First, staying positive will let you accomplish more things in life. For Example, It can help you accomplish getting a job, finishing school work and getting into colleges.

Next, with positive energy it will help you get through the day much smoother. Also, you can accomplish anything you set your mind to.

Next, staying positive lets people know that you respect others. This allows you to get a good images in any environment. When getting good images people would be interested in giving you job opportunities. Also, when showing good attitude and respect could lead to success in life.

Also, when getting a job you need to always stay positive to show your first impression to your boss. First impressions show how someone thinks of you and determines if you get the job or not. If you dont show positive attitude, then you probably wont get the job and it shows bad first impression.

In conclusion, the key to life is your attitude and the only person who can control it is you. Studies show that your attitude determines your success in life. So, now you know why staying positive is a key to success in life by accomplishing more, respecting others and first impressions.

A positive mindset is widely seen as the most important factor in achieving success. Research shows your outlook shapes your life outcomes because it reflects who you are. Specifically, keeping an upbeat attitude helps you achieve more, earn others’ respect, and make great first impressions.

To start with, staying optimistic lets you reach far more goals. For example, a positive mindset can help you land a job, finish schoolwork on time, and get into the college you want.

Positive energy also makes busy days much easier to handle. When you stay upbeat, you feel motivated to chase any goal you set, no matter how hard it seems.

A positive attitude also shows you respect others, helping you build a good reputation in any setting. People with strong reputations are more likely to get job offers, as respect and pleasant behavior lead to long-term success.

This matters most when applying for jobs, where positivity makes a good first impression on employers. First impressions often decide if you get hired. Negative attitudes leave poor impressions and make you unlikely to get the role.

To sum up, your attitude is the core of your success, and only you can control it. Studies confirm your mindset determines how successful you will be. Staying positive helps you achieve more, earn respect, and make great first impressions.

Offering distance learning as an option for students to attend classes from home by way of online or video conferencing by schools is a good idea, but I take a position on this issue to say that, students would not benefit from being able to attend classes classes from home due to the following reasons.

First of all,some students when offered distance learning will not pay attention to their lessons. They will distracted either by their cell phones or electronic devices. And we all know students always like to be on their cell phones at anytime and anywhere. Also,Students can be distracted either by their parents or siblings which may cause them lack behind ahead of their lessons. So when all of this happens , students may be delayed which will cause them to fail and waste of time. For example,my cousin came to the United States of America with his siblings and he was permitted to to take one of his subjects or courses online. And anytime he gets home,he doesnt get a peace of mind because of the disturbances and worries from his siblings. Due to this,he fell apart in his studies which caused him to fail the course.

Another reason is that,some students finds it difficult and boring to learn on their own pace. Because they encounter a lot of problems in their studies. Students finds it very hard to understand lessons without the presence and explanation of a teacher. And again,students finds it very boring when learning on their own because there is no form of oral conversation between the teacher and student. Some students prefer being active in studies rather being dull or inactive. So when all these happens,the students may skip the contents because he or she doesn't get any understanding,

or close the contents and go to sleep. For instance,I had a friend who was struggling with these same problems,he feels bored and difficult to understand in distance learning. So anytime he gets to sit for the lessons,he feels sleepy during a short period of time. He sometimes drink a whole cup of thick coffee but it doesn't make any changes. So what he does is to off the computer and go to bed. And this hinders his academic performance each year.

Lastly,students feel fatigue or weak in distance learning since they don't get time to take rest after school. Some students even have to close work after school before taking the online class. With these,it makes student lazy and sleepy when he or she sits in fronts of the computer to learn. And me myself is experiencing this problem. When school closes, I have to walk half a mile before I gets home,and from there,I work on my assignments and take my shower. So by the time I will be done,then it is getting late, and I still have to take this classes online. I feel tired in learning at times which retards my level of learning.

From these reasons, I would like to conclude that,students would not benefit from distance learning because there are so many disadvantages from it which has brought low level academics in their studies.

Thank you.

Many people argue that offering distance learning, where students attend classes from home via online tools or video conferencing, is a positive step for schools. However, I hold the opposite view: I believe students do not actually benefit from studying remotely, for the following reasons.

First, students who study from home are far more likely to lose focus during lessons. It is common for young people to get distracted by their phones, tablets, or other electronic devices, which they tend to check constantly no matter where they are. On top of that, family members like parents or siblings can interrupt their learning, making it hard to keep up with class material. When these distractions pile up, students fall behind, risk failing their classes, and waste valuable time. For example, my cousin moved to the United States with his siblings and was allowed to take one of his courses fully online. Every time he tried to study at home, his siblings would bother him or create noise, so he never had a quiet space to focus. As a result, his grades dropped badly, and he ended up failing that course.

Another major issue is that many students struggle to learn at their own pace without in-person support. They often run into problems understanding course material when there is no teacher present to explain concepts clearly. What’s more, remote learning can feel very dull because there is little to no real-time conversation between teachers and students. Most students prefer active, engaging lessons rather than sitting alone in front of a screen. When lessons feel uninteresting and hard to follow, students may skip parts of the material because they don’t understand it, or even close their laptops and take a nap. I had a friend who faced exactly these problems: he found distance learning boring and confusing. Every time he sat down for an online class, he would start feeling sleepy within minutes. He even tried drinking a full cup of strong coffee to stay awake, but it didn’t help at all. Eventually, he would just turn off his computer and go to bed, which hurt his grades year after year.

Lastly, remote learning leaves students feeling exhausted, since they rarely get time to rest after the school day ends. Some students even have part-time jobs or chores to finish before they can join their online classes, which makes them feel lazy and sleepy as soon as they sit in front of their computers. I have experienced this problem myself. After my in-person classes end, I have to walk half a mile to get home, then finish my homework and take a shower. By the time I finish all that, it is already late, but I still have to log in to my online lessons. I often feel too tired to focus properly, which slows down how much I learn.

For all these reasons, I conclude that students do not benefit from distance learning. The many downsides of studying from home lead to worse academic performance and lower overall achievement for most learners.

Thank you.

I believe students should be allowed to design their own summer projects for three key reasons: they can produce far more creative work, they enjoy the process more, and they face less pressure during the break.

First, letting students choose their own project topics unlocks much more creativity. Instead of sticking to a fixed task set by a teacher, they can pick areas they actually care about. For example, they might try out a science experiment they found online that is interesting for both themselves and their classmates, or write about a family member or historical figure who inspires them, explaining why that person matters to them. Some students might even come up with completely original project ideas, like a new small invention, show off their work to the class, and explain how they developed the concept and who it could help.

Second, students have way more fun when they get to create their own projects. They’re far more eager to work on a task they picked themselves than a dull, one-size-fits-all assignment handed out by a teacher. When given the freedom to explore their interests, they can come up with far more creative work than they would with a fixed topic. They don’t have to follow a strict checklist of requirements, so they can actually enjoy the work instead of worrying about ticking every box. They can even team up with friends to work on a shared project, which makes the process even more enjoyable.

The third benefit is reduced stress over the summer. When students design their own projects, they don’t have to stress about whether their work is perfect or if they’re meeting every single requirement on a teacher’s checklist. They can set their own pace and create their own personal checklist of goals for the project, then share their process with classmates so others can try the same idea for fun someday.

In conclusion, these are the main reasons why I think students should be given the freedom to design their own summer projects.

I think students should never be forced to enroll in music, drama, or art courses. Instead, these should only be offered as optional electives. Every student has different strengths and interests, after all. If a learner is made to take a class they have no interest in and will never use later in life, it can easily lead to them failing the course. I hold this view because making these classes mandatory is pointless, unfair, and completely irrelevant to most students’ goals.

Many young people plan to work in fields that have nothing to do with singing, painting, or acting. Taking these courses does not make students smarter or teach them useful new skills, and they have almost no connection to core academic learning. For students who have no interest in the arts, sitting through these classes is just a waste of time that brings no enjoyment.

Another key reason is that forcing students to take these classes is deeply unfair. Struggling in a mandatory art or music course can cause a student to fail overall, delaying their graduation. It is wrong that a single optional-seeming class could stop a student from moving on to college. No one should have to repeat an entire grade just because they performed poorly in a class that offers no real value to their future plans.

To sum up, music, drama, and art classes should never be mandatory for all students. They are not essential to a young person’s education, and they do not give students any advantage when applying for jobs. The vast majority of careers do not ask for any background in the arts as a requirement for hiring.

Is it more effective to tackle tasks alone or collaborate with others? While personal preferences vary widely when it comes to solo versus group work, I firmly believe that collaborating with others is the best way for people to grow, as it helps them gain more knowledge and grasp concepts more clearly.

First, collaborating with others supports growth in both academic and professional settings by exposing people to new information. For instance, hearing teammates share different ideas and perspectives expands what you know. I remember my English teacher splitting the class into groups of four last term: he handed each group a worksheet, wrote several questions on the board, and asked us to work through them together. After we finished, we had a full-class discussion where each group shared their answers. It quickly became clear that every group had approached the questions differently, with unique ideas and viewpoints. We all picked up new insights from one another.

After all, we all learn something new every day as we navigate life.

Second, group work helps people improve because they develop a deeper understanding of the material. If you get stuck or don’t fully grasp a concept, you can ask a teammate for clarification immediately. For example, my history teacher once assigned a task due by the end of class. When she gave the instructions, I didn’t quite follow what I was supposed to do. I turned to a classmate in my group and asked him to walk me through the instructions again. Once I understood, I could share my own thoughts and contribute meaningfully to our group’s work.

When we all support each other, we can achieve far more than we would alone.

Many people argue that working alone is better, since it allows for better focus. They say they won’t get distracted by others, so they can complete tasks more quickly. One of my friends always works solo for this reason: she claims that groups often end up chatting instead of working, distracting each other, and by the end of the session, they’ve only finished a few questions. However, this argument falls apart when you consider that working alone means you have no one to turn to if you get confused. You might get stuck on a single part of the task and make no progress at all, and having no one to talk through ideas with can make work much harder.

In conclusion, group work offers a wide range of benefits. Beyond the ones I’ve already mentioned, collaborating with others lets you make new friends, learn more about your teammates, and even discover new things about yourself. Working with others eases the pressure of meeting deadlines or feeling clueless about how to start a task. Even though some people hold the opposite view, I remain convinced that working in groups is far better than working alone.

At the end of the day, we all need a little support from others now and then to grow and improve.

I support the plan to start an afterschool homework club. Many students struggle to finish assignments on their own, so having teachers available to assist them would be incredibly helpful. This extra support would mean far fewer learners fail their courses. There is also the fact that some children lack computers or other electronic devices at home, which they may need to complete online assignments, making finishing homework much harder. Admittedly, there is a small benefit to not running the club: without teacher support, students would learn that life is not always straightforward, and you can only get ahead if you are talented or work as hard as possible. Another major advantage of these clubs is that they let students socialize with classmates, build new friendships, and also see how their peers approach and complete their own assignments, which can give them useful new study ideas.

Of course, there are potential downsides to consider. Some students might try to take advantage of the club by cheating, copying answers from classmates and then leaving early as soon as they have what they need. To prevent this, the club should have a rule that no one can look at another person’s work until all assignments are finished. Others may treat the club like a social hangout and chat the entire time instead of working. However, there will always be students who take the club seriously. These learners do not fool around, tell jokes, or distract others from their work.

Overall, I believe we should launch an afterschool homework club, as there are far more arguments in its favor than against it. This program could help many students improve their study habits, learn to manage their time better, and earn fewer poor grades over time. Most young people who choose to join care about their academic performance, so they are very likely to follow the rules and focus on their work. It is true that even without this club, students who need to boost their grades still have chances to improve and finish their current year with solid marks to prepare for the next grade. However, adding the club gives these learners extra support that makes success much more achievable.

People should take charge of their own choices instead of relying on advice from self-proclaimed "experts" to avoid poor guidance.

For one, no one understands your personal needs, preferences, and limits better than you do. You are the only person who truly knows what you like, what you want, and what works for you, both mentally and physically. When you make choices for yourself, you factor in these unique details that no one else can fully grasp. Think about a situation where someone buys you a gift that you hate, don’t want, or that is the complete opposite of what you need. If you had made the decision yourself, you would never have asked that person to pick out that item in the first place, would you? That’s a clear sign that your own judgment is more reliable for your life than someone else’s.

Making your own decisions also lets you learn from your own slip-ups and poor judgments. Take online clothes shopping as an example: every day, plenty of people order items without trying them on in stores first, only to receive the wrong size. After that happens once, they learn to either visit a store to try clothes on first, or get their measurements taken before placing an order. Another common mistake is buying something that looks nice in photos without reading the product description or instructions. When the package arrives at your home, it might be much smaller than you expected, missing parts, just one piece of what you ordered, or nothing like the picture. This is a valuable learning experience: you’ll know to always read full product details before ordering anything next time.

Lastly, not every person who claims to be an expert can actually help with your specific situation, and some aren’t even good at their jobs. For instance, you might pay a lawyer a huge amount of money, only for them to lose your court case entirely. Another example: you visit a doctor because you are in severe pain, and they tell you nothing is wrong, then prescribe an expensive painkiller that you already have at home. Therapists can be untrustworthy too: some will prescribe medication you don’t need, just because they are allowed to write prescriptions. Not every therapist behaves this way, but the majority do.

All in all, these so-called "experts" sometimes have no idea what they are doing, and others are just trying to make money off innocent people. At the same time, it is completely normal to make mistakes occasionally, and learning from your own misjudgments is a key part of life. That is why it is always better to make your own decisions, to avoid bad guidance from others.

School assignments are often challenging, and many students need extra support to complete them. Running a homework club after classes end might seem like a fun, useful addition to the school day. Such a club would definitely help learners who struggle to finish their work on time or don’t fully understand the material. However, there are plenty of students who simply cannot spare time after school for extra activities.

An after-school homework club would not work for every student. Not everyone has free time once the regular school day finishes. Many kids have other commitments: they might practice for a sports team, attend dance or singing lessons, or take music instrument classes. These activities leave them with very little time to finish homework, even once they get home. That said, a homework club would be great for students who have no afternoon plans, as they could stay to complete that day’s assignments or catch up on overdue work.

I count myself among those who oppose an after-school homework club. I often have sports practice to attend, so I don’t have time to stay back after class. Even so, I do my best to complete all assignments and hand them in the following day. Teachers, too, may not be able to stay after school. They have their own responsibilities: they might need to feed pets so their animals don’t go hungry, or care for their own children to keep them safe. This is another clear reason why an after-school homework club is not a good idea.

Most students would also struggle to get home from an after-school club. Their parents might be at work, feeling unwell, or not at home at all to pick them up. I also doubt the school would be able to properly supervise all the students attending the club, which is another major issue with the after-school format. What if students get hungry while staying late? It’s unlikely the school would provide meals or snacks. If the school wants to run a homework club, it would make far more sense to schedule it during the final class block of the day, so students can use that period solely for homework.

Scheduling the club during the last class of the day would be a much better option. Students would use that block exclusively to finish their assignments. This way, learners who have after-school commitments won’t fall behind on homework, even if they have sports, lessons, or other activities right after school. It would also give everyone a chance to take a short break from their regular lessons. This setup would help teachers too: while students work on homework, teachers can use that time to grade papers or check completed assignments.

Another possible option is holding the club during the first class block of the day. This would let students who didn’t finish their homework the night before complete it before their regular lessons start. That said, my preferred option is still the final class block. It gives everyone, including teachers, a chance to reset after a long day of lessons. All students would get their homework done, so no one has to worry about missing deadlines, and everyone has more free time in the afternoon.

What if schools paired students from different grade levels? Matching older and younger learners together creates positive outcomes for all students. The arrangement lets younger students pick up new learning techniques, gives them useful tips about what to expect in high school, and teaches everyone practical ways to handle stress.

The first major benefit of cross-grade pairing is that students get to learn new ways of tackling schoolwork. Older students can walk younger peers through their own study habits, for example. If a younger student gets stuck on a homework problem, they can ask their older partner for help: the older student can explain the solution step-by-step and share the skills they use to work through tough assignments. They might even share handy shortcuts for tricky subjects, like math or science. Picking up these new approaches helps younger students when they run into concepts they don’t understand later on.

Another key advantage is that older students can give younger peers honest advice about what high school life is really like. They can warn them about heavy homework loads and explain how much harder coursework gets in higher grades. They might also recommend fun electives to try, like theater or cheerleading, based on their own experiences. Younger students can even share their own interests, telling older partners which classes they’re excited to sign up for in the future. On top of that, older students can outline the core skills younger learners need to master before starting high school. Getting this heads-up helps younger students feel prepared, and older students play a big role in that readiness.

Finally, older students can share their best strategies for managing stress, which is a huge help for younger learners facing bigger academic challenges. They can explain the test-taking tricks that work for them, like how to prepare for exams or the study routines they follow to stay on top of work. They might also walk younger partners through their time management habits: for example, sharing what time they set aside for homework each day, or how they organize their study space to avoid distractions. Learning these stress-management tools will serve younger students well once they reach high school.

All in all, pairing younger and older students is a great idea for three clear reasons: it lets students learn new study methods, gives younger kids valuable insight into high school life, and teaches practical stress-management skills. Even though it’s a less common school arrangement, cross-grade pairing offers a worthwhile experience that benefits everyone involved.

A growing number of schools now permit students to use cell phones during lessons for academic purposes, and many people argue this is a beneficial practice. However, I strongly believe phones should be banned from classrooms entirely. My stance is based on three main reasons: they cause constant distractions, they stop students from learning effectively, and owning a phone is a privilege that should not be misused during class time.

First, phones are a major source of distraction for students. Even when teachers only approve their use for specific learning tasks, many students will switch to unrelated activities like texting friends or scrolling through social media instead of completing assigned work. Over time, this makes students think it is acceptable to pull out their phones at any point during lessons, even when they should be focused on the teacher.

Second, allowing phones in class hurts students’ ability to learn properly. They lose the chance to learn in the traditional way, without digital devices. Students who take handwritten notes rather than relying on their phones have a much better chance of memorizing lesson content and doing well on tests. When teachers lead hands-on activities in class, students can fully engage with the material and even teach their classmates, something that is hard to do when everyone is focused on their devices.

Finally, cell phones are a privilege for students, not a basic right. Teachers should not allow their use during class time because many students do not understand when it is appropriate to use their phones. Even if schools set very strict rules about phone use, students almost always find ways to get around those restrictions.

To sum up, this is why I believe some schools should not allow phones in classrooms. Students get distracted, miss out on better learning opportunities, and phones are a privilege. I believe schools should not allow students to use their phones during class.

While some people claim that being inactive has its uses, since it gives them more free time than they would have if they were busy with scheduled activities, I firmly believe we should never choose to be idle. When we stay busy, we can achieve so much more—whether that means taking part in group activities, spending extra time reading, or testing out new experiences.

Thomas Jefferson once wrote the famous line, "Determine never to be idle." This rings true for so many people and students today, who waste their time doing nothing instead of using it productively. We can get so much more done if we take part in activities rather than sitting around idle. For instance, when I arrived in the United States on January 8, 2017, I stayed home for two full months without attending school or doing anything productive. I grew tired of wasting time, so I told my mother I wanted to do something useful instead of being idle. I decided to sign up for the Generic_City Soccer Team to fill my time and use it wisely. I submitted my application, and the coach accepted me. I started training with new teammates, and I made plenty of new friends along the way.

Instead of wasting time being idle, why not spend more hours with our books? The more time we spend reading, the faster we learn and the better our reading skills become. Take my friend Generic_Name, for example: his parents rarely let him hang out with friends for long periods, and they never allowed him to sit idle without a book to read. Generic_Name spent most of his free time reading for years, and he grew into an excellent reader in his English class. His teacher often asked him to read storybooks and passages aloud to his classmates. He inspired many students at his school, and most of them wanted to be like him, so they started setting aside more time to read at home too.

On top of that, people who prefer to be idle, or who think inactivity has value, are usually not determined and have no plans for their future. They avoid joining activities or interacting with others, and idle people are often lazy because they refuse to try new things. Even if you don’t end up being perfect at something, trying new things when you have free time can teach you a lot. For example, I once sat at home doing nothing with three friends: Generic_Name, Generic_Name, and Generic_Name. One of them suggested we try out UFC GYM, so we went there and signed up for training. The gym gave us a one-day free trial to see if we liked it. We went back the next day and trained for an hour. Even though I didn’t stick with it, I had tried something new and gained some useful experience from the process.

For all these reasons and examples, I encourage every person who is currently idle, as well as anyone who thinks inactivity has a purpose, to get involved in activities, spend more time reading, and try new things whenever they feel themselves starting to waste time. You can achieve so much just by testing out new experiences. We can get far more done when we stay busy, so we should all follow Jefferson’s advice: determine never to be idle.

For instance, if you meet someone for the first time and quickly decide their personality is unpleasant, make an effort to get to know them better. Another useful step is to spend time together in places you both enjoy. That said, some people simply have naturally different personalities, and you have to learn to accept that.

Finally, everyone faces challenges in life that can shape their personality over time. It is also important to ask people how they are doing, as they may be struggling with anger, sadness, or depression and just need someone to listen. Supporting each other through tough times makes a big difference.

Even if you don’t know a person well, it never hurts to check if they are okay. With patience and care, it is possible to change their personality and make them a better person.

The roots of modern tech trace back to Alexander Graham Bell’s invention of the first telephone. The devices he created look nothing like the smartphones millions carry today. Bell’s telephone was bulky and heavy, more like a brick than a portable gadget, and was designed only for home use, not something you could easily carry around with you. It wasn’t an instant hit either—most people were used to living without telephones, so they didn’t see it as a must-have item at first. Over time, other inventors built on Bell’s work, tweaking and improving the design. The size and weight were drastically reduced, and new features were added beyond just making voice calls. Originally, phones only let people talk to each other without being in the same room, let alone the same building. As more people wanted to create their own versions of the phone, multiple companies popped up to produce electronic devices, rather than just one single manufacturer. In the early 2000s, Apple—now one of the world’s biggest tech companies—launched the first iPhone, and it flew off shelves globally. Since then, Apple has released countless products: cell phones, earbuds, tablets, laptops, smartwatches, portable chargers, and almost any other gadget people might use in their daily lives.

While tech addiction among young kids is a real problem, it can also help them learn when used properly. Parents play a huge role here: many who let their children use devices set strict rules about what content they can access and how long they can use the gadget each day. Letting little kids use technology isn’t inherently bad, either. There are plenty of TV shows designed to teach them basic skills like shapes, colors, and object recognition, as well as how to move their bodies and communicate with others before they even start school—giving them a head start on their peers. ABCmouse is just one of many great online tools that make learning fun for kids, so they enjoy studying instead of dreading it.

Technology is used by people all over the world, even in space! It’s everywhere, both inside and outside our homes. Inside, we rely on security cameras, thermostats that keep our homes warm, air conditioners that cool us down on hot days, refrigerators and freezers that store our food and drinks, WiFi routers, televisions, and smart doorbells—and that’s just the tech in a typical house. Outside, we use tech to commute to work in our cars, follow traffic signals, and use GPS to navigate to our destinations. If you have a paper due or need to look up information for any reason, you don’t have to wait for a library to open—you can do all your research from anywhere with a quick tap and swipe on your phone or computer. Medical machines are critical for human survival: they treat severely injured patients and care for newborn babies in hospitals. Tech is still evolving, too. Every day, inventors and scientists use it to develop new ways to cure diseases, track their origins, and figure out how to prevent them entirely.

The creation of technology has improved life for everyone in countless ways. Without it, far more deaths and accidents would happen that tech now helps us avoid. The rapid progress we’ve already seen will only lead to even better tools, so we can prepare for future disasters that might otherwise harm the world. Tech has been an incredibly positive force for the millions, if not billions, of people who use it every day.

Former British Prime Minister Winston Churchill once said, “Success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm.” I fully agree with this view. Failure plays a massive part in achieving success. At its core, failure is about learning from the errors you make and gathering as much experience as possible from the process. It means refusing to quit, figuring out how to improve your approach, and working toward your goal until you get even better results than you first imagined. This is exactly why failure is so central to the journey toward success.

One clear way failure contributes to success is by teaching us to learn from past errors. Throughout history, entire societies, countries, and even our whole species have grown by examining what went wrong in the past. A perfect example is the League of Nations, which was formed after World War I with the goal of keeping global peace. It ultimately failed to achieve its purpose. But instead of giving up, global leaders studied why the League did not work, and used those lessons to create the United Nations. To this day, the UN remains one of humanity’s greatest successes in maintaining international cooperation. This is just one of countless cases that prove failure and success are deeply connected.

Refusing to give up is another key part of this link between failure and success, because quitting is never a solution. Consider the story of Pelé, widely regarded as one of the greatest footballers of all time, and the youngest player ever to win a World Cup. From a very young age, he was told he would never become a professional footballer, with many people claiming his talent was not enough to make it. But he never gave up. He poured all his effort into training, and when opportunities came, he proved exactly what he was capable of, eventually becoming a global legend. During his first World Cup appearance, he suffered a knee injury while training for the opening match, which sidelined him for half the tournament. Doctors told him he needed daily physical therapy to recover, and warned he would not be fit to play in the rest of the tournament. Still, he refused to quit: he trained every single day, and in the third round of the tournament, he was cleared to play in a match. This is a powerful example of the resilience people show when they refuse to give up and dedicate themselves fully to their goals. It also clearly shows how pushing through failure helps people achieve what they set out to do.

Another way failure paves the way for success is by teaching us the value of trying again. This is perhaps the most important part of the connection between the two: once you analyze what went wrong in previous attempts and learn from those mistakes, you are ready to make another effort and reach the goal you have been working toward. Space exploration is a perfect example of this. It is widely known that early space missions failed at an extremely high rate, with many rockets exploding due to system malfunctions or other technical issues. But after countless failed attempts, where scientists carefully studied every error, humans eventually managed to launch satellites and send people into outer space. It took many failures to get to this point, but now we can send spacecraft across the galaxy to explore distant stars and other far-off places in space. Failure showed us exactly what we were doing wrong, and we used those lessons to improve. This clearly demonstrates how failure is tied to success through repeated, persistent effort.

Some people argue that failure has no connection to success at all. They claim that it is possible to achieve goals on the first try, that we learn nothing from our mistakes or failed attempts, and that failing repeatedly makes you lose all your motivation. I believe these people are mistaken. First, very few people achieve major goals without any prior failures. Second, we always learn something from our mistakes, often picking up valuable lessons that we would never have gained otherwise. As for the idea that failure kills enthusiasm, that is entirely up to us: we choose whether to let setbacks discourage us or to keep our passion alive. That is why I disagree with this view. Failure is inseparable from the pursuit of success, whether we like it or not, because every failure gives us new experience and knowledge. Even if it sounds unlikely at first, failure is a core part of what makes progress possible, and there is always something valuable to learn from it.

As the examples above show, failure and success are deeply linked. Failure is not something negative: it lets us learn from our errors, gain practical experience, and identify what we need to change. The most important thing to remember is that we control whether we lose our enthusiasm after setbacks. This is exactly why I believe Churchill’s words are completely accurate. Moving from failure to failure, we learn from every mistake we make on the path to success. We use those lessons to create better plans, then try again, often achieving far better results than we originally hoped for. That is why I am certain failure is always connected to success.

A common question today is whether students benefit from learning from home.

Schools are meant to be places where students feel at ease, and there are many different types of learning environments to choose from. In my view, learning from home comes with both upsides and downsides. For one, students won’t be interrupted by rowdy classmates, making it easier to finish assignments on time without distractions. By contrast, students in traditional classrooms often face a big drawback: classmates who don’t take their studies seriously can be a bad influence. Some get distracted easily and end up failing courses, forcing them to repeat a year or stay in school longer than expected. Home learning works very differently here. If a student fails a class, they can retake it at home without anyone judging them for struggling. In regular schools, having to repeat a year is often seen as something to be ashamed of, which is a big issue worth considering.

Another key difference is the level of individual support. Homeschooled students usually get far more one-on-one time with their teachers. While traditional schools try to offer the same, classes are often so crowded that teachers simply can’t give every student the attention they need. Many young people want to go to a physical school but can’t, due to reasons like a disability or being a public figure. Celebrities, for example, might want to avoid unwanted attention, so they have no choice but to learn from home. Homeschoolers in this situation often wish they could attend a regular school, since staying home all day can feel isolating and trapped, and many get tired of spending all their time in the same space. Most people benefit from getting to socialize with peers a little bit, after all.

Homeschooling also lets students finish their studies faster than they might in a traditional setting. It offers a lot of flexibility, but misses out on some perks of public schools. For example, almost all public schools provide free lunch and free tuition, while homeschoolers have to cover all their own costs. You’ll need to pay for your own food, wifi, computer, and other supplies. Even so, getting an education is always worth the cost, since it will pay off in the long run.

Earning a qualification from the comfort of your own home benefits you now and will continue to do so in the future, once you receive your diploma. At the end of the day, whether you go to public school, private school, or learn from home, all paths will benefit you in countless ways.

A year ago, I was convinced that business was the degree I wanted to pursue, but I struggled a lot with my classes. I couldn’t get good grades no matter how hard I tried, and I ended up failing the course. I felt incredibly stressed and had no idea what my next step should be. I knew business wasn’t the right fit for me, but I thought it was too late to switch paths. When I spoke to my academic counselor, she told me I could still change my major. I decided to pick a different field, and now I’m confident I’ve found the right one for me. I might still change my mind again later, since I tend to be indecisive sometimes. I also learned that this kind of experience is totally normal. When I talked to my classmates, many of them shared that they’d gone through the exact same thing.

Some people argue that it’s smart for students to decide on a career early, since they can pick high school classes that will prepare them for their chosen field. But I strongly disagree. Committing to a career when you’re young is a bad idea, for two main reasons: first, you might pick a path that isn’t actually a good fit for you, and second, many students are still undecided about what they want to study, and that’s okay.

Supporters of early career commitment point out that high school students can choose classes that align with their future field, which helps them build relevant skills. But they often overlook how stressful this can be for students. Almost every day, I hear classmates or friends complain, “This class is way too hard for me, but I can’t drop it because it’s supposed to help my future career.” Hearing those words makes it clear to me that many of them are miserable and overwhelmed.

The best way to support students is to let them switch majors if they need to. Maybe the path they started with isn’t right for them, or they picked a field on a whim because they were undecided. There are plenty of reasons why early career commitment is a bad idea, but I’ll focus on two key ones here.

First, committing to a career early often leads students to pick a path that isn’t right for them. Many kids grow up wanting to follow in their parents’ footsteps: they want to study the same subject their parents did, even attend the same university. In other cases, parents put pressure on their children to pursue a field the parents want, not what the child is interested in. Either way, students end up choosing a career based on someone else’s wishes, not their own. Later, they realize the field isn’t a good fit, which makes them unhappy and stressed. Some even want to drop out of school entirely, convinced that education is too hard for them. In reality, the problem isn’t school itself, but that they picked the wrong major. If someone did a survey of how students feel about their chosen career, I think the likelihood that they’d say it’s not the right fit for them would be over 100 percent.

The second reason early career commitment is a bad idea is that many students are genuinely undecided about what they want to study. There are hundreds of different career paths to choose from, so it’s unrealistic to expect a young person to pick just one and stick to it. Students often discover that skills they built for one field transfer well to another, so they decide to switch paths. Sometimes these switches don’t work out at first, but trying new things is all part of learning. Making the wrong choice about a major is just a normal part of life, and students grow from that experience. Some even decide to study two or more fields, taking different classes to reach their goals. I think being undecided is actually a good thing for students, as it pushes them to experiment with different courses and figure out what they really enjoy.

To sum up, committing to a career at a young age is a bad idea, mainly because students might pick a path that isn’t a good fit, and many are still undecided about what they want to do. Sometimes young people make impulsive choices, picking a career on a whim without realizing it’s not right for them. Other times, they simply can’t make up their mind about what to study. The best way to support students is to give them the freedom to explore different options until they find what works for them. I believe that when students are allowed to take their time figuring things out, they’ll feel much more confident in the path they eventually choose.

Working in groups is often seen as the better option for school projects and class tasks. Teachers usually believe that students gain more from collaborative work, since group members can talk through problems and support each other. When you work alone, it can be really tough to figure out a question you don’t understand, with no one to ask for help. Many students agree that group work helps them learn more, as they can share ideas and fill in gaps in each other’s knowledge. Teachers also notice that students improve when they discuss topics together, whether they are in a group or working alone but chatting with peers. Collaborative work and solo study both get students more engaged, doing more tasks and staying focused during class.

There are clear reasons why so many people prefer group work. When you collaborate with others, you can talk through tricky questions and figure out answers you might not get on your own, which also helps you feel more confident in your work. It’s a lot like sports: a team needs to communicate, practice, and work together to win, and the same rule applies to school or any other group setting. Another good example is classic Looney Tunes cartoons, where Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck team up to perform an opera act that makes audiences laugh. Their success comes from working as a team, just like students do when they collaborate on school tasks.

On the other hand, plenty of students argue that working alone is the better choice. They say you can achieve more on your own and think through problems more deeply than you would in a group. Even though many students and teachers believe group work is more effective, working solo has its perks: if you or a friend need help, you don’t have to rely on each other, and can just ask the teacher instead. Many students actually produce better work when they’re alone, and come up with more creative ideas that go beyond what’s covered in class. For instance, lots of successful singers work solo: they prefer to create music on their own, which lets them make better songs, plan their own paths, travel wherever they want, and live a happier life on their own.

In conclusion, roughly half of students prefer working in groups, while the other half would rather work alone. Teachers usually let students choose whichever option suits them best, with no requirement to pick one over the other. Lots of students show they can handle both types of work equally well, since the method you use doesn’t matter much in the end. Teachers always give enough time to finish tasks, whether you’re collaborating with a group or working by yourself.

One of my close friends was homeschooled after she faced severe bullying at her regular school, to the point where she was ready to quit education entirely because she could no longer cope with the harassment. Her school counselor stepped in with a better solution: enrolling in online classes. Since my friend had always earned strong grades, the counselor wanted to make sure she could still graduate and build a stable future. Many schools now even offer distance learning programs, which let students join classes from home via online platforms or video calls. I firmly believe homeschooling (usually through online coursework) is a huge advantage for students dealing with difficult school circumstances, those at risk of dropping out, and it is also far simpler and faster than traditional schooling.

The first major reason homeschooling is so beneficial is that it supports students facing difficult school environments. This could mean frequent fights with peers, ongoing bullying or harassment, conflicts with teachers, or even feeling like regular school is a waste of time when you could be earning money at a job instead. Switching to online classes lets you avoid these negative situations entirely, cutting off the source of stress while still letting you make academic progress. You can work through your coursework without the distractions of a toxic school environment, and still graduate on time without any issues. If you are struggling with any of these problems, I’d recommend speaking to your school counselor about distance learning options, or asking your parents if homeschooling is a possibility for you.

Second, homeschooling is a lifesaver for students who are considering dropping out of school. Most students who leave traditional school do so for financial reasons: they feel they need to start working immediately to support their families, so they quit their studies. Others are teenage parents whose families refuse to support them or help with their needs, leaving them with no choice but to drop out. Online learning lets these students continue their education nonetheless, which can help them qualify for better jobs later on. It also gives them a sense of relief knowing they don’t have to give up on graduating, even if they originally thought dropping out was their only option. I still remember my time working as a student counseling aide, when a distressed student came to me to ask where he should leave his school laptop because he was about to drop out. Generic_Name, who was nearby, asked him what was wrong. He explained he wanted to drop out to help his family, who were struggling financially. He had no idea online classes were an option, and when Generic_Name told him about the distance learning program, it completely turned his mood around.

Finally, homeschooling is far simpler and faster than traditional schooling. You can schedule your classes around your free time, take breaks whenever you need to, and pick back up when you’re ready. It is much less stressful than attending a regular school. Studies show that homeschooled students face far less stress than their peers in traditional classrooms. Generic_Name, a science teacher at SCHOOL_NAME, shared that 88% of students in regular schools feel stressed about homework and tight assignment deadlines, while only 5% of homeschooled students report feeling stressed. In short, homeschooling removes the pressure of traditional school, giving you more free time to pursue other interests. You can wake up at whatever time works for you, work through your classes at your own pace, and take breaks whenever you want. To me, that sounds like the ideal way to learn!

Some people argue that homeschooling has downsides, saying you won’t have a teacher available to answer questions or explain difficult topics in person. But online classes are essentially one-on-one: there are no other students in the session, just you and your instructor, which makes it far easier to focus. I’d much rather learn this way than sit in a classroom full of friends who are messing around, not paying attention, and falling behind on their work. All things considered, homeschooling through online classes is a huge benefit: it supports students dealing with toxic school environments, helps those at risk of dropping out stay on track to graduate, and offers a faster, simpler path to finishing your education.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once wrote, "To be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment." I completely agree with this idea, because staying true to who you are and handling things on your own leads to far better results. As Emerson suggested, being authentic lets you grow by trying new experiences, and there are countless reasons to stay true to your own identity.

First of all, being your true self can lead to a much happier, more fulfilling life, and it often opens doors to opportunities you never expected. When I talk about this, I mean that sticking to your own beliefs and goals gives you a clear direction toward a successful future. For example, setting your own personal guidelines or carving out time to focus on things you are passionate about is an excellent first step. A mentor once told me that if you are willing to work hard for your dreams and genuinely want to achieve them, you will reach your goals by staying authentic to who you are. Before long, you will feel proud of yourself for pulling off tasks you once thought were impossible.

Second, completing tasks through your own hard work sets a great example for countless children around the world. Believe it or not, being a role model for others is one of the greatest accomplishments, since they will want to act or grow to be just like you. What’s more, trying something new every day helps you improve over time. As the quote goes, "Hard work beats talent when talent doesn't work hard." It is also helpful to remember that everyone learns new skills by making mistakes. Messing up is not a major problem—making a mistake just means you are trying to do better and grow by learning the correct way to handle things.

Third, and certainly not least, friendships are closely tied to this idea. A very important question to ask here is: how can you be sure your friends are genuine? This is a common concern, and it is exactly why being yourself is the greatest accomplishment. After all, friends can pull you into harmful habits like drug use, excessive drinking, and other bad behaviors. That is not to say you should avoid having friends altogether. Instead, it means you need to pick your friends very carefully, because hypocrisy is everywhere—some people might want to hold you back from having a bright, successful future. Hypocrisy is one of the most dangerous things in the world, as it can trick people into thinking they need to act or live a certain way that is not true to who they are.

In conclusion, staying true to yourself will help you grow and unlock opportunities you never could have imagined. Start by doing things you are passionate about or genuinely enjoy—that is a great first step toward being authentic. Learn to tell the difference between what is good for you and what is not, and never forget to keep fighting for your dreams.

I disagree with the popular saying "A problem is a chance for you to do your best" for three main reasons: not everyone learns from their errors, some problems cause irreversible harm, and success is about avoiding mistakes rather than facing them.

I do not agree with the claim that "A problem is a chance for you to do your best", mostly because not everyone manages to learn from their mistakes. Some people cannot even remember errors they made long ago, so they end up repeating them. For instance, my brother failed his driver’s test the first time he took it, and when he retook it later, he failed again because he made the exact same mistake. On top of that, problems can leave people with trauma that makes them afraid to try again. I remember missing a tackle during a football game once, and I was so scared of failing a second time that when I got another chance to make a tackle, I hesitated and missed it again because I kept thinking about my earlier mistake.

The saying "A problem is a chance for you to do your best" is also incorrect because some problems leave lasting harm that cannot be undone. For example, if someone is given the death penalty for murder, they can never undo that crime or make things right again. Similarly, some people turn down great opportunities when they first get them, and they can never go back to accept them later. My sister once won a special award, but she refused to accept it at the time, and now she cannot change that decision.

My disagreement with the quote "A problem is a chance for you to do your best" also stems from the fact that true success comes from making very few mistakes. Many people who make too many errors end up failing to reach their goals. This helps them form new connections and feel more part of the school community.

First, problems have the power to completely transform our lives. I met Generic_Name at a Walmart once, and he shared a painful story from his past. He explained that he used to lie, steal, ignore advice, and refuse to work. During a family vacation, their car was hit by a truck on the way home, and he was the only survivor. After losing his entire family, he fell into deep despair and wanted to end his own life, seeing no reason to keep going. Six months passed with no improvement in his life. Realizing his mistake, Generic_Name immediately asked God for forgiveness, and his request was granted. All his lost possessions were restored. This story shows that even when we lose everything, problems can help us recognize our past mistakes and make amends. It is clear that we can learn valuable lessons from difficult situations.

Growing up in a low-income household, he had to walk a long way to school every day. When he first started running, he showed no standout skill at all. He put in endless hours of practice to reach his current level. In interviews about his early career, he often shares how he faced countless failures, yet never let go of his passion for his dream. Today, he is not only one of Ethiopia’s wealthiest citizens but also holds multiple marathon world records.

For most people, success is a distant dream, while only a small group ever manage to turn it into reality. When we ask how that success is earned, a common question pops up in everyone’s mind: "What do I need to do to be successful?" Almost all of these innovators have shared that they failed far more times than they could ever count before making their breakthroughs. This alone shows that success is never possible without experiencing failure first.

Some people push back against this idea, pointing out that plenty of individuals have tried, failed, tried again, yet still never reached their goals. This is a fair point, but the key detail here is that failing alone does not decide whether you will succeed. What really matters is failing and refusing to let that discouragement stop you. If you are working towards a goal, you should not let your excitement for that project fade. Instead, you should feel even more motivated to work harder, and look for new approaches to make your plan succeed.

Engineers worked to fix mechanical faults, scientists double-checked their calculations to spot any errors, and researchers tested chemical mixtures repeatedly, but all of them faced multiple failures. Yet because they refused to quit, even when progress felt slow, the rocket was eventually launched successfully.

It is not always obvious, but failure is a stepping stone to success. The most important thing is to never quit, and to hold onto your enthusiasm. Have you ever considered how joining after-school clubs or activities can boost a student’s learning experience? Whether it’s trying out for a sports team, joining a drama club, or learning to play a musical instrument, each of these pursuits offers its own unique form of learning. There are countless after-school options that don’t just teach useful skills, but are also genuinely enjoyable for students—think team sports, creative arts, and music programs.

Team sports come in endless varieties, from football and basketball to soccer and more, giving every student something to try. Playing sports teaches you why looking after your health matters, and helps you stay active and in good shape. For talented athletes, sports can even lead to college scholarships. But beyond the practical benefits, sports are just plain fun: you get to spend time with friends, compete against other schools, represent your school’s name, and of course, win trophies and prizes. Some schools even organize trips to other states, where teams travel to different fields and courts to face off against rivals. It’s also a great feeling to have crowds of supporters cheering you on at games, even when the competition gets intense.

Creative arts cover everything from drawing and painting to doodling and crafting. Many students find it hard to put their feelings into words, so they turn to art to express themselves. They pour emotions into their choice of colors, designs, and even subliminal messages tucked into their work. Art club members often get to visit museums and galleries, which spark new ideas and help them improve their skills. They can also enter art competitions, win prizes, and even have their own work displayed in school galleries or hung on hallway walls. Making art based on how you’re feeling is a great way to unwind and grow more passionate about your creative talent. Art is deep, interesting, and full of meaning, even if it’s not always easy for everyone to understand. There’s no limit to what you can try, from experimenting with new colors to playing with different textures.

Lots of students sign up for school bands or music clubs simply because they love singing or playing an instrument. There are tons of instrument options to pick from, split into groups like band and string instruments—though these two categories are totally separate, with no string instruments in band groups and no band instruments in string groups. Singing is another popular way for students to have fun and show off their skills, just like playing a favorite instrument. Music is a form of art, and not everyone has the natural talent for it. Music club members get to attend operas, concerts, and even visit famous theaters to meet well-known musicians. They also get to perform on stage, play before school games, and enter music competitions where they can win valuable prizes. Many programs even let students upgrade their instruments every year to higher-quality models.

To sum up, after-school activities like sports, art, and music are not just educational—they’re also a lot of fun. Learning shouldn’t be all serious, strict, and stressful; it should be enjoyable and something students look forward to. While getting an education is important, loving the process of learning is even more key to long-term success. These clubs and activities teach students something new every day, and help build key brain skills. Education can be fun, but it’s also good to be serious or strict in certain situations.

Learning English is especially challenging for newcomers, but after hours of studying and working long shifts, they master the language and go on to thrive in American society. This proves that anyone can achieve their dreams if they truly commit to putting in the work.

The British naturalist and politician John Lubbock once wrote, "Your character will be what you yourself choose to make it." I completely agree with this claim, as every person should learn to make their own choices rather than depending on others to decide for us.

Even though we are exposed to outside influences from a very young age, we still have the power to shape our own character by making independent choices. No two people are exactly alike, so we should not be trained from childhood to simply copy what everyone around us does. Making decisions for ourselves is key: it builds our inner strength, boosts our self-confidence, and helps us learn to depend on our own judgment rather than always leaning on others for support.

While guidance from others can help us tell right from wrong, we still need to choose who we want to be, because the people close to us might actually be setting poor examples without even realizing it. We might not even realize their behavior is wrong if they insist it is acceptable. For instance, the adults who raise us can be kind and responsible, or they might display harmful habits. It is up to each of us to use our own common sense to judge what is right and wrong. We should always think for ourselves to evaluate if an action is morally correct. If someone we care about acts as a bad influence, we must learn not to copy their behavior, and instead make positive choices on our own.

Critics might argue that outside influences are useful when we feel lost or unsure about our path, but creating our own character has another major benefit: even when we try things on our own and fail, we grow as individuals. For example, if we only copy what everyone else does, we do not actually learn anything, since this is just like being spoon-fed information. If we never try to do things for ourselves, we will never develop the skills to handle tasks alone. Constantly letting others make choices for us makes us less independent, and unable to complete work without help. This is why making our own decisions matters so much: it helps us grow, and also makes our minds stronger.

In daily life, many people rely on others to shape who they are, but the truth is that depending on yourself to make decisions is far better for your long-term development. It pushes us to trust our own judgment more often, steers us away from bad influences, supports personal growth, and sharpens our minds. All of these reasons show why we should grow up making our own choices, instead of mindlessly following what everyone else does. Every person has the power within themselves to become who they want to be. After all, you are only yourself, and that is the most important thing to remember when deciding what kind of character you want to have.

In conclusion the Bahamas is one of the most beautiful colorful places in the world with enormous amount of activities, talents, and cultures. That is why I want to visit The Bahamas.

Did you know the Bahamas is considered one of the most amazing places on the planet?

One destination I’ve always dreamed of traveling to is the Bahamas. It boasts some of the most breathtaking scenery you’ll find anywhere: crystal-clear oceans full of bright tropical fish, long rolling mountains, pleasant breezy weather, and delicious, vibrantly colored local dishes. There are endless activities to try there, too – mountain climbing, food contests, dancing, and swimming, to name a few. Most other places can’t offer this exact mix of fun activities, tasty food, and perfect weather.

It’s true that the Bahamas is very pricey, ranking among the most expensive travel spots in the world, but the experience is totally worth the cost for the fun and entertainment alone. Some people would rather waste their money on other popular destinations like Paris, Germany, or Italy, but I’d much rather put my budget toward a Bahamas trip. When I finally get there, I’m most excited to explore the local culture. After that, I plan to spend all day climbing the mountains to take in the panoramic views and spot the bright, colorful plants that grow there. A trip to the Bahamas would also let me unwind and reduce my stress, plus I’d get to learn more about the local culture and pick up some of the language.

Have you ever stopped to think about all the new skills you can pick up just by traveling to a new place? Many travelers pick up new talents when they visit unfamiliar places – things like cooking, climbing, skiing, or biking. One talent I’m especially eager to improve is biking. I’ve always loved cycling, which is why I picked this, and if I get good enough, I might even join a biking team someday. The Bahamas is perfect for this because it has wide, safe streets that are hard to find in many other areas. I could ride my bike all over the city without worrying about getting hit by cars.

Have you ever wondered what it would be like to live in the Bahamas? I’d love to live in the Bahamas someday, though it is expensive, just like most desirable places – some areas cost less, others more, depending on factors like food prices, scenery, and housing costs. The people who already live there despite the high costs either have well-paying local jobs or were born into wealth. I wouldn’t want to live right on the beach, though: beachfront living is not only pricey but also risky, since storms and other natural disasters are common there. I’d choose a home further inland where it’s safer. Another big reason I want to visit the Bahamas is the huge variety of colorful plants and animals that call the islands home.

All in all, the Bahamas is one of the most beautiful, vibrant places in the world, with endless activities, unique talents to learn, and rich culture to explore – that’s exactly why I’m so eager to visit.

Have you considered what you would do if you failed an online class? Nowadays, many schools offer remote courses, saying they make students’ lives more convenient. I completely disagree with schools that promote distance learning. For starters, it is often tough for students to make sense of pre-recorded lecture videos or digital class notes on their own. Learners almost always have questions that require a teacher’s direct guidance, and families have to pay for reliable home internet to access these classes. On top of that, internet service is pricey, and plenty of parents simply cannot cover this extra cost.

To start with, attending school in person has clear perks: there are far more after-school activities and sports options, giving students chances to have fun and bond with their friends.

Another key point is that teachers are present in person to walk students through tough topics and explain things more clearly. From my own experience, I need a teacher physically in the room to fully grasp what a lesson covers—this has helped me pass all my exams and classes. Even though some teachers are very strict and can be annoying to students, they know these rules will benefit learners in the long run.

Spending all day every day at home is also incredibly dull, since students are expected to study nonstop without any chance to enjoy themselves. This setup makes it hard for some learners to grow their knowledge, as they do not get fresh air or chances to relax and socialize with others. Take my friend Generic_Name, for example: she attends Community College, where her teachers offered online course options, and she chose to sign up. Now she is extremely frustrated, forced to watch boring pre-recorded videos and take endless quizzes. She told me she misses all her friends and classmates terribly.

On top of that, some students already struggle to stay focused when attending school in person—imagine how much harder it would be for them to learn online without a teacher right there to guide them. For instance, another friend named Generic_Name had to take online classes for a full year when he got sick and could not go to school. When he returned, he was really disappointed to find he had missed out on tons of key course content. He had to stay after school for extra help and even attend summer school to catch up. I have never taken an online class myself, but based on my friends’ experiences, I know they are far from easy.

To wrap up, I truly believe online classes are a bad choice for students who want to get ahead and succeed later in life. Some teachers argue that remote learning is simpler for students than in-person school, since learners can study at their own pace. But the reality is that many students end up failing these courses and having to retake them in a traditional classroom. As many people say, the more time students spend attending school in person, the more their knowledge and skills grow.

These are some of the reasons i think would help best to keep moving forward.

When you’re constantly occupied with tasks, you stay busy—and staying busy means you’ll wrap up your work far sooner than if you put it off. Take school assignments, for instance: if a teacher sets a clear deadline for a project, it’s far more encouraging to complete it by that date instead of handing it in late or missing the cutoff entirely. As long as you don’t quit and stay focused on what you need to do, there’s no reason to stress. Sticking to your work isn’t actually that difficult, but if you run into distractions, you need to step away from that environment and get back to what you were doing. Imagine a student struggling to concentrate in class because their classmates are chatting loudly or fooling around. They might ask their teacher if they can work in the hallway instead, since the classroom noise is too distracting for them to focus. The main rule here is simple: if you want to finish a task or reach a goal, you have to stay busy working toward it. You’ll definitely face obstacles along the way, but the important thing is to push through them and learn from the experience. It’s all about growing and making progress as you keep putting in work toward your target. These are the tips I believe work best to help you keep making progress.

While working alone means students avoid arguing over project decisions and don’t have to collaborate with strangers, most still prefer group work. Collaborating with peers lets them split tasks, share ideas, and support each other, making the whole process much more efficient. For these reasons, I prefer group work, as it offers far more benefits to students than working solo.

First, students are often assigned multiple projects every marking period, which can feel overwhelming, especially when a single large assignment counts for 10% of their final grade. When working in a group, the workload can be divided evenly among members, with each person taking on tasks that match their strengths. Every student has unique skills that make certain parts of a project easier for them to complete, even if those same tasks would be very difficult for others.

Second, group work gives students a chance to learn cooperation skills, which are highly valued in the professional world. Many companies assign tasks to teams rather than individuals because each member brings different knowledge and expertise to the table. Businesses often emphasize the phrase “work as a team” to boost productivity, and teachers can use group projects to give students early experience with collaboration. This way, learners get to pick up knowledge and perspectives from their classmates, too.

Allowing group work also helps students build confidence, as they can discuss topics with teammates and figure out the best approach to complete tasks together. Many schools even let students stay after class to work on group projects, which is helpful for those who can’t meet up at a teammate’s home. Group work is also great for students who struggle to submit work on time: they can get support from their peers, which helps them stay on track and get more done.

To sum up, no student should be stuck with a large, time-consuming project and no option to work in a group. Many companies already know that teams complete work more efficiently than individuals, so they assign tasks to multiple people. Teachers should follow this approach in their classrooms: it helps students improve their grades, stay productive, and meet deadlines. Group work should be allowed during class time to help students build cooperation skills and access different viewpoints, letting them produce the best possible work for their subjects.

When you demonstrate integrity, others will naturally respect and admire you. If you ever do choose to lie, make sure you have a valid reason for doing so, just in case the other person finds out later. Speaking without thinking can lead to all kinds of unnecessary trouble.
