Winston Churchill’s famous words hold real weight in the lives of people across the United States. Right now, plenty of folks who stumble or fall short will pick themselves back up to keep chasing the dreams they care about. Yet there are also those who, after facing a setback, decide it’s better to walk away and stop trying entirely. It’s worth looking at both of these mindsets. At its core, Churchill’s message reminds us that quitting should never be the first option when things get tough.

The first key reason to keep going even after failure is that setbacks teach us valuable lessons. If you don’t succeed at something the first time, or you make a slip-up, it’s not the end of everything. You’ll walk away knowing exactly what to adjust so you get it right the next time around. It’s always worth remembering that you can still achieve your goals and find success, as long as you stay committed. Standing up for what matters to you will never lead you astray.

Another big reason to never give up is that reaching your biggest, most meaningful goals takes persistence. If you want something badly enough, you have to put in the work to get it. Many people who mess up or don’t get the result they wanted will quit, claiming they’ve wasted their time. But the truth is, no one wins every time or gets everything right on the first try. Everyone faces failure at some point, and it never feels good in the moment. Still, we keep pushing forward because we want to reach that success, and feel proud knowing we didn’t throw in the towel when things got hard.

On the flip side, people who quit the moment they hit a hurdle have already lost. Anyone who thinks they can land a great job, get into a top school, or chase their dreams without making a single mistake is bound to give up the second they stumble. The people who actually land those dream jobs or get into top schools didn’t get there by luck. They worked hard for it, and even when things went wrong, they didn’t walk away because they had a clear purpose driving them. It’s common for people who fail to tell themselves they’re not smart enough or not talented enough. But if you weren’t capable, how would you have made it this far? When you’re struggling with something, remember that the people around you are there to help you work through your problems. Friends and family are the support system you can lean on when times get tough.

To wrap up, whenever you set a goal or want to achieve something, it’s crucial to never quit halfway through. A goal is something you’re working toward, and with steady effort, you’ll reach it sooner than you think. If you get stuck or run into a problem, you always have the people closest to you ready to lend a hand. Choosing not to give up on what you’re pursuing doesn’t just help you hit your target, it also builds your confidence, making you feel more sure of yourself as you move through life.

Think about the last time you put your phone down to actually look at thesky above you. For most people, the very first thing they do when they wake up is grab their phone to check notifications. We rely on technology for almost everything these days—it is woven into every part of our daily lives. Tech keeps advancing and changing all the time, but are we as people growing alongside it? So many of us share our entire lives online, constantly comparing our own experiences to those of others. It is no surprise that rates of depression are so high: people see all the nice things others have, but they are too distracted to notice the value of what they already own. Even though we all scroll through the same content online, each of us interprets it in our own way.

Wasting time is one of the biggest issues tied to tech use. Most people’s eyes are fixed to their personal screens for hours on end—they act like sheep, following every new trend without question. They only care about the newest gadgets, the biggest scandals, and flashy status symbols, like that popular shirt with a red logo that reads ‘Supreme’ in white letters. They compete for the most likes and online clout, caring more about the fake life they build on social media than their real, offline relationships. They say cruel things to others over FaceTime or text messages, but would never dare say those same words to someone’s face. Many are terrified of not fitting in, so they feel they need the latest, biggest, most expensive device—they assume a higher price tag means higher quality. All of this stems from technology, as people waste hours staring at glowing screens. This habit affects both the mind and body: a huge number of people slouch constantly, developing curved, arched backs. Back problems are everywhere these days. I have dealt with back issues since childhood from hunching over devices, and I predict that before long, almost everyone will have a curved spine, while only those with straight posture will hold positions of power. That makes sense when you think about it: you cannot stand tall and confident if your back is permanently arched.

Of course, technology does have real benefits. It can help you find answers for your homework, meet a romantic partner, start a whole new life, or even find a place to live. Tech is not bad by nature—it only becomes a problem when people misuse it or use it too much. It makes our lives easier in countless ways, but it also causes harm, and most people fail to see this balance.

Should schools team up with local businesses? People hold different opinions on this issue, but when we think about how these partnerships help students plan their future careers, it’s clear that such collaborations are a good idea.

Critics of school-company partnerships often miss a key point: while not every student will be excited about these programs, plenty are very interested in them. If schools do not work with businesses, many students will struggle to discover what jobs they might want to do later in life.

When schools have these partnerships, students are far more likely to land roles they actually enjoy. They will not face as many struggles when looking for work after graduation, either. If someone is doing a job they truly like, it is much easier to push through tough tasks and stay motivated.

These partnerships also let students take on work in fields they are passionate about, which can become their long-term dream careers. When young people are happy in their roles, they are much more likely to thrive and achieve success in their professional lives.

To sum up, schools should definitely build partnerships with companies. This way, students can access jobs that match their skills and interests, letting them do work they are good at and enjoy.

Every single person is born with some natural ability or skill. Take me, for instance—my special talent is drawing. This skill comes in handy for all sorts of situations, from finishing school projects to helping out with school plays and other events. Getting good at any activity you love isn't easy, though; it requires putting in plenty of time and effort to reach a level you're happy with. While everyone has their own unique talent, the only way to actually grow that skill is through hard work, regular practice, and doing it over and over again.

First, hard work is thefoundation for improving any talent or skill. When I first picked up a pencil to draw, I was absolutely terrible at it—mostly because I never put in any effort to practice. But once I started dedicating time and energy to getting better, my drawings started to improve noticeably. That experience taught me that progress only comes when you’re willing to work hard. Pushing myself to practice also lets me prove to myself what I’m truly capable of. Putting in effort feels rewarding because it’s a way to challenge myself to improve, both in my skills and in life as I grow older. Clearly, hard work alone can help someone achieve great things.

Second, regular practice is essential for honing any talent. My best friend’s skill is playing soccer, and he’s incredibly good at it because he trains every single day. Even though he’s smaller and slimmer than most other players, he doesn’t let that stop him—he can hold his own against opponents twice his size and weight. I saw this firsthand when I went to watch him play in a tournament last year. It was a perfect day for soccer: bright sun, clear blue skies, and mild temperatures. We waited a few minutes for the match to kick off, and once it did, my friend’s skills were on full display. He moved so fast down the field, dodging defenders left and right, he looked like a cheetah chasing its prey. By the end of the tournament, his team had the most points and took home the win. My friend was overjoyed that all his hours of practice had paid off. Afterward, we went to a nearby restaurant that smelled sweet like fresh flowers, and the food was absolutely delicious. This just goes to show that consistent practice can help people reach amazing heights.

Third, doing your chosen activity constantly is key to getting better at it. My dad is a good example of this—when he first decided to learn guitar, he had zero experience. He asked a friend who already played to teach him the basics, then spent hours every day repeating the same chords and notes until he got them right. Beyond that, having a developed talent is useful for handling everyday tasks. For instance, if I’m playing a soccer game, my drawing skill won’t help much—but if my talent was soccer, I’d perform well. Similarly, if I have a school project to finish and drawing is my strength, I’ll get a good grade because I’m using a skill I’ve worked hard to improve. It’s clear that constant repetition is one of the best ways to sharpen any talent or skill.

To sum up, every person has some natural talent or skill—they just need to know how to nurture it. Combining hard work, regular practice, and constant repetition of the activity is the best way to improve any skill. Have you ever thought about how useful it is to have a talent or skill of your own?

Can students of different ages work well together? Absolutely. Older students usually have more experience in school, so they tend to be more knowledgeable than their younger peers. They can also support younger learners with their studies. Schools should set up programs that pair older and younger students, as these partnerships let them help each other with schoolwork, build teamwork skills, and share practical tips and helpful advice whenever needed.

How exactly can older students support younger ones with their schoolwork? As mentioned, older learners often know more, since they have spent more time in the classroom. At the same time, younger students often pick up new information more quickly than older students. For example, my older sister is very clever. Whenever I ask her for help with a tricky assignment, she always makes time to explain how to solve the problems I don’t understand. Once she walks me through one question, I can usually figure out the rest on my own. That’s a clear example of how older students can boost younger ones’ academic work.

Working together also teaches both age groups about teamwork, a skill that is extremely valuable. Teamwork helps people communicate better with others and pick up great ideas from different perspectives. When older and younger students collaborate on a task, both benefit: they improve their teamwork skills and produce better results on their shared project. I remember once I had to complete a project with an older student. They were a huge help: they showed me how to structure the project from start to finish, pointed out my mistakes, and explained how to fix them. Their intelligence made the whole process easier, and I learned a lot about working in a team. This is how mixed-age groups can build stronger teamwork skills together.

These pairings also let students share useful, workable knowledge and give each other good advice when someone is struggling. When I was in third grade, I had to take my first SOL exam, and I was terrified. My older brother gave me great advice: he told me to stay calm and focus on the material. He also helped me study, which made a huge difference. This shows that older students can offer really helpful guidance, but younger students can give good advice too. Overall, learners of all ages can teach each other useful things and share valuable tips.

Schools should definitely create programs that pair older and younger students. These initiatives let learners share advice, pick up useful skills from each other, practice teamwork, and support each other with schoolwork. Older students often have good judgment when helping younger peers, which means they can offer solid advice. Teamwork is a skill everyone needs, as working with others and hearing their ideas is so important. Sometimes younger students even help older ones, depending on the task or the specific students involved. No matter what, older and younger learners who team up for schoolwork always support each other. For all these reasons, schools should set up programs that match older and younger students to learn together.

When given the choice between working alone or in groups, many students might prefer solo work to avoid distractions. While focusing individually can help some learners stay on task during lessons, collaborating in groups is actually far more valuable. Group work benefits students in three key ways: it lets them exchange thoughts, helps them perform better in class, and allows them to learn from their peers.

First, group work lets students share their ideas freely. Whether they are tackling a major school project or a small daily homework task, every member can voice their opinions. They can also look up information together to back up their points, which leads to higher-quality work. On top of that, group members can build on each other’s ideas, turning separate suggestions into a strong, unified final output. This makes group projects far more successful than those done alone.

Another reason group work is better is that it helps students improve their performance in class. When working together, learners can discuss material they find confusing and go to the teacher with questions as a group. This also saves teachers time: instead of explaining the same concept to ten different students one by one, they can give one clear explanation to the whole group. Additionally, students can learn from the errors their group mates make, so they avoid making the same mistakes themselves. This helps them do better in lessons and stay on track with their studies.

Group work also gives students the chance to learn from everyone in their team. If one student struggles with a topic or needs extra help, other group members can step in to explain it to them. They can support each other to make sure the whole group understands the lesson material, not just a few people. Working together to research topics also helps them find more reliable, detailed information than they might find on their own. This learning from one another is one of the biggest advantages of group work.

Overall, students should prioritize group work over working alone. Sharing ideas means every member of the group can pick up new perspectives from their peers. Collaborating also helps them do better in class, which makes it easier to pass the school year. Most importantly, learning from others prepares them for future situations where they will need to work with teammates. For all these reasons, group work is far more beneficial for students than working solo.

Should school weeks be shortened to four days, with each day lasting 10 hours? I don’t see any benefit to this change. Students who work will lose valuable shift hours, learners will waste the extra day off instead of studying, and young people will end up using electronic devices even more than they do now.

Many high schoolers hold part-time jobs after classes end. They need time to get home, rest, and prepare for their shifts, but longer school days would make working hardly worth it—they might only be able to fit in 3 or 4 hours of work per day. This is especially hard for seniors, who often rely on these earnings to pay daily bills or save for college tuition. In my view, the best option is to stick with the usual five-day school week, which lets students work at least six hours a day.

School staff often assume students will use the extra day off to finish homework or review material, but they overlook how many learners need in-person support. Some students feel more focused studying in a school setting, but with one less day on campus, far more will fail projects or exams. For example, a student who used to spend time at the school library after class won’t be able to do that anymore, since the library will likely be closed by the time their 10-hour school day ends. We should keep the existing schedule to support all students who benefit from it.

Supporters of the four-day week claim cutting one day of school will save energy and reduce costs, but they forget students will just go home and spend the entire extra day on their phones, watching TV, or playing video games—all of which use electricity. When students are at school, they can only use electronic devices during short breaks or lunch, so their total energy use from screens is far lower than it would be if they stayed home for a full extra day.

For all these reasons, I believe it is far better to maintain the standard school schedule, with students attending class for their usual hours five days a week. This way, working students won’t lose valuable shift hours, learners will have more time to study and complete work on campus, and they will spend less time on electronic devices than they would at home. While the goal of cutting costs and saving electricity is well-meaning, many students simply won’t use the extra day productively, so the change would do more harm than good.

you will learn how to make wise choices by learning from the lessons that an expert or authority could offer you.

Jobs play a huge role in most people’s lives, shaping their daily routines and even their sense of identity. There are thousands of career options out there, each suited to different interests and personality types, and most people put a lot of effort into picking the right path. That’s why encouraging students to commit to a career at a young age is a smart choice: it lets them learn what a job is truly like, discover fun, engaging activities to fill their days, and avoid unnecessary stress about their future once they reach adulthood.

The first major advantage of picking a career path early is that students get to see what that job is actually like in real life. Many students have vague dreams about jobs like medicine: they might say they want to be a doctor, but they have no idea what medical training involves, or what it’s really like to treat patients day after day. You can’t fully understand these details just from reading about them—you need hands-on experience to know if the work suits you. Students who settle on a career early can also do targeted research to fill in gaps in their knowledge. For example, a student interested in dentistry can look up exactly what qualifications they need, what a typical day in a dental office looks like, and what skills the job requires. Getting involved in career-related activities early gives students access to all these resources, so they can make informed choices instead of guessing.

A second key benefit is that committing to a career early helps students find fun, engaging ways to spend their free time, and even discover things that matter deeply to them. Lots of students have no set plans after school or during holidays, which often leaves them feeling bored and unmotivated. For these students, joining after-school programs that teach career skills or explore different job paths is a great solution. Many young people don’t have a regular hobby that brings them joy, but trying out different career-related activities can help them find a passion they actually care about. Instead of wasting time with nothing to do, they can build useful skills and enjoy themselves at the same time.

The final major reason to pick a career early is that it saves students a lot of stress and worry once they become adults. Most teenagers have no clear idea what they want to do for work later in life, and these young people often struggle to find and secure jobs after graduating. But if a student spends extra time in school learning about a specific career path, they won’t face that same struggle. They will already know exactly what they want to do, so they can focus on reaching their goal instead of panicking about their future. When high school students graduate, many feel huge pressure to pick a job immediately, which causes a lot of stress. Students who already committed to a career path early feel far less pressure, because they already know what interests them and what they want to become. Even students who have no idea what they want to do yet can benefit from spending time researching careers and attending career fairs, which can give them a few ideas to work with. Getting involved in career planning early means students won’t be overwhelmed by stress later on.

Some people argue that students should not commit to a career at a young age, because they are not yet well-informed enough about different job paths. However, this view misses the fact that students who avoid career planning early are actually more likely to face problems finding work later in life. The best way for students to fully understand what a job involves is to take part in career fairs, or get involved in career-related activities early, so they can set themselves up for success. In the end, committing to a career path early helps students become more knowledgeable about their chosen field, find a fun hobby to fill their free time, and avoid stress and trouble when looking for work as adults.

One person’s choices and behavior can have a real impact on how those around them act. Philosopher Albert Schweitzer once said, "Example is not the main thing in influencing others; it is the only thing." I fully agree with this view. After all, most people today look up to and mimic the people who are trending on social media. We also tend to follow the patterns we learn from parents, teachers, or other authority figures. This essay will explain why leading by example is the most effective way to get others to take action.

To start with, seeing someone else do an activity you find interesting can easily push you to try it yourself. For instance, if you love food and watch someone cook a new recipe, you might feel inspired to make your own meal at home. Most people rarely start a new habit or activity without some outside influence. Take Juuling, for example: most kids would never have tried the e-cigarette product unless they were persuaded or pressured by friends who used it.

Another key point is that setting a positive example is one of the best ways to guide others toward good choices, much like how most parents teach their children. No one can do something they have never been shown or learned how to do, so they naturally look to people who have the skills they want to pick up, and admire those individuals. Others can only follow a behavior if someone models it first. This is similar to how a wolf pack operates: the alpha leads by example, and the rest of the group copies their actions.

Some might argue that words alone, like speeches, can also sway people – Martin Luther King Jr.’s famous "I Have a Dream" address is a common example. While speeches may have been the most powerful tool for influence in the past, most people in today’s society are far more moved by actions and real-life examples. If that were not the case, why would children keep participating in the viral "challenges" that make headlines almost every week?

To sum up, leading by example remains the most effective way to encourage others to take action. When people model behaviors, they inspire those around them to do all kinds of things. Whether those actions are positive or negative is entirely up to the person setting the example, and the choices they model for others.

Anyone who knows the work of Ralph Waldo Emerson likely remembers his famous quote: "To be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment." If you disagree with his emphasis on the importance of individuality, here is why you should rethink that stance. At its core, his point is that every person deserves the freedom to make their own choices, and to act and think independently.

Of course, there are clear upsides to fitting in with the people around you. Pleasing loved ones and adopting a shared group identity can promote good behavior and help you develop positive personal traits that mark you as part of that community, giving you a strong sense of belonging. It also feels rewarding to connect with the shared values and common interests that define your group – these traits become so tied to who you are that you start to feel proud of your community, similar to the patriotism or nationalism people feel for their country.

But this does not mean you should stop thinking for yourself. You have every right to question your community if its core beliefs have serious flaws. For example, when a group or authority treats a principle or opinion as an absolute, unchangeable truth – a concept called dogma – you should push back. You should also be open to doubting advice from friends and family at times: even loved ones can give bad guidance about a specific choice, though you can still trust them in most other matters.

In the end, the most important thing is to be yourself. Think independently, embrace the unique traits that set you apart, and claim your right to express your own will and personality.

Energy and natural resources are among the most critical elements for human survival and progress. Over centuries, they have supported every aspect of our lives, from the money we earn to the goods we use and the power that runs our homes and cities. These resources are essential for maintaining our current way of life, so every person has a responsibility to look after them. Yet the harsh truth is that many people ignore this duty, either because they do not understand the long-term consequences of waste or because they simply choose not to think about it. We must fix these harmful habits and work to protect what we have left. This essay will outline practical plans to conserve resources, along with their benefits, potential downsides, and advice for putting them into action.

First, let’s look at the advantages of conserving resources. One key proposal is to switch to a four-day work week, where people work 10 hours each day, paired with school days that last just two hours. This setup would cut down on resource use in several ways. We would use less energy, food, internet data, and water, while also having more free time to spend with family or on hobbies. It would even reduce wear and tear on our clothes and shoes, since we would spend less time commuting or moving around for work and school. On a larger scale, this plan would lower pollution levels, making the environment healthier and improving overall quality of life. It would also let us save extra resources to use during global emergencies or shortages. Clearly, adopting this plan could help us protect a wide range of valuable resources.

However, this plan also comes with significant drawbacks. Implementing it would create several issues. Students would have far less time to learn, and workers would have fewer total hours to complete tasks. People would also lose out on social connections built at school and in the workplace. Advancing in a career or becoming a qualified professional would take much longer and be more difficult. Slower technological progress would be another major problem, which would ultimately hold back human development. We might end up losing access to useful tools and resources that make daily life easier, all because we cut back on work and study time.

In conclusion, while many people would gain from this proposal, it would also cause serious problems due to its downsides. Anyone considering adopting this plan must fully understand the risks involved. We need to carefully weigh these risks to avoid creating more issues than we already face. Rather than wasting time, we should start building a better world with improved lifestyles, and develop new projects to conserve resources. Governments should lead these efforts, as they have the authority to implement changes across entire countries. After reflecting on this topic, I have made caring for resources my personal goal. Putting in effort rather than remaining passive always yields better results. When we push ourselves to do more than the bare minimum, we are constantly growing and improving. Every single action we take, no matter how small, pays us back in some way—most people call this a reward. Working hard to achieve a goal builds self-confidence, because we learn firsthand that taking action lets us reach what we want, which in turn motivates us to keep trying. It is true that some people believe they can gain things without lifting a finger, but real accomplishment only comes from hard work, giving your best, and actively working toward a goal. If we do nothing at all, we will never achieve anything meaningful in life.

I learned this lesson firsthand back in sixth grade, when I really wanted to enter the annual math competition prepared by Generic_Name. Only the top math students were allowed to participate, and the school offered after-school review sessions to help students prepare. But I couldn’t attend those sessions, because I had paid swimming lessons every afternoon that I couldn’t miss. At first I was upset, but then I realized that if I really wanted a spot in the competition, I had to find another way to practice. I started waking up two hours earlier every morning to work on math problems, and I spent my lunch breaks in the library doing extra exercises. All that sacrifice paid off when the list of competition participants was posted—my name was on it. My mom always says that even if you fail at something once, you’ll learn from that mistake and not repeat it next time. In the end, your effort and hard work will help you achieve any goal you set for yourself. That is a lesson I will carry with me forever.

Every time we take action, no matter what it is, we get something in return—some might call it recompense. When you take the time to do something with patience, will, and gratitude, especially if it helps others without expecting anything back, you get a deep sense of self-satisfaction from making someone else happy. For example, imagine seeing a hungry child digging through trash for food, with no money or family to care for them. If you give that child a meal, you feel the warmth of knowing you made their day a little better. I had a similar experience when I went with my mom to clean the house of a 79-year-old woman who only had her dog for company. I asked my mom if I could join her on weekends to keep the woman company, and I had no idea how much she would mean to me. She was the kindest, sweetest person I had ever met, and she even called me her granddaughter. I was devastated when her son, who lived in Generic_City, came to take her back to live with him. But before she left, she told me: “I may be leaving, but don’t worry—you will always be in my heart. I will cherish every moment we spent together making me happy.” That day, I learned that even small actions can bring rewards that change your life forever.

Working hard toward a goal also builds unshakable self-confidence. When you want something and put in the effort to get it, you prove to yourself that no task is too hard if you try your best. For instance, if you have a pile of school assignments to finish, but you push yourself to complete them all anyway, you start to realize: “If I set my mind to it, I can do anything.” This confidence helps you in every area of life, especially when you have to make big, life-changing decisions. I saw this with my sister, who was torn about whether to pursue the college degree she really wanted. She was scared she might fail, but she believed in herself, enrolled in the program, and kept going. I admire her so much for that—she knew confidence would help her move forward and achieve what she wanted, even when fear tried to hold her back. Sometimes, we have to let go of the fear of failure and embrace the confidence that lets us believe in ourselves.

Choosing to take action is always better than doing nothing and hoping you’ll get something for free.

When we take action, we grow more than we ever would by being passive. We always get something back from our efforts, whether it’s the joy of helping someone else, or the pride of reaching our own goals. Most importantly, we build the confidence to know that we can achieve anything we want, as long as we work hard for it. Everyone should remember that we have the chance to improve our lives and reach any goal we set, but we have to be willing to put in the work, stay confident, and take action to make it happen.

Dear Principal,

I recently learned that the school cafeteria is planning to switch to a new, healthier lunch menu. As a junior here, I strongly believe this proposed change is a mistake, and I want to share my perspective to help support both the school’s growth and our students’ health. I think we should stick with our current lunch options. I know many people will disagree with me at first—they probably think we’ve eaten the same meals for too long, and want to try new dishes or copy what other schools serve. But I’m confident that once they hear my reasoning, they’ll realize our current cafeteria food is far better than they give it credit for.

My first objection to the menu switch is that it would do away with many students’ favorite cafeteria dishes—including several of my own. The food we serve now is tasty, fresh, and nutritious. There’s also more than enough for every student to get a full meal, so there’s no real need to adjust the menu at all. Changing it would just waste time and school funds that could be used for more pressing issues. There’s an old American saying: “When life gives you lemons, make lemonade.” It means we should make the most of what we already have, rather than trying to replace it with something untested.

On top of that, our current lunch menu is already healthy. I’m certain of this because I’ve never heard a single student complain about the meals we serve now—that alone shows our current lunch is special in its own right. It also includes some of the best healthy American dishes out there.

We all know most American food options are unhealthy junk that makes students gain weight slowly over time. But our current menu is full of fruits, vegetables, and fresh green salads that help us avoid excess weight gain and keep our bodies at a healthy size. I’ve been eating the cafeteria’s green salad regularly for months, and I’ve noticed great changes in my own health—it’s really impressive how much better I feel. So principal, don’t you agree that switching to a new lunch menu is a bad idea?

For example, our current cafeteria meals include protein and Vitamin D, and my weight has stayed steady ever since I started eating here. I hope you’ll take all of these points into account as you make your final decision. I know you want what’s best for the school, and that improving our community is your top priority. Thank you for your time,

Is it surprising to learn that studying from home can significantly lower students’ stress levels? Most academic stress stems from overwhelming amounts of homework that all need to be submitted by the next day. When students work from home, they no longer have to deal with this extra homework burden, since all their work is completed in their own space. Letting students follow their own daily schedules also makes them more motivated to finish assignments. Homeschooled students have more time to review material, and while they get to set their own rules, they also learn to be responsible for following them. Overall, learning at home rather than in a traditional school helps students achieve higher grades.

One major benefit of homeschooling is that it can be done from any location, at any time. Since students don’t have to rush to get to school early, they can get a full night’s sleep and wake up feeling refreshed, with a schedule that fits their needs. They can also adjust their study time to match their parents’ availability, rather than parents having to rearrange their own plans to accommodate school drop-offs or distance learning sessions. Many students struggle in traditional classrooms because they can’t keep up with the pace teachers set for the whole class. Distance learning lets these students work through material at their own speed, on a timeline that works for them. There are also no strict, unnecessary rules about being late or what to wear, so students can focus fully on their schoolwork instead of worrying about following arbitrary regulations. For many learners, distance learning improves their academic progress by offering flexible timing and letting them study in a way that suits them best.

Another key advantage of learning from home is the lack of distractions. In a traditional classroom, taking tests or writing notes is often interrupted by noise or other disruptions that make it hard to focus. At home, there are none of these typical classroom distractions, so students can concentrate fully on their work, which leads to better grades. A common source of distraction in schools is other students messing around, which makes it uncomfortable for those trying to pay attention. Studying from home lets students learn in a relaxed, comfortable environment without this stress. In school, students are stuck sitting at a desk listening to lessons for six hours straight, with very little time to eat or take bathroom breaks. At home, they can grab a snack or step away whenever they need to. This reduces pressure and helps them earn higher grades than they might in a traditional school setting.

Of course, there are some drawbacks to distance learning. Public and private schools offer far more extracurricular and academic opportunities than homeschooling does. For example, college recruiters rarely visit students’ homes to share information about career paths or degree programs. Making friends is also much harder without regular in-person social interaction, since traditional schools provide plenty of free time for students to socialize. If large numbers of students switch to homeschooling, public school funding will drop, leading to budget cuts and teacher job losses. Cheating is also easier at home: while teachers in traditional schools can monitor students closely during exams, homeschooled students can quickly look up answers on a separate device. Even with these issues, the choice between home and traditional schooling should come down to what students need, not just their personal preferences.

For all these reasons, schools should offer online or at-home class options. Learning from home is less distracting and far less stressful for most students. Flexible deadlines and schedules support both students’ mental health and their academic performance, making them more likely to earn good grades. While traditional schools do give students chances to build friendships through social interaction, it is very unlikely that missing this daily social time will negatively affect students once they reach adulthood. Already, many students around the world take some or all of their classes from home successfully. In the near future, all school districts and education systems should make distance learning a widely available option for students who prefer it.

Is learning from home via online videoconferencing a good way for students to study?

Taking classes remotely from home using videoconferencing tools is not a good way to study, as students miss out on the same quality of learning they get in a physical school setting. If remote learning becomes the standard, students lose the chance to form close bonds with their classmates and teachers. On top of that, many students will not treat their coursework with the same seriousness they do in school, since they lack direct guidance from teachers, advice from counselors, and oversight from school administrators.

First, learning from home is nothing like being in a physical classroom. In school, students take assignments, quizzes, and tests far more seriously than they ever would at home. When they are in a live class, if they don’t understand a topic, they can ask their teacher right away, and the teacher can give clear, detailed explanations and examples to make sure everyone follows along. By contrast, online students can’t stay after class for extra help, retake missed quizzes or exams, use school learning centers where peers help with homework, or even study alongside a classmate. As a result, their grades are likely to slip, since they won’t get all their questions answered or problems solved.

Second, if remote learning becomes the norm, students will not develop their communication skills, since they won’t form relationships with classmates, talk through their worries with peers, or even socialize with friends during lunch breaks. School often feels like a second home over time: students get inspired by their peers, see classmates as friends or even family, and know there are people who can help with both schoolwork and personal issues, from teachers and counselors to friends. On the other hand, learning online at home leaves students bored and lonely, with no one to talk to about their doubts or questions. What’s more, a large number of teenagers today struggle with mental health issues like stress, anxiety, and depression. Going to school takes their mind off problems at home or part-time jobs, and gives them easy access to supportive adults and friends who can offer help and advice. Studying alone at home just can’t match that.

Finally, remote learning is a bad fit for students who tend to slack off if not closely monitored. At home, there’s no teacher standing nearby to remind them to finish their work, pay attention, or stay awake during class. They also won’t feel the same pressure to complete homework and turn it in on time. Group work in school teaches students a lot: they learn from teammates, motivate each other, and have fun while working toward goals. Seeing peers work hard pushes them to do the same. But when working alone, these students often do the exact opposite. They end up thinking they can do whatever they want, and will not treat their courses with the level of seriousness they require.

To sum up, learning from home via videoconferencing is not a good option for students. They do not get the same quality of education as they would in a physical school, miss out on developing communication and social skills, and are less likely to take their coursework seriously.

Several school districts now run programs that let high schoolers finish their studies and graduate a full year sooner than the standard four-year timeline. From my perspective, most teens who jump at this chance and want to wrap up high school early are just trying to rush through their education to get it over with. They opt to take extra classes during summer break instead of going on beach vacations or hanging out with their friends. Sure, graduating ahead of schedule sounds appealing at first—who wouldn’t want to be done with school sooner? But in the end, the trade-off isn’t worth it.

I’ll admit school isn’t always exciting or entertaining, but the lessons and knowledge you gain there really help you succeed later in life. Finishing a year before your classmates doesn’t make you superior to them, and it definitely doesn’t prove you’re smarter than other students. It’s just a way to take a shortcut to avoid the rest of your high school experience.

I don’t think graduating early is a smart choice for most students, mainly because senior year brings so many unique, valuable experiences you can’t get anywhere else. You also get chances to learn about different colleges when representatives visit your school, plus help with building your resume and other resources that set you up for a successful future. A lot of students call senior year the best year of high school, and for good reason. If you graduate early, you’ll miss out on all those fun memories with friends, plus the special events and activities schools host for their final-year students. Not everyone will agree with this, but senior year gives you one last, gentle push to get ready for the next stage of your life. The final year of high school acts as a roadmap for starting adulthood, when you’ll have even bigger goals to work toward.

Another big reason I’m against this early graduation trend is that many students take this “easy way out” just because they want to be done with school forever. In my experience, the teens who push to graduate a year early are often the ones who skip class regularly, turn in incomplete work, show up late to school, and generally have a bad attitude—I’m talking specifically about the students who are a bad influence on others. High school isn’t a race, and life isn’t a competition to see who can get the nicest things first. The best things in life come from putting in hard work, not cutting corners. Some of these early grads don’t even go to college at all; they head straight into the workforce. Let’s be real: graduating early doesn’t make you cool. I also think jumping into full-time work right after high school isn’t the best move, because most of these students end up in low-wage jobs at places like fast food chains—think Chick-fil-A, McDonald’s, Burger King—that barely pay enough to get by. A proper education opens doors to better, stable jobs that pay well, so you don’t have to switch jobs every few months just to make ends meet.

For any student planning to finish high school in just three years, it’s essential to have a clear plan, whether that includes going to college or not. If you do want to go to college, you need to know that a lot of colleges expect applicants to have completed a full four years of high school. Admissions teams also look at your full school record to get a sense of what kind of student you are, and they may reject applicants who rushed through their high school years. The bottom line is that not all colleges will accept students who only did three years of high school. For those who don’t plan to go to college, you need an even better plan to survive in the real world. A lot of students don’t take school seriously, but they don’t realize that education is the key that unlocks opportunities for their future.

If I were to support school districts letting students finish early, I’d focus on the potential benefits. There are definitely some students who choose this path because they love learning so much that they want to get a head start on their career or college studies. That’s a great reason, and I’m not saying that’s a bad choice at all—it’s just not something I would do personally. Only students who are more than ready for the next step should be allowed to graduate early. In my view, the opportunity to finish high school a year sooner should only be open to students who have perfect attendance, always turn in their work on time, and earn high grades.

To sum up, school districts should not let high school students graduate a year early as a general rule. Students need to earn the right to graduate by putting in the work and showing they’re committed to their education. Senior year gives high schoolers one last boost of support before they start the next chapter of their lives. School might not be perfect, but it can absolutely set you up for a great career.

One personal goal I’m determined to achieve is losing weight, and I have three key reasons for this. First, it would greatly improve my physical health. Second, I want to show other people struggling with their weight that change is possible, giving them hope. Third, shedding extra pounds would make me feel better about myself overall, raising my self-esteem and easing my self-consciousness.

Let me explain my first reason more clearly. Carrying excess weight comes with serious health risks that I want to avoid. For example, obesity is a major risk factor for type 2 diabetes, a chronic illness linked directly to being overweight. Many people with extra weight also struggle with basic daily tasks, like walking long distances, because the extra pounds put strain on their bodies. I’ve even noticed this in my own life: I often find gym class exercises that most of my classmates breeze through really tough to complete. Avoiding these health issues is a huge motivator for me to lose weight.

My second reason for wanting to lose weight is to motivate other people who are also carrying extra weight to try making changes themselves. If I can get in shape, it will show others that someone who was once in their exact position succeeded, so they can too. I have a personal motto: “when you help someone, you help everyone.” For instance, if I encourage one person to start their weight loss journey, they might then feel inspired to support someone else in doing the same. I hope to start a sort of ripple effect: I inspire one person, they inspire another, and the cycle continues. Knowing that my own weight loss would not just benefit me, but also help others, would make me feel incredibly proud of my achievement.

My third and final reason is that losing weight would boost my self-esteem and make me less self-conscious. Anyone who has personal insecurities knows how much you want to get rid of them. My weight is one of my biggest insecurities, so I know that shedding extra pounds would make me feel more confident and stop me from worrying so much about how I look to others. I truly believe that losing weight would let me feel better about who I am, and that alone makes it worth the effort.

To sum up, my main personal goal right now is to lose weight. There are other smaller reasons I could mention, but these three are by far the most important to me. I want to get in shape to protect my health, to inspire others to make positive changes, and to feel more confident in my own skin. Losing weight is my top priority, and I love the idea that achieving this goal would also let me help other people along the way.

Many people compare modern technology to an extra limb, since we carry devices like smartphones everywhere and rely on them constantly. It’s true that we interact with tech daily, but this constant use often reduces face-to-face human interaction and creates endless distractions. While some argue that technology improves our lives overall, I believe its negative impacts are far more significant.

To be fair, technology is not all bad. It has become a core part of daily life, and it offers real benefits. For one, most modern jobs depend on tech tools that make work faster and more efficient. We also use devices to stay in touch: smartphones let us message loved ones to check their location or just catch up. Schools rely on tech too: computers and tablets help students complete assignments, access online resources, and even support teachers in delivering lessons.

Yet one of the biggest downsides of technology is how distracting it can be. Take schools as an example: smartphones are everywhere in classrooms, pulling students’ attention away from lessons and even disrupting their classmates. When students use devices without permission, their grades tend to drop, and they often lose interest in school entirely. These gadgets are more than just distractions, too — many people develop addictions to them. Distraction also creates serious safety risks. Using a phone while driving, whether texting, adjusting music, or checking a GPS, takes your eyes off the road. This split attention can easily lead to car accidents, since you are not fully focused on your surroundings.

Another major issue is that heavy phone use reduces meaningful human contact. It is common to see people, especially teenagers and young kids, walking with their heads down, staring at screens instead of looking up at the world around them. Many teens hardly talk to their parents, friends, or other family members anymore because they are glued to their devices. Over time, this hurts social skills: some people no longer know how to start a conversation or even say a simple hello when meeting someone in person. It is worrying to see how technology is damaging our ability to connect with others, cutting us off from real-world interactions.

Even though supporters point to the benefits of technology, I still believe its negative effects are more noticeable. Tech is now deeply woven into human life, and we could never remove it entirely. It distracts us constantly and weakens our connections to other people. The technology itself is not the problem — it is how we choose to use it that turns it into a harmful, addictive force. If we only used tech when it was truly necessary, our lives would be far better off.

While school plays a hugely important role in shaping a person’s life, it already takes up the majority of both students’ and teachers’ daily schedules. Take a typical public middle school in Maryland as an example: the first class starts at 8:15 a.m., and the final bell rings at 3:00 p.m. That adds upto 7 hours and 25 minutes spent in school, a long stretch of time to be absorbing information without a break. The local school board should not move to lengthen the school day, as doing so would cut into time students need for key activities now and in the future. These include completing homework and studying, joining after-school programs like sports teams, and volunteering for community events.

First, extending the school day would leave students with even less time to finish homework and study. Most students already spend over seven hours at school, with 6 to 8 classes that each run for 45 minutes. At least three of these classes typically assign regular homework, which students need enough time to complete carefully. If the school day were made longer, students would have fewer hours left to work on these assignments, which could lead to lower grades or failed classes due to missing work.

Second, longer school days would reduce time for after-school activities including sports and clubs. Health experts recommend that everyone gets at least one hour of exercise per day, but not all students take physical education (P.E.) classes. Even for those who do, a standard 45-minute P.E. session is not enough to meet this daily exercise requirement. Adding an hour and a half to the school day would leave students with less time to practice with after-school sports teams. Clubs, much like sports, are a core part of school life: they give students access to opportunities they cannot get during regular class time. A longer school day would mean students involved in clubs have far less time to participate in these valuable programs.

Third, extending the school day would cut into time students need to volunteer for community events. Community service is a common requirement in most school curriculums. For example, I have personally had to complete 75 hours of volunteer work in the past, which I earned by helping teachers with younger students or organizing classrooms before the school year started. These tasks almost always took place after school, usually lasting around two hours each. If the school day were lengthened, students would have less time to rack up the required volunteer hours, and could even fail to meet graduation requirements if they do not complete enough service work.

All in all, it makes far more sense for the school board to avoid adding any extra hours to the school day. This way, students can keep enough time for other important commitments, including sports, clubs, and community service work.

Is it true that we achieve more when we’re constantly busy? The answer is yes, but only if the activities we fill our time with actually benefit us. This is because staying consistently active with purposeful tasks makes us far more likely to reach our goals and succeed in life. That said, not all busy work counts. We have to be picky about what we spend our time on: if an activity won’t help us in the long run, there’s no real value in doing it, since it won’t move us closer to our future aims.

Take playing sports as a clear example. If you spend your free time practicing a sport regularly, you’re not just staying physically active—you’re also creating new opportunities for your future. Talented athletes can often win scholarships to top universities, which makes higher education much more affordable. On top of that, regular sports practice involves consistent exercise, which keeps you in good shape. This leads naturally into the next point about general fitness.

Another great habit to build is regular exercise, whether that’s going to the gym, taking fitness classes, or just moving your body every day. Staying active this way helps you maintain good health both now and as you age. When you make exercise a consistent part of your routine, you’re far less likely to develop serious health issues later in life, since your body stays strong and resilient. Adding a balanced, healthy diet to your routine only boosts these benefits, giving you even more advantages for the years ahead.

Working consistently is another reliable way to get more done and improve your life. When you hold down a regular job or take on paid work, you have a steady income coming in. That money covers all sorts of essential costs, from tuition and textbooks to transportation, groceries, and clothing. You can also set aside savings for unexpected emergencies, giving you a safety net for tough times. Plus, having work to focus on keeps you busy and purposeful, instead of sitting at home with nothing productive to fill your time.

To sum up, staying busy with meaningful, beneficial tasks is always the best way to make progress and achieve your goals. I don’t see any value in being inactive: if you’re not working toward things that help you, you won’t get very far in life. To be successful, you have to keep moving, focusing on productive activities that will pay off down the line. That’s why I firmly believe we accomplish far more when we’re always doing something worthwhile.

Encouraging students to reflect on their future goals helps them shape their own thoughts about what they want to pursue long-term. A career that aligns with their personal interests can bring real benefits to their lives, so guiding them to prepare early can shift how they view their passions and what they need to achieve success. While it takes time for young people to settle on a clear career path, starting this process early gives them space to explore their options. If they make thoughtful choices, these early opportunities can lead to major positive changes in their lives.

As students move forward with their studies, they start to form clearer stances on the subjects they are learning. Thinking about the future at a young age lets them tap into their natural creativity, both in how they think and what they care about. When students pick a career direction as early as 8th grade, many communities give them the chance to map out their own path and adjust their goals to match what they truly want. This shift moves them away from a carefree, playful mindset and toward one where they start making intentional choices as teenagers. In the long run, this process helps them work toward graduating as capable, respectable adults. Most students who start early end up figuring out what they want to do later in life, and as they plan ahead, they become more organized and gain clearer direction for their future.

This approach can make a huge difference for teenagers, proving they are capable of making positive, confident decisions. Schools can even test this method with all middle schoolers, tracking how their ideas develop as they move from middle to high school. While most students end up picking solid, or even excellent, career paths, the value goes beyond just choosing a job. It is about building the habit of thoughtful decision-making as a teenager, letting them take charge of what they believe will bring them success.

That said, pushing very young students to plan their future studies is not always the best move. Not every student wants to focus on long-term career plans before starting high school, so forcing these opportunities on them can waste time and effort. Some students change their minds about their career choice repeatedly once they enter high school, and by the end of four years, they still have not settled on a path. Many end up disliking the career they picked earlier, give up on that choice, and even drop out of college entirely. However, this does not mean early planning is useless. Even if a student ends up in a career they did not originally pick, they can still succeed and build a good life if they work hard. Changing the career they thought about in middle school is normal, and many keep adjusting their goals until they find what they truly want as young adults.

For all this to work, students need to think carefully about their choices, with support from parents who understand their children’s strengths and teachers who guide them on how to reach their career goals. It can be hard for society to tell which approaches help students and which do not, but as young people gain more knowledge, they get better at picking careers that benefit them. Many students who want a clear career path get help from their community with relevant courses as they start high school. Once they have this foundation, they can focus more on what their chosen career actually involves and how they will handle the demands of the job.

Staying consistently busy with purposeful tasks allows us to gather a wide range of life experiences, finish the tasks we set out to do, and lay the groundwork for what we hope to pursue later. Over time, the lessons we learn from these experiences also guide us to make better choices about what actions to take or avoid in the future. By contrast, when we are idle, we gain nothing useful at all, and we miss out on building the experience we will need for our long-term goals. This plays a huge role in shaping both the quality of our lives and the direction we want our lives to take. I strongly agree that we achieve far more when we stay active, and this habit shapes how all of us live our day-to-day lives.

One key reason I believe staying active shapes our daily lives is that it lets us pick up new skills, whether for a job we are interested in or a completely new topic. While getting a formal education is a core part of most people’s lives, it is not the right path for everyone, and success in any area always depends on how much effort you are willing to put in. In many places around the world, plenty of jobs do not require a degree at all, only hands-on experience in a specific field that sparks your curiosity. Getting involved in activities like volunteering for your community, handing out food to people experiencing homelessness, or mentoring younger children cuts down on idle time and keeps you active. It all comes down to how willing you are to put yourself out there and commit to the task at hand.

A second reason I think staying active makes you feel accomplished is that it gives your life a clear sense of purpose, and a feeling of pride that you cannot get any other way. For example, I have spent time helping school-aged kids with their homework after class, and every time I do this, it gives me a warm sense of pride knowing I am supporting my local community. This has brought me a lot of personal satisfaction, and shown me how important it is to teach young children that putting time and energy into a task leads to real accomplishment. I have had a similar experience playing lacrosse: whenever I fail to hit my target mile time, I push myself to train harder and improve. Playing lacrosse has taught me that self-satisfaction never comes easily, it takes patience and consistent effort. This has motivated me to take on more challenges, and helped me realize that if I invest my time and energy into something, I will always end up feeling accomplished. Doing work you enjoy and getting that sense of satisfaction helps you find your purpose, and makes you feel more fulfilled in your own life.

One final way that staying active boosts your sense of accomplishment is that it makes you aware that you have a meaningful purpose to live up to. I think a lot of people do not take the opportunities they are given seriously, even though it can be hard to seize those chances at first. I always feel most accomplished when I do work that shows others I care about them, rather than just trying to boost my own reputation. I recognize that many different things influence the choices we make, but it is also important to show the people around you how much you matter to them.

To sum up, the more effort you put into tasks, the more accomplished you will feel, and the happier you will be with yourself. This can give your self-esteem a big boost, and show the people around you that you are willing to dedicate yourself to your goals. Many people I have spoken to say their local community has helped them grow, and made them want to give something back in return. Even small, simple acts of activity can make someone’s day far better than doing nothing at all. There is a difference between working to meet your basic needs and working toward what you truly want, and both help you understand the value of feeling satisfied as an individual, and as part of a community.

In my opinion, schools should use cell phones in the classroom for educational purposes. Some school staff members may claim that cell phones should be forbidden in the classroom even for eductional purposes. Because, they think students will lose their attentions. However, I firmly believe that shools should allow students to use cell phones in the classroom for educational purposes.

Students will be effective academically as long as they use cell phones in the classroom. There are several reasons for my opinion. My first reason is that as a student, whenever I use cell phones in the classroom, I can search things easily and take pictures when nedded if my teachers allow me; which will help me on my studying when I go home. Another reason for my opinion is, if I don't have my phone with me, I will be eager until the bell rings and get my phone back without concentrating on the class. For example, I have a friend whose father took her cell phone forcing here to study the whole school year. Stubbornly, she stops doing what he tells her to do. Instead, she persistently hang-out and have more fun. As a result, she got F's for all of her classes. Therefore, using cell phones in the classroom helps the learning-teaching process.

Consequently, the positive effect of using cell phones in the classroom is more influential.

There is an ongoing debate in schools right now: should students be allowed to use their cell phones as learning tools during class, or should these devices be completely banned from classrooms? I strongly believe that schools should let students use phones for educational activities during lessons. Some teachers and administrators argue that even educational phone use should be forbidden, since they worry students will get distracted and lose focus. However, I am convinced that allowing phones for school-related tasks is the right choice.

When used properly, cell phones can actually help students perform better in their studies. There are a few key reasons I hold this view. First, as a student myself, I find that being able to look up information quickly or snap photos of complex notes or diagrams during class makes it much easier to review material when I get home. Another important point is that if I don’t have my phone with me, I spend the entire lesson distracted, counting down the minutes until the bell rings so I can get it back, instead of paying attention to the teacher. I have a clear example of this from a classmate: her father took away her phone for the whole school year, hoping it would force her to focus on her studies. Instead of doing better, she rebelled and refused to follow any of his rules. She spent all her time hanging out with friends and having fun, and ended up failing every single one of her classes. This shows that banning phones does not always lead to better learning—in fact, letting students use them appropriately supports the whole teaching and learning process.

Cell phones also play a very important role in emergency situations. For example, if an armed stranger entered the school or we had a lockdown and I heard an intruder nearby, I could dial 911 immediately to get help. Beyond that, if a crisis like a fire, hurricane, or severe thunderstorm hit while I was in class, I might need to call my family to let them know I’m safe—this would give my loved ones peace of mind about my situation. Another key point is that people tend to want things that are forbidden to them. If schools ban phones entirely, students will likely sneak them into class and use them for non-school activities behind teachers’ backs, which is far more problematic than letting them use phones openly under supervision. Overall, the benefits of allowing educational phone use in classrooms are far more significant than any potential downsides.

To sum up, schools should permit students to use cell phones for educational purposes during class. While some people argue that phones have no place in classrooms during lesson time, I remain convinced that they belong there for school-related tasks. The positive impacts of using phones for learning are far more powerful than any negatives, and phones are also much quicker to use than laptops or other bulky electronic devices when students need to complete small tasks in class.

Group projects make it easier to finish tasks by the deadline, and they also help create a positive atmosphere in the classroom. Group work in class is a huge support for students, as they can rely on each other for help. When someone works alone, they often get stuck and hesitate to ask for assistance, which makes it harder to do good work and keep making progress.

Having a partner or team to work with makes daily tasks far simpler than tackling everything alone. Every teacher should try to set up group activities that help students feel at ease and supported in the classroom.

A growing number of schools now let students use their phones in class for learning activities. For young people who are already used to using their devices daily, this policy can boost their educational experience in several meaningful ways. Most importantly, it makes tackling school tasks feel less stressful, helps learners stay on top of assignments and grades, and ultimately supports better academic performance.

First, using phones in class gives students extra time to complete assignments and homework. Many courses assign heavy workloads, so learners often need more time than they have outside school to get everything done. On top of that, personal challenges can get in the way of studying at home. For instance, I sometimes get so caught up in personal worries that I can’t focus on homework, and the stress makes it impossible to get any work done. Then there are students like me who work part-time after class: I often come home exhausted from my job, and the tiredness is so overwhelming that I can’t bring myself to do homework. Having been through this, I truly believe letting students use their phones for schoolwork during class time would make a huge difference.

Another key benefit is that students can easily check their grades and upcoming assignments. Learners who miss class due to illness or other reasons often don’t know what work they’ve missed, and many don’t have spare time at home to log in and check. It’s also common for students to forget they have homework: I’ve had plenty of days where I get home, start doing household chores, and suddenly realize it’s already bedtime, leaving no time to finish assignments for the next day. Letting students check their missed work during class solves this issue. They can even ask their teacher for permission to work on missing tasks during free moments, and get extra help if they’re stuck. I had a friend who struggled with math, for example: he used class time to check his math assignments on his phone, then asked the teacher to explain confusing concepts. This small change helped him improve his grades a lot, which shows how useful this policy can be.

Critics of this policy argue that phones are too distracting, claiming students will spend class time texting, playing games, or ignoring lessons entirely. But this view is misguided. Students actually learn better when they’re allowed to use tools they’re comfortable with, which makes the learning process feel more engaging rather than boring. Teachers can even use phones for fun, interactive activities: some already let students play trivia games on their devices, which helps students learn while enjoying themselves. Content viewed on phones is also easier for many students to memorize, since it aligns with how they already consume information daily. Older generations sometimes worry that too much technology, including phones in class, will make young people’s brains less sharp, but this is not true. Phones just give us new, more effective ways to learn.

To sum up, allowing phone use in classrooms brings clear benefits: it helps students finish homework and classwork, stay updated on grades and assignments, and ultimately learn more effectively. We are the first generation to grow up with constant access to this technology, and we should use it to gain more knowledge. The future of education is in our hands, and making learning easier for ourselves is a choice we should embrace. Schools are only looking for better ways to help us learn and succeed, both in our studies and in our future lives.

When it comes toRalph Waldo’s famous statement, I fully agree with the core message he is sharing. His point is that pushing yourself to master skills beyond the bare minimum is the only way to make real progress and build a meaningful life.

At the heart of this is the idea that you should chase your own dreams, not the plans other people make for you. No one else has the right to map out your future, because only you know what truly matters to you. If you trust in your own abilities and refuse to quit, you can master any skill or goal you set your mind to. That said, plenty of people will try to tell you that you are not talented enough, or that you should abandon your ambitions entirely.

Mastering even one meaningful thing can open doors you never expected. This often starts with small, foundational steps, like finishing your education. Once you have earned a degree or diploma, you can qualify for better jobs that let you grow professionally and personally. For many people, building a family is another huge milestone—loved ones can offer support and connect you to opportunities you might not find on your own. No matter what goal you pick, putting in maximum effort is essential. If you slack off or give up too easily, you will never become the person you want to be, and you will stall instead of growing.

So what should you do? Follow your own goals, of course. If you pursue the career you actually want, you could end up a famous singer, or even the president, even if no one else thought you were capable of it. Thinking creatively and trying new approaches lets you achieve things you have always dreamed of. You do not need to show off or act flashy to become a pro athlete, for example—you just need to trust in your skills. People will try to tear you down, but as long as you believe in yourself, you can always bounce back from setbacks.

How do you avoid letting other people make choices for you? You have to center your life around your own wants and needs, even when that feels uncomfortable. Sometimes people will pressure you to give up on a goal you have worked hard for, but you should never listen to their criticism or demands. Surrounding yourself with negativity will only hold you back. Ignore what others say about your plans or how you choose to reach your goals. Instead, carve out your own path and prove what you are capable of. When you succeed, you will make the people who supported you feel proud of everything you have achieved.

When someone shares a positive, thought-provoking idea, I have to agree with them—and Ralph Waldo’s point is exactly that. We have to push ourselves to master skills beyond the bare minimum, or we will never grow as people. Never give up on the dreams and goals you have set for yourself. Ignore the plans other people try to force on you, and make your life reflect what you actually want. Once you achieve the goals you set for yourself, you will gain access to amazing opportunities and go far in life. If you refuse to work toward the things you care about, you will end up stuck with no direction. That said, it is fine to ask for advice from people you trust to have your best interests at heart.
