Most people enjoy visiting beaches or public pools, and I’ve often thought about which water-based activity brings the most joy. For me, joining a swimming club is the top choice. Swimming is a great pastime because it helps me relax when I’m angry, I can hang out and play with friends in the water, and it turns exercise into something fun and effortless instead of a chore.

First, swimming helps me feel calm whenever I’m upset or angry. Last year, right after the school term ended and everyone had gone home, I jumped into a pool and swam laps. The experience lifted my mood immediately: I could hear water droplets falling as I kicked my legs, the soft sound of waves hitting the pool wall made me feel sleepy, and the rush of water flowing past me as I swam made me feel more awake and alive when I got out. Another time, I went on a school field trip to the beach that lasted two days. As the trip drew to a close, I felt sad and frustrated because I didn’t want to leave. I changed into my swimsuit, grabbed my camera, and walked out onto the sand. The crash of the waves sounded loud enough to almost swallow me whole, and I heard birds chirping as I snapped photos of them. It turned into a peaceful, happy day I still remember. That’s why I say swimming is so enjoyable: it’s a great way to calm down.

Second, swimming is way more fun when you’re with friends, and it’s even a good way to meet new people! Once, I was swimming by myself and felt fine, since I don’t mind being alone. But as soon as my friends arrived, they had me laughing in no time. We spent the whole time doing silly tricks, racing each other across the pool, which was a blast. One memorable time, my friends were swimming underwater and bumped heads with each other. When they popped up to the surface, all three of us couldn’t stop laughing. Plus, learning to swim is much easier when you’re having fun, and it’s even better with friends. For example, a friend can help you practice floating if you’re struggling. Even the basic dog paddle is hard for some people, though it comes easily to me. Learning on your own can feel boring, but practicing with friends makes the whole process enjoyable. That’s another reason swimming is such a great activity: you get to share it with people you like.

Lastly, swimming makes exercise feel way more exciting and less like hard work. I used to take swimming lessons every Friday after school. I didn’t enjoy them at first, but by the third lesson, I was hooked. At 10 years old, I weighed 145 pounds, but after starting the lessons, my weight dropped to 111 pounds. You don’t always notice results right away, especially when you start having fun with what you’re doing. At first, I wasn’t interested in swimming at all – I only joined the lessons to lose weight. I didn’t see any improvement in my swimming skills, and I wasn’t losing any weight either. But after a few weeks, the weight started coming off, and I got better at swimming too. I realized later that this happened because I’d grown more passionate and determined about swimming, so I didn’t even notice the small changes at first. After everything I’ve experienced, swimming always lifts my mood. That’s how much of a positive impact it’s had on my life.

To sum up, swimming is more exciting and easier than other forms of exercise, it lets you play with friends, and it helps me calm down when I’m angry – all reasons why it’s such an enjoyable activity. I think it’s important to share this story because it’s based on my real experiences. So far, three people have told me this story helped them try swimming too. Without a doubt, joining a swimming club is one of the most fun activities you can pick.

When it comes to trying to be someone, is it better to improvise or follow the script all the time?

Everyone needs to have their own individuality and be original instead of trying to be something else because that way you learn more about yourself. Also, you are acknowledging different methods about how to be better than yourself. And one of the most important things, you could make a good influence in someone else's life and teach him/her how to find their path in their own way. No matter what happens, you always have to follow yourself.

While you are listening to your favorite songs from your playlist, you are dancing according to the tempo and doing the dancing moves that you usually do. After dancing for a long while, suddenly you let the music take control over you and you make a back flip without practicing it before. You are very surprised because you did something that you did not know you could do and after that, you keep practicing that move and perfectioning it and it comes out natural. That is how you learn more about yourself.

After a long time taking bad decisions, he finally decided to make things better for the people who cares about him and specially for him. It took him over 5 years for him to get back on his feet; with his own effort and the support from his family and friends, he started to make a good difference for the world. Right now, Robert is one the best actors in Hollywood, he has an excellent life with his wife and kids on his side, and is a great influence for millions of people. That is how you acknowledge different methods to be better that yourself.

That is how you follow your own script with your own terms.

You acknowledge new ways to become better than yourself like if you were in a videogame, you are going to the next level slowly. Take this example: imagine you’re in your large home basement one day, playing your favorite playlist at full volume. You start dancing to the beat, doing the same moves you always use. After a while, you stop thinking about the steps and just let the rhythm guide you—suddenly, you throw a backflip, even though you’ve never practiced it before. You’re shocked at first, but you keep working on that move until it feels completely natural. That’s exactly how staying true to yourself helps you learn what you’re really capable of.

Choosing your own path also means you’ll find all kinds of ways to become a better version of yourself, not comparing to others but growing past who you used to be. You’ll do whatever it takes to grow, as long as it fits your values. A perfect example is Robert Downey Jr. There was a time when his life was in shambles: he struggled with drug addiction, got into legal trouble repeatedly, and even faced court hearings for his bad choices. After years of making harmful decisions, he finally decided to turn his life around, not just for his loved ones, but for his own well-being. It took him more than five years of hard work and support from family and friends to rebuild his career and his life. Today, he’s one of Hollywood’s most respected actors, has a happy family with his wife and kids, and inspires millions of people around the world. That’s what it looks like to find your own way to improve yourself.

Some people argue that trying to be yourself is just copying other people’s advice. But that’s not true. When you listen to tips from others, you’re not mimicking them exactly—you’re adapting their suggestions to fit your own perspective and personality. That way, you’re still writing your own life script, while giving credit to the people who helped you. For example, say you meet a girl at a party and want to get to know her, but you have no idea how to approach her without messing up. You ask a friend for advice, and he shows you how he talks to people at parties, giving you a few ideas. Before you walk over to her, he reminds you: “Just be yourself.” You take his tips, but do things in your own way. The girl ends up liking you, everything works out, and later you even help other friends who are nervous about dating. That’s how you follow your own path, on your own terms, even when you ask for help.

To sum up, staying true to yourself at all times matters more than trying to copy someone else’s life. It proves you don’t need to mimic others to be a worthwhile person. You’ll learn more about your own character than you ever could about a fictional anime character, find new ways to grow like leveling up in a video game, and positively impact the people around you. At the end of the day, being yourself means listening to your gut instinct, as long as your choices bring some kind of good to your life or the lives of others.

I believe that success is built out of failures, even if this isn’t the case for everyone.

We pursue success to improve our lives, but reaching that better life always comes with tough hurdles—what we call failures. These challenges can make you want to quit the very thing that would help you succeed.

Failures play a key role in success because you can’t learn without messing up at least once. Learning comes from figuring out what you did wrong: if you made a mistake before, you can identify it, learn from it, and avoid repeating it next time. That’s how you get it right eventually.

A lot of people give up way too fast on their goals or what they’re working toward. Some lose their excitement for success, while others don’t. I think if you change how you view failures, you’re more likely to reach your goals. My aunt always says, “Focus on what you can achieve, not on what you might fail at.” She’s never given up on anything she’s wanted to accomplish in life.

For example, I’m from Generic_City, and my whole family is Hispanic—we speak Spanish at home. Learning English wasn’t easy for me, and at first I didn’t think I’d ever be able to speak it well. But I reminded myself that anything is possible. Everyone is born for a reason, not just because their parents wanted a child.

There was a period where I struggled with stress, anxiety, and depression. I was failing my classes, and I felt so awful that I wanted to quit everything immediately. Failure kept piling up, one after another, until I finally told myself, “You’ll be okay. You’ll do what you love, succeed, and make your parents proud of you.” I started thinking positively and fixing my mistakes. Nothing lasts forever—I overcame my depression, though I still deal with some stress and anxiety. But those things don’t hold me back anymore.

Failures can make people feel hopeless, lose their motivation, and give up easily if they’re weak. But if you’re strong enough to believe you’ll make it, you will. You’ll keep your hope, excitement, and faith high, so nothing can stop you from succeeding.

Think of failures as extra challenges added to your life journey. To reach the top of a mountain, you have to hike all the way up until you can see the ocean on the other side. It’s not just failures you’ll face—there will be huge obstacles, and sometimes people will even try to trip you up on purpose.

Some people will hope you fail in your field, while others will be thrilled to see you reach the top. A lot of people fail along the way because they don’t understand what failure really means.

To sum up, I agree that success is moving from one failure to the next. Even if you lose hope or excitement along the way, you have to keep pushing toward your goal. I’d guess more than half of people are fighting for their future, putting in all their effort to succeed—and if they can do it, so can we. Failures are a valuable part of success, helping to lay the groundwork for achieving your goals in life.

I fully agree with this idea, as it’s incredibly tough to stay true to who you are in today’s world, where everyone seems to judge every little choice you make. People constantly pressure you to act exactly how they expect, dictating what you should and shouldn’t do, without ever caring about your own perspective.

A clear example comes from my own family. They’re always telling me what to do, and if I make a mistake, they’re quick to judge me. They even try to choose who I’m friends with, what clothes I wear, even what shoes I put on. In a situation like this, it’s almost impossible to be your genuine self, because they never give me a chance to show who I really am.

Another example is how strangers treat us. No matter what we do, we can never fully meet other people’s expectations. If someone sees you hanging out with a guy who has tattoos, they assume he’s a bad person. If you’re a plus-sized girl, people call you ugly; if you’re thin, they find fault with that too. Wear a short skirt? They’ll label you as wild or inappropriate. The truth is, we can never do anything right in their eyes.

Everybody can judge, but we have to be strong, and try to show the world who we really are and what we enjoy doing. We face lots of tough moments because of this constant judgment. You might feel down or upset when people criticize you, or get exhausted from pretending to be someone you’re not. Sometimes, you might even start thinking negatively about yourself, telling yourself things like “I can never do anything right” or “I’m not a good person.” That’s why it’s so important to be who you want to be—loving yourself has to come first. No one can care for you more than you care for yourself. Of course, you need to take responsibility for your own choices, but you have to feel at peace with those decisions. Show the world who you really are: if you feel good about yourself, that positivity will shine through.

All of these are reasons why staying true to yourself is so difficult, and that’s exactly why I agree with Ralph Waldo Emerson’s words—they really connect with me. I feel like a winner, happy with the person I am, because I’ve stopped worrying about what other people say or think. This is my life, and I make my own choices. Even if people call me a wild, outspoken woman, I’m fine with that, because I feel good being that way. I love being happy, being my authentic self. I truly value who I am, and I don’t have to pretend to be anyone else. The little girl who always did whatever others told her to is gone—she’s part of my past, not my present. I’m still learning to embrace who I am, but reaching this point feels like one of my greatest achievements. Being yourself is wonderful: I feel relaxed now, satisfied with the choices I’ve made, and I’ve finally shown the world who I really am. My life is full of joy and laughter. I’m a little wild, and I love that about myself—my personality is one of a kind, and that makes me really happy.

Students are eager to gain hands-on knowledge from people working in various professions, since these fields may shape their future careers. Schools should regularly offer opportunities for this kind of learning, as it has a direct positive impact on students’ long-term career paths. Many young people have clear dreams about entering specific industries, and they are motivated to learn the skills needed to join those fields. They also deserve the chance to ask questions about how these experiences will help them earn a college degree and build a stable career. Most importantly, these programs benefit students greatly, and they can share what they’ve learned with their parents.

Schools should support this type of learning because it prepares students for college, and after graduation, they will be ready to start long-term careers in fields they are passionate about. Absorbing as much knowledge as possible is key to helping students gather the information they need to reach their personal goals. While some young people struggle to decide what they want to do with their lives, which can feel like a difficult choice, real-world exposure can make this decision easier. It feels great when students can explain their career plans to their parents and other loved ones. Sometimes, stepping out into the world and encountering a new field or experience can be a total surprise—and that unexpected spark might be exactly what sets a student on their ideal career path.

Whether a student sticks with the career they dreamed of as a child or switches to an even better option later, these experiences help them grow. There are many practical benefits too: when students take on part-time work related to their interests, they can buy their own necessities, which reduces the financial burden on their parents. It is also helpful for parents to encourage their children to earn their own money, save for college, and enjoy greater independence. Schools already have the right approach by teaching core subjects, but they should also include career-focused lessons that go beyond standard curriculum. For students with specific interests, like athletics, it is important to balance these career explorations with school responsibilities: homework, projects, and other assignments. Staying on top of these tasks is essential for passing classes and graduating on time.

For those unfamiliar, a homework club is a supervised session where teachers are on hand to assist with assignments or clear up confusion about tricky course material. These clubs let students deepen their understanding of topics, bond with classmates through collaborative work, and feel more confident about their academic progress. They are a huge support for learners of all levels. There are plenty of productive ways to use this time: teaming up with a friend to finish a group project, preparing for an upcoming test or quiz, or even getting all your assigned work done ahead of schedule.

One of the biggest advantages of attending these clubs is the direct support from teachers. Working on a project with a classmate becomes easier when you have an adult there to guide you, and collaborating this way helps you build stronger connections with your peers. If you ever get stuck on a part of an assignment or have a question about a project, the homework club is the perfect place to get clear, helpful answers. What makes these clubs special is the sense of community they create: as more students show up, everyone starts helping each other tackle problems, turning the space into a collaborative group where no question goes unanswered. Tackling big projects alone can feel overwhelming, but with the resources available at your school’s homework club, you’ll never be without the support you need. If you’re struggling with any academic task, this club is the best place to turn for assistance.

Another key use for homework club time is preparing for tests and quizzes. Teachers can help you make revision flashcards, work through study guides step by step, or even host a game of Kahoot to make revising more fun. For anyone who hasn’t heard of it, Kahoot is an interactive game that reinforces what you’ve learned before an exam, basically a study guide turned into a friendly competition. Lots of students find it hard to focus on revision when they’re at home alone, with distractions like phones, TV, or siblings pulling their attention away. At homework club, you’ll have a quiet, structured space to study, with teachers making sure you stay on track. I’d suggest everyone try to attend at least three times a week, whether you need help with test prep or any other academic issue. Going to these sessions will boost your chances of passing your exams, as the club gives you all the tools you need to feel prepared.

The final major benefit of homework clubs is getting your assigned work done early. Teachers break down every task clearly, and I promise you’ll pick up even more knowledge than you would in a regular class session. Whether you need help with math, science, history, or English, there will be staff on hand to teach you extra details about the topic. Finishing your work at the club means you won’t have to stress about it when you get home, freeing up your evening for hobbies or relaxation. During these sessions, teachers don’t just give you answers: they explain assignments in far more detail than they might have time for in a busy classroom, helping you grasp the underlying concepts of the subject.

Homework club is easily one of the most valuable after-school activities a school can offer. It helps students master course material, builds their academic confidence, and lets them connect with classmates in a low-pressure setting. These clubs are vibrant communities filled with supportive students and dedicated teachers. The range of support available is huge: staff help you meet project deadlines, prepare for exams, and get your daily homework done ahead of time. We can make sure every school has a homework club, but it will take effort from students to push for this change. None of this would be possible without the amazing teachers who volunteer their time to run these sessions, as the club would lose all its value without their guidance.

I strongly believe that staying active is far better than spending most of your time idle. Keeping busy, whether by helping others or ticking off household tasks, lets you contribute meaningfully to the people around you. What’s more, regular movement keeps you in good physical shape—if you’re up and moving often, that counts as solid exercise without needing a gym membership.

I personally love working out and helping my family with day-to-day tasks, and I’m not alone in this. Most people feel happier and more content when they’re up and doing things, rather than sitting still for hours. I can’t stand being inactive for too long, and I know plenty of others feel the same. For some careers, like personal training or coaching, being active is not just a preference—it’s a core part of the job.

Staying idle for long stretches can cause real problems, too. If everyone else is pitching in to get work done but you’re not helping, it can annoy the people who need your support. I’ve found that if I laze around for days on end, I start to feel unwell—and this is true for most people, not just me. Our bodies are built to move, so some form of regular exercise is essential. That’s a big part of why staying active is the better choice.

Of course, there are rare times when being inactive is actually the right call. For example, if you’re at a movie theater, you can’t jump up and run around the room—you’ll get thrown out. Similarly, if there’s danger or trouble happening outside your home, it’s far safer to stay inside and keep a low profile rather than getting involved.

To sum up, while inactivity does serve a purpose in a few specific situations, staying active is still the better approach for daily life. You’ll accomplish far more when you keep busy, and putting in hard work instead of lazing around is the only way to meet your long-term life goals.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once argued that the greatest accomplishment a person can have is staying authentic, even when the world constantly pressures them to become someone else. I firmly believe this is true, as staying true to who you are helps you grow independent, build the confidence needed to reach your goals, and develop the strength to support the people around you.

First, staying authentic helps you become self-reliant, which is key to handling your own choices and responsibilities. Relying on yourself to reach your goals is far better than depending on others, since people rarely stay in your life forever. Friends, partners, or mentors may come and go, but you will always have yourself. When you achieve things on your own, you prove to others—and yourself—that you do not need anyone else’s help to succeed. All you need is your own determination.

Being your true self also pushes you to improve, and as you make progress, your self-confidence grows. There is nothing more valuable than trusting in your own abilities. Building confidence does not have to be hard, either—just as it is easy to gain weight, it is simple to build confidence through positive self-talk, like reminding yourself "I have what it takes to succeed" regularly. With enough motivation, you can take on almost any challenge, whether that means trying an extreme activity like skydiving or just showing up on time to work every day. You might start getting better grades in school, or perform better in your job. At the end of the day, confidence is essential for success in any area of life.

As your confidence grows, you will also gain the strength to lift up others who are struggling. Maybe a friend is dealing with depression, or a family member is going through a tough patch. You can use your own experience to motivate them to keep going, no matter how stressful life gets. Everyone has to face hard times before things get better, so it is important not to dwell on the past. Everything happens for a reason, after all. I have personally faced a difficult period for the past six months, but that never made me want to give up. I am a strong, independent woman, and I will never stop working to maintain my confidence.

In conclusion, Emerson was completely right about the value of staying true to yourself. While the world may try to push you to change in negative ways, holding onto a positive mindset is the best way to resist that pressure. If you stay independent and confident, you will not only reach your own goals, but you can also help the people around you do the same. Never give up, stay positive, and remember that confidence and motivation are the keys to a happy, successful life.

Many young people are expected to pick a career path by the time they enter high school. As soon as they start high school, some begin working in a specific field to earn money and get ready for their future career.

Committing to a specific career at such a young age is a bad idea. It distracts students from their schoolwork, interrupts their ongoing education, and takes time away from activities they enjoy.

First, focusing on a career too early pulls attention away from core school responsibilities. High school classes get harder every year, and teachers place a lot of importance on academic performance. Students have piles of homework, regular tests to study for, and need to stay focused to graduate and get into a good college. If they spend hours working a job tied to a specific career before finishing high school, they may struggle to keep up. For example, a high schooler who starts working at a hair salon after classes might have a big test to study for and several assignments due. But their work shift runs late, leaving no time to review material or finish homework. Over time, their grades drop, they fail exams, and this can hurt their self-esteem.

Another key reason is that high school students are still in the middle of their formal education and personal growth. They are young, still developing, and need these years to focus on learning rather than tying themselves to one career path. During high school, most students are only just starting to figure out what they want to do long-term. Getting a solid education first will help them earn more money, live healthier lives, and build a stable future. For instance, a student who has not yet finished high school is not fully educated and is still building key skills. They need to stay focused on their classes, graduate, and then attend a good college to study the field they are actually interested in—their dream job. Taking on a specific career too early could pull them away from that goal entirely.

Finally, early career commitments can steal time away from hobbies and activities that students genuinely enjoy, which hurts their wellbeing. Doing things they love is important for staying healthy, reducing stress, and having positive outlets outside of school. When a high schooler takes on a job in a specific career field, they often have no free time left between classes, homework, and work shifts. If they add a part-time job in a specific career field, they will have no time left to play football, and not enough time to keep up with schoolwork either—causing unnecessary stress.

To sum up, high school students should prioritize their studies and overall education instead of committing to a specific career early just to earn some money. Early jobs in a chosen field can distract them from schoolwork, pull them away from hobbies they love, and interrupt their personal growth. They need to keep learning, work hard in their classes, and get into a good college so they can prepare for their actual dream job, earn a good income, and build a happy, stable life.

Many people believe that first impressions can never be altered. We learn from past experiences that our behavior, the language we use, and how we look all reveal our true personalities. Most people agree with this idea, since we have the ability to adjust our actions, the words we speak, and our appearance over time.

First, the way you behave when meeting someone for the first time matters more than almost anything else. The old saying that actions speak louder than words holds a lot of truth here. Once you’ve acted a certain way in front of a new acquaintance, you can’t take those actions back. If you come across as unkind or rude when you first meet someone, they will assume you are not someone they want to spend time with. That’s why it’s so important not to make mistakes during that initial meeting.

When you talk to someone you’ve just met, avoid using offensive language. If you swear or use rude words, they may think you don’t know how to communicate politely. Whether you use fancy vocabulary or just speak casually, every positive conversation helps build trust with the other person over time. Try not to stumble over your words or stutter too much – while it’s normal to stutter sometimes, making an effort to speak clearly helps. If you do slip up, some people will be kind enough to give you another chance. Also, avoid using too many hand gestures when talking to someone new.

On top of that, your appearance plays the biggest role in first impressions. You can’t change the way you looked during that first meeting, as your appearance covers both how you present yourself on the outside and your inner character too. Most people pay more attention to how someone looks than how they act or speak when forming a first impression. If you have a messy or unappealing appearance, others may assume you are a bad person and avoid being friends with you. A neat, pleasant appearance might make people want to befriend you, but this also depends on their own perspective. Generally, if you like how someone acts, speaks, and especially how they look, and their first impression was positive, you’ll probably want to get to know them better. Once formed, these first impressions stick in your mind and cannot be erased or changed.

Of course, there are exceptions. Sometimes you might be able to change someone’s mind about you later. Everyone has bad days where they act out of character, and some people will accept that you’re just having a rough time, not that your behavior is your normal self. Even so, there is always a chance to make a second good impression, even if the first one was not great.

To wrap up, many people argue that first impressions cannot be changed, and most agree with this view. The three key factors that shape these impressions are your actions, your words, and your appearance. We all learn from our own life experiences over time. It’s always important to be mindful of how you act, speak, and present yourself to new people, since we cross paths with new acquaintances almost every day.

Inactivity always serves a valid purpose. Thomas Jefferson once argued that we can accomplish an incredible amount when we stay busy without ever stopping. I firmly believe that inactivity always serves a purpose. To complete any task successfully, we need to take breaks along the way, and this also keeps our bodies from breaking down while we work. That said, some people argue that we get more done if we never stop working.

First, taking breaks is essential to finishing what we start. This is exactly why most people have Saturdays and Sundays off work now. Our bodies simply cannot keep functioning if we never take a pause. If we push ourselves too hard without rest, the buildup of pressure makes it impossible to sleep. Even animals rest after a long day of hard work so they can keep going the next day.

Another key reason inactivity serves a purpose is that it stops our bodies from shutting down while we are busy. If we skip rest, we might start falling asleep while working, which can lead to all kinds of accidents. We could even get hurt on the job, depending on what type of work we do. Worst of all, driving while exhausted from nonstop work can cost us our lives, or take the lives of others.

Of course, some people claim that we achieve more when we work nonstop, getting more done and finishing tasks faster. For one, we might learn new skills more quickly if we practice all day without resting. They also argue that focusing only on a task leads to better results. For example, construction crews building apartments or houses could finish sooner if they never took breaks. It would take far less time to reach the end goal, much like a nonstop journey to a destination. They believe that never stopping is the best way to reach your goals.

In the end, I still believe inactivity always serves a purpose: we need breaks to finish tasks, and rest keeps our bodies from breaking down. While some argue that constant work leads to more accomplishments, the choice of whether to take time off and be idle or keep working is entirely up to each person.

I fully agree with Emerson’s statement about the value of individuality. It feels deeply comforting to know I can be my true self in this world, even when society constantly tries to mold me into someone I’m not and shape how I view the world. Staying authentic lets me make my own choices, like traveling to see beautiful natural places: wandering through vast forests, climbing rolling hills, and taking in stunning scenery. Experiencing these wonderful sights is truly amazing.

I can embrace my true self even when the world pushes me to become something else, and that authenticity makes appreciating nature even more special. There is nothing quite like visiting natural spaces, from spotting all kinds of colorful wildflowers to admiring the delicate beauty of blossom trees. These simple natural wonders feel far more meaningful when I experience them as my genuine self, not as the person the world wants me to be.

When I think about how the world constantly tries to turn me into someone else, I find peace in visiting big forests. At first glance, a forest might just look like rows of trees, but when I explore as my true self, I notice so many new details. I see how forest life shifts and grows over time, spot fresh fruit hanging from branches, and stumble across lovely patches of flowering bushes. Every visit feels full of interesting surprises.

Sometimes I reflect on how a world that tries to force me to conform still wants me to take in all its beauty. This makes me think of standing on high ground, like a mountain or a hill. I prefer rolling hills to tall mountains, since mountain peaks are often freezing and battered by strong winds. Big hills are usually covered in soft grass, and when I climb to the top, the clear view of open grassy land dotted with trees reminds me of what landscapes looked like long ago.

Staying true to who I am and living authentically in this world brings me so much joy. This idea sums up my whole perspective. Some people might disagree with Emerson’s statement, arguing it is boring or does not make sense, but to me it is completely logical. It perfectly captures how the world pressures people to conform, yet choosing to be yourself is the greatest accomplishment of all. That is exactly why I stand by Emerson’s words: being my true self is the best way to live in this world.

Taking classes from home is not a good choice for students, as traditional schools offer many benefits that remote learning cannot provide. While everyone learns in their own way, in-person classes are almost always the better option. Students can choose the learning environment that feels right for them, and regular school also lets them pick the subjects that interest them most. Attending a physical school gives students access to opportunities they simply won’t get at home: they can meet new people, join clubs, and get face-to-face help from their teachers whenever they need it.

One of the biggest advantages of in-person school is the chance to socialize. Not everyone wants to stay isolated and never interact with peers. Having someone you can talk to openly is really valuable, and going to school lets you meet hundreds of people and build new friendships. Consider the case of Generic_Name: she had to choose between homeschooling and regular classes, and picked the home option at first. She was excited to avoid early mornings, and things went well for the first few weeks as she adjusted to the new routine. But soon, she realized she had no friends and felt incredibly lonely. When she told her mom how she was feeling, her mom pointed out that she wouldn’t be struggling with loneliness if she had chosen traditional school instead. After thinking it over, Generic_Name decided switching to in-person classes was the best choice. When you go to regular school, you don’t have to feel isolated, and you’ll have plenty of chances to make friends.

Traditional schools also offer the chance to join clubs and extracurricular activities, something remote learning rarely provides. Public schools have all kinds of groups and hobbies for students to try, which help prepare them for life after graduation. Students can pick teams or clubs that match their interests: for example, a student who loves football can join their school’s team, which is only possible at a physical school. Being part of a school sports team could even lead to scholarships for bigger leagues down the line. Beyond that, clubs let students explore potential career paths, try new things, and gain hands-on experience that they can’t get through remote classes.

Some people argue that remote learning is better because it gives students time to work part-time jobs, stay out of trouble, or care for younger siblings at home. But students who attend in-person classes get direct access to teacher support, which is far more valuable. Not every student picks up new concepts quickly, and sometimes we need a little extra help from someone who understands the material well. One great thing about traditional schools is that teachers often stay after class to help students with difficult work. It’s true that paying attention in class can be hard when other students are noisy or the material is tricky, but teachers can go over your grades with you and give tailored advice on how to improve. Talking to a teacher face-to-face helps you understand better, as they can give detailed, step-by-step explanations.

To sum up, going to school lets students make friends, try new activities, and improve their grades with teacher support. While some people might prefer homeschooling, it’s clear that traditional school is often the better choice. School is a great way to get out of the house for a few hours each day, which many people appreciate rather than staying home all day. You can have fun with friends, and school lunchtimes are a unique experience that remote learning can’t offer. After-school activities also keep students out of trouble and help them figure out what path they want to take in life. Schools offer plenty of ways to have fun, not just through play, but through learning too.

Everyone has a talent or skill. In my case, Its music. Although my music skills are still improving, I would still consider it a talent or skill.

I've learned to play different instruments such as: the guitar, percussion, xylophone, and the violin, which is what i'm currently playing. At first I joined chorus in 1st grade and finished in 5th grade. I really enjoyed it ,so I chose to learn an instrument, which ended with me joining band. In band, I learned how to play the recorder. I played it from 2nd grade to 3rd grade. After learning the recorder I switch instruments to a xylophone, that played during 4th grade.

Since I didnt really like playing the xylophone, I chose to do percussion for 5th grade. I was also learning the guitar during 4th grade through 5th. when I entered middle school I decided to turn things around by choosing to do orchestra. I learned everything I had to know in 6th grade ,so I was ready to play the violin in 7th grade. I really felt passionate about the violin so I kept playing ,and still am ,and yet will continue until high school.

My music skills can be useful at times, for example: my parents once asked me to play a song for their wedding, they thought it was marvelous. Last year, I sang a song ,that I composed, for my sisters' birthday. She really enjoyed it. I like participating in music contests, concerts, etc. This year I went to New York for a violin concert, it was amazing.

My music skills have yet to improve, but until then I will continue trying new ways of music.

Students already have more than enough time in class as things stand! I am completely against the school board’s plan to extend the school day by adding extra hours. I’m not saying this only because I’m a student myself—this change would impact every learner in our school, not just me. For one, longer days would lead to worse behavior among students, since sitting in the same building for even more hours would leave everyone exhausted and frustrated. It would also hurt grades, because tired students simply can’t focus or work as effectively as they do when they’re well-rested. On top of that, if the school day was longer, students would have no time left to finish homework or study for upcoming quizzes and tests.

This plan doesn’t just hurt students, either. It would cause major problems for teachers and the school as a whole. Most teachers have their own families, and many have young children—lengthening the school day would mean they get home later and have less time to spend with their loved ones. Another big issue is that many students have regular appointments, just like I do.

For example, I visit my orthodontist monthly for morning appointments, and I already miss two or three classes each time. When I get back, I’m hit with a pile of missed assignments to make up. If the school day wasn’t extended, I could easily ask my orthodontist to move my appointments to the afternoon instead. Sick students would also be worse off: missing a single day with a longer schedule means even more makeup work than usual. The school would face extra costs too. They’d have to provide more food for students, use more paper and bathroom supplies, and print new student agendas with extra bathroom passes. Longer days would also lead to more conflicts and fights between students, since everyone would be more on edge from exhaustion. Worst of all, adding an hour and a half to the school day would mean we get out at the exact same time as elementary schools. That would put way more school buses on the road at once, leading to more car crashes and accidents.

Most students already wake up very early for school, myself included. Adding more hours would leave us completely drained—we wouldn’t be able to focus on lessons, and teachers would struggle to teach effectively when the whole class is tired. As you can see, extending the school day would hurt students, teachers, and the school in countless ways. The school board needs to rethink this proposal entirely. They should also listen to what students actually want: I know I’m not the only one who thinks this plan is a bad idea, since it affects everyone in the school community. Of course, some students might have different opinions, but that’s exactly why the board should hear from more people.

To sum up, the school board should not add extra hours to the school day, given all the negative consequences this would bring for students, teachers, and the school. Longer days wouldn’t just make students tired—they would also make it impossible to learn subjects as well as we do now. Teachers would suffer too, since they’d be more exhausted and more likely to get frustrated with students. This plan could also cause bigger conflicts across the school, leading to more fights and a need for extra breaks for students. When it comes to getting work done, is it better to tackle tasks alone or as part of a team? I firmly believe that working in a group offers far more benefits, for several key reasons.

My main arguments for this are simple: group members can support you when you get stuck, splitting up tasks saves time and reduces stress, and collaborating lets everyone pick up new knowledge about the topic. Now that I’ve outlined my core points, let me explain each one in more detail.

First, working with others means you never have to struggle through a problem alone. If you hit a roadblock, your teammates will usually step in to help. They’ll walk you through the issue until you fully grasp the concept, and often share multiple methods or tips to solve similar problems in the future. I saw this firsthand in math class recently: my teacher paired me with a friend for an assignment, and I couldn’t wrap my head around the core concept. I asked my friend for help, and she sat with me to explain the material step by step. She showed me several different ways to approach the problems, and without her support, I’d still be completely confused about what to do.

Another big advantage of group work is that you can split responsibilities among team members. When everyone has a clear, specific task, the whole project moves much faster. You don’t have to shoulder all the work yourself, which cuts down on stress and prevents burnout. I experienced this just last week in history class, where my teacher assigned me to a group with three other students. We divided the work evenly: I tracked down citations for all the information we used, Chloe researched the main topic details, Marcus found relevant images, and Sean located supporting videos. We wrapped up the entire project by the end of class, and even earned an A on the assignment.

The last key reason I prefer group work is that it helps everyone learn more about the topic at hand. Your teammates might come across information or ideas you hadn’t found on your own, which makes the material clearer for everyone and can even lead to new insights. This also pays off when it comes to tests or quizzes: since you’ve worked through the content with others, answered questions together, and picked up new details, you’re better prepared for assessments. This wraps up my final core argument for why group work beats working alone.

To recap, group work lets you learn more about the subject, saves you from doing all the work solo, and ensures you have support if you get stuck on a concept. These are the reasonsI think collaborating with others is far better than working alone every time. Teaming up with others gives you way more advantages than trying to handle everything by yourself, and it’s clearly the more beneficial option. I’ve laid out clear, valid reasons why I believe working in a group is better than working alone.

In daily life, everyone faces choices—some prefer to weigh options alone, while others turn to friends, family, or mentors for advice. Though many argue that seeking outside guidance leads to better choices, I believe making decisions independently brings far more benefits. People who decide for themselves build self-confidence and learn to take responsibility, and they are more likely to lead happier, more fulfilling lives down the line.

First, making your own choices helps you grow more confident and accountable. When you pick a path on your own, following through builds your belief in your own judgment, and you learn to own the outcome. Take a young adult who moves out of their childhood home, for example. They become fully responsible for their daily needs because they chose to live independently, which pushes them to handle challenges alone and grow more responsible. Another example is high school students picking their own courses. When they choose classes themselves, they gain confidence in their ability to judge what works best for them, and it helps them figure out what to study in college later.

Making your own decisions also leads to greater happiness. When you reach a goal you chose for yourself, the reward feels far more meaningful. If a student skips college to train as a professional soccer player and works hard to succeed, they will be happy in their career because they followed their own path. I have a personal example, too: when I was a sophomore, I picked next year’s classes to prepare for college, instead of taking easy courses others recommended. When I started those classes, I was glad I’d made that choice—they helped me a lot with my college prep. You end up happier when your choices match your own goals.

Some argue that seeking guidance is better because it prevents bad choices. I disagree. If you always rely on others to tell you what to do, the choices you make may not fit who you are, leaving you unhappy later. For instance, if your parents pressure you to become a doctor, and you go along with their plan, you may end up miserable in a job that doesn’t suit you. Relying on others too much can stop you from becoming a confident person.

In conclusion, making your own decisions helps you build self-confidence and responsibility, leading to a happier, more fulfilling life. When you choose your own path, you can achieve your goals and grow as a person. Everyone should trust their own judgment and take charge of their choices.

Schools and businesses should seriously look into switching to a four-day weekly schedule, as it helps cut down on energy use. Under this system, both schools and companies would operate for ten hours each day across the four working days.

For students, the extra two hours added to each school day mean more time to complete assignments and keep up with coursework. Those struggling with low grades can get the extra support they need during regular hours, instead of relying on after-school help. Teachers also benefit, as they will no longer need to stay late after classes end. With the extended daily time, educators can cover more material thoroughly, helping students learn more effectively.

The extra day off each week gives students valuable time to rest and recharge. They can spend more time with their families, and those with part-time jobs can pick up extra shifts to earn money they need. Students overwhelmed by heavy homework loads can use the free day to catch up, ensuring all tasks are finished on time. There is also room for hobbies, sports, or other extracurricular activities that they might not have time for otherwise.

Cutting one day off the weekly schedule also saves a significant amount of energy. Many natural resources, including water and electricity, are finite, so reducing unnecessary use helps preserve them for the future. A four-day week means schools use far less power overall. For large buildings like schools, electricity bills are a major expense, so this change would lead to big cost savings too.

For all these reasons, schools should switch to a four-day weekly schedule. This change cuts costs, conserves energy, and ensures that schools do not face energy shortages in the years to come.

Have you ever set a curfew for your teenage child? Do you believe such rules are necessary for young people? Ensuring teenagers stay safe is a top priority, particularly once the sun goes down. The world today is far more unpredictable than it was in past decades. Right now, a local city council is discussing whether to introduce a mandatory curfew for teenagers. If this rule passes, would any teen found outside after the set time be considered a lawbreaker? And do these curfews actually protect young people from harm, or do they unfairly limit their freedom?

Why is the city council even considering this curfew rule? There are several key reasons behind the debate. First, officials want to prevent teenagers from putting themselves in dangerous situations while they are still young and may not judge risks well. Second, they aim to shield young people from the many threats that exist in public spaces after dark. Finally, they hope to reduce risky behavior: many teens make poor choices, such as underage drinking or other activities that are not appropriate for their age. All these factors are driving the council’s discussion of a potential curfew.

If the council does approve the curfew, does that automatically mean every teenager out after hours is breaking the law? Public opinion on this is split, but I believe the answer depends entirely on the reason for being out. For example, teens traveling to or from work, dealing with an emergency, or accompanied by a responsible adult would not be violating the rule. They are not out unsupervised, so there is no real risk. However, if a teenager is out to meet friends, attend parties, or socialize without a valid reason, then yes, they would be breaking the law. So the answer is not a simple yes or no: it all comes down to the circumstances of why they are outside.

Do curfews actually keep teenagers out of trouble, or do they unfairly interfere with their daily lives? Most young people would argue the latter: they feel the rules limit their freedom and stop them from having fun with friends. But there are clear benefits to these rules. For one, curfews keep teens safe from unpredictable dangers that can arise after dark. Another key point is that many teenagers sneak out of their homes at night without telling their parents, which is never a safe choice. Teens need to ask themselves: is going out without permission really worth the risk? Even if you think nothing bad will happen, there is always a chance that something could go wrong. Young people should consider whether curfews are truly limiting their lives, or actually protecting them from harm.

The city council’s debate over a teenage curfew remains ongoing. While some residents believe the rule should become law, others oppose it. The core of the discussion is always the same: officials want to keep young people safe and prevent them from getting hurt or making bad choices while they are still young. As for whether being out after curfew counts as a crime, it comes down to context. Valid reasons like work, emergencies, or being with an adult do not count as violations, but going to parties or hanging out with friends without permission would. When it comes to the impact of these rules, most teenagers see them as an unfair interference in their lives. But many parents, and likely most officials, argue that the curfew is simply a way to keep young people safe, rather than putting them at unnecessary risk.

AVID is a super enjoyable school program for anyone who has a personal dream they want to reach. I say this for a few key reasons. First, it doesn’t just help you grow as a person, but it also pushes you to plan for college. Then there are the tutorials: these aren’t just there to check what you already know, but to help you get better in any of your classes. On top of that, you get to go on awesome, fun field trips that most other students don’t get to experience. Lastly, being in AVID feels like having a second family, no matter where you are.

In AVID, you learn to be responsible and hardworking. For example, we have weekly binder checks to make sure we stay organized, which is a skill that helps in all parts of life. It’s like a regular class, but everyone in AVID shares the same goal: we all have dreams we want to achieve, so we know we have to keep trying and never give up until we reach them. A lot of teenagers don’t care about college, but some of us do. If you start hanging out with the wrong crowd, it can drag you down really far, like sinking to the bottom of the ocean where you can’t climb back up to where you were before. I’m not saying you can’t be friends with those people at all, but in my opinion, you shouldn’t get too wrapped up in their lives the way your other friends might.

Tutorials are a huge part of AVID. They show your teachers and classmates how much you know, how determined you are, and how much effort you put in. You have to stand in front of your group and explain what you’re struggling with, which also lets you learn from your peers, almost like sharing your knowledge back and forth. Tutorials also show off your personality: if you’re not shy, you’ll speak up in front of the group. Some people prefer to stay quiet, keep to themselves, and just listen during tutorials instead of talking.

We also get to go on field trips that most middle and high school students never get the chance to take. We visit colleges and learn all about them, which helps us understand what college life is like. The trips are fun too: we get guided tours around campuses, and we meet new people while we’re there. It’s such a cool opportunity to do things that not all students are allowed to do. One of the most fun parts of AVID is that we do fundraisers to pay for trips to Kings Dominion. When you get there, you feel like you’ve really earned it, because you’ve been working hard all year with no big fun breaks. That reward keeps you motivated to keep going, even when you’re tired. For me, my niece is the person who pushes me to work hard. AVID works the same way: you put in hard work doing tutorials and taking Cornell notes, and at the end of the year, you get to go have fun with your friends, ride roller coasters, and celebrate everything you’ve accomplished. It’s such a great experience.

Most students in AVID, including me, would agree that the program feels like a family. We all do activities that everyone enjoys, no one talks badly about anyone else, and even though we all come from different places around the world, no one is mean to each other. We stick together, and we all learn the same things. If a fellow AVID student feels like giving up, the rest of us make sure they don’t, because we’re a family. Whenever we’re feeling down, we always say our motto: 'dream, believe, achieve.' This program helps you do better in school, but it also makes you proud of yourself, and makes your parents and family proud too.

To sum up, I think AVID is such an enjoyable activity because you get to meet so many new people, and you might even find your best friend there. You get to do cool activities and join special programs that other students don’t have access to. It’s also like a family, so if your home life isn’t very supportive, AVID can fill that gap. You can be your true self there, no need to pretend to be someone you’re not. It’s a huge opportunity to be part of this program, so you should take a risk and join. You never know, it could lead you in a really positive direction, help you become a great person, and achieve the life you’ve always wanted.

Many people claim a positive mindset is the secret to a successful life, but that is not true. The real key to achieving your goals is putting in consistent hard work. Having an upbeat attitude does not automatically mean you will finish high school with an advanced diploma, land a decent job after university, or even reach the targets you set for yourself. For example, plenty of students spend years studying a degree they dislike, only choosing it because it promises better job prospects later. None of that happens just because you think happy thoughts. To build a successful life, you have to put in effort, study regularly, and step outside your comfort zone to take on challenges.

Hard work and persistence are what actually help you reach your goals. Take a common goal, like buying a new car within the next year. If you only rely on a positive attitude, you will be disappointed. You need to meet plenty of practical requirements: you have to find affordable car insurance, pay monthly premiums, and cover the cost of the car itself if you buy a new model. All of this means you will likely need to work extra hours, which will cut into your free time and leave you with less money to spend on other things than before. The point is simple: just feeling optimistic will not magically put a brand-new car in your driveway. You need to put in real effort to earn the money and handle the responsibilities that come with owning a car.

Can a positive attitude alone get you an advanced high school diploma? Absolutely not. Earning that qualification takes 12 full years of consistent work, not just good vibes. It is unrealistic to say you stayed positive every single day of those 12 years. Think about the days you were sick at school, with no one available to pick you up because your family was out, and you had to tough it out until the final bell. Were your thoughts all sunny and upbeat then? Probably not—you were just focused on getting through the day. Everyone has moments where they want to quit everything and move to a remote island to escape the pressure of modern society. A positive attitude is not the key to success in school, and it is not the key to success in life either.

University students go through years of struggle that no amount of positivity can fix. Many study a major they do not even enjoy, hoping that once they graduate, they will find a well-paying job to support their family. They work part-time jobs, pull all-nighters, write hundreds of essays, finish homework at midnight, and struggle through group projects. Sometimes they cannot even afford to pay for the next semester’s tuition. All of this hard work is what paves the way to a successful life, not just a cheerful mindset. After graduating, they still have to hunt for jobs, pay back student loans to the bank, and prove in interviews that they are more qualified than dozens of other candidates.

To sum up, a successful life comes from actually reaching your goals: graduating high school, finishing university, and landing a job that fits your skills and needs. Not everyone gets to achieve this, because not everyone has the chance to attend high school or university. Many people spend their days hoping for a miracle, working tirelessly and dreaming of winning the lottery so they never have to work again. But relying on a positive attitude alone will never get you anywhere near the success you want. Real, consistent hard work is the only thing that delivers results.

I believe that real self-esteem grows out of actual achievement, not empty praise.

To start, praising students for assignments they didn't put full effort into hurts their long-term growth. If a student knows they didn't try their hardest on a task, but still gets positive feedback, they might start to think they don't need to work harder next time. That mindset actually drags down their self-esteem in the long run, because they never learn to value their own hard work.

There is a big difference between praising genuine effort and praising lazy work. If a student works hard on a difficult paper, feels confident they did their best, and gets recognized for that, it builds real self-esteem. They know their achievement is earned, not given away for free. Even if the assignment was challenging, they pushed through instead of taking shortcuts. That desire to improve, rather than stay stuck at the same level, is exactly what helps self-esteem grow.

Another key point is that teachers have a responsibility to help students get better. If a student turns in work they know is below their ability, and the teacher still praises it, the student will assume they don't need to try harder. Over time, this leads to lower self-esteem, because they never feel the pride that comes from actually achieving something difficult. Good teachers should not hand out praise for lazy work. Instead, they should talk to the student one-on-one: tell them their work is okay, but not their best, and remind them that you know they can do better. That kind of honest feedback pushes students to grow, rather than letting them stay comfortable with low effort.

My counterclaim is that teachers should not let students get away with lazy work. I say this because sometimes students might think their teachers don’t pay attention to them, or don’t care about the work they turn in. Even so, if a student approaches a teacher with a problem, the teacher will remember that student and make a point to check in on their work more often.

In conclusion, true self-esteem does not come from praise for effortless assignments. If teachers praise students for low-quality work, that becomes the level students stay at, since they got positive feedback for putting in little effort. This means teachers leave students with no desire to improve or expand on skills like writing.

Sincerely,

Seeking multiple opinions helps people make smarter decisions because they gain new viewpoints, access more choices, and discover alternative solutions to problems. Ignoring the value of getting more than one input can lead to seriously bad outcomes.

First, hearing different perspectives from others is a key reason to seek multiple opinions. Take Generic_Name, for example, who went to the mall one day but could not find a specific store she really wanted to visit. She stopped a man and asked for directions, and he told her it was on the second floor. When she got there, though, the store was nowhere to be seen. She asked another person instead, who explained it was actually on the first floor, right next to the ice cream shop. Generic_Name went back down, grabbed an ice cream, and easily found the store. She was so relieved she had asked a second person—if she had only trusted the first man’s directions, she would never have found the store at all.

Second, having more than one opinion gives you more reliable information to work with. Imagine Generic_Name had just moved to New York for her first day of high school, and neither she nor her parents knew where the school was located. Her parents suggested she walk toward the school and follow other students her age. She spotted a girl with blue eyes and brown hair, and thought, “She looks like a high schooler,” so she ran up to introduce herself. The girl confirmed she was also headed to high school, so they walked together. When they arrived at the building, though, Generic_Name realized her classroom was in a completely different part of the school, and she was totally lost again. Instead of trusting just one person’s directions, she stopped several people in the hallway to ask where she needed to go. Everyone gave her the same answer, so she knew exactly where to go. If she had only asked one person, that person might have been wrong, and she would have ended up in the wrong classroom.

Finally, seeking multiple opinions can help solve urgent problems when they come up. For instance, Generic_Name once had a sleepover with two close friends. They decided to cook food in the kitchen, even though her mom had warned them not to. While they were having fun preparing snacks, the oven suddenly caught fire. Generic_Name panicked—she had no idea what to do, shouting, “AHHHHH! WHAT SHOULD I DO?” One friend told her to call 911 immediately, while the other insisted she just throw water on the fire, calling her dramatic. Generic_Name thought calling emergency services was the smarter choice, so she did that. The firefighters arrived quickly and put out the fire, solving the problem before it got worse.

Overall, seeking multiple opinions helps people make better choices by giving them access to different viewpoints, more options to pick from, and new ways to solve problems. Generic_Name found the store she was looking for, got to her correct classroom on her first day of school, and kept her house from burning down. It is easy to see that very bad things could have happened if she had only relied on a single opinion each time.

We’ve all heard the saying that you should never judge a book by its cover, and this is especially true when it comes to people. In this context, a person’s “cover” is not just their physical looks, but the first impression they make on others. Just like a book’s cover might not reflect the story inside, first impressions often do not match the reality of who a person really is. It is only once you start “reading” — that is, getting to know someone — that you realize appearances can be deceiving. There are several key factors that shape the first impression we form of someone: their personality, the situation they are in, and how they choose to present themselves. All of these can make first impressions one of the worst ways to judge a person.

A person’s personality plays a huge role in the first impression they give off. Everyone is unique, but when it comes to first meetings, a lot of how others see you comes down to whether you are shy or outgoing. I met my best friend when I moved schools during my junior year of high school. Before I got to know her, she barely spoke to me or anyone else in our classes, and I assumed she was a bit strange. Later, I realized I was exactly the same way — I rarely talked to new people because of my own shy personality. I knew that once I warmed up to someone, I would drop my guard and show my real self, so I guessed she might be the same. Over time, we started talking more each day, our friendship grew, and I discovered she was not odd at all. Just like me, she was actually outgoing, but her shyness made her seem quiet and reserved at first. For people like us, shyness creates a polite, distant front when meeting new people. My initial impression of her could not have been more wrong: someone who seems shy at first might actually be very outgoing, they just feel uncomfortable putting that side of themselves on display right away. This makes first impressions of shy people almost always inaccurate.

First impressions are also unreliable because you never know what situation the other person is dealing with. When you meet someone new, you have no way of knowing what kind of day they have had, what struggles they are facing, or what disappointments they might be processing. They could have recently lost a loved one, or be a new student trying to navigate unfamiliar routines and daily stress. All of these circumstances can put up a wall between them and others, and making a good first impression is probably the last thing on their mind. For example, on the first day of my senior year, I rushed to my first class even though I had plenty of time to get there. When I walked into the room, all I cared about was finding a seat quickly, whether it was next to someone or not. At lunchtime, I sat alone and ate fast so I could get to my next class early. I was so focused on being on time, finding a seat, and getting everything right that I never even thought about making a good impression on my classmates. As a result, they probably thought I was nervous and unfriendly, but really my behavior had nothing to do with my personality — it was all because of the stressful situation I was in that day.

There are countless factors that shape how we perceive someone when we meet them for the first time. A person’s natural personality, the situation they are currently in, and the way they happen to present themselves all influence the assumptions we make about them. Because these impressions are based on surface-level information, they are often incorrect. If all friendships were formed based on first meetings, far fewer people would have close friends. First impressions are almost always a poor way to judge someone, because you only get a clear sense of who they really are once you take the time to get to know them. Only then can you understand their true character and values, rather than relying on a superficial first impression or a metaphorical book cover.

All students look forward to having an amazing summer break. While many enjoy the long summer holiday because they can put school worries aside for a while, others argue for shortening the summer break and extending winter, spring, and fall breaks instead. Both sides have valid points, but I firmly support keeping a long summer vacation with shorter breaks during the other seasons. My two key reasons for this are that short breaks make it impossible for students to make long-term plans, and frequent short breaks disrupt effective learning routines.

First, short breaks leave students unable to make long-term plans for their time off. Many students dream of traveling to other countries or taking extended trips, but with a short break, they’re constantly stressed about upcoming schoolwork and assignments even while away. It’s also frustrating to rush through sightseeing when you don’t have enough time, leaving you wishing you had more days to explore. For students with family living in other countries, visits are rare, so they want to make the most of the time they have together. They might not see each other again for a year, or even a decade, so they’d rather stay for as long as possible. If the break is too short, they have to cut the visit early, which stops them from fully enjoying the time with their loved ones. For these reasons, I believe a long summer break is far better.

Another key reason is that having short bursts of school followed by frequent breaks is not an effective way to learn. Think about professional athletes: every sport has a season, and players and coaches focus fully on their duties during that time. They don’t take 3 or 4-week breaks in the middle of the season because that would disrupt their rhythm and performance. The same logic applies to students. For example, someone learning a musical instrument needs to practice consistently. Practicing for 10 hours one day and then not touching the instrument for a week won’t help them improve at all. Even if practice sessions are shorter, using the instrument every day builds habit and helps them get better over time. While it can be tough to adjust back to school after a long break, it’s much more effective for students to settle into a steady school rhythm for most of the year, rather than switching between short school terms and short breaks constantly. That’s why I support a long summer vacation.

Supporters of shorter summer breaks do have valid points: not every student learns the same way. Some work very hard for a short period, then take a break, and that method works for them. But this approach has a big downside: students are likely to forget what they learned during the break, because they crammed so much math, science, English, and history content into a short time. Even if these students get good grades from cramming for tests or assignments, they usually have to relearn the material again soon after. For most learners, a long summer break is better than a short one.

As I’ve mentioned, summer break is the highlight of the school year for most students, and nearly everyone makes plans for how to spend it. Before summer starts, some students worry about the upcoming break and argue for shortening it to extend other seasonal breaks. While that’s not a terrible idea, people need to remember that longer winter or fall breaks would get in the way of their summer plans. They should also realize that a longer summer break gives them far more opportunities to do the things they love. How you use your time is up to you, but a longer summer break opens up far more possibilities.

We develop our personality traits through two main paths. The first is actively selecting the qualities we want to have, shaping our character ourselves. The second is having our traits formed by outside factors we can’t influence, leaving us with no say in the matter. Picking our own traits is by far the more logical approach, as it fits with how most people are able to manage their own feelings.

Personality traits come in all kinds: some people are cheerful, others are lively or amusing, and there are countless other possibilities. These qualities mostly grow out of the choices we make and the actions we take, which in turn shape how we respond to different feelings. While we can usually keep our emotions in check, there are moments when they get the better of us and we lose control.

There are certain traits, though, that feel completely out of our hands. They surface on their own, often because we’re not able to regulate ourselves in the moment. Strong feelings like rage, deep sadness, or even depression can strip us of control entirely. When that happens, we might act in ways we never would otherwise, sometimes doing real harm. This is why personality traits can be either a force for good or a source of trouble, depending on the situation.

Public opinion on this is split. Some people argue we have the power to pick our own traits. Those who take this view say that when they act, they feel in charge of their emotions, which helps them make choices that work best for them. Others insist our traits are entirely beyond our control. They explain that emotions just surface on their own, especially when they’re working or handling daily tasks, and they have no way to stop them. They add that these unexpected feelings are almost always negative, like anger or sadness.

There are endless debates about how personality traits work, but the truth is they are not good or bad by nature. It all comes down to whether the person can manage them. Even people who struggle to keep their emotions in check can use small, simple strategies to stop feelings from taking over. That is why taking charge of your own personality traits is so different from letting outside forces shape who you are.

While year-round schools do schedule more frequent breaks throughout the academic year, they cut back significantly on summer vacation time. This setup ends up creating higher stress levels, shorter summer breaks, and reduced earning opportunities for both students and the wider community.

The first major problem with year-round schooling is increased stress. For students, a big source of pressure is deciding what to wear each day. Many want to stand out by never repeating outfits, so they feel forced to buy new clothes even if their closets are already full. Teachers face stress too: they have to plan lessons for a longer school year, and handle far more assignments to grade with no long summer break to catch up.

A second downside is the much shorter summer vacation. Most year-round school calendars only give students 3 to 4 weeks off in summer, which is far less than many families want. That short window makes it impossible to take long trips to other countries. Parents are also impacted: many responsible caregivers won’t leave their children behind to travel alone, so they miss out on summer trips too.

The third issue is reduced earnings. Students can’t take on summer jobs when they only have a month off, so they make far less than they would with a traditional 3-month summer break. This loss of income isn’t limited to students: governments also lose out, as they have to cover the cost of electricity, water, and other utilities for school buildings that stay open year-round instead of closing for summer.

Supporters of year-round schooling often point out that students get more frequent breaks throughout the year. However, this doesn’t make up for the drastic cut to summer vacation time. Another common argument is that shorter breaks stop students from forgetting what they learned. But studying non-stop without a long summer break just adds more stress, which harms learning in the long run.
