Should schools restrict how many extracurricular activities students are allowed to take part in? While schools may need to step in under very specific conditions, their overall control over this should be minimal. Families should be the ones to decide whether a student stays in or leaves extracurricular activities. This only changes if a student begins to fail classes, their parents ask the school to withdraw them from some activities, or if their attendance at activity meetings becomes poor. In those cases, the school can help determine the next steps for the student.

First, I believe there should be clear boundaries for how many activities a student can enroll in, but the final choice should always lie with the student and their family, as they know the student’s schedule best. If a family notices their child has little time left for homework or studying for tests, they should discuss the issue with the student and listen to their perspective. Whether the family decides to let the student keep doing the activities is their call. However, if they choose to pull the student out of any extracurriculars, they must inform the student’s guidance counselor and the person in charge of each activity.

If a student starts failing classes or their grades keep dropping across most subjects, their guidance counselor should meet with them to find out the cause. If too many extracurricular activities are the problem, the counselor should discuss with the student which activities they can pause until their grades improve. This approach motivates students to understand that staying in extracurriculars depends on keeping their academic performance up.

Finally, if a student has poor or inconsistent attendance at activity meetings, they should not be allowed to keep participating. Students should only be allowed to miss up to five meetings per month without facing any penalties. If they exceed this limit, the activity leader should notify their parents of the reason, and the student can be kicked out of the club. Barring other issues, the student may also be suspended from attending meetings for a set period of time instead of being fully removed.

In conclusion, schools should have almost no say in whether a student joins or stays in extracurricular activities. To put it simply, families hold the most power in this decision, unless a student’s grades are dropping or they start failing classes, their meeting attendance is poor, or they stop showing up to activities entirely.

There is ongoing discussion about whether students should be allowed to use their phones in class for school-related tasks. Opponents argue that as soon as students get their hands on their devices, they will start messaging friends instead of focusing. Supporters, on the other hand, claim that using phones for educational purposes helps students complete their assignments more effectively. I strongly disagree with this positive view: I believe allowing phones in classrooms will only distract students, make them ignore teachers, and cause them to stop putting effort into their schoolwork.

The first major issue with classroom phone use is that it pulls students’ attention away from their work. Instead of focusing on lessons, many will put on music, scroll through social media apps like Snapchat, Instagram, or Facebook. For me, the moment a teacher asks the class to take out our phones, my first reaction is to text a friend, not open a school-related app. I have found that using my phone during class makes me lazy and less willing to finish assignments. When I leave my phone in my bag, I feel more responsible about completing both homework and in-class tasks. I saw this problem happen during a group project last year: one of my partners spent the whole work period listening to music on his phone instead of contributing. When it was time to present our project to the class, the rest of us knew exactly what to say, but he had no idea what our project was even about. He ended up failing that assignment entirely.

Another key problem is that students will stop listening to their teachers entirely. If phones are allowed, even I would be tempted to watch my favorite TV show during lessons instead of paying attention. This creates a huge issue: teachers will waste time repeating instructions that no one is listening to, and they will quickly get frustrated. I doubt many students would focus on the teacher at all, unless their parents pressure them to get good grades. Without that outside pressure, I can say for sure that most students would ignore everything the teacher says. When students don’t pay attention to class instructions, they are far more likely to fail their courses.

A third reason schools should ban phones is that they make students avoid doing their work altogether. If I know I can use my phone during class, I will put off assignments because I feel too lazy to start them. When students skip homework and in-class tasks, they earn failing grades, which can hurt their chances of success after high school. I learned this the hard way when I was a junior in chemistry class. I was using my phone during a lab experiment, and I accidentally spilled a chemical on the device. It stopped working immediately, and when I told my parents what happened, they were furious. They pointed out that my bad grades in the class were directly linked to my habit of using my phone during labs, calling me irresponsible for letting my device distract me from schoolwork.

To sum up, allowing cell phones in classrooms is a bad idea because most students will end up avoiding work entirely. Many young people are addicted to their devices, and having phones in class only makes it harder to focus or complete tasks. Phones are not beneficial for learning, as they make students lose the ability to focus and work independently. Phones do not help students get smarter; instead, paying attention to teachers and putting effort into schoolwork is what builds responsibility and academic success. Education is the key to success, and holding on to that key means committing to hard work, not getting distracted by phones.

While many students hope to graduate a year early to jump straight into college or the workforce, there are strong reasons why high school should remain a four-year requirement. Teenagers need time to grow and mature, and mandating four full years of high school supports this. Here is why this rule is necessary.

First, high school prepares young people to handle the challenges of adult life. Plenty of students need the full four years to get their mindset ready for their future plans. Finishing in just three years would force them to cram all required coursework into a shorter period, leaving no space for sports or other after-school activities they enjoy. Instead of having a well-rounded high school experience, they would have to pour all their energy into simply passing their classes.

Second, the four-year timeline helps students build independence. Over four years, they learn to balance schoolwork with after-school activities, which teaches useful time management skills. They also grow more reliable, as they practice completing tasks on schedule, which boosts their self-confidence. If they rush to finish in three years, they have no time to take breaks. Without adequate rest, they will struggle to meet all the expectations placed on them.

Some might argue that students who graduate in three years still have enough knowledge to take on the real world. However, those who complete all four years will have a much clearer sense of what they want to do once high school ends. In conclusion, students should stay for the full four years to gain a better understanding of what lies ahead.

I believe the school principal should choose to let students use their phones during lunch and other scheduled break times, rather than banning all phones from campus entirely. Most students now own their own mobile devices, and plenty of us need to reach our parents, guardians, or other family members for various reasons.

I told her we were stuck on campus, I wasn’t sure when we’d be allowed to leave, and I’d update her as soon as I knew more. That quick message gave my family peace of mind, and I wouldn’t have been able to share that info at all if phones were banned entirely from school grounds.

Permitting phone use during breaks is a smart move for another reason too: if students know they can check messages and chat with friends or family as soon as class ends, they’ll be less tempted to pull out their phones during lessons. This would help improve student grades, since fewer people would be distracted by their devices when they’re supposed to be focusing on the teacher and class material. On top of that, students would appreciate being able to use their phones openly during breaks without fear of getting in trouble or having to hide their devices.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once wrote, "To be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment." I completely agree with this statement. When people pressure you to become someone you’re not, staying true to who you are can feel incredibly difficult. Back in 8th grade, a person I considered a close friend pushed me to change my personality. They told me I wasn’t cool enough to hang out with them anymore, and at first, I blamed myself for not fitting in. Over time, though, I realized that real friends never demand you change who you are, no matter what. Staying true to yourself is easily one of the toughest challenges a person can face. This is often because you might be too shy, doubt yourself, or fear how others willjudge you.

I always hated thinking about myself because I never believed I was good enough for anyone, or capable of achieving anything. I kept all my feelings locked away inside, never telling anyone how I really felt. At one point, I even thought about killing myself, but I was too scared to actually try anything. To cope, I acted like everything was fine, even tricking myself into thinking I was happy, but that didn’t last. Now that I’m in 11th grade, I’ve met someone very special—my current girlfriend—who makes me feel truly happy whenever I’m with her. Every day, I think about how lucky I am to have met her. Ralph Waldo Emerson’s words ring truer than ever to me now: "To be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment." As an individual, I agree with his quote because in this world, not everyone wants to see you succeed in your efforts.

Students gain clear advantages when they take school courses from home rather than attending in-person classes, as they can move through material at a speed that suits them. They no longer need to wake up early in the morning, which means they avoid feeling exhausted before the day even starts. When students are too tired to focus, they rarely complete their assignments properly. With online learning, students can work on tasks whenever they have time, so they never have to rush to submit incomplete work before a class session ends. This setup is also helpful for learners who fall seriously ill and need to miss weeks of in-person classes, as it lets them keep up with their coursework without falling behind. Schools also do not need to worry about snow days disrupting the academic schedule when classes are held online. Another perk is that students can stay in the comfort of their homes, with no need to travel or move between classrooms all day. Without classmates to chat with during lessons, students often find it easier to concentrate on their work. It also supports students who often miss in-person classes, as they can do their schoolwork from home rather than skipping school entirely and falling behind. Since they are more likely to complete all their tasks, students often earn higher grades with online learning. If they struggle to understand a topic, getting help is simple: they can look up explanations online or ask a family member at home for support. Students can also take short breaks whenever they need to, so they do not get worn out from working for long periods. Completing schoolwork online also helps learners build useful computer skills that will serve them well later. They often access higher quality learning materials this way, which benefits them in the long term. Another plus is that students can show their parents finished assignments right away, so they can spend their free time as they wish afterwards. Most students rarely share updates about their in-school work with their families, so this makes a big difference. This system makes life easier for people who dislike attending school in person or struggle to wake up early in the mornings. It also saves time for both students and teachers, as they no longer need to spend the entire day on school grounds. More people may grow to enjoy school when classes are online, since they can complete work at any time of day as long as it is submitted by the deadline that same day.

Modern tools and digital systems let people complete all sorts of tasks without needing in-person contact, and this change has only brought good things. Tech keeps making everyday life simpler for everyone, and it also gives us a glimpse of what the world might look like a few years from now. Some people ask why this progress could ever be a bad thing, since all developers are really trying to do is make our daily routines less stressful. Take ride-hailing apps as an example: if you need to get somewhere quickly but don’t have your own transport, you can just open an app, share your live location and the address of your destination, and a driver will come pick you up. Technology is amazing, and it seems to get better and more useful with every passing day.

Smartphones today have apps for almost every possible need. Imagine you’re at home, starving, but you really don’t feel like going out to get food. You can just download an app like Grubhub, which will bring meals right to your door so you never have to skip a meal. Grubhub is a food delivery service that partners with restaurants all over, so you can order from almost any place you like. All you need to do is pick the food you want, confirm the restaurant’s location for pickup, and enter your home address so the delivery driver knows where to drop your order off. It’s that simple—your phone handles the whole process with just a few taps on the screen. Most of these apps are free to download, too; you only pay for the food itself, which makes sense because very few things in life are truly free.

Computers are another huge part of modern technology. Desktops and laptops are used every single day for school, work, and countless other tasks. For students especially, computers make it easy to do research and find information you might not have known before. Laptops are just as useful, if not more so: they’re portable, foldable computers that you can take anywhere, which is perfect for people who travel often or work remotely. Laptops keep improving, too—now there are touchscreen models, and even ones that fold all the way back into tablet mode. It’s wild to think about how much they’ve changed, and it makes you wonder what tech will look like just a few years from now. All these advances are getting us ready for the future of technology.

Technology makes our lives easier little by little, every single day. Without it, I wouldn’t even be able to complete this test, and I wouldn’t be able to contact emergency services quickly if I were ever in danger. For me, tech is nothing but a force for good, and I can never see it becoming a negative thing. We rely on technology to keep us informed about what’s happening in the world around us, and that’s a really important part of modern life. Tech is useful now, and it will stay useful for as long as people keep using it.

When it comes to handling school tasks, students can choose to work independently or collaborate with peers. I firmly believe that group work offers far more benefits for learners.

Take my friend Generic_Name: he’s more than capable of doing schoolwork alone, yet even he has struggled with concepts that only clicked after getting help from others. I’m also confident working on projects solo, but I’ve found that other people’s input always makes my work better.

I’ve seen clear proof of how useful group work is. Generic_Name was always one of the smartest students in our class, regularly topping the grades. But even he couldn’t manage every task alone. Once, our teacher assigned a project due that same week. Generic_Name decided to do it entirely by himself. When he handed it in, he was shocked to learn he’d failed. He couldn’t figure out why, so the teacher pulled him aside later: he’d misunderstood the assignment prompt entirely. When he asked how to make up the points, the teacher assigned a new project two weeks later, with one rule: he had to work with a partner this time.

Generic_Name followed the advice, and asked a classmate to team up with him. When the project was due, he was nervous since he rarely worked with others. To his surprise, they got a perfect score. The teacher explained why: when multiple people share ideas, it’s easier to spot gaps in understanding. If one person misses a key detail, someone else in the group will catch it, making the final work far clearer.

Another experience that convinced me happened in high school, with a two-part project. First, we all did the first section alone. When we finished, the teacher told us to pick partners—I chose Generic_Name. We compared our solo papers; even though they were on the same topic, they were totally different. Then we had to write a new paper together on the same subject. After everyone finished both parts, the teacher had us pass papers to the right, so each person had three: two solo papers, and one group effort. We voted for the one that made the most sense. Every single person picked the group-written paper. When asked why no one chose the solo ones, students said those only had one perspective, so they felt incomplete.

Some argue that working alone is better, but Generic_Name and I learned you need multiple viewpoints to build a strong argument. If I’d kept working alone forever, my way of thinking would be very different now—and not in a good way. The same goes for Generic_Name. Thanks to learning teamwork skills and how to listen to others’ perspectives, we can now make decisions with input from others instead of doing it all alone.

I recommend talking to your teacher about assigning more group projects—you’ll be surprised how much you learn. Ask your parents how these skills apply to the real world too; you’ll be shocked by how often you use them, and how much easier they make your daily life. When you don’t have to make every decision by yourself, even tough choices feel way less stressful.

While some schools push for remote learning where students study from home, many others argue that in-person schooling brings far more benefits to learners. To start, students who attend physical classes can access a broader range of subjects than those taking virtual lessons. If all students switched to home learning, there would be no need for on-site teachers and support staff at school buildings.

In-person schooling also allows students to cover more material across different subjects. When learners study at home, they often struggle to focus on their assignments. It is easy to get distracted by phones, television, or other electronic devices, and there is rarely anyone there to monitor their progress. Students need teachers not just to deliver lessons, but to guide, educate, and encourage them to stay engaged with their learning. As is clear, attending school in person offers far more value to students.

Beyond that, if students stop attending school in person, countless jobs for teachers and school staff would disappear. Entire communities rely on these roles, so widespread remote learning would cause major job losses. Students also benefit from building personal relationships with their teachers and school staff, something virtual classes cannot provide. Face-to-face instruction lets teachers connect with students directly, which leads to a higher quality education. When students learn on site, there are always trained staff available to support them, and this setup delivers better academic results overall.

Some people argue that remote learning is the better choice, claiming that virtual classes offer students more flexibility and learning opportunities. However, there are just as many who believe in-person schooling is superior. Schools are designed to help students master a wide variety of subjects, and learners who attend physical classes consistently perform better academically. The structured environment of a school building supports deeper, more effective learning than studying alone at home.

For all these reasons, students should attend school in person. Schools exist to help young people learn across all subject areas, and on-site learning delivers clear benefits for learners. Keeping students in physical classrooms also ensures that teachers and support staff keep their jobs. Most importantly, learning directly from a teacher face-to-face makes a huge difference: having someone there to explain concepts, answer questions, and guide you through material helps students learn far more effectively.

Modern technology brings both major benefits and serious drawbacks. While some tools make our lives easier, others cause real harm to individuals and society. We might wonder if we now rely on tech so much that it’s essential for daily life, or if we’ve just grown too lazy to handle basic tasks without it. My view is that when technology replaces face-to-face human interaction, it damages people’s lives in three key ways: it triggers isolation and depression, makes people lose touch with reality, and hurts both physical and mental health. On the whole, tech often brings more harm than good in these areas.

First, tech-driven isolation and depression are a growing problem, and having both at once makes the situation even worse. Social media is a major culprit here: countless young people face cyberbullying online, which leaves many feeling deeply upset and hopeless. In some cases, these kids withdraw completely, skipping school and avoiding friends or family. Video games are another issue. Many people love gaming, but some get so absorbed that they stop noticing they’re cutting themselves off from the people around them. Almost everyone now owns a smartphone, and it’s common to see people staring at their screens all day, never stepping outside or interacting with others in person. This constant reliance on devices has a huge impact on mental wellbeing, often leading directly to depression.

Another major issue is that heavy tech use can make people lose their grip on reality. The internet makes it easy for bad actors to manipulate others, especially young children. Kids spend hours watching TV and YouTube videos, and most are very trusting of what they see online. False information spreads quickly: children might believe fake claims, or even be brainwashed by biased content. Adults are not immune either. For example, many conspiracy theories claim governments use advanced tech to brainwash the public, and plenty of people fall for these unproven ideas. Even video games can blur the line between fiction and reality. Some young people play so much that they start to think the actions they take in games are possible, or even acceptable, in real life.

On top of this, as technology keeps advancing, the risks to our physical and mental health only grow. Eye doctors warn that spending hours every day on screens damages your eyesight over time. Tech also changes people’s personalities: many try to copy influencers or online personalities they see, altering how they dress or even act, sometimes in ways that don’t fit their real lives. There’s also the danger of copying harmful content. Plenty of people watch videos of others doing extremely dangerous stunts, then try to copy them. These attempts almost always fail, leaving people with serious injuries that send them to the hospital.

To be fair, technology does have genuine benefits. It can save lives in medical emergencies, and advanced tools help countries win wars. Tech makes daily tasks far more efficient, simplifying life so people have less stress than they used to. There’s no doubt that technological progress could reshape the world for the better. But these positives come with big risks. Tech devices can malfunction at any time, sometimes leading to fatal accidents. Many people assume tech will keep making life easier, but it often does the opposite. If we let machines handle every task for us, we will stop getting the physical exercise we need, and our health will decline rapidly. We also can’t ignore the damage tech does to the environment. Manufacturing and using digital devices creates huge amounts of pollution, destroying the planet we call home.

All in all, technology is causing terrible harm to us, even if we don’t notice it until we stop to look at how it’s changed our lives. My core belief is that replacing in-person human connection with tech leads to overwhelmingly negative results. It cuts people off from the real world, triggers isolation and depression, and does serious damage to both physical and mental health. We can choose to ignore these problems, but technology is here to stay, whether we like it or not.

If you had to select one lesson to teach elementary school students, would you pick math, since many kids enjoy working with numbers, or science, given how much they love hands-on experiments? I would absolutely choose science, as we encounter scientific concepts in our daily lives constantly, from flipping a light switch to tossing a ball into the air. Beyond that, most students find science the most enjoyable subject, thanks to all the experiments it includes. The main reasons I would teach a science lesson are that it is engaging, straightforward to teach, and applies to everyday life more than any other subject.

First, science is an incredibly fun subject to teach, for both kids and adults. The biggest reason it is entertaining is the wide variety of hands-on experiments students can do. For instance, if you want to explain kinetic and potential energy, you can design a simple experiment involving throwing a ball to demonstrate how energy shifts between the two forms. Another reason science is enjoyable is that it is accessible to everyone. When one student conducts an experiment, the whole class can participate by watching and noting what happens. Finally, science lessons are the most fun to plan because they encourage collaboration and sharing observations. If your class does an egg drop challenge, students can compare their designs with peers across the school, learning from both their own mistakes and other people’s successes. All these elements make science a joy to teach, as it revolves around interactive experiments rather than passive learning.

Second, science is by far the easiest subject to teach to students and even adults. Unlike other subjects, it does not require constant memorization of abstract rules. For example, English classes often ask students to memorize word roots, and math requires drilling formulas until they stick. With science, you only need to learn key terms, and you are ready to go. Another factor that makes science simple to teach is that experiments are easy to follow if students pay close attention. If you watch an experiment closely, you will grasp every step, whereas math often requires repeated practice before a concept clicks. Third, science works well for visual learners because it involves drawing diagrams, which is often easier to understand than rote memorization. If students struggle to follow verbal explanations, you can sketch out a process for them to make it clear. This approach works especially well in science, as the subject relies heavily on both drawing and hands-on testing. In short, science is the simplest subject to teach because it is intuitive and low on dry memorization.

Third, I would choose to teach science because it is the subject people use most in their daily lives. Nearly every part of our routine ties back to scientific concepts. For example, turning on a light involves radiation, and running an air conditioner relies on air moving in currents. These are just two small examples of how science shows up everywhere. Science also helps people make sense of everyday tasks through lessons. If you do not know how to use a compass, a science lesson on magnetic fields will give you the answer. On top of that, science is essential for fixing broken items and understanding how common tools work. It can explain how electrical circuits function, how to repair a faulty circuit, or why a light turns on instantly when you flip the switch. For all these reasons, science is the most practical subject for real-world use.

To sum up, the lesson I would most like to teach elementary school students is science. It brings smiles to students’ faces because it is engaging, it is the simplest subject to teach since it relies more on visuals and hands-on work than long lectures, and it is the most useful for everyday life. I should start preparing my science lesson for the elementary students soon, as they will learn a lot while having the most fun possible. Would you choose to teach science too? Why or why not?

Have you ever wondered what life would look like both with and without success?

I fully agree with Winston Churchill’s famous saying: “Success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm.” Failure plays a hugely important part in all of our daily lives. When we fail, it can push us down many different paths. But if we take the time to learn from our mistakes, we can figure out exactly where we went wrong. Some people have the drive or extra energy needed to push through tough obstacles, while others do not — and that is completely okay for this kind of situation. It is easy to lose faith when things get hard, but giving up on yourself as a person is never the right choice.

Resources and tools shape who we are today, and help guide us toward building strong, positive character traits. They are often right there waiting for us when we need them most. For example, if you are working on a school project, you might use the internet to find evidence that supports your argument. You might not even realize that the exact tool you needed has been sitting there all along, ready to be used — and once you do use it, success follows soon after.

If we never faced failures or made mistakes, we would never understand what errors we were making. Life would be far harder, more stressful, and deeply overwhelming. The more mistakes we resolve, the more new issues seem to fill up our plate. We would never be able to undo our existing problems, and that would only waste more of our time.

I strongly believe that success grows out of the mistakes and obstacles we meet along our path. These setbacks show us what to do and what to avoid, so we do not fall into the same trap twice. Adjusting to these lessons takes time and effort, so we all need to put in work as we move forward.

To sum up, no matter what obstacles we face in life, it is normal to feel the urge to give up sometimes — but we should let that feeling pass. If we keep going, we can achieve anything we set our minds to.

A common topic of discussion these days is whether technology has a positive or negative impact on people’s daily lives. I strongly believe technology brings more benefits than drawbacks, mainly because so much of modern life now takes place online. For me, the biggest perks are easy access to digital books, the ability to connect with others through laptops or smartphones, and the convenience of typing notes or documents on digital platforms. Many people argue technology is harmful, but most of their concerns come from negative stories they see on the news, not personal experience.

Gone are the days when you had to carve out time to visit a bookstore and hunt through shelves for the book you want. These days, almost every title is available digitally, making it far quicker and simpler to find what you’re looking for. If you’re on a long road trip with nothing to do, you can just pull up a book on your smartphone or any other portable device. Parents, who rarely get time to relax and read, can easily catch up on a book during road trips while their kids nap in the back seat. Digital books are also far easier to carry, since they’re stored right on your phone—no more lugging heavy paperbacks around, or panicking when you’ve misplaced a physical book. Plus, you’ll never lose your place in a digital book: you can add bookmarks to save pages, and if you come across a word you don’t know, you can look up its definition instantly, even translate it into another language if needed.

For people who live in different countries or states, staying in touch used to be a real struggle. Waiting for a letter to arrive could take a week or more, and even phone calls were expensive and inconvenient. Now, any device with a camera—tablets, laptops, smartphones—lets you do video calls instantly. You don’t have to wait days for a response to a letter; you can send an email with a rough draft of a project in seconds, and others can edit or give feedback on it right away. Video calls also let you chat with multiple people at once, for as long as you like. Lots of people complain they can’t meet up with friends or family because their schedules are too busy, but with digital tools, you can just pick a time that works for everyone and call from wherever you are.

Technology is only going to keep improving in the coming years. Right now, we’re still at the early stages of what’s possible—lots of people love using tablets, laptops, smartphones, and headphones, and many like to show off new devices when they get them. But it’s important to take good care of these gadgets, since they can be pricey. Looking ahead, we’ll likely see even more tech developments, and physical paper and pencils may become obsolete as almost everything moves to digital platforms.

Most people are happy to see technology grow, because it makes life easier. Even young kids use tablets to learn basic skills like letters and numbers. Many schools now provide tablets or laptops to students, since these tools help them learn more effectively and give them reliable ways to complete their schoolwork. Students especially appreciate tech because they can quickly research topics for projects or homework, and watch instructional videos that explain difficult concepts in a clearer way.

Technology offers so many ways to communicate, even if you don’t want to speak out loud—there are endless tools to access what you need without hassle. I think tech will play a huge role in people’s lives very soon. Everyone should get comfortable with the digital tools available now, because these technologies will only become more widespread in the future. Some people might miss physical paper and pencils, but digital tools are a safer, better way to connect with others and get things done, letting us communicate faster than ever before.

No one goes through life completely self-sufficient. We all need people we can count on at some point, because no one is born with everything they need to navigate the world alone. Staying true to who you are is always valuable, and if you ever feel the need to grow or shift parts of yourself, that choice should only ever be yours. If someone else tries to force changes on you, that’s a problem—they might have unrealistic ideas, or be overly negative about things in life. To me, being yourself means refusing to let others dictate who you become; the only person who should decide that is you.

I strongly disagree with Emerson’s claim that individuality is always a good thing, and I have plenty of reasons and examples to support this view. Some of the most important people in my life are my mom, dad, sister, and very close friends who feel more like family than just acquaintances. Having these connections is essential—they make getting through daily life far easier, and they give you space to grow and change as you move through the years. If you cut all those ties, you’d likely end up living in total, crushing isolation. These relationships aren’t trivial or unimportant; you have to trust the people in your life to get through tough times together.

When I was around twelve to fourteen years old, I used to struggle with my grades every time the school year started. I felt a constant knot of anxiety every morning when I headed to class, convinced I couldn’t push myself to improve my marks or get better at talking to other people. I was only focused on my own problems back then, and when I got home from school, I’d feel depressed and repulsed by myself. But everything shifted when I realized I needed help from the people around me. Over time, I was able to grow and change thanks to the support of others. The world isn’t forcing you to change—you’re changing yourself just by living alongside other people, and you might not even notice the shift. That’s a good thing, because if you can grow with support, anyone can do the same.

Another downside of having no one in your life is that it gets incredibly dull and unfulfilling. If you live completely alone, there’s no one to talk to or keep you company. But when you have a wide circle of friends and get to know new people, you share experiences that make life genuinely enjoyable. Hanging out with friends lets you have fun—you can play games together, chat, travel, and pick up new life lessons along the way. A lot of people claim we live in a society where no one cares about anyone else and no one wants to help. But that’s not true, and it’s not other people’s fault. The people around you can influence you in both positive and negative ways. Constant negativity can push someone to act badly, which is why people who are always bitter often end up isolated. They fear or hate others because they’re convinced no one cares about them, but that’s rarely the case. All it takes is being willing to let others into your life, or asking for help, to start growing.

To sum up, extreme individuality can be deeply harmful, pushing people down bad paths. Having others in your life is necessary because we can lift each other up—no one is worthless. Leaving someone to fend for themselves is sad, while helping others makes you a better person and leads to an easier, happier life. But as I said before, never let anyone force you to change who you are. Staying true to yourself is good, but isolating yourself completely is not. You are the protagonist of your own life, and your life is yours to shape.

Younger kids also remind older students that it is fine to not have all the answers. For example, if an older student is helping a younger peer with a problem they don’t understand themselves, they can always ask a teacher to explain it first. That shows everyone that needing help is not a weakness, no matter how old you are.

Most students look forward to the long summer vacation, though a smaller group argues it should be shorter. Currently, most schools schedule a three-month summer break, but some suggest cutting this to just one month, then extending winter break and adding a week of vacation in both spring and fall. I do not support this change. It is true that after three months away, students may forget some of what they learned in the previous school year. However, the long summer break is valuable because it gives families more time for trips, lets students take full-time summer jobs, and helps reduce stress for learners.

First, a long summer break gives families the time they need for meaningful vacations. Many people use this time to travel long distances to visit relatives they do not see often, or simply to spend quality time together having fun. For instance, a family living in Virginia would need several days just to drive to Florida or other popular destinations. A short one-month break would not leave enough time to plan the trip, travel there, and actually enjoy staying at the destination. Not all vacations are for visiting family, either—some are annual traditions or special rewards for the whole family. No matter the reason for the trip, having enough time is the most important factor for a successful vacation.

Another key reason to keep the long summer break is that it lets students take full-time jobs, which helps them earn more money. Many parents want their children to understand the challenges of real life, including how hard they have to work to afford the things they want. Teenagers especially start wanting more expensive items as they get older—this is often the age when they learn to drive and want to buy their first car. For example, a teen who wants a car might ask their parents to help pay for it. Parents may offer a set amount, but it might not cover the full cost. In that case, the teen needs to get a job to make up the difference. While a part-time job could eventually cover the cost, it takes much longer. A full-time summer job, made possible by the long break, lets them reach their goal faster.

Finally, a long summer break is essential for reducing student stress. Going to school all year with no long break is tough for many young people, especially if they are also dealing with problems at home. Juggling both schoolwork and personal issues can be overwhelming, so a long break gives them time to rest and reset. For example, a student who keeps failing tests might be struggling to find time to study at home. Bad grades can lead to parents scolding them and putting pressure on them to improve, which only adds to their stress if they are already dealing with other challenges. A long summer break lets students clear their minds and step away from these pressures, lowering their overall stress levels.

In conclusion, even though some people worry students will run out of things to do during a three-month break, the benefits are too important to ignore. These include more time for family vacations, opportunities for full-time summer work, and lower stress for students. A long summer break means more fun and less pressure for young people. Most schools have offered three-month summer breaks for years, and families are used to this schedule—there is no good reason to change it now. It is better to stick with the system that already works for most people. After all, a long summer break solves many common challenges for both students and their families.

Our species has survived for as long as we have because we learned to stick together and share tasks. This proves the old saying that two heads are better than one – there are plenty of jobs that no single person can handle alone. We’ve come a long way since those early days: we now build structures with complex, detailed designs, and we’ve created transport that lets us cross entire oceans in just hours. I often wonder if even the most talented individual could have achieved any of this alone. That’s exactly why teamwork matters so much.

When you become part of a team, it’s usually because you have a specific skill or talent that adds value to the group. For example, imagine you work for a company that builds websites for government projects. You hold a degree in coding and graphic design, and you were hired as a content creator. Think of yourself as a carefully shaped cog that fits perfectly into a bigger machine. This machine runs at a steady speed, never pushing too hard on any of the parts that make it work.

Second, when you work in a team, the workload is split fairly among members. Take a construction crew: the cement worker always measures out the right amount of cement for each portion, to avoid wasting materials. In a good team, you’re only given as much work as you can handle, so no one ends up overworked. It’s the same in a busy kitchen: one person peels carrots, another stirs the cake batter, and a third prepares the toppings. Every single person has a clear task to finish.

To sum up, teamwork offers countless benefits for everyone involved. Just like a well-oiled machine, successful teamwork relies on clear communication. The end result is a group that functions as a single unit: there’s almost no room for mistakes, because everyone knows exactly what the others are working on. Think of that same kitchen: one person peels ingredients, another mixes them, and a third polishes the final dish. Teamwork is the most important lesson we can learn. After all, there will always be tasks that are impossible to finish on your own.

The statement is "the first impression is almost impossible to change" which is a different feeling for everybody, but for me, I disagree. In fact, the first impression is really important and sometimes true, but I think the first impression does not define a person, an object or a situation. Having a first impression is a human reflex, like having an opinion or a judgment. We are doing it unconsciously.

The first impression is most of the time not real, you need to search deeper to make an opinion and when you really have an opinion, then, the first impression is not important anymore. For example, when you meet someone, your first impression might be that you think she is supercilious and even a little bit mean. Therefore when you really get to know her deeper then you will find that she just had a bad day and that she is nice and sociable. Sometimes it's the contrary, a person seems really nice but in reality she is not, so your first impression was wrong. It is not good to stay on a first impression because most of the time it's wrong.

Moreover, the physic, behaviors or attitude can change an impression. If the person do not smile and seems to be rude but in reality is the nicest person, then it will be awkward for you because you thought she was bad. Sometimes a person can have a bad reputation because of the first impression he shows and it is not his fault, some persons just don't smile every time. Sometimes you can be disappointed because you didn't get to know the person because of your first impression.

The first impressions is not only for people but also for a situation or an object. For example if you are in a library and you want to buy a book, the first thing you are going to do is looking at the cover of the book. If it's pretty you will more easily choose this one instead of a book with a black cover and only the title, because it is your first impression. But your first impression is wrong because you didn't take time to read the resume and you will find soon that the pretty book is actually boring instead of the black book which is really interesting. An object can look nice but have a bad quality. The first impression is the color and the shape of the object, like the physic and the attitude of a person.

In conclusion I would say that the first impression is sometimes right but most of the time it's not. In my opinion, you must not keep in mind your first impression of a person, it's most of the time wrong. You have to get to know the person to build your own opinion. It is normal to have a first impression, like judging, but you must not take the habit to stick with your first impression.

There is a widespread claim that first impressions are almost impossible to alter, and people have varying reactions to this idea. For my part, I do not agree. While initial impressions can carry weight and are sometimes accurate, they do not define who a person is, what an object is like, or how a situation will play out. Forming quick first impressions is a natural human reflex, similar to making snap judgments or having instant opinions, and we do it without even thinking.

Most first impressions are not rooted in reality. To form a genuine opinion, you have to look past that initial snap judgment, and once you’ve built a real view of someone or something, the first impression stops mattering entirely. Take meeting a new person, for instance: your first thought might be that they are arrogant and unfriendly. But after spending more time with them, you could learn they were just having a terrible day, and are actually warm and easy to get along with. The opposite happens too: someone might seem perfectly pleasant at first, but turn out to be unkind once you know them better, proving your initial impression was off. Clinging to first impressions is unwise, because they are wrong more often than they are right.

Beyond that, a person’s appearance, behavior, or attitude can easily shift how others see them. If someone rarely smiles and comes across as rude, but is actually the kindest person you’ll meet, you’ll likely feel embarrassed for misjudging them so harshly. Plenty of people get stuck with bad reputations based on surface-level first impressions they never asked for — some people just don’t smile all the time, and that’s not a flaw. You might also end up disappointed if you write someone off based on a first impression, and never take the chance to get to know them properly.

First impressions aren’t limited to people, either — they apply to situations and objects too. Imagine you’re at a library looking to buy a book. The first thing you’ll probably notice is the cover. If one has a bright, eye-catching design, you’re far more likely to pick it up over a plain black book with nothing but the title on the front, all because of that initial impression. But that first impression might be misleading: if you don’t read the blurb first, you could end up with a boring book with a pretty cover, while the plain black one is actually fascinating. Plenty of objects look appealing at first glance but are poorly made. A first impression of an object is just its color and shape, much like a first impression of a person is just their physical appearance and demeanor.

To sum up, first impressions are sometimes accurate, but far more often they are not. I believe it is a mistake to hold onto your first impression of a person, since they are wrong most of the time. The only way to form a valid opinion is to take the time to get to know someone properly. Having instant initial impressions is a normal part of being human, much like making quick judgments, but you should not make a habit of sticking to those first thoughts.

Being self-reliant is a crucial part of finding success in life, as it means taking charge of your own actions and choices. I believe everyone should have the right to make their own decisions, since having the freedom to choose what works for you is essential. People need to be able to form their own thoughts and judgments.

Why is this freedom so important? When people are allowed to pick what they want, they avoid having outsiders—like officials or so-called experts—force choices on them that they dislike or don’t need. Imagine someone wants to buy a pair of flashy new sneakers, but a parent or manager disapproves and insists they buy a plainer pair instead. I would never want someone else making choices for me, because they can’t possibly know my personal tastes or preferences. If you let others decide everything for you, you’ll end up unhappy: those in charge will pick options that suit their own likes, not yours. Take a cafeteria visit, for instance: if you aren’t allowed to choose your own meal, a staff member might hand you a dish you hate, just because they decided it was better for you.

There’s another key reason to value self-reliance: the ability to think independently. If someone can’t form their own opinions or make their own judgments, they will run into all kinds of trouble in daily life. For example, if an authority figure asks them a question and they freeze up because they’re used to letting others decide, that person will step in and make a choice for them—one that the original person will almost certainly dislike.

To sum up, having the right to make your own decisions is a huge benefit, because most people want to be in control of their own lives. No one likes being told exactly what to do or how to think by someone else. When you are self-reliant, you get to pick the path that works best for you, and shape your life the way you want it to be.

Although, students will have a healthier life, other people cannot decide what students should eat.

In conclusion, changing the school lunch menu is a bad idea because students might be allergic and students' favorite food will be eliminated. Should schools update their lunch menus? Students are the ones who get to pick what they eat, and many would rather have a burger than a salad. Changing the school lunch menu is a poor choice, for two main reasons: some students have allergies to certain vegetables, and many beloved menu items would be removed entirely.

First, adjusting the lunch menu could cause problems for students with food allergies. Take Generic_Name, for instance: he has severe allergies to both tomatoes and lettuce. If the school changes its menu to include more of these vegetables, he would stop going to the cafeteria at lunchtime altogether. Because of his allergies, he has to avoid these ingredients completely. School leaders should think carefully before going ahead with menu changes, to avoid harming students like Generic_Name. Overall, updating the lunch menu would not benefit all students, and could even create issues for those who have to avoid certain foods.

Second, changing the menu would remove popular foods that many students love. For example, pizza and hamburgers are favorite meals for lots of young people. If the cafeteria swaps these out for new options, many students simply won’t buy lunch there. When students skip meals, the cafeteria ends up throwing away uneaten food. This waste is unnecessary, and could easily be avoided by keeping the current menu as it is. In the end, altering the lunch menu is likely to lead to more wasted food, not less.

Some people might argue that updating the lunch menu is a positive move, since it would help students eat more healthily. There is some truth to this point. However, changing the menu is still a bad idea, because no one else has the right to decide what students should or shouldn’t eat. Even if a new menu leads to better health, it is not up to school staff or officials to make that choice for students. Students should be allowed to pick their own meals.

To sum up, changing the school lunch menu is a bad idea for several clear reasons. First, it could harm students with vegetable allergies, like Generic_Name. Second, removing favorite foods would lead to more wasted food in the cafeteria. Finally, even if a new menu is healthier, no one else should choose what students eat except the students themselves. In the end, students are the ones who should decide if they want to eat healthier options, not school administrators.

Should schools cut summer break short and add those days to winter vacation instead? What’s the reason for tweaking the current holiday schedule anyway? Can’t we just leave things as they are? Would students even be happy with this switch? Would these changes actually help learners do better in their classes?

For starters, plenty of students would be unhappy with this adjustment. Winter weather is often freezing, which makes it hard to spend time outdoors, go for walks, or play outside. A big part of why they dislike the idea is that summer break lets them be outside and visit fun places, which isn’t possible in the cold. If kids stay out in winter for too long, they could catch a cold, end up missing school days, and fall behind their classmates.

On the flip side, a few students might actually support the change, since summer heat can get unbearable, and people can get dehydrated if they spend too much time outside in high temperatures. That said, summer days still have plenty of great perks: trips to the beach, amusement parks, camping trips, and travel are all common summer activities. There are lots of reasons students would want more summer break, too: extra days off, pleasant weather for outdoor fun, trips to the pool, chances to explore nature, and it even helps them spend less time on screens.

If this vacation shift actually happens, I’d be really disappointed. I love spending time outside in warm weather, so having less summer break and more time off in winter sounds awful to me. I also can’t stand snow days when school gets canceled, honestly. I’m happy with the current vacation schedule as it is, since everyone gets to take time off during the season they enjoy most. I’m also sure most students would want to keep the current setup, because they’d rather have more vacation days overall, not fewer.

To wrap up, it’s unlikely the vacation schedule will change, since students clearly prefer the current setup. They want to enjoy their time off, not dread it. My main point is that if students don’t like a new schedule, they’ll probably dislike returning to school and might even ignore lessons entirely. So if school leaders want to adjust the vacation calendar, they should first ask students if the change works for them. If not, they need to come up with a different solution that everyone can agree on.

While it is true that letting students use smartphones in class would make looking up class-related information far easier, schools should still ban these devices during lessons. This ban is necessary for three key reasons: phones act as major distractions, give students a chance to cheat on exams and quizzes, and lead to laziness, gaps in learning, and procrastination.

Supporters of allowing phones in class make several valid points. Some argue that students who finish tests early deserve a short phone break to relax with entertainment, and that listening to music helps certain learners concentrate better on their work. Others point out that phones let students work on group projects more easily and look up extra details on topics they don’t fully understand. There is also the argument that dictionary apps on phones are a huge help for international students struggling with a new language. Proponents add that tools like Kahoot and other educational game apps make it simple for students to review class notes and practice what they’ve learned.

The strongest argument against allowing phones is that they make cheating far too easy. If students have access to their devices during class, they will almost certainly try to use them to cheat on quizzes and exams. For instance, it is common for students to snap photos of answer keys and send them to classmates mid-test. Beyond that, almost all study materials can be saved on a small smartphone, so many students will stop putting effort into studying altogether. Why would they spend hours revising when they can just pull the answers off their phone during the exam? This completely undermines the purpose of education, making any policy that allows phones in class totally unacceptable.

Another major issue is that phones are incredibly distracting. Picture a quiet classroom where everyone is working, when suddenly a phone notification pings, drawing the attention of dozens of students. No one enjoys being interrupted, but allowing phones in lessons is a mistake that negatively affects everyone in the room. For example, some students play loud, inappropriate music on their phones while others are taking tests, a problem that happens in schools everywhere. Even students who are trying to focus can get distracted by a classmate using a phone nearby, which disrupts their own work too.

Finally, phones contribute to laziness, gaps in student knowledge, and procrastination. When students have constant access to phones, they often waste time scrolling through apps instead of paying attention to lessons, which leads to serious learning gaps. Since they can look up any answer in seconds, they stop thinking critically about the material they are studying. They might get good grades by copying information off their phones, but they are not actually retaining any of the knowledge. The more schools let students use phones in class, the more they harm their students’ long-term learning.

In conclusion, students should be banned from using cell phones in classrooms. These devices are major distractions not just in lessons, but in other public spaces too, make cheating during exams far too easy, and lead to laziness, poor retention of knowledge, and procrastination. If phones were allowed in all schools, students would have no reason to attend classes at all, since every piece of information they need is already available online. Schools want students to develop real skills through hard work, not just copy answers from websites on their phones. Every school administration should carefully consider the negative impact of allowing phones in lessons before making any policy changes.

Do curfews actually stop teenagers from getting into trouble? Right now, our city council is stuck deciding between setting a 10 p.m. weeknight curfew or a midnight curfew for weekends. Any minor caught out past the chosen time would be violating local law. Laws are created for good reasons, even if we don’t always agree with every rule, we still have to follow them. I strongly believe the council should approve a curfew for all minors. When it comes to protecting young people, their safety has to be our top priority, and curfews are a key part of that. We cannot ignore the many dangers present in the world today.

Have you ever stopped to think about the risks your child faces when they are out without supervision? The world is full of unpredictable dangers right now. I’m not saying something bad will definitely happen every time a teen stays out late, but the truth is, anything is possible. Without an adult’s guidance or watchful eye, all sorts of bad situations can arise. Far too many young people are injured or killed for reasons no one could have predicted. A curfew is one simple way to reduce the chances of these tragedies happening to your kids. Even a midnight weekend curfew carries some risk, but it is still our job as adults to teach minors the difference between right and wrong. If we explain clearly why curfews matter, they are more likely to take their safety seriously. It’s very possible they will push back against the rules at first—I can speak from experience here: when I was a teen, I wanted to spend as much time as possible with my friends, and I ignored my mom’s rules more than once. But eventually I realized how much my safety meant to her, and how worried she got when I stayed out late.

Take the case of Generic_Name, a teenager from New York, for example. He was a wonderful kid: his mother often talked about how much he loved spending time with his nephews and the rest of his family. He rarely went out with friends, preferring to stay home, and he was extremely close to his sister—the two were almost always together. Generic_Name got good grades in school and never got into any trouble. I’m bringing up his story because he was murdered just a few blocks from his own house, outside a small grocery store. I don’t know the exact time, but it was after dark. A group of men saw him, dragged him out of the market, and stabbed him under the arm. He begged for help, but no one came to his aid. He tried to walk to the hospital on his own, but unfortunately, he collapsed and died on the sidewalk. The men were caught a few months later, and they claimed they had mistaken him for someone else. Generic_Name had done nothing wrong—he absolutely did not deserve what happened to him. Maybe if he had waited until the next day to go to the store, or if his mom had gone with him, things would have turned out differently. The point is, being out alone, especially at night, is never fully safe, but the risks drop drastically when you are with a parent or trusted adult.

Some people argue that they want to give their own children the freedom they wish they had as kids. They might think there is no issue with letting teens go out whenever they want, and that curfews are unnecessary. It’s true that everyone wants to live life to the fullest and have fun. But enjoying life does not have to mean staying out past a set curfew—there is plenty to do during daylight hours too. Yes, you might trust your own child completely, and believe they will make good choices when they are out. But can you say the same for every other person your child might encounter in public? Daytime is far safer than nighttime, mostly because there are so many more people around. If something goes wrong, you can shout for help, run to a crowded area, or signal that you are in danger. I believe that people can only reach greater success by consistently taking action and staying busy with meaningful tasks. The more often you push yourself to get things done, the more likely you are to achieve your goals.

One of the clearest examples from my own life is when I joined my school’s swim team. There were plenty of days when I felt like quitting altogether. Sometimes I was too exhausted, other times I was just lazy, or buried under piles of homework after class. But one night, I realized that giving up would waste all the hard work I’d already put in. After that, whenever I felt like stopping, I reminded myself to keep going. I showed up to every single practice without fail, repeating to myself that I would never give up. Before long, I started seeing real progress: I became a team leader, and my coach told me he’d always known I would put in the extra effort, because he’d believed in me from the start.

There were also times after swim practice when I really wanted to spend time with my friends. I wanted to go shopping with them, walk through the park, visit the beach, or go to their parties. But I knew that if I wanted to be a good leader for the swim team, I had to prioritize what was best for my own progress first. I could only make plans with my friends once I’d taken care of my own responsibilities. After I became a role model for the team and started attending every practice without missing a day, I finally had time to hang out with my friends again. They totally understood what I was trying to do, because I’d taken full responsibility for my swim team commitments first. By the end, I had plenty of time left for both my friends and my family.

Looking back, the biggest lesson I’ve learned from this experience is to never give up if you want to be successful. I don’t regret a single choice I made. In fact, I’m really proud of how far I’ve come, especially becoming a strong leader for my swim team. In the future, I’m chasing my dream of becoming a world-famous swimmer, competing on live television. If I ever get the chance to give a speech on TV, I’d tell everyone: “Accomplishing more through consistent effort is the only way to turn your dreams into reality. Always take responsibility for your own choices, and don’t let anyone tell you otherwise.”

Whether you look around your neighborhood, school, or workplace, almost everyone sets goals or makes plans for what they want to achieve down the line. Some people have the time and motivation to work toward these goals, while others struggle to find the hours or drive to get started. Everyone has their own method for reaching success in the things they care about: some choose to sit back and do nothing, while others take active steps to make progress. Thomas Jefferson once said, "Determine never to be idle....it is wonderful how much may be done if we are always doing." I completely agree with this statement—constantly taking action helps us accomplish far more than we would if we stayed inactive.

First, taking consistent action helps you map out, reach, and finish your long-term goals much faster. For example, if you are assigned a task, you cannot just sit around waiting for someone else to step in and help, or hope that some miracle will suddenly get the work done for you. If your goal is to finish high school and earn a scholarship to attend college, you need to put in consistent effort studying to make that happen. The same applies if you want to land a stable, well-paying job later on: you will need to study hard, build a strong resume, and gain relevant skills. Staying active with your work means you complete every task you are given much more efficiently.

Beyond that, staying busy with productive tasks keeps you more engaged and active overall. For instance, if you fail an exam—or even several—you cannot just shrug it off and act like your grades do not matter. You need to take action: study harder, and aim to do better on the next round of tests. Whenever I fail a quiz or test, even though I hate having to retake them, I start preparing for the next assessment right away, and even get ready for all the units we will cover later in the term. I prefer to learn content ahead of the class because I do not pick up material as easily during lessons, so I prepare in advance instead. Taking notes, making plans, and staying organized pushes you to take action rather than sitting idle and letting your future plans fall apart. Having a clear roadmap for your future makes it much easier to actually achieve what you set out to do.

On the other hand, some people argue that staying idle while working toward your goals is less stressful. They point out that students who push themselves to be constantly productive often rely on pills to stay awake, especially in high school. These students want to achieve more, graduate with top marks, get into good colleges, and land great jobs, so they pour all their energy into studying, sometimes even drinking excessive amounts of caffeinated drinks and taking pills to avoid sleep. Some end up getting sick but cannot stop because they have become dependent on these habits. While this concern is valid, the benefits of consistent action far outweigh the risks. Staying active helps you build responsibility, which will serve you well in the future: most employers ask for prior experience or proof that you are qualified for a role. Since no one can predict exactly what will happen in the years to come, being prepared and having a solid plan in place is the best way to set yourself up for success.

In short, I make a point of planning my future goals and learning material ahead of my classes. Consistently taking action keeps you involved in meaningful tasks, helps you learn new things, and improves your academic performance, all of which set you up to be successful later in life. It also makes you a valuable employee in the workplace, where your teachers, coworkers, and mentors will admire and respect you—you might even become a role model for others. With this mindset, you can get into the college you have always dreamed of and achieve every personal goal you set for yourself.

Back in high school, I had a teacher who seemed unfriendly at first. He rarely talked to students and never re-explained lessons, so I asked my counselor to switch classes, but she said no. After a few weeks, I realized he was actually a great, kind teacher. Every time I asked for help, he made sure I understood the material, helping me do well on quizzes and tests. There’s a saying that first impressions are almost impossible to change, and some think you can know someone’s character from just one meeting. But I believe first impressions can shift. Someone might have been having a terrible day when you met them, so you should always get to know their true character before judging them.

Everyone has bad days, and that’s totally normal, as life is full of both good and bad moments. If you’re having a rough day, you’re naturally not going to be as friendly or upbeat with others. For instance, someone might be dealing with issues at home, at work, or at school, and that stress will definitely show in how they act. They might be short-tempered or unapproachable with you, but that’s just a reaction to their current situation, not their true personality. Just because someone seems unpleasant when you first meet them doesn’t mean they’re actually mean. They could just be going through a tough time. That’s why you can’t judge someone until you know their real character.

In daily life, you can’t go around judging people based on one thing they did or how they look. Most people are familiar with the phrase “Don’t judge a book by its cover,” which means you can’t assume what someone is like just from their appearance. Someone might seem warm and friendly on the outside, but turn out to be untrustworthy once you get to know them, leaving you hurt if you believed their initial nice persona was real. On the other hand, people who come across as grumpy or unfriendly at first might actually be very kind once you take the time to talk to them, and you might even need their help at some point in the future.

To sum up, first impressions can absolutely change, whether because someone was having a bad day when you met them, or because you get to know their true personality over time and start seeing them differently. It’s so important to learn who someone really is before judging them—you never know if the person you dismissed early on might end up being the exact person you need help from down the line.

I am convinced that having a positive outlook is the most important factor for achieving success in life. To be clear, this means being kind and offering encouraging feedback about the things people do and say. When we act this way, we demonstrate our maturity, and we also set a good example for the people we live and interact with every day.

A good friend of mine, let’s call her Generic_Name, takes part in many sports, including soccer. Her team used to lose almost every match, but she would always remind her teammates that everything was okay, and they just needed to practice more. Before their next Saturday game, all her teammates were terrified: they were so sure they would lose, they felt defeated before even stepping onto the field. Generic_Name told them that losing is not the end of the world, and letting fear take over would not help them win at all. In the end, the whole team promised each other that no matter the result, they would be happy just to have the chance to play together.

On the other hand, there is my 12-year-old younger brother, also named Generic_Name. He has never been a fan of math, and I often help him with his homework. One day, I saw his test results and every answer was correct. I was not surprised at all, since he had been working so hard. Whenever he got a question wrong, he would just shrug and say it was fine, he would try again. After school one day, he told me his teacher had given him a candy for doing well, but he had given it to a friend. I was shocked, and immediately asked why. He explained that his friend had studied just as hard but did not get any candy, so he felt bad for him.

All in all, a positive attitude is truly the key to success. Whenever we start to feel weighed down by negative energy, we should pause and remember that things could always be worse. By choosing to stay positive, we gain far more than we ever lose when we let negativity take over.

Little, everyday acts of kindness can make a huge difference in people’s lives, often by lifting their mood in unexpected ways. One easy way to show this is picking up litter that someone else dropped. These small gestures can even help others reach their goals later on, and doing them makes you a more helpful person, since you’re directly supporting someone in their daily life. For example, if you see someone drop their books or phone, bending down to pick it up for them is a quick, kind act.

Kindness can reach far more people than you realize, too. Even if you’re upset with someone, choosing to be kind to them still matters. Speaking to others politely, even when you’re frustrated, is a simple way to show care. Kindness also helps in countless situations: it can brighten someone’s day even if they’re feeling sad or angry with you. Helping a classmate with their homework is another easy, meaningful way to be kind.

Every small kind act leaves a mark on the people you help, simply because you’re offering them support. I believe being kind is incredibly valuable, especially when you reach out to someone who’s having a bad day or is upset about something that happened. Offering to translate a sentence from English to Spanish for someone who needs it is one small way to help. There’s something really nice about being useful to another person, and you can show kindness in so many ways—even helping someone with their homework again counts. Even the tiniest favor makes a difference, and counts as a kind act.

Being kind doesn’t just help the person you’re assisting—it can boost your own mood too, even if you’re showing kindness to yourself. Another easy act of kindness is helping your family or friends wash the dishes after a meal. Even the smallest gesture works, because you’re still choosing to be kind to someone else. These little acts can change people’s lives, since you’re doing something nice for them, and they often help you feel good about yourself too, just from the act of being kind. One more example is offering to help someone pet their dog, like holding the leash while they sort something out, or joining in to give the pup some attention.

I truly think that being kind to others lifts your own mood, because you know you’ve done something good for someone else. Kindness is also incredibly useful: you’re directly helping someone, and it helps you grow into a better person over time. Picking up litter you see on the ground is another easy way to show kindness. Even if someone is feeling down, a small kind act can cheer them up. If you notice someone sitting alone and looking lonely, going over to say hello is a simple, powerful way to be kind.
