Would you want to add two extra hours to your school day, even if you already work four days a week for 10 hours each? Personally, I strongly disagree with this idea. There are three main reasons: many students need time with their families, lots of us have other important responsibilities after school, and we all deserve some free time instead of working nonstop.

First, plenty of students want to use their free time to connect with family members. Some have relatives who live far away, so they jump at any chance to visit before those family members leave town again. Others spend time with elderly grandparents, who may need help with daily tasks as they get older, or just want company. There are also students who haven’t seen their cousins in months and want to catch up. For many young people, family time is precious because they don’t get to see loved ones often, sometimes not for years at a time.

Second, a lot of students have other obligations that make staying in school longer impossible. Many of us have sports practice right after classes end, so we can’t afford to stay two extra hours. Others need to rush home to babysit younger siblings while their parents are at work. Some even have part-time jobs to get to right after school, and skipping shifts could get them in trouble with their bosses. We have plenty of other responsibilities besides schoolwork, so adding more hours to the school day just creates more stress.

Third, students need free time to relax and do things we enjoy. Instead of being stuck in school or at a job all day, many of us want to hang out with friends, go shopping, or just spend quality time with our parents, who we don’t see enough of during busy weeks. Free time is rare for young people, and we shouldn’t have to give up the little we have to sit in school longer.

In my view, adding extra hours to the school schedule is a bad idea. We’re still young, and we should get to enjoy our free time before we get older and have even less of it, between more school and full-time work. Piling on too much work also makes some students so burnt out that they start to give up on their assignments entirely. For example, when I get home from school, I have to take care of my little sister because my mom isn’t available to do it.

I definitely wouldn’t want to be stuck in school for two more hours every day. It would mean leaving campus late, and if I had a four-day work week with 10-hour shifts, I’d have no time left to do schoolwork at home. By the time I get back from work, I’d be so exhausted that I’d just fall asleep instead of finishing assignments.

Plenty of students gain advantages from this setup, including higher attendance rates, fewer conflicts, and support for those with specific disabilities or ongoing health issues. That said, some disagree, claiming that skipping in-person classes will make young people lazy and less responsible. Overall, distance learning offers clear benefits for both students and schools.

One major way distance learning helps students is by improving their attendance. When learners can join classes from their own homes, they have far fewer chances to skip sessions. Most students hate having to wake up early, get dressed, and commute to school every morning. Forcing them to start their day so early just to sit through eight hours of lessons often makes them feel lazy and tired.

Sadly, some students are born with or later develop disabilities that stop them from attending physical schools. These young people still have a legal right to access quality education. Distance learning is a huge help here, as it lets them take part in classes from the comfort of their homes. While there are many upsides to distance learning, supporting children with disabilities to get an education is by far the most important reason to use this system.

Another clear benefit is that distance learning cuts down on common school problems. Many students face terrible treatment at physical schools, including bullying, and some even like to stir up unnecessary social drama. When learners study from home, they avoid these negative interactions with peers, so there is less drama and more focus on education. Schools would also see far fewer reports of bullying if more students switched to distance learning setups.

Of course, not everyone agrees with this view. Critics argue that studying from home makes young people irresponsible and lazy. However, students should be free to choose the learning format that works best for them. If a student becomes lazy while doing distance learning, that is a personal problem, not a flaw of the system. Many people actually find that distance learning makes students less lazy and more responsible.

Have you ever visited a completely new destination? When you’re in an unfamiliar place, what do you do to fill your time? For me, I’d spend my days taking in the sights, swimming, and either climbing or walking to get around.

If I had the chance to travel anywhere on Earth, I’d pick Jamaica without hesitation. It offers endless spots for fun activities, a huge range of local dishes, and all kinds of unique wildlife.

Jamaica’s mix of landscapes is what draws me most for activities. You can head to the beach or hike up a mountain, both full of things to do. At the shore, I’d swim in the fresh water, then lie back on the sand to enjoy the pleasant weather. I’d also climb the island’s mountains to breathe in the fresh air, and once I reach the top, I’d take in the stunning views spread out below. While swimming, I’d keep an eye out for small water creatures living in the shallows.

Another big reason to visit Jamaica is its incredible food options. You can find all sorts of dishes in different places: restaurants serve classic rice and beans, tropical trees grow fresh coconuts and bananas, and local creeks are full of crayfish and other fish. If I caught a crayfish or any other fish, I’d fry it up myself. With so many different foods available, I could switch up my usual diet entirely while I’m there.

Finally, Jamaica is home to so many different types of animals. I’d spot chickens and other birds, some flying overhead and others running along the ground. Stray dogs wander the streets, too. In the water, I’d look for fish with claws as well as those with regular fins. Frogs are everywhere, some poisonous and some completely harmless. Goats roam free, often nibbling on people’s garden plants, and you might even come across snakes with sharp fangs, some of which are poisonous.

All in all, I’d choose Jamaica because it has endless activity spots, a wide range of delicious food, and all kinds of unique animals. It stands out from other destinations thanks to its rich natural environment, which is exactly why it’s my top pick for a dream trip anywhere in the world.

Have you ever stopped to think about your own work style—do you prefer collaborating with others or handling tasks entirely on your own? How do these preferences help you succeed in a job, at school, orin other areas of life?

There’s a long-running debate about which approach works best: many argue that teamwork is the superior way to get things done, while others swear by working independently. Both sides have clear advantages, which I’ll outline below.

Personally, I believe group work brings more benefits. For one, collaborating with others exposes you to fresh perspectives and ideas you might never come up with alone. It also speeds up the completion of tasks, since the workload is split among all team members. I saw this firsthand during a driver’s ed project with my friends earlier this year. We started by sitting down separately to brainstorm individual ideas, then met up to narrow down our favorite suggestions together. After that, we each took charge of a specific section of the project, and managed to finish the entire thing before the class period ended.

That said, plenty of people prefer working alone, and they have valid reasons. When you work solo, you can focus entirely on your task without distractions from others. You also have full control over your creative process, without having to compromise with teammates. I remember a girl in my biology class who chose to complete her final exam project by herself. She spent hours researching her topic, staying completely focused on finding the exact information she needed. Once she had her research, she designed a highly creative poster that fit the project’s theme perfectly—her teacher was so impressed she awarded her an A.

In the end, though, I still find that group work benefits me the most. The shared workload feels far lighter, and combining everyone’s ideas leads to better outcomes. It also lets me share my own thoughts and hear others’ perspectives on the topic—perks that solo work just can’t offer.

I went through some tough personal issues in the past, and it was really rough. Imagine if those problems had been so severe that I couldn’t even leave the house to get to school? Not every student thrives in a traditional classroom setting — plenty would rather learn from home using digital platforms or video meetings. Even students who constantly get in trouble at school often do better when they study from home. At home, there’s no one to get into mischief with. You just finish your assignments and move on to the next task, with no more trouble or disruptions.

Adults, especially parents, often argue that going to school and interacting with peers is good for young people. Is that actually true? I’m not totally convinced, but I do know one thing: students should get to choose the learning setup that feels right for them, and our parents should support that choice. For the record, students who learn from home aren’t doing less work than those who go to school. We all complete the same assignments, which are graded the same way. Everyone has to submit work by the deadline, or it counts as late. We take the exact same tests and quizzes too. The only real difference between students who take classes online and those who go to school in person is that online learners aren’t sitting in a physical classroom. We’ll probably never find out for sure, and I doubt there’s a way to get a clear answer to that question.

It’s really tough for children and teenagers to go to school and handle interactions with other kids — I get that completely, because I struggle with it too sometimes. Of course, not every classmate is difficult to deal with. But overall, online classes and video conferences aren’t as bad as some people make them out to be. If I had the chance to learn from home, I would definitely take it.

Some research suggests that students who settle on their dream career before starting high school are more likely to build a successful professional life later on. Yet committing to a career path so early is often a source of heavy stress and pressure, as these students feel they have to reach their goals faster than their peers. Deciding on a career at a young age is a mentally taxing choice that is not worth the cost: it raises stress levels, makes students focus only on future work instead of their own growth, and ignores the fact that high school often changes what people want to do.

The first reason students should avoid committing to a career too early is that it creates constant stress throughout high school. While high school may seem like the perfect time to lock in your future plans, that is rarely true in practice. If you fixate on a single career path during these years, you are far more likely to feel overwhelmed. You might tell yourself that following a strict plan will help you reach your goals quicker, but you will also worry that one wrong step could ruin your chances of success. This puts you in a tough spot that is hard to escape. You will focus so much on your chosen career that it becomes hard to concentrate on or study for other classes. High school is a time when your education shapes who you are, and it is very common to change your mind about what you want to do not long after you start. For that reason, it is better not to put yourself in a position where you feel constantly stressed.

Pressure is a huge part of life today, even though people often pretend it is fun. That is not the case. Facing constant pressure is one of the hardest things to deal with, because you feel like you have to succeed just to make other people proud. When it comes to early career commitments, you might feel pressured to stick to your choice to impress your parents, teachers, or school administrators, to prove that you can follow through on your plans. As the weeks and months pass, this pressure only grows. When it gets too high, you may start to feel depressed, sad, and unlike yourself, because you are chasing a goal to please others, not because you truly want it for yourself.

High school has a way of changing everyone’s mind about what they want to do. The moment you walk through the doors, you realize it is nothing like the high school movies you may have watched. It is a place where students and teachers go about their own work, focused on their own tasks. Middle school and high school are completely different environments. Classes are much harder, and high school offers a wide range of elective courses to choose from. Of course you are going to change your mind about your plans once you try new things. Why would you lock in a career path at a young age when you have not even taken these other classes yet? You can never be sure what you actually enjoy until you have tried out different options.

For my part, I would never commit to a career at a young age. I have learned this from my own experiences and from watching others. Take the classes you enjoy in high school, and if you like them, keep going with that path. If not, switch to something else. What you see on TV is very different from real life. Everyone is unique, and you are no exception. A career is just a label, not something that should define you before you have even finished growing up. Do not push yourself to decide so early.

Choosing a career path while still in high school gives students a valuable head start on planning their adult lives. In many cultures, young people are encouraged to settle on a professional direction before they even begin secondary school. I firmly believe deciding on a career this early is a smart choice.

First, picking a career ahead of time lets students reach their goals faster. For instance, if they start learning the basics of their chosen field during high school, they may not need to spend the full four years most people do in college. They could finish their degree in just one or two years, since they already have the foundational knowledge from relevant high school courses.

Another key benefit is that it pushes students to take their future more seriously and act with greater maturity. Career-focused classes can motivate them to work toward a better life, even if they previously had no interest in studying for a profession. It also teaches them that they are responsible for their own choices, and that building a stable career is a crucial step that will shape their entire adult future.

Not everyone agrees with this approach, though. Some argue that it is a waste of time, pointing out that students will have extra work to juggle, including additional classes and more intensive studying. This added pressure could leave them feeling exhausted both mentally and physically, so these critics insist it is better to wait until college to pick a career.

However, waiting until college is often too late. Students usually have to declare a major soon after starting college, and if they haven’t thought about it beforehand, they might rush into a field they do not actually care about. This can lead to spending extra years in school, dropping out entirely, or ending up with a low-quality job and an uncertain future.

To sum up, committing to a career path at a young age is a positive decision. It helps students get ready for their future, letting them reach their goals sooner than their peers. It also gives them a clear idea of what to expect when they start college. Deciding on a career early benefits students in countless ways, as outlined above.

Education plays a massive, lasting role in shaping how people grow and adapt in our fast-changing world. It influences everything from how a future worker handles a sudden problem at work to the way they come up with solutions for it. Whole generations have been built around access to learning. Basic skills like math and literacy, taught in classrooms, paved the way for humans to reach the Moon and tackle worldwide emergencies. All of these advancements have helped create the world we live in now. For these reasons, I strongly believe the school board should not lengthen the school day, for three key reasons: the current 7-hour schedule already provides plenty of time for both physical and mental growth, a longer day would expose students to more stress and unproductive pressure, and adding an extra 90 minutes would clash with the existing schedules of students, their families, and school staff.

First, let’s look at the current 7-hour school day. Students already face plenty of challenges from the moment they walk through the school doors. Some might have missed the bus, or arrived too early with nothing to do. Once classes start, they’re working to grasp new concepts, often while trying to finish a page of homework due that same day. Between classes, they might stress about a messy locker or forget something important inside. Even at the end of the day, many are worrying about group projects or arranging time with friends when they both have assignments due the next morning. In short, a student’s day is already packed with demanding tasks and stressful moments, even without extra time added.

If the school day is made longer, these small, everyday struggles would only get worse, and new problems would pop up too. Students would have more assignments to complete, and homework loads would grow even heavier. Spending too much time focused on one subject could make classes feel boring and unengaging, while other subjects might have their class time cut short to fit in the extra 90 minutes. Many of the small issues that come up during a normal day already feel overwhelming to students, and adding more time would make far more situations feel impossible to handle.

Another major issue is that a longer school day would clash with the schedules of students, their parents, and school staff. Many students take part in extracurricular activities like baseball or swim team, which need enough time after school to practice and compete properly. Parents might also struggle to adjust their work schedules to pick up their kids or spend time with them after school, which could lead to all kinds of negative outcomes for families.

Teachers and school staff would also be affected. They would have to stay later to finish grading, prepare materials for the next day, or clean up their classrooms after the extra time. Everyone connected to the school, and even people outside it, would be stuck trying to balance two completely different, conflicting schedules that no longer line up.

To be fair, there are some potential benefits to a longer school day. Students would have more time to study subjects in depth, and they might be able to finish most of their homework during school hours instead of at home. Lunch and gym classes could also be extended, giving students more time to socialize. But even these benefits come with downsides, and unproductive, stressful elements would still be present no matter what changes are made.

As I’ve said before, I am firmly against extending the school day. The extra time would create conflicts for countless people, increase stress and negativity for students and staff, and the current schedule already includes more than enough activities, lessons, and learning opportunities to keep everyone busy.

Parents might have to cut back on work hours to adjust to the new schedule, which could hurt family stability. Homework and class requirements would likely get harder and more numerous, putting even more pressure on students and teachers. The current 7-hour day is already full of diverse lessons, activities, and challenges that demand full focus and energy. While there are both pros and cons to lengthening the school day, we need to think carefully about what this change would really mean: its effects could be permanent, and not in a good way.

A common topic of debate is whether true self-esteem comes from receiving praise or from personal achievement. Some argue that praising low-quality work harms learning by reducing expectations, and they claim that actual accomplishments are the only real source of self-esteem. I disagree: I believe praising students’ work is the true source of self-esteem, as it helps them become more independent. When students are praised for their efforts, they gain the ability to work independently more efficiently, build greater confidence, and learn more effectively.

First, praising a student’s work helps them complete tasks more efficiently. It shows them they are capable of working on their own and preparing for successful future careers. When someone is recognised for their efforts, it boosts their mood and motivates them to take on more work. However, students should only be praised if they have put genuine effort into their assignments. Praising work that lacks effort would only encourage them to stop trying altogether, since they would realise they can get the same recognition as peers who worked hard and cared about earning good grades for their dedication.

Second, high self-confidence allows students to work more consistently and put in more effort, because they know they are capable of earning good grades. When a student is willing to invest time and energy into their work, they deserve more praise. Recognising their efforts builds their self-confidence further, which in turn helps them learn more. A student’s genuine desire to learn is the strongest form of motivation, and it lets them complete more work efficiently, with greater confidence in their abilities.

Third, students who show a strong desire to learn, stay on task, pay attention in class, submit work on time, and put consistent effort into their studies should always be recognised and praised. These behaviours show maturity and a clear goal to graduate and build a successful career. Students who put in this level of effort prove their maturity through their commitment to learning. In contrast, many other students do not care about graduating: for them, being popular, ignoring teachers, disrupting lessons, and doing whatever they want matters more than getting an education.

Strong self-confidence, independence, and a willingness to learn more are all positive outcomes of praising students’ work. When teachers show appreciation for their students, it demonstrates that they care about them and are willing to help them push forward and be there when they need support. This makes students want to come to class every day and engage with lessons, as they find their teacher enjoyable to be around and good at working with students. For all these reasons, praising students’ work is highly beneficial.

Didyou know that 80% of students who attend after-school programs and receive extra academic support achieve better results than those who do not participate? These programs help learners who need additional guidance to succeed, boost their grades, and provide extra time to finish missing assignments and homework.

When a student misses a class session and falls behind on the lesson, they have the chance to stay after school with their teacher to learn the missed content and finish any outstanding work they did not complete during class. Lots of students also stay to study with friends and teachers ahead of exams, getting support with challenging topics that improve their grades and help them succeed later in life. It also gives teachers a chance to explain lessons in detail without disrupting regular class time or leaving other students confused.

Completing overdue work during normal class hours can be difficult, but after-school programs give students the time to finish these tasks with help from teachers and peers, and ask questions about anything they do not understand. Some students also need extra time to finish tests or quizzes, so staying after school is the only way to complete these without losing points or hurting their grades.

Some students argue that staying after school is a waste of time with no real benefits, and others do not care about missing work or skipped classes. However, this is not true. Attending these sessions is a far better way to improve grades, and it is a valuable opportunity, as teachers give up their own time to help students finish missing work, go over lessons again so everyone understands the content, and avoid confusion or failing their courses.

In retrospect, after-school programs are a valuable opportunity that most schools provide, letting students get extra help from teachers to finish missing work, succeed in school, and boost their grades. This is why we should persuade more students to attend these sessions for support — and why I am in favor of school after-school programs.

Showing off stunning natural landscapes, historic temples, unique cultural traditions, diverse local cuisines, traditional clothing, and the rights all citizens enjoy can all make a strong impression that encourages them to plan a trip.

To sum up, making an impression means acting in a way that grabs someone’s attention for a particular purpose. This could be convincing someone to adopt your religious beliefs, encouraging them to vote for a specific political party and pick a strong leader for their country, or persuading them to visit your home country by sharing its best qualities.

Think about a young learner sitting at the kitchen table for all their lessons, with no classmates in sight. How would their parents feel about this setup? Is learning at home really more valuable for a child than attending a public school? The answer is clear: students gain far more from going to a public school instead of studying at home, as they get to stay physically active, access reliable learning resources, and learn to exchange ideas with others.

First, public schools are great at encouraging students to stay active. Teachers make a point of getting kids moving, knowing that physical activity is key to both health and focus. A perfect example is physical education (PE) classes, which are a core part of most school curriculums. These classes give students structured time to exercise, train, and play games, whether indoors or outdoors. Even students who are reluctant to join in are often motivated to participate by fun, low-pressure activities led by their teachers.

Beyond keeping students active, public schools also provide easy access to the information and support learners need. Having clear, accurate resources helps students fully grasp what they are learning, which is why it is so important for them to have access to expert guidance. For instance, many schools offer after-school tutoring sessions where students can get extra help preparing for tests or working through tough topics. Teachers are always there to answer questions, and students should never hesitate to ask for support—educators will always do their best to explain things clearly.

Public schools also give students the chance to share ideas with their peers, which is another major benefit. Working with others helps learners grow, especially when they collaborate on group assignments. Most students enjoy partnering up or working in small teams to solve problems, as they get to hear different perspectives and debate their views. They can listen to classmates’ opinions, figure out if they agree or disagree, and learn from each other. Being part of a group is always more helpful than studying alone with no one to bounce ideas off.

To sum up, public schools help students stay active, access the information they need, and share ideas with others. This is exactly why attending a public school is so important for children. Homeschooling is very different, and it can be extremely challenging for many learners: they work alone without partners, get less physical activity, and may not get all the expert information they need from their parents. Just imagine a student in that situation—how would they feel? Public schools are the far better choice for most children. If every student got to learn in a public school setting, we would see a huge positive shift in their futures. Schools build students’ knowledge a little more every single day, and that growth starts with showing up to learn.

Many people argue that first impressions are almost impossible to change, but I disagree completely. I’m convinced that initial perceptions of a person can absolutely shift over time. Most first impressions tend to be inaccurate, based on quick unfair judgments, or entirely on wrong assumptions.

My name is Generic_Name, and I’ve had countless people form first impressions of me — classmates, teachers, even strangers I’ve only met once. Almost every time, their initial take on who I am turns out to be wrong, because the real me is nothing like what they assumed after just one meeting.

First impressions are judgmental 80% of the time. People judge others based on surface-level details: what they wear, what they look like, and how they act in a single moment. I’m a perfect example of this. In middle school, I was known as a troublemaker, but when I started my freshman year of high school, I was too nervous to act like myself at first — it was my first year in a much bigger school, after all. For weeks, my classmates thought I was a quiet, shy kid. Only after I got more comfortable did they start to get to know me, and realize I was still just as much of a troublemaker as I’d been before.

I’ve also been guilty of making these quick judgments myself. Every time a new student joined my school, I’d immediately form an opinion of them based on how they dressed, what they looked like, and how they acted in their first few days. This year, there was a girl — let’s call her Generic_Name — who always wore hunting clothes, had thick glasses, and had a quirky, funny-looking style.

One day, I teased her about her appearance, and she snapped back at me. She ended up sharing her full life story with me, and I felt terrible for judging her so quickly. I apologized right away for what I’d said. Now, whenever I think back to that moment, I remind myself to never make too many assumptions about people I don’t know well yet.

To sum up, I still firmly believe that first impressions can be changed. You just have to be willing to open up and express who you really are. Sometimes that means sharing your life story with people, like you’re telling them the plot of a book, so they can see the real you.

Most students enjoy summer vacation, but some educators think that summer break is too long and students do not retain information as easily as they would in the fall. Because of this a lot of educators think we should have year- round school years. This would be shorter breaks in the summer (3-4 weeks) and longer more spread-out breaks throughout the year. I disagree with this statement and believe that summer break should stay the way it is.

The first reason I disagree with this statement is that it would ruin certain summer activities or even business plans. Think about all the activities in the summer that kids usually take part in, this could be sports, some sort of trip, etc. All of these activities students would preferably do during summer break. They have this preference because they see the summer as a perfect time to do all these activities without having to balance their education as well. They can put most of their time on this activity. The same preference applies to things like summer jobs or internships. During the summer they can learn important values like how to save and earn money. Or if a certain student has a chosen career path they can explore this career path by going in a internship for that spesicifc job. For all of these activities students at the very least would be discouraged to participate in if there was a year-round school year.

The second and probably most important reason is pertaining to the students mental health. An article, by Complex News writing about kids mental health stated, that over 40% of kids by the end of their freshmen year in high school are depressed or overall feel exhausted and depleted mentally. The article continues to say that this number from the time of their freshmen year only increases after each school year. Students use the summer break as a way for their brain to refresh from the long almost ten month school year. Students need this time to relax their brain and get ready for the next year of education. As a student, I can say that during school my brain goes into this state where I am mostly just focused on school work. And I can admit that my brain at multiple points during the year is worn down and damaged by always be in this state. My brain does not get a chance to heal from this until the summer, when school is over. So if we were to hypothetically have a year-round school year, this would mean that the brain would also be in this damaged state year round. If this were the case than the brain of the student would eventually just break and shut down. No student should have to experience that because of a year- round school year.

Although the strongest reason for this year-round school year is that students cannot properly retain enough information for the next school year, I think I have a much stronger counter claim and solution to this problem. A very simple way to take care of the problem of retaining information, is to make mandatory (but simple) assignments from the previous year for the student to complete so that they don't forget this information. This way students can have their long summer break to refresh their brain and do their activities, without them having to forget any information. You get the best of both worlds with no need for a year-round school year.

In conclusion I think my assertions for the summer break to stay the way it is is much stronger than year-round school year argument. Having a year-round school year would be unnecessarily tedious and dangerous as it would negatively affect summer activities and mental health. As someone said once upon a time "Don't fix it if it ain't broke."

While most students look forward to summer vacation, some teachers and school administrators argue that the long break makes it harder for students to remember what they learned during the school year, compared to the fall term. For this reason, many educators support switching to a year-round school calendar, which would cut summer break down to just 3 or 4 weeks and add longer, more spread-out breaks throughout the rest of the year. I strongly disagree with this proposal, and believe the traditional summer break should remain unchanged.

My first objection to year-round schooling is that it would disrupt popular summer activities and even hurt small businesses that rely on the summer rush. Consider all the typical summer pastimes students take part in: sports camps, family trips, outdoor hobbies. Most students choose to do these during summer break specifically because they don’t have to split their time between these activities and schoolwork. They can devote all their energy to whatever they’re doing, whether that’s improving at a sport or traveling to a new place. The same logic applies to summer jobs and internships. These give students hands-on experience with managing money, like learning to save earnings or budget expenses. For students who already have a clear career goal, summer internships let them test out that field and gain relevant experience. If school ran year-round, far fewer students would bother signing up for these opportunities, since they’d have to squeeze them in around classes instead of having a full block of free time. This would also hurt businesses that run summer programs, since fewer students would be available to join them.

The second, and arguably most critical, reason to keep traditional summer break is the impact on students’ mental health. A report from Complex News on children’s mental wellbeing found that more than 40% of students feel depressed or completely mentally drained by the end of their freshman year of high school. The report adds that this percentage only rises with each additional year of schooling. Students rely on summer break to give their brains a proper rest after nearly ten months of non-stop classes and homework. This downtime lets them relax and mentally prepare for the next school year. Speaking as a student myself, I know that during the school year, my mind is almost entirely focused on assignments and exams. I can admit that multiple times a year, my brain feels worn out and strained from staying in that constant work mode. It only gets a chance to recover once summer starts and classes end. If we switched to a year-round calendar, students’ brains would stay in that exhausted, overworked state all year long. Eventually, this constant strain could lead to total burnout, which no student should ever have to experience just because of a school schedule change.

Supporters of year-round schooling often point to the main benefit: that students forget too much material over a long summer break. However, I have a far more effective solution to this problem that doesn’t require drastically changing the entire school calendar. Schools could assign mandatory, but very simple, review work based on the previous year’s lessons for students to complete over the summer. This way, students still get their long break to rest and pursue their summer activities, but they won’t lose the information they worked hard to learn. It’s a win-win situation that makes switching to a year-round schedule completely unnecessary.

In conclusion, the arguments for keeping traditional summer break are far stronger than those supporting a year-round school calendar. Switching to year-round schooling would be an unnecessary hassle that could harm students’ ability to join summer activities and damage their mental health. As the common saying goes, “Don’t fix it if it ain’t broke.”

I strongly disagree with the idea of lengthening the school day by an extra hour and a half. This change would be too much to handle for both students and teachers. It is also deeply unfair to ask teachers to work longer hours than they already do. Another issue is that students at our school would be stuck in class longer while nearly every other school lets their students go home earlier. When students get too little sleep, their grades and in-class performance drop quickly, and the same problem applies to teachers, whose energy and focus also suffer without enough rest.

Adding 90 minutes to the daily schedule would leave students feeling exhausted, since they need time both to review their lessons and get proper rest. This extra time would also ruin after-school plans: students would be too tired to take part in activities, or they would not have finished homework due the next day. Most students already wake up very early for class, and when they get home, they are often desperate for a nap, but they cannot rest because they have household chores to finish.

On top of that, students would have no time left to finish the chores their parents ask them to do, as they are already busy with homework or sports practices like soccer, swimming, or gymnastics. Extending the school day by an hour and a half would disrupt their balance of schoolwork, hobbies, and sleep, leaving them overwhelmed.

Teachers would also be unfairly burdened by this change. They would have to stay at school later than usual, leaving them with almost no free time to spend with their families, including their own children. They would also have to do even more work preparing class materials and grading assignments. This means they would be stuck at school for extra hours instead of being with the people they care about.

For all these reasons, I am completely against adding an extra hour and a half to the length of the school day.

Back on September 2, 2015, Generic_Name was starting his first year of high school. He already had a clear long-term goal: becoming a doctor, though he was unsure which type of medical professional he wanted to be. Before his high school classes even began, he spent time researching different medical specialties to narrow down his choice. Eventually, he settled on surgery, completed all required coursework for the field, and years later, he now works as a surgeon. He earns a high salary, lives in a comfortable home, and is living the life he always imagined.

In many communities, it is common for students to decide on a career path before they start high school. I strongly agree with this expectation. Choosing a career early lets students plan the steps they need to take to reach their goal, and it also helps reduce unnecessary stress later on. These are the core reasons I believe committing to a career by high school entry is a smart move.

The first major benefit of picking a career before high school is that it opens up clear opportunities to prepare for the job. To land your dream role, you first need to understand what the work actually involves, which often means looking into different workplaces or shadowing professionals in the field. You will also know exactly which classes to prioritize: for instance, a student who wants to be a history teacher should focus on history courses, while someone aiming for a medical career will need to take as many science classes as possible. Another key opportunity is that you can start planning for long-term goals, like earning a good income, early on. This is exactly why deciding on a career before high school helps you access all the resources you need to reach your professional goals.

The second key reason to choose a career early is that it cuts down on stress significantly. When you have a clear goal in mind, you feel more in control, and the more clarity you have, the less anxious you will feel. You will also know exactly which classes you need to take, so you will not waste time or energy on extra courses that have nothing to do with your plans. If you ever feel stuck, do not be afraid to ask for help, since teachers and family members are always willing to support you. The more you reach out for guidance, the less overwhelmed you will feel. This is why identifying a career by high school entry helps students avoid unnecessary stress.

Some people disagree with this view, arguing that it is fine to wait until after high school starts to pick a career. They often claim that high school is a time to socialize with friends, and that students do not need to worry about their grades or future plans yet. Others believe their true passion will suddenly appear later, maybe even in their final year of high school. But this approach is risky. Waiting until senior year to figure out your path makes it hard to choose the right college, leaves you without a clear plan, and will only lead to more stress in the long run.

To sum up, many societies expect students to have a clear career idea by the time they start high school, and I fully support this expectation. There are several good reasons for this: it gives students access to the opportunities they need to prepare for their job, starting with knowing which classes to take. It also helps them avoid feeling overly stressed about their future. When you know what you want to do, you feel more secure, and the more clarity you have, the less stress you will face. These are the core reasons why I agree that students should commit to a career path before entering high school.

School is a period when students are given various assignments, and it is up to each individual to complete them. How well you handle your schoolwork shapes both how your teachers perceive you and how much you develop over time. That said, there is one common school practice I strongly disagree with: teachers praising students who are not putting in their full effort. I believe genuine self-esteem grows out of real achievement, and it is unfair to encourage those who are not truly trying their best.

The first reason I object to this method of building students’ confidence is that it makes them overly reliant on others. These students grow used to having someone constantly lift them up, but the real world does not work that way—you cannot depend on others to carry you through every challenge. They come to expect praise even for the smallest, most minimal efforts, and grow attached to that constant praise. What would happen if that support suddenly disappeared? Without anyone to motivate them or hand out unearned praise, they would likely stop putting in any effort at all.

My second concern is that these students never experience the satisfaction of genuine accomplishment. When you work hard to reach a goal, you feel a real sense of pride, happiness, or relief once you finish it. If teachers praise students for half-hearted efforts, they never learn to push themselves to actually complete tasks, because they already feel like they have done enough. They lose the drive to keep going, which will hurt them later in life. In the future, they will likely fail assignments and bigger tasks, because they believe their low-effort work is good enough when it is not.

To be fair, there are some benefits to teachers motivating students. It can help them build confidence and self-esteem, which serves them well later in life. A teacher’s encouragement might even inspire students to motivate their peers to work hard too. I just think teachers should not go overboard: praising a student just for writing their name on a paper, for example, is taking things too far. Sometimes being strict is necessary. Picture yourself stuck in a classroom with bare walls all around, after a long, frustrating day of dealing with strict teachers, noisy classmates, and endless schoolwork. Now imagine you have to stay in that same room for an extra 90 minutes. How would you feel by the time you finally get to leave? On top of that, students will struggle to perform well when longer days mean even more assignments and homework to complete. This is exactly why the school board should reject plans to add an extra hour and a half to the regular school day.

First, many students take part in sports teams, clubs, and other after-school activities. After a full day of classes plus an extra 90 minutes, they will be completely exhausted, which means they cannot perform at their best. For example, my friend plays soccer, and after her school day was extended by an hour and a half, she fainted during practice because both her mind and body were completely worn out. What’s more, students will get home from school or after-school activities well after sunset. This is not only unfair to them, but also creates safety risks for young people traveling home in the dark.

Next, longer school days leave students with no spare time to spend with family or friends, as they will be buried under homework and projects. Teachers face the same problem: they will have no time to be with their own children, since they have tests to grade and endless paperwork to finish. Similarly, students will lose all motivation to relax or have fun, because schoolwork will be the only thing on their minds. They will also have far less time to get enough sleep each night.

Furthermore, constant exhaustion will eventually leave students with no energy to even attend school. Over time, this can lead to depression and a persistently negative mood. Many students may even grow to resent school so much that they stop wanting to come at all, which puts them in a very high-risk situation.

In conclusion, the school board must not approve adding an extra hour and a half to the school day. Longer class time means more work, which will make it hard for students to function well. Many students have sports and other after-school commitments, but they will get home after dark, which is unsafe. Both students and teachers will lose time to spend with their families and friends, as they are overwhelmed with assignments and grading work. Students will also lose motivation to enjoy their free time, and will get less sleep. Eventually, this exhaustion will leave students with no energy to attend school.

To many middle schoolers, high school feels like a place where they can finally do whatever they want, just one step away from heading off to college. While that’s a common perception, the reality is that high school students have to juggle countless required courses, all meant to bring them closer to their future goals. But classes like art, music, and drama offer something that standard core subjects simply can’t. They act as a welcome break from the pressure of writing lengthy essays or solving complex math problems, letting students relax, have fun with friends, and explore creative activities like singing, painting, or acting. More than that, these courses teach young people how to socialize and communicate effectively with their peers.

High school is far more demanding than many people realize. Students often feel overwhelmed trying to pass all their required courses, prepare for standardized tests like SOLs, and get ready for college all at once. That’s exactly where creative classes come in: they provide a much-needed outlet to cut down on that stress. The atmosphere in these courses is almost always upbeat and relaxed, giving students a chance to learn by interacting with others and enjoying themselves. You never know— a student who never thought they’d like music might take a few months of classes and realize they’re passionate about it, even deciding to pursue a career as a musician. The same goes for art and drama. These classes don’t just offer a break from the pressure of advanced core subjects; they also teach students lessons they never expected to pick up.

Think about an extremely shy student who has never felt confident enough to speak up in class, not even to ask a question during math— a subject where most students end up asking at least one question per unit anyway. If that student never learns how to communicate properly, how will they ever give a speech later in life, or find the courage to speak up for themselves in a big company? Even if they have incredible talent and a brilliant mind, they will struggle to succeed. Being able to express yourself is a basic requirement in life if you want to keep moving forward. Nothing comes easy, but communication is a social skill everyone has to master.

Of course, not everyone agrees with this view. Many people argue that these classes are a waste of time, claiming students get nothing out of them and just use the 90 minutes to hang out with friends and procrastinate. But what about students who have no friends, who sit quietly in the corner of the classroom and never say a word, even when teachers try to get them to participate? These are the students no one ever hears from, sometimes even the ones teachers don’t notice are there at all. Shouldn’t schools care about these young people? Shouldn’t school be a place where they can grow, spread their wings, and start chasing their own unique opportunities?

I once heard a line in a commercial while watching TV with my mom: “Tu voz abre puertas,” which translates to “Your voice opens doors.” But those doors will never swing open if you don’t speak up, ask questions, and seek out the answers that will push you further in life. No matter how smart a student is, if they can’t make themselves noticed, their brilliant mind will go to waste.

In today’s fast-paced, competitive world, being skilled in just one area is rarely enough, yet most people prefer to stick to routines where they feel safe and comfortable. It is common for individuals to avoid trying new tasks, even when they have already mastered their current responsibilities. So what is the best way to keep making progress? Ralph Waldo Emerson’s well-known idea offers a clear answer: stepping outside familiar habits to explore new fields is key, because repeating the same actions over and over will never lead to real growth.

Take the working world as an example: many roles require people to branch out into new areas to improve. Photographers, for instance, usually focus on taking still images, but those who also learn to film video can move into cinematography or even work as visual journalists. They recognize that trying new related fields is the most effective way to advance their careers. This same logic applies to personal growth too. A student who moves to a foreign country to continue their studies, or a doctor who researches a new branch of medicine to find treatments for rare illnesses, both step outside their usual routines. Exploring areas that feel completely unrelated to their daily work helps them grow in meaningful ways, proving that trying new things benefits everyone.

What’s more, growth is impossible without making changes. Consider skilled tradespeople like carpenters or construction workers: many dream of starting their own businesses, but they fear failing. Even though they are experts at their craft, they are too nervous to take on new roles like managing a company. These entrepreneurs should take the risk to launch their ventures and invest in new tools or equipment to expand. If they just keep doing the same hands-on work without putting money or effort into growth, their business will never get bigger. Some people argue that sticking to one task makes you a true expert, like professional athletes who practice the same moves daily. But even top athletes have to adjust their skills and learn new techniques constantly. If they never changed their routine, they would never stay competitive or become the best in their sport. This same principle holds true for any field where someone wants to succeed.

To sum up, Ralph Waldo Emerson’s view is completely correct: people can never reach their full potential if they keep doing the exact same thing day after day. To grow, everyone should push past the tasks they are used to and try new things. In most cases, taking that first step into unfamiliar territory brings clear rewards. Change is always a positive force in life, as long as you have the will to embrace it. Success does not come from mastering just one skill, but from building expertise in many different areas.

I largely disagree with the idea of schools offering distance learning as an option for students to attend classes from home via online platforms or video calls, though this has nothing to do with the fact that I currently study at a public high school. There are several clear reasons for my stance.

First, remote learning can damage students’ communication abilities. When you take classes online, you are stuck at home instead of being on campus, so your only real interaction is with your teacher. I have never taken an online course myself, so I cannot say for sure whether it is better to have no peer contact or to socialize regularly, but I personally believe it is harmful for students to only engage with their instructor. Other students often grasp concepts that you might struggle with, and they can explain things in a way that makes sense to you. If you are not physically present with your classmates, you lose out on this kind of support.

My second, and perhaps most strongly held, objection is that online learning also harms students’ ability to participate actively in their education. At my school, we do lots of hands-on activities linked to the material we are studying, and these make the content stick in our minds far better than just listening to a lecture. It is also much easier to ask questions and clear up confusion when you are face to face with your teacher, rather than sending emails or using other messaging tools. Teachers might not reply to messages right away, which can leave you stuck on a topic and hurt your grades. For this reason, I think in-person clarification is always better.

Finally, studying from home makes it far too easy to get lazy and skip classes, which can badly hurt your grades. This is a big risk if you are not a highly productive, dedicated student. For example, I know I would struggle with online learning because I tend to be lazy. I would almost certainly miss classes, either by sleeping in or coming up with other flimsy excuses. That said, there are plenty of very organized, responsible people who can handle this setup. For students who are fully committed to their education and able to stay on track, distance learning can work well.

These are my main reasons for mostly disagreeing with offering distance learning as a standard option for students. I do think it is a good thing that schools provide remote learning for people who have a valid reason for not attending classes in person, but personally, I do not support making it a widespread choice.

Relying on technology has cut down on face-to-face human interaction, and this trend has a harmful impact on people. Most notably, it damages basic social skills in today’s youth, makes online bullying easier, and lets internet trolling run wild.

First, technology gets in the way of students developing proper social skills. For instance, many students walk into classrooms glued to their phones all day long. Even during class time, instead of chatting with peers, they sit at computers playing video games. This habit traps people in their own little digital bubbles, stopping them from understanding both themselves and the people around them.

Second, the internet makes it far too easy to bully others. People can post humiliating videos that destroy someone’s self-esteem, even pushing them to attempt suicide. Others might post embarrassing photos of someone drunk, tag them in these posts on Facebook and Instagram. I once watched a YouTube video about a girl from Australia who was harassed online and at her school. The problem got so bad her family had to move house at least three times to escape the abuse.

Lastly, unmoderated chat rooms can put people in contact with dangerous strangers, including serial killers. Social media also spreads fake news and rumors fast: for example, there were false posts on Twitter claiming Michelle Obama was running for president in 2020.

To sum up, cutting back on in-person contact harms young people by damaging their basic social skills, enables online bullying, and fuels internet trolling. In my view, everyone should switch off their phones for one or two days a week, and go out to eat with friends without bringing their devices. At school, teachers could stand outside classrooms with a collection box for phones, so students can’t use them during lessons. Online bullying often spills over into real life and drags on far longer than it would otherwise. We need stricter rules to tackle this, as overusing technology stops people from talking openly about the problems they face.

If a person only ever practices skills they have already mastered, they will make no progress at all. They will stay stuck in the same position, with no room to grow. Stepping out of your comfort zone and trying new activities is the only way to develop. There are three main reasons for this: first, exploring different tasks makes you more capable across many areas. Second, picking up new skills boosts your overall competence. Finally, you might discover hidden talents you never knew you had. It is far better to try new things than to stay stagnant and never improve.

The first key reason trying new things helps you grow is that it makes you stronger in areas you never focused on before. Building competence in multiple different skills can push you to levels you never imagined reaching. For example, someone who tries different sports might become not just a good runner, but a well-rounded athlete who excels at many physical activities. Once you have a wide range of strengths, you can even support friends who are struggling with tasks you have mastered. When you become a capable, well-rounded person, there are very few challenges you cannot handle.

Next, learning new skills directly improves your overall ability. Picking up unfamiliar talents can benefit you in countless ways. Trying a variety of new activities can even improve your physical and mental health, as you stay active and engaged. As you start to notice your own progress, seeing clear results will boost your motivation to keep going. If you master many different skills, you may even be able to teach others who look up to you and want to learn from your experience. Improving your abilities in this way is an incredibly rewarding process.

Finally, trying new things lets you discover talents you never realized you had. Realizing you can do something you once thought was impossible will come as a big surprise. When you uncover more skills you are capable of, you can take part in far more activities than before. People with a wider range of abilities have a clear advantage, as they can complete tasks that others cannot. It is surprising how many people go through life without ever realizing they are capable of things they never thought possible.

To sum up, trying new things allows you to become far stronger and more capable than you are today. Learning new skills will boost your overall competence, and you may even discover new hobbies, sports, or talents you never imagined you could master.

Have you ever met someone new, or sat for a high-stakes job interview, and left them with either a positive or negative impression of you? Some people argue that first impressions can always be fixed, since everyone deserves a second chance. Others, however, believe that first impressions are permanent, as they reveal a person’s true nature. I agree with this second group: first impressions are impossible to change, because they reflect your personality, your attitude, and your core character.

First, first impressions show your personality, which is why they are so hard to alter. A friend of mine wore completely unsuitable, messy clothes to a formal job interview and was rejected immediately because of her outfit. Months later, she still couldn’t find work anywhere, no matter how many applications she sent out. This proves you need to dress properly and mind your tone when meeting others, to show you’re respectful, responsible, and mature. First impressions don’t just show personality, though – they also reveal your attitude.

Your attitude is another part of first impressions that is nearly impossible to undo. I used to be rude, pick fights over small things, and insult people even when they needed my help. Once, an elderly woman asked for my assistance with carrying her groceries. I refused and insulted her, and she warned I’d face hard times in life, but I ignored her and walked away. Years later, I tried to change my ways, but people still blamed me for every problem that popped up, even when I wasn’t involved. I even wished someone had been rude to me back then to make me see sense. That’s when I remembered the old woman’s warning. I wanted to apologize, but she’d passed away by then. I’m left with the weight of that unkind moment, almost like a curse. That taught me a key lesson: always respect everyone, even strangers.

First impressions also lay bare exactly who you are as a person.

A recent news story illustrates this. A woman was caught on camera licking an ice cream she’d taken from a store fridge, then putting it back without paying. This single act destroyed her public reputation. Now everyone knows what she did, and what kind of person she is. She didn’t just humiliate herself – she brought shame to her family and home country. This proves first impressions cannot be changed.

Some say first impressions can be altered because everyone gets a second chance. But this is rarely true. Even if you change your behavior, most people stick to their first impression of you. Some might think you’re having an off day, others might notice you’ve improved, but plenty never let go of that initial judgment. For this reason, first impressions are essentially impossible to change.

In short, your character, true self, and behavior are all clear in first impressions, which are incredibly hard to shift. Most stick for good. Think: when you meet someone new, will you be respectful or rude? Appropriate or inappropriate? Will you take responsibility for how you come across, especially to people older than you? That first choice will stay with you.

When weighing the pros of solo work against collaborating with a team, which option do you think is more valuable? For me, group work comes out on top. It lets you finish tasks faster, pool creative thoughts, build teamwork skills, and even save time when tight deadlines are approaching.

First off, tackling tasks with a group speeds up completion. You don’t have to stress over every single detail on your own, since different members can handle separate parts of the project at the same time. Trying to do everything solo, by contrast, drags the process out, and you might run out of time to finish before a deadline. When everyone chips in, the workload feels lighter, and you’re not shouldering all the responsibility alone. Working by yourself can also be incredibly stressful, as you have to generate every idea and solve every problem yourself. With a team, you can split up tasks fairly, which makes the whole process move much faster.

Second, sharing ideas with teammates is a huge plus. It’s also more enjoyable to work alongside others, hearing all kinds of different perspectives. Maybe one person in your group has a really creative streak and can come up with solutions you’d never think of alone. If you don’t exchange ideas, there’s little point in being part of a team at all — everyone should have a chance to speak up and contribute. Working solo means you lose out on that extra support and feedback; when you finally present your work, others might have critiques or suggestions you never considered. Solo work can also feel isolating and tiring: if you get stuck on a problem, there’s no one there to lend a hand. Plus, handling every task by yourself often means juggling too many things at once, making it harder to finish on time.

Lastly, group work builds teamwork skills, and we all know that working together usually leads to better results than going it alone. Collaborating well with others shows that every member can take charge and lead in their own way. It’s also a lot more fun: you might get paired with new people, or work with friends you already know, which makes the whole effort feel more engaging. When everyone focuses on their assigned section while others handle theirs, the entire project moves along much faster.

To sum up, I’d always choose group work over working alone. Teaming up makes tasks feel easier and cuts down on the amount of work each person has to do. I’d never want to work solo, since I’d have no one to bounce ideas off or share my thoughts with. Handling an entire project by yourself is tough, and the final result might not turn out as well as you hoped. You also get far fewer ideas when working alone, while a group brings tons of different perspectives to the table. Solo work is rarely as fun as collaborating with others, too. With a team, you can split the workload fairly, but doing everything yourself usually makes the task twice as hard. That’s why I’m convinced group work is far more beneficial than working on your own.

While some people argue that schools should not offer online classes, saying that students might get others to do their work for them when they are not in a physical classroom, so they learn nothing, the truth is that schools should definitely provide online learning options. Most students today have part-time jobs, and far too many end up dropping out of school entirely to work full-time. Offering online classes would let these students keep studying while still holding down their jobs.

There is strong evidence supporting the case for online classes. Research shows that 80% of high school students have part-time jobs after school. They get home late, still have homework to do, and end up sleeping far too little. Then they have to wake up by 7 a.m. to get to school on time, which is really hard. Many fall asleep in class and have no motivation to do any schoolwork. Online classes fix this, since students can take their lessons whenever it works for them.

Another common problem is that many students have to walk to school. In winter, they have to deal with bitter cold weather, which often makes them fall ill. Last year, I saw a student break his arm after slipping on a snowy, slippery sidewalk on his way to school. I also watched a boy get beaten up by a group of guys while he was walking home from classes. If these students could take online classes, they would not have to make that daily trip, so these kinds of incidents would not happen.

Additional research highlights how effective online classes are. It shows that 70% of students who take online courses go on to succeed in their studies, which proves this learning format really helps learners. They can get more rest at home, and do not have to wake up early every morning.

In conclusion, schools should provide online learning options. Colleges and universities already offer online courses, and the majority of students who take these classes go on to succeed. This is the most helpful thing schools can do for their students.

Who would actually choose to stay inside all day? Most people would much rather get outside! There are tons of fun ways to fill your day in the fresh air, like working out with your friends. Plus, you’re not just handing out refreshing drinks to people, you’re also earning some extra cash!

You can lounge on a floatie, play games like tag in the water, or even try out new water activities you never thought you’d be able to do.

Teenagers also really like putting on their headphones and walking around their neighborhood. It’s a great way to explore the local area and get familiar with nearby streets, plus it helps take their mind off any worries or stress they have.

Parks are another favorite spot, especially for younger kids who love running around playing games like hide-and-seek or tag. Teens like going there too—some bring a book to read in the grass, or pack a picnic with friends. Picnics are always a hit because you get to chat with your friends and snack at the same time!

All of these are great ways to make the most of your time outside, instead of sitting in front of the TV day after day!

People need to grow up, be responsible, act fairly, and be happy.

People need to act like adults: take responsibility, treat others fairly, and focus on staying positive.

The argument related to distance learning has often been a topic of interest to many people. Nowadays, many scholars support the idea of distance learning and it has been getting a great acceptance among many societies. Although some people think distance learning make students careless in doing their work, nevertheless, students would benefit from being able to attend classes from home because it saves the time they would spend by going to school and makes them more effective and efficient in their technology usage.

For example, it can take ten to forty minutes for a student to go to school. This shows that going to school takes students' precious time and makes them unproductive. Clearly, no one wants to waste his/her time on transportation.

For instance, students who spend their time on technological materials know more how to accomplish technology related tasks in a short period of time compared to students with no experience. This proves that taking online classes prepare students for higher education and learning. Obviously, the use of technology is growing fast in this age.

Overall, students would benefit from being able to attend classes from home. This is because distance learning saves the time they would spend by going to school and makes them more effective and efficient in their technology usage. In conclusion, schools have to offer distance learning as an option for students to attend classes from home.

A lot of people think they should ask experts or authority figures for advice when facing big life decisions. Others prefer to make their own choices instead.

Choosing your own path is valuable because it lets you learn from your own errors. When things go wrong, you figure out how to pick yourself up and keep going. People who make their own choices understand the potential outcomes of their actions, and this helps them grow as individuals while building the skills to overcome any challenges they face. That said, it is not wrong to ask for advice sometimes—older people often have more life experience in certain areas, after all.

First, making mistakes helps you learn not to repeat them. If others just tell you what to do, you never learn to fix your own errors. Asking for help is fine, but don’t let others make every choice for you. If you need support, watch how the person you ask handles the problem. Everyone makes mistakes, so you must learn to decide for yourself eventually.

Second, people whose parents made every choice for them struggle when parents are no longer around. When hard times come, they want their parents’ help but don’t know how to cope alone, since they are used to adults doing everything for them. They never learn to pick themselves up and handle tasks independently. Relying on others to solve every problem leaves you stuck when the same issue comes up again with no one to guide you.

Third, people who regularly make their own choices already understand the possible consequences of their actions, and they know how to overcome those outcomes and grow as a person. Many people avoid making their own decisions because they are scared of what might happen, but facing that fear is exactly how you mature. This is also how you become a better, more capable person in the future. If you are too afraid of the results of your own choices to make them at all, it means you have not yet fully grown up.

In conclusion, everyone makes mistakes, and people who make their own choices learn from them. You avoid repeating errors by experiencing them firsthand—if someone never makes a mistake, it means someone else guided them through life. No one is perfect, and we grow through our own decisions. People used to others making every choice for them don’t know how to pick themselves up in hard times. Parents and mentors won’t always hold your hand, so you must learn to stand alone. Those who make their own decisions know consequences exist, but they can handle them, grow, and become better people. For these reasons, making your own choices is best. Asking for help is fine, but don’t rely on others for every decision.

Dear Principal, I am writing this letter to share my thoughts on the proposal to switch our school’s lunch menu to a more nutritious, health-focused option. I strongly believe this change would be a positive step, as it would cut down students’ intake of unhealthy foods, support their overall health, and motivate them to build better eating habits.

Right now, many students eat unhealthy meals at school almost every day. Switching to a healthier menu would directly reduce how much junk food they consume regularly. Eating poor-quality, processed food day after day can harm students in countless ways. For one, it raises their risk of developing serious conditions like heart disease, or even obesity at a very young age. Beyond helping students, this menu change would also benefit teachers and school staff, who would also eat less unhealthy food each day.

A healthier lunch menu would also help students stay in better physical shape, as it would provide the proteins and nutrients they need to grow properly. This would boost their performance in both sports and their regular classes. Another plus is that it would let students try new dishes, instead of the same repetitive meals they have eaten year after year. It is also important to note that this change is not meant to force students to eat foods they dislike, but rather to help them maintain good health.

I know some students might object to this change at first, since it would remove some of their favorite menu items. But in the long run, it will do them a lot of good. It will push them to start eating healthier, which benefits them both now and in the years to come. It could also inspire them to encourage their friends and family to adopt better eating habits, helping everyone avoid diet-related illnesses caused by too much unhealthy food.

To sum up, I firmly believe switching to a healthier school lunch menu is a great decision. It will reduce students’ consumption of unhealthy food, support their health, and encourage them to build better eating habits. These are the key reasons for my view, and I hope this letter helps you see that rolling out this plan will make our school a better place for everyone. Thank you for your time, Principal.
