I strongly believe that anyone can reach their goals if they put in consistent effort and chase what they truly want. No achievement comes easily—there is always hard work and persistence behind every person who has made it. Everyone should have clear personal goals, and never pursue a path just because others pressure them to. When you work on something you love, even making mistakes feels fulfilling: you’ll work to fix issues and grow. But if you only do what your parents expect of you, you will never feel truly happy with your progress.

School should be a time for students to balance studying with relaxation and fun, not a source of overwhelming pressure. Every child deserves access to the same education and opportunities, and no one should face discrimination. While students should be free to follow their interests, they also need guidance to avoid making harmful choices. The American school system is perfect for students: it lets them study core subjects while also taking classes they are passionate about, giving them the chance to learn more about their chosen career. This balanced approach keeps stress levels manageable and helps students focus on planning for their future.

Some U.S. high schools let students graduate in three years instead of the usual four. But there is no real benefit to finishing early to start work or college sooner. What difference does one extra year really make? All it does is add unnecessary stress and anxiety.

Often, students only choose early graduation because their parents push their own dreams onto their children. I’m not saying parents have bad intentions, but pressuring kids this way is not the right path to success. All students need free time to unwind and forget about school stress, but many parents are so focused on their children becoming top achievers that they won’t let kids enjoy normal childhood experiences. Good grades are not the only measure of success. What matters most is how much you actually learn, and how you will use that knowledge later in life. To graduate early, students have to take summer classes and give up their free evenings—this is not healthy for young people. They need time to rest their minds so they can focus better when they do study. They should also be able to take elective classes they enjoy, as these often help the most with future success.

I have a personal example: my cousin graduated high school early to start college ahead of schedule. He was extremely bright up until his junior year, with a deep understanding of current events that he loved sharing with our family to help us learn too. But by the end of junior year, he became obsessed with graduating early. He worked nonstop and eventually got into college, but now he regrets that choice. He missed out on so much of his senior year, and the gaps in his preparation are causing him a lot of stress now. If all students finish high school in the standard four years, they gain all the necessary knowledge about how college works before they get there. Then they can make informed choices about their future paths. We hear too many stories of students taking their own lives due to academic pressure, so it is clear that no one should force themselves to do things they don’t enjoy. Instead, they should focus on what they truly want to pursue.

Hard work is the key to success, but that does not mean you should grind away at something you hate. Instead, put that effort into achieving goals you actually care about. No one else should dictate what you want to achieve. If you have a clear personal goal and a plan to reach it, stick to that path—that is how you will become a top achiever in your chosen field.

Students should be allowed to use their cellphones for school-related tasks, as having these devices on hand can simplify many parts of their daily classwork. For one, they can act as calculators during math lessons, saving students from struggling with manual calculations. In history class, learners can quickly look up facts they need to complete assignments instead of waiting to access a shared computer. If a teacher plans a phone-based activity, students can participate right away using their own devices. Overall, letting students keep their phones in school makes them more engaged with their schoolwork.

In math class specifically, phones are useful even beyond basic calculations. If a student’s physical calculator runs out of batteries, their phone can step in to help them finish math problems on time. Many phone apps also let users draw straight lines for graphs or geometry work, which speeds up assignments when class time is tight. Teachers can also let students snap photos of board notes, so they have a clear record of what work is due the next day. All in all, phones support students whenever they run into unexpected issues during math lessons.

History class is another area where phones offer clear benefits when used responsibly. If a teacher asks the class to look up which year a major event happened, students can find the answer in seconds using their phones. If a student has to leave class early, they can ask to take a photo of the board notes to copy down later. Teachers can also plan fun, subject-related activities like Kahoot quizzes that students join with their phones. For learners curious about current events, apps like CNN 10 give easy access to reliable news updates. Phones are a huge help for students as long as they are allowed to use them for school tasks.

Of course, some people disagree with letting students use phones in class. They argue that phones are a distraction, and that students should rely on books to find information instead. Others worry that phones make it easier for students to cheat on quizzes and tests. However, not every student will act this way.

To sum up, cellphones should be permitted for educational use, as this makes students more engaged with their work. When teachers let students use their devices for class tasks, it creates more opportunities for interaction between students and teachers. Those who prioritize self-reliance should still turn to experts and authorities for guidance when making major life decisions, rather than relying solely on their own judgment. When we refer to experts, we mean people with far deeper knowledge of a subject than the average person—much like the relationship between a teacher and a student. Teachers have completed years of study and training to qualify to teach subjects like science, putting in significant effort to build their expertise in that field. This is why valuing self-reliance does not mean rejecting outside help: consulting experts can actually help you achieve your goals in life. That said, there are small, personal choices you can absolutely make on your own. For instance, personal choices like whether to drink alcohol or smoke primarily affect only you. For these, you just need to consider who your actions will harm—and as we know, that is only yourself, no one else. If you do not take responsibility for your own choices and well-being, no one else will step in to do it for you.

In my view, self-reliance plays a key role in every person’s life, as it is closely tied to our ability to make choices. There are times when we are convinced we are making the right call every single time, but we have to remember that as humans, no one is perfect. We all make poor choices sometimes. A clear example of this is the teenage years: at that age, people are more vulnerable than at any other stage of life, as they are easily swayed by outside influences. This is exactly when guidance from experts is most needed, and there is no better expert for a young person than their parents. Most parents want the best for their children, so they will share wisdom about what truly matters in life, driven by their love and care. Of course, this is not true of every parent—some do not pay attention to what their sons or daughters are doing—but many do prioritize their children’s well-being. Beyond parents, there are also professional experts who hold formal qualifications in their field, having spent years studying their chosen career. Turning to these professionals can be incredibly helpful for achieving your goals, as their expertise can guide you to make smarter choices throughout your life and grow into a better person.

Poor decisions can have serious negative effects on our lives. We all have to make choices at some point, and while some turn out well, others do not—and occasionally, a choice that seems good at first can lead to harmful outcomes. Take the example of someone who wants to invest their savings to open a restaurant. At first glance, this sounds like a great idea, as many people assume food businesses only generate profit. The reality, though, is that running a restaurant is far more challenging than it seems. Many people do not take the time to think through the potential consequences: they forget to account for all the expenses they will have to cover using the restaurant’s earnings, such as rent, staff wages, and supplies. They also fail to consider that if the business does not take off, they could lose every cent they invested. When people lose all their savings this way, they may fall into deep depression, and in extreme cases, some have even taken their own lives. This is exactly why it is so important to consult experts rather than making the decision to open a business alone. These experts have far more knowledge than the average person, having earned degrees and spent years studying business. They understand the ins and outs of the industry, and can advise you on what steps are best for your situation. With their guidance, you are far more likely to succeed in business and avoid losing your hard-earned money.

Some might argue that making decisions entirely on your own is better, as you will not be able to blame anyone else if things go wrong, and you will learn to take responsibility for your choices. However, there is no need to wait until you make a costly mistake to learn that lesson. As the saying goes, two heads are better than one: seeking expert advice early on can help you make smart choices from the start, rather than fixing bad ones later.

To sum up, seeking guidance from experts is one of the most effective ways to handle major life choices. They are there to share their knowledge and help us improve, which is exactly why these roles exist in our society. We have to accept that we cannot handle every challenge alone, and that turning to experts or our parents for support is not a sign of weakness. To succeed in life, it is worth looking for advice from a variety of trusted sources. While there are times when we need to stand firm on our own, when it comes to making important decisions, being willing to reach out to others and ask for help is the best way to ensure we make choices that serve us well.

I want to work as a guidance counselor because my top priority is supporting young people through their struggles, both at school and in their personal lives. I want every student to know that I’m available to listen to whatever they’re going through, no matter how big or small the issue feels. I plan to share tips on building self-confidence, and remind them that even when everything seems to be falling apart, things will improve eventually. If a student is being bullied, I’ll stand by them and offer guidance, just as I’d help them work through any personal challenge they’re facing.

I also want to help them understand that tough emotions are normal, so they know it’s perfectly fine to feel sad or hurt sometimes, and that those feelings won’t last forever. I’ll teach them they don’t have to let others push them around – they’re in control of their own choices, not anyone else. I’ll encourage them to be brave, take chances, and look at the world from new perspectives. I’ll make sure every student knows there’s always someone in their corner to help them get through moments that leave them angry, upset, or overwhelmed.

My goal is to brighten their days with small moments of joy, and put a smile on their faces when they’re struggling. I was inspired to pursue this career because my own guidance counselor supported me and my family when we needed it most, and I want to pay that kindness forward to other families. Genuine self-esteem grows when people receive encouragement to keep pushing forward and chase their dreams. A close friend once told me that no one should be allowed to make you feel small, and you should always pick yourself back up after a setback. This idea reminds us that we should value our own self-belief over the hurtful words of others that try to hold us back. Building thick skin to ignore negative, doubting people is key, because courage, confidence, and trust in others all play a big role in strengthening self-esteem.

First, having confidence in yourself is essential if you want to reach the goals you set in life. For instance, I felt completely unsure I would pass my SOL exams, but my teacher kept encouraging me to stay positive and avoid overthinking the material. When I finished the test, my teacher told me the next day that I had passed. She later pointed out that I should have more faith in my own abilities. This proves that when someone offers genuine praise, it helps the other person build confidence in themselves.

Second, courage is vital for getting past the fears that can hold us back. Take a relay race, for example: if a runner starts falling behind, it’s easy to give up, thinking “I’ve lost, there’s no way to catch up when I’m already last.” In moments like that, hearing a friend cheer you on and push you to keep trying makes all the difference. The boost of courage they give you keeps you running all the way to the finish line. This shows that supportive words of courage can push someone to keep going even when things look bleak.

Finally, many young teenagers should listen to the advice adults give them, instead of brushing it off. Some people argue that teens should be free to do whatever they want, but that’s incorrect—teens still need to learn important life lessons from older, more experienced people. For example, when I was younger, I shoplifted from stores with a group of friends. My mom warned me to stop hanging out with teens who got into trouble, but I ignored her. We ended up getting caught by store staff, who called our parents to pay for the items we stole. This proves that when teens listen to the praise and guidance from adults, they are more likely to make smart decisions that keep them out of trouble.

In conclusion, words of encouragement can do a lot to help someone feel good about who they are. Whether you’re taking a big test and hoping to pass, playing a sport and wanting to win instead of giving up, or listening to people who always have your back, support from others matters. All of this shows that courage, confidence, and trust in others are key to building strong self-esteem.

Asa member of the Generic_City school community, most students have been shifting their views on the upcoming changes to our cafeteria food options. Recently, the cafeteria announced it will roll out a healthier school lunch menu, which means cutting some of the most popular student dishes and introducing entirely new meat options. I firmly believe this change is a positive step. The school clearly made this decision to encourage students to adopt healthier eating habits and build stronger, more energetic bodies.

Switching to healthier meals will help students realize they need to adjust their diet and daily routines. It will also motivate them to take up sports, just like the school’s athlete students, and eventually lead them to prioritize their health by eating more vegetables, fruits and dairy products. Many will even start going to the gym regularly to build a fit, toned body.

On top of that, eating unhealthy food leads to serious illnesses and social isolation in adulthood. This new menu strategy will also lower the risk of cancer and other conditions later in life, which often stem from poor nutrition knowledge. Carrying excess weight makes daily life harder and limits what people can do. Staying flexible and active is essential for a good quality of life. Statistics show many people die young from heart attacks caused by unhealthy food with harmful ingredients that act like poison.

My main reason for supporting this change is the huge importance of healthy eating. Eating well boosts brain function, so students will notice better academic progress as they focus more in class. It also improves physical appearance, making people look healthier and more attractive. On top of that, it gives us a greater sense of confidence and energy in our daily lives.

To sum up, while many students are in favor of this menu change, there are still plenty who criticize it. I plan to strongly support this initiative by helping other students understand just how valuable it is for their long-term health and success.

Is Ralph Waldo Emerson’s famous quote accurate? He argued that "unless you try to do something beyond what you have already mastered, you will never grow." I fully agree with this idea, as it reminds us that everyone has the potential to pursue greater achievements in their own lives. More than that, coming across this line encourages people to reflect on their personal goals, and whether they are pushing themselves enough to reach new heights. Below, I will explain why Emerson’s words hold true.

To begin with, Emerson’s message has inspired countless people, boosting their self-confidence. A single powerful phrase can shift how people view their own potential, pushing them to aim for ambitious goals and break through limits they once thought were fixed. When people internalize this idea, they start to trust that they can exceed even their own expectations. Take, for instance, those who quit pursuing their dreams early on: without this push to grow, they often lose direction entirely, unsure of what they want to achieve or what they are even capable of.

Beyond that, those who step outside their comfort zones and go beyond their existing limits tend to lead more successful lives. They gain a clear sense of what they can handle, and learn the skills needed to truly succeed. This gives them a sense of capability, making them feel ready to tackle any task set before them. Many report a huge sense of relief, like a weight being lifted, once they realize how much they were missing out on by staying in their comfort zone. For example, many people overthink their goals and create unnecessary obstacles for themselves because they are not willing to push beyond what they already know, rather than because the goals are truly out of reach.

Another key point is that pushing past mastered skills helps people gain far more experience in their field. Once they see the benefits of growth, they actively seek out new challenges to build even more expertise. They want to develop a resilient mindset and a fulfilling, successful way of living. What’s more, people with extensive experience can land job opportunities almost instantly, as their track record proves their ability to grow and adapt. No external factor can stop someone with this mindset from believing they can achieve even more. For instance, those with the most diverse experience face far less difficulty finding stable work.

To sum up, Emerson’s quote plays a vital role in many people’s lives, cementing its place as one of the most motivational lines ever written. It leads people to value themselves far more than they ever thought possible. Anyone who refuses to attempt tasks beyond their current skill set has not yet reached their full potential. While many people have the ability to aim higher, fear holds them back from doing so. Ultimately, the greatest benefit of following Emerson’s advice is the extra professional experience and personal growth people gain along the way.

This essay will explore the key challenges and benefits of both group-based and solo work, with a focus on how these modes of working affect individual team members, rather than the group as a whole. We will first break down how groups function compared to working alone, then look at the specific experiences of people contributing to group projects, including both the advantages they gain and the obstacles they face.

Think back to the last time you had to complete a project. You probably considered several approaches, but the first choice you likely faced was whether to tackle it alone or with others. Most people are familiar with solo work: when you work individually, you are the only person responsible for every part of the task. But groups are a different structure entirely—how are they created, and what rules or patterns govern how they operate?

A group is simply a set of people who join forces to achieve a shared goal or complete a specific task. Group dynamics refers to the structure of the group, the processes it follows, and how well it operates as a unit. These dynamics apply to all kinds of groups, whether they are formal work teams or casual friend groups. Since groups are everywhere in schools, workplaces, and community organizations, understanding how they work is a key part of studying organizational behaviour.

To dig deeper into group dynamics, we look at the reasons groups form in the first place, and how they grow and change over time. Researchers have put forward many different theories to explain these processes.

Group work comes with plenty of benefits, but it also has significant downsides. For one, individual members have far less control over how the task is completed than they would if they were working alone. There is also a common issue where a few group members take over most of the work, while others contribute very little or stop participating entirely. In these cases, the group might still reach its goal, but the less active members do not get the full value from the experience. On the other hand, groups that collaborate well can produce far better results than people working solo. A team brings together a wider range of skills to apply to real-world tasks, and talking through ideas with others can be incredibly helpful for building a deeper understanding of a specific topic.

Working as part of a team also helps you build important interpersonal skills, like clear speaking and active listening. You will also pick up teamwork abilities such as leadership, and learn how to motivate and work well with others. Many of these skills will be useful throughout your time in education, and all of them are highly valuable.

To get the most out of group work, you need to manage your team’s processes effectively.

Should students be required to take online classes from home? Do these classes actually help them in the long run? I strongly believe that students should not have to attend online classes at home.

For one, many students already have part-time jobs, and their schedules are too packed to fit in extra online coursework. There are also people who are not enrolled in traditional schools but choose to take online classes instead — that’s a valid option for them, but it shouldn’t be forced on regular students. Students who work night shifts, for example, have no spare time left for home-based online classes. Another key reason is that schools are meant for academic learning, while home should be a space where students can relax, have fun, and do whatever they like outside of school hours. Students deserve to enjoy their free time when they are not in class, and adding online classes at home eats into that. I personally work night shifts, so I have no time to spare for online classes. A friend of mine takes online classes at home, and he’s found that they take up a big chunk of the free time he used to have for hobbies and rest.

Supporters of mandatory online classes argue that they help students stay focused in school and start planning for their future careers early. But this view is flawed. Life is not only about preparing for what you’ll do after graduation — it’s also about enjoying the present and doing what makes you happy. Many parents want the best for their children, but they forget that life is short, and kids should get to enjoy it while they can.

Looking ahead, I think some students will still choose to take online classes in their spare time alongside regular school, if they want to focus on specific goals. Others will stick to in-person school only — they may want a good career, but they don’t want the kind of “excellent,” high-pressure life that other students chase. They’d rather have a balanced life that leaves room for enjoyment.

Completing tasks on your own brings far more advantages than collaborating with a team. When you work solo, you can focus in a quiet, calm environment without constant interruptions, and you never have to wait for others to weigh in on your decisions. For people who are naturally shy, being surrounded by colleagues can feel uncomfortable or even overwhelming. While group work does have one clear perk—everyone can swap ideas and perspectives—working alone is ultimately the better choice.

Job tasks are already stressful enough on their own, and adding non-stop chatter and constant feedback from others only makes that stress worse. Picture a workspace where the whole team is talking over each other, and one person is already feeling overwhelmed—that person will struggle to focus or come up with fresh ideas. They will likely head home at the end of the day far more stressed than someone who spent the day working quietly on their own. Solitary work helps people unwind, and when you are calm, creative ideas flow much more easily.

Sometimes a great new idea pops into your head mid-task, but if you are working with a group, you have to run that idea past everyone and wait for universal approval—a process that eats up valuable time. It is also common for team members to disagree on new suggestions, which slows progress even further. When you work alone, you save all that time you would have spent consulting others, and can put it toward actually completing your work instead. Group projects often turn into chaotic discussions with multiple people talking at once, leading to disagreements, confusion, and wasted hours. That is why working solo is far more time-efficient: you can focus on your own tasks without getting caught up in unnecessary consultations.

For people who are shy, being in a large group setting can be incredibly difficult. I speak from personal experience here: as a shy person, group work is always a struggle for me. I have to force myself to talk to others and share my thoughts, which makes it impossible to work calmly or even think clearly. There is also the constant worry that colleagues will judge my work, disagree with my ideas, and make me redo everything. Most of the time, I end up hiding my own work and just going along with what the rest of the group wants instead. This is far from ideal—when you feel like you are being watched or judged, your brain cannot function properly, and all that pressure often leads to subpar final work.

Some might argue that collaborating with others lets people share ideas and opens up new opportunities, which is true—getting to hear different perspectives is definitely a plus. But the benefits of working alone far outweigh that single advantage. It is much better to enjoy a calm, low-stress workday than to gain extra ideas but end up exhausted and overwhelmed when you get home.

Working on your own in a quiet, peaceful space lets you focus entirely on your own thoughts, think through every point of your task, analyze all the details, and stay relaxed and calm, with no shyness or stress to hold you back. This is the kind of work benefit that everyone deserves to have.

This story makes it clear that a negative attitude can destroy the things you value most, while a positive one can heal your mistakes and set you up for success.

Lastly, a positive attitude reflects your true personality, which changes how others perceive you. You can’t expect people to just decide you’re successful or capable on their own. Instead, people form opinions of you based on how you act, both in your future plans and your past behavior. For example, would anyone call you a successful student if you have no interest in further education? They may even give you more chances to show what you can do, which can push you further toward success.

To sum up, a positive attitude is essential for both your daily life and long-term success. Adopting an upbeat mindset shapes each day into a good one. You also need positivity to find the right path toward your goals. Most importantly, a positive attitude shows the people around you who you really are, catching their attention and leading to opportunities that can help you become successful. If you want to achieve your goals, cultivating a positive attitude is the first step you need to take.

Letting students bring and use mobile phones in the classroom leads to three major problems: ignoring the teacher’s lessons, misusing the devices for non-school activities, and disrupting the entire class’s learning. When students have phones in hand, they rarely pay attention to what the teacher is saying, since they are too focused on their screens. Many also choose to use their phones for fun instead of schoolwork, and their constant use distracts those around them too. These are the key ways phones hurt learning in class.

First, it is almost impossible to learn properly when you are using a phone during class. Checking messages or scrolling through apps pulls you off task, so you end up missing the day’s lessons entirely. Sometimes, things you see or hear on your phone might make you upset, and you might take that frustration out on classmates. Even a small vibration from a notification will make you want to check your phone, which takes your full attention away from the lesson. You cannot focus on your studies and stare at a screen at the same time, no matter how hard you try.

Second, using your phone for non-educational purposes will not help you master the material you need to know. If you spend class time playing games or chatting instead of using your phone for school tasks, you will fall behind on what you are supposed to learn. You might also get in trouble with teachers for misusing your device. Phones should only be out when a teacher specifically says you can use them for an assignment, not for personal use during lessons. This is a big reason why phones should not be used for unrelated purposes in school.

Third, phones cause disruptions that make it hard for other students to learn. A sudden ringtone or notification sound will stop the whole class, as everyone turns to see whose phone is making noise. If you are not paying attention to the lesson because of your phone, you will not understand how to do your work, and you will also bother classmates who are trying to focus on the material they need to build a good future. You should never get in the way of your classmates’ chances to succeed in life.

In short, having a phone in class works against your goal of learning and succeeding in school. You should not ignore what your teacher is explaining, or distract your classmates while they are trying to learn. Mobile devices should only be used for educational purposes during class, never for personal entertainment. Most importantly, just because you might not care about your own success does not mean you should ruin your classmates’ chances to do well. For all these reasons, cellphones should not be allowed in classrooms at all.

I went through a period of depression myself not long ago. I was constantly teased for having a larger head and being very thin — I know it sounds silly now, I even laugh about it when I tell the story. The bullying got so bad I stopped wanting to go to school at all. I didn’t want to leave my house or speak to anyone; it was a really low point. One day, a close friend noticed I’d been skipping school and asked why. I opened up to him about everything. He told me straight up to ignore all the nasty comments people made about me, and to live my life to the fullest. From that day on, we’ve been best friends for life — we always have each other’s backs. A few weeks later, I told my mom about the bullying too. We talked for hours about how I shouldn’t let other people’s cruelty hold me back, since life is too short to waste time on negativity. That conversation completely changed how I see the world and myself.

Trying to stay true to yourself is incredibly hard in today’s world. Something as small as a comment that your shoes look ugly can shake a person’s confidence completely. They start buying items they don’t even like, and doing things they have no interest in, just to fit in. Some even start making bad choices, all to blend in with people who have expensive clothes and trendy shoes. Judgment from others stops so many people from being their genuine selves.

Cruel comments can have really terrible effects — sometimes victims are pushed to suicide just because of someone else’s careless words. We all need to start treating each other with basic respect. Parents should teach their children to be kind to others from a young age, too. People shouldn’t let others’ opinions control how they live, and everyone deserves to live life to the fullest.

Being your genuine self is the greatest accomplishment anyone can have.

Looking for fun activities to try at your local park? There are plenty of simple, enjoyable options to choose from. You can walk your dog, share a picnic with family or friends, visit animal exhibits, or ride bikes, skateboards, and scooters around the grounds.

One of the best things to do at the park is take your dog for a walk. As you walk along the paths, you get a good workout without even realizing it, while your pet gets to sniff around and discover new sights and smells. It’s also a great way to spend quality time outdoors together, soaking up fresh air and greenery that both of you will enjoy. Most dogs love being out and about, so the park is the perfect spot to let them explore while you relax.

Another popular park activity is hosting a picnic with family or friends. Sitting on a blanket sharing food and conversation is a simple pleasure, especially when the weather is warm and sunny. Once you’ve finished your meal, you can wander off to explore more of the park’s trails or green spaces. If you’ve brought someone who’s never visited before, they’ll likely love the experience and want to come back again soon.

Many parks also have animal exhibits that are fun to visit. You might spot creatures you’ve never seen up close before, like bears, fish, turtles, goats, chickens, or even pigs—some parks even hold pig races for visitors to watch. Staff or other guests are often happy to share facts about the animals, such as where they come from or what they eat. Most parks also provide safe food you can use to feed the animals, which makes the experience even more interactive.

Last but not least, you can bring wheeled gear like bikes, skateboards, or scooters to the park. It’s a great place to practice if you’re still learning how to ride, since there are far fewer cars than on the street, making it much safer. As you glide along, you’ll get to take in the park’s pretty scenery, and it’s even more fun if you bring friends to ride and play with. The open space means you’ll have plenty of room to move around without worrying about traffic.

Is leading by personal example truly the most effective way to shape how others act? Copying the behavior of those around us is not always a smart choice, since not everyone sets a positive tone. At times, people may be in a dark, negative headspace, act recklessly, or engage in silly, careless horseplay. Other times, though, individuals can be charming, well-mannered, and have a real positive influence on others.

I grew up in the Generic_City area, where I saw firsthand the damage caused by drugs, gangs, and violence. The behavior modeled by these groups is far from positive, and following their path almost always leads to terrible consequences. I once had a friend whose father shot himself after making a series of poor choices—he felt so trapped by his mistakes that he thought ending his life was the only way out.

That said, plenty of people choose to make a positive impact on their communities. During my three years of high school, I watched many students put others first instead of acting selfishly. A lot of them volunteered their time to help local causes, hoping to encourage others to do the same. I even got the chance to host a Halloween party for kids at a local church—it was a lot of fun, and I really enjoyed the experience.

To be honest, I do not think I am a particularly good role model, but I do not consider myself a bad one either. I make mistakes all the time—that is how I was raised to learn. Growing up, I was taught that the only way to grow is to mess up, then reflect on what went wrong. Only after analyzing your errors can you truly get better, and eventually inspire others to improve too.

All in all, I am not fully convinced that setting a personal example is the best way to influence others, since the behavior people model is not always positive. Poor decisions made by some can lead to harmful examples that hurt more than they help. Really, I think it is more important to be the best version of yourself that you can be. After all, every person is one of a kind—there is only one you, but so many other people out there. Staying true to your own unique self is far better than trying to copy anyone else.

Lots of schools now partner with local companies to give students hands-on chances to explore different careers, whether through short internships or job shadowing programs that let them see what a role is really like. I fully agree that these opportunities are a great idea, as they let young people test out fields they might be interested in before committing to them long-term. Getting to experience a workplace firsthand makes it much easier for students to figure out their life goals early, which puts them on track to secure stable, well-paying jobs down the line.

The biggest benefit of letting students try out careers through internships is that they can clarify exactly what they want to do with their lives, which lays the groundwork for a successful future. I have a cousin named Generic_Name, who has three children of his own. A few years back, he was accepted to Liberty University, but first he visited the campus to see if any of the courses interested him. After that visit, he enrolled and studied there for several years, graduating with straight A’s. These days, he runs his own small business and is happier than he’s ever been.

Another key reason these internship and exploration programs are useful is that they help students land high-paying jobs later on. I have another cousin, also named Generic_Name, who is the toughest and bravest person I know. He joined the Air Force several years ago, and while he loved serving, he admitted the training and work were really challenging. He chose the military because his parents couldn’t cover the cost of college for him. After finishing his service, he also decided to enroll at Liberty University, and he loved every minute of his time there. He graduated in 2015, and now works for the FBI—I could not be more proud of him. A few weeks ago, I visited his house, and he turned to me and said, “Generic_Name, the Air Force was incredibly tough for me at first. I felt like my time there was wasted. But now I understand that God put me in that position because he had big plans for me. I feel like I’m on top of the world right now, happier than I’ve ever been. I also make great money at my job—the pay is amazing. Someday I want to buy a huge mansion.” I saw tears in his eyes, and I felt so proud of him. I thought to myself, “I want to feel that same sense of accomplishment. I want big things for my own life too.”

Some students argue that college isn’t important, which is a view I can sort of understand. I was talking to a friend once about how much I wanted to go to college, but she didn’t care at all. She looked me straight in the eye and said, “What’s the point of college anyway? It’s just like going back to a place I hate. My parents never went, and they’re doing just fine.” Others claim college is the worst experience possible. My friend also said, “Why do schools even bother letting students figure out what they want to do? We don’t need college, and we don’t need a future. I actually like working at Wendy’s.” Hearing her say such negative things about higher education just made me more determined to work harder in school and get better grades.

To sum up, letting students explore different careers through internships isn’t just a good idea—it’s a brilliant one. As I’ve said before, these experiences help young people figure out their long-term goals, and set them up to land well-paying jobs. My cousins’ stories have really inspired me: because of them, I want to push myself harder and achieve more. Maybe one day I’ll work for the government, and be able to give my future children a happy life.

Picture finishing all your school tasks quickly and with no mistakes! Homework clubs are designed for learners who struggle to complete assignments on their own, and they let students work alongside their classmates too. These clubs benefit students in three key ways: they let you finish work ahead of time, they encourage peer support, and they boost overall learning abilities.

First, students get their work done sooner. This means they have free time later instead of rushing to finish assignments, and it stops them from turning in late work. I remember back in 7th grade, I often skipped homework, knowing it was a bad choice. The result was terrible grades and being grounded for weeks. I used to hate doing homework, but that experience taught me a lesson, so I started staying on top of my assignments once my grounding ended.

Second, students can support one another. Those who find homework hard can get help from classmates, and everyone finishes tasks more easily. For instance, when I stayed after school to work with my English teacher, I noticed I completed most of my assignments because I stayed focused, and I asked the teacher for help whenever I got stuck. This pushed my grades from failing up to passing. That’s why I recommend homework clubs to any student who wants to get their work done on time.

Third, these clubs strengthen your learning skills. They build collaboration and communication abilities, and can even improve your performance across all school subjects. I saw this firsthand when I was in 4th grade: I didn’t know a single word of English, so I joined an English as a Second Language program. Teachers taught me new vocabulary every day until I felt comfortable speaking English in class and with other students. I got to the point where I no longer needed the program. At first, I was afraid to talk to people, worrying they’d make fun of my poor English, but I was wrong. I made my first friend in 5th grade, a boy named Etka. We were both in the ESL program, but he spoke much better English than me, and he helped me get better at communicating too.

Overall, after-school homework clubs are a great resource for students. They let you finish work early with help from both teachers and classmates, and most importantly, they sharpen your learning and communication skills for the long term.

The majority of high schoolers choose to complete the standard four-year program, then apply to college in their final year. This timing lets them get guidance from school counselors and teachers as they prepare applications. Finishing high school early can be tough for teens, since everyone learns at a different pace, and some pick up material much faster than others. While school districts should let students decide if they want to graduate early and give them more control over their future plans, the traditional four-year timeline has clear benefits. Students who follow this standard path avoid the extra stress and pressure of early graduation, plus additional coursework, and they get to pick elective classes that interest them.

All students know passing their classes and tracking credits is essential to graduating. For those who graduate early, this pressure can be harmful. The stress and anxiety from rushing to finish early make daily life harder, and often lead to mental health struggles. Many parents check grades constantly, which frustrates students. Kids are often told they must get good marks, and if they don’t, guardians might take away privileges or control other parts of their lives as punishment.

Almost every student worries about falling behind or low grades, but these fears are less intense for those on the four-year timeline. Teachers often encourage early graduates to take extra summer or evening classes to move ahead. Students on the standard path don’t need these extra classes. They still have assignments, but are not forced to rush through work. Everyone should be responsible for their own schoolwork, even if that means taking more time to finish.

High schools let students try new subjects by choosing electives. Unfortunately, early graduates often miss this chance, seeing electives as a waste of time when they need required courses. In contrast, four-year students can take as many electives as they like. These classes let them challenge themselves and get better at any topic that interests them.

To sum up, the traditional four-year high school program is better for most students. They can get support from teachers and school staff when needed. Anxiety and pressure distract students from learning, pulling attention from studies. Extra time in the four-year program should not be spent on extra work, since students have assignments and barely time for more courses. Electives are valuable: they let students learn new skills and take a break from core class stress.

Minister Churchill’s core message is that the path from failure to success is rarely straightforward in life. This leads many to ask: what can we do to build successful careers and achieve our goals? This is a sentiment most people would agree with. Not everyone will reach their goals, and making mistakes is a universal part of the human experience. We need to keep pushing ourselves, even if it takes years to get where we want to be. Failing at something does not mean the end of the road—instead, it is a chance to figure out what approach works best for each of us. While moving from failure to success is never simple, anyone can reach their goals if they are willing to put in the effort and tap into their own potential.

To start with, many people argue that working through failure to achieve success is a valuable process. Take my friend as an example: when he first started playing basketball, several of our mutual friends told him the sport wasn’t a good fit for him. But over time, he practiced nonstop and eventually became much more skilled on the court. As the old saying goes, practice makes perfect. Another case is my sister, who had her heart set on attending the University of Virginia. She studied tirelessly to meet the admission requirements, even though our family didn’t think her grades were good enough. A few weeks later, she got her acceptance letter. Life is never going to hand us easy wins—we have to accept that challenges are part of the journey, and the only way forward is to work harder.

What’s more, this struggle is something nearly everyone goes through. There is no single person alive who has lived their entire life without facing any setbacks. Even in school, it is almost impossible to find a student who never struggles with their coursework. No one is born smart—we have to work to build our knowledge and skills. For instance, I get good marks in math and history, but I struggle with English and science. This just goes to show that everyone has their own strengths and weaknesses. No one is perfect, so we all need to put in extra study time and effort to improve where we fall short.

On the flip side, some people argue that working through failure to find success is a waste of time, claiming it will not help their future careers. They point out that there is an overwhelming amount of material to get through in school, college, and even in the workplace just to achieve success. They also complain about the need to work long hours to cover housing costs, utility bills, health and car insurance, and provide for their families. Most of the people who dismiss this process as a waste of time are those who end up in difficult situations, such as homelessness, or who have completely given up on pursuing any meaningful goals.

Finally, there are clear reasons why everyone should commit to working through failure to reach success. For one, achieving your goals boosts your self-esteem and makes you feel proud of what you have accomplished. Another benefit is that if you complete all the requirements for your chosen career early on, you won’t have to juggle those tasks later in life when other responsibilities pile up. Studying and mastering the material you need puts you in a position to achieve great things. Even if you don’t reach every goal you set, that is okay—you still have chances to try again. The key is to keep studying and working hard, so you never have to look back with regret.

Picture the thrill of walking out of high school a full year ahead of schedule, ready to start college or jump into a full-time job. While that achievement feels rewarding after years of hard work, reaching this goal means sacrificing hobbies, free time, and favorite pastimes along the way. This is exactly why letting students graduate high school in three years to enter college or the workforce early is a bad idea. The main issues? They’ll have to take extra classes in summer or evening sessions, they’ll miss out on fun elective courses, and the whole process puts way too much pressure on young people.

To fit all required graduation credits into three years, students have to take classes during summer breaks or after regular school hours in the evenings. Plenty of high schoolers rely on summer jobs to earn spending money or save for college, but summer courses would leave them no time to work. Beyond that, evening classes clash with after-school activities: if a student wants to join a sports team or a club that meets after the final bell, they won’t be able to, since they’ll be stuck in class instead.

Another big downside is that students who graduate early rarely get to take elective classes. To earn a diploma in three years, they have to squeeze in all mandatory core courses, which are also the classes colleges look at most during admissions. With schedules already packed full of required subjects, there’s simply no room left for fun electives like art, drama, music, or photography.

Supporters might argue that finishing high school early is a smart way to get a head start in life, but this ignores the immense stress it places on young people. They have to stay on top of classwork for every subject, finish homework nightly, study for quizzes and tests, and complete long-term projects and presentations, all while making sure they don’t fall behind. All these demands pile up quickly, leaving students with almost no time for their own hobbies or downtime.

All things considered, letting students graduate high school a year early to start college or full-time work is not a good choice. They’ll be forced to take extra classes in summer or evening sessions, miss out on valuable elective courses, and deal with unhealthy levels of stress. Schools should stop offering three-year graduation tracks that push students to enter college or the workforce ahead of schedule.

Can first impressions never be altered? I strongly disagree—these early perceptions are far from set in stone. When we meet someone new for the first time, many of us put pressure on ourselves to blend in or pretend to be someone we’re not. As time passes, though, people’s views of us shift naturally, and that initial first impression stops holding as much weight. Another common reason early perceptions are misleading is nervousness: when you first meet someone, you might come across as quiet, reserved, or even unfriendly, even if you’re actually super outgoing. It just takes time to get comfortable around new people, and most folks don’t show their true selves right away in those first interactions.

I have a personal example that proves first impressions can absolutely shift. The first time I met my boyfriend’s mom, I was extremely shy and on edge. I worried I was giving off a bad vibe, or looking bored, even though I was just trying to be polite and avoid saying or doing anything too over-the-top. After spending more time around her, though, she started to see my real personality. She realized I was way more outgoing than I’d seemed at first, and her whole opinion of me changed for the better.

Another example comes from my relationship with one of my closest friends. We met through a mutual friend, and my first impression of her was that she was annoying and couldn’t ever take things seriously. Over time, though, I got to know her true personality, and I realized I’d judged her way too quickly. As we grew closer, that initial negative impression faded completely—now I love her, and that first meeting has no impact on how I see her today.

To sum up, I don’t think first impressions are impossible to change. It’s not something that happens overnight, of course—shifting how people see you takes time. But depending on your actions, those early perceptions can definitely shift, for better or for worse, as you get to know each other better.

We often hear that we are the ones who shape our own character. But is that entirely true? Do we pick our own personality traits, or are they molded by outside forces we can’t control?

To break this down, we can look at a few key points:
1. Some people are influenced by friends
2. Everyone has their own life traits
3. Not everyone has bad traits

In my view, everyone has the power to choose what kind of person they become. Still, plenty of people let others influence their traits instead. This includes friends, family, and even strangers who don’t know you well and don’t want to see you succeed—these people can hold you back from developing the traits you want. On the flip side, there are those who stick to their own positive qualities, which leads them to happier, more successful lives. It’s also worth noting that not everyone has bad traits. Some people will be a good influence on you, encouraging kind actions and steering you down the right path. Ultimately, it all comes down to how you process information: you have to decide for yourself whether an influence is good or bad for your life.

1. I believe every person has their own way of living, shaped by a mix of good and bad qualities. Bad traits can come from anyone: friends, family, even people you barely know. I think this is partly because not everyone grows up in a supportive, happy home. A difficult upbringing can lead someone to develop negative traits that stick with them. On the other hand, people raised in loving families often pick up positive qualities that guide their lives. But even if you have good traits, spending time with people who have bad ones can ruin the progress you’ve made.

2. Next, it’s clear that everyone’s traits shape their life outcomes. Take successful people, for example—those with big homes and expensive cars got there by developing good traits that will also benefit their children and grandchildren. In contrast, bad traits lead to nothing but misery and negativity. If you have good qualities but become close friends with someone who has bad ones, you risk being influenced and controlled by that person. Romantic relationships are another major source of influence. A bad partner can be one of the worst influences you’ll ever face, turning every part of your life upside down and breaking you down mentally. Some partners, though, will guide you in the right direction. Toxic relationships involve constant arguments, unfair self-blame, and hurting each other with words or actions. These experiences leave scars that never fully heal, and can pass negative traits on to your future self.

3. Finally, not everyone lets outside forces control them. Smart, successful people often face pushback from others who are jealous of their achievements. These people will try to drag you into negative behavior, or even ruin your life entirely if they can. You have to stand up for yourself and stay away from any bad influences that might lead you down a negative path. To anyone who feels pressured to change who they are: remember that you are the one who chooses your character. That choice determines what kind of life you’ll lead. Take a moment to reflect: are your traits positive, or negative?

Theprincipal’s new rule requiring all students to take part in extracurricular activities is completely unfair and unethical. No one wants to spend their limited free time on tasks that offer no real value to them. Students already have mountains of schoolwork to handle, and adding mandatory activities on top of that will only hold them back from reaching their academic targets.

When students are forced to join these programs, they lose time they would normally spend on their regular school tasks. They will have far less time to finish homework or work on long-term projects, which pushes them further away from their academic goals. On top of that, they will have almost no time left to spend with their families. This can cause tension in those relationships, and even lead to distance between students and their loved ones.

Mandatory participation in these activities also adds a lot of unnecessary stress for students. Their daily routines will now include an extra program packed with more work—work they never chose to do, but are required to complete. All this extra pressure means students will be too stressed to get enough sleep, which is very bad for their health.

This constant pressure can also damage students’ grades. When they have to spend time on activities they do not want to do, it adds even more stress and distracts them from their personal priorities. They will focus on mandatory activities instead of their schoolwork, and before long, their grades will start to drop.

For all these reasons, it is clear that forcing students to join extracurricular activities does far more harm than good. These programs are not good for students’ health or their academic performance. The only fair approach is to let students decide for themselves if they want to take part, rather than forcing them to do so.

Revamping the school cafeteria’s menu is a lot like taking a beloved treat away from a pet that’s been looking forward to it all day. One key reason why altering the current school lunch options is a poor choice is that it will leave students frustrated and upset. When learners are dissatisfied with sudden changes to their school routines, their parents often step in to voice complaints, which can quickly damage the school board’s public image. I once saw a TV show where administrators made sweeping changes to school policies without asking students or parents for input first, and the reaction was huge. Students were so angry they organized a strike and refused to attend classes entirely.

Another major issue with removing popular items from the cafeteria is that many students will simply stop buying lunch at school altogether. For instance, I remember going to a family dinner where they served meatloaf, a dish I absolutely cannot stand. I felt guilty, but I couldn’t force myself to finish even a few bites, so I ended up throwing most of it away. A similar situation happened when my friends and I went to a buffet that had very few dishes we actually liked. We ended up picking some chicken wings, but they tasted terrible, and none of us could eat more than a bite or two. It’s a simple fact: when people are faced with food they dislike, they are very unlikely to eat it, or even give it a try in the first place.

Finally, changing the cafeteria menu would cut down the number of choices available to students, which is incredibly unfair to those who don’t like the new dishes being served. If the only options are foods they can’t stand, they will have nothing to eat for lunch. Think of it this way: imagine going to your favorite clothing store, only to find that all the styles you loved have been removed and replaced with items you hate. You would feel deeply let down by that change, right? That is exactly how students would feel if their familiar lunch options were swapped out for new, unfamiliar ones.

Some people argue that switching to healthier school lunches would be far better for students’ well-being. While this is a reasonable point, it is flawed because it ignores the fact that lots of students will be deeply unhappy with the decision, regardless of how good the food is for them. These are all key reasons why changing the current cafeteria menu is a bad idea for the school.

In certain communities, teenagers are pushed to decide on a long-term career path before they even start high school. The classes they take during these four years are often tailored to steer them toward a specific job field. However, most young teens simply aren’t ready to make such a big decision at that age. I think their ideas about what they want to do for work will shift a lot while they’re in high school. Students shouldn’t be forced to pick a career when they first enter high school—they lack the life experience to know what they truly want, they might pick the wrong field, and end up upset about wasting years studying for a job they’ll later decide isn’t right for them.

Without enough real-world experience, young people often struggle to figure out what they actually want for their future. When they first start high school, most are around 14 years old—an age where few are thinking seriously about their long-term career. As they learn more about different job options, their views on what they want to be start to shift. By 16, most teens have matured more and can look at future plans with a clearer, more realistic perspective. It’s unreasonable to expect a child to map out their entire professional life when they’re still so young.

Forcing teens to settle on a career as soon as they enter high school makes it far more likely they’ll pick the wrong path. Most students understand that a bad career choice can have long-lasting effects on their lives. Imagine picking a job field at 14, only to realize years later that you hate it—you could end up stuck in unfulfilling work for decades. On the other hand, people who work in roles they enjoy tend to put in more effort and produce better results.

It’s normal for people to change their minds about likes and dislikes almost daily, and career preferences are no different. No one wants to waste time, especially when it comes to something as important as their future. Making young teens choose a career too early can set them back, forcing them to redo years of study later on. Picking the wrong field means dealing with the consequences and starting over with a new choice. Taking time to do proper research and plan carefully will set students up for better success in their future careers.

The truth is, most high school students aren’t ready to pick their future career yet. Many have no clear idea of what they want to do with their lives later on. Some may end up choosing a field they have no real interest in, and changing their mind later will leave them frustrated about the time they wasted on a path they didn’t care about. Students need to gain enough experience and learn about different options before committing to a specific career path.

People seek independence for countless reasons, but the most common one is the desire to take charge of their own choices. Being able to decide things for yourself is a key part of life—it proves you are responsible and self-sufficient. Of course, not everyone makes wise choices. Some people pick helpful, positive paths, while others make poor decisions that can harm those around them in many ways.

Common examples of harmful choices include using illegal drugs, driving under the influence of alcohol, and joining street gangs. All of these can bring immense pain to the people closest to you. Joining a gang puts you at constant risk of fatal violence, often for no meaningful reason at all. If you lose your life to gang activity, the only thing you leave behind is grief for everyone who cares about you. Drunk driving is equally reckless: you endanger not just yourself, but also other road users who have families waiting for them to come home safely. When you choose to drive after drinking, you may end up sending innocent people to the hospital, and you alone are responsible for that consequence. As for drug use, it never benefits your health or your life. The only way to avoid this trap is to never try drugs in the first place. Your family and loved ones will only be disappointed if you get involved with drugs, but beyond these bad choices, there are plenty of positive decisions people can make.

Making your own choices also helps you plan for life after high school. For example, you might decide what career you want to pursue, what subject to study in college, or whether you’re ready to start a family. All of these are positive, forward-looking decisions. Good jobs are very difficult to land if you have no relevant experience, as most employers look for candidates who are prepared and eager to work. If you go to college first and already know what job you want, you can pick the exact courses you need to qualify for that role. This preparation helps you in countless ways, and later on, it lets you start a family without constant stress about having enough money to support them.

While adults are navigating all these big life choices, many young kids are also starting to seek independence and make their own decisions. When children take these first steps, their family members often realize their kid can handle things on their own. In other words, parents come to see that their child no longer needs help with every little task. This shift shows parents that their child is growing into a mature young man or woman. Parents understand that letting kids make their own choices teaches them to think for themselves and develop as individuals. It also proves to parents that their child can take care of themselves when they are on their own.

All of these points show that making decisions can be difficult for many people. At the same time, it is a key way to learn how to live independently, and it is a step that both children and adults must take to keep moving forward in life. Independence is something people all over the world strive for—so once you have it, what will you choose to do with it?

I am strongly against the plan to extend the school day by an hour and a half. Right now, the time we spend in school each day is already more than enough. If the school board tacks on an extra 90 minutes to the daily schedule, every student will end up exhausted, which means we won’t be able to absorb what’s being taught during class time. Juggling long school days with regular homework already puts a lot of stress on most of us. For many students, the current schedule is already pushing us to our limits. Adding another hour and a half would almost certainly make most of us resent school, potentially leading to higher dropout rates or a total loss of interest in classwork and homework. We’d also have way less time to study for tests or finish big projects at home, especially since plenty of students work part-time jobs after class.

Students need free time to stay happy and keep physically healthy. As a middle schooler myself, I can say that right now, I manage to fit in both schoolwork and free time without too much trouble. But if 90 minutes were added to my daily schedule, I’m not sure I’d still have time to hang out with friends, get my work done, and spend time with my family. Not having enough free time to play with friends or do hobbies I enjoy would definitely hurt my health. For students with part-time jobs, the extra school time would leave almost no time to rest, see family and friends, or take care of themselves. That would take a real toll on their mental and physical health, as well as their overall happiness—they wouldn’t have time to exercise or do fun activities to clear their minds.

Many teachers also work part-time jobs, and this change would make that nearly impossible. Most teachers take on extra work because their teaching salary isn’t enough to support a large family, or they want to save money for the future. Everyone has their own personal reasons for this. But if the school day is extended by 90 minutes, teachers won’t have time for decent part-time work. Most already stay after school once or twice a week to help students who need extra support or want to retake a test. They’d also struggle to take care of their own families: married teachers with kids wouldn’t have time to care for them properly, and single teachers who live with aging parents wouldn’t be able to look after them. This would force teachers to either quit their jobs or demand a raise, so they wouldn’t need to work a second job and could still have time for their families.

School bus drivers already face risks driving in the dark early mornings, when it’s hard to see the road clearly while transporting a bus full of students. While adding 90 minutes to the regular school day might not be a huge issue for them, the real problem is the after-school program. Right now, after-school programs run for two hours. If we add an hour and a half to the school day, that program would end three and a half hours later than usual, when it’s already fully dark outside. Driving in those conditions would be extremely difficult and risky, putting both the drivers and all the students on the bus in danger.

After-school programs are a huge help to students: they let us make up missing work, retake tests, or redo homework to improve our grades. They also let students earn service hours by helping school staff with tasks, which gets work done faster for the school. Sadly, if the school day is extended by 90 minutes, these programs would likely have to shut down. The extra school time would leave teachers, bus drivers, and students too exhausted to participate. Most students wouldn’t stay after school anyway, since they’d be completely exhausted by the time the regular day ends.

Does extending school hours help cut down on energy use? One suggested plan is to switch to a four-day school week, with two additional hours added to each school day to save power. I believe this is a terrible idea for schools to take on. This change would create major difficulties for students who have commitments outside of class.

Lengthening the school day by two hours brings plenty of issues for both students and staff. Students who work part-time jobs or take part in after-school activities like sports teams or clubs will be hit hardest. They will also feel exhausted after the longer day, and have far less time to spend with friends. Teachers face problems too: some may live in neighboring towns or counties, and need to leave on time to collect their own children from school. All in all, this plan would mess up the daily routines of everyone involved.

Supporters of longer school days point out a few benefits. Students would have extra time to finish assignments during class, get more time for tests and quizzes, and learn more material overall. This could mean teachers assign almost no homework. Students might also fit in more classes, which could let them graduate earlier, since they are spending more total time in school. On top of that, a four-day week means three days off to rest. Some even say students could finish school earlier overall, because of the extra hours added each day.

Even with these possible benefits, I still think this plan is a bad choice. It would cause too many problems for students and teachers alike. Many students will hate the change: some have after-school jobs, others need to pick up younger siblings, and plenty have sports practice or other activities. Teachers who live 30 minutes away from school need to collect their kids on time, and stop at the store to buy groceries for dinner. That is why I oppose adopting this proposal pushed by the administration. There is a big difference between the needs of students and adults. Right now, our main responsibility is school, since we spend seven hours there every week. I really hope the school does not consider putting this plan into action.

Is it possible to reach our goals by staying constantly active? As Thomas Jefferson once said, 'Determine never to be idle... It is wonderful how much may be done if we are always doing.' Does doing nothing productive help us get more done? Definitely not—lying around at home or standing idle all day won’t lead to any achievements. Instead, we make far more progress when we stay busy with purposeful tasks.

Staying productive also helps us pick up new skills. For instance, my mom once signed me up for a soccer team out of the blue. I had no idea I’d be joining, and I didn’t even want to play at first. But I went along with it anyway. That experience taught me how to kick a soccer ball properly, how to play as a goalie, and even improved my running speed. Another time, I had an English vocabulary test coming up, and I didn’t recognize half the words on the list. Instead of giving up, I studied until I had memorized every single one.

Getting out and doing things also lets us meet new people who can help us reach our goals. I’ve always been more of a homebody, but every soccer season, joining a team pushes me to interact with new teammates and coaches. These connections help me figure out how to be a better teammate, and work on my speed and mindset to grow as a soccer player. Another example: when I struggled with a math equation I couldn’t solve, I reached out to a new math teacher. He explained the problem clearly, and now he helps me with any math questions I have whenever I get stuck.

Just think about how much we could achieve if we stayed active all the time. We’d tick off so many goals if we spent our time doing purposeful things, instead of lounging at home watching TV all day. Even small pockets of free time can be used for tasks that will benefit us later, and push us to think more critically. Sometimes we might think we don’t need help, but it’s better to ask someone to explain things we don’t understand, rather than staying stuck in the same old way of thinking.

Of course, there are exceptions. Some people don’t have much spare time to stay constantly active, so they might seem idle while working toward long-term goals at their own pace. In some cases, inactivity makes sense—maybe someone can’t afford to join a program, or doesn’t have a way to get to where they need to go. But even then, they can’t just sit around doing nothing and wait for good things to fall into their lap.

To sum up, we can reach our goals by consistently doing things that will benefit us down the line. As Thomas Jefferson wrote, 'Determine never to be idle... it is wonderful how much may be done if we are always doing.' Staying active helps us learn new skills, meet people who support our goals, and get far more done overall. By contrast, doing nothing but lying around at home will never lead to any real accomplishments.

After that, they will present their lists to the rest of the school. As an added incentive, students with low grades will be able to earn extra credit by participating.

Another common reason students skip the program is that their friends tell them it is a waste of time. But this is not true at all: the program directly affects our daily lives. Once students realize this, they will want to take part and work to make our neighborhood a better place for everyone.

Participating also comes with a benefit: students receive good grades for joining, since it counts as extra credit. Once they see these benefits, their friends will hear about the program and want to join in too.

To sum up, a school community center would be an excellent space for students to gain all kinds of useful knowledge. I truly believe this is a great idea for our school. It will teach students to identify local needs, find ways to improve our community, and understand why being part of a strong community matters.
