Many people believe that aiming for very ambitious goals is a wise choice, while others argue that it’s better to set easier, low targets. Some worry that if you set a high goal and don’t reach it, you’ll lose motivation and quit, but they overlook that achievements vary widely in size and type. I think people should always aim high with their goals, because doing so helps you accomplish more, stay more driven, and feel a greater sense of success.

Some people disagree with this stance, saying that setting a goal that’s too hard and then failing can make you feel less motivated. They think that if a big goal doesn’t work out, you might quit altogether and stop trying. They believe that giving up on a goal can leave you feeling empty, and make you not want to try again later. This shows that many worry about failing, and when they do, they lose the will to keep going. But supporters of high goals have other important points that these critics miss.

For one, setting high targets pushes you to achieve more overall. When you aim for something very ambitious, you often end up tackling multiple smaller goals along the way, not just one big one. Hitting several of these smaller milestones feels great, and gives you a real sense of pride in your progress. Even if you fall short on one goal, that doesn’t mean you can’t accomplish others. All goals are different, and failing one doesn’t stop you from reaching other, equally challenging targets.

Another key benefit is that high goals make you feel more successful. Once you complete a tough, ambitious target, you get a real sense of having achieved something meaningful. This boosts your confidence and reduces anxiety about your abilities. It also proves to yourself that you’re capable of far more than you might have thought. Building this confidence helps you later in life, too, because you’ll have the self-belief you need to take on new challenges. You’ll also feel like you’ve made the most of your life, instead of looking back and regretting not accomplishing anything important.

High goals also keep you more motivated. Working toward a big, meaningful goal takes a lot of hard work and focus—you have to put most of your energy into reaching it. For most people, this clear focus is exactly what drives them to keep going. Your brain gets a boost of energy when you’re working toward something you really care about, and that pushes you to keep making progress until you reach the finish line.

That’s why aiming high with your goals is such a good idea. The extra motivation, greater sense of success, and increased overall achievement all help you grow in life. It’s normal to be scared of failure, or worry that something might go wrong. But the truth is, everyone fails at some point—no one is perfect. You have to move past that fear if you want to reach your full potential and accomplish what you set out to do.

Students work hard there is no arguing that. They have schoolwork, homework, extracurricular and maybe work, all these things make a students life stressful so it is important that they get a break every once in a while. I believe that students should get a long summer break, instead of a year-round school year, because, firstly, there are other activities that can be done during the summer that keep students minds active, secondly their health is at risk and lastly, summer break is beneficial to school staff as well.

From time to time, people need to get a break from their day-today life they need to take a moment to relax and enjoy their life and maybe discover an interest that they may have. Although school is important and necessary for success later on in life, so are outside experiences that can contribute to the development of a student's 'real life skills'. During summer break there are multiple activities that can be done in order to keep a student's mind active, whether it may be sports, summer camps, summer jobs etc. All these activities allow for their minds and bodies to stay active. Eventhough, they are not keeping their brains engaged in terms of school work and studying they are exposing themselves to new activities that might require them to think critically, open-mindedly and collaboratively; which I feel is essential for real life. For example, a student might be at summer camp and they are put in a group with four strangers and are given a challenging task that requires them to collaborate with the other member of the group, critically analyzing the situation and coming up with solutions and be open-minded to listening and trying to understand the perspectives of their peers. This also reflects their environment in school therefore, it can be said that they are keeping their minds active while outside of school.

Although, not all students might be involved in activities outside of school, some are taking a break from the stress of life itself. Due to all the demands in their life during the school year summer break is a good way to take a breather and take care of themselves mentally. Depression has been very common in teenagers in recent years, and although it may not be entirely due to the stress of school, school does contribute to the detirriation of their mental health. In addition, over-working ones self has negative impacts overall whether they are depressed or not. Too much stress in ones life can have negative effects on their health overall. High blood pressure, hypertension, severe weight loss are a few examples of the effects stress. Furthermore, when stressed our body releases a neurotransmitter called Cortisol, this neurotransmitter in excess can impair a persons thinking and reaction time; which is very important for students as they are required to think in order to complete school work and homework, therefore, if they dont take breaks their grades are probably going to drop due to their inability to think effectively, further contributing to their detirriating mental health.

Lastly, summer break is and essential time for everyone that is involved in schools, such as teachers, administrators, councilors etc. Although schools are intended to educate students, its the school staff that make this possible. This is why we need to give our school staff a break because all the points I stated above also applies to them. In addition, with a long summer break teachers are able to have more time to thoroughly think about their lesson plans for their students as well as have an extended amount of time to live their lives and enjoy time with their family and friends, after all, teachers are humans too and they need to be able to life their lives and forget that they are required to do so much for such little pay.

To emphasize further, I believe that schools should give students a long summer break instead of a year-round school year because a students mind will stay active during the summer through various activities that require students to think open-mindedly, critically and collaboratively. Also, students need a break in order to de-stress for the sake of their health mentally and physically. Lastly, a long summer break is needed for school staff as well because they also need to take a break, as well as the students.

There is no doubt that students work incredibly hard. Between regular classes, homework, after-school activities, and often part-time jobs, their schedules are packed, leaving many feeling overwhelmed. All these competing demands make student life deeply stressful, so it is vital that they get a chance to rest every so often. This is why I firmly believe schools should keep a long summer vacation rather than switching to a year-round calendar, for three key reasons: first, summer activities keep students’ minds active; second, time off protects their health; and third, school staff deserve the same break.

Everyone needs to step away from their daily routine now and then, to relax, enjoy themselves, and maybe even discover a new hobby or interest. First, summer break offers plenty of chances for students to stay mentally sharp through activities that aren’t tied to schoolwork. While classroom learning is key for future success, real-world experiences are just as valuable for building practical life skills. Summer camps, sports teams, part-time jobs, and other seasonal activities keep both their minds and bodies engaged. Even though they aren’t memorizing facts or writing essays, these experiences push students to think critically, work with others, and consider different perspectives — all skills that are crucial for adult life. For instance, a student at summer camp might be placed in a group with people they’ve never met before, given a tough problem to solve as a team. They have to listen to others’ ideas, analyze the situation together, and come up with a solution that works for everyone. These are the same skills they use in school group projects, so they’re still exercising their brains even when classes are out.

Not every student fills their summer with structured activities, of course. Many just use the time to step back from the constant pressure of the school year and focus on their mental well-being. Teen depression rates have risen sharply in recent years, and while school isn’t the only cause, the stress of academic demands definitely worsens mental health for many. Even for students who aren’t struggling with depression, overworking has clear negative effects. Constant stress can lead to high blood pressure, hypertension, and severe weight loss, among other physical issues. On a biological level, too much stress triggers the release of cortisol, a hormone that in high levels slows thinking and reaction times. This is especially harmful for students, who need to process information quickly to keep up with schoolwork. If they never get a chance to rest, their grades may slip because they can’t think clearly, which only adds more stress and hurts their mental health further.

Finally, long summer break isn’t just good for students — it’s essential for all school staff, including teachers, administrators, and counselors. Schools exist to educate students, but it’s the staff who make that education possible. All the points about stress and burnout apply to them too. A long summer break gives teachers extra time to carefully plan lessons for the coming year, and also lets them live their own lives: spend time with family, pursue hobbies, and recharge. After all, teachers are people too, and they deserve time to step away from their demanding jobs, especially when they often put in long hours for relatively low pay.

To sum up, I strongly believe schools should keep a long summer break instead of moving to a year-round schedule. Students can keep their minds active over the summer through activities that build collaboration, critical thinking, and open-mindedness. They also need time away from school to reduce stress and protect their physical and mental health. And finally, school staff deserve that same extended break to rest and prepare for the year ahead, just like the students they support.

Renaissance master Michelangelo once shared a powerful insight: 'The greater danger for most of us lies not in setting our aim too high and falling short; but in setting our aim too low, and achieving our mark.' While not everyone agrees with this view, I believe aiming high is far more beneficial. When we set ambitious goals, we open ourselves up to achieving far more meaningful results. People who aim high also tend to generate more creative, original ideas than those with narrow, rigid mindsets who settle for low targets. What’s more, high aims lead to far more opportunities across different areas of life.

First, setting ambitious goals creates far more opportunities in all areas of life. Most people define their goals before taking action or making plans. Think about job hunting: would you have more options if you only applied for easy, low-skill roles like dishwashing, or if you applied to every field you’re qualified for? The same logic applies to education. For instance, a student unsure of their future career path could either join the military right after high school, or attend college where they’ll be exposed to countless academic and professional opportunities. Choosing college greatly expands their job prospects, and they may land a far more fulfilling role than they would have if they’d enlisted.

Beyond practical opportunities, ambitious goals also help people develop more original, authentic ideas compared to those with inflexible mindsets who stick to low targets. People who aim low often hide their true thoughts or aren’t even aware of their full potential, since they avoid taking on challenging tasks. In contrast, those who set high goals push themselves to tackle difficult projects and consider more complex ideas. This stimulates brain development and helps people think in ways that stand out from the crowd. Consider famous artists: none of them would have produced their iconic works if they’d placed limits on their own abilities. Every groundbreaking piece of art exists because its creator refused to settle for small, safe goals, and instead aimed as high as possible.

Setting high goals also lets us accomplish far more than we would with low targets, even if low goals feel more likely to succeed. Take school assignments, for example: would you get a better grade if you only did the bare minimum required, or if you aimed to produce the best work possible? Almost everyone would pick the second option. When you set low goals, you’re more likely to give up when faced with obstacles, even if the task is important. But with a high aim, you’re motivated to keep going until you finish. In short, aiming high is always better than settling for the easiest path.

Critics might argue that aiming too high leads to unnecessary suffering, which is sometimes true — but that doesn’t mean we should swing to the opposite extreme and set low goals. The key is to find a balanced approach, just like we’re told to eat balanced meals as children. You should understand your own abilities and set goals that stretch you, rather than picking something so easy it requires no effort. Some people claim that avoiding high aims means less hard work and lower stress. While this is technically true, not all stress is harmful. In fact, stress can sometimes push us to grow. I experienced this myself as a student in Japan: I hated school and was too lazy to complete any work, which left me feeling so stressed I stopped going entirely. Staying home didn’t ease my stress at all, and I felt terrible about myself. Eventually, I decided to return to school. While stress mostly impacts people negatively, it can also have beneficial effects.

Ultimately, the core message here is that avoiding challenges and picking the easy route is never the best choice. Aiming low may seem like a safer, simpler option, but the real danger is that people stop believing they’re capable of great things. The best approach is to set goals you won’t regret, pushing yourself as far as you can. No one needs to be perfect or exceptional, but everyone should try their hardest in this short life, so they can reach the end with no regrets.

Many people claim that first impressions are nearly impossible to alter, but I completely disagree with this idea. I believe people’s impressions of others can shift for several reasons: as individuals grow and mature over time, as they are influenced by the behavior of those around them, and as they go through difficult or unfair life experiences.

First, people’s impressions of someone often change as that person grows up and matures. My own mother often points out that I am nothing like the child she raised years ago, both in how I look and how I act around others. When I was 7 or 8 years old, I was very shy around new people, and I would go out of my way to be polite just to avoid causing any conflict. Back then, I would never have considered smoking or talking back to adults, the way many little kids worry about keeping a good impression. As I’ve gotten older, that shyness has faded, and my behavior has shifted completely, so people’s view of me has changed along with my maturity.

Second, the people around us can shape how others see us, too. My younger brother is a perfect example of this. He used to be extremely shy and rarely spoke to anyone outside our immediate family. But after watching how I interact with others—calm, confident, and unafraid—he started copying that behavior. Now he chats easily with people he likes and enjoys hanging out with new friends. This shows that the influence of others can leave a positive or negative mark on someone’s behavior, which in turn shifts the impression others have of them.

Third, how life treats a person can completely shift others’ impressions of them. A week before my 14th birthday, my father was arrested. I was heartbroken and didn’t want to celebrate at all—I kept thinking life was so unfair. The next morning at school, everyone still thought I was my usual happy, carefree self, since I’d always been upbeat before. But when they started wishing me an early happy birthday, they could tell I wasn’t in a good mood. People noticed I wasn’t smiling or joking like I usually did, and their impression of me changed fast. Instead of greeting me every morning, they gave me space, assuming I was depressed—which I was, for quite a while. Now, people take me more seriously because I stopped making jokes all the time. That difficult life event completely changed how others saw me.

To sum up, I firmly believe the common claim that first impressions cannot be changed is wrong. There are plenty of reasons why someone’s initial impression shifts: personal growth and maturity, the influence of friends and family, and unexpected, difficult life events. No one can ever know exactly how these factors will shape how others see a person over time.

These days, a lot of people believe that it is far better to set a modest, achievable goal and reach it than to aim for something massive and end up failing. I, however, completely disagree with this idea. The famous Renaissance artist Michelangelo once argued that aiming too low and hitting that target is actually a huge risk for many people. He spoke from experience, having made countless mistakes and faced failure many times before he became widely recognized as a master of his craft. Michelangelo famously preferred to fail at something grand rather than play it safe and succeed at a tiny, unimportant task. I stand with Michelangelo on this. Chasing big goals, even if you do not reach them at first, lets you learn from your errors, teaches you to take calculated risks, and pushes you to grow as a person.

Michelangelo’s incredible body of work exists only because he kept learning from his early failures. He did not let his mistakes stop him; instead, he used them to get better with every project. We can see this same pattern in everyday life, too. Take the cooking competition show Masterchef, for example. Every episode, talented chefs have to impress a panel of judges with their cooking skills, and one contestant is sent home each time. Getting eliminated can feel like a crushing blow to their dreams, but every chef who appears on the show has already taken a big risk by auditioning. Even if they go home early, they can look back at what went wrong, improve their skills, and try again later. I have personal experience with this, too. When I was a teenager, getting my learner’s permit was a huge deal, since it was my first step toward independent driving. I was extremely nervous during the test and failed by just one question. Instead of giving up, I went over every question I got wrong, studied those topics more carefully, and passed easily the next time I took the test. These examples show that failing at a big goal gives you the chance to learn, grow as a person, and build the courage to take more risks later.

Taking risks is almost always part of chasing big goals, whether that relates to your education, your career, or other major life choices. I believe that taking these risks is far better than sticking to safe, small decisions, even if things do not work out the way you hoped at first. The TV show Shark Tank is a perfect example of this. Entrepreneurs come on the show to pitch their business ideas to wealthy investors, hoping to get funding. Not everyone succeeds, of course. But even the people who walk away without an investment do not give up. They keep pushing forward, often taking out their own loans or finding other ways to grow their business. Learning to take risks also makes you more comfortable speaking in public and sharing your opinions, skills that are useful in every part of life. Another good example is job interviews. Choosing to do an in-person interview instead of an online one is a bigger risk, since it is more stressful and challenging. But it also gives the hiring manager a better chance to get to know you, and it shows that you are willing to put in extra effort. You are much more likely to get the job this way than if you take the easy route of a video call. Taking risks like these makes you a stronger, more capable person overall, and even the mistakes you make along the way help you improve.

Both Michelangelo and I believe that failing at a big goal is better than succeeding at a small one. When you set a large, meaningful target, you feel more confident and focused on the task at hand, since you know it matters. You learn to look at your mistakes, work through them, and do better the next time you try. Small goals, on the other hand, require very little effort or hard work. If you only ever aim for easy, simple tasks, you might get used to taking the easy way out, and eventually become lazy about pushing yourself. Setting a higher, more challenging goal is far better, because it forces you to build new skills and learn new things. Big goals help you grow in ways that small, easy wins never could.

As that great artist once said, setting a small, unambitious goal for yourself is actually a dangerous trap. Failing at a big goal is still better, because you walk away with lessons from your mistakes, experience taking risks, and personal growth that you would never get from a small win. Smaller goals are just a way to avoid hard work, since they are so easy to reach. It is always better to challenge yourself, so you are prepared for whatever life throws at you. Even if you take the harder path and fail, that does not mean you can never try again. To sum up, setting a big goal and falling short is not only acceptable, but better than setting a small, easy target that requires almost no effort to reach.

If you approach life with a good attitude, you can offer support to these people, and you will feel a deep sense of pride from doing something helpful for others.

If you are job hunting, it makes you more likely to get hired, since most companies now prioritize candidates with a good attitude. Employers know that such workers will interact well with customers and be willing to help anyone who needs assistance.

To sum up, a positive attitude is truly the key to a successful life. It supports you when you make bad decisions or face problems you are going through, and even lets you be a source of support for friends. With this mindset, your life will be better and so much fun, and you will be far more likely to achieve success in life.

Is a positive attitude the key to reaching your goals, or just a helpful bonus that makes success come more easily? In reality, having a pleasant, upbeat way of treating others opens up far more doors than you might expect—it can help you thrive in your career, build strong romantic relationships, and grow a wide circle of friends. Take work, for example: if you support your teammates and consistently do high-quality work, your boss is far more likely to notice your effort and dedication, and promote you to a better role. The same goes for romance: if you’re warm, charming, and show genuine care for others, you’re much more likely to meet someone who returns your affection and treats you with the same kindness you give them.

First, showing a good attitude is one of the most effective ways to move up in your career. Most employers value team members who get along well with others, since this makes the whole workplace run more smoothly and benefits the company as a whole. Last year, my uncle was in the running for a promotion at his job—three employees were being considered, including him. When it came time to decide, most of his coworkers voted for him, saying he was the friendliest person for the role and the best fit for the job. This proves that when people like your attitude, they’re more likely to support you, trust you, and follow your lead.

Next, having a great attitude and open communication is key to building a happy, lasting romantic relationship. Most successful partnerships work because both people respect each other and talk through issues instead of letting them build up. For example, my parents almost never get into big fights—they always choose to sit down and talk through problems until they find a solution. They’ve taught me that you don’t need to be aggressive or difficult to resolve conflicts. This shows how a good attitude can keep love alive and prevent relationships from falling apart or ending in divorce.

Of course, some people argue that a good attitude isn’t always necessary to succeed. Many people think that having a bad attitude doesn’t have to be an obstacle to building a successful career. For example, the president of my country, El Salvador, has a very unpleasant attitude, but he has a flawless political career and still serves as president. People often say, “He’s president because we need him, not because we want him to lead us.” This shows that even if you manage to gain power or career success with a bad attitude, people will never truly like you if you treat them poorly.

People with warm personalities and positive attitudes find that opportunities come much more easily, simply because of how they interact with others. On the other hand, people with off-putting attitudes, no matter what they say, will struggle to make friends if they refuse to change their behavior. To sum up, being a charismatic person who gets along well with most people will make your life noticeably better and more rewarding, all thanks to having a good attitude.

First impressions are not set in stone, and how they shift can vary a lot from one person to another. Everyone reacts differently when they encounter a person, place, or thing for the first time. But as you learn more about whoever or whatever you’re looking at, your initial opinion can shift completely.

These first reactions matter because they are the very first judgment we form about something. Often, though, that initial take can shift in just an hour, or even a full day later.

Take a school class as an example: if the first day feels dull and uninteresting, you might leave with a bad impression. But if the second day’s lesson is fun and engaging, your opinion of the class will probably turn around fast.

Sometimes, your own attitude shapes that first impression too. If you approach a new situation with a negative mindset, you’re far more likely to form a negative first impression of it. And if you lash out or react poorly when you have a bad first impression, that can say a lot about your own character.

That said, not all first impressions are changeable. Plenty of people hold onto their initial reaction forever, no matter what new information comes to light.

Even if you start out with a positive impression of someone, that can flip on its head if they do something hurtful or out of character.

The same goes for jobs. You might start a new role thinking it’s easy, fun, and a great place to make friends, especially if your first day goes smoothly. But if you meet your boss the next day and they treat you rudely, your entire opinion of the job will shift instantly. You might even start dreading going in, all because of that one bad interaction. First impressions are such important moments because they shape that very first thought we have about a person or thing. A good first impression of someone can even turn into a lasting friendship down the line.

To sum up, first impressions can change, and how they shift depends on the person and their own attitude. But that’s not always the case—some people never adjust their initial thoughts, no matter what. Think about how limiting that is: if you never let a first impression change, you might write someone off just because you don’t think they’re ‘cool’ enough at first glance. You could miss out on a great experience or friendship, all because you didn’t take the time to learn more about their life. That’s a real shame.

Have you ever imagined how much more engaging school could be if a program brought together students of different ages to work on projects, try new activities, and learn side by side?

Imagine a school initiative designed to let you learn more efficiently, grasp concepts in new ways, and get extra support for subjects you struggle with day to day. In my view, students almost always feel more comfortable and confident talking to peers their own age. Peers can break down confusing topics in ways that are easy to understand, since they’re learning the same material too. On the other hand, many students feel pressured when speaking to adults, which stops them from asking for help when they need it.

Think about whether you’d prefer a program where everyone can come together to get help when they need it, while also making new friends. Most days, you probably only hang out with your usual group of friends, but there are plenty of other students in your school you’ve never even spoken to. A program open to all is a great way to meet people you might not cross paths with otherwise.

This kind of program wouldn’t just help you bond with other students and get to know people across the whole school. It wouldn’t stay contained to scheduled meetings either: you’ll start connecting with people you pass in the hallways every day, and everyone involved can share new ideas or skills with each other, teaching you something fresh every time you interact with another participant.

If you like this idea and want to bring a program like this to your own school, the first step is simple: talk to a teacher or your principal. Share whatever ideas you’ve come up with, and work with them to get the initiative off the ground. It’s a small change that could make school a far better place for everyone.

Their parents hold down jobs to cover basic family costs like groceries, clothes, and utility bills, so there is no one else to care for the kids. While some might think this is a chore, most students actually enjoy spending time with their siblings, playing games and keeping them company. It also teaches them responsibility: they have to make sure their siblings stay safe, give them meals so they do not go hungry, and change their clothes if they get messy. When the younger kids take naps, students can tidy the house without interruptions, which means their parents do not have to worry about housework when they get home tired from work.

High school students already have a heavy workload to manage. Homework piles up quickly, and big projects can be especially challenging. Even though some assignments feel like too much work, students know they need to complete all their tasks to keep their grades from dropping. When projects get too difficult, they often ask classmates or friends for help. Studying with friends is also a fun way to bond and spend time together, and working hard to pass high school is rewarding because it makes their parents proud.

On top of schoolwork and sibling care, many students also hold after-school jobs. Having a job lets them earn their own money, so they do not have to ask their parents for cash every time they want to buy something. While working after a long day of classes can be tiring and make them feel sleepy, the income is worth it, and they no longer need to rely on pocket money from their parents. It is even better if their friends work the same job, as they can commute to work together and have fun while on shift.

For all these reasons, 89% of Generic School students are firmly against the plan to add an extra hour and a half to the school day. Most have after-school jobs to get to, and many need to rush home to care for their siblings while their parents are at work. Adding more time to the school day would throw off their ability to balance all these key responsibilities.

Thomas Jefferson held the view that taking action is always preferable to sitting idle. We achieve far more when we stay consistently active. Accomplishments come in all sizes, from massive breakthroughs to tiny daily wins. For example, if you’ve always wanted to play an instrument but don’t know how, the only way to reach that goal is to start learning. Even far-fetched ideas, like building a machine to visit other dimensions or travel back in time, require active effort to become reality. Simple, everyday tasks count too: tidying your home, making a meal, finishing homework. As long as we keep moving, we keep making progress.

Choosing action over inaction lets us achieve more in the long run. If humanity had never taken any action, we would not have any of the comforts and tools we rely on today. We can reach goals on our own or by working with others. Think of sports teams: players collaborate to win matches. Video game companies are another example—whole teams of people work together to create games for players to enjoy. Even within those games, people can choose to play solo or team up with others to win. It is always better to tackle your work, finish homework, and even make time for small joys like playing outside or hanging out with friends.

That said, inactivity does have a valid role to play, mostly as rest. Sleeping, relaxing, or taking time to unwind helps us let off steam after putting in hard work. After spending hours on work or school tasks, we might go home, take a nap, eat a meal, watch some TV, or get a full night’s sleep. This rest helps us feel motivated to keep going the next day, whether we have a job to return to or classes to attend. Even ticking off small daily tasks counts as an achievement: picking up groceries, cleaning the house, or cooking a meal all add up. Completing any of these means you have accomplished something useful.

Sleeping all day, though, leaves no room for achievement. Laziness is harmful, because once we get used to taking the easy way out, it becomes a hard habit to break. We risk getting comfortable with doing nothing at all. Instead, it is far better to stay active and motivated to complete the tasks we need to do, so we can keep making progress and reaching our goals.

Thomas Jefferson once posed a question: do we achieve more when we stay constantly busy, or does doing nothing have value too? Naturally, not everyone answers this the same way. Some people prefer to laze around and avoid pushing themselves forward, while others are driven to work hard and create new chances for themselves. I fully agree with Jefferson’s view, as it comes down to three key habits that help people seize opportunities: putting in the effort, making the most of your time, and staying open to new paths.

Of course, not everyone shares this outlook. Many people insist they cannot create better options than the ones they already have, often because their lives are difficult. For example, plenty of people grow up without wealth, so they feel they lack the resources to chase new chances. But we have to accept a basic truth: nothing worth having comes easily. My own grandfather shared a story with me shortly before he passed away about his early life. It was incredibly tough: his family was not wealthy, and with five children to feed, they sometimes only ate one meal a day. But he never stopped saying, "One day, everything will get better." He held onto that belief even through the hardest times, and eventually found new opportunities to build a better life for all of us. That is why I remind myself every day: if you want something, you have to fight for it.

On top of that, we can turn even our wildest dreams into reality if we use our time wisely. Hard work lets you achieve things you never thought possible, like buying a nice car, owning a large home, or affording other luxuries. But these rewards only come if you put in consistent effort. What’s more, when you work hard and build a good life, you also gain the ability to help other people improve their own lives. Anyone who refuses to give up and keeps working will always accomplish far more than someone who stays idle.

The last key habit is to stay open to new possibilities every single day. This means you should never settle for just one route to your goals. If one path doesn’t work, you should always be willing to try another. I remember sitting down one day to figure out how to reach my own dreams quickly, and I realized that people who actively look for different options are the ones who actually achieve what they want. It is a simple truth: if you never step out of your comfort zone, nothing will ever change.

To sum up, the core message here is that you can unlock countless opportunities and dreams if you are willing to keep moving forward. People who refuse to push themselves beyond their current limits will never experience anything new, which is a shame because they will never know what amazing things they could have achieved. But if you work hard and always keep an eye out for new chances, you can have everything you want in life. Say you dream of buying a car that costs one million dollars: if you put in the effort, you will earn the money to afford it. You have to fight for what you want, use your time well, seek out new opportunities instead of wasting your days, and stay open to different paths. Time moves incredibly fast, and you might regret being lazy later if you don’t act now. If you follow these steps, life will become much easier to navigate and enjoy.

I fully agree that individuality is important. I love seeing people make their own life choices, which feels great. Most of my friends just copy what others do, but I prefer to follow my own desires and do what I actually enjoy.

My family is often really negative when they share their opinions, and I dislike that—I want to speak my mind, but they never listen. That’s why I embrace my individuality: I trust my own judgment and do what I want.

Too many people depend on others, which is not healthy. My history class covered this, explaining how people in the past lacked individuality. I think folks rely on others because they crave attention. Life today is very different—now people care too much about what others say about their looks or actions.

I’m happy with who I am. I’m kind and have many good qualities, so I do what I want and don’t care what others say about me.

At first, I wasn’t sure what to write, so I just kept going. If I knew more English, I’d write even more. Since I had no other ideas, I decided to share my personal story.

I moved from Puerto Rico to the US two years ago, and my life changed completely. I now value everything I have, because I understand the sacrifice behind each thing. I still want to improve myself, even though adjusting is hard—the language and customs are totally different.

Meeting people from other places is mixed—some are great, others not. I love learning new things, but it upsets me that Puerto Ricans are US citizens, yet many treat us like undocumented immigrants just because Spanish is our first language.

These two years have been tough. School was a huge obstacle—walking into a classroom and feeling totally alone is hard. When you can’t communicate, you just watch others participate. I started skipping school and acting out because I had no support at home or school.

Now, I don’t feel like I belong here. The only reason I stay is my mom—I want to give her everything she deserves. She always provided for us, even when life in Puerto Rico was hard, always giving us the best she could.

While some people argue that students should be allowed to use cell phones in classrooms, since they can access the internet to complete class assignments, I believe phones do not belong in the classroom. They cause disruptions and lead students to chat with others instead of focusing on lessons.

First, cell phones cause constant trouble in the classroom. For example, when a teacher is giving a lesson, some students might listen to music or watch movies on their phones instead of doing classwork. This distracts nearby classmates, who cannot focus on the lesson because of noise or the student’s screen. It can also lead to conflict: if a teacher asks a student to stop using their phone and the student refuses, an argument may break out. If a student repeatedly misuses their phone during class, the school might even suspend them for breaking rules.

Second, students often use phones to chat with friends while the teacher is talking. This means they pay no attention to the lesson, so they miss important information and fall behind in their learning. Worse, some students use chat features to share rude or inappropriate photos of classmates as a joke. This can embarrass the people in the photos, hurt their confidence, and make them feel too anxious or afraid to come to school. No one should feel unsafe or unwelcome in class because of someone else’s phone use.

Third, phones make it easy for students to cheat on tests. If a teacher steps away from their desk during an exam, a student with a hidden phone can look up answers or message a friend for help. This lets them get a good grade they did not earn, which is unfair to other students who studied hard. Over time, this also hurts the cheating student’s own learning: they never build the confidence to do work on their own, and they miss out on gaining real knowledge.

Fourth, phones reduce class participation and waste valuable learning time. When students stare at their screens all day, they do not raise their hands to answer questions or join group activities. Spending hours every day watching movies or listening to music on a phone is also bad for physical health: it strains the eyes and overworks the brain, which is only focused on entertainment instead of learning. When you need advice, you probably shouldn’t rely on just one person. Most people reach out to several people to explore more options instead of basing their entire decision on a single person’s view, which helps them make smarter choices and cut down on unnecessary costs from limited options.

One big advantage of asking several people for advice is that you get a wider range of choices to pick from. Chances are, you’ll end up following suggestions from the people you consult, whether those lead to good or bad results. There’s always an opportunity cost to any decision—you might make a smart move that improves your life, or a poor one that causes problems. These choices can shape everything from your long-term future to your mood for the rest of the day, affecting your personal growth or the impact you have on others. All sorts of different outcomes are possible.

Another benefit is that you get to hear lots of different perspectives on your situation. You can rule out suggestions that line up with past experiences you’ve had, whether those were great or awful. You can take on board what others tell you, learning from their input even if it points to a tough time ahead or a positive outcome. Once you’ve learned from these experiences, you can support other people facing the same or similar problems. You might use what you’ve learned to help yourself if you ever run into the same situation again, or even share your knowledge with others who need guidance.

There are downsides to asking multiple people for advice, too. Hearing so many different opinions might make you doubt the decision you originally had in mind—though sometimes that shift in thinking leads to an even better choice. Different people will give you conflicting responses about your situation, which can make your problem feel even more confusing when you have to pick which advice to follow. The process of comparing all the suggestions can add extra stress and pressure. Even after you’ve made your choice, it could turn out to be the worst day of your life, or the absolute best. It’s never easy to settle on which piece of advice to trust.

Many schools now provide distance learning, letting students take part in classes from home via online platforms or video conferencing. Other schools do not offer this option, as they believe learning remotely is not an effective way to study.

I disagree. Other schools refuse to offer distance learning because they think it is not a good way to learn.

First, students gain little from taking classes at home. If they struggle to understand a topic, there is no one nearby to explain it to them right away.

Second, remote learning is not the most effective way to study. Students need the structure of a physical school to master the material they are required to learn.

While you can pick up some knowledge studying from home, attending classes in person at a school is always the better option for students.

Schools that refuse to offer distance learning do so because they believe it is not a useful way to learn. Their reasoning matches the points above: students do not benefit from studying at home, as they lack immediate support when confused. Remote learning is less effective than in-person classes, since students need the environment of a physical school to learn what they need to know. While home study is possible, attending school in person remains the best choice for learners.

Some schools do offer distance learning, as it works well for certain students. However, it is not the right choice for everyone. Many students have after-school jobs and other responsibilities, such as young immigrants who move to the country alone without their parents. These individuals have to balance work and study at the same time, so I believe distance learning does not benefit them. For example, people who move to a new country are often seeking better opportunities and a brighter future. They need to learn a new language, which is not easy for everyone — some pick it up quickly, while others take much longer.

Online classes can be a great option for some students, though, particularly those who have valid reasons for not attending school in person. For instance, some students have young children to care for and cannot leave home to go to school. For these people, distance learning is a valuable opportunity to study and work toward their goals. They just need enough motivation to keep going, and they can achieve what they set out to do.

Overall, I believe most students do not benefit from taking classes at home. Homes are full of distractions, from electronic devices to young children or other family members, which make it hard to focus on studying.

Video conferencing is a useful learning tool for some people who prefer studying from home, but if you have a question or doubt, you cannot ask the video for help. That is why I believe the best way to learn is to attend school in person and work hard every day to study for the future you want. Your future is in your own hands — if you make bad choices, you will face the consequences later. It is important to think carefully about what you want and take deliberate steps toward it. In life, everything you do to others, whether good or bad, will come back to you eventually. You will feel the impact of the mistakes you made that hurt other people in the past.

In today’s busy world, there are endless tasks we need to complete, both personal and for the wider community. As Thomas Jefferson wrote, "Determine never to be idle... it is wonderful how much may be done if we are always doing." Imagine how much we could achieve if we all worked together to build a better life for everyone. Improvements like this don’t just help one individual—they make the whole community better off.

We should make up our minds not to sit around waiting for change to happen on its own. Instead, we need to prepare our own lives to make that change a reality. Being useful matters—we should take action that helps both ourselves and the people around us. If we all pitch in to improve our society, we can definitely make it happen. Take small daily choices, for example. Instead of littering when we’re out walking, we could pick up trash we see. This simple habit would show clear progress from past years, keeping our communities clean. It proves we can improve every day without needing orders from others.

I’ve watched groups of volunteers all over the world make huge positive changes to the planet, clearing up polluted rivers and messy parks. If we stop waiting for others to fix problems, we can follow their example and make our own impact too. We just need to keep taking small actions for a better life. At the end of the day, it’s all about being helpful and improving daily—that’s the real secret to progress.

Taking action should be a core goal for every community. We need to be more engaged with our surroundings, to make positive changes and turn impossible things into reality. Stay determined and keep acting—doing something is always better than waiting for others to step up while you do nothing. Let’s keep our communities productive and wonderful.

To reduce energy use and save resources, many companies have switched to a four-day work week where employees work ten hours each day. Some people suggest schools should adopt this same model by adding two extra hours to the daily schedule. I strongly disagree with this idea. Extending the school day by two hours would be extremely stressful for students, leave them with almost no time to complete homework, and create major issues for schools overall.

First, this change would be a huge disadvantage for students who have commitments outside of class. For instance, I work a part-time job after school that starts at 4 p.m. If my school added two hours to the day, I would have to quit my job, since classes would end too late for me to get to work on time. This does not only affect me, either—many other students also have after-school jobs, childcare duties, or family responsibilities that they would no longer be able to manage with a longer school day.

Second, adding two hours to the school day would be incredibly tiring for students. Longer classes would make it hard for us to focus on what teachers are saying, as we would get worn out much faster than usual. We would also get home very late and exhausted, leaving almost no time or energy to finish homework. Since students need to rest for the next day of school, many would skip assignments entirely, which would hurt their grades in the long run.

Another major issue would be lower attendance rates. Students would be so exhausted from the longer school days that many would skip class entirely, especially if they are still tired from the day before. Regular attendance is required for students to pass their courses and move forward in school, so this is a serious problem. A model that makes students miss more class is clearly not a good solution.

In conclusion, even though a four-day school week means only four days of classes, adding two hours to each day is not a workable plan. As a student, I know this change would disrupt my daily routine, leave me stressed and tired during class, and hurt both my attendance and my grades. For all these reasons, my school should not adopt this model.

While personal accomplishments can boost students’ self-esteem, it is also true that learners put great effort into every task they take on. Even when their work is not perfect, offering praise encourages them to try their hardest. Recognition can be given to those who reach specific milestones, but all achievements, big or small, help build a student’s self-esteem. Ultimately, self-esteem stems from either external praise or personal success.

Does genuine self-esteem only come from praise? When students work hard in class, acknowledging their effort raises their self-esteem. This not only helps them perform at their best, but also sets a positive example for their peers, lifting everyone’s confidence and work ethic. Students feel valued when others compliment their work, which benefits them in the long run. Praise is one of the most meaningful things you can offer learners, as it helps them grow into adults with strong self-esteem and a solid commitment to hard work.

Self-esteem also grows out of personal achievement. Even small successes in schoolwork, no matter how minor they seem, play a key role in a student’s development and help maintain healthy self-esteem. Students who complete tasks well tend to have higher self-esteem, which in turn motivates their classmates to aim for similar success. Any achievement, whether in a classroom or another setting, helps sustain and boost a student’s self-esteem over time.

To sum up, both praise and achievements are essential for students. Every accomplishment or word of recognition they receive helps them build strong self-esteem, and both serve as important life lessons. Reaching a goal encourages students to keep making good choices and maintain high self-esteem. Meanwhile, praise pushes students to do their absolute best, even when tasks are challenging, helping them learn, improve their self-esteem, and work toward new achievements. Recognizing students’ efforts also makes it more likely they will earn further accomplishments in the future.

From my own life experiences, I strongly disagree with the common idea that first impressions are almost impossible to change—after all, people are always capable of growing and adjusting their behavior over time. I think a lot of people believe this myth because when they first meet someone, that person might not seem interested in talking to them, so they assume that’s just how the person is forever. It’s very common to make a bad first impression, but that doesn’t mean things have to stay that way. You shouldn’t judge or label someone based only on how you first interacted with them, since people can always change later.

One big reason this idea is wrong is that someone’s mood on the day you meet them can totally shape how they come across. If a person is having a terrible day when you first talk, they might not feel comfortable chatting or engaging, which makes their first impression seem far worse than it really is. A perfect example of this is my relationship with my best friend. We first met in math class, and he didn’t even want to be my partner or speak to me at all. When I asked him for help with math problems I couldn’t figure out, he completely ignored me and never responded.

To wrap up, I firmly disagree that first impressions are set in stone. In my group of friends, there are two people who gave me a really bad first impression when we first met, but we’re all close now. All of this goes to show that you should never claim first impressions are literally impossible to change, because people can always adjust how they act later on.

I once created a prompt to learn more about people who have been targeted by bullies, and I’ve noticed something striking: how much people’s attitudes shift once they actually get to know someone. I’ve put in a lot of effort to get along with others, but not everyone is kind. There are still plenty of people who bully others for no reason, often judging people harshly without even trying to meet them first. That’s a big part of why I often keep to myself—too many people spread rumors about others without knowing the full story, and I hate that. Worse still, the people who are being bullied are usually too terrified to speak up, because they’re afraid the bullies will target them even more.

I’ve learned to ignore most of what other people say—if they want to gossip, that’s their issue, not mine. But I’ve noticed that when people get hurt or end up in trouble, they often come to me for help, even if they didn’t like me before. When I’m feeling angry or down, I turn to soccer. Playing helps me clear my head and forget about the worries weighing on me, at least for a while. If I could change one thing, I’d use that love of the sport to help others too.

I’d organize community soccer games where anyone who wants to play can join in, so they can set aside their worries just like I do. That’s the whole point of sports, after all—they’re meant for people to have fun together without conflict. There are plenty of other ways to connect with others too: going to the movies with friends, watching soccer, basketball or volleyball matches together. I truly believe every problem has a solution, but the core issue is that we don’t show enough respect to one another. If we all made an effort to treat others with respect, everything would be completely different.

At the end of the day, what everyone wants is to feel safe, in communities free of gangsters who only drag people deeper into poverty. We should get all families involved to work together to put a stop to people who hurt others. So many people work hard in school to build a better life, hoping to pull their families out of difficult situations and away from harmful paths. Finishing high school makes it far easier to earn a good living later. Even a basic high school diploma can get you a solid job—it might not be your dream role, but it’s at least a steady way to support yourself.

There are practical ways to stay safe too. If someone steals your belongings, you can report it to the police, who may be able to help you get your things back. People should never let fear show, because if you act scared, others will take advantage of that. We’re all capable of being clever, but we need to be smart in every part of our lives, not just in areas we’re good at. Just because you’re intelligent in some ways doesn’t mean others will treat you kindly. If you let your anger show, people might lash out at you in ways that cause real harm.

Most people are kind at heart, but when they get mad, they can change completely. They might get so angry that it’s scary to be around them. To avoid conflict, I think the best approach is to invite people to play sports or hang out with your friends. You could go to the beach together, have a good time, and keep tensions low—that way, you might even become close friends, or at least stay on good terms. But there’s one rule: never show your weak spots. If you end up in a disagreement with a friend, they’ll already know exactly how to hurt you most. That’s why I believe no one should know your biggest vulnerabilities, whether they’re physical or personal. That’s all I wanted to share with this prompt.

Experiencing failure plays a massive role in eventually becoming successful. When we fail, we learn exactly what not to do next time, so we can avoid repeating the same errors. For example, imagine I dreamed of becoming a professional soccer player. I had played for top clubs, been named my team’s best player, and never once been cut from a squad. One day, my coach told me about a professional tryout happening the next week, and said he wanted me to prepare for it. He gave me a strict schedule of workouts and healthy meals to follow to get in top shape. Every day, I had to eat well and train hard. Some days I felt unmotivated, wanting to skip training and eat junk food instead, but I pushed through those feelings. When tryout day arrived, I was as ready as I could possibly be. We started with warmups, then moved to drills. I played amazingly well, probably the best person on the field that day. At the end of the day, the coaches gathered all the players and announced who had made the team. My name was not on the list. I had failed to become a pro soccer player.

This is the moment where your attitude matters most. I could either quit soccer entirely and choose a completely different path, or I could pick myself up and try again. Failing puts your dedication to the test: it shows how committed you are to your goal, and whether you’re willing to face failure again and again to reach success. A great example of this is the story from the book *The Pursuit of Happyness*. The main character invents a machine and wants to sell it to make money. No one is interested in buying it at first. He is a father of one child, and they live in a motel. When he can’t pay his bills, they are kicked out and end up homeless for a few weeks. Even while homeless, he doesn’t stop trying to sell his invention. He faces rejection every time he tries to pitch it to someone, but he keeps going. Finally, after many struggles, one person agrees to buy the machine. That buyer tells others how useful it is, and soon more people start purchasing it too. He becomes successful because he never gave up on his dream, even when he was rejected over and over again. At the end of the day, failure is the key to achieving real success.

I believe working 10 hours a day is better than an 8-hour schedule. You save energy, electricity, and daily time. Four 10-hour days add up to 40 hours a week, the same as a standard 5-day workweek. You can still work overtime on Fridays and Saturdays if you want extra shifts.

A 10-hour daily schedule also works better than the standard 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. routine for schools. I think my school should adjust its hours to save time and resources. We should add 2 extra hours to the school day, making it 10 hours long. This lets students get more sleep once they get home and work their part-time jobs. Extending the day by 2 hours means we can switch to a 4-day school week, giving students 3 days off.

This setup helps schools cut down on energy and water costs. Teachers would also get three full days off per week, which is a great benefit for them. We should move to a 4-day school week across the board.

Many students struggle to wake up early, but a 4-day week gives them more time to finish homework at their own pace. Well-rested students focus better in class and get longer weekends to catch up on schoolwork. Getting enough sleep keeps high schoolers fresh and active during the day, which helps them hit their academic goals more easily.

Right now, most high schoolers have a tough time all year because they cannot finish homework on weekends. Many also work 32 to 38 hours a week at part-time jobs, so they have zero free time on Saturdays or Sundays.

Many students struggle to build this confidence, often because of how they were raised or how their peers and teachers treat them. Putting in consistent effort makes even tough schoolwork feel manageable eventually. Some people argue that praising students for low-quality work hurts their learning, as it makes them stop aiming for higher standards. Instead, students should focus on completing work they fully understand, even if it means taking small risks, as this helps them put in the effort needed to grow more confident. Not everyone agrees with this approach, mostly because building genuine self-confidence is far from easy. It takes time and hard work to achieve, and many people underestimate how difficult the process can be. A common question comes up here: does real self-esteem come from constant praise, or from personal achievements? The answer is clear: true self-esteem grows from accomplishments. These are the successes you earn after taking risks and putting in work, both in school and in daily life. Every student will face incredibly hard times when they feel like giving up, or like they are not capable of succeeding. Many also deal with personal problems outside of school. But pushing through all these struggles, taking risks on tasks, and working through challenges is exactly what builds lasting self-confidence.

While many believe that doing nothing at times has value, the truth is that people need to stay busy and productive throughout their lives. Everyone needs a sense of purpose and tasks to focus on. Most people recognize that a person who does nothing all day can negatively affect those around them, so it is important for everyone to keep working toward goals. Leading an active life brings far more benefits. People who take action and stay busy achieve more success, which can improve not just their own lives but also the future of their children and even the next generation of their family. On the other hand, someone who is inactive is often lazy, neglects their own responsibilities, and may even stop caring about the needs of others.

Around the world, there are many people without jobs who make no effort to find work. They feel too lazy to go out and search for employment, choosing instead to waste their days doing nothing useful. When people spend their time without work, they make no progress toward a better future, which is why so many stay trapped in poverty. They could build a good life if they stopped wasting time being idle. In many countries, people who refuse to work end up begging on the streets for money from strangers. These individuals often have plenty of opportunities in life, but they never stop to consider them. An inactive person does not care whether they have a job or not, only wanting free time with no responsibilities. Being lazy serves no real purpose in life. Worse, many children suffer because their parents refuse to work. Young kids are forced to get jobs or beg on the streets alongside their parents, just because the adults are too inactive to hold down a job. This inactivity hurts children deeply, as they are dragged into the same cycle of poverty and begging.

Laziness is common across all age groups, including students. Many learners are inactive in school, for example, when given group projects, they try to take the easiest tasks instead of contributing fairly. This habit causes problems later when they grow into adults, as they expect life to stay as easy as it was during their school years. Most students are lazy and want everything handed to them without effort. As adults, they will struggle when they realize work is not easy, even when job opportunities are right in front of them. Instead of taking available work, they avoid it and waste time staying at home. Some even look for jobs that require almost no effort, which is why many end up unemployed. Students need to learn to be active and hardworking. Being inactive from a young age has a huge negative impact on the future. Young people need to set clear goals and avoid falling into the habit of laziness.

Today, many people are unemployed and claim this situation is better for them, as it lets them spend more time with family. However, there is no reason to be lazy just because they do not have a job. Everyone should contribute something to their family or their country, no matter their employment status. Many experts say that if global unemployment dropped, economies would improve significantly. A strong economy is vital for the future of every country. If fewer people were inactive and unwilling to work, economies would grow, and there would be far less poverty worldwide.

To sum up, living an inactive life has no real purpose. Everyone needs to stay busy and work toward meaningful goals in their daily life. People who consistently take action can shape their own future for the better. Active people always work with clear purpose, and this makes them successful in whatever they do. Being inactive means having no direction or goals, so no one should ever choose to live that way. People should never act lazy or waste their potential. Everyone can benefit from being more active, which will help them achieve greater success in life.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once wrote about the importance of individuality, but I disagree with this view. In life, there are countless times when we need support from others, not just the ability to stand alone. True success is not just about being independent—it is about learning how to manage your life well, even when that means relying on other people. In this essay, I will discuss the value of working together with others. First, I will look at how collaboration affects job performance and outcomes. Next, I will talk about society, and why being fully individual is not always practical or helpful. Finally, I will explain how we make decisions, and how working with others can help us achieve our goals. All of this will show that individuality does not stop you from becoming the person you want to be.

Workplaces offer many examples of why pure individuality is not always best. You might work with a colleague whose behavior you find annoying or hard to deal with. Instead of keeping to yourself and acting as an individual, you should try to work with this person. After all, you may need their help or expertise one day. Making an effort to collaborate breaks down the walls of individuality between you, and helps you build better relationships with the people around you. Another common job issue tied to individuality is staying in a role you hate, instead of pursuing the career you always dreamed of. Just because you are currently in a job you dislike does not mean you cannot work toward your goal. Quitting a job you hate to follow your passion is not a sign of being unindividual—it is a smart choice. Most companies rely on teamwork to reach their goals, and you can do the same in your own role, working with colleagues instead of isolating yourself.

When it comes to society, some people prefer to spend most of their time alone. We often call these individuals asocial. They choose solitude because it makes them feel comfortable. Other people avoid being around others because they prefer to handle tasks on their own, or because they want to be the center of attention—we can call these people individualists. Not all of these people fit the same pattern, and there are often deeper reasons for their behavior, such as their upbringing or past experiences. Navigating social situations can be far more complicated than it seems, especially if you know people who prefer to be alone. However, you can still try to connect with them, and many of these people do change over time. Some seek help on their own, while others improve because a close friend or family member supported them and helped them grow.

All of us make decisions in life, and some of these choices can lead us to act wrongly or become a different person than we intended. Choosing to change who you are is not just a matter of wanting it—it requires a deliberate decision. You can either let the outside world pressure you into choices, or you can decide for yourself what you want to do. Many people choose to let others control their lives, because they think it is better or simply because it is the easier path. Even a president cannot run a country alone, making choices however he wants—he knows he must work with Congress, because he cannot achieve anything by himself. Like a president, we all have the same choice: we can collaborate with others, or we can try to go it alone. You can set your own goals and fight for what you want, instead of letting the world constantly push you to become someone you do not want to be.

In conclusion, we all have the power to choose which path we follow in life. In this essay, I discussed how collaboration affects job performance and results, how we can live in society and resolve conflicts with others, and how we can make our own decisions to become who we want to be, set goals, and fight for them. All of this shows that Ralph Waldo Emerson was wrong about the value of pure individuality. We do not have to be constantly pushed around by the world—we can take control, work with others when needed, and become exactly the person we want to be.

British naturalist and politician John Lubbock once wrote the now-famous line: "Your character will be what you yourself choose to make." While Lubbock’s words ring true, it is also worth noting that our past experiences play a big role in shaping who we are and who we may grow into later in life. But we should never let our past or our current circumstances take over our lives entirely—we hold far more power than we realize, through the small and large choices we make every day.

Take someone who grew up with abusive parents, for instance. They might worry they will turn out the same way, but overcoming that difficult upbringing can actually make them far stronger, building their character more than they ever thought possible. We always have a choice in how we shape our character. People might label someone as "mean" or "selfish" for not sharing, but that is not necessarily their character—it may just be part of their personality. You are the only one responsible for building your own character, and not everyone has to like it. What matters most is that you are happy with it, because at the end of the day, you only have yourself to rely on. That is far better than living to please people who judge you unfairly.

As the saying goes, you can never judge a book by its cover. No one can truly understand your character until they know your full story and where you come from. The way you build your character can leave a lasting legacy, often without you even realizing it. People will admire how you grew through tough times, and ask questions like "How is she so strong?" or "How did she become so independent?" When you share your journey, the struggles you have faced and the steps you took to overcome them, people will be proud of how far you have come. Remember, you are the only one who controls what character traits you develop.

It is impossible to fully define your character just by saying "I have been through this before." Think of someone who loses a family member to a long illness. They might spend weeks in deep sadness, refusing to accept the loss. But eventually, they will pick themselves up, determined to make their loved one proud of the person they raised. They will try to make every day count, showing how well they are coping even when sadness hits out of nowhere. Pushing through that grief makes their character stronger than they could ever imagine.

Everyone faces moments of self-doubt, wanting to give up because they feel they are not good enough to achieve their goals. But once you start reaching small milestones, the world feels a lot less intimidating. Your brain might try to trick you with negative thoughts, telling you that something is impossible—but why focus on that? Those thoughts only hold you back. Your character is not meant to drag you down; it is there to push you forward, past all the obstacles life throws your way. Only you have the power to break through those barriers.

So never hold back from making a choice you know is right. Trust your gut, and let your values guide you. Do not let anyone tell you that something is impossible—prove them wrong, and make your mark. Let your character stand out, because you are unique, no matter what anyone else says.

Life is not about picking only the easy, comfortable options. It is about doing what feels right for you, and fitting your own needs. As Lubbock’s quote reminds us: "Your character will be what you yourself choose to make." This is your life—enjoy it, and let every action, every choice, help build the character you want to have.

I fully agree that a person’s attitude plays a central role in their life.

Attitude matters more than most people realize, because it shapes how we act around others. Whenever you speak to someone new, they pick up on your attitude right away. If you come across as respectful, warm, and humble, they will see you as a kind person, and will want to keep talking to you. Even if you run into that same person days or weeks later, they will still be happy to strike up a conversation again, all because of the positive impression your attitude left.

Take a common example: the first time you meet the father of your daughter’s partner. The very first thing he will notice about you is your attitude and how much respect you show. If you act with kindness and courtesy, he will decide you are a good person worthy of his daughter, because your attitude shows you are respectful and humble. He will feel proud of how you carry yourself, trust you, and treat you with respect in return. After all, if you want others to respect you, you first need to learn to respect them and approach every interaction with a positive attitude.

Later in life, when you have children of your own, teaching them to be good people should be your top priority. The most important lesson you can pass on is how to treat others with a positive attitude. Kids who learn to be respectful and kind from a young age grow up to be good people, and they come to see how beautiful life can be when you treat others well. You will feel proud of yourself too, knowing you gave your children a solid, valuable education. Truly, attitude is one of the most important keys to a happy life.

Attitude forms the foundation of how we move through the world. When you consistently show a good attitude, the people around you will see you as someone with strong values. You will know how to communicate clearly and kindly with others, and your humble approach will make you easy to get along with. Sadly, many people today lack this quality: their attitudes are rude, they show little respect, and they struggle to hold conversations about even simple topics. Instead, aim to be the kind of person who respects everyone, no matter their age. Above all, keep your attitude humble and polite. This way, people will recognize you are a good person, and they will treat you with respect at all times.

Respect and attitude are the true keys to life. These are the most important things you can learn, and you need to practice using them every day. Ideally, schools everywhere would teach these values to all children, because education is the most important thing for building a good future. At the same time, your attitude must always be your top priority: stay humble and respectful, no matter who you are talking to.

I fully agree with Ralph Waldo Emerson’s view that you can only grow if you try to do things that go beyond what you have already mastered. If you stick to tasks you have already perfected, you will never get better, because you are just repeating the same actions over and over. You will not move forward or pick up any new skills, since you are not challenging yourself at all. To grow, you need to take on new tasks and learn as you go, picking up fresh skills along the way.

Too many people fall into a routine of doing the exact same thing every day, never trying anything new. They need to push themselves to try unfamiliar activities if they want to learn new things.

Spending time practicing things you have already mastered is a waste of your energy. You could be using that time to try other new activities instead. There is no need to stick to the same tasks forever.

I stand by this opinion, and I believe Emerson’s words are spot on. Trying new things is key to learning, as taking on different challenges helps you gain new knowledge and skills.
