Would you really want to spend extra hours stuck at school when you could be enjoying your free time instead? Joining an after-school homework club can wreck all the hobbies you care about, which is why these programs are a bad idea for students. There are three key reasons to avoid them: they cut into family time, leave no room for sports, and stop you from gaming.

First, joining a homework club means you’ll barely see your family. If you’re stuck at school for extra hours, you’ll probably miss out on plans your parents made. Take Generic_Name as an example: when the final bell rang one day, he realized he had to stay for the after-school homework club. He called his mom to let her know, but she told him the family was heading to Red Lobster, his favorite restaurant, for dinner. Generic_Name was really upset that he had to skip his favorite meal just to sit in a club at school. This clearly shows how these clubs can ruin quality time with loved ones—he missed a special dinner all because of an extra school program.

Second, these clubs often clash with sports practices and games. If you’re in a homework club and play a sport, you’ll almost certainly show up late to practice. Generic_Name is a basketball player who also attends an after-school English homework club. Every Wednesday, he has to go to the club right after classes, followed by basketball practice. One week, he arrived at practice just five minutes late. His coach counted it as his first strike. When Generic_Name tried to explain he’d been at a school club, the coach told him he had to choose between school commitments and basketball. Generic_Name ended up getting three strikes total and was kicked off the team. He lost the sport he loved, and his dream of playing basketball professionally was ruined. This proves homework clubs can destroy your athletic goals.

Finally, if you love video games, a homework club will limit when you can play. You’ll get home so late that there’s no time left for gaming on weekdays. Generic_Name is a popular gaming YouTuber who streams for his followers every day. But after joining the homework club, he gets out of school at 6:30 pm, and the 30-minute drive home means he doesn’t arrive until 7 pm. He still has leftover homework from the club to finish, so there’s no time to stream on weeknights. Now he can only play games on weekends. He also bought a new game recently, but he’s only allowed to play it on Saturdays and Sundays. Since he stopped streaming regularly, he lost half of his YouTube followers. All of this happened just because he joined an after-school homework club.

Overall, after-school homework clubs are a waste of time if you have other plans after class. It’s hard to balance two big commitments at once, so it’s better to skip the club. If you love sports, focus on those instead—you can always do homework on your own schedule at home. No one wants to spend even more hours at school than necessary. If you don’t want extra time in class, stay away from after-school homework clubs.

Keeping a good attitude is the best way to achieve success in life. There are two main types of attitudes people can have: a positive, helpful one, and a negative, unhelpful one. A good attitude can help you handle all kinds of situations. For instance, if you disagree with your boss about your salary, you can either approach the conversation with a calm, positive attitude to reach a compromise, or lash out with a bad attitude and risk getting fired. Good attitudes also make tough or boring stretches of time easier to get through. Say you and your family are having a miserable time on a trip—if you stay upbeat, you can lift everyone’s mood and turn the trip around.

There are plenty of small things that can put you in a good mood, too. You’re more likely to have a positive attitude when you’ve slept well, when the sun is shining, when you receive a gift, or when you get to eat your favorite meal or visit your favorite restaurant. Hanging out with friends at your house, visiting family, or being on a fun trip also boost your mood, along with many other everyday moments.

On the flip side, a negative attitude can lead you down a bad path. Plenty of people walk around with a bad attitude most of the time, and it’s very hard to get along with them. These people often have few friends, or none at all. For example, if you come to school stressed out and in a bad mood, and your teacher does something you don’t like, you might snap and yell at them. That could get you sent to the guidance office and land a bad mark on your report card. Or if someone has a bad attitude and picks a fight, things can escalate quickly and end very badly.

Lots of everyday situations can put you in a bad mood, too. You’re more likely to have a negative attitude when you’re exhausted, when you have a huge workload, or when it’s raining and you can’t go out. If someone is rude to you, if you’re angry at someone, or if you’re hungry and the only food available is unappetizing, that can also ruin your mood, along with plenty of other small annoyances.

I always have the best experiences when I keep a positive attitude. Eating my favorite food, getting a present, or spending time with my family always lift my mood. For example, yesterday was my cousin’s birthday at a fun venue—I stayed upbeat while playing with my cousin and eating great food. I also feel positive on family trips, since I love visiting new places. Another example: my science teacher was in a great mood last week, so he gave us an extra day to submit our projects.

There are so many benefits to keeping a good attitude. For one, say you have a big exam coming up. You study hard and feel prepared, then wake up on exam day feeling upbeat and confident. That positive mindset will help you do your best, and you’re likely to get a good grade. But I think the biggest benefit of all is just enjoying yourself—when you’re happy, that’s the best feeling a person can have.

To sum up, a good attitude can help you in almost every part of life, from work and school to family gatherings. Now that you know this, the next time you’re feeling down or going through a rough patch, remember that the best way to handle it is to keep a good attitude.

One of the most pleasant ways to spend time outside, especially during the summer months, is to hop on your bicycle. You’ll get to spot all sorts of interesting sights along the way: local shops, even some famous stores, flowing rivers, chirping birds, and even passing cars. You can pack a picnic basket with food to stop and eat somewhere nice, too. As you ride, you’ll pass plenty of other cyclists out enjoying the day, and if you get hungry, you can easily pull up to a store to grab a snack or a drink. You’re not limited to a set route, either—you can pedal to famous spots like museums or popular restaurants, watching the crowds of people there as you go. There’s something amazing about being able to ride wherever you please, taking in all the beautiful scenery around you. You might ride past a river where other people are snapping photos, or cycle by the zoo to catch a glimpse of colorful flowers. You’ll also meet plenty of fellow bike lovers out on the same adventure as you. Every ride lets you spot new, lovely details you might have missed otherwise, and the whole experience leaves you feeling thrilled and energized.

This activity is so enjoyable mostly because of the flexibility it offers. You can bring your own food along if you prefer, or stop to buy treats as you ride. It’s also a great activity to share: you can take your kid along on the bike, or invite friends and family to join you for a group ride. Riding with others makes the experience even more fun—you can all stop for a picnic together, or explore different neighborhoods as a group. As you wander, you’ll also spot cool details you might not notice when driving or walking, like pretty public art designs on building walls. Every ride feels like a small adventure where you get to discover new spots and learn more about the area you live in.

What exactly do partnerships between schools and companies involve? I believe they are a fantastic opportunity for students who want to explore their options before heading to college. By getting involved, students can test out different work fields and figure out what kind of roles they might enjoy. If a student is curious about a particular career, they can visit a partner company to see exactly what daily work there looks like. When schools team up with local businesses, it makes it far easier for students to identify which types of work actually interest them. I think I would be a great fit for this program because I enjoy being around others, I want to clarify which career paths suit me, and I’m eager to get hands-on experience in different jobs.

Plenty of people prefer to keep to themselves, but I really thrive when I’m around others. I find that being surrounded by people always lifts my mood and gives me a positive boost, no matter where I am—whether that’s at a workplace, a school event, or anywhere else. Even if you end up working with people you don’t get along with at first, you’ll still have to collaborate with them in most jobs. I had a similar experience at school during a group project: I didn’t know any of my group members at first, and felt too shy to speak up. But once I started chatting with them, we got along so well that we’re still friends now. Even when I meet strangers, striking up a conversation makes me feel like I’ve known them for years.

Most students already have a clear idea of what they want to do after graduation, but I’m still unsure. I constantly ask myself what I’m good at, but I’ve never been able to figure out my strengths. Not everyone gets their dream job right away, but if I’m selected for this program, I’ll get the chance to explore different types of work that interest me. Knowing what career I want to pursue would make a huge difference for me. So many people end up stuck in jobs they hate, only working there to support their families. I believe everyone should have the freedom to choose work they actually enjoy.

Imagine starting a job at a company you know nothing about—how could you possibly do well? I think it’s essential to try out a role first, so you know exactly what to expect. When I wanted to work at a restaurant, I had no idea what the day-to-day work involved, so I asked a friend who already worked there to tell me all about it. If you don’t have personal experience, you can always do research, but some roles require hands-on background. I’ve always dreamed of being a nurse, so I’ve spent time learning about the field on my own. If I’m selected for this program, I’ll get to explore nursing roles up close and gain the practical experience I’ve been looking for.

You may be hesitant to select me at first, but I truly believe you should. I love being around people, I want to identify which types of jobs suit me best, and I’m eager to gain practical experience in different roles. As I’ve said before, being around others always gives me a positive feeling.

I think you should choose me for this program because it will give me the chance to discover which types of work I’m truly interested in. My goal is to pick a career that I’ll enjoy going to every day, not one I’ll dread. Dear Principal,

I believe switching our cafeteria’s current lunch options for healthier alternatives is a fantastic plan. Introducing new, nutritious dishes and types of cuisine many students have never tried before would benefit everyone here. As a student, I fully support this idea because it means we’ll all have access to better, healthier food.

Rolling out a new lunch menu will definitely please a lot of students, since many of us are bored of eating the same meals almost every day. That said, it could also upset others who love the current options and never get tired of them. To balance this, I suggest you speak with the cafeteria manager and ask for a list of the most popular dishes among students. Then, you and your team can decide whether to overhaul the entire menu or just make small tweaks. In my opinion, the best approach is to keep all the food students already love, and only replace the dishes that are least popular with new, healthy options.

This way, students will be satisfied because you’re not removing their favorite meals, while also adding new options they’ll be excited to try. Offering varied, healthier lunches will set our school apart from others, making us a model that other institutions might follow. This is especially important because the problem of repetitive, unappealing cafeteria food isn’t unique to our school—students across the country are dealing with the same issue. If other schools in different states see our success, they may adopt the same changes. This would help more than just students: it would also let parents save money. Right now, students who dislike the current menu ask their parents to buy food from outside, and some families simply can’t afford that extra cost. It would also cut down on students skipping class to buy outside food, which protects the school’s reputation and benefits students and parents alike.

Trying new foods is something many students, myself included, really enjoy. The current cafeteria offers both unhealthy and healthy options, but the balance is off—we need far more nutritious choices. Some students also have allergies to ingredients in the current menu, so they can’t eat the cafeteria food and only eat meals from home. Since we spend most of our day at school, we don’t have the chance to go out and buy safe food. Introducing a healthy, varied lunch menu would fix this: we’d get to try new, nutritious dishes, and no one would need to skip class to buy food elsewhere. Skipping class is risky, and it also worries parents when the school calls to report unexcused absences, since they have no idea where their children are or what they’re doing.

To sum up, I think students will be happy with these changes if you first ask the cafeteria manager for a list of the most and least popular dishes. This approach will make sure all students are comfortable with the new menu: they’ll keep their favorite foods, while students who dislike the current options won’t need to skip class to buy food elsewhere. Parents won’t have to worry about their children going hungry or skipping class, and no one will risk getting sick from not eating. Eating healthy food has so many benefits, from better physical health to more protein and less unhealthy fat in our diets. Parents will also save money since they won’t need to buy outside food for their kids anymore. Updating the school menu is a great idea that most students will support, and those who are hesitant will get used to it over time. This change will help every student at our school, and other schools will notice the positive impact and follow our lead. A healthier student body means less risk of health issues for everyone. This is my honest opinion, and I hope you’ll take these student perspectives into account when making your decision. Thank you!

Every individual has the freedom to make their own life choices, as they are free to pursue goals they have worked towards for years. No one enjoys being forced into tasks they have no interest in, and everyone deserves the right to decide what career they want to build or how they want to live their daily life.

That said, the choices people face often fall into two categories: the challenging path or the simpler path. The challenging path requires putting in consistent effort: studying to earn good grades, working hard to build a career, and pushing through setbacks. The simpler path, by contrast, relies on having money or resources to invest upfront to skip certain steps. This route is quicker, but it is not an option for everyone, as it depends entirely on what they can afford and whether they are willing to use those resources. A person’s financial situation also plays a huge role in how they plan their future. For example, people with a lot of wealth can take shorter, more direct routes to their goals because they do not have to stress about covering basic bills or monthly payments. Someone with less money, however, will have a much longer road ahead: they have to worry about rent, car payments, groceries, and other daily costs, which means they often have to work extra hours just to stay afloat while chasing their goals.

I have seen this play out in real life with people I know. A friend of mine used to balance school and a part-time job while he was finishing high school. He had planned to enroll in college right after graduation, but he made a choice that changed his life forever. He decided to drop out, telling me, “Working pays more than going to school right now.” He quit his studies to do nails full-time. While this job can bring in good money some months, the income is very unstable, and he has no interest in putting in more effort to advance. He could have gone to college, earned a degree, and landed a much higher-paying, more stable job later on, but he lost that chance. He can never go back and change that decision now. My brother had a similar experience: he attended college for two years before deciding he no longer wanted to study. He dropped out to start working immediately. If he had stuck with his degree, he would almost certainly have a better job today.

This shows that people need to think carefully about how their choices will affect their future, and make decisions based on both their current resources and what they hope to have later. While everyone has the right to make their own choices, they often need guidance and support from others to make the best ones. Many people, however, have no idea what they want to do with their lives. They do not know what hobbies or jobs interest them, so they feel stuck. These people need help exploring options that might appeal to them as they grow older.

All the options available to a person, plus the environment they grow up in, shape the future decisions they make. Support from family and friends can help them make far better choices for their own lives. Everyone has to take charge of their own path, work hard to build a happy future, and gain the freedom to do whatever they want. If people put in enough effort during their own lives, their children will have a much easier time making choices about their own futures down the line.

Most people face a bigger risk not from aiming too high and missing their target, but from setting their goals too low and actually reaching them. I believe that setting a high goal, even if you fall a little short, is far better than aiming too low. If you start with almost no goal, or set your target very low, you might hit it easily by trying hard, but that’s not as meaningful. I agree with Michelangelo’s idea that you don’t have to be the best to succeed—putting in effort lets you achieve anything. But I also disagree with parts of this quote, because there’s no rule that says your goals have to be small. You can aim high if you want! It doesn’t matter which path you take to reach your target, either. Life often leads you to unexpected places and pushes you to make choices you didn’t plan for. For example, I’m currently taking the SOL exam. Even if I aim high to pass, move up to 12th grade, and earn my diploma, I could also set a lower target and still reach that same milestone. Putting in effort means you can do anything, but at the same time, it doesn’t really matter how much effort you put in—you’ll always reach your goal eventually. Everyone faces this, whether in their daily life, at work, or in school, at some point. This experience is common across the entire human race. Another thing I think the quote is saying is that many people have a habit of setting low standards for themselves.

This is a really engaging topic to write about, and I have to say I agree with the core idea. After all, if you face non-stop failure in life and eventually grow tired of that pattern, you’ll often shift your mindset to pursue success instead. Constant failure is very tough to deal with for many people, after all. That said, some people disagree with this view. They argue that failure makes success impossible: for example, if you’re applying for a job and keep falling short of what your potential boss asks of you, you might not land the role. The same logic applies to school, where you can’t keep failing either.

I also fully agree with Winston Churchill’s famous statement on this topic. He was right that you can’t achieve success without putting in effort, since making it in life is far from easy. Anyone who wants to build a successful life has to be willing to try hard. We see plenty of people today who have no job, no permanent home, and not enough to eat, often because they never managed to succeed in life. Success is also about moving from one setback to the next, because failure is a normal part of life. No one is born successful the moment they enter the world.

To sum up, I believe failure can eventually lead you to success.

Many people struggle to finish all their assigned work when they are already busy with tasks. This happens either because they have no time left for other assignments, or because they spend all their energy on difficult tasks first and never get around to finishing the rest. However, being idle also serves a useful purpose. People who are not currently doing any work have plenty of free time to complete tasks and get things done, since nothing else is taking up their attention.

The main reason why inactivity can be useful is that people with free time are able to tackle any unfinished work they still have. This means they have no valid excuse to avoid doing tasks. In contrast, people who are already working hard have a fair reason to say no to extra work if they are given too many assignments to handle at once. However, anyone who finishes their required work early and still has spare time should be given additional tasks until they have no free time left during the school day or their work shift.

There are two key reasons related to how people handle work when they are already busy. First, some people get a lot done when they are actively working, because they focus on tasks and do not waste time at school or work. However, this is not always the case. Other times, people cannot finish all their work when they are already busy, because they run out of time for other assignments. They may also rush to get everything done, make many mistakes on their tasks, and end up with bad grades or poor performance reports. This is why many people choose not to take on extra work when they are already handling other tasks.

To sum up, some people manage to finish all their work, while others do not. Being idle can be useful for people who have already completed their assigned tasks, but no one at school or work should just sit around doing nothing. Instead, they should be given more work until it is time for them to leave class or end their work shift.

Who has the right to tell others what holds value in their lives, or which choices they ought to make?

Every person has the freedom to shape their life as they wish, choosing the path that feels right to them. When someone builds up self-reliance, they no longer need outside voices dictating their every move.

It is far better to make your own choices, even when you feel uncertain. Mistakes are not failures, but chances to grow: if you pick the wrong option, you learn how to do better next time. This process builds a sense of security that makes future decision-making easier, and it lets you discover what truly matters to you, without relying on others' input.

Of course, everyone makes poor choices now and then, but that is not a bad thing. It is simply part of figuring out how to get things right. Many people turn to experts when facing major decisions, out of fear of picking the wrong path. There is nothing wrong with seeking advice, but you should trust your own judgment before paying someone else to tell you what to do, or which choices to pick.

When you make good choices on your own, you feel confident in your actions, which builds the self-reliance you need for later decisions. Even if you pick the wrong path, you learn from those missteps so you can make better choices down the line, without needing a professional to guide you.

Why let someone else decide what is truly important in your life? You do not need outside guidance to figure this out. Instead, take the time to reflect on what holds meaning for you, and make your own choices about what matters most. After all, every person is unique, so what works for one person may not work for another, even when it comes to core life values.

To sum up, making your own decisions is key. It helps you feel more confident when facing future choices, lets you grow from any mistakes you make along the way, and allows you to work out for yourself what truly matters in your life.

I fully agree with this statement. Putting full faith in yourself can turn even the most impossible-seeming tasks into reachable goals. This applies to things like applying for your first job, or chasing any career path you dream of pursuing.

This mindset is especially valuable when you’re in college: it helps you save more money and work towards getting whatever you want out of life. As you build this confidence, you’ll pick up new skills and learn more about your own strengths, like figuring out what types of jobs suit you best. All of this shapes how others see you.

When people get to know your personality, they’ll pick up on this confidence right away. Your first impression will be so firmly rooted in your self-belief that it’s almost impossible to shift, because you’ve put in the work to build that version of yourself. You’ll realize you’ve gained valuable experience along the way, too.

Of course, not everyone makes the same first impression, since we all have different personalities and goals for ourselves. Some people never change how others see them at first, usually because they don’t push themselves to trust their own knowledge, even when they have plenty of it to draw on.

On the other hand, people who do shift how others perceive them are usually far more self-assured. They’re willing to put in the time and effort required to grow, rather than wasting their days on meaningless tasks.

For people who don’t care about building a future career, and are content to be unambitious, this kind of growth is impossible. Their first impression never shifts, they won’t achieve any real success, and nothing about their life will change for the better.

I agree that the truth can be painful sometimes, but being honest is still the right choice. There are moments when you might not feel the need to speak up, but pointing out someone's mistakes to them directly is often helpful in the long run. When people are open and truthful with one another, it builds stronger, more reliable friendships.

Being honest with your parents is especially important too. If you get into trouble, they can step in to help you work through problems, whether that's issues at school or something else going on in your life. On the other hand, if you aren't truthful with people, you risk losing their trust forever. They'll start to see you as someone who can't be relied on, and that's hard to fix.

Think about it this way: if you mess up and try to hide it with a lie, you'll probably get found out eventually. When that happens, things will turn out way worse than if you'd just told the truth from the start. So it's always better to be upfront and truthful, because hiding the truth never works out in your favor.

Sure, honesty can hurt people's feelings, and no one likes delivering bad news. But holding back lets people get their hopes up for nothing. Later, they'll thank you for the truth, reflect on their choices, and value having you in their life. It's worth being honest even when it's hard—at least you're truthful, and you can both move on.

I'll admit honesty isn't perfect—there are times it feels like it does more harm than good. But I'd much rather have honest people around. Hearing the truth right away, even if it stings, is better than finding out later from others. That hurts way more, especially when you realize someone didn't trust you enough to be honest from the start. It makes you feel small, and I'd rather avoid that.

I also think being honest is good practice for the real world. As you get older, you'll have a job, maybe a family of your own, and you'll face all kinds of challenges. Life isn't always fair, and things won't always go your way. But if you're used to being honest and dealing with the truth, even when it's hard, you'll be better prepared to handle whatever comes your way.

Not everyone is happy with the current length of summer break, as many students and parents argue it is far too short to fully relax and enjoy vacation time. These critics suggest adjusting the summer break schedule, starting it in June and ending in August instead of the current May start. They also propose canceling spring break entirely, noting that the time usually set aside for that mid-spring break could be better used for SOL testing and preparation.

Removing spring break would free up an extra week in the school calendar. That week could be dedicated to SOL practice or testing, rather than a break, giving students more time to get ready for these important exams. Instead, schools could host more engaging, fun activities for students and classes throughout April, so learners still get a chance to unwind before the end of the school year.

Shifting the summer break to run from June through August makes far more sense than letting it start in May, when the weather is often still unpredictable. May weather is often still cool and not summer-like, while June brings reliable warm sunshine, perfect for starting vacations with family and friends to enjoy more outdoor fun without worrying about chilly days.

Cutting spring break also works because it falls so close to summer anyway, so removing it does not take away a break that feels separate from the long summer holiday. Without that break, students would have more time to sit for SOL exams and study for final tests, reducing stress as they prepare for end-of-year assessments. They would also get more time in regular classes, where teachers can offer extra support and cover more material, helping students who are struggling to catch up. Schools could use the freed-up spring break week to host activities that let students learn while still having fun, blending education with enjoyment.

This could include more sports, skill-building sessions for both students and teachers, and trips to music venues, universities, art museums, and other local attractions that add to the school experience.

We agree with those calling for these changes to the school calendar, as they balance more study time with better scheduled vacation periods. A 3-month summer break running from June to August, with no spring break, would give students more time in school for SOL prep and final exam study, while still leaving plenty of time for summer fun and relaxation.

I do not support school district programs that let students earn their high school diploma in three years, as this timeframe is far too short compared to the standard four-year schedule. Completing graduation requirements in three years means students have to work much harder, often taking classes during summer breaks and in the evenings. This leaves their minds exhausted, as they barely get any time to rest. They also often cannot fit important elective courses into their schedule, as the shortened timeline forces them to prioritize only core required classes.

While finishing high school earlier may seem like a benefit at first, this faster pace does not actually help students. Instead, it just adds more stress, as they have to put in extra hours studying during summer and evening sessions. Overall, I believe that graduating in three years is a poor choice. The standard four-year timeline is far better, as it gives students the time they need to learn properly.

Another key issue is that students on the three-year track have to work extremely hard. Attending classes in the summer and evenings leaves them feeling very tired, while the standard four-year schedule gives them more time to rest and stay focused before they move on to university. With four years of high school, students have more time to study, think about what career path they want to follow, and make decisions without rushing.

This four-year timeline is much more helpful for students. It offers more time than a three-year schedule, so they do not feel overly pressured, and they have more free time to handle personal tasks and hobbies. Taking four years to finish high school also better prepares students for university and the workforce. They have more time to focus on learning new material and gain more knowledge before entering the next stage of life. This extra time in high school is very valuable, as it helps students make informed choices about the careers they want to pursue in the future.

A few years ago, I applied to a local private high school, and during my meeting with the principal, he mentioned that students were expected to have a clear career path in mind before enrolling. This experience made me realize that students really should decide on a specific career before they start high school.

I fully agree with this idea, because when you know early what you want to do, you can focus your studies and practice to become a skilled professional later on. The key is to pick a career that actually interests you, then work hard to pursue it.

For example, I’ve always been drawn to mechanics. I love cars, and I think working as a mechanic would be a great fit for me—not only do I enjoy fixing vehicles, but I also know it can pay well. That’s why I’ve already decided to follow this career path, and I plan to practice my skills whenever I can while I’m still in school.

The same logic applies to hobbies that could turn into careers, too. I’m passionate about soccer, and playing is my favorite summer activity—I practice almost every day. One of my biggest dreams is to become a professional soccer player someday, because I truly love the sport. No matter what career you pick, if you enjoy it, you’ll want to practice constantly.

Every student has a career they’re interested in, even if life sometimes gets in the way of their plans. But if you work hard and stay committed, you can still achieve your goal. My older sister is a perfect example: she wanted to be a nurse since she was little. She spent years studying hard and practicing basic nursing skills, and now she’s been working as a registered nurse for six years. She achieved exactly the career she’d always wanted.

In the end, it’s important to take time to figure out what you want to do with your future. There are so many options out there, but the best choice is always a career that makes you happy. Once you find that, work as hard as you can to make it a reality.

Do we achieve more when we stay consistently busy working on projects? History shows that people who put in steady effort are the ones who develop new technologies, from car radios to televisions. Those who avoid putting work into new ideas will never advance technology as quickly as we have. All tech requires ongoing effort to refine and upgrade. Beyond that, these innovations create jobs and give people stable ways to earn a living. When more people contribute work to new projects, it transforms how we live: it improves daily life and drives worldwide change. Some of the most common items that have evolved over time are computers, televisions, and radios, all of which we use on a daily basis.

This pattern holds true when we look at the radio, for example. The radio was one of the most significant breakthroughs of its era. When it first launched, the engineers and developers working on it faced major challenges getting the frequency settings correct. Their success was a massive achievement, and the device quickly became popular with everyday people. Over time, the radio kept growing and improving because people kept putting in work to refine both the technology and their own expertise. That steady effort even paved the way for the first television, which was a huge sensation when it debuted. The determination of those who worked on radio also helped expand jobs in the entertainment industry, opening up far more employment opportunities for others.

The first television was a game-changer: unlike the movies of that era, it had sound and let people watch moving images on a screen at home. This drew more people to work in television production, and demand for TV sets among regular households was extremely high. People were willing to work harder to reach their goals, and those developing TV technology were determined to build on what they already had. For the first time ever, elections were broadcast on television, so anyone who owned a set could watch the coverage to decide who to vote for. The teams working on TV were committed to making the technology reliable and convincing consumers to buy their products, a push that eventually laid the groundwork for the development of computers.

Early computers were basic, with no sound and only simple programming functions. The people working to improve them wanted to add features that would convince more consumers to purchase them. Developers built into these machines exactly the tools they wished to see included. Today, we can use computers to take tests like the Sol project, along with many other tasks.

I strongly believe that students gain no real benefits from taking classes remotely, whether through online learning platforms or video conferencing tools. Attending school from home is not a good option for learners of any age.

First, studying at home comes with far more distractions than a physical classroom. At home, students might be tempted to play video games or do other unrelated tasks while their class is in session. When lessons are held remotely, schools have to come up with extra measures to keep students engaged, but these are never as effective as in-person instruction. In a regular school setting, the teacher is right in front of the students, which makes the learning process much more focused. Students pick up new ideas more easily when their teacher can give them direct, immediate attention, rather than speaking to a screen.

Second, remote learning is a particularly poor choice for many students, including myself. My home is always busy: I have three brothers and one sister, so there is rarely a quiet space to focus on online lessons. All the noise and activity around me makes it almost impossible to pay full attention to the class, which hurts my progress.

To add to this, distance learning is not a smart alternative to traditional schooling. While students tend to have more energy and focus in the morning, which helps with memorizing new information, online video conferences are still too basic and ineffective to replace in-person classes. Even if a student is wide awake during a morning remote lesson, they will not get the same benefits as they would in a physical classroom.

In conclusion, I do not think students should take classes from home or rely on any form of distance learning. They learn far more when they attend school in person. Most parents share this view, as it is clear that face-to-face classes are much more effective than learning from home.

Should people make their own choices, or let others decide for them? There are clear reasons why everyone should take charge of their own decisions.

First, making your own choices builds self-confidence. When you go through the process of weighing options and reaching a conclusion on your own, you learn to trust your own judgment. This is very different from letting others pick for you, which never helps you grow more sure of yourself.

Next, choosing for yourself is closely tied to happiness. The decisions you make shape almost every part of your life, so when you pick paths that fit your own needs and wants, you are far more likely to feel satisfied with how your life turns out.

Making your own decisions also helps you handle life’s challenges. You will definitely face difficult moments at some point, and while these times are never easy, being used to making your own choices gives you the skills to work through problems instead of waiting for others to save you.

It is true that people who leave all decisions to others may have an easier life. They never have to stress about picking the right option or dealing with the consequences of a bad choice. But even with that simpler path, it is far better to make your own decisions.

Modern technology makes it possible to finish countless everyday tasks without ever interacting with another person face-to-face. You can borrow library books, buy groceries, and play games all without saying a single word to another human. This shift has drastically cut down on how much in-person contact people have in their daily lives.

Humans have a fundamental need for social connection—after all, our species has lived and worked in groups for hundreds of years, and we are more interdependent now than we have ever been in history. That is exactly why meeting new people and building relationships is so important, and why we all need to step away from our devices every once in a while.

While digital tools let us borrow books, shop, and game without leaving home, this kind of constant isolation goes against our biological need for human interaction. We have grown far too comfortable ordering everything online, and this habit needs to change. Children in particular are getting hooked on video games and online shopping from a very young age. I know these tools make life much easier, but if someone only interacts with others through a screen, how will they ever make new friends? How will they meet people in the real world?

This overreliance on technology is severely limiting meaningful human contact. Toddlers are given tablets to play with before they can even walk, so it is no surprise that so many kids spend their free time alone, staring at a screen. You will often see young people walking around by themselves, or scrolling on their phones during class or work, completely focused on their device and nothing else around them.

While I think it’s always positive to stay true to who you are no matter where you are, being authentic is far better than pretending to be someone you’re not. Putting on an act never feels comfortable, after all. When you stay true to yourself, you’re really choosing to trust your own judgment. You don’t have to listen to every person who comes up to you and tells you to change who you are. Instead, you reach your goals by relying on that self-trust. For instance, staying authentic shows the people around you just how strong you can be, and it lets you keep moving forward to get better at what you do.

We live in a world where many people change who they are just to get ahead. That’s why it’s so important to trust yourself enough not to change into someone bad, or into whatever version of yourself society tries to force you to be. Keep trusting yourself and stick to your own path of self-improvement, to show those around you how firmly you believe in yourself. That way, you stay true to the best version of yourself. I also think this can push the people around you to grow too: when they see you staying authentic, they realize they can do the same thing.

Sometimes you’ll meet people who are really determined to change you. Or you might be part of a society that has already shifted, where everyone follows a totally different set of rules to get ahead in life. These people will try to pressure you to act exactly how they want, to follow their path—even when you know their way is not how you can grow. Choosing to stay yourself and improve your life under your own set of rules makes sense here. You can see that something about their path is not right, even if the rest of society is changing to fit it. Often, when those people try to improve their lives, they listen to others’ bad advice, and they don’t even realize that when they reach their goals, they’ve hurt other people or caused problems they don’t know about.

I don’t think it’s right to copy what others do just to please people around you. We should each follow our own unique path in life. As Ralph Waldo Emerson once wrote, society is always trying to make us change, even as it claims to be pushing for the greatest possible improvement. That’s why I have to believe in myself: I know I can reach my goals successfully if I focus on what I need and want. No one should be allowed to pull me away from my goals, because there will always be people who want to stop you from reaching your dreams. To become the best version of myself, I will work incredibly hard. There are always people who will try to make you fail on your way to your goals, who will laugh at you if you stumble, and who will try to block you from achieving what you want. But I truly believe that if you trust yourself and set big, meaningful goals, you can achieve them. No one will be able to stand in your way.

When you stay true to yourself, trust in your goals, and respect yourself, other people will respect you too—just as you respect them. You’ll also reach your dreams the right way, without cutting corners or hurting others. But I see that many societies are full of people who have already changed who they are, and now they try to change me too. I can see that they might be improving their lives, but they’re doing it the wrong way, and there’s no real respect between people in that kind of environment. That’s exactly why I believe I need to stay true to myself.

In the end, I truly think staying true to yourself is the best choice. Do the things that make you happy, first and foremost. If you see society changing around you, and people try to pressure you to change too, stick to your guns—even if you’re doing the right things to improve yourself. Those people might tell you to do something else, but you know that’s not the right path. Their way of doing things could hurt other people, even if they’re only focused on their own improvement. All things considered, I believe the best path is to be yourself, and always do things the right way.

I believe one of life’s greatest achievements is living in an environment that constantly challenges me to give my best effort. I agree with Emerson’s statement that individuality is the foundation for reaching all our personal goals.

For me, it is essential to acknowledge that achieving my goals requires consistent hard work. Putting in effort drives me to compete, push my limits, and become the best version of myself. Individuality plays a huge role here: it helps me trust my own abilities, and encourages me to seek out opportunities that improve my life.

Working independently motivates me to put in far more effort. When someone runs their own business, they take full responsibility for fixing problems and delivering high-quality work—the same applies to solo tasks. If you work alone, you’re driven to do a perfect job to impress your colleagues. For instance, when I work without a partner, I push myself to do exceptional work so I can rank among the top workers. Completing my own projects makes me feel proud, especially when I earn awards for being a strong performer. Everyone wants to be recognised for their work and receive rewards, but earning those honours requires having real skill in your role. Many people share this mindset: handling our own work leads to far better results. Working solo sparks motivation to work harder and boost output, and individual projects always deliver strong outcomes. Workers who take on their own tasks produce more in factory settings, which ultimately helps them access more resources.

While competition can sometimes weaken teamwork, individual competition remains one of the best ways to push past obstacles. For example, when a new employee starts a job and earns higher pay for doing excellent work, their colleagues may feel jealous. This sparks competition across the factory, as everyone wants to earn more money instead of receiving the same salary as others. They may complain that it is unfair the manager gives the new hire more pay, but the truth is the new worker has specialised skills that make them more valuable. Over time, this kind of workplace competition boosts overall factory production, as every worker strives to hit output goals and find new ways to produce more than their peers. For instance, if a worker finishes their assigned tasks early and earns free time as a reward, other staff may feel frustrated and look for new methods to produce more than the top performer, so they can earn the same reward. Healthy competition relies on both individual work and collaboration in large groups, and it is a great way for individual effort to create positive emotional drive. Many companies encourage high output by offering bonuses or extra time off to the worker who produces the most. As a result, factories where staff work separately see a huge impact: every worker tries to produce the maximum amount of materials. Challenges like these are very effective for roles that require independent work.

Striving for accomplishments to become the best version of yourself is a universal goal. Everyone wants to earn recognition in life, but becoming successful requires hard work above all else. Criticism, bullying, and negative comments from others do not matter—the only thing that counts is staying true to who you are. The best possible situation is living in an environment that frequently demands you take on new challenges. Even when you face many difficulties, you must stay patient and push through the bad times. If you want to stand out from the crowd and achieve your goals, you need to work independently. Sometimes, no one else is available to help you, so fighting through challenges on your own helps you grow into a respected member of society. Competition is everywhere in today’s world: for example, almost everyone watches soccer on TV. A soccer team has 24 players, and they compete to decide who will be the team leader. This mirrors real life, where leaders are people who work hard and support their teammates. The same applies to company leaders: to lead a business, you have to compete with other candidates who want the same role. Ultimately, successful people are those who make their own individual decisions.

Completing tasks on my own pushes me to put in full effort and dedication. Group work, however, is often affected by unpredictable factors, much like a bet. People who stand out from the crowd with unique qualities can offer great help to others. These individuals make a real difference in the world: they strive to succeed in high-demand, competitive environments, and work to build influence in their roles. Individuality plays a huge role in making the world a more successful place. For example, government officials are highly skilled and compete with one another, which drives major achievements in public administration. This is why I agree with Emerson’s statement: competition brings us real benefits, and fuels progress for governments, factories, and entire countries. Being part of a competitive environment pushes us to become the best version of ourselves.

I don’t need everyone in my life to stay true to who I am. I can get through life perfectly fine on my own, without relying on anyone else. Every goal I’ve reached, every milestone I’ve hit, has been down to my own hard work — the people around me have never lifted a finger to help me.

In the world I know, I can’t trust anyone. Most people don’t want good things for me — they hope I fail instead. Some try to push me into bad choices, and even school doesn’t help me build a stable, successful life. The people around me actively don’t want me to succeed, but I’m sure I’d have a much better future if I didn’t have to deal with any of them.

I don’t need anyone around me to reach my goals. They’ll never step up to help me succeed when it counts. Take my old friend Generic_Name, for example. She used to be really kind to me, but she started changing after a while. She tried to convince me to skip school with her, saying classes would never help me build a good life. She also had constant fights with her parents and refused to stop making bad choices. I eventually stopped talking to her — my parents no longer liked her, and even though I wanted to stay friends, her actions were too harmful. I had to focus on my own future instead.

To make something of myself, I have to work hard toward my goals without relying on others. When I’m in trouble or need help, they’re never actually there for me. For instance, yesterday I took a math test with other students, and one of them asked me to let him copy my answers. I refused, because the teacher would have been angry with me if we got caught. After we finished the test, he came up to complain that I didn’t help him. I told him he should have studied beforehand — you can’t count on other people to bail you out when you have a test to take.

Another key part of succeeding is never giving up, even when people tell me I’ll never make it. I’m graduating this year, but my cousin keeps telling me I won’t because I’m not smart enough. I don’t care what she says — I know I’m doing my best to graduate on time. She says horrible things to me all the time, and sometimes it makes me want to cry. But I don’t need anyone to become the person I want to be, not even my own family.

After all this, I’m sure I don’t need people in my life. They’ll never be there to support me when it matters. Spending time with the people around me only brings trouble, since so many of them try to talk me into bad choices instead of good ones. In the world we live in, people can even kill you or cause irreversible damage. It’s better to be on your own — then you don’t have to worry about anyone else’s actions affecting you.

Do I agree with Winston Churchill’s quote that “Success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm”? Yes, I fully agree. No one wins every time, and we rarely get things perfect on the first try.

For example, last year I took an English exam in class. I practiced a lot, hoping for an A+ or at least a B+, but I failed completely. I was heartbroken, but my teacher offered a retake. I took that second chance and passed with an A- — I was thrilled. Failing that first test taught me that stumbling while chasing a goal doesn’t matter. What counts is staying strong and trying your hardest to succeed.

Another example is my aunt, who wants to travel to El Salvador (my home country) to visit my grandmother this year. When she first called the airline, tickets were too expensive for her budget, so she waited a few months. Seven months later, prices had risen further, but she didn’t want to wait longer. As she went to buy the ticket, she found her ID had expired, so the airline couldn’t sell it to her. She was upset she’d forgotten to renew it. She applied for a new ID weeks later, but was told to wait three months. Three months have passed, and she still hasn’t received it. She’s sad she can’t visit yet, but she hasn’t lost her excitement to travel to my country this year.

Churchill’s words ring true. No one is perfect, and we need to fail to learn lessons and grow stronger. Some people disagree, saying the quote is false because they’ve lost many times trying to succeed. They even call people who fail twice “losers” or “stupid” — unfair labels that are wrong. In my view, these people either had bad experiences, or lost their own enthusiasm and became too weak to keep trying.

To conclude, failing is part of life if you want to succeed, as my exam and my aunt’s travel struggles show. These experiences teach us to grow stronger, and never lose the enthusiasm that drives us to succeed in life.

Principals should allow students to bring mobile phones to school, as these devices can be very helpful in urgent situations. For one, a student might face a personal emergency and need to contact their parents right away. Parents could also run into unexpected trouble, like a car accident, and need to tell their child not to wait for a ride home after school. Students who walk to campus face higher risks such as kidnapping, so having a phone lets them call for help if they are in danger.

For example, if a classmate faints, a student can quickly call the school nurse for assistance. For these reasons, schools should let students carry phones as long as they follow these clear rules.

There is growing support for schools to adopt a four-day weekly schedule, like some workplaces that have already switched to this model. Many supporters say this would save energy in many settings.

I think this plan would be a bad idea for saving energy. It adds two hours to the school day, so students spend ten hours on campus daily, using far more energy than before.

Longer school days also mean using more natural resources. We would waste far more paper on assignments, and use much more water for drinking and cleaning, than we do with a normal five-day week. These are supplies we would not use as quickly with a shorter daily schedule.

Ten-hour days also waste electricity. Every classroom uses computers, monitors and tablets for far longer each day, using power we could save with a standard eight-hour schedule, which adds to unnecessary energy waste.

These are my main reasons for opposing the four-day school week as a way to save energy and resources in schools.

Setting a good example is the best way to show other people how to do things better. When someone is teaching and provides clear examples, it makes you feel like the teacher really wants to help.

When I was little, my grandmother taught me all kinds of practical skills and gave me plenty of helpful advice. Now, I want to share what I know with my friends and other people, teaching them things they might not have learned yet. I can show them how to play soccer, how to track down hard-to-find items, and plenty of other useful tricks.

Over the years, I’ve picked up so many skills I never expected to have, like fixing toys, repairing computers, and handling all sorts of other small tasks.

I really appreciate teachers who explain things clearly, because that makes it so much easier to learn. Some teachers don’t put effort into their lessons, or they get angry at students for no reason. That’s exactly why so many students end up saying they dislike a teacher—either they’re mean, or they don’t teach properly.

Sharing examples is the best way to wrap your head around concepts you’ve never quite understood before. Behavior matters too, both in class and at home. How you act is a huge part of life, because other people will notice if you have good manners. If someone has a good reputation for their behavior, I’d be happy to ask them for advice or examples on how to fix a problem or improve a skill.

Examples aren’t the only way to influence people, though. There are plenty of other factors, like simply watching how others work. Just by observing the people around me, I’m picking up new skills that will help me in the future.

I don’t have concrete plans for after high school yet, but I know I’m most passionate about technology and electrical work—those are the two things I care about more than anything else. Life can change in a second, and you can lose everything, or even pass away, before you know it.

We live in the 21st century, a time when most people value their independence and make their own choices. Society has transformed dramatically over the past decades, and modern individuals are generally sharp enough to handle everyday decisions well. That said, many still take big risks by making major choices without first checking in with professionals or official authorities.

For any significant life or work choice, it is always wise to ask for advice from people who know the field well. Turning to someone with experience makes it far simpler to weigh different options and pick the best path. When people try to handle major decisions entirely on their own, they often end up making costly mistakes. Take famous public figures: almost all have personal advisors, usually managers, who handle key choices to keep their careers on a steady upward path. If celebrities tried to make every big call by themselves, far more would see their careers crash and burn.

All major choices should be well-considered and backed by input from experts. A clear warning of what happens when you skip this step comes from the book *Into the Wild*: the story of Christopher McCandless. Chris decided to travel alone into the Alaskan wilderness without asking for any advice from people familiar with the area. He did not pack proper supplies, and refused to ask for help when he needed it. McCandless died in the Alaskan wilds because he was completely unprepared for the harsh conditions he faced. If he had listened to even a single piece of advice from someone who knew the risks, he would almost certainly have survived. His death was entirely the result of choosing to ignore all guidance.

Almost everyone hopes to build a successful life, but only a small portion actually achieve that goal. To reach your goals, you either need to make consistently smart choices, or turn to experts for help when you are unsure. Very few people manage to build a successful career entirely on their own, and even those who do will eventually need a manager or advisor to help them stay on track long-term. People who regularly ask for input from professionals and authorities tend to have a clear edge in business and work. It is far more trustworthy to make a major decision after getting expert advice, rather than trying to handle everything by yourself. Going it alone makes you far more likely to make a bad call.

In short, all people should make a habit of seeking advice from experts and authorities when making important decisions. Getting outside input is always more helpful when facing life’s big choices, or you risk ending up in a situation as tragic as Christopher McCandless’s in *Into the Wild*.

New technology has made daily life far more convenient, and education is no exception. Years ago, the only way to work toward a career was to attend a traditional school in person, with no alternative options available. Today, many schools offer remote classes that students can join from their own homes. This is a major benefit for people who live far from campus and cannot commute easily or quickly. You no longer need to stress about travel logistics, since countless online platforms now provide chances to reach your academic and professional goals. This is especially valuable for people who never got the chance to go to school and assumed they had missed their window to learn—but that is no longer true. Online classes let anyone achieve their goals, no matter their age. Whether you are young or old, you can log in and study whenever your schedule allows.

Many parents now choose to sign their children up for online schools, believing this option is better than sending them to a traditional campus. There is some truth to this: at a regular school, you cannot keep an eye on your child throughout the day. You might not even be sure if they are actually attending classes, let alone know who they are spending time with. You have no way to know if the friends your child is hanging out with are a good influence, or if they are being bullied by other students.

In a traditional school setting, it is hard to keep track of what is really happening in your child’s day. With online learning, though, you can be present while they study if your schedule fits. If your availability does not line up with their study hours, you can hire a trusted tutor to support them instead. Online schooling also means your child is not surrounded by peers who might mistreat them or make them feel down, which removes a major source of stress. This way, you can closely monitor how your child is progressing academically.

I believe enrolling your child in an online program is one of the best choices a parent can make, and the same goes for adults looking to further their own education. These online schools offer huge benefits for everyone, not just kids. For example, people who dropped out of school years ago can finally pick up where they left off—it is never too late. They can study at times that suit their routine, in a comfortable space like their own home. For my part, I would much rather take online classes than commute to a traditional school every day.

Do you prefer to make your own choices, or do you turn to experts for advice? I strongly believe that everyone should have the freedom to make their own decisions. For one thing, no one is always correct, including so-called experts. The advice or guidance others give you is not guaranteed to be accurate or suited to your situation. Another key reason is that no one knows your personal goals, values, and preferences better than you do. The choices you make in life should reflect what you actually want, not what someone else thinks is best for you. It is also never a good idea to blindly copy what other people do. You will see plenty of people around you making good or bad choices every day, but that does not mean you have to follow their lead. Every choice you make should be your own, not a copy of someone else’s.

Trusting other people’s advice is not always the safest option. Would you really want your best friend to decide important things for you? Probably not, because you can never be 100% sure if they are giving you good advice, or even telling the truth. No one is right all the time, and you do not want to get into trouble or make a choice that does not fit your life just because you listened to someone else. On the other hand, if you make smart choices at school or in other parts of your life, you can set a positive example for others, helping them avoid making the same mistakes. This is exactly why you should avoid letting others make choices for you: their bad advice could land you in a situation you never wanted to be in.

Life offers countless paths, but the final choice is always yours. You get to decide what you want to do, and you should not let other people judge your decisions, because they have no right to interfere in your personal choices. After all, everyone has the freedom to live their life as they see fit. If you make a poor choice, you are the only one responsible for it. You cannot blame someone else, since you were the one who made the decision, and you are the one who ended up in that situation. Think about kids in school: many get into trouble because they do not think for themselves. Of course, there are plenty of great students who avoid trouble by refusing to copy what their peers do. But there are also tons of students who make bad choices simply because they follow the crowd, watching others act poorly and copying them. This is never the right way to act, because it leads to trouble, and they miss out on valuable learning time because of their bad decisions.

When it comes down to it, the choices you make are yours alone. Only you know what you truly want. If you do not want to do something, you should never force yourself to do it. Do not be afraid to say no to something just because you worry it might be a bad choice. Instead, take a moment to think carefully about what you are doing first. Always ask yourself: is this a good choice? Remember, you are the one who has to live with the consequences. Everyone is an individual, and no one should have control over your life. For example, when I was choosing new friends at school, I was very careful about who I spent time with. I did not want to be influenced into making bad choices by people around me. No one has the right to make decisions for someone else. Every choice ultimately comes down to you.

To sum up, always remember that you should make your own decisions, not let others choose for you. In the world we live in, it is clear that no one makes perfect choices all the time, and that is completely normal. No one is perfect. Everyone has made at least one bad decision in their life. The key is to take time to think carefully about the choices you make, so that once you decide, you will not look back and regret not making a wiser choice. Do not be too hard on yourself, and do not stress too much about always picking the "right" option for your life.

Many people believe first impressions can be changed. Plenty of people make bad first impressions, acting disrespectful or saying unkind things, but anyone can shift how others see them if they want to be a better community member.

First, even people who seem rude or disrespectful at first can learn to be considerate. If you meet them again, your view may shift completely—you’d never expect someone so unpleasant to turn out to be kind. Their respectful behavior can easily make you rethink your initial opinion.

Next, a bad first impression might not reflect someone’s true personality. They could just be having a terrible day. It’s never fair to judge anyone based on one interaction. Everyone has good and bad days, so someone who seemed negative at first may just be having a rough time, and act much better the next time you meet.

That said, negative first impressions tend to linger in your mind, making it hard to see someone differently later. These initial reactions are often an automatic part of how we process new people.

In conclusion, never judge someone before you get to know them. People show their true selves over time, and can absolutely change the negative first impression you first formed of them.

Should schools offer distance learning programs that allow students to attend classes from home using online tools or video conferencing? Many people are in favor of this setup, as they believe remote classes are more beneficial and effective for learners. Students can absorb more information, produce higher-quality work, and have extra time to spend with their families. When students take classes online, they open up a wide range of opportunities: they can pursue their dreams and work toward achieving any goal they set their minds to.

The first major benefit of online classes is that they are more effective for learning, and students can manage their time at home to handle all their necessary tasks. For example, I want to graduate and continue my studies, but this has been difficult for me because I have almost no free time. I struggle to finish homework or prepare for quizzes, as I have to work to cover my personal expenses, rent, and car payments. That is exactly why I prefer online classes: they give me plenty of extra time to handle my personal responsibilities, so I can both work and study at the same time.

A second key advantage is that students can produce better work and earn higher grades. With more flexibility, they can submit homework or projects that include more detailed, well-researched information. For instance, when learners have extra time, they can put more effort into their assignments, focusing on responsibilities like homework and projects because they want to perform well. They can use the internet to find plenty of relevant information to improve their work. Since online students are more relaxed and have better time management, they only need to study for a few hours a day, unlike in traditional schools. In-person classes are far more exhausting: students have to wake up very early, and they receive piles of homework across multiple subjects. Remote learning is much simpler and less stressful than attending school in person.

Critics argue that online classes are a waste of time, claiming students get nothing done at home. They say when learners are at home, they just play on their phones or use their devices for non-school activities, so they do not study or learn as much as they would in a traditional classroom. However, remote learning is actually wonderful because it gives students more time to spend with their families. They can plan fun days with loved ones, doing activities like playing football, watching movies, going to the cinema, or visiting any other places they enjoy.

In conclusion, online classes offer clear benefits for students who attend school from home. Learners can absorb more material, produce higher-quality work, and have more time to spend with their families. These advantages are valuable because students can fit more activities into their schedules, doing whatever they want with their extra time. Taking online classes gives learners many perks: they can both work and continue their studies remotely, and work toward important goals like securing a good job and finishing their education.

When you need guidance on a problem, is it better to ask a single person for their thoughts, or to gather input from several people to hear different views?

I believe it is much better to ask several people for advice, since this lets you hear many different angles on whatever problem you are dealing with.

Another key reason to get input from more than one person is that different people will judge your situation based on their own experiences. For example, if you are thinking about taking a big risk, your mom might tell you to avoid it because she wants to keep you safe. But if you ask a friend who loves trying new, bold things, they might encourage you to go for it.

Finally, basing a big decision on just one person’s advice can be very risky. If that one person gives you the wrong guidance, you might end up making a choice that brings a lot of stress or difficulty into your life. On the other hand, hearing from several people makes it more likely you will get good advice that helps you make a smart choice, which can make your life much easier.

To sum up, asking multiple people for advice helps you see both the pros and cons of a choice by considering what different people have to say.

While some students plan to choose a career path while they are still in school, others prefer not to think about their future job at all during their studies.

First, many young people realize that picking a career early is crucial for their future. When you are still in school, you have time to focus on your long-term goals, work toward improving your life, and eventually support your family. For example, if you start planning early, you can build a stable career that lets you care for your parents as they get older and can no longer work full-time.

Second, countless people around the world want to improve their lives and provide better futures for their families, and picking a clear career path is key to that. There are so many options to choose from: technology roles, teaching, technical trades, and police work, to name a few. Even more difficult career paths can help you grow and get ahead, so it is worth deciding which one fits you best early on.

However, not all students want to plan for their future. Many feel they are too young to worry about careers while they are still in school, so they put off making decisions. That said, I still believe it is important to think about your career path early, as this allows you to support your family later—not just your parents, but also uncles, sisters, and brothers. Unfortunately, many students only go to school to socialize: they make friends, date, and hang out, rather than working to improve their lives. Some even get involved in harmful behaviors like drug use, excessive drinking, or fighting, which stops them from progressing at all.

In conclusion, I agree that students should figure out their career path as early as possible, ideally before they finish school. It is much easier to plan your studies and work toward a goal when you know what you want to do early, rather than waiting until after you graduate. Having a clear career plan also helps you stay focused, earn a steady income later, and support your family as they grow older.

So the learners can take these subjects as an elective. For example: if a student takes an art class, in fact he/she is not taking it as a required class, he/she takes it for their choice and wants to get extra credit. Or if a person has 4 required classes and he/she takes an art class instead of one of the 4 classes, and he/she thought, "These are the 4 classes that I need for graduation," indeed they are going to take a wrong class because as we know the art classes are not needed for graduation. So we have to take a class that we need for graduation.

Although some educators take the art or music classes of course seniors because they might have less classes. In this case, they choose these classes as choice and the juniors can take these as well to get extra credit.

Let's talk about the required classes:

Required classes are: English 11, Geometry, Math, CIS, World History, and etc...

These classes that students need to take and complete the school credit and receive a better score for graduation.

Each subject has different SOL tests.

When the students reach those classes, they need to pass the SOL test, as well as SOL is one of the important parts of required classes that learners need to pass during a year. The SOL test comes twice for students of course!
