Music, Drama, and Art courses are not compulsory for students to take during their studies. Instead, these fall under elective options, meaning learners can choose to enroll in them based on their personal interests.

For instance, if a student signs up for an Art class, they are not taking it to meet a mandatory requirement, but rather because they want to earn extra credit or pursue a personal interest. There are cases where a learner might replace one of their four required courses with an Art class, mistakenly thinking it counts toward the credits needed to graduate. This is a mistake, though, because Art courses do not fulfill graduation requirements. To graduate, students must complete the specific mandatory classes first.

Some educators allow seniors to take Art or Music classes because they often have fewer required courses left to complete. In these cases, seniors pick these electives by choice, and juniors can also take them to earn extra credit.

Now let’s go over the mandatory courses students must take. Required classes include English 11, Geometry, general Math, CIS, World History, and several others. Students must complete all of these to earn enough school credits for graduation, and doing well in them also helps boost their overall graduation scores.

Each of these subjects has a corresponding SOL test. When students take these mandatory courses, they also need to pass the associated SOL exams, which are a key part of meeting graduation requirements. The SOL tests are offered to students twice a year. Learners must score over 300 points to pass, and if they fail to do so, they are permitted to retake the test.

Even though electives such as Art, Drama, and Music are available, they do not count toward mandatory graduation requirements. These subjects are not compulsory, so they should be treated as electives that students can choose as favorite subjects to support their future plans.

I strongly believe that starting an afterschool homework club is a great idea, as it would give many students the support they need to get better grades and perform well across all their classes.

Think about it—don’t you appreciate extra help when you’re struggling with a task? Students feel exactly the same way. Schoolwork and homework can get really tough, and most students want extra guidance to get through it.

I know this from my own experience. Sometimes I need extra help with my schoolwork, so my parents pay a tutor to come to our house. But not every family can afford that. If we set up a homework club, it would support students who can’t pay for tutoring, and their parents wouldn’t have to spend a lot of money to help their kids do well in school.

Right now, students might only get a short time with teachers after school, sometimes as little as 47 minutes. If we’re going to run a homework club, we should make sessions longer than that. More time means students can get more work done.

To sum up, we really need a homework club. It will help many students improve their schoolwork, pass more tests, and even make tough assignments feel easy to handle because they have all the support they need. It will also save parents a lot of money on tutors. If some teachers don’t want to stay for extra time, they can let students work together and help each other while the teacher rests.

All in all, I think this is a great idea that will help many students with their schoolwork.

"Success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm". We usually define failure as falling short of a goal, or even losing the drive to keep functioning as normal. As humans, we all know that after a setback, it is easy to lose the energy to start over and chase what we really want. Yet British Prime Minister Winston Churchill famously argued that the key is to never let those failures drain your excitement for what comes next.

To start with, failure is an unavoidable part of every human life. It pops up in almost every chapter of our lives, often when things seem to be going well. Most of us wonder why setbacks always seem to strike during our most meaningful moments. We tend to blame ourselves, thinking we must have done something wrong, or not tried hard enough to land a job, pass an exam, or sort out our personal problems. This leads many to ask: why does failure play such a huge role in our day-to-day lives?

The truth about failure is that it is not just a negative outcome. It is a chance to look at what went wrong so we can improve. We need to accept that failing is useful, even good for us: it stops us from repeating the same errors we made before. Every single failure brings a new experience and a fresh lesson that pushes us closer to success.

Take scientists as an example. They run countless experiments to reach one specific result, and they fail far more often than they succeed. But those failures often lead them to discover things they were not even looking for in the first place. This proves that no matter how many times you fail, there is always a solution out there, and new things to learn along the way.

On top of that, staying positive is a real struggle for most people. We all try our best every day to keep a bright outlook, and to frame our mistakes as positively as possible. But this effort often becomes even more stressful right after a major setback.

It is important to remember that feeling stressed or unsure of yourself is actually a good thing. We are all human, and our emotions actually make us stronger than we realize. That said, many people do fall into depression after a failure. This is why so many of us lose hope: we give up on our goals, grow tired, and sink into low moods.

For instance, students at Generic_School read a book last year called "The life of an Indian". It tells the story of a poor Indian boy living on a reservation, who had almost no hope for his future. One day, his teacher introduced him to life outside the reservation, helping him find hope and believe in himself. He chose to chase his dreams instead of staying trapped in poverty on the reservation. He failed countless times, but instead of backing down, he worked through every issue he faced.

This story shows that staying positive after failure is not always as hard as it seems, even for someone growing up in such tough circumstances. Of course, not everyone can manage this mindset. But we all want to be happy, and failure can become a powerful ally in our pursuit of that happiness.

To sum up, learning from our mistakes is the best path to success and personal growth. We need to keep in mind that every failure brings a new experience and a fresh lesson. No matter how many times you fall short, there is always a way forward.

As humans, if we learn to believe in ourselves, keep a positive attitude, chase our dreams, and accept that failure is a normal part of everyday life, we will become far more successful. We will gain the insight to understand how life really works, and realize that life is not as difficult as we often imagine.

A common topic in today’s debates is how to save energy and resources, especially since many businesses have switched to a four-day work week where employees work ten hours a day. Should our school adopt this same model by adding two hours to each school day, so we have four longer days instead of five standard-length ones? Some people argue that this change will not help conserve energy or resources at all. They say longer days mean the school uses far more electricity to power lights, computers, and smart boards, and that students are likely to waste more water by leaving bathroom taps running. They also point out that more time in school leads to higher utility costs overall. However, I believe our school should follow this model. Adding two hours to each school day would help us focus on conserving energy and resources, and most importantly, give us more time to make the world a better place and raise environmental awareness.

First, adding two hours to the school day helps us save more energy for future generations. Schools can also teach students how to use energy wisely at home, such as which light bulbs are most efficient to use, and share tips to help families lower their electricity bills.

Another reason is that we can save water, a key resource, at school. Most students use the bathroom at least twice a day and flush toilets regularly, so putting up student-made posters about the importance of saving water would help. We can also cut down on plastic and paper use, since the school spends money buying these supplies. The money saved could go toward improving our school, and students would learn to be more mindful of how they use resources.

The last key reason is that adding two hours to each day gives both students and teachers extra time to work on meaningful projects. For example, we could create public campaigns to teach the wider community how to slow global warming and care for the planet. Students could also build an online page to share tips with other students and people outside our school about how to live more eco-friendly lives.

To sum up, I believe our school should add two hours to each school day as part of the four-day weekly model. This would help everyone in the school become more aware of how to save energy and resources, and ultimately protect the world we live in. Our world will only become a better place when we all make a conscious effort to change our habits and protect it.

Being your true self is a unique privilege you alone can claim, and it paves the way for countless successes in the world. It is never easy to resist the pressure to change who you are, especially when society constantly tries to shape you into someone else. That is exactly why staying authentic counts as the greatest achievement a person can reach.

Maintaining a positive mindset also gives you a stronger sense of security in your own identity. When you approach situations with optimism, you are far more likely to recognise and seize important opportunities that come your way. Having a clear commitment to staying positive is the best way to steer your life in a good direction. On top of that, living as your true self is the most effective way to show the world what real, meaningful achievement looks like.

The most important thing in life is to hold onto your dreams. Having clear goals inspires you to chase countless achievements, and it is often the first step toward coming up with original ideas that help you stand out. Life is never simple, but it is also far from impossible to navigate. Your dreams are the core goals you can work toward and reach entirely on your own terms.

While some people argue that staying authentic is not the greatest accomplishment, many others firmly believe it is. They point out that anything is possible if you have a clear purpose driving you. This perspective makes sense, but there are extra key points to keep in mind: when you set a goal for yourself, you have the power to do everything required to achieve it. All the sacrifices you make along the way will open up amazing opportunities. Hard work and dedication are the main forces that push you to keep moving forward, and turning your life’s purpose into action is what truly makes it matter.

When you stay true to yourself, you are far more likely to reach a wide range of goals. A negative attitude will only hold you back, since everyone can achieve far more of their aims when they keep a positive outlook. You have to find inspiration within yourself to reach that highest level of success. Being your authentic self means coming up with your own ideas and making a real difference, which is what true great accomplishment looks like. Many schools now offer distance learning, letting students attend classes from home via online video calls. Is this a good idea? I strongly believe taking classes online is an excellent option, mainly because it saves students valuable time and reduces stress.

First, it works well for students with jobs. Most workplaces will not adjust shifts to fit a student’s class schedule, so students often have to rush between work and school. With online classes, they can log in right after their shift ends, with no commute needed. They also have time to eat and rest first, which helps them focus better. Plus, online learning frees up time for other activities, like sports or hanging out with friends.

Next, online classes solve issues related to health, transport, and weather. If a student is sick, going to school risks spreading illness to classmates. Sick students may not be fit to drive, and not all have cars. Even those who do often pay for campus parking, an added cost. Bad weather like heavy rain or snow can also make commuting dangerous or difficult. Online classes remove all these barriers.

They also help students with family responsibilities. Students who are parents can care for their children while learning, so they do not miss class or worry about childcare. This gives them peace of mind, knowing they will not fall behind. Students with disabilities who cannot travel to campus alone also benefit, as they can join classes from a safe, comfortable space. They can even take a break if unwell, then catch up on the lesson later. Parents also get to spend time with their kids and check on their school progress while taking their own classes. Of course, juggling studies, work, and family keeps them busy, but having the option of online classes makes it all much more manageable.

Overall, technology makes daily life easier, and online classes are a great example. They save time, cut stress, and let students balance their studies with work, family, and other duties. For anyone with a busy schedule, online learning is a top choice.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once argued that the highest achievement anyone can reach is staying true to their own identity, even when the world around them pressures them to become someone different. While some people push back against this idea, I fully agree with it. Modern society often tries to force people to adjust their opinions, abandon their cultural traditions, or change their core beliefs to fit in. I think this is true for three key reasons: first, you should never give up on being your authentic self. Second, you must always value and take pride in who you are. Third, you should never turn your back on your background and roots.

The world will always try to push you to change, but you cannot give up on who you are. It does not matter if others disapprove of your choices or personality — the only person who needs to feel at ease with your identity is you. Your comfort and sense of self are what matter most. You should always love who you are and take pride in your identity. Everyone makes mistakes sometimes, but that does not mean you have to change your core self. Instead, you can learn from those errors and grow. Loving yourself is important because every part of your appearance, your personality, and your character is what makes you stand out. These traits make you unique, different from every other person in a world that wants everyone to fit into the same mold.

It is also vital to never forget your roots. If you come from a different country or cultural background, you might feel pressured to hide that part of yourself and pretend to be something you are not. But you should resist that pressure. In a world that constantly tries to turn you into someone else, proving that you can succeed while staying true to your background is one of the greatest things you can do.

So why wait any longer? Do not let the world change who you are. Remember to never give up, always fight for what is best for you, love and take pride in yourself every day, and hold onto your roots. Every part of who you are makes you unique and special — and that is your greatest achievement.

I disagree with the view that heavy smartphone use is positive, because it causes many harmful effects—most notably, it makes people lose real communication with those around them.

First, relying on phones cuts down on chances to go out shopping. Back when I lived in my home country, I’d ride my bike or walk to the local store whenever I needed something. But after moving to the United States, I almost never go out for groceries or supplies. My mom just orders everything we need online or calls the store, and they deliver the items right to our door.

Second, phones change how friends spend time together. Last week, I messaged a friend back in my home country and asked if they still play physical games like soccer on the local field or street games after class. He said most kids now only care about popular mobile games, and no one really wants to play outside in the streets anymore.

Third, young kids get obsessed with phones and stop doing other activities. My little brother is only two years old, but all he wants to do is watch videos or play simple games on the phone. If my mom takes the device away, he starts crying immediately. He never plays with my other brother or does any other kid activities—he just stares at the screen all day.

Fourth, frequent phone use makes visiting family or new places less about real connection. Every time I go to see my extended family, I get bored within minutes if I don’t have my phone, so I end up scrolling through apps instead of chatting with my relatives. Even when I travel to new places, I focus more on taking photos to post online than actually soaking in the sights.

Finally, heavy phone use leads to addiction. I have a classmate at school who cannot put his phone down, even during lessons. He spends class time playing games or watching videos, and when the teacher catches him and tells him to put the device in his backpack, he ignores her. Sometimes he sits at the back of the classroom just to hide his phone use from the teacher.

Imagine your school principal announces that every single student must take part in a mandatory school activity. This rule is a bad idea, for two big reasons: first, many students really need time to rest, and second, plenty of young people simply don’t enjoy sports or group activities. On top of that, kids deserve time to unwind and do whatever hobbies or tasks they actually want to do, not just what’s forced on them.

First, students need rest because they already have piles of schoolwork to handle every day. They need to save their energy for both school tasks and any activities they actually choose to do. When kids get to rest, they feel more ready to take on other responsibilities later. Hanging out with friends is another key way for kids to relax—chatting with peers is fun, and it counts as rest because they aren’t running around or following strict activity rules. If a mandatory activity takes up this free time, students won’t get to catch up with friends, which is just as important for their wellbeing as sleeping or sitting quietly. Rest is essential for young people, since they need energy for all the other parts of their daily lives.

Another issue is that so many kids prefer indoor pastimes over group activities. Lots of students have fun playing video games with their friends online or in person, which they enjoy far more than mandatory sports or clubs. There are also plenty of young people who don’t like going outside at all, and would rather stay in to read, play games, or hang out with a small group of friends. Some might not have any interest in typical school activities, or they may not have many close friends to join in with, which makes forced group activities feel uncomfortable or boring. Most kids would much rather do their own thing than follow a rule that makes them take part in something they don’t enjoy.

Forcing all students to take part in a school activity is not a good policy. We already know that kids need rest, and that many simply don’t like group activities or sports. If I were the principal, I would let students make their own choices. If someone wants to stay inside during free time, that’s fine. If a student is too tired to join an activity, that should be allowed too. And if a kid wants to sign up for a club they actually like, they can absolutely do that. Giving students control over their own time is much better than forcing everyone to do the same thing.

The moment we enter the world, we emerge from our mother’s womb, and our very first instinct is to let out a loud wail. If a newborn doesn’t cry right away, medical staff will gently pat their back to coax out that first cry. From that initial sound, we each develop a unique way of vocalizing, with a pitch and tone distinct to us alone. Hospitals also take our fingerprints at birth, which are completely one-of-a-kind—even identical twins, who may look nearly the same, will never share matching prints. From that point on, we begin to form our own individual personality. Even as tiny babies, our brains start processing information: we learn to cry when we’re hungry, need a diaper change, are in pain, or just want someone’s attention. Once we reach the toddler stage, we pick up how to walk by watching the people around us, and learn to speak by listening to the voices in our daily lives. We figure out how to hold our own bottle, grip a fork or spoon, and handle almost all our basic daily routines—all by observing and mimicking the adults and older kids near us.

When we reach the 6 to 12 age range, most of us have a strong desire to fit in, whether that means joining the popular group at school or copying trends we see on TV. We watch celebrities and see all kinds of possible careers: musicians, actors, painters, police officers, firefighters, dentists, doctors, mayors, chefs, and athletes in every sport from soccer to tennis—the list goes on and on. The key point here is that we are constantly shaped by outside influences. As we move into our teenage years, between 13 and 19, we start to find our own voice, even as we’re still learning to make fully independent choices. We each take our own path and make our own decisions. Our parents don’t follow us around all day dictating every move; they do offer plenty of advice, since they’ve already been through those years and want to spare us from failure or pain. But sometimes making mistakes and failing is exactly what we need to learn our limits and what works for us.

Once we become adults, the safety net we had while living with our parents disappears. We no longer have that privilege, and we have to fully grow up and solidify our own identity. Getting a job comes with real responsibilities, and that’s when we find out what kind of person we really are: are we responsible or unreliable? Outgoing or shy? Easygoing or strict? Patient or quick to anger? Forgiving or holding grudges? I like to think we are all born to grow and adapt to the sometimes harsh world around us, and our behavior is shaped by the experiences we’ve lived through. For example, someone could grow up in a terrible, rundown neighborhood but still have the happiest outlook, far better than a wealthy teenager complaining they didn’t get the car they wanted. Compare that to a child who watched their mother get abused by a deadbeat father, or a kid who stayed up all night worrying if their mom would come home safe, or a child who went to bed hungry. Life circumstances don’t have to define us. I don’t believe we are born with fixed labels. We all have the power to decide what to make of our lives, instead of sitting around begging for pity. A huge part of your character comes down to your mindset: if you have a broken, weak mentality, you’ll give off negative energy and become an unreliable, unmotivated person. But if you have a strong mindset and the drive to get things done, you’ll develop a well-rounded, respected character. To sum up, we create and build our own character ourselves—no higher power assigns us a label or decides what kind of person we will be in life.

Have you ever failed at something so many times that you eventually became really good at it? If that is the case, this prompt is for you. I strongly believe that failure plays a vital role in the journey towards success. I once heard about a young boy who was terrible at catching footballs. If you never practice the things you are bad at, you will never get good at them. This means you will fail again and again, many times over. Failure is also a natural part of life. You will face setbacks in every area of your life, but it is always your choice to pick yourself up and keep trying until you reach perfection. If you never experience failure, you will never achieve true success. So if you fail, do not let it get you down. Keep trying, and soon enough, you will get the results you want. Although you might think this is untrue because some people are naturally gifted, keep in mind that no one is ever good at a skill the first time they try it. Ever. I want you to try something you are not good at, practice it consistently for about a month, and see your progress. I would love for everyone to give this a try, so you can see that failure truly plays a major role in achieving success.

Summer should be a time to soak up good weather, spend time with family and friends, and even hang out with pets—basically, focus on fun, not schoolwork. No one wants to spend their summer stressing over homework or trying to finish assignments.

Students definitely need to unwind after a long, busy school year. But it’s not just young people who need this—working adults also need lengthy breaks from their jobs. They often feel exhausted or burned out from work, just like students do. I’m not trying to compare adults to young people—I know adults have far more responsibilities in their daily lives. But students’ need for breaks is easy to understand: they need to save energy and get enough sleep. Adults need these things too, yet many jobs only mandate a single week of vacation time, sometimes even more, which still leaves workers feeling extremely stressed and tired. That’s why they’d love a long vacation to spend time with family, just like students do—so now that students get this chance, they should make the most of it.

On top of that, most students adore summer for the warm weather, the gentle breeze, and that unmatched feeling of freedom. When you don’t have to worry about grades, extracurricular activities, or school projects, it makes a huge difference whether you get a long break or a short one. I can also see things from teachers’ perspectives, though—they don’t want to spend the first weeks of the new school year reteaching material students forgot over the break, which would be really stressful for them too. But let’s be honest: who doesn’t want a long vacation? Plenty of teachers even save up money specifically to enjoy their summer break.

As a student myself, I relate to the idea that we need vacation time to relax. But there’s another key reason why longer summer breaks matter: a lot of students use the time to work full-time jobs. I know some teachers do this too! They use the extra income to cover necessary expenses, or even save for college—that’s actually the main goal for many students. Some students don’t get as much financial support as others, so summer work is a big help. I get where teachers and educators are coming from too—their job is to help us reach our goals, and a schedule with a 3-4 week summer break, longer winter break, plus a week off in spring and fall sounds great. Some students prefer the weather during those seasons, even though they love fall too, so that setup would work almost the same as regular summer vacation, just a little shorter.

To wrap up, the summer break we already have is perfect. The main reason is that so many students love it—the weather is pleasant, beaches are open, and there’s enough time to travel out of town to visit family and have fun. It’s also great for students who want to work over the summer to earn extra cash or help cover their expenses.

What exactly does self-reliance mean? I’m glad you asked. Simply put, self-reliance is the ability for both students and adults to make choices that affect themselves or the people around them. There’s so much we could discuss on this topic, but I think it’s best to start with the current events and challenges we’re facing right now. These issues don’t just impact us as individuals—they affect the entire United States. Take government shutdowns, for example: they don’t only hurt ordinary people, but also damage businesses of all sizes, from small shops to large farms. Asking for help and advice can make a massive difference when dealing with these problems. Relying on just one perspective isn’t enough—we need more people to join the conversation, discuss these issues openly, and share their ideas and knowledge. That way, we can come up with better solutions together. We shouldn’t teach our children to just follow others blindly—we should raise them to be leaders, and building self-reliance skills is a huge part of that. Even the best leaders ask for help when they need it. They start with small decisions, gain more knowledge and experience over time, and eventually have all the expertise they need—but even then, they keep asking questions to learn even more. These skills aren’t limited to one area of life, either. We can apply self-reliance and the habit of seeking guidance to our families, our jobs, and our daily lifestyles.

Self-reliance isn’t just for students, though. Combining self-reliance with a habit of seeking out extra information makes us better at our jobs and more satisfied with our lives. As we learn these skills, we also pass them on to others—and make no mistake, these skills are extremely useful. Everyone needs them. Self-reliance is closely tied to leadership: it means standing up for what you believe is right for your own career and life. Even if you’re confident your answer is correct, you don’t want to risk being wrong. That’s why asking for guidance and listening to other people’s ideas gives you more options to choose from. I know we all want to be right, but sometimes seeking out other answers and perspectives gives you more to think about, which benefits not just you, but everyone around you. We don’t even have to look far to see why this matters: take the military, or big global decisions. Do these affect us? Absolutely. I bring this up because there are so many issues people ignore that really need to be solved.

Serving in the military is a job, a way of life, and a career that rests entirely in your own hands. The men and women who serve our country have to make incredibly tough choices. Before they even start, soldiers need to be fully prepared—their mindset and skills are the most important things, which is exactly where self-reliance comes in. You can’t always wait for a commander to give you orders when you have the lives of other soldiers on the line: you have to make split-second decisions yourself. That’s why boot camp drills are designed to train soldiers’ minds and skills, so they’re ready to handle these issues without panic. Even during training, asking questions and gathering information is key—it gives you better feedback on the work you’re doing, and helps you build the skills you need. These abilities aren’t just important for the military, either. In civilian life, we all have big decisions to make too, whether it’s about our children or our careers, and we need to stay alert to these challenges.

No matter your age, race, gender, or background, learning these skills is incredibly important, both now and in the future. These abilities will take you far, and one day you’ll even be able to teach your own kids about money, business, and more. But right now, we all need to pay attention to what’s really happening with our government, and push for change. We don’t want to go through another stock market crash, so use your voice, your skills, and everything you have to help others, not just yourself. The world needs more people speaking up, and our government needs to get back to where it was before. Our jobs and homes are at stake, and how we spend our time and money matters. Seeking out answers to tough questions makes a huge difference for our entire society and local communities.

Most of us get our jobs through bosses, who in turn get their funding from the government. When the government shuts down, we lose a lot of income—countless business owners lose their companies and even their homes. These are the real issues we need to focus on, not trivial things like whether we should buy the newest 2019 car model. What matters is setting an example for others: show them how to seek guidance, share new ideas, and never be afraid to ask questions. Asking never hurts, and it helps you see things more clearly and from new angles. Don’t be scared to speak up—we’re all here to learn every single day. No one is perfect, and we’ll keep learning right up until we’re old. Never stop looking for answers, and always share your ideas with the people around you.

To wrap up, I’ll leave you with this: always seek guidance, and never stopasking questions. Thank you so much for your time, and I hope you have a wonderful day.

One of the most enjoyable ways to spend time outside is hosting a casual cookout with family and friends, grilling up favorites like hamburgers, hot dogs, carne asada, tacos, and barbacoa. You can also play all kinds of games together: kick a soccer ball, toss a football, ride bikes, race each other across the grass, or play a casual game of baseball. Bring a speaker to play music, but keep the volume down so you don’t get a noise complaint from the police. Invite your children’s boyfriends or girlfriends, along with their parents, to join the fun, and don’t forget to pack extra snacks for the whole afternoon. Spending time outside with loved ones feels a lot like a mini camping trip. If there’s a nearby river where fishing is permitted, it’s a great idea to try catching a few fish to cook and eat later. But above all, the main goal is to enjoy yourself with everyone there. Take time to notice how beautiful the natural surroundings are, let the sound of birdsong help you forget your daily worries, and reconnect with your family. It’s a good reminder of how much the people around you care about you, and how important that love is. Many people don’t have close family or friends and feel lonely, so we should be deeply grateful for the people in our lives who appreciate us. When evening comes, build a small fire to roast marshmallows, then sandwich the gooey roasted marshmallows between two cookies. While you eat, gather the whole group to share scary stories or tell silly jokes. The best part of being outdoors, though, is not just the fun you have with family and friends, but also getting to breathe in fresh, clean air from nature. Community parks, state parks, and national parks are incredibly valuable spaces for local communities. They’re places where people can have fun with friends, partners, or spouses, host small parties, go for a run, walk their dogs, or just take a quiet stroll to relax their minds and reflect. They offer a chance to leave your problems behind, even if just for a little while. We need to take good care of these parks, too, since they are home to many birds, wild animals, and native plants that need the space to grow and thrive.

Former British Prime Minister Winston Churchill once said, 'Success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm.' I completely agree with this statement. To achieve success, you have to put in a lot of hard work. You will definitely face failures along the way, but the key is to keep trying and never give up.

There are always many obstacles standing in the way of success, and you need to find ways to get around them. You might stumble or face setbacks, but that does not mean you should quit. Every failure teaches you a valuable lesson if you are willing to learn. Churchill’s point is that experiencing failure is a necessary part of reaching success, as long as you hold onto your passion. For instance, imagine you want to attend university but cannot afford the tuition fees. You might feel hopeless at first, thinking your goal is impossible. But instead of giving up, you can look for solutions: you could work a part-time job while studying, earn enough to cover your fees, and eventually complete your degree.

To reach your goals and become successful, you need to work hard, stay persistent, keep a positive attitude, solve problems as they come up, always do your best, and keep learning new things. Above all, remember Churchill’s wise words: true success comes from moving through one failure after another, never letting go of your enthusiasm.

I believe the answer is not a simple yes or no—it really depends on the individual. In some ways, reduced face-to-face contact due to technology has brought good changes, while in others, it has caused harm.

On the positive side, technology can be a lifeline for people who feel lonely. Loneliness can really damage a person’s mental health—it’s one of the worst feelings, though of course there are worse fates, like being in prison, losing your job, or even death. I’ve met people who would rather face those terrible situations than spend time completely alone. For them, being able to read books, shop online, play games, listen to music on apps like Pandora, orwatch shows on YouTube or Netflix is a genuinely positive use of technology. It gives them something to do and helps them feel less isolated.

But as my grandfather always said, nothing in the world is perfect—there have to be downsides for upsides to exist. Every good thing comes with a negative side, and technology is no exception. One big downside is that phones and other devices make people lose interest in ordinary, everyday social activities. For example, some people don’t even care about family gatherings anymore. I’ll admit I never cared much for those either—I always preferred hanging out with my cousins and childhood friends than sitting at home listening to boring adult conversations. But these days, it’s almost impossible to have a normal chat with someone because they’re constantly staring at their phone, doing who knows what. To me, that’s incredibly rude. It sends the message that you don’t care what the other person is saying, and that can make people really dislike you.

There’s no denying that technology is one of the best inventions ever. It makes communication way simpler, provides endless entertainment, and keeps us updated on everything happening in the world—even events in space. We don’t have to read entire books just to find a quick answer to a question anymore. Technology has streamlined so many parts of daily life: you can do almost anything from home, like shopping or ordering food, without even stepping outside.

But all these conveniences make people lazy. You start asking yourself: why should I bother doing this task when my phone or computer can handle it for me? Why go on a real date to talk to someone when I can just chat with them on my phone? Why have a face-to-face conversation when there are so many other things to do on my device? If you keep making these excuses, you might wake up one day and realize you have no one left in your life.

To sum up, technology is a wonderful tool, but only if you use it when you actually need it. Don’t let it take over your thoughts or replace real human connection.

Group work is far more effective than working alone. Collaborating with others gives you access to far more support, as the old saying in my home country goes: "Two brains think more than one." Consider a typical school assignment: a teacher tells the class to create a poster with illustrations, colored sections, and written content, letting students choose whether to work solo or with others. A student working alone has to handle every single step themselves, which is incredibly tiring. In contrast, a group can gather at one member’s house and split tasks: one person handles the writing, another does the sketches and colors, so the work gets done much faster and with far less stress.

Of course, some people argue that working alone is simpler. They don’t have to arrange meetups with partners, or worry that a teammate might mess up their part of the project, or not finish it at all. Sure, solo work takes much more time, but you have full control over every detail, and the final product turns out exactly how you imagined.

This same idea applies to team sports too. If you play a group sport, trying to go it alone is a terrible strategy. You need your teammates’ help to win as a whole team. If you refuse to work with them, the opposing team will easily steal the ball from you, your teammates will be annoyed that you didn’t pass when you should have, and you’ll end up losing the match.

As education systems evolve, most schools now run programs designed to nurture students’ natural talents, and those with a passion for the arts can easily sign up to discover what they are good at. On top of that, learners always need to unwind after sitting through two or three hours of academic lessons. Taking an art class can be a great way to recharge and boost energy levels for the next focused study block, but it ends up being a waste of time for students who have no intention of practicing those skills.

For many high schoolers, daily study feels dull because they struggle to figure out where their interests lie within the school system. In this situation, the best way to turn things around is to find enjoyable activities that cut stress and help learners recharge after long stretches of academic work. There are plenty of options to pick from: joining a band, taking part in a school play, or signing up for a painting or drawing class, all of which can boost motivation for schoolwork. We believe these classes should be mandatory for all students, since they let us choose activities that match our own interests.

On top of that, signing up for an art class does more than just give the brain a break. It also makes it easier to take in new information in the next study block, improving overall learning efficiency. For example, after a tough lesson packed with complex material, doing something creative like singing, acting, or drawing helps clear mental clutter, so the brain feels relaxed and ready to absorb more content. Of course, how well a person relaxes depends on their personal taste in hobbies – you only feel truly refreshed if you are doing something you genuinely enjoy.

We agree that every student should take at least one arts class, but only if these courses are set up as electives that let learners pick options aligned with their natural strengths. If classes are not electives, a large number of students who have no real interest in music, drama, or visual arts will end up in these sessions, making the experience unpleasant for everyone else. For instance, uninterested students might doze off or make loud noise, ruining the chance for others to enjoy their much-needed break.

To sum up, arts classes play a key role in helping students feel refreshed after a long, tiring day or several back-to-back study blocks. They recharge energy, improve focus, and boost motivation, making school feel less stressful and more enjoyable. However, these classes must remain electives, so students only sign up for ones they have the time and interest for. This way, no one wastes time sitting through a class they do not care about.

Modern technology makes it possible to get countless daily tasks done without ever interacting with another person face-to-face. While some worry that this reduces human connection, I believe the overall impact of technology on people’s lives is overwhelmingly positive. It lets us stay in touch with loved ones far away, work remotely without commuting, and meet people from all over the world.

The first key benefit of technology is that it bridges the gap between people who live far apart. We can video call family members who are miles away, share updates about our daily lives, and stay close even when we cannot be together in person. Without these tools, keeping in touch with relatives in other cities or countries would be nearly impossible, and we might grow apart or even forget each other over time. This is why technology is one of the best tools we have in our lives, and why everyone should have access to it. It also proves useful in urgent situations: if someone gets into a car accident, their family can use location tracking on their phone to find them quickly. It also makes daily communication far easier: if you are too sick to go to work, you can send a quick message or call your boss to let them know, rather than having to drag yourself to the office just to pass on the news.

Another major advantage is that technology enables remote work, which saves both time and money. Working from home means you do not have to commute, so you avoid spending money on gas or public transport, and you do not waste hours stuck in traffic. This is especially helpful for parents who want to stay home with their children while still earning an income, as they can balance work tasks and childcare in the same space. It also benefits people who cannot drive or have mobility issues, as they can take on jobs without needing to travel long distances to an office. Even when you travel, you can keep up with work tasks using your phone or laptop, so you can explore new places while still earning a paycheck.

Technology also makes it easy to connect with people from completely different backgrounds. On social media, you can meet people from other countries, learn about their cultures, languages, and traditions, and even ask them questions about their daily lives, religious beliefs, home countries, and more. It also acts as a vital tool when you travel to places where you do not know the language or local streets. If you get lost in a foreign city you have always wanted to visit, or cannot ask locals for help because of a language barrier, you can use translation apps on your phone to communicate with them, or map apps to find your way to your destination.

Overall, technology has had a positive impact on people’s lives. It helps us handle countless everyday tasks, and acts as a useful tool that we rely on for almost everything we do.

Technology plays a huge role in modern daily life, serving as a useful tool that supports people in countless ways, from handling daily tasks and staying in touch with others to accessing entertainment. These days, tech is evolving at an incredibly fast pace across society. A quick search on a smartphone, tablet, or computer lets anyone catch up on breaking news from around the world, or easily message their parents, friends, and classmates no matter where they are.

There is no doubt that technology brings overwhelmingly positive changes to our society. It makes shopping easier, offers endless entertainment options like games and music streaming, and gives people free access to countless useful tools. GPS navigation, language translators, and digital book libraries are all available at no cost to anyone with a connected device, removing barriers that once made these resources hard to reach.

There are many reasons why technology has become so essential to people’s everyday routines:

First, it offers practical help every single day. For example, if someone gets lost in an unfamiliar area, they can pull out their phone and use GPS to navigate to their destination safely. The same tool makes it simple to find the way to a local store or supermarket, proving how valuable tech is for handling small, everyday issues that come up unexpectedly.

Another key benefit is the entertainment it provides. When someone feels bored and is not sure what to do, they can stream music from any artist or genre in the world. It is also far easier to download games or books on a phone or tablet than to visit a physical bookstore: you just type the title you want, and the device pulls up multiple options instantly. The internet also has thousands of games suited to all interests, including sports, adventure, puzzle games, and more, so there is something for everyone.

Technology also changes how we communicate, erasing distance barriers entirely. Popular apps like Facebook, WhatsApp, Instagram, and Messenger are intuitive and easy to use, so almost anyone can figure them out without trouble. These platforms make it simple to stay close to family members or friends you have known since childhood, letting you view their photos and video clips even if you live on opposite sides of the world. For this reason, technology is a true treasure in our lives, as long as we use it responsibly to avoid causing problems.

It also helps people solve all kinds of practical problems. If you are unsure how to cook a new recipe, fix a car issue, or repair something around the house, a quick search will pull up step-by-step video tutorials on platforms like YouTube or Google. These sites share tips and clear guides for almost any issue you might face. You can even find contact details for mechanics or other professionals who can help with more complex problems that videos cannot fix.

Technology also makes job hunting far more accessible. Most companies let people submit applications online, which is much simpler than mailing physical documents. Since almost everyone has internet access via a smartphone, computer, or tablet, this process is open to most people. Businesses use tech to promote their products and reach customers far beyond their local area. The internet lets even small companies go international in days, boosting their profits quickly.

To sum up, technology is an incredibly valuable tool for human life. It supports us with communication, entertainment, job searches, and problem solving, even helping people navigate unfamiliar places or learn new skills. With a connected device, we have endless resources to handle all kinds of needs. Platforms like Facebook and Instagram let us keep up with favorite artists, athletes, friends, and family no matter how far apart we are. Technology brings people closer to loved ones, and was created to support people as they grow. Everyone should recognize how much it improves daily life for people worldwide.

I fully agree with Ralph Waldo Emerson’s view that staying true to yourself in a world that constantly pushes you to conform is the ultimate achievement. Many people claim they care for you and accept you exactly as you are, but the reality is very different. The moment you open up and show your true self to them, they start trying to mold you into someone else. It’s also common for others to fixate on your past mistakes rather than recognizing the value you bring. That’s why being authentic is the most important thing you can do. When you embrace who you are, you prove to others that you are happy with yourself and unfazed by their criticism. Love every part of who you are, inside and out, and never give up the things you’re passionate about just because someone tells you to. Prioritize your own happiness over pleasing others. Don’t hold back your talents or hide what makes you unique – you only get one life, after all. Feeling content with yourself will always matter more than making everyone else happy.

My uncle had $100 in his wallet last week. He handed me $10 but kept the remaining $90 for himself. I urged him to set that cash aside for the next day, since he would definitely need it later. But he ignored my advice and blew the entire amount on new shirts, pants, and hats. The very next morning, he came to me asking for money to fill up his car with gas. He was so excited about having extra cash to buy things for himself that he refused to listen when I warned him he’d need the money soon. Even though he knew he’d have expenses the next day, he spent every cent on items he wanted instead of what he needed.

These kinds of situations show exactly why seeking input from others can lead to better choices. Another friend of mine once had some cash in his pocket and suggested we all go see a movie at the theater. Every other friend in our group told him that was a bad idea. The film was already out on DVD, and buying the disc would cost way less than theater tickets for everyone. When he heard all our advice, he looked at the situation from a different angle instead of just his initial plan. Even though he really wanted to see the movie on the big screen, he realized going to the cinema would be a huge waste of money. That’s how we convinced him to just buy the DVD instead.

It’s common for people to ask more than one person for advice when they’re unsure what to do. My dad once gave me some money to buy whatever I needed, and I knew full well I would need a white shirt the next day for an event we were going to. But I was so obsessed with a new video game that I bought it instead, even after my dad reminded me I’d need the shirt. The next day, I had to ask my parents for extra money to buy the shirt, and my dad just said, “I told you to get it yesterday, but you didn’t listen.” I knew I needed the shirt, but I still ignored his advice. After that, I learned my lesson—now I always set aside some cash for unexpected expenses like that.

Looking back at all these stories, they all prove how important it is to listen to the people around you. Every bad situation I mentioned happened because someone refused to take advice from the person right next to them. So, what about you? Do you think it’s okay sometimes to get advice from more than one person?

I fully agree that building a successful life starts with how you treat others and manage your own mindset. To get ahead, you need to show the world you’re unique by staying kind no matter what others say or think about you. Handle every situation calmly, and tackle problems with a positive attitude—losing your temper never leads to good solutions. That’s why it’s so important to be good to everyone you meet, keep a sense of inner peace, and build strong, positive bonds with the people around you. No matter what comes your way, face it with a smile.

When you’re kind to everyone, you lift their mood and yours too. Choosing to be good sets you apart from the crowd, since we see so many rude or unkind people in the world today. Just because you meet someone with a bad attitude doesn’t mean you should stop being nice. Instead, stay away from people who bring negativity, and give yourself the chance to find others who think like you—they’ll feel like family. These are the people who will make your life better and help you reach more success. For example, I always try to be kind to my family, my friends, and even strangers. I’ll share a bit about my friends: they’re truly special to me, and we care deeply about each other. Why? Because I took the time to really get to know them. Now I understand what they enjoy, how they spend their free time, and most importantly, they see me as someone who’s successful because I always treat them with a good attitude. I want these people in my life, and I truly believe they’ll all have wonderful futures—I can already see they’re on track to be very successful themselves.

I also believe peace of mind is a key part of a happy life. When you have inner calm, you get so many positive feelings that make you feel comfortable in your own skin. Even when something happens that upsets you, that’s exactly when you need to work hardest to keep your peace. I know it’s not always easy—lacking inner calm can hurt you in many parts of your life. To feel at peace, do things you truly love, find hobbies that never get boring, and don’t get angry over small things. Holding a grudge for days or even a weekend over one problem is terrible for you—nothing beats having a calm soul. When I was 12, my younger brother did something that really upset me at the time. I still remember it clearly to this day, and I’ll be honest: carrying that anger inside me felt awful. I’m 20 now, and I worry that that bitter feeling might stay with me forever. I try not to dwell on it, but when I do think about it, I remind myself how much I love my brother. We’re very close now—he’s always there to listen when I need to talk, and sharing everything that’s going on in my life with him brings me true peace of mind.

Building good connections with the people around you also helps you keep a positive attitude. If you spend time with people who are always upbeat, or who talk about things that will help you grow, they’ll shape your future for the better. These people know what they want out of life, and what’s bad for them—they’re interesting to talk to, you can learn a lot from them, and you can share your own ideas too. In life, you’ll meet all kinds of people, good and bad. Some might seem great at first: they’ll invite you to parties, ask you to hang out all the time, and you’ll think they’re the perfect friends to help you succeed. But let me tell you, sometimes the people who really want to help you aren’t the ones throwing parties—they’re the ones offering you opportunities that will actually improve your life, not hurt your future. I know it’s easy to think the people pushing you to do better are being mean, but that’s not true. I knew a boy in seventh grade who had a bright future ahead of him. He got great grades, always turned in his homework, and was a genuinely nice person. But when we got to ninth grade, he started hanging out with a group of kids who skipped homework, got bad grades, and didn’t care about their futures at all. A few months later, his grades started to drop. Every time I asked where he’d been, he’d say he was out with his new friends doing things he shouldn’t have been. He ended up becoming just like them, and I don’t think he even went to college. That’s exactly why I say: if you want a successful future, you have to surround yourself with people who will support your goals.

After going over these three key points—being kind to everyone you meet, keeping peace in your soul, and building positive connections with those around you—it’s clear how important a good attitude is. Show kindness to everyone, keep a positive mindset, and stay upbeat no matter what’s happening in your life. That’s the real secret to success.

Whether technology’s reduction of in-person human contact counts as a positive or negative change is a common debate today. Tech is now present in almost every part of daily life. Without it, we would have far fewer opportunities to learn new skills or access information. We no longer need to meet face-to-face to hold a conversation: even a basic phone lets us text someone living on another continent. Tech simplifies countless daily tasks, and I believe it mostly brings positive changes, as shown by the examples below.

Tech supports countless parts of human life, which proves its positive impact. For one, many people depend on tech for their jobs. They can look up answers to work questions instantly without bothering colleagues, and if tech did not exist, they would not be able to do their jobs at all, meaning they would lose their income. Schools are another clear example: both teachers and students rely on tech regularly. Most students type assignments on computers and submit them online. If they have a question about a topic, they can search for answers on the internet immediately. In US schools, for instance, roughly half of all academic tasks involve tech—students and teachers use digital tools far more often than physical textbooks to find information. Doctors also benefit hugely from tech. They use advanced medical devices to perform surgeries that save far more lives than procedures in the past, when they had to rely only on printed medical textbooks. Beyond that, factories use automated tech to handle tasks like packaging products. This means factory workers do not have to do hard physical labor, since machines take on most of the heavy workload.

Of course, tech is a tool that people can use for both helpful and harmful purposes. Most people use it responsibly: secretaries, teachers, doctors, and many other workers rely on tech to communicate with colleagues or store important files. Many parents also use tech to keep their children occupied. In Latin American countries, some parents even call digital devices the “new babysitter”—phones, tablets, and similar gadgets are an easy way to distract kids when parents need to finish chores or work, so they do not have to hire a separate caregiver. But not everyone uses tech ethically. Some people learn to use digital tools to commit fraud, trick others by pretending to be someone else on social media, or even coordinate kidnappings. There are many cases of scammers targeting elderly people, or tricking children through online games and social media to get personal information. Others become hackers who steal bank account details, with no concern for the people they hurt. These bad uses show that even though tech offers more opportunities, not everyone chooses to use them for good.

Tech also shifts how people live and form their opinions. For one, advanced security systems and smart home devices make many people feel safer in their own houses than they did in the past. It also creates new job opportunities: content creators like YouTubers can share their hobbies and interests with a global audience, even if they never meet a single viewer in person. Tech has even changed how older generations interact: in the past, they had to write physical letters to stay in touch with distant friends, but now they can send a quick text or hop on a video call instead, no in-person meeting required. This reduction in face-to-face contact is not always a bad thing. For example, if you play online games with friends who live on the other side of the world, you can chat with them through the game’s voice or text features—you do not need to see each other to build a friendship. This shows that limiting in-person human contact can have real benefits too.

That said, reducing face-to-face human contact does have downsides. At work, for instance, you need to talk regularly with colleagues to build strong professional relationships. The same goes for romantic partnerships: you cannot maintain a healthy relationship with only text messages—you need in-person time together to connect properly. But there are exceptions: in school, you might discuss a homework question with a classmate over a messaging app, or look up a verified answer online instead of just accepting what a friend tells you. To sum up all my examples, both in-person communication and tech-based interaction have their pros and cons. It is true that some people turn to tech instead of books because they are too lazy to read, and digital sources do not always provide correct information. But when it comes to this balance, I believe we should prioritize in-person human connection over communication through technology.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once wrote, "Unless you try to do something beyond what you have already mastered, you will never grow." I completely agree with this statement, and I have three key reasons to support my view. First, people cannot grow if they only prepare for one single path in life. Second, having knowledge in multiple areas gives a person a clear advantage over others. Third, avoiding challenging tasks that push your limits will stop you from developing further.

To start with, if individuals do not build up a range of skills and knowledge throughout their lives, they will lack direction and have far fewer opportunities in today’s society. They simply will not have the right qualifications to apply for good jobs. For example, someone searching for a better role with new responsibilities will find it impossible to succeed if they only know how to do one basic task. How can they contribute productively to their community or country if they are not prepared to take on important, specialized work?

Next, having diverse knowledge makes it much easier to find high-quality, well-paid jobs. Knowledge is one of the most powerful tools a person can hold. Many people believe that knowledge is something money cannot buy, no matter how wealthy you are. If you focus on learning new things consistently, you will always have an edge when it comes to growing and advancing in life.

Finally, I believe people will never grow if they never take on difficult, unfamiliar challenges. We should always seek out new experiences that push us out of our comfort zones. For instance, imagine a person who goes to university and qualifies as a teacher. If they stay in that same role forever and never pursue more demanding careers, such as becoming a school principal, they will never advance beyond their initial level.

In conclusion, I fully agree with Emerson’s statement. His words clearly explain what personal growth really means: unless you push yourself to try things you have not already mastered, you will never develop. These reasons are why I stand by his view.

Online classes and video conferencing are one of the best ways to support two key groups: students who cannot afford to attend traditional college, and older adults who never had the chance to continue their education due to money troubles. Financial struggles are a huge barrier to education for many people today. Students often have to cover the cost of housing, whether they live in on-campus dorms or rent off-campus apartments, which pushes many to leave dormitories entirely because they cannot keep up with payments. A lot of students also hold down part-time or full-time jobs to cover basic expenses. Juggling both work and study is very hard for students, as they have to carefully split their time between job shifts and classes to keep their lives manageable and low-stress.

Transportation and parking pose additional challenges for many learners, which is why a lot of them choose to take classes from home to avoid arriving late. Even colleges with huge campuses often do not have enough parking spots for all their students, and not every learner owns a car or other vehicle that needs a parking space. When students can join classes remotely, they have the flexibility to start their lessons at any point during the day, even after a long, tiring shift at work.

Students who attend classes online from home often get more work done faster and accomplish more overall. Without the usual distractions of a physical classroom, they can focus better on the material, understand lessons more easily, and even enjoy the learning process more. They can ask questions directly to instructors online, and they have extra time to rewatch recorded lessons until they fully grasp the content. Many lecturers also assign less homework and fewer projects to online learners, so they have enough time to complete other assignments from their courses.

Remote learning frees up time for learners to handle other responsibilities, and makes it easier to show up to lectures on time. It also gives people who never had the chance to attend college – including older adults – the opportunity to work toward their lifelong education goals. For students who do not have access to transport, online classes save money and help them stay more organized, with better time management skills.

In several societies, teenagers are expected to pick a future career before they even enter high school. Those who begin planning their career early definitely increase their chances of turning those plans into reality. Younger students who start this process early also have the option to consult their school counselors for guidance. A lot of learners argue that choosing a career early is beneficial: they say it lets them enroll in relevant college courses later, helps them land a job right after graduation, and means they won’t have to stress about career decisions in adulthood. However, I firmly believe that deciding on a career too young is a mistake. It often leads students to drop out of related courses, forces them to overthink their choices, and ends up wasting their time.

First, young people who pick a career early are far more likely to abandon their related classes. For example, if a student signs up for a course tied to their chosen career, they often lose motivation after just three weeks of attendance. This loss of interest makes it hard for them to keep up with coursework, leaving them struggling to catch up. That’s why it’s always better to think carefully before committing to any career-related class.

Another issue is that picking a career too early causes unnecessary stress and overthinking. Even adults take a long time to settle on the right career path. Most prioritize finding a job first, since their main goal is to earn money quickly. They often wait until they have enough savings and have spent time with friends before dedicating themselves fully to a career. Young students lack the maturity to balance these priorities, making early career choices even harder.

Finally, starting career planning at a young age is often a waste of time. Most kids would rather play video games or pursue hobbies than focus on future work. Many also assume career planning is just another school assignment, so when asked to write down their goals, they often put “don’t know” and go back to their favorite activities. This is why it’s essential to create a detailed plan before trying to map out a career while still young.

Deciding on a career at age twelve or younger is particularly reckless. It leads to excessive overthinking, pushes kids to abandon the plan and return to their old hobbies, and creates negative feelings toward school courses. Most young children will drop a career-related class after just two or three weeks, and many will write “don’t know” when asked to list their career goals. While figuring out a future career takes time, it’s important not to rush the process, and to stick with it even if you struggle to keep up at first.

I firmly believe that telling the truth all the time is the right choice, since being honest simply means sticking to the facts and never deceiving the people around me. There are clear reasons why honesty is the best policy. For one, people are far more likely to trust me when I answer their questions or ask for help with a task, even if those same people are not fully truthful in their own work. To me, honesty is the most important part of who I am. As people grow and learn, they get wiser, and I plan to keep honesty as a core part of my life from the very beginning. Another big reason honesty matters so much to me is that it helps me feel secure. I know I won’t fail exams or get bullied later in life, because I’m always truthful about my abilities and actions.

Of course, being honest doesn’t always work out perfectly. Sometimes telling the truth upsets people who trusted me, and they might decide never to trust me again for the rest of their lives. That’s a really upsetting situation: I was only trying to stay positive to make a friend or family member feel better, not dwell on bad things that might never actually happen, but they still get mad at my honesty. After a conflict over honesty with a loved one, they might reject my commitment to telling the truth, stop trusting me entirely, and even seek out people they think are smarter than me. Years later, that same friend or family member might apologize for not trusting me before. We could repair our relationship, they might come to value my honesty again, and we’d never have another fight about truthfulness or our bond.

But there’s another possibility: what if they start trusting other people’s honesty instead of mine? That could lead to huge, never-ending arguments between us. The better option is to avoid a massive fight altogether. I can sit down face-to-face with the person involved, have a calm talk that doesn’t hurt anyone’s feelings, and avoid being cut off from my friend or family member forever. This approach works better because I can rally other honest people I know to help my loved ones focus on positive relationships instead of negative ones. That way, they won’t get stressed, have emotional breakdowns when sad thoughts come up, or spiral into dangerous thoughts like suicide, overdose, or getting into a fatal car crash.

Even if people tell me they don’t trust me and reject my honesty, I never have dark thoughts about ending my life. I will stand by my commitment to truth, even if I let down people who trusted me. My honesty is not a failure, no matter what. I will be truthful for my whole life, and I will never give up this core part of who I am. If I’m worried I might fail an exam on my first try, I’m always honest with myself: I won’t fail, I’ll work as hard as I can, pass, and feel proud of my own truthfulness that I can rely on. If I forget to study and end up failing, that’s not honesty’s fault. It’s my own mistake for not preparing, which is why I got most answers wrong—I was guessing instead of knowing the material. Even if I feel like honesty isn’t useful to me at a certain moment, I’ll turn to it whenever I really need help to succeed, so I don’t end up failing in life.

I wish everyone would make honesty their top personality trait. It helps people work through conflicts that can’t be solved quickly, and I might even need that help myself sometimes. Most people disagree that you should be honest all the time, and they don’t list it as their most important trait. They first need to learn what honesty really means, and how it can help them succeed in life. A lot of people believe only very intelligent people have strong honesty, and they trust those smart people’s words for no good reason. But they’re wrong—honesty is equal across all people. Less intelligent people are just as honest as smart people, and vice versa.

People who aren’t very smart now can grow over time, and their honesty will make others support them as they become more intelligent. For smart people, they might keep growing, or there’s a small chance their intelligence drops. Even then, people often keep trusting them, even if I can see their intelligence and honesty have slipped—meaning they’ve started lying, even though they used to tell the truth. That’s why smart people who were honest in the past might start lying about most things later, if no one teaches them to never stop being truthful.

If you lose your way and stop being honest, the best people to teach you again are family members or teachers. You don’t mess around as much with family or teachers as you do with friends—friends might lead you into a different crowd where you forget about honesty, leaving everyone confused about why they can’t trust you anymore. As I grow and stick to honesty, my friends and family are often surprised at how I learned to be truthful, and how many people trust me now. They feel like they’re in a totally different world, and they wonder: “How did they change so much? I thought they’d stay the same their whole life.” Once they realize how I’ve grown, they’ll probably tell everyone about the person I’ve become. That’s why honesty is the most important trait for everyone’s life, and why it is the best path to follow.

While some might argue the opposite, beginning with modest goals lets you tackle small, fixable errors first.

We should think about setting our aims a little lower at first, so we can start by checking over the areas that need improvement. These small adjustments are what will make you tougher and more capable of handling all kinds of challenges down the line.

Those who begin with the most humble starting points are often the ones who end up reaching their dreams. They are the ones who prove capable, because they set realistic, low-stakes goals and hit their targets step by step. Making mistakes along the way actually helps them grow: each error builds their character, making them far stronger and better equipped to take on even more complex tasks in the future.

Many people set overly ambitious goals right away, convinced that this will let them reach the top quickly, and that any problems that come up will sort themselves out without any hard work or even a moment’s thought. But it is better to start a little lower than that. This way, you can build the resilience and work ethic needed to reach your goals, just by putting in steady effort, instead of aiming too high and falling short. Take someone who vows to take on huge projects, risking everything they own: if they take one wrong step because they didn’t stop to plan first, they lose it all. Starting with smaller goals helps you avoid unnecessary risks, letting you move forward step by step and pick up new skills as you go.

Choosing low-risk goals also stops you from losing the things you worked so hard to earn or achieve. Understanding that this approach is what helps you get far in life means you won’t let your progress stall. Instead, you take the time to look at the things already in your life and make them better, working on them one step at a time. Some say it is good to challenge yourself every now and then, but you should never risk what you already have to do so. There is no point putting in all that effort to build something, only to lose it all in one unthinking step because you didn’t move forward gradually.

My view is that everyone should pause to think before taking action. This is what will actually get you to the top, instead of watching your progress crumble in front of you. Rushing to take risks without sparing a single thought for the consequences will never lead to long-term success. If you do want to challenge yourself, make sure you think through all the details first.

Would you prefer your child head to college or start working right after finishing high school a year early? Why wouldn’t you?

Quite a few schools now offer programs that help students prepare for their future goals, whether that means pursuing higher education or entering the workforce.

Yet many students feel ready to chase their goals without sitting through four full years of high school. For young people eager to wrap up high school and prep for their next steps, a four-year schedule can feel needlessly complicated. I believe there are plenty of ways for these students to get ready for what comes next. They can start college sooner, land jobs earlier, and gain real-world experience that helps them become professionals far faster than the traditional path allows.

For example, starting college a year early lets students learn more about their future careers and get a clearer idea of what they want out of their work.

Another key benefit is that students who finish high school early can get jobs more easily. This helps them avoid low-wage roles like restaurant work or other poorly paid, unstable jobs, letting them build a solid foundation for their future instead.

Lastly, finding success early in life is a major plus. Parents are always proud of children who follow a good path and achieve their goals ahead of schedule.

To sum up, I believe finishing high school in three years is a better option for many students. They can learn more, gain more practical experience, and find success in their daily lives much faster. This path also lets them build up more knowledge and skills in a shorter time, making them stand out more quickly than peers who follow the traditional four-year schedule.
