Dear Council,

I strongly believe the city council should introduce a curfew for teenagers, as it will help keep them away from trouble. There are many teens who hang around outside and disturb local residents. A 10 P.M. curfew makes sense for these young people, since they often loiter on streets, make loud noise, and do little except cause problems for others. At the same time, there are also teens who use this time to study for school or get rest for the next day – a curfew would support them too. If the council adopts this rule, it should be written into law that any teenager found on the streets after 10 P.M. is breaking the law.

Many teens end up in jail for engaging in illegal activities. Some carry guns, even though most are under 18 and not legally allowed to own firearms. Occasionally, innocent teens get grouped with those caught with guns or other illegal items. Often, the guns teens are found with are not even theirs – some are dumped in bodies of water, and the person who discovers the weapon is wrongly blamed for all past crimes linked to that gun. The city council and this curfew are both meant to support young people, with the goal of helping all teens avoid trouble.

Some argue that a curfew interferes with young people’s lives. While it is true that such a rule limits their freedom to some extent, many of these teens are engaging in harmful behavior that puts them at risk. The curfew is only intended to protect and guide them.

Overall, I am convinced that keeping teenagers off the streets after 10 P.M. is a good idea, as it will help them stay out of trouble.

First impressions are not permanent, since what we first notice about a person or situation is rarely the full truth. Many people assume something is negative simply because their initial quick judgment of it was unfavorable, without stopping to consider they might be missing key details.

We should avoid forming firm opinions about people or things based only on first impressions, because we are very likely to be mistaken. It is easy to misjudge something we think is wrong, and we often form quick opinions about others without knowing anything about their personality, background, or values. What we see at first glance is almost never the whole story, so our initial assumptions can easily be inaccurate.

I learned this lesson firsthand in 10th grade, when I misjudged a classmate. Even though we shared several classes, I refused to speak to him or spend time near him. My first impression was that he was rude to both other students and teachers, so I kept my distance, figuring he would be unkind to me if we ever interacted.

Later, I realized he became one of my best friends, and turned out to be the nicest person I had ever met. He was someone I could trust completely and enjoy hanging out with. Even if you believe first impressions cannot be changed, taking the time to reflect on them or get to know the person better can totally shift your initial view.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once argued that people only grow when they try tasks beyond their current mastery, and he was right. To understand this quote, mastery means being able to do a skill perfectly every time, with no errors. Growth starts with setting clear goals. Even tiny steps toward them move you closer to your bigger achievements. Progress is rarely fast or easy. Some skills take years to learn, let alone master, but with confidence and self-belief, you will eventually get there.

For example, if you ride a bike, learn to ride a motorcycle. If you bake cupcakes, try a full cake. If you can float, teach yourself to swim. Small challenges like these build on existing skills, making them stronger. As you improve, you can take on bigger projects and reach higher goals.

You will never reach your goals unless you push yourself. With dedication, you can hit them and go further than you thought possible. Struggling with a task at first does not mean you will never master it—keep trying until you succeed, or you will never grow. Now, the choice is yours: grow as a person, or stay the same and never achieve your life goals.

Thomas Jefferson, who served as US president, wrote a message to help people make a habit of doing their work regularly.

Sticking to a regular routine of completing our tasks has so many benefits. When we work at something consistently, we finish what we start, get better at the task over time, and it eventually feels effortless.

Of course, doing the same work day after day can feel dull for us sometimes. But even when it’s boring, regular practice helps us master a skill properly.

I make a point of doing my schoolwork, my part-time job, and my sports training every day. This routine helps me remember what I’ve learned, and practicing regularly lets me build skills until I’m good enough to teach them to someone else. Take reading, for example: if we read every day, we pick up so much knowledge about all kinds of topics. On the other hand, people who skip their work or job responsibilities are just lazy. They never learn anything new if they don’t stick to a consistent schedule.

If we look around, it’s easy to see the difference between people who stick to regular habits and those who don’t. Consistent people are always better off than those who aren’t. Think about it: doing homework every day, going to bed on time, training for sports regularly, showing up to work on schedule—these habits all lead to better results.

We should also encourage the people around us to build these consistent habits. Reminding others to stick to their work routines is a great way to support them.

I didn’t always follow this rule myself. When I first started school, I struggled because I rarely did my homework or studied regularly. That changed when my friends encouraged me to start doing my work every day. I’m so glad I listened to them. Now, I want everyone to make consistent work a habit they never break. There are even more benefits, too—if we eat healthy meals regularly, we’ll stay in good shape and won’t need to visit the doctor as often.

Just keep doing it, always.

I strongly believe that first impressions of people or things are never fixed—they can shift over time, and everyone reacts to these initial judgments differently. No two people will ever hold exactly the same attitude toward a situation or person.

There are plenty of people who never adjust their first impressions at all, usually because they simply don’t care what others think. For others, though, their views shift completely based on past experiences they’ve already lived through. A really negative impression can push someone to reconsider their behavior, while those who ignore what others say will keep acting the same way day after day. But once they get a new perspective that makes them pause, they start to reflect on their mistakes and pick them apart. Real change only happens when someone truly feels the need to become a better version of themselves, and it never happens overnight. Some people take a long time to shift their habits because they keep repeating the same errors without thinking them through first.

Romantic relationships, especially experiences of betrayal, can completely transform how someone sees their partner or the idea of dating in general. Every relationship faces challenges, whether that’s jealousy, toxic behavior, or negative influences from others. Tragically, many young people lose their lives because they act on a first impression that their boyfriend or girlfriend has cheated on them, without stopping to think about how painful it would be for the other person to be wrongly accused of betrayal. A relationship should never be about trying to make other people jealous of what you have. Change is often difficult, but it’s one of the best ways to build a happy, healthy partnership.

I can speak to this from my own life. For a long time, I was convinced that I could never change my personality. That changed when someone told me my attitude had let a lot of people down, and I felt incredibly ashamed of myself. I started having negative thoughts every single day, convinced I would never be as capable as the people around me. Back then, I thought changing my behavior was impossible because I was so used to doing things that felt right to me, even if they bothered other people. But one day, I made up my mind to change who I was, no matter how hard it would be. I was determined to make that change, whether I got support from others or had to do it on my own.

To return to my main point: first impressions of people and situations are always open to change. Adjusting your behavior is a clear sign that you’re not the same person you used to be, and every past impression—good or bad—can teach you how to avoid making the same mistakes in the future. Lots of people claim it’s impossible to move past old mistakes, but if you work at it day by day, you can get better at letting go. No one is perfect, but we can all improve by shifting our attitudes, including learning to be more careful about who we choose to trust.

I don’t think school principals should make every student clean up litter or do community service, because lots of students have family plans and other responsibilities outside of class. Younger elementary schoolers might be able to handle this kind of work, since they usually have fewer after-school commitments and more free time. Some middle school students could help too, as long as they aren’t overloaded with other tasks—for example, kids who don’t play school sports might have extra time to pitch in. It’s likely that some school leaders will try to make all students do mandatory community service, maybe because of widespread behavioral issues. Others might single out students who break rules and assign this work only to them. Students who follow the rules, like me, can always volunteer to help on weekends instead. I’m usually tied up with other responsibilities on weekdays, so weekends work better for me. Principals should only require students who misbehave during the week or on weekends to do this work. Doing repeated cleanup or service tasks will likely get tiring for them, which could push them to improve their behavior to avoid the extra work.

Choosing between working alone or with a group is a common dilemma. While collaborating with a team you like and trust, where everyone knows their role, can be incredibly rewarding, solo work offers distinct advantages. For one, you never have to worry about someone stealing your ideas or copying your work—a problem that comes up far too often in group settings.

Too often, group work turns into a situation where everyone does less than they would alone. When you rely on teammates to pick up the slack, you start to feel less confident in your own abilities. It can make you feel like you always need someone else to lean on, rather than trusting your own skills.

Group work isn’t always terrible, but it can be frustrating. I’m a student, and I do enjoy working with my friends sometimes—but they always end up copying my work, which I hate. It makes me worry that they won’t be able to do well in life without me doing the heavy lifting. It’s disappointing to see them rely on being in a team to get good results, especially when they didn’t actually contribute anything to the project.

For me, working alone is far better than collaborating with a team. That’s not to say I dislike working with other people—it’s just how I operate. When I work in groups, I never feel like I’m getting anything out of it, because my teammates are either cheating off me or not helping at all. Working by myself feels more genuine. I stay motivated, knowing I don’t have to worry about what others are doing, and I find I can get way more done without needing to rely on anyone else.

Over time, I’ve learned a lot of important lessons. Most of all, I’ve realized you have to put your own needs first, and always have your own back. In my view, group work should really be avoided entirely. You might wonder why—but the answer is simple: you should never feel like you’re not good enough on your own. Prioritizing yourself is always the right call.

I strongly believe that allowing students to attend classes from home would bring them many advantages, as they can prepare more easily for lessons and concentrate better without the usual school-day distractions.

One key reason I hold this view is that many students feel too shy to show their true abilitiesin a traditional classroom. For instance, a top-performing classmate might tell them they are not good enough, or that their English speaking skills are too weak to keep up. But when learning from home, these students can work toward their goals without facing that kind of harsh judgment in person.

Take a student working alone at home, for example. If no one is there to tell them exactly how to complete a task for their online class, but they have lots of questions about the material, they will learn to find answers independently. That builds self-reliance, which is a valuable skill.

I’ve also found that studying from home adds flexibility to daily routines. If I’m home, I can look up extra information for my assignments, and if I get hungry after a long day of working and studying, I can quickly make a snack in the kitchen before returning to my room to finish homework. If I have a question, I can just send a text to my teacher for help, instead of waiting until the next day’s class.

Overall, learning from home with no social pressure can make the experience far more comfortable, especially for shy students or those who need a teacher’s undivided attention to explain difficult material. It also helps students who hate waking up early for morning classes: they can choose to study later in the evening instead, without worrying about getting dressed or commuting to school on time.

I also know from personal experience how helpful remote learning can be. A friend of mine got pregnant while in school, and continuing in person was incredibly difficult for her. I saw her many times, exhausted with her growing belly, still dragging herself to campus. After she gave birth, she sometimes brought her baby to class, which was stressful: if the baby cried or needed to nurse, the teacher would be right there with her, and she felt uncomfortable. Later, when she returned to full-time in-person classes, she struggled with leaving her baby at home alone. Hearing her story made me realize that if given the choice, I would definitely pick remote classes over in-person school.

Of course, there are some challenges to consider. What if a student cannot afford the fees for online classes, or their family does not have the resources to support remote learning? Another issue is that some students might skip in-person classes to sleep in, or show up to school without paying attention to the teacher. But for students who need to work to support themselves, remote learning is a great solution: they can work a few hours a day, then spend the rest of their time studying at home. They could also alternate days: work one day, take online classes the next. This makes it much easier to pass their classes and required exams like the SOL. The key is to never give up on your goals. If you don’t understand something, ask for help. Research information on your own, put in your best effort, and ignore people who try to make you feel like you don’t belong. Show those who doubt you that you can succeed.

During the school year, it is easy to learn through online videos or video calls. These videos often explain math problems and other course materials very clearly, step by step.

There are plenty of other benefits to learning from home too. Students can spend more time using computers for research, focus better on homework without classroom distractions, look up information on their phones whenever they need to, and study at any time of day. They won’t get distracted by chatting with friends during lessons, and can finish assignments faster without interruptions.

Remote learning also saves students from winter hassles: you don’t have to worry about freezing temperatures on the morning commute, or picking out the right school clothes. You can go to your “class” from home in a good mood, without running into people you’d rather avoid, which helps prevent conflicts with other students. Many students struggle with low self-esteem, which takes a toll on their mental health. Giving these students the option to take classes online would be far better for their well-being. That is my firm opinion on the value of learning from home.

A common debate today is whether students should be required to settle on a career path as soon as they start high school, with most of their coursework chosen to steer them toward that specific field. I firmly believe that expecting young teens to commit to a career so early is a bad idea. Most high schoolers are still too young to make thoughtful, well-informed choices, and they often act without thinking, leading to poor decisions about their future.

For one thing, high school students are rarely mature enough to know exactly what they want to do for work. They have almost no real-world exposure to different careers, so they can’t possibly understand what a given job actually involves day to day. Most teens have never held a proper job, let alone learned about what people in their intended field do regularly, so they’re not prepared to make such a big, long-term choice.

I think making this choice too early is a mistake. For me, I plan to spend my first two years of high school exploring all kinds of career options. Once I reach my junior and senior years, I’ll take the time to pick the courses that are the best fit for the path I’ve chosen, so I can get proper preparation and hands-on experience for my future job.

Another issue is that teenagers often act impulsively or change their minds as they grow. If you pick all your classes for a specific career freshman year, but later decide you want to do something completely different, all those early courses will have been a waste of time. Take my friend, for example: he signed up for a technology class his first year of high school, but when he looked up how much people in that field earn, it was far less than he expected. He ended up switching to a materials and processes class to learn construction skills, like cutting materials and building houses.

It’s also very common for young people to make the wrong call about their future. Instead of rushing to pick a career in freshman year, I think the smarter choice is to wait, focus on doing well in all your classes, and take the time to find the best possible path for you. This requires being responsible, caring about your schoolwork, and taking your future seriously.

After considering all these points, I’m convinced that the best approach for high school students is to focus on getting good grades and learning as much as possible in their early years. By the time you reach senior year or start college, you’ll have more life experience and a better understanding of different careers. That is the ideal time to choose the courses that will guide you toward the specific career you actually want to pursue.

Do I agree or disagree with the claim that "Unless you try to do something beyond what you have already mastered, you will never grow"? I fully agree with this view. Having lived for 17 years, I’ve learned that sticking to what feels comfortable leaves you stuck. If you only chase easy paths, you will never work to reach your full potential as a person.

It is possible to stay in your comfort zone, of course, but it does not help you progress. You end up wasting time and energy that you could spend improving yourself and sharing what you know with others. Everyone should always work to become the very best version of themselves.

I believe everyone should agree with this statement, because refusing to improve yourself is never the right choice. It is not that staying comfortable is inherently good or bad, but pushing yourself to learn more is incredibly rewarding. You can gain more education, which may even lead to better job opportunities, and more importantly, you can use that knowledge to support people who cannot help themselves. We humans have a duty to help anyone we can, even if the help is small. Sometimes people will not ask for assistance, but that does not mean they do not need it—you can still offer support when you see someone struggling.

Of course, some people may disagree with this view. They might be focused only on their own needs, or they may feel they have already reached a good enough place in life and do not need to put in more effort. They believe they have already mastered every problem and situation they will face, and that there is nothing left for them to learn. But they are mistaken. Humans can always learn new things, and we should always strive to be better—better people, better parents, better children, and so on. The key is to never settle for "good enough" when you can do more.

We need to learn not to stay in our cozy, familiar routines. Try to improve just a little bit every day, or pick up a new skill. Focus on helping yourself first, but also reach out to others when they need support—or when you need it, too. Talking to people and learning from them will never hurt you.

As the writer Ralph Waldo Emerson once said, "Unless you try to do something beyond what you have already mastered, you will never grow." This is absolutely true. We should all work to become better people, and grow into someone that others can look up to.

Have you ever spotted a lost item on the ground, picked it up, and acted like it was yours? That counts as a lie, and it’s a really harmful habit. You never know if the cash or toy you found belongs to someone who will come back searching for it — only to find it gone, because someone else walked off with something they spent their own money on.

When I was younger, I often saw people drop their belongings. Every time that happened, I’d either pick the item up and return it directly, or flag the person down to let them know they’d left something behind.

Most people’s first instinct when they find something lying around is to keep it, but that’s not a smart move. You have no idea who the item belongs to or where it came from, and taking something that isn’t yours is no different from stealing.

A common piece of advice is to leave lost items exactly where you found them, since the owner will almost always come back to look for their things. No one leaves their belongings somewhere on purpose and then walks away without a second thought.

I know schools often teach this rule, because when I was in elementary school, signs were posted all over the building reminding us to leave found items where they were and never take things that don’t belong to us. Most kids followed this guidance, but some didn’t care — and that’s not acceptable, especially when they don’t even need the item, they just want it.

There’s a big difference between needing something and just wanting it. If you truly need an item, it’s something essential that’s hard to replace — but even then, you can usually buy a replacement at a nearby store. Wanting something, on the other hand, means you don’t actually require it. You might take it to show off to friends, to play with for a little while, or just because you feel like it, even though you’re not facing any hardship and could easily buy the item yourself if you really wanted to.

Never take items you find.

Always return things to people who drop them.

Think about the impact of your actions.

Don’t give in to peer pressure.

Be helpful to others.

Treat people with kindness.

This lesson matters more than ever today, because many people ignore these rules and just take whatever they find. A lot of parents don’t teach their kids right from wrong anymore, so it falls to schools to step in and educate young children about proper behavior.

You might wonder why you should always return dropped items. Think about how you’d feel if you lost your favorite toy — something you saved up to buy and loved playing with — only to have someone else pick it up and keep it. You’d probably feel furious, sad, and hurt. That toy is gone forever, because the person who took it didn’t care about you, didn’t need the toy themselves, and only took it because no one else was around to stop them.

Now imagine the opposite: you drop that same favorite toy, and someone sees it, runs after you, and hands it back. You’d feel happy, relieved, and grateful. That person didn’t want to keep the toy for themselves, or even think about taking it — they just wanted to do the right thing. They knew they weren’t the owner, and that you were standing right there. You might not have even realized you dropped the toy until later, when you went to use it.

I learned this lesson the hard way a few years ago, when I lost my iPad. Someone saw it, picked it up, and kept it — and they didn’t care at all. I never even noticed who took it, because I was distracted and didn’t realize what was happening. When I finally noticed my iPad was gone, I was devastated. I had to use my mom’s phone until my dad could buy me a new one.

This is exactly why teaching kids this lesson is so important. Taking things that don’t belong to you is never a good idea, and you don’t need to do it. A lot of people don’t care about this rule until it happens to them — then they wonder why they’re the one who lost something. If you take an item someone else lost, don’t be surprised when someone else does the same thing to you. They’ll take your lost item and keep it, and you’ll probably never get it back.

A lot of lost items are extremely expensive, like smartphones. People rely on their phones constantly, and get furious if they even crack the screen, since a damaged screen can make the device glitch. If someone loses their phone entirely, they’ll be even angrier. Modern smartphones cost over $1,000, sometimes much more. If someone loses their phone and finds out another person took it, they’ll be devastated. They might search everywhere, do anything to get it back, because phones are essential. People use them to call for rides, avoid getting stranded, or reach emergency services if they’re in trouble.

If someone stole my phone, I’d be furious and heartbroken. A lost or stolen phone is incredibly expensive and not easy to replace — a new smartphone can cost as much as a used car you’d find for sale online.

Is it possible to stay completely true to yourself in every situation and still achieve the greatest successes the world has to offer?

I am completely convinced that if you stay authentic to who you are at all times, you can reach incredible heights, and your daily life will feel much easier too. When you have constant faith in your own abilities, nothing in this world is beyond your reach. As the saying goes, "the heavens are the limit"—you can achieve anything you set your mind to. Why is this the case? Because the power to succeed lies within you, and most importantly, you have faith. There is a well-known proverb that says "faith can move mountains," and it is absolutely true: if you truly believe in yourself, no obstacle will seem too big to overcome.

Take Martin Luther King Jr. as an example. He had a famous dream that everyone would look the same color, with no differences based on skin tone. Revamping the school cafeteria’s lunch menu is a very poor choice, as many students will refuse to eat the new options, some may suffer allergic reactions that put their health at risk, and tons of uneaten food will be tossed out, making the school waste money on trying to please students.

These days, young people are extremely fussy about what they eat. Most students inspect their meals closely to make sure everything looks exactly right. If a dish has a strange smell or looks unappealing, they’ll either throw it in the trash or skip eating entirely and wait until they get home to have a meal. I, Generic_Name, am super picky—if I’m going to eat something, I want it to look perfectly prepared.

Schools should stick to their current lunch menus because many students have food allergies that staff may not know about. Kids often feel embarrassed about their allergies, thinking they’re something odd or unusual, even though having them is totally normal. Most students are reluctant to share their allergy details with others, fearing they’ll be teased by their classmates. That’s why changing menus is risky—schools simply don’t have full, accurate information about every student’s dietary needs.

While many schools have enough budget to pay for various student resources, administrators often push to update lunch menus hoping to boost how happy students are with their meals. But they fail to account for just how many picky eaters there are—most of these students won’t touch the new food, and it all ends up in the trash. This is a huge waste of school funds, and if students don’t even appreciate the new options, that money would be better spent on other programs or items that kids actually want.

Ultimately, keeping the lunch menu exactly as it is is the best choice. Changing it does not deliver the results schools hope for: it wastes money, leaves students hungry when they refuse to eat the new food, and puts allergic kids at risk. If schools just leave the menu unchanged, they’ll save money, keep students content, and make sure no one gets sick from an unexpected allergic reaction.

Have you ever wondered why some students graduate high school at a much younger age than their peers? While some might claim that graduating in three years is a bad idea, I believe it is actually a smart choice. It helps young people become more mature and ready for the real world, and teaches them to take full responsibility for their own lives.

First, graduating in three years pushes young people to become more mature and ready for adult life. Most teenagers today don’t understand how the real world works. For example, many teens drink and drive, getting into accidents that hurt themselves and others, but they don’t think about the consequences. Their parents often bail them out of trouble, so they don’t care if they harm someone. All they know is that someone will always take care of them. If teens graduate in three years, they have to face real-world situations sooner, which teaches them what actions are right and wrong. Another common issue is that parents take full responsibility for their teens: they pay for car insurance, and if their child breaks the law, they stand up for them, insisting their kid is innocent even when they’re wrong. This makes teens believe the world works this way, so they never learn from their mistakes. Graduating in three years helps them realize they have to answer for their own choices, no matter what.

Second, graduating early teaches young people to take full responsibility for their own lives. They have to pay for things like rent, electricity, and phone bills on their own. For instance, my mom still pays my phone bill, so I never really think about where the money comes from — I just know the bill gets paid. If teens have to cover their own bills, they become more careful not to let costs rise. I used to waste a lot of electricity and water, but since my mom is the one paying those bills, I didn’t realize how much my usage was costing. Teens who don’t have to handle these expenses never learn to be mindful of how much they use.

Some people might argue that graduating in three years is a bad idea. They say you’ll miss out on typical teenage experiences, won’t have time to have fun, and will feel too stressed to enjoy the moment. They believe you should make the most of your teenage years instead of rushing into adulthood.

All in all, graduating in three years is a good choice. It helps you grow more mature for the real world, and learn to take full responsibility for yourself. You’ll understand what adult life really looks like, instead of being shielded from it by others.

I strongly believe that true self-esteem grows out of personal achievement. When students put in consistent hard work, they earn more accomplishments over time. Each time they win an award or reach a milestone, they feel proud of their efforts, which helps form genuine self-esteem that lasts.

Many students work incredibly hard: they turn in all assignments on time, balance part-time jobs after class, yet still struggle to develop real self-esteem. For these students, the missing piece is self-confidence. After all, it is impossible to build lasting self-esteem without first feeling confident in yourself.

There is also another group of students: they show up to school, have no after-school or weekend commitments, and already feel confident in themselves, but they still have no idea how to build genuine self-esteem.

This is why students should always put their best effort into earning achievements. Reaching these goals gives them the motivation they need to develop stronger self-esteem.

Self-esteem is something students can build entirely on their own, as long as they put in hard work, show up to school on time, and use tools like checklists or calendars to plan out their tasks in order of priority.

These days, far too many students are not putting in enough effort. I cannot tell if this is because technology has made them lazy, or if they simply lack the drive to try, but either way, they are not working toward any meaningful achievements at school.

It is frustrating to see so many students waste their potential. If they would just take out their textbooks and study for at least two hours every evening, they would earn far more achievements at school, which would help them reach all their personal goals.

To build true self-esteem, students need to focus on earning achievements first, then develop self-confidence. Only after doing both can they become the best version of themselves.

Teachers also play an important part in this process. After all, most students spend more waking hours with their teachers during the week than they do with their own parents.

This does not mean teachers need to sit down and have deep conversations about self-esteem or confidence with every student. That should only happen if a student is curious enough to ask their teachers or classmates how to become a confident person who has already built strong self-esteem.

At the very least, teachers should point students toward the right path to earn achievements and reach their goals. This small step is often enough: once students start thinking about how to earn achievements, they will usually begin working on their own confidence and self-esteem on their own.

I have personal experience with this. When I moved to the United States in 2017, I did not speak a word of English and had no friends at my new school. Anyone who has been in that position knows how difficult it is to attend classes when you cannot talk to anyone, and you have no social circle. On top of that, I was an extremely shy person.

Whenever another student tried to start a conversation with me, my face would turn bright red and I would start blushing uncontrollably. This all stemmed from a complete lack of self-confidence.

Since then, I have worked as hard as I can to learn the language and make friends at school, so I can collaborate with them on work or hang out in my free time.

Now, I can speak, write, and read English fluently. I am far more confident than I used to be, I have become the best version of myself, I have a large group of friends, and I actually look forward to going to school every day.

To sum up, self-confidence and hard work toward achievements act like a key that unlocks self-esteem, which always grows out of personal success.

Students should stay focused on their schoolwork, or whatever else they are studying, so they can earn achievements that will help them build self-esteem.

Parents should also encourage their children to build self-esteem, just as students need to push themselves to do the same, so that they can grow into confident, self-assured people.

US President Thomas Jefferson once wrote, “It is wonderful how much may be done if we are doing.” This simple line means that steady, regular effort—whether we are working to improve our own lives or to help our communities—can lead to far more progress than we might expect. This makes us wonder: do we achieve more when we stay constantly active, or does taking time to do nothing also have value? Some people argue that inactivity is useful, as rest gives us the energy to grow stronger and keep working later. Others believe that staying busy is better, since consistent hard work helps us reach our personal goals and lets us contribute productively to society.

Every day, millions of people wake up and put their full effort into their work, trying to do their best. But what about those who do not have formal jobs? Even if you cannot find paid work, you can still contribute to society or your own personal growth. You might volunteer, help neighbors, or take on community projects—the key is to stay active. It is important to note that everyone needs rest, but if you spend too much time idle, you will struggle to reach your dreams and long-term goals.

Staying active is always a good thing when you are focused on positive, meaningful tasks. Working hard and feeling passionate about what you do gives purpose to every effort. Every person who works has a reason for doing so: some need to cover expenses, others want to support their families, and some simply love their work or the sense of achievement it brings. We all work toward something, and that drive keeps us going. My mom always tells me that if you want something, you have to chase it and make it happen. We all deserve a good, stable future, which is why it is so important to never stop taking action. This is exactly why staying busy with purpose is far better than doing nothing at all.

We also have to consider society’s expectations. In the real world, you have to stay active, whether or not you have a grand dream, because you need money to buy food, pay rent, cover bills and taxes, and meet all your basic needs. That means having a job, of course, but it also means looking for other ways to stay productive. As mentioned before, helping others is a great way to stay active, and it helps you grow as a person too. Even if a task is unpaid, if you love what you do, or if you simply want to be a useful, productive member of society, you will find value in doing good work.

Staying active matters for all of humanity, as it is what keeps our world running and growing. Our dreams and goals are what push us to take action every day. Take a moment to think: are you a productive person, or do you lean toward inactivity? That choice might change how you see your life. To sum up, Thomas Jefferson’s quote encourages us to reflect on what we are doing now, and what we should be doing with our lives. Taking a break is fine, but never lose sight of the goals and dreams you want to turn into reality.

Many people today believe that hard work is the only path to success, and that a positive attitude does not matter. However, this is not true—having a positive outlook is actually a key factor in achieving your goals. A positive mindset helps you make progress in places like the workplace, schools, colleges, and even when running your own business. As we go through life, we learn many important lessons, and one of the most useful is to stay positive no matter what hardships we face.

Employers across all industries actively seek out staff with a positive attitude, and there is a clear reason for this. They want team members who will contribute to the company’s growth and success. Workers who approach their jobs with optimism tend to be far more productive, which ultimately helps the entire organization reach its goals.

A positive attitude is also critical for succeeding in school and college. Students who view their studies with optimism are much more likely to achieve long-term success in life. Take, for example, learners with a negative outlook: they are far less likely to do well in school, since they tend to give up as soon as they encounter a challenge. By comparison, students who stay positive keep pushing through difficulties, which helps them reach their academic goals.

This same logic applies to people running their own businesses. Successful business owners share a key difference from those who struggle: when they hit hard times, they stay positive and work to solve the problems they face, which eventually leads to success. Those who are not successful, on the other hand, usually give up when things get tough and develop a negative attitude that holds them back.

Many people still argue that hard work is the only key to success, but that is not the whole truth. A positive attitude is just as vital, and it offers many benefits—including helping you achieve your goals in life, as we have seen. I firmly believe that having a positive outlook is a key part of succeeding in life.

I agree with Ralph Waldo Emerson’s view that earning a master’s degree helps people progress further in their careers. People who hold this qualification tend to perform better in their field, access more job opportunities, and secure higher-ranking roles than those without a master’s.

Of course, not everyone shares this opinion. Some argue that people without a master’s sometimes deliver better work than those who hold the qualification.

First, people with a master’s degree usually perform better at tasks related to their field, since they have spent years studying and practicing the required skills. For example, a chef with a master’s in culinary arts only needs to memorize new recipes, while someone without the degree has to learn about ingredients, tools, and how to use kitchen equipment from scratch.

Second, holding a master’s opens up more career opportunities, as the degree acts as proof that you are fully prepared for the role. Many companies require candidates to hold a master’s for certain jobs or senior positions. For instance, if you want to work as a restaurant manager, most establishments will ask for a relevant master’s degree, and these roles also come with higher pay.

Third, master’s holders are more likely to land higher-level positions than people without the qualification, as the degree demonstrates your expertise and experience. For example, if a restaurant is hiring for kitchen staff, a manager, and dishwashers, a candidate with a master’s will probably be given the manager role. Someone without the degree is far more likely to be assigned to wash dishes, and they would need to work much harder and wait longer to be considered for a management position.

To sum up, people with a master’s degree work more effectively in their field, access better job opportunities, and qualify for higher positions than those without this qualification. For this reason, I fully agree with Emerson’s statement that it is impossible to grow professionally without a master’s degree.

Having a positive attitude is one of the most valuable traits a person can have. Without it, people often treat others poorly, making those around them feel uneasy. I fully agree with this, as a positive outlook helps secure employment, navigate daily life, and build a happy home environment.

First, I work in a restaurant and keep a friendly, upbeat attitude with every customer. I’ve seen how damaging negativity can be: a manager there always has a sour, unhelpful attitude, which is not the right way to behave at work. A positive attitude makes it easier to keep a job and work well. I work more efficiently when I stay upbeat, and I think this mindset often comes from our parents, who teach us to be positive from a young age.

Second, I have friends who are very negative, which can be draining. We should always strive to stay positive, even when things get tough. Some people claim a negative attitude is useful, but that is not true—negativity leads to bad decisions and pushes people away. My mom and grandma have always told me not to be negative, which is why I stay positive in all situations.

Third, a positive attitude benefits everyone. Happy people naturally project positivity, and anyone can learn this mindset. People without it often struggle to find work, as most employers want upbeat, reliable staff. A girl once applied to my workplace and came for a training day with my boss, but she showed no positivity during the session, so she was not hired. This proves positive attitude is essential for almost any job.

In conclusion, anyone wanting a successful career must learn to stay positive. If you tend to be negative, work to change this habit, as negativity holds you back in work and other parts of life. We should all stay positive, as our attitude shapes how we treat others. No one wants to make people sad with a bad attitude, so choosing to be positive is always better. Make a habit of staying upbeat, and it will improve your life.

As Thomas Jefferson noted, "Determine never to be idle… it is wonderful how much may be done if we are always doing." While staying busy with meaningful pursuits like advancing your career or volunteering can boost your wellbeing, spending too much time idle often leads to serious health issues.

This raises an important question: do we achieve more when we focus on things we care about, or can laziness and inactivity also help us reach our goals?

In reality, inactivity brings no advantages. It harms your physical health, leaves you unmotivated, and gives your life no clear direction. Avoiding hard work and activity often leads to a life that feels unfulfilled and unsuccessful. While some people prefer to stay home all day, skip school, avoid getting a job, and ignore their responsibilities, this lifestyle puts them at risk of developing serious health problems. Of course, some disagree, but these truths hold for most. Isolating yourself from the rest of the world is also damaging and deeply unhealthy.

On the other hand, staying active has clear value. It gives your life meaning, and brings plenty of benefits: better physical health, progress toward career and academic goals, and chances to support the people around you. Getting a job is one example of active living. Setting aside time each day to work toward your interests is always a smart choice. Whether you are learning new skills at school or university, every step you take toward your goals improves your life.

Joining in with activities and staying busy will always make your life better. To return to Jefferson’s words: "Determine never to be idle… it is wonderful how much may be done if we are always doing."

Of course, everyone has their own views on activity and idleness, and no two people are exactly alike. But the core benefits of staying busy are clear for most.

There is an ongoing debate about whether schools should force all students to take art classes, or if they should instead offer a range of elective courses for students to choose from. Think about how rewarding it feels to do work that brings you joy, that plays to your strengths, and helps you figure out what you are truly capable of achieving. Many people argue that every student should be required to take elective classes, as this approach helps young people discover their interests, develop their talents, and access new opportunities — all of which will benefit them greatly later in life.

It is absolutely vital that students get to pick the electives that interest them most. If a student is assigned a class they have no desire to take, they are likely to feel uninterested in attending, and many will start skipping sessions entirely. Skipping class leads to poor grades, which in turn makes students feel frustrated and unmotivated. When they lose motivation, they may give up on the class altogether, meaning they earn no credits. Since students need a certain number of credits to graduate high school, failing to earn them means they cannot move on to college, which limits their ability to get well-paying jobs. Companies are unlikely to hire someone without a college degree, and long-term unemployment can even lead to homelessness, which is an incredibly difficult situation to escape. This is exactly why letting students choose their own electives is so critical.

Most people agree that every individual has their own unique set of strengths. Electives give students the chance to find these skills by letting them take classes they excel in. When a student is good at a subject, they will actually look forward to attending class, which leads to better grades and a desire to learn even more. Earning credits for these classes is also a key benefit. Having strong skills opens up many opportunities later in life, as employers are always eager to hire people with diverse talents. For instance, a student who shines in drama class might be hired as an actress, gain fame, star in their own movies, and earn a high income. It is also worth noting that students are not limited to just one skill — developing multiple talents and gaining varied experience will only help them more in the long run. This is another major reason why helping students identify their skills through electives is so valuable.

The future is a top priority for most students. Those who take electives they are passionate about can use these classes to build a solid foundation for life after high school and college, when adult responsibilities begin and life changes significantly. Developing relevant skills makes the future far less daunting, as even when tough times come, they have the tools to get through them. This period is also when students start chasing their dreams: the skills they gain from electives help them build a better future, as they know exactly what they are working toward and what to expect. Most will even find their true calling and end up in a career they genuinely love.

Of course, some people argue against requiring electives altogether. They claim that many students lack the motivation to take these classes seriously, do not want to participate, and treat elective courses as a waste of time rather than a real learning opportunity.

There is ongoing debate about the pros and cons of switching from the traditional five-day school week to a four-day schedule, with all regular school activities moved to just four days instead of five. Moving to a four-day school week is an option that should be adopted not just by some businesses for their workers, but by all high schools and colleges too, once people understand the reasons behind it.

Switching would mean losing 10 hours of class time per week, but those lost hours can easily be made up by adding two extra hours to each of the four school days. This would lengthen each class period, giving students more time to focus on lessons, finish assignments and projects set by teachers. The extra time each day also lets students spend more time with friends and teachers, so they can get extra support if they are struggling with a subject.

We could also use the extra two hours added to each school day for activities like library time, which is perfect for students who love reading, or for extra sports practice and other after-school hobbies.

The day off school each week can be used for doctor’s appointments or other health-related needs. Right now, many students skip class by having their parents write notes saying they have appointments, which disrupts their learning. Scheduling these appointments on the non-school day would cut down on the number of classes students miss.

We should also think about teachers who are parents themselves. They would get an extra day to spend time with their children and do regular family activities, which is a big benefit for them.

We also need to consider high school seniors, who are going through a tough time deciding their future. They need extra time to research university options, apply for higher education, and even look for weekend jobs. Freshmen, who just moved up from middle school, also benefit: they get extra time to adjust to high school routines and try out new extracurricular activities that are different from what they did before.

The free day, which could be Monday or Friday depending on the school’s choice, is also perfect for community service. With parental permission and adult supervision, students who want to participate can help clean up streets and rivers, or do other community service work. Schools could also partner with big companies to create programs that help students find jobs on this free day, or part-time work on weekends.

To be clear: this schedule means four full days of school, with no short days spread across five. Students get three full days off each week. They can use this extra time to hang out with family and friends, do whatever they and their parents want. Depending on whether the school picks Monday or Friday as the off day, students don’t have to wake up early that morning. They can use the time to rest and get all their responsibilities done.

One group this might not seem convenient for at first are students with part-time jobs. Adding two hours to each school day cuts into the time they have for work. But students in this situation can use their off school day to work full-time shifts, meaning they get three full days of work each week instead.

It is also true that juggling two different activities a day, like going to school and then heading straight to work, is tiring and leaves no time to rest. But with a four-day school week, even with the extra two hours each day, students have time after school to rest, finish homework and projects. They can use the three off days for whatever work suits them.

Even though there are some disadvantages, we have solutions for every common complaint about this plan. For more than 90% of students, the benefits far outweigh the downsides.

After going over all the benefits, potential downsides and solutions for this four-day school week plan, I firmly believe that all students should have three days off each week and attend school for just four days. How each student uses their free day might look different: some will stay home, follow family routines, help with household chores, work, or study. If we all support this plan, we can join forces to fight for this new right for high school and college students. Together, we have the power to make this change a reality.

It is entirely possible to gain knowledge and skills without stumbling through personal errors. Instead of figuring things out on their own, people ought to turn to experts and authority figures for advice on major life matters, rather than making independent choices. This approach brings three key benefits: it helps people learn more effectively, ensures everyone has a trusted adviser, and stops the world from falling into the chaos it faces today.

First, following expert advice leads to far more effective learning. When people ask specialists for help, they avoid countless unnecessary errors that would otherwise slow their progress, making their lives smoother overall. Take someone who consults experts regularly: they are far more likely to access better opportunities than those who go it alone. Consider a student struggling with a math lesson, for instance. If they approach their math teacher or another qualified math expert for clarification, the concept will be explained clearly, and they will grasp it quickly. In contrast, a student who refuses to ask for help will almost certainly fail the class. The same applies to new employees: starting a job is much easier when a supervisor or experienced colleague walks you through your responsibilities. Without that guidance, a new hire is bound to make repeated mistakes that could have been avoided. Clearly, those who listen to expert advice pick up new skills and knowledge far more successfully.

Second, having a trusted adviser is essential for everyone. Everyone faces challenges, but not everyone has someone to turn to for direction. I remember a new student who joined my school last year: he was unfamiliar with the school’s rules, so he broke a major policy and got into serious trouble. If an older student or staff member had explained the rules to him beforehand, he would have avoided that issue entirely. Too many teenagers act on impulse because they lack a guiding figure in their lives, and the result is that these young people end up in constant trouble. On the flip side, teens who receive guidance from a trusted expert or authority figure tend to succeed in whatever they try. It is clear that everyone needs someone to point them in the right direction, so they can avoid making avoidable errors.

Third, widespread expert guidance would prevent the world from slipping into the ruin it is in today. If every person had access to reliable advice, the planet would be a far safer place for everyone. For example, many countries are currently in crisis because their leaders do not know how to run a nation properly. If qualified experts took charge of these governments, citizens would no longer face danger. Similarly, many teenagers live independently without any adults to teach them right from wrong, so they often engage in harmful behavior without even realizing it is wrong. As mentioned before, if every single person had an expert to guide them, the world would not be in the state it is today—instead, there would be peace everywhere.

To sum up, if everyone had access to an expert guide throughout their life, the world as a whole would be a far better place. People would make wiser choices in all areas of their lives, and no one would face unnecessary danger. Young people and children would have brighter futures across the globe, and the world would be far more peaceful, with everyone learning more effectively. Whenever someone is unsure about a problem, they can simply consult an expert who will steer them in the right direction. Ultimately, life would be simpler and more pleasant if everyone reached out to experts when facing challenges, so no one would make a huge mistake.

Across the globe, a growing number of companies and educational institutions have switched to four-day work or study weeks to reduce waste of resources and energy. While some argue my school should not follow this model—and should avoid adding two extra hours to each school day to offset the lost day—because they claim we never waste resources or energy unnecessarily, I believe we should adopt a four-day week with extended daily hours. This change would let us protect the environment and manage our energy use more effectively.

People who oppose this plan have valid points, of course. Their main argument is that our school does not waste resources or energy unnecessarily: we use these things to support our studies and give students better learning opportunities. They also insist that switching to a four-day week would make no meaningful difference.

However, adopting a four-day week with longer school days would first help us build a healthier environment. A recent article published in my local county reports that our school’s resource consumption has risen by 70% in recent years. It adds that the overuse of resources has led to far more trees being cut down across the county, which is damaging the local environment. This has given both our school and the wider county a bad reputation, since we do not recycle or reuse materials properly.

Another key benefit is better energy management. Our school has the highest number of students in the entire county, and as enrollment has grown, so has our use of computers, smart boards, and other tech devices. A website focused on energy conservation notes that 80% of the energy schools use goes to computers and similar technical equipment. Moving to a four-day week with extended daily hours would reduce how often we need to use these devices, making our school more efficient overall.

Many still argue against the four-day week and extended hours, claiming our school never wastes resources or energy. But as I have shown, this change would bring real benefits to our school and the community as a whole. Wouldn’t you agree? Think about it this way: if this same waste was happening in your own home, wouldn’t you cut back on energy use to lower your monthly utility bills? Think about it!

Philosopher Ralph Waldo Emerson once noted that the greatest achievement a person can have is staying true to who they are, even when the world around them pushes them to change. Today, the things we do, our attitude, and our achievements all show the world who we are. Across the globe, many people believe that going above and beyond what is expected of you is a sign of being humble. For instance, at work, in school, or in your local community, taking on tasks that are not officially your job is often seen as a kind and generous act that highlights your good character, and shows others that you are willing to stand out by doing more than what is required. I fully agree with Emerson’s view. When you stay true to yourself, people notice something unique about you. You become the kind of person others want to learn from. Your first attempts at new things might not be perfect, but you keep going, even when everyone around you expects you to act like everyone else. There are three key reasons why being yourself matters so much.

First, being yourself encourages others to follow your example. If you make a habit of going above and beyond, like helping someone even when it is not part of your official duties, people will notice. For example, if you are a student and you take time to explain a math problem to a classmate, even though that is the teacher’s job, your kindness will make an impression. Over time, many people will start to copy your behavior, because they see how much good it does.

Second, staying true to who you are makes you an inspiration to people in every part of your life. This could be at home, in your neighborhood, at school, at college, or even at your place of worship. For instance, if your neighbors see you mowing your lawn, keeping your home tidy, or helping other people in the area with small tasks, you become a role model for them. That is exactly how you achieve the goal of inspiring others through your actions.

Finally, your achievements when you are being yourself can shift how other people think. When others see the progress you make in your life by doing things your own way, they will start to wonder how you managed it. You can share your story with them to show that if you could do it, they can too. For example, families come in all shapes and sizes: some members work low-paying jobs, while others run their own businesses. If you are the kind of person who always supports your family, you will spread positive energy and hope to everyone around you.

To sum up, as Emerson said, we as humans often try to go above and beyond to achieve great things in life. More than half the world already acts this way, because most people recognize the benefits of helping others. Most importantly, the world responds positively to this message: when you always do a little extra, your greatest achievement can serve as an example to those around you. More than just an example, you can become a source of inspiration for countless people across the globe.

Many schools ask students to finish summer assignments to make sure they keep learning while school is out, but a key question is: should teachers pick these projects, or should students get to design their own?

I strongly believe students should create their own summer projects. Every student knows exactly which topics they struggled with during the school year, or which areas they want to improve. When students take charge of their own summer work, it gives them a chance to keep learning, and working on their own ideas and plans helps them build new skills. By the time they return to class in the fall, they will feel much more prepared. As an ESL student myself, I always make my own summer projects to avoid forgetting the material I worked hard to learn over the previous school year. In other words, students really benefit from working on projects they choose during their break.

The first main reason for this is that students feel far more comfortable with projects they design themselves. Since they chose the topic and planned the work, they already understand exactly what the project involves, which makes it much easier for them to complete. If schools let students pick their own projects, they will feel less stressed and more willing to put in effort.

Another key reason is that student-designed projects help learners hold onto the knowledge they gained during the school year. If students keep working on projects they care about over the summer, they are far less likely to forget what they learned. Stopping all academic work over the break can make students feel lazy, and for groups like ESL learners, not practicing with self-chosen projects can lead to forgetting almost everything they studied.

Overall, I am fully convinced that students should design their own summer projects. This approach is better for learners in so many ways: they will not forget the material they mastered during the year, since they are still engaging with the content in a way that makes sense to them. Students can thrive without constant teacher direction over the summer, and they get to be more active and show off their unique skills. If they put in the effort, they can definitely succeed. There are countless benefits to letting students create their own summer projects.

Is it better to work in a team or tackle tasks on your own? There is no doubt that collaborating with others brings far more advantages. When you work with others, you can turn to teammates for support, and collective effort makes it much easier to achieve your goals. While some argue that solo work is the better choice, group collaboration leads to greater success: it is far simpler to seek advice when you get stuck, and this support helps you succeed both in your studies and later in life.

Supporters of working alone often claim it is the more effective approach. They say solo work gives you full control over your schedule, making it easier to plan your tasks and put in your best effort. Some also avoid group projects because they worry that lazy or careless teammates will drag down the quality of their work. However, this view is mistaken: working with a group actually boosts your chances of success far more than working alone ever could.

Many people far prefer team-based work, and for good reason. Having others to turn to for help is incredibly useful. For instance, many people struggle to plan out tasks like homework assignments or school projects on their own, but group work solves this problem, as you can easily get help from peers who might have better ideas for how to structure your work.

Another key benefit of group work is that it lets you build on other people’s strengths. When you collaborate, you can combine multiple good ideas into one strong plan, which leads to much better results than you could achieve on your own. If one teammate comes up with a great concept, the whole group can adapt it to improve their shared work.

Even people who normally prefer working alone can gain a lot from group collaboration. Shared work means that one person’s smart idea can help the entire team finish their tasks faster and more effectively. What’s more, you can swap drafts or plans with teammates, so they can review your work and point out areas where you could improve your efforts.

My special skill is drawing—something I really enjoy doing. Whenever I pick up a pencil, I love sketching natural scenes like the night sky with stars and the moon, dense forests, and rolling ocean waves. Drawing is a form of self-expression that lets people share all kinds of creative ideas. There are so many different art styles out there, but my top favorite is definitely drawing with pencils or pens.

When you draw, you have total creative freedom—you can make whatever you imagine, and if you mess up, it’s easy to correct the mistake. I also really love painting, another type of drawing, because it lets you put your emotions on the canvas. Whether you’re feeling sad, happy, angry, or upset, you can use colors and brushstrokes to show exactly how you feel. Art is one of my favorite talents because I can create anything I want, and people are often willing to pay huge amounts for drawings and paintings they love. They don’t care if a piece costs billions of dollars—if it’s beautiful, they’ll pay that price without hesitation.

A lot of people have a natural talent for art, but some are so hard on themselves that they think their work isn’t good enough, so they throw it in the trash. What they don’t realize is that plenty of other people would love their work and be happy to pay for it. Art can sell for massive amounts of money, but not everyone chooses to sell their work. Some keep pieces as keepsakes or to show off to their family. Sometimes they sell work to relatives, but they don’t charge millions or billions for these pieces, since they’re just for loved ones. Other people keep art with mistakes they didn’t fix or throw away, hoping a wealthy collector will buy it someday.

I think more artists should try selling their work, because they could earn a lot of money from their paintings and sketches. Art is really tough work that requires a lot of patience. You might make a mistake and feel like you have to start over completely, but most people don’t do that—instead, they turn that mistake into something beautiful. That’s the thing about art: even if something looks ugly at first, you can fix it up and make it look amazing.

Some people think art is boring, but that’s not true. If you love creating art, you’ll never find it dull—it brings you joy. Sometimes when you’re so excited to paint that you can’t hold back, you just start putting brush to canvas without worrying if it looks bad. You let your hands move on their own, because you’re too excited to plan out what the final piece will look like. I do this too sometimes—letting my body take over while I create—and it actually feels really good, leaving me happy and energized.

Many people get really stressed when their work doesn’t turn out the way they planned. I feel that way too sometimes, when my drawing doesn’t look as good as I wanted it to. But as I mentioned earlier, patience is key—art is not easy, it’s hard work. Over time, though, you get used to it. It’s still challenging, but not nearly as tough as it was when you started. I’m skilled at art, but I’m still learning, and it’s really difficult at times. I have to stay patient and keep practicing, because practicing is the best teacher.

Do students actually gain anything from taking classes remotely from home? I don’t think so—in fact, I’ve seen firsthand how this setup fails students, like a friend of mine who took online classes and ended up with no real progress. She never completed the work she was meant to do, using the flexible schedule as an excuse to run errands and handle personal tasks instead, and got zero value out of the experience. Overall, students do not benefit from home-based classes because they abuse the freedom, skip required work, and learn almost nothing.

First off, many students take advantage of remote learning’s flexibility to prioritize non-school activities. For example, they hand in assignments weeks past the deadline, claiming they had other urgent responsibilities to handle. Not every student who learns from home slacks off, of course, but those who do often push the limits further: they skip studying to go to parties, hang out with friends, or spend time with partners, all while ignoring their academic duties. They also constantly invent excuses for why they missed a deadline, never taking responsibility for their own lack of effort.

The bigger issue is that these students avoid assigned work entirely. When given a project or homework task, they often choose to be lazy, knowing there’s no teacher in the room to remind them to stay on track. They waste hours on socializing or hobbies instead of finishing the assignments that would actually help them build skills for the future. Most of the time, they understand the course material just fine—they just can’t be bothered to put in the effort, even when they know the work will benefit them later.

Worst of all, students rarely learn any meaningful content when taking classes from home. All they do is socialize, party, and hang out with friends or partners instead of engaging with their lessons. Instead of completing assigned tasks, they cheat: copying work from classmates or looking up answers online. Most see remote learning as a chance to take a break from school responsibilities, so they waste time playing around instead of taking their studies seriously. All that partying leaves no time for actual learning, so they absorb almost nothing from their courses.

To sum up, students do not benefit from attending classes from home. They abuse the flexible schedule to handle personal tasks instead of schoolwork, skip assigned work because there’s no one to hold them accountable, and learn next to nothing because they spend all their time socializing or cheating. Instead of studying, they party and hang out with friends or partners, leaving every assigned task unfinished.

Many long-held beliefs about students not putting in their best effort at work are actually wrong. These students hold the view that real achievement comes from strong self-esteem. I have a clear stance on this matter: we should focus our attention on what lies ahead. People vary greatly in their outlook. Some only focus on getting through each day, never considering their long-term future. They act as if life is just about getting by, not realizing there is more to life than just day-to-day survival. I believe students are justified in their thinking: achievement is never easy. We all earn accomplishments in life, and without those wins, life feels empty. In my view, truth is the most important thing of all. Truth reflects what actually happens, and when truth is absent, everything changes completely.

A key point from the prompt is that students emphasize the need for self-confidence, and that confidence is a powerful force in life. It is important to distinguish between two related terms: confident and confidence. Confident describes a person who feels or shows they are certain of their own abilities and choices. Confidence, on the other hand, refers to a firm trust in someone or something. For example, you might say, “I have every confidence in my ability to do this job.” Students have plenty of confidence, and they are often given strict orders to learn more: an order is a command delivered in a way that leaves no room for refusal. To learn is to gain knowledge or a new skill, and students believe that combining learning with work is the best approach.

Achievement refers to something completed successfully, usually through hard work or skill. It is both the act of finishing a task well and the proud feeling that comes with that success. Students do not lower their standards as they learn—lowering means reducing the amount or quality of something. They know life offers chances to build a better future and enjoy every moment. Even though hard work is necessary, it is also vital to cherish time with family, minute by minute, year by year. Life should not revolve only around a job. Everyone needs to take time to pause, reflect on their life, and look toward the future.

What exactly is the future? The future refers to a time that is further ahead, a point more distant in time. For example, a board of directors might say, “We need more time to consider this matter further.” You might also say, “I can’t remember anything further back than 1995” when referring to a greater distance in time, or use it for physical distance: “The town is further down the road.” In formal conversation, many people use “further” to describe distances, but it has other uses too, like “We need a further week to finish the project.” Do not let your profession be the only thing that enriches your life. A profession is a job that requires specialized training and education, often at a high level. Employment refers to work done specifically to earn money, and it is very hard to find stable employment right now. But do not shape your future around work alone.

I believe students put their best effort into building a career. A career is the series of jobs a person holds in a specific field, with increasing responsibility over time. I have a friend who had a very distinguished career in medicine—she worked in the medical profession. It is important to tell the difference between a profession, a career, and a trade. A trade is a hands-on job that requires specialized training, often focused on manual work. Right now, students do not have full-time jobs yet, largely because they are seen as lacking work experience.

Many people focus only on the fact that students lack experience. Experience refers to events that happen to you, the feelings those events bring—for instance, “It was the first time I had ever experienced failure.” Being experienced means having the exact knowledge or skill needed for a task. The students have shown me something important: their sincerity is a key strength. Sincerity is the quality of being honest and genuine, meaning exactly what you say without pretending. When someone acts sincerely, they show their true feelings and beliefs clearly. The students make a valid point here.

Students deserve praise, which means expressing admiration for their efforts. They also take precautions in their work: a precaution is an action taken now to prevent future danger or problems. For example, “We took the precaution of locking our valuables in a safe” or “These are standard precautions against fire.” Students do not just implore others for help when situations get difficult—implore means to beg someone urgently when you need something very badly.

They understand the importance of work: “The decision was of great importance to the future of the business.” They know this job matters, but they also value tolerance—the ability to accept opinions, behaviors, or people different from yourself. The opposite is intolerance, which means refusing to accept differences, or the ability to endure pain or difficult conditions. Students work together and blend their strengths to improve themselves.

Other people often lack compassion and are not considerate toward students. “They had considerable difficulty getting the students to agree”—considerable means large or significant in amount. Students form their own opinions on work, and they prioritize truth above all. They consider matters carefully before making choices: to consider something means to think about it in a specific way, weighing all factors. They avoid taking risks that are too great, and they show respect to others. They are not angry about their lack of job experience. Instead, they are intelligent and secure, free from insecurity. I admire that they are not insecure—they have a strong sense of security in who they are.
