Why is it important for people to trust their own gut feelings and original thoughts? In my view, everyone should take charge of their own choices, since relying on personal instincts and unique ideas is key. Above all, you have to have faith in yourself—if you don’t believe in your own abilities, no one else will either.

First of all, making your own decisions starts with trusting your own judgement. Since your ideas come from your own mind, not borrowed from others, you don’t need to second-guess yourself as much. If you’re coming up with your own plans, there’s no need to ask others for input. For instance, if you’re working on a writing task, you can create original content instead of copying someone else’s work or taking information from the internet.

Another key reason to follow your instincts is that you won’t have to rely on others when problems arise. If you trust your gut, you don’t need to wait around for someone else to solve issues for you, and you won’t feel the need to constantly ask for outside guidance. This is because you already have confidence in your own abilities.

Beyond this, self-belief is essential because if you don’t have faith in yourself, others won’t either. Take a class presentation as an example: if you’re standing in front of your teacher and you’re convinced you’ll mess up, your teacher is likely to doubt your abilities too. This can hurt your final grade, since you’ll spend the whole presentation pausing to ask your teacher if you’re saying things correctly or making mistakes.

To sum up, I believe people should always make their own decisions, but only after building confidence in themselves first—you can ask for help later, but self-trust comes first. Remember, if you don’t believe in your own worth, no one else will either. Finally, I hope everyone learns to trust themselves above all else. If you only listen to other people’s opinions and ignore your own inner voice, you’re not recognising your own value.

Many schools now run programs that pair younger students with their older peers. People often wonder why these programs exist, or how the two groups can support one another. These initiatives actually benefit both age groups: younger students learn what responsibilities come with being an older student, and get a clear idea of what to expect when they grow into that role. At the same time, older students also pick up new perspectives from interacting with younger kids.

Older students are well placed to share lessons from their own past mistakes, since everyone makes different errors as they grow up. By talking about these experiences, they can guide younger peers to make better choices, and the two groups end up supporting each other in the process.

Younger students also get the chance to reflect on their own mistakes through these programs. Often, older participants will visit younger classes to offer support, helping kids learn from their errors and teaching them practical life lessons about making good choices.

Younger students rely on older peers much like older students depend on adults. Just as adults can step in to say "don't do that", older students can correct younger kids when they go off track, and the two groups can help each other with any problems or questions that come up. For example, some younger students struggle with English, and older peers can often explain things in a way that's easier to understand. It works both ways too: if an older student doesn't know something, they can ask a younger peer for help. There are all kinds of joint activities these programs organize, and older students can even step in to break up fights between younger kids, reminding them to make better choices. After all, everyone makes mistakes in life, and no one is perfect, so mutual support is key. The main difference between the two groups is that older students have more responsibilities than younger ones, though still fewer than adults. I remember my dad telling me that when he was young, he once needed help but didn't want to talk to an adult about it. He advised me that if I ever need guidance, I should ask an older peer to help me make good choices and learn from my mistakes. We can all support each other this way. Older students play a big role in helping younger kids understand the world: they know what is right and wrong, and working together helps build harmony between the two groups. Younger students can learn from the common mistakes their older peers once made. That said, a common issue is that some older students don't want to help younger ones.

There are all sorts of interactions between the two groups, and sometimes problems pop up. Older students might refuse to help younger ones, while younger kids might ignore advice from their older peers. It’s a similar pattern to how older students sometimes ignore adults or teachers: when someone tells you not to do something, you might be tempted to do it anyway, only to face consequences you didn't want later. That’s why we need older students to teach younger kids what is good and bad, just as older students need adults to guide them. Adults can’t hit kids to make them listen, of course—they can only explain what choices are harmful or helpful. The same goes for older student mentors: they should guide gently, not use force. The two groups need each other’s support, and can even look out for each other’s safety.

While critics often claim that learning from home hurts students, since they miss out on chances to work on group projects with peers, I believe remote classes actually benefit students far more: they feel more relaxed, and they are much safer too.

Opponents of remote learning often point to research to back up their claims. Roughly 200 published articles note that students taking online classes often produce lower-quality projects, since they cannot gather feedback and ideas from classmates. After all, a group of people can come up with far more creative, varied ideas than a single student working alone.

That said, there are clear benefits to remote learning, starting with comfort. A survey conducted at my school found that most students prefer online classes specifically because they can sit however they like, instead of following strict school seating rules. I completely agree with this – I enjoy being able to adjust my seating position whenever I want, which is not allowed in a traditional classroom.

Safety is another major advantage of learning from home. Recent years have seen over 100 school shootings across the country, proving that physical classrooms can be dangerous places. Gangs in schools are another serious risk: they can expose children to all sorts of harmful behaviors and negative influences that can damage their development.

From my perspective, remote learning also eases stress for parents, who no longer have to worry constantly about their children’s safety while they are at school.

As we can see, even though some say students would not benefit from home learning because they cannot stay connected with classmates, the truth is that attending classes remotely lets students feel comfortable and safe, which makes it a far better option.

The new policy to conserve energy by extending school hours should not be followed by students, because working ten hours a day will place an enormous amount of stress on them.

Many learners will be negatively impacted by this change, especially those who already hold after-school jobs. These students rely on their earnings to support their parents, so if they are forced to cut back their working hours, their income will drop, leaving them unable to contribute financially at home.

Beyond paid work, lots of students also look after younger siblings or handle household tasks after class, such as mopping floors, washing dishes, and preparing dinner. They also need time for their own hobbies, all of which makes daily life run more smoothly both at home and at school.

After-school hours are also when many students play sports like soccer, football, basketball, or tennis. Others simply want quiet time alone to read or go for a walk. These small joys are easy to lose if teachers vote to extend the school day. If teachers decide to extend the school day, students will still need to work the same total number of hours per week. The only difference is they will have to work two extra hours each day to reach the required 40 hours of work per week. Those two extra hours will be taken away from the activities they enjoy, which make their lives happier.

Think about why students work after school: many need that money to help their parents put food on the table. This is exactly what a lot of mothers did years ago. They found ways to support their own parents by taking on part-time work, using the earnings to buy food for their families. I always believe those mothers are heroes, sent by God to do everything they can to help their parents. It is incredible that students today already have the chance to go to school, because their own parents have sacrificed so much by working hard. Now, these students have the chance to build a better future for themselves.

Every student hopes to build a successful future for themselves. I believe that once young people finish their studies at school or university, they deserve the chance to work in roles that offer real growth opportunities. These positions let them put the skills they have learned into practice and show what they are capable of.

At the same time, I think graduates should give their full effort in these roles. Doing so helps them hold onto the knowledge they picked up during their studies, rather than forgetting it as soon as they leave the classroom. I also feel that younger students, such as those aged 14 or 15 who are not yet old enough for full-time work, should have the right to take on part-time jobs. No one should stop them from getting work experience early, as this helps them grow.

In my view, all students have the right to prove their abilities. This gives them fresh ideas, builds up their work experience, and helps them navigate life more confidently. Practicing their skills also makes them sharper and more capable, as they are pushing themselves to do their best. Beyond that, working early helps them become independent, and they will also come to appreciate all the effort their parents put into supporting their education.

Finally, I think students should be free to choose the career path that suits them best, or pick the option that will help them build a better future. That is my main view on this topic.

Is true success really just moving from one failure to the next? Winston Churchill, the former British Prime Minister, once claimed that "success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm." I disagree with this view of how failure fits into the journey toward success. When you chase a goal or a lifelong dream, you might face setbacks or achieve small wins along the way, but the key is to never quit. You have to keep pushing until you hit your target. While everyone experiences failure at some point, success comes from hard work and fighting for what you want, not from piling up mistakes. Above all, you must never let your enthusiasm fade—that passion for your goal is something no one should ever lose.

First, it is impossible to find someone who has never failed at least once in their entire life. Across the world, countless people have made mistakes, faced setbacks, or let themselves or others down. Common examples include struggling to land a job, getting poor grades in school, or falling short of a personal goal. No one is perfect, and everyone makes errors eventually. Failure is not limited to your own personal ambitions, either. You might fail your family or friends by lying to them or breaking promises, which counts as a failure too. That said, a tiny fraction of people—maybe just 1%—have rarely experienced failure. My cousin is one of these rare cases: she has never disappointed her parents, always earned top grades, and scored highly on all school tests. She graduated with a full scholarship and now studies at Virginia Tech University.

To reach your goals or turn your dreams into reality, you have to put in serious hard work. If you fail once or multiple times, don’t let yourself sink into sadness or depression—you are strong enough to handle setbacks. Life always offers new opportunities and second chances if you look for them. Never give up easily; fight for what you want and work toward your biggest dreams. No one ever promised that life would be simple, and the truth is that it is often difficult. If you want something, you have to earn it through effort. I know how discouraging it feels to fail at something, but you can always pick yourself back up. If one path doesn’t lead to success, make new plans—there are countless other options and opportunities out there. Don’t get stuck focusing only on a single goal. Explore other interests that appeal to you; you might find something you love even more.

Another key point is that people should never lose their enthusiasm. If you feel passionate about something, pursue it fully—don’t let anyone else take that drive away from you or handle it for you. Enthusiasm is a rare and valuable trait that is worth working hard to keep. Not everyone has this spark: they lack the deep interest, the warm passion, or the excitement for the things they want to do or achieve. You should be proud of yourself if you have enthusiasm for a goal. People without it do not care about their lives or futures; they just take whatever comes their way without putting their heart into it. They settle for what they get instead of chasing what they want. For example, when I was a child, I was always a top student with excellent grades. But when I moved to the US, I had to start over because I didn’t speak any English. To succeed in my new school, I had to work extremely hard to improve my English skills.

In conclusion, I stand by my disagreement with Churchill’s statement. Success does not have to mean moving from one failure to the next. You will definitely face setbacks along the way, but if you refuse to give up and put in the hard work, you can achieve your goals and fulfill your biggest dreams. Never lose the enthusiasm you have for your ambitions—the passion and interest you feel will keep you motivated when things get tough. Always work hard for what you want, and you will eventually succeed. Life is never easy, even for people with a lot of money.

When we make smart, well-considered choices, daily life feels far more enjoyable and less stressful. For instance, handling tasks properly from the start adds more excitement to our experiences, instead of creating avoidable problems later. The simplest way to keep life smooth and fun is to pause and think carefully before taking any action, rather than rushing into things.

Too often, we waste time on actions that do nothing to help our long-term goals. Take skipping school as an example: if I cut classes, my teacher will contact my parents, and I will get in trouble. Worse yet, missing school hurts my future prospects. It could stop me from reaching my goals, and even if I do find a decent job later, I might earn less than peers who finished school, or miss out on benefits they get as graduates.

Many people act without thinking first, which leads to bad decisions. I learned this the hard way when I lived in my home country. Back then, I made a huge mistake: I skipped class with friends to play soccer, without pausing to consider the consequences. I ended up failing the course, got terrible grades, and my parents were called to school. I got in big trouble, all because I didn't stop to think before acting. That experience taught me that we should always think carefully before making any choice.

It is easy to focus on short-term fun instead of thinking about how our actions will affect us years from now. My older brother is a good example of this. When he was in 9th grade at TCW, he spent most of his time hanging out with friends, and didn't take the SOL tests seriously at all. He didn't think they mattered much. But when he reached 12th grade, he had to pass the SOLs to graduate. He told me later, "Don't make the same mistake I did. I wasted so much time, and then I had to work hard to catch up."

I strongly believe we should always think carefully before making any decision. If we don't take time to weigh our options, we risk messing up our long-term goals and our future. Thinking carefully is key to succeeding in life. When more people pause to think before acting, we can even make positive changes to the world around us.

Online courses are a great support for students with packed schedules, but they also benefit anyone who simply wants to take the classes. For people with little free time, online learning is an excellent choice. Many busy learners struggle to balance cooking, homework, and commuting to campus, especially if they need to work to earn money. These competing demands often feel like barriers that make it hard to attend in-person school. When they take classes online, they can plan a more flexible schedule, eat at home, finish assignments, and still have time for other household tasks. For instance, parents with young babies can care for their children while attending class from their living room. Likewise, people with full-time jobs can go to work as usual, then log in to their online lessons during their free time. Another key advantage is for students who live far from their school and do not have access to a car or public transport. For these learners, taking classes online from the comfort of home is far more convenient than traveling long distances. Online learning also works for students already enrolled in traditional schools who want to keep studying over the summer break. They can easily sign up for online courses or video conference-based classes instead of taking a full break from learning. In my view, both fully online classes and video conferencing options help a wide range of students. Whether someone has a very busy schedule or just has a personal interest in the course material, they can benefit from taking these classes.

How does technology impact our daily lives and face-to-face connections? I agree it is not the best human invention, as it harms our lives and relationships. Many say tech is bad because it keeps families apart, or they just dislike it. These people are right—tech disrupts how we live and interact. Here are key ways it hurts: phone and game addiction, compulsive online shopping, and less meaningful communication with others.

First, people get hooked on phones or games, which is bad because it makes them self-centered. For example, if someone needs help, a screen-obsessed person might ignore them, choosing their device over assisting. This applies to adults and children alike. We should be kinder and pay more attention to people around us, not just our screens.

Second, online shopping is popular with women, and it can help them gain independence by buying their own clothes. But some develop a serious addiction. For instance, while many shop online conveniently, others buy far more clothes than they need, struggling with compulsive shopping.

Third, people who rarely communicate with others lack inspiration for their lives and futures. If someone never does anything motivating or helpful, they blend into the crowd with no clear goals. They become just another person, not someone with a unique path.

In conclusion, we need to be a positive influence for tech-addicted people, as this habit harms their lives and futures. This is why I agree technology is not the greatest invention humans have made.

The famous physicist Albert Einstein once stated that 'imagination is more important than knowledge,' and I fully stand by this claim. Imagination brings us joy, lets us support others, and even helps us land dream careers—all points I’ll explain below.

First, using your imagination can boost your own happiness. When you picture things you love, even if they’re impossible in real life, it brings a sense of joy. For instance, you might dream of soaring through the sky like a bird, even though humans can’t fly naturally. You can imagine how that freedom would feel, whether it’s refreshing, cozy, or tiring. You can also picture what you’ll look like at 100 years old, playing with details in your mind. These little mental escapes lift your mood easily.

Next, imagination can be a powerful tool to help others. Think of a young child crying in a shopping mall because onlookers are staring at her unusual outfit. Instead of ignoring her, you can use your creativity to comfort her. You might say, 'Don’t cry, sweetie—everyone is looking at you because your outfit makes you look like royalty! You’re a princess greeting her subjects, so you have to be kind and poised.' This small shift in perspective can often stop her tears immediately.

Many parents argue that imagination won’t help you find a good job, but I disagree. Take home design as an example: if you want to work as a home designer but lack creativity, you’ll end up making ugly, impractical spaces. You’ll likely get fired quickly and struggle to earn a living. On the flip side, a writer with a vivid imagination can create thirty-plus excellent books, earning far more than even a doctor in some cases. Imagination is the key to building a career you actually love.

To wrap up, I completely agree with Albert Einstein’s famous words. Imagination brings personal joy, helps us support the people around us, and opens doors to fulfilling, well-paying careers. I truly believe imagination is the most important thing in the world.

One useful skill I rely on is reading text aloud. This habit helps me grasp the content I’m reading far more easily. When I speak the words out loud, the information stays fixed in my memory, which makes it much simpler to explain the material later. It also comes in handy when I need to write an essay based on what I’ve read.

For me, reading aloud makes a huge difference because my comprehension improves significantly. There’s also a nice sense of control when I read out loud — I can track how smoothly I’m reading. I can tell if I’m reading at a steady pace or pausing awkwardly at every single word. If I come across a term I don’t recognize, saying it aloud often helps me make sense of its meaning.

Reading aloud also boosts my ability to retell stories or explain concepts clearly. I find I can give much more detailed, accurate explanations after reading out loud, since more specific details stick in my mind. Once I finish a reading session, I rarely forget what I’ve just covered. By contrast, when I read silently without speaking, I lose track of most of the information. I’ve noticed this benefit works for other people too — many others understand content better when they read it aloud.

This habit is especially helpful when I’m assigned an essay. Reading the source material aloud gives me plenty of ideas to include in my writing, and I can expand on the story or topic much more easily. By the time I sit down to draft my essay, I’m not anxious about what to write at all — the full content of the book or text is fresh in my mind. I also like reading aloud while I write essays, as it helps me check that my writing matches what the original text is saying.

In conclusion, I strongly recommend reading out loud. Doing this helps me fully understand the material I’m reading, makes essay writing far simpler, and ensures the content stays fixed in my memory long after I finish reading.

There are countless advantages to completing tasks as part of a team. Working in groups is preferable for a wide range of reasons: everyone can support one another, students produce higher-quality work together, and every group member gains new skills. Collaborating also helps students build friendships with peers they might not otherwise interact with, while boosting communication and generating far more ideas than solo work. Group work is especially useful for students who feel unsure where to start on an assignment. I believe teachers should assign more group tasks, as this allows students to support each other and produce better results. Working in a team is also valuable for life beyond school: it helps you succeed in future jobs, get along better with family, and complete tasks to a high standard.

Group work benefits students in several clear ways. First, having more people involved means more diverse, higher-quality ideas that help every member of the team. Many students feel stuck on assignments and do not know how to proceed, but a group member can step in to explain concepts, helping everyone understand how to complete the task well. Collaborating in a team is far more useful than working alone in many respects: communicating with peers makes it easier to grasp difficult material, which helps students produce good work, pass their classes, and avoid failing. Group work also introduces you to classmates you have never had the chance to speak to before. When a teacher forms a new team, you get to meet new people and expand your social circle.

Second, group work helps students develop useful skills, especially communication. Teammates can support each other with written work and improve how they speak to others. Strong communication is essential in most situations, as it lets you ask for help when you do not understand a task. All group members can practice working together daily to produce excellent results. Students who have a stronger grasp of the material can join groups to support peers who need extra help. This is especially valuable for students who struggle with the course content, or for those who face language barriers that make assignments difficult. Working with people you have never met before can also turn into lasting friendships. Group work benefits not just students, but the school as a whole: students understand lessons better and earn higher grades. The advantages extend beyond the classroom too: good teamwork skills help you get along with family members and avoid conflicts at home, and they prepare you to work well with colleagues in future jobs. Think of a soccer team: players help each other, share new strategies, and work together to win, which is exactly how group work functions. When a team has strong communication and positive relationships, members can support each other effectively. Being generous with your time and knowledge pays off, as others will help you when you need it. Overall, group work is far better than working alone. If you work by yourself and get stuck, there is no one to turn to for help. However, teachers sometimes prefer solo work to stop students from getting distracted by peers or copying each other’s work. While working alone can improve focus, it is not always the best option. I would love to see more teachers assign group tasks, as I do not think students prefer working alone. Teamwork is often easier and faster than solo work.

In conclusion, I firmly believe teachers should assign more group work to students. In my view, collaborating in teams is far more helpful than working alone. When people work together, they generate better ideas, complete higher-quality work, and incorporate more diverse opinions, which leads to excellent results. Strong communication and positive relationships are essential for effective teamwork. Students who understand the material well can support peers who need extra help, and group work gives everyone the chance to meet new people. I hope teachers continue forming groups so students can learn more than they would on their own. These teamwork skills are valuable for life: if you get a job where you have to work with colleagues but cannot collaborate effectively, you may even lose your position. Relying only on solo work can cause problems if you have not learned to work with others. Teamwork always brings more ideas and perspectives, leading to better work and supporting your future career and personal life. Some students dislike group work because they do not know their teammates, but I think if teachers assigned more collaborative tasks, students would grow to enjoy them and communicate more with peers. Personally, I prefer group work because when I am unsure how to proceed, my teammates help me complete tasks to a high standard, and we all share our unique ideas.

This backs up my conclusion: people never forget the first impression they take away from meeting someone. I haven’t seen those teammates for a year and a half, yet their initial view of me as a skilled soccer player has stuck completely. Time flies, but that first impression hasn’t faded at all.

Some people claim that first impressions can be altered, no matter if they are positive or negative. But they admit you have to work extremely hard to make that happen, and it will take a very long time.

All students put in effort during their time in school, proving they can keep pushing forward even without frequent compliments, even if progress takes a year or two to show. Constantly praising a student for every good grade or minor assignment they complete is not helpful. I think real self-esteem grows from genuine achievement earned through hard work. This is because effort leaves clear marks on a student’s output, helps them avoid becoming arrogant or self-absorbed, and means they won’t demand rewards if praise stops coming. That said, getting an occasional compliment for a job well done does feel nice.

When a student puts in genuine effort, it’s obvious both in the quality of their work and their attitude. Plenty of students have given their absolute best without receiving any compliments in return. To truly finish a task well, a student needs to find their own internal drive to do the work. If a learner gets praised for every little thing, what real lesson are they learning about hard work? They’ll start to believe that every good thing they do deserves a reward.

It’s common to see students act arrogantly when they earn a top grade. While those students may have done solid work, there are often peers who put in the exact same effort but didn’t get the same high mark. Some students get their feelings hurt when they receive a low grade, only to have a classmate brag about their better result right to their face. These self-absorbed students are narrow-minded: rather than offering to help a struggling peer, they choose to make them feel worse. Not all students are like this, though — some prefer to keep their grades private.

Students who receive constant praise will start to expect a reward for all their efforts eventually. They won’t work to achieve things for their own sake, but only to earn the compliment or prize. This means they never learn what real hard work actually is, since they assume every good deed comes with a payoff. That’s not how the real world works. The best feeling comes from finishing a tough task you worked hard on without any praise along the way. Students feel far prouder of themselves when they know they achieved something entirely on their own, with no external validation.

To sum up, I believe true self-esteem comes from hard work, taking pride in your own grades, and not expecting handouts from others when you’ve put in the effort. These students will show their dedication through their work, and seek out their own academic achievements because it makes them feel good about themselves. Those are the learners who truly deserve praise.

One activity I find truly fun is taking part in science experiments. One big reason I enjoy them so much is that they feel totally different from other school assignments. For example, a math project usually just means working through endless practice problems, and a language arts project is basically just writing another essay. There’s nothing hands-on about those, unlike science experiments.

I still remember one dissection project where we got to look inside a frog. I know that sounds gross to a lot of people—and to be fair, the smell was awful too. But I was totally fascinated by what I saw. Frogs have way fewer organs than humans do, or maybe some had been removed before we got the frozen frogs, but there just weren’t that many inside. Another thing that caught my attention was the color: the organs were blue and pink, nothing like the red insides of humans. The tissues felt a bit dry because our teacher told us the frogs had been frozen for a while, but that actually made it easier to cut into different parts. Our teacher said we could explore however we wanted, so my group and I poked around as much as we could. The only really nasty part was finding a few flies in the frog’s stomach. That made me shudder, but it didn’t make me want to quit the project at all.

After we’d looked at all the internal parts, our teacher started listing the name and function of each organ. Then one of my friends did something silly: he poked the frog’s eye. To this day, I have no idea what he was thinking. Since the eye wasn’t fully frozen, liquid squirted out the second he touched it, and he got splashed all over. Thankfully it didn’t hit me, but my friend was covered in the gross fluid. The teacher sent him straight to the bathroom to clean up, and after that, she decided it was best to end the project early. Even with that messy moment, I still had a blast.

Another recent experiment was tied to our current unit on light, which we had been studying for weeks. We did the whole project in a dark room, which fit the theme perfectly. It was way simpler than the dissection, and honestly not as exciting at first. We had to spray a special liquid in front of a flashlight, and the idea was that we’d see the waves that light travels along. Our teacher took ages to explain how it worked, which was a bit boring, and when we first sprayed the liquid, I couldn’t see anything at all—I was pretty disappointed. But after about four seconds, the waves started to show. They were really faint and only visible for a few seconds, but I still really liked the project. The only downsides were that it was over super fast, and the teacher’s explanation took way too long.

What I’m trying to get across with these personal stories is that science experiments can be far more engaging than many people expect, and they’re definitely not the boring chore some make them out to be. You might think you won’t like them, but you should really give them a try. I promise you’ll find at least one project you enjoy, because they make regular classes so much more interesting. In my opinion, hands-on experiments are the absolute best activities we do in school, way better than sitting through lectures or doing worksheets. They teach you in a way that’s way more direct than other types of schoolwork. That’s exactly why I think they’re the top choice for learning.

When you enjoy what you’re doing and keep a cheerful mindset, even a regular workday can feel fun and satisfying.

Beyond work, a positive attitude also sets you up for success in life overall. When you hold hopeful thoughts about your future, other people are more likely to want to support you. You’ll find more opportunities come your way, since most people enjoy being around someone who is upbeat and kind. You’ll also come up with better ideas for your career, a business, or how you want to live your life, and you’ll maintain strong, happy relationships with both family and friends.

The way you interact with others shows what your life is like, and a cheerful outlook makes it easy to show that respect. When you act positively toward people, you can brighten their whole day. At home, keeping a good attitude leads to happy, quality time with your family, and overall, you’ll run into far fewer problems in your daily life.

In conclusion, I believe a positive attitude is one of the most important keys to a good life. It helps you build strong relationships at home, at work, and with friends, and opens up more opportunities for you. Collaborating with a group of people is far more advantageous than working by yourself. What makes team tasks better? When you work with others, your teammates can assist you with coming up with concepts, drafting content, finding relevant examples, and gathering useful information. If you work on your own, there is no one to back up your thoughts or help you refine them.

There are plenty of perks to working as part of a team. For one, you can chat with your group members about the task at hand, ask them questions when you get stuck, and compare example ideas together. They can also share tips on how to approach the work, and the whole group will stand behind your ideas, making them stronger.

Working solo does not come with many upsides. The few good things are that you get to use only your own ideas, and no one will interrupt you while you work. You can also add your own examples, but this is much harder because you have to find all the information yourself, and there is no one to support or improve your ideas.

Take a high school English class as an example: the teacher tells students to form groups of four to complete a project. The students agree, and they divide the tasks. One volunteers to gather all the necessary information, another handles writing up the content, a third adds relevant examples to the project, and the last one reviews the entire project and prepares to give the class presentation. This setup is far better because the group shares the workload, so you feel much more relaxed knowing others are supporting you.

Now consider the alternative: a high school teacher announces a project and says students can work in groups or choose to work alone if they prefer. One student decides to work solo because they do not want anyone to interrupt their process, and they get to use only their own ideas. But there is no one to discuss the project with, so they often feel nervous during class, get distracted easily, and find the work boring.

Why do some people avoid group work? Often, it is because they have conflicts with other members of the team. Maybe they do not feel comfortable around the people in their group, or they feel anxious when working with others. Others simply prefer to work in a quiet, silent environment without any chatter.

So why do most people prefer working in groups? The main reason is that they enjoy collaborating with their friends, and they feel at ease chatting with group members. They also like answering questions from their teammates and getting instant input on their ideas.

British Prime Minister Winston Churchill once noted that success is built by moving from one failure to the next without losing enthusiasm. Failure plays a key role in achieving success, as it helps people grow, learn, and build strength in their lives.

First, failing helps you improve in many areas, including school, work, and your personal life. No one gets everything right all the time. When you do fail, you should take time to figure out what went wrong and why, then come up with new strategies to do better next time.

Second, mistakes teach you important lessons. If you make a mistake, it usually means something about your current approach is not working. You might need to change things like your work style, the skills you use, how you study, or how you communicate with others, then try new methods to get better results.

Finally, failure makes you stronger. If you fail, don’t stay down. No one wants to be destitute, and most people hope to live a wealthy, secure life, so the best thing to do is pick yourself up and keep going. Push yourself, work hard, and remember you are in control of your own choices.

To sum up, failure does not hold you back. Instead, it pushes you forward: it helps you improve at what you do, teaches you from your own mistakes, and encourages you to find new strategies to become a better person, worker, or student.

There are many advantages to tackling assignments as part of a team rather than working on your own. Collaborating with others makes the whole process far smoother and quicker. When you have multiple people in a group, everyone can share their own thoughts and suggestions for the best way to approach the task. By contrast, working solo means taking on all the responsibility yourself, which takes far more time and effort since you are handling every step alone.

Working in a team means you can pool everyone’s skills to handle even very difficult assignments that might feel impossible alone. Splitting up tasks also means you have fewer individual responsibilities, since different group members can take on different parts of the work. This division of labor also cuts down the total time needed to finish the assignment compared to doing it all yourself. What’s more, discussing the task with others gives you a clearer, deeper understanding of what needs to be done, thanks to the range of ideas and perspectives everyone brings.

A key part of any successful group is having a designated leader. This person is responsible for checking that every member has finished their assigned tasks, and they can also assign work to everyone fairly, which helps avoid arguments about who does what. If you run into a personal issue, like a family emergency, you can let the leader know you can’t finish your part. They can then inform the rest of the group and find someone else to take over your task. If you were working alone, you would have no one to rely on in this situation, and the assignment would likely go unfinished. While a good leader is helpful, they are only effective because of the rest of the group—every single member’s contribution matters for the team to succeed. No one person, not even the leader, can complete the work alone.

All in all, working with a group offers far more benefits than working alone. You gain a better grasp of the assignment thanks to everyone’s input, take on less individual responsibility, and finish the work in much less time. The combined effort of the whole team makes success far more likely than going it solo.

Many schools now let students choose distance learning, which lets them join classes from home via online platforms or video conferencing tools. I believe learners gain a lot from this option. It allows them to focus better in a familiar environment, helps those who can’t travel to campus due to health problems or illness, and supports people who have to balance school with work or other responsibilities.

First, studying from home gives students more freedom to focus than a traditional classroom. At home, there are fewer loud classmates or other distractions, so learners often work through material faster and find lessons more interesting. Regular in-person classes often have shorter, more interrupted learning periods, while distance learners can set aside longer, uninterrupted blocks of time to concentrate on their work.

Second, many students cannot attend in-person classes due to health issues or sudden illness. Thanks to online learning and video conferencing, these learners no longer have to fall behind. They can access the same classes as their peers in traditional schools, so they can keep up with their studies without having to step foot on campus.

Finally, a lot of learners have other responsibilities, especially full-time jobs, that make it impossible to attend daytime classes. These people work all day and only have free time in the evenings or at night, which does not line up with regular school schedules. Online learning solves this problem: they can join classes or review materials at any time that works for them, even late at night. The biggest advantage of remote learning is this flexibility, letting people study on their own schedule.

To sum up, students should be able to take classes via online platforms or video conferencing from home, as modern technology offers clear benefits for learners. People can study whenever and wherever works for them, focus better in a quiet home environment, and balance school with work or other duties. Even students with health problems that keep them from attending regular school can keep learning alongside their peers from the comfort of their own homes.

Have you ever wanted someone to lie to you instead of being honest? I firmly believe we should tell the truth at all times. Sure, being honest can sometimes hurt someone’s feelings, but think about your own preferences: would you rather someone lie to you, or tell you the truth?

Telling the truth helps you avoid bigger problems down the line, since lying often leads to even more mess. Being honest also builds a positive reputation, which is the complete opposite of what happens when you choose to lie. When you share the truth with others, they are far more likely to trust you.

When you’re truthful with the people around you, they come to rely on you, and that makes you someone they feel comfortable confiding in. You can feel proud of yourself for sticking to the truth. Think about it: if someone lied to you all the time, would you want them in your life? You wouldn’t feel safe sharing private things with them, since they’ve proven they aren’t trustworthy. What’s more, more people will want to be your friend when you’re known for being truthful and never hiding facts.

Avoiding lies also boosts your reputation in the long run. Whether you’re talking to your teachers, friends, or family, if you’re always honest, they’ll take your words seriously, because they know you won’t make things up. People will come to know you as a truthful person. On the other hand, lying damages how others see you, and that harm to your reputation can be hard to fix.

The famous American jazz musician Duke Ellington once said, "A problem is a chance for you to do your best." At first glance, this seems to mean that facing a challenge gives you an opportunity to solve it before the situation gets any worse. However, I disagree with this idea. Not every problem can be fixed, no matter how hard you try. If you attempt to handle a problem on your own when you are not prepared, your efforts might actually make the original issue far more serious than it was to begin with.

Take a common household issue, for example. Imagine your kitchen sink breaks, and you have no idea how to repair it. You call a plumber, who comes to fix the pipes, but then has to leave for another job before checking if the repair held. Later, the sink starts spraying water again. You decide to try fixing it yourself, since you watched the plumber work earlier. But your attempt only makes the leak worse, and soon water is flooding your home. Now you have to call the plumber back, pay for a second visit, and deal with water damage. If you had just called the plumber as soon as the leak started again, he could have talked you through a temporary fix over the phone, or returned sooner to prevent the flood.

Another clear example involves pet ownership. Many families have children who grow very attached to their pets. When that pet passes away, some parents think getting a new, similar pet will make the child feel better. But this often does more harm than good. The child may stop eating, have trouble sleeping, or even stop talking for a long time, because the new pet can never replace the one they lost. I went through this myself when my dog Lucky died. My brother and I were heartbroken — we barely ate or spoke for days. My dad tried to get us a new dog, but both of us knew it would never be the same as having Lucky back. His attempt to fix our sadness only reminded us more of what we’d lost.

A third situation shows how even small, kind actions can make a problem worse. Imagine you are at school and notice a classmate looking very upset. You ask what’s wrong, but he doesn’t respond. You then remember you have a group project to do together, so you suggest coming over to his house after school, adding, "Ask your dad if I can come over." Suddenly, the boy starts to cry. He tells you his father died in a car accident the night before. By mentioning his dad, you made his sadness even worse than it was just a few minutes earlier, all from one careless comment.

For all these reasons, I have to disagree with Duke Ellington’s quote. Trying your best to handle a problem does not always lead to a good outcome. Whether it’s trying to fix a leaky sink without the right skills, replacing a beloved dead pet with a new one, or trying to cheer up a grieving friend, your efforts can easily make the original problem far worse than it was before.

You don’t need to give someone a physical gift to make them happy. Simply treating them with kindness is enough to brighten their entire day.

I stand firmly in agreement with Prime Minister Winston Churchill’s perspective on success and failure. To start with, many people assume achieving success is simple, but as we grow older, life becomes far more challenging. Experiencing repeated failures does not mean you are doomed; instead, these struggles prepare you for easier times ahead. While most people lose their way after facing constant setbacks, holding onto hope and staying focused on your goals is the key to eventually succeeding. You must keep chasing your dreams, even when times get tough, and even when you feel like you are getting no answers or clear signs that you are on the right path.

My second point is that failure is unavoidable at every stage of life. For example, teenagers face it in school, working adults encounter it in their jobs, and it also shows up in financial struggles or housing issues. Everyone needs to learn how to handle these setbacks: we should come up with solutions, map out clear plans for our lives, and figure out how to fix the problem. If we cannot solve it alone, there is no shame in asking for help from others.

Thirdly, getting through failure teaches you new things about yourself that you never realized before. Most people who overcome setbacks find strategies to avoid repeating the same mistakes. This is also when you build up the confidence to keep going, and you start practicing every possible method to make sure you do not fail again in the future.

To sum up, almost everyone goes through difficult periods in life. It is always a good idea to talk to someone you trust about your struggles, and to actively look for answers. This way, you can find a solution and resolve the problem either on your own or with the help of someone important to you.

When people face problems and need help finding solutions, they often turn to more than one person for input. This helps them make smarter decisions and avoid harmful choices, such as stealing money or selling drugs. Good advice can also guide others toward doing what is right.

Relying on just one person’s perspective rarely leads to the best possible choice, while hearing from multiple people gives you more options. You can weigh different opinions to find what works best for your situation, rather than being limited to a single idea. For instance, if you get stuck on a difficult math problem, trying only one method might leave you stuck. Listening to different approaches can help you solve it faster. Similarly, when students misbehave or ignore school rules, they need guidance to make better choices. Following class guidelines and working to improve the classroom environment makes the space safer for everyone. If you refuse to consider other ideas, you may struggle and even fail. The key is to pick the approach that works best for you—that is how advice helps people make choices that suit their own needs.

Ignoring rules or making poor decisions often leads to bigger problems. Children need guidance just as much as adults do. It is common for people to make foolish mistakes, like stealing from others or selling drugs, and good advice can help keep them safe from harm. People who engage in these behaviors need to understand the consequences of their actions and learn about better alternatives. You do not have to consult multiple people if you feel comfortable talking to just one person. However, if you are consistently making bad choices, getting input from more than one person is far more helpful. For example, someone who repeatedly steals money needs guidance to turn their life around—that is exactly what advice is for. Advice is not only for people who do wrong things; even good people, including children, can benefit from it. Kids make silly mistakes or act out at school, and advice can help them correct their behavior.

Overall, advice is a valuable tool for making decisions, and it is especially useful in schools to help students make better choices. It works much like school rules that everyone is expected to follow, guiding people toward positive actions.

There’s a common saying that first impressions are almost impossible to change, and I completely agree with this for three main reasons.

First, when you meet someone new and observe how they behave, you immediately form strong feelings about them, whether that’s love or hate. Second, you may never meet that person again, so the way they act during this one encounter is what you will use to judge them. Third, even if you see the person every day, the way they acted toward you at first leaves you with feelings that will never change.

This is exactly why first impressions are so hard to change. These feelings you develop toward someone, whether love or hate, come directly from the way that person behaves.

For instance, I once met a man for the first time, and I had no idea what to expect from him. After talking to him, I disliked how he spoke and his personality, so my first impression of him was very negative, and I never changed the opinion I’d formed of him. I never saw that person again for the rest of my life. This just proves that once you form an impression of someone, you rarely shift your view.

After all, changing how people think is extremely hard.

There is a well-known saying that claims you will never grow unless you step outside of the skills you have already mastered, and I completely agree with this idea. That does not mean, however, that being good at one thing guarantees you will fail when you try something unfamiliar. The only thing that truly stops personal growth is giving up. Take changing your lifestyle as an example: starting to eat healthy meals and go to the gym is never easy, but it is still worth making an effort. We push ourselves to try new things for two main reasons. First, we want to test our limits in situations we never expected to face. Second, exploring new activities helps us find hobbies or passions we might end up loving.

Consider learning to cook as a clear example. Even if you have never followed a recipe or held a knife properly before, that is no reason not to give it a go. We take on new challenges to prove to ourselves that we can handle situations we once thought were impossible to navigate. Curiosity also drives us: we want to see if we can master new skills. Raising a child is another good case—you are never fully prepared to teach a little one right from wrong, or make sure you have all the tools they need to grow. At the end of the day, trying new things matters because humans can do things machines cannot, most notably learning and adapting to entirely new tasks.

If we set our minds to a goal, we can master almost any skill, as long as we are willing to put in the work and push past fear. When we believe in ourselves, we realize that nothing is impossible if we commit to it. Look at major moments in US history: the country fought for independence from England centuries ago, abolished slavery, and ended the racism that was once widespread across the nation. These huge accomplishments show that even the hardest challenges can be overcome, all because people were willing to try new, bold approaches, even when the outcome seemed uncertain. Of course, we will fail at some of the challenges life throws at us—there is no doubt about that. Mastering a new skill is never easy, and there will be times when our minds and bodies feel too tired to keep going, when we want to quit and tell ourselves we are losers or quitters.

This self-criticism is a form of emotional punishment, far more damaging than any physical pain. Over a lifetime, the deepest hurt most people feel comes from giving up on something before mastering it, leading to crushing emotional pain. The hardest challenge of all, one we have struggled with since birth, is controlling our own emotions. This is a skill most of us have not yet mastered.

Many of us struggle to figure out what makes us feel angry, sad, or happy, but people who have mastered emotional control got there by trying, putting in the effort to understand their feelings. Therapists are a great example of this: they study emotions deeply so they can help people who do not understand why they react the way they do to certain situations.

All of this drives us to keep trying new things. As humans, we are naturally curious about what interests us, and we want to see if we can master new skills. To return to the core idea: growth only happens when we test ourselves with tasks that go beyond what we already know how to do. So keep trying new activities that catch your attention—you might just surprise yourself with what you can achieve.

Thomas Jefferson once advised people to "determine never to be idle," adding that it is incredible how much a person can achieve if they stay busy. This raises an interesting question: do we get more done when we are constantly active, or can periods of doing nothing also be useful?

Personally, I always strive to finish every task I can as quickly as possible, just to keep up with my responsibilities. Staying inactive is neither good for your health nor helpful for your future growth. Keeping busy helps you feel more prepared and organized, ready to handle whatever comes your way. It is also important to set clear goals: they should be realistic and easy to measure, so you can track your progress.

There is no doubt that we achieve more when we stay occupied and keep working toward our aims. That said, not all inactivity is bad. Sometimes, taking a short break from tasks is necessary: it gives you time to rest, think, and work through your own ideas and perspectives.

Jefferson’s advice to never be idle refers to avoiding laziness, and I completely agree. We all have moments when we want to do nothing at all, but giving in to that laziness will never help you reach your goals. As Jefferson himself put it, the amount you can achieve when you stay consistently active is truly amazing.

Jefferson makes an excellent point with this quote. There is so much valuable meaning packed into his short words, and I believe everyone interprets this message in their own way.

True success comes from pushing ourselves to reach our goals, and it’s important to remember that no one is born with all the answers. We are all here to learn, and often, that learning happens through failure. I fully agree with Winston Churchill’s view that failure plays a central role in achieving success. My reasons for this are simple: failure helps us grow and show our best selves, it allows us to inspire others, and it gives us valuable personal experience.

First, failure pushes us to bring out our best qualities and feel proud of our progress. When we fail, we learn to dig deep and show what we are truly capable of. For example, last year I lost my job because I was too young to meet the company’s age requirements. Instead of giving up, I started my own business this year, and now I employ several people. This shows how failure does not have to crush your motivation. You might face setbacks once or twice, but that does not mean you will never succeed — success will come eventually if you keep going.

Second, your attitude after failure matters more than the failure itself. You can use your experience to encourage other people who have lost their motivation and given up on their dreams, showing them that they too can push forward and achieve what they want. A great example is my cousin, who failed 12th grade three times. After her first failed year, her confidence plummeted and she stopped working toward her goals. But this year, she is finally set to graduate: she spent the past year preparing properly for her classes, and she will get her diploma soon. Her story is a perfect example of failing repeatedly, then finally reaching success.

Some people argue that failure is harmful to society, but I strongly disagree. To achieve any success, we have to start learning from the very beginning, and failure is part of that learning process. This leads to my third reason: the experience we gain from repeated failures teaches us exactly what steps to take to succeed later. The famous author Ralph Waldo Emerson once stated, "Unless you try to do something beyond what you have already mastered, you will never grow." From my own life experiences, I completely agree with this idea. Growth only happens when someone pushes themselves to complete tasks outside their current comfort zone, which helps them reach new goals. People can grow in many areas of life, including their education, professional work, and personal hobbies.

Schoolis one key place where people develop useful skills for the future, like reading, writing, building vocabulary, studying history, and solving math problems. Beyond academics, students also learn how to communicate with others and behave appropriately by making friends and interacting with peers. Even further education, such as community college, helps people build job-specific skills that prepare them for their future careers.

Professional careers are another major area for growth. Advancing up the ranks at work is a clear sign of career growth. For example, I currently work at a company called Searchs, where I now serve as a supervisor. When I first started there, I was hired as a cashier, and after putting in time and effort, I worked my way up to my current role.

Personal hobbies also offer plenty of room for growth. People can improve their hobbies by learning new techniques and practicing regularly. Drawing is one of my favorite pastimes. When I was six years old, I could only draw simple stick figures. Over the years, I have taken many art classes to sharpen my drawing abilities, and now I can create detailed, realistic human portraits.

Pushing yourself to go beyond what you already know how to do can help you learn new skills, climb the career ladder, or improve your personal hobbies.

A local city council is currently discussing introducing a 10 pm curfew on weekdays and a midnight curfew on weekends for all teenagers. I am fully in support of this proposal, as I believe curfews are an effective way to keep young people out of harm’s way. Under such rules, teens would be required to be home at reasonable hours, which keeps them safe. If they fail to follow these regulations, they will face unnecessary difficulties.

The first reason I support this policy is that it stops teenagers from being out on the streets late at night. Many communities have individuals who use illegal drugs or act erratically, which creates serious risks for young people wandering around after dark.

Another key point is that teens are far safer at home with their families than anywhere else. Staying in allows them to spend time with loved ones, maybe finishing homework or having meaningful conversations about the positive things that God has in store for them.

A third important factor is the need for young people to follow the law. If they choose not to obey curfew rules, they will end up in significant trouble with authorities.

To sum up, the city council’s proposed weekday 10 pm and weekend midnight curfew for teenagers is a smart move. I remain convinced that these rules keep young people safe from danger. For one, teens have no reason to be outside after 10 pm, when risks are higher. For another, home is the safest place for them to be. Finally, following this law is beneficial for their overall well-being and lives.

Writer Ralph Waldo Emerson had a valid point when he noted that the world often tries to shape people into versions of themselves they never chose to be.

I believe we all make daily choices that can either help us grow into better versions of ourselves or lead us down the wrong path. To get where we want to go, it is important to set clear future goals and make concrete plans to reach them. Something I learned during my time in prison stuck with me: you have to value yourself more than you value anyone else. If you do not respect your own worth, there is no point in setting goals at all—they will just sit there untouched, never coming to life.

Everyone has their own opinions, but some people wrongly blame the world for the bad choices they make. This is never true. When people know they have messed up, they often try to shift the blame onto others instead of owning their mistakes.

What I will say is this: with all the challenges we face today, we need to come together and support one another. Not just as a team, but as a family. When one of us stumbles, we should lift each other up. When one of us is hurting, we should help each other heal.

There are always steps we can take to make things better. Hard times never last forever. In moments of struggle, we should look back at how far we have come, even from times when our future looked hopeless. The world may try to change you, break you, or push you to the sidelines, but the goals you have set and the people who stand by you will help you achieve the dreams you have always wanted.

The prompt presents a quote from Ralph Waldo Emerson: "Unless you try something beyond what you have mastered, you will never grow." Most would call this very wise, but since there’s so little wisdom in the world today, sharing wise words often feels pointless. Personally, I agree with this statement. Aside from the physical growth I’m still experiencing as a teenager, I’m almost done growing in other ways. To return to the main point: Emerson’s quote makes me ask myself, if I never try things beyond my current skills, am I really growing at all?

If I stick to my usual routine and never try anything new, I won’t get very far in life. I can’t actually think of a good reason to disagree with Emerson’s statement. In my seventeen years of life, I’ve tried plenty of new things, and I can honestly say those experiences have shaped me into the person I am today. A lot of people avoid new opportunities because they judge them too quickly—whether it’s a new activity or a new person—without giving them a real chance. But if people actually opened themselves up to new experiences, it could change their lives for the better, or even for the worse.

At the end of the day, whether you try new things comes down to personal perspective. If I want to improve myself and be a more helpful member of society, I’ll choose to step outside my comfort zone. But if I decide to stick to the same boring daily routine forever, I’ll probably end up bored with everything eventually. Some people might argue that repeating the same routine is exactly how they found success—for example, athletes have to practice the same moves over and over to get better at their sport, and dancers rehearse the same routine countless times before performing it for an audience. That’s true in some cases, but for other people, trying a completely new routine is what leads to success. Of course, not everyone has the same natural talent.

To sum up, trying something new always changes you a little, for better or for worse—it can either help you grow or even damage your life. Some people grow old and wise, but others never gain wisdom as they age, staying young and reckless instead. Ralph Waldo Emerson was absolutely right when he said, "Unless you try something beyond what you have mastered, you will never grow."

Many schools now give students the choice to join either fully online courses or live video conferencing sessions. But a major issue is that not every family owns a home computer, which students need to access these remote learning options. Some parents are against these remote learning setups, as they work full-time and have no one available to care for their children while classes are on.

Live video conferencing tends to work better for students than standard online classes. The live teacher can walk students through assignments more clearly, and step in to help with any tasks they are stuck on. Many learners prefer having a real person guide them so they can get immediate support with their work.

Taking classes from home has clear benefitsfor many students. Some even like remote learning more than attending a physical school, since regular classrooms feel overwhelming due to the large number of other students. These learners prefer working quietly on their own, with a patient teacher who moves at a slow pace and has enough time to assist them.

Home-based classes also offer more flexibility when it comes to scheduling. Students can pick the specific days and times that work best for their personal routines.

You can never truly succeed in life without facing failure first. While failure means not reaching a goal or finishing a task you set out to do, it still plays a key role in helping you eventually achieve success. In fact, going through failures can push you closer to reaching your long-term goals.

I agree with Ralph Waldo’s statement, because if you never fail, you will never spot your own mistakes. For instance, if you sail through life only ever succeeding, you will have no idea how to react or fix things when a failure finally happens. In the end, failing actually leads to more lasting success overall. It also teaches you the hard work and effort that people put in to reach their goals. Once you have failed yourself, you understand exactly what is required to achieve success in the future.

At the same time, I disagree with Ralph Waldo’s statement, because I think people who never fail might accomplish fewer goals. For example, if you never experience failure at all, you will not know how to handle it when it finally happens. Of course, it is great to have constant success in life, but you should be prepared for the unexpected—that is when everything falls apart if you are not ready. In fact, success is not a bad thing at all; it is actually very positive.

In my view, success is not better than failure—instead, the two work together like a team. I ultimately agree with Ralph Waldo’s statement, because unexpected challenges will always pop up in life.

Have you ever relied on examples to pick up a new skill, or do you find you learn more effectively through other methods rather than being given sample work? As Albert Schweitzer once noted, "Example is not the main thing to influence others." This suggests that there are plenty of other approaches to guiding or inspiring people without relying on providing examples.

One key way people can be influenced more effectively is through hands-on assistance from others, rather than just being shown examples. I saw this clearly in my ceramics class last term: our teacher almost always just showed us samples of finished clay pieces, and rarely offered personal guidance. She would explain a technique once, then leave us to work, which made it really hard for me and many classmates to figure out what to do—most of us forgot the instructions quickly. But whenever she stepped in to help a student one-on-one, that person’s final project always ended up being the best in the class, all because of the direct support she gave them.

Another common issue with using examples is that they can leave people feeling confused, especially when they shift someone’s original perspective on a task. For instance, imagine a drawing assignment where a teacher tells the class to create a piece based entirely on their own imagination—whatever unique ideas come to mind, with no set rules. But if that same teacher then shares example drawings of what to make, students might start to wonder if the teacher actually wants them to copy those samples instead of using their own ideas. This shows that examples can backfire for certain types of creative tasks, because they end up muddling people’s understanding rather than clarifying it.

Of course, some people argue that using examples makes it easier to influence others, since examples demonstrate the instructor’s own experience and give clear steps for completing a task. There are definitely learners who respond better to seeing samples, and find they understand concepts faster that way. But I still believe there are more powerful methods of influencing people that make examples far less effective, or even useless, in many cases. For all these reasons, I am convinced that there are far better ways to guide or inspire others without ever relying on examples.

Is a positive attitude the most important factor for achieving success in life? Many people argue that maintaining an upbeat mindset can make a big difference in how you navigate daily life. In my view, a positive attitude serves as a key to success in countless areas of life.

I fully agree with this idea. One of the most valuable traits a person can possess is a positive outlook, as it opens doors to far more opportunities than you would encounter otherwise. When you approach life with optimism, you naturally connect with more people, which often leads to new chances to grow both personally and professionally, no matter where you are in the world.

From my perspective, an upbeat attitude benefits almost everyone. It improves your overall well-being, making you feel happier and more energetic throughout the day. For instance, when you go to work with a positive mindset, you tend to feel good all day long. You also interact with colleagues and friends in a kind, thoughtful way that does not upset or bother anyone around you.

It is clear that people who maintain a positive attitude are far more likely to succeed in life. I have seen this firsthand in my own family: my grandparents have built very successful lives largely thanks to their optimistic outlook. They always have faith in the plans they make, and one of my grandfathers often says that the only thing you truly need to get ahead in the workplace or in life generally is a positive attitude. He believes that if you have this trait, you can achieve almost anything you set your mind to. There are many moments in real life when you want to take action but feel unsure if you can follow through. That is exactly when a positive attitude pushes you to try anyway. For me, having a good attitude is one of the best qualities a person can have. It leads to more opportunities, and people with this mindset often start their day by smiling at themselves in the mirror as soon as they wake up.

While having a positive attitude is undoubtedly a great asset, not everyone sees its value. People who lack this optimism often have very different perspectives, and they may not even understand what steps they need to take to develop the same upbeat mindset as those who always look on the bright side.

Looking ahead, I believe a positive attitude will only become more important, both in people’s personal lives and across the world as a whole.

To sum up, if you develop and maintain a positive attitude, you are far more likely to achieve success in all areas of your life.

Many students would jump at the chance to have a longer summer break, as it gives them extra time to hang out with family and friends. Beyond that, looking at the benefits, a longer vacation acts as a well-earned reward for learners who have worked hard throughout all school year. It lets them step away from the stress of assignments, exams, and grade worries entirely. This time off also helps students recognize how valuable their education is, which sets them up to succeed later in life with plenty of opportunities. They’ll also learn to handle challenges on their own, using the key skills and knowledge they picked up during the school year.

Some educators argue that students forget most of what they learned during the school year after a long summer break, returning to class knowing almost nothing, a common concern among teachers. There is some truth to this: most people don’t spend their break thinking about stressful school topics. Instead, they focus on enjoying time with loved ones. That said, many students still read books every few days or check the news to stay in the loop with current events, so they don’t fall behind on what’s happening in the world. Besides, young people pick up new information and process ideas faster than older adults, so they’re unlikely to completely forget important course material that easily.

A lot of students also travel during summer vacation, whether to other states or even foreign countries. For these learners especially, a longer break is a great idea: it gives them enough time to fully explore the places they’re visiting. This kind of travel can even help them learn about new histories and cultures, and they can share these unique experiences with classmates and teachers when they get back, which adds to their overall knowledge. While being away from school for a month or more can impact how focused a student is when classes restart, this mostly depends on how much they let themselves get distracted during the break. For some, the break isn’t even a proper vacation: they use the time to work part-time jobs to cover their personal expenses, or they have family responsibilities to handle. Others choose to volunteer for community organizations or join other various activities that keep them busy.

All things considered, a longer summer vacation gives students plenty of time to reconnect with friends and family members they didn’t get to see much during the busy school year, especially loved ones who live far away. It lets them make up for all the missed time spent apart, and this benefits everyone in the general community, not just the students themselves.
