The point made in the comment I read is really valuable. So many people go through their whole lives sticking to just one routine, never experimenting with anything new. They might worry that new experiences will be pointless later on, or simply feel like they don’t really need to branch out. But the truth is, the more new things you try, the more you grow as a person, and all those experiences become the foundation for your future choices.

Think about how we grow up: as we get older, we pick up all kinds of lessons that shape us into better people. Take a young person who’s eager to learn new skills, for instance. Even if they’re still a teenager, they might understand things that usually only adults know, which makes them seem more mature than others their age. This also means they take on more responsibilities, because the knowledge you gain directly influences how you live your life, the decisions you make, and the paths you choose to follow.

School is a perfect example of this. It’s a space where we learn constantly until we graduate, and the more we know, the more chances we have to succeed later in life. That’s exactly why I agree with the comment I mentioned earlier. Let me explain why. Lots of people never step out of their comfort zone: imagine a teacher who’s been in the classroom for five years and no longer feels passionate about teaching. They could switch to a completely different career, which would help them grow by giving them fresh experiences. Trying out new jobs, or even going back to study a new subject, adds so much to your experience bank. It’s easy to get stuck doing the same thing forever, but there’s always a way forward. Reaching your goals is never simple, though—you often have to give up things you really care about.

That might mean putting your hobbies, time with family, or social events on hold for a while. But in the end, you’ll get everything you ever wanted, because you earned it through hard work. When you start to see your success, you’ll realize every choice you made to get there was the right one, and you’ll have grown so much thanks to all those varied experiences. There’s no limit to what you can achieve. For example, say you own a small restaurant and want to expand it. You remember that you studied business in the past, and also worked as a manager at another restaurant before. That experience means you know how to manage your budget and create a solid marketing plan, so you can grow your business successfully. On top of that, you’ll grow as a person, with a much richer set of experiences than before.

On top of all this, I think the person who wrote that comment is completely right. As I’ve said, the more you learn, the more experience you gain, which can lead to better job opportunities and a happier, more fulfilling life. If you never push yourself to try things outside of what you already know how to do well, you’ll never really grow. Your experiences are what shape who you become.

Plenty of activities exist that people find fun and engaging. So what makes educational activities so enjoyable? For one, they let you learn new things, but they also let you bond with friends, and they teach you to grow from your mistakes.

First, educational activities are fun because they open up chances to learn new things. Trying out new activities you’ve never done before will not hurt you, but it can bring plenty of rewards. Take dancing or hands-on experiments, for instance: giving them a try might reveal a hidden interest you did not know you had. Every new task you take on teaches you something useful. The more time you spend learning or practicing, the more facts and skills you pick up along the way.

Second, educational activities are enjoyable because they give you time to hang out with friends. When you work on projects or tasks together, you can help each other solve problems and get better results. Friends play a huge role in most people’s lives, and spending time with them during these activities strengthens your bond. Every shared memory you make reminds you how valuable good friends are. They offer support in all sorts of ways, from helping you finish a tough assignment to lending an ear when you are feeling down.

Third, educational activities are enjoyable because they teach you to learn from your mistakes. Many people say that “failure is the key to success,” and this is absolutely true. Every time you make a mistake, you push yourself to do better and fix what went wrong. If a project or activity does not go as planned, you can look back at what happened, figure out the problem, and make changes to improve next time.

To sum up, educational activities are fun because they let you take part in activities you genuinely like. They help us grow as people and expand our minds, which improves our ability to think through problems and use our imagination.

It’s easy to notice that many people’s actions these days seem really strange, which makes my heart race when I see them. But I’ve learned that the most effective way to influence others is through your own behavior. This works because good actions build trust, prove you’re willing to help those around you, and leave a huge positive mark on the people in your life.

First, your own behavior is key to building trust. When you act reliably, others learn to respect you and know you care about them. Take friends, for example: their actions build trust because they step up to help when needed. If I got badly hurt and couldn’t walk, I’d know they weren’t messing around, and I’d trust them completely to help me. Teachers also build trust through their behavior, which is almost always positive and sets a good example. They focus on supporting their students, which makes students trust them when they need help. Even if some students feel like teachers don’t believe in them, most people see that teachers have faith in their students, push them to work hard, and want the best for their futures. Family members build trust too, and they always have a big influence on me. Spending time with them has even made their personalities more positive than they used to be. In short, your behavior builds trust by helping others, staying positive, and strengthening your relationships with the people around you.

Another way your behavior influences others is by showing you’re willing to help. My family often helps people in need, and those we’ve supported never forget us. A while back, my whole family went to Generic_City on a volunteer trip: we built houses for people who needed them and cooked meals for hundreds of low-income locals. Friends help others too, especially me when I’m going through a tough time. They always know how to comfort me and make me feel better when I’m sad or angry. Teachers help students because they want everyone to pass their classes. Even when some students struggle or fail, teachers do everything they can to help them improve. They push students to try their best, work hard, and actually learn the material. My own teachers always go out of their way to help me prepare for quizzes and tests. Helping others is one of the best ways to influence the people around you, whether that’s friends, teachers, or family, and it makes them more likely to support you and others when help is needed.

Your behavior also leaves a huge positive impact on others. When you act kindly, more people will respect you and even grow to like you. I see this with my friends: when I show them I care, they usually return that love. We should all make an effort to show care and kindness, so people don’t end up disliking us. For family, a positive attitude goes a long way. Acting friendly is like building a bridge straight to their hearts, and it slowly improves their mood over time. Firefighters are another group that leaves a massive positive impact on others. They care deeply about people’s lives and always rush to protect those in danger. There’s a story about a group of firefighters whose tools were old, rusty, and broken, but when someone called about a house fire with a wife trapped inside, they still rushed to help. They managed to get her out safely, and her husband was so grateful he started sending the fire station $2,000 every month to buy new equipment. That story shows just how much the husband appreciated them. Big positive impacts come from showing love, lifting others’ spirits, and being willing to take risks to protect people.

Some people might point out that your own behavior affects others, which is exactly what I’m saying: your actions influence people by showing you help others, creating a huge positive impact, and building trust. We should see if our behavior can influence others and change the world.

What if an event is taking place, but you have to do cleanup as part of community service? Doing the right thing is always the correct choice. Community service benefits local areas greatly: it helps neighborhoods improve over time, making all residents happier. Not everyone wants to help, though—some have other commitments, or simply don’t want to volunteer. This is just like school, where only some students take part in community service.
First, community service matters because it makes city leaders such as the mayor proud. Residents often grumble about messy public spaces, saying “What a mess!” That’s exactly why community service volunteers are needed. Trash left on the ground will start to smell terrible after a few days, which annoys many people. Everyone should put garbage in bins instead of littering.
Second, event staff have to finish cleaning before the event starts. Some people claim this wastes too much time, but that’s wrong—they just want to support the community and its people. School is no different: some friends refuse to help, while others do.
Finally, there is often a lot of mess to clean up, and much of this work happens at night. Janitors clean overnight so spaces are tidy the next day. Some people clean alone, others in groups.

Is Winston Churchill correct when he says that failure plays a key role in the journey to success? I believe failure is a major factor in achieving success, but only for people who are truly determined to change their lives. First, you can learn something from every failure. Second, failure reveals people’s true character. Third, and most importantly, avoid repeating the same mistakes over and over.

Churchill once said, “Success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm.” To start with, every failure offers a lesson, because we are all human and bound to make big mistakes at some point. People who learn from their errors are often the best at supporting others facing the same struggles. We should always take lessons from setbacks, since more failures will definitely come our way in the future.

Next, failure brings out who people really are. You might assume your close friends will support you when things go wrong, but only those who truly care will step up. Sometimes, someone you previously thought did not like you might be the only one to offer help. For instance, a loyal partner will never leave you the first time you face a setback.

The more often you face the same setback, the harder it becomes to stay motivated. We will always encounter new failures in life, but if you cannot move past even one, dealing with multiple setbacks at once will feel impossible.

To conclude, everyone experiences at least one failure in their lifetime. The most valuable part of any setback is moving forward with the lessons you have learned, making sure you never repeat the same error again. Anyone has the option to change their life, but the key is that they must truly want that change and be ready to transform themselves.

The current debate asks whether schools should shorten summer vacation, a suggestion often tied to the belief that long breaks make it difficult for students to remember what they learned during the academic year.

For most students, summer is a rare opportunity to travel with their families to new places, have fun, and completely set aside any school-related stress. After months of attending classes and completing assignments, learners deserve this extended break to shake off stress and focus on activities and interests outside of school. It is also the ideal time to visit relatives who live in other cities or even other countries, especially if you have not seen them for a long time. Summer feels like dedicated time for personal enjoyment, as the two-month break allows students to try activities that are impossible to fit into the shorter breaks scattered throughout the school year. Students who failed a course can use the summer to retake classes and earn back any credits they need to move forward. Young athletes benefit greatly too, as they have more time to practice their sport, stay in shape, and play without the pressure of homework or upcoming exams. Students who love reading get plenty of free time to spend at the library, working through piles of books they have wanted to read all year. Those who enjoy traveling can visit any destination they choose, then take photos or write journals to share their experiences with classmates when the new school year starts.

There are many downsides to shortening summer break, starting with the obvious: students would spend more time in school overall. Families would no longer be able to take long trips, as students would have to attend classes instead, which would add a lot of unnecessary worry to their lives. Most students would feel burned out and stressed from schoolwork if they do not get a long summer break to rest. Summer would also lose its fun factor for many students, as it is the time when friends usually gather to relax and enjoy each other’s company.

I believe school boards should not reduce summer break, first because students can travel with their families to new places, have fun, and not worry about school responsibilities. Students deserve this break after months of being in school, as it lets them release stress and focus on things outside of academics. They can also travel to different regions or countries to see family members they have not visited in a long time. Summer is a time for personal enjoyment, as the two-month break lets students do activities that are not possible during the shorter school term. Students who need to retake a failed class can use the summer to recover credits they need to progress. Student athletes have more time to play their sport and stay in shape, without the distraction of schoolwork. Avid readers have plenty of time to themselves to spend hours at the library reading countless books. Students who love to travel can go anywhere they want, then take photos or write in journals to tell their classmates about their summer adventures when school resumes. This is my reasoning, and I strongly agree that summer break should not be shortened, as cutting it would leave everyone feeling overwhelmed and burnt out.

Back then, phones were banned from classrooms, but times have changed, and now schools permit students to use their devices during lessons. This essay will answer the question: What effects does allowing students to have and use mobile phones in classrooms have?

Whether curfews keep teenagers out of trouble or unfairly limit their freedom is a common debate. I strongly believe these rules are necessary to protect young people, not restrict them unfairly. Curfews are designed with good intentions to look out for teens, who are still young and more likely to take risks when out late at night. In the end, the only people who truly benefit from these rules are teenagers themselves.

For example, teens out in the middle of the night often get into trouble. With no authority figures around to supervise, they may do whatever they want without thinking of consequences. Curfews set clear boundaries that stop them from making reckless choices.

After all, you rarely see people out on the streets doing anything positive late at night. Most are at home resting or spending time with family, so teens should follow the same routine.

Late nights also come with higher risks of crime. Someone might steal your belongings, hurt you or other people, or you could get caught up in danger if you witness a crime and try to help.

Some argue that going out at night is fun, but I disagree. Nightclubs are particularly risky because you don’t know the people around you, and anything can go wrong. For example, a mass shooting at a Las Vegas club almost three years ago killed many people.

To sum up, curfews are an important way to keep teenagers safe, and these rules are ultimately good for them.

A positive attitude is essential for becoming a successful person, as it brings happiness and excitement to our daily lives. You just need to be kind to yourself and those around you — if you maintain a healthy, optimistic way of thinking and feeling about the world around you, your attitude will naturally stay positive.

Take a customer service worker, for example. If a customer says rude things, like claiming you are not good at your job, you should not let that shift your attitude. You know your role, so you never need to doubt yourself or change your mindset. You know the customer is always right, so you stick to your positive attitude and keep working hard.

Staying positive helps in countless ways. If you look at someone with a tired, angry, or frustrated expression, you can tell they lack a positive attitude in their life or their surroundings. Putting on a pleasant face matters because others can see you are ready to get started, stay active, and bring good energy — this positive mindset makes your days feel smoother and more enjoyable.

Even though following your dreams and reaching your life goals requires self-awareness, mutual respect, and knowing your worth, your attitude is the clearest sign of whether you are doing well. If you want a good job and secure great opportunities, your attitude shapes your personality — people will see you as the top candidate for roles, and a positive mindset lets you take on big projects down the line.

Another clear example is a job interview. You need to show off your skills and clearly explain what you are capable of. Stay honest and friendly with the person who might hire you — they will look at your attitude to decide if you are the right fit for the role.

It is no secret that a positive attitude is the best tool for building great projects and achieving big things. Your mindset can help you earn more money, land good jobs, buy a home, and build a better future. A positive attitude spreads good energy, making everyone around you happier — including the people who love you. If you approach life’s greatest challenges with the best possible positive attitude, you will thrive.

Should students be allowed to take classes from home? While some learners in our country may gain advantages from remote learning, I mostly disagree with this approach. Attending school in person offers far greater benefits for most students. Some may choose distance learning via online tools or video calls, but only when they have no other way to earn the credits needed to graduate.

First, schools give students the chance to take part in sports they enjoy, a major perk of in-person learning. Most young people love physical activity, and schools provide the space and resources to pursue this. For me, playing soccer lifts my mood when I feel down — it’s fun, helps me forget my worries, and lets me bond with others who share my passion. Playing sports also keeps many students away from risky behaviors like drug use or joining gangs. Young people need positive environments to chase their goals, and school sports programs provide exactly that.

Second, in-person classes keep students from getting bored. All learners want to feel motivated, happy, and engaged — they don’t want to spend all day staring at a computer or stuck at home. That’s why most prefer going to school: they get to spend time with friends and meet new people. For example, when I’m confused about homework, I can ask my teacher or a classmate right away. Schools also organize trips to universities, theaters, and museums, which let us learn about our history and culture firsthand.

Finally, schools offer elective classes and specialty academies that let students explore their interests. Many join these programs to figure out what they want to do in the future. Schools across our country offer electives in fields like cooking, piano, cosmetology, art, fitness, medical assisting, dentistry, band, law enforcement, detective work, electrical repair, and emergency medical services. These classes help us identify future study paths. Only in-person schools provide extra support like guidance on taking out bank loans for university, accessing other university financial aid, applying for scholarships, and choosing the right university for your chosen career. For example, my school helped me figure out what I want to study and assisted me with taking out a bank loan for my university tuition.

In conclusion, most students are not interested in distance learning options that let them attend class from home via online platforms or video calls. The majority prefer in-person school because they can play sports, avoid boredom, and access diverse elective programs. However, some students have no choice but to take remote classes: those with no family, others who need to work full-time and lack time or transportation to attend night school. For these learners, remote learning is the only way to earn the credits needed to graduate.

I strongly disagree with the statement, as knowledge is far more valuable than imagination. Imagination is little more than daydreaming, but knowledge gives you the tools to turn ideas into real, major achievements. For instance, with enough knowledge, you could start your own company, hire staff, and organize deliveries to customers—all of these are concrete, real-world results.

Building this knowledge does take time, though. You need to finish school, go to college, and earn a degree, which requires patience. You also have to develop a focused mindset and encourage yourself to keep pushing forward, even when progress feels slow.

Once you have this experience, you can also help others who need guidance. You have already been through the process of finding a job or launching your own business, so you can share practical advice and urge them to apply themselves fully. The person you help can then support someone else, creating a never-ending cycle of encouragement. You can share your own success story with them, so they can follow a similar path, then pass their achievements on to others too.

Imagination is not reality—it only exists when you are asleep or lost in thought. Knowledge, on the other hand, is what you will need to handle real-life situations.

People often say that first impressions are nearly impossible to reverse. While some believe they can shape how others see them the instant they meet someone, that’s not accurate. First impressions form in a fraction of a second, leaving no time to plan a response or adjust your behavior. A few impressions can be shifted later depending on the circumstances, but most will stick no matter what you do. I agree with this idea, since an impression is essentially the feeling, emotion, or mental image that stays with someone after an interaction.

Certain impressions can have a really negative impact on our lives. Take, for example, a time when someone only makes one impression, even if it’s not the one they wanted to leave. Imagine a student sitting in class who isn’t feeling well, and accidentally lets out a very loud fart that the whole room hears. He might want to act like nothing happened, but that’s impossible—he knows everyone heard the noise. He’ll feel ashamed, his face will flush red, his ears will burn, and these physical reactions are completely out of his control.

The emotions that come with a first impression are usually not something you feel every day. If you have embarrassing moments constantly, though, you might get that strange, fluttery feeling all the time. When a first impression comes from a rare, awkward situation, it almost always brings shame, confusion, discomfort, or even pain. But when the awkwardness is part of your daily life, it tends to bring happiness instead. For example, when my family asks me embarrassing questions or we share awkward little moments, I feel happy almost every time. These are everyday occurrences, even if they make me a little uncomfortable, so they don’t bother me the way new awkward moments do.

People who go through lots of first impressions, especially awkward ones, often learn to act calm in many situations. Those who used to feel embarrassed or ashamed every time something awkward happened can now handle these moments normally, all thanks to their past experiences. I’ve had plenty of these experiences myself, so instead of feeling shame or embarrassment now, I just feel at ease. When my mom asks if I have a girlfriend, I just smile or tell her I don’t, and it feels totally normal. Or when my friends at school ask if I’m dating the girl I like, I just answer yes or no like any other student—I don’t feel any shame at all. All the experiences I’ve had over the years have made me comfortable with these moments now.

I hope that in the future, when someone asks me something embarrassing that would normally make me feel ashamed at first, that initial feeling of shame won’t show. Instead, my past experiences will take over, so the moment doesn’t become more awkward than it already is. I don’t want to lose my mind and turn a small awkward moment into the worst experience of my life.

Some people argue that young students should not settle on a career pathtoo early, often claiming they lack the time to balance such a commitment with their current schoolwork. However, I strongly believe it is far better for students to decide on a future career when they are still young.

When you figure out what you want to do for work at a young age, you will have years to learn about that field before peers who wait until later even start thinking about their future jobs. Choosing a path early also saves you from wasting time testing out every possible option just to figure out what to do after you graduate high school.

Some critics repeat the claim that young students have no time to commit to a career early, but I still stand by my view that early commitment is beneficial. Take my own experience as an example: I already knew what career I wanted to pursue before I started high school. Now that I am actually in high school, I can focus my energy on learning as much as possible about that specific field.

Students who identify their career goals before finishing high school will have a much clearer sense of what steps to take next with their chosen path. While some argue against early commitment because young students have not yet entered high school, many others, including me, believe it is smart to decide on a career even before starting high school.

In conclusion, young students should commit to a career path early. By the time they grow up, they will have far more knowledge and experience related to that field than their peers who waited to make a choice.

I fully agree with the statement that first impressions cannot be completely erased or altered, no matter how much effort someone puts into changing them.

First impressions stick in people’s minds and are nearly impossible to forget. They can be tied to someone’s attitude, how they carry themselves, or small habits like the way they speak, walk, or eat. Even if you try to shift how someone sees you, the new impression will never match the original. For example, a man who has loved a woman since childhood: even if a new person tries to win her over, that newcomer can never replace the deep first impression the childhood friend left.

This holds true even when people try to copy the thing that made the first impression in the first place. Take the example of someone cooking a meal to impress a friend: if the friend loves that dish and tries to recreate it exactly, it will never taste quite the same. They might not know all the secret ingredients the original cook used, and even if they are told every single component, the final result will still feel different. That original first impression of the meal is fixed, and no copy can match it.

We know first impressions are almost impossible to shift because they work a lot like strong feelings, which can’t be easily altered. Sometimes, these impressions aren’t even based on truth: for instance, a student might lie about their personality or family background to impress their classmates. Even if those classmates later find out the truth, the initial impression they formed will still linger, and it’s nearly impossible to replace it with a new, honest version of the person. Lies can create first impressions just as easily as honesty, but both are equally hard to change.

We need to accept that first impressions are permanent. Instead of trying to alter how others see us, or copying other people’s behavior to make a good impression, we should focus on being confident in who we are. Trying to redo a first impression is often painful, and even if you put in the work, the result will never feel the same as the original moment.

As a student, I believe we need to find a middle ground for our school lunch menu. Making lunches entirely healthy has both advantages and downsides. For one thing, many students don’t look after their health by choosing junk food, even though they love their favorite meals. For example, in my class, when everyone eats pizza for lunch, it upsets their stomachs, and the only nutritious item they have is milk. There’s hardly any other healthy option available.

Another key point is that eating well on school days makes your body feel more comfortable and calm. What’s more, choosing healthier meals supports your long-term health as you get older. Serving nutritious food at school is a great way to keep students from getting sick, and we need protein to grow properly.

My third point is that if the school takes away our favorite dishes, most students won’t touch the healthier alternatives. I remember when we didn’t have Fried Chicken Friday for lunch — that’s everyone’s favorite meal. The whole school was so disappointed that most students skipped lunch entirely just because there was no fried chicken.

So to sum up, I think we should strike a balance: have some days where we serve healthy meals, and other days where we can enjoy our favorite foods.

When the menu is balanced, students will be much happier because they get both their favorite dishes and something nutritious to eat. In my view, I really hope you let us have both options, so every student stays happy and their bodies stay healthy too.

I fully support the school board’s proposal to extend the school day by one and a half hours, as this change would give students more time to learn in every class and create benefits for the entire school community.

My main reason for backing this plan is that many students currently struggle to complete class tasks like worksheets or note-taking within the limited time we have now. Adding an extra hour and a half would give us the extra time needed to finish all required work without rushing, and even catch up on any assignments we didn’t complete in earlier classes.

This change would also be a big help to teachers, not just students. Right now, many educators feel pressured to rush through lessons to fit everything into short class periods. With the extra time, they can teach at a steady pace, finish all planned material, and won’t have to stress about running out of time before a lesson is done.

I also believe that a longer school day would let us learn far more overall. If a student is struggling with a certain topic, teachers will have extra time to re-explain the material step by step, offer more support, and help everyone improve their skills in that subject.

Another key benefit is that the extra time can help students get better at subjects they find difficult, which often leads to higher grades. Teachers will have more opportunities to walk students through tricky problems, so they won’t feel lost or struggle as much during tests. Over time, this support helps students feel more confident in subjects they used to dislike.

The extra hour would also give teachers more time for essential tasks like lesson planning, grading, and other daily responsibilities. They can use this time to catch up on any work they didn’t finish earlier, which reduces their workload and helps them prepare better classes for students.

If we do not add this extra time, there are clear downsides. Teachers will continue to struggle to get through all their planned lessons, and students won’t have enough time to ask for help with topics they don’t understand. This often leads to students falling behind: they have to finish work the next day, while their classmates have already moved on to new material.

For all these reasons, I strongly agree that the school should extend the day by one and a half hours. This change will create clear advantages for both students and teachers, making the school day more productive and less stressful for everyone.

Is attending school from home via online classes actually beneficial for students? Plenty of people argue that virtual learning is a great option, claiming it gives them more time to finish homework, or that logging in from home is simpler than commuting to a physical school. However, I strongly disagree. In my experience, online learning is far more challenging because there is no one there to walk you through tricky concepts, and students end up learning next to nothing. I believe in-person school is the better choice: students rely on teacher support, many enjoy the social aspects of going to school, and even the distractions there serve a purpose.

Not everyone can work independently—while some students prefer to handle assignments alone, many others need direct guidance from teachers. Take my sister, for example: she often stays after school to get extra help from her teachers. She says they break down topics she doesn’t understand, and she’s learned so much from their explanations. When she failed a math test last semester, she stayed late with her teacher to go over every question she got wrong, and ended up mastering the material afterward. Teachers always find time to support students, even when they have their own work to do, because their top priority is making sure we pass our classes.

Another key reason in-person school is better is the social connection it offers. Many students look forward to going to school to hang out with friends and join in fun activities. My brother Generic_Name, for instance, loves playing school sports—he says it’s way more fun to practice and compete with his teammates in person than alone at home. School also teaches us how to interact with other people, which is a key life skill. We get the chance to show up every day, learn new things, and work toward a diploma that will make us proud when we graduate.

Supporters of online learning often argue that virtual classes are better for students who prefer to work alone, and that going to school just distracts them from their home environment. But most students need both healthy distractions and social interaction. School is a place where many feel safe and welcome. My friend, for example, says she gets distracted at school sometimes—but that’s a good thing: she might join a sports team, work on a group activity with classmates, or chat with teachers and staff who have more life experience than she does. Even listening to music while doing homework with friends is a fun, productive distraction.

To sum up, teachers play a vital role in student success: they explain confusing topics, offer extra support, and guide us through material we can’t figure out on our own. With online classes, students are left to struggle through everything by themselves. In-person school is the best way to figure out what you want to do with your life and who you want to become. Schools offer resources like games, libraries with books you can borrow, and mentorship from staff. I firmly believe students should attend physical school instead of taking classes online. Teachers are incredibly supportive—they go out of their way to help whenever we’re stuck. School is a foundational part of life, too: you need a solid education to get into college and eventually land a good job in the future.

John Lubbock, a British author, once argued that each person has full control over shaping their own character. This idea is comforting, but it also raises worries about how young people adjust their personalities when they feel unhappy with who they are, often overthinking their flaws and doubting their natural traits. While our natural personality traits should be the main thing that defines us, it is fair to ask: do outside forces sometimes take over control that should be ours, pushing us to act against our true selves?

We do not always base our self-worth only on our own thoughts, as human beings are social creatures who care about others’ opinions. How other people view our habits and personality can make us feel insecure, pushing us to change ourselves even more than the traits we inherited from our parents or learned in childhood. Most of these pressures come from society, especially the internet, where unregulated content spreads ideas that go far beyond what we might expect or even prepare for. No one controls all these influences, but there are so many out there that everyone can find the ones that fit them best and stick with those, rather than letting random content shape who they are. Overall, society is shifting to accept more diverse ways of seeing the world, which gives people more options to define themselves.

On a personal note, I have seen how much people can shift their outlook, sometimes in ways they never planned. Since moving from California to Virginia, I have changed a lot to fit in with local norms, adapting to what people here consider “normal” even when it feels unfamiliar at first. Some influences are truly hard to avoid: we often see content online that makes us want to copy it eventually, whether it is fashion, speech, or behavior. For example, many rappers reference inappropriate topics like women, violence, or drug use in their music, and we hear about their actions every day through social media and streaming platforms. This is worrying, especially for someone like me who recently moved to a new place and is still adjusting to a completely new environment. My home state of California is full of artists and musicians who purposefully try to influence as many people as possible, since more attention means more moneyand fame for them.

Both children and adults are swayed by the people around them, but we still have the power to pick which ideas we let shape us, even when those influences feel impossible to escape. We choose who we become, and we choose the path we follow, because our decisions always align with what we truly want, not just what others expect of us. For that reason, I am proud of the world we live in today, even with all its flaws and pressures.

Every year brings new developments, some of which threaten us directly: wars, rising pollution, new viruses that can be deadly and spread faster than we can prepare. We are often influenced by others to live in fear of these issues, since they pose real risks to our lives and the lives of people we love. Behind every one of these impactful influences, there is a lot of careful planning and thought, whether it comes from leaders, media, or other powerful groups.

The common saying “have a nice day” is more meaningful than it seems, even if it is often said without much thought. It is what helps us move forward every time we get stuck in a rut, reminding us that small kindnesses matter.

Individuals should turn to experts and official authorities for advice when making major life decisions. After all, people who insist on deciding everything on their own often lack proper knowledge, relying only on their gut feelings and personal ideas. This leads them to believe their choices are correct even when they are not, or when they go against established rules.

Consider laws that govern everyday activities, for example. Using illegal drugs is banned in most states, and even legal substances like alcohol require you to be at least 21 to purchase. Carrying firearms is permitted in many places, but you must have a valid permit and meet age requirements. Driving is another case: you can get a license at 16, but if you do, you are required to have an older, experienced copilot in the car with you until you gain enough practice. These rules are set by authorities to ensure public safety, and ignoring them can lead to serious consequences.

Workplaces also have clear rules that employees must follow, including set schedules and assigned duties. A fixed schedule lets everyone know exactly when to arrive and leave, which keeps the entire organization running smoothly. If staff members showed up whenever they pleased, it would disrupt operations. For instance, imagine you work as an accountant, and the company relies on you to handle morning account tasks. If you decide on your own to skip the morning shift and come in the afternoon instead, the company will face delays with its finances, and you would be held responsible for that mistake. Assigned duties are also tied to your specific skills, so you cannot just decide to take on other tasks on a whim, or you risk losing your job.

Social norms and public rules also limit what individuals can do in shared spaces. You cannot decide to burn down a library just because you think it is a good idea, or hit strangers on the street to amuse your friends. You also cannot trespass on private property to pick a flower you like, even if you think it is harmless. These are not choices that anyone is free to make on their own.

To sum up, people should not be allowed to make all their own decisions about important matters. This is not to say that individuals have no right to shape their own lives or choose their path. Rather, it means no one should be free to do whatever they please, especially when it breaks rules or harms others. Ifully agree with Thomas Jefferson’s view that people can achieve far more when they work together. Too often, people stay passive and end up missing countless chances to grow or improve. It is far better to be part of a community, push for shared benefits, and stay active yourself. Small, consistent active choices can transform many aspects of people’s daily lives.

When we are part of a group, we are less likely to put off daily responsibilities. If we regularly take part in events or tasks that help either ourselves or others, we do two important things: we set higher standards for our community, and we strengthen our own personal mindset.

Reaching a major milestone is not the only way to feel accomplished. Even completing ordinary, everyday tasks in the most helpful way possible counts as real progress.

We should always fight for the outcomes we want, and never let a single chance slip away. I know this from personal experience: I used to be very passive, and I let so many good opportunities pass me by. Losing those chances because I refused to take action still bothers me today.

Now I know that the best way to get what you want out of life is to put in effort every single day. Looking back at my past mistakes, I see that pushing yourself to keep going is the only way to reach real success.

Active people also make it easier for others to reach their own goals. There is nothing more rewarding than helping someone else while making good use of your time. Most people have big dreams, but those dreams only come true if they are willing to put in the work. Even small acts, like lending a hand or joining a local community project, can lead to huge positive changes in society. We only have so many hours in a day, so we should spend that time working toward our goals. Being an active, engaged person really can make a difference, even on a global scale.

To sum up, it does not matter where you come from or what your background is—everyone should make an effort to be more sociable. This helps us reach our goals, gain the benefits we want, and fight for the things that matter most to us. We should never waste a single opportunity, and we should always offer help to those who need it, so we can all grow into better people.

Many schools now give students the choice to take classes from home using online tools or video calls. I believe this option would be a huge help to certain groups of students. For one, lots of high schoolers work late shifts, which clashes with early school start times—often around 7:30 a.m. For these students, getting to school on time means skipping much-needed sleep, which hurts their ability to learn.

Take my friend as an example. He often works after school, usually from 5 p.m. to midnight. After his shift ends, he has to wake up at 5 a.m. to get to school on time. It’s really hard on him—he’s always exhausted during his first morning class because he didn’t get enough rest. He still needs to finish high school, though, since that’s his only path to a better future. He’s not alone, either: plenty of high school students work part-time or full-time after class. Distance learning would let them keep their jobs while getting more sleep. That extra rest would also give them time to finish homework and study for tests, which would improve their grades. Right now, a lot of these working students get low marks simply because they don’t have enough hours in the day to keep up with schoolwork.

Another group that would benefit is pregnant high school students. I’ve noticed that many pregnant high school girls avoid going back to regular school after they get pregnant, often because they face unfair judgment from others who think they’re too young to have a child. Distance learning lets these girls take all their classes from home, avoiding that unfair treatment. It also makes it way easier for them to graduate. A lot of pregnant students start out in traditional schools, but drop out once their baby is born because they have to stay home to care for the infant. With distance learning, they can keep up with their coursework even while raising a newborn, so they don’t have to put their education on hold.

All in all, offering distance learning as an option is a great idea. It supports students who face big obstacles to attending regular school, whether that’s a conflicting work schedule or personal circumstances like pregnancy. By letting them learn from home, schools give these students a real chance to finish high school and build better lives for themselves. It’s a simple change that could make a huge difference for so many young people.

There is no doubt that maintaining a positive attitude is central to achieving success in life. I fully agree with the idea that people who approach life with optimism and kindness play a major role in making society better. However, it is clear that far too many people have negative mindsets that they need to shift. After all, those who cultivate a positive outlook tend to enjoy happier home lives, perform better in their careers, and even uplift the people around them.

When someone has a positive mindset, they tend to treat their family members with more care, which in turn strengthens communities and pushes society forward. They also often inspire others to adjust their own negative habits. For instance, many people today struggle to be patient with children, family members, or even strangers in their community. This is why so many need to work on shifting their mindset, and leave behind the poor choices they have made in the past. Someone with a negative attitude will rarely be able to support their family or help others when they are in need. That said, a growing number of people are trying to change their outlook, because they recognize that adjusting their mindset is the right step to build a happier life with their loved ones and within their community.

A positive attitude also makes a huge difference in the workplace. People who stay upbeat tend to collaborate better with colleagues, and can answer customer questions with a smile and kindness. In contrast, many workers have a negative mindset: when a customer asks them a question, they snap in response, which only makes the customer frustrated too. This shows that everyone needs to practice patience, not just with family or customers, but with every person they interact with. Even if a customer comes in with a bad attitude and speaks rudely, an employee who has cultivated patience can keep their composure and reply politely, instead of matching the customer’s anger. The truth is, people need to learn to manage their reactions if they want to succeed in their jobs.

Beyond personal and professional benefits, people with a positive attitude can also transform the lives of those around them. They help others make wiser choices at school, at work, and in how they treat the people in their lives. For example, teachers often work to improve their students’ mindsets, encouraging them to be more respectful to both staff and classmates. This is because teachers want their students to build better lives for themselves: when these young people grow into adults with positive outlooks, they will make far better decisions. After graduating, they will be able to land good jobs, treat customers with respect, support their families when they are struggling, and contribute to a healthier society overall. In short, having someone with a positive attitude in your life can push you to become a better person.

To sum up, a positive attitude remains one of the most important ingredients for success in life. It strengthens bonds with family and improves connections across society. Many people land great jobs specifically because they show respect to their bosses, customers, and coworkers. Adopting a positive mindset can change not just one person’s life, but the lives of countless others, paving the way for a brighter future for everyone.

I believe school principals should let students bring mobile phones to school, as long as the devices are switched off and put away during class time. Students can use their phones during lunch breaks and other free periods, though. This is mainly because many students need to contact their parents when the school day ends at 3:50. It also helps in case of unexpected emergencies, when a student might need to call home urgently.

It is true that plenty of young people own phones, and some might be tempted to use them to message friends during class instead of paying attention to the teacher. To stop this, there should be a clear rule: any student caught using their phone during class time will get a detention. I am confident most students will follow this rule and keep their phones away during class.

For these reasons, I support the idea ofletting students bring phones to school primarily for emergency situations. They can also use their devices once the school day is over, which is convenient for everyone.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once claimed, "To be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment." I strongly disagree with this statement. True personal achievement does not require letting the world take away your freedom—instead, you must take charge of your own path to become the person you want to be. It seems Emerson did not fully consider the implications of this quote before writing it. After all, staying true to yourself relies entirely on your own choices: you have to make your own decisions, pursue what you love, and refuse to let outside forces control your life.

First and foremost, staying true to who you are means never handing control of your life to the world around you. This starts with making your own decisions. If you let others pick your path for you, you will likely feel lost and worn out later in life, since you gave up your right to choose for yourself instead of deciding your own future. When you make choices that align with your true self, you know exactly why you made them, and that clarity will benefit you in the long run. By contrast, people who let the world decide their future often grow deeply unhappy with their lives.

The second key to achieving real success without letting the world control you is to stay true to yourself and pursue what you genuinely enjoy. If you want to reach your biggest goals, you should focus on work that you actually like doing. When you do things you love, you will never grow tired of putting in effort, and the work will not feel like a burden—it will feel like a natural part of who you are. To make this dream a reality, you must never let the world dictate what you do or push you into paths you do not want to take.

Choosing to stay true to yourself and refuse to let the world control your life is the best decision you can make. When you make your own choices, you learn to tell right from wrong, pick the right career, and set meaningful goals—because no one knows you better than you do. You should never let the world ruin your life: take charge of your own decisions, and show the world that you can succeed on your own terms. Too many people hand over their choice-making power to others, only to ruin their own lives later. They end up feeling lost and unsure of what to do next, all because they did not make their own decisions and let the world choose for them.

In conclusion, you should never let the world change who you are. If you hand over the power to choose your path to others, you will never feel truly satisfied with your life, and you will end up with an unhappy, unfulfilling future. Always stay true to yourself: pick activities you love, whether that is a sport, a hobby, or a career you have always wanted. When you choose things you enjoy, they will never feel like a chore. You might let the world make small choices for you sometimes, but in the long run, you will grow bored and regretful if you are not following your own passions. If you want to achieve real, meaningful success, the most important thing is to never let the world change you.

I fully agree with Albert Einstein’s famous claim that imagination holds more value than knowledge. Imagination is the starting point for all knowledge: when you let your mind wander, you spot chances to learn things you never would have thought to look for otherwise. That said, letting your imagination run too wild can sometimes overwhelm your brain, like when you dive into a complex topic that’s far beyond your current understanding, and your mind feels like it can’t keep up.

Of course, there are moments when knowledge proves more useful than imagination. When you face tough, concrete obstacles, your accumulated knowledge kicks in, acting with more maturity than wild daydreams. Think of the time you got stuck on a tricky math test question: your imagination wouldn’t help you solve that, but the formulas and methods you’d studied would. Even reading books regularly expands your vocabulary, which is a clear benefit of building up knowledge over time.

There are also plenty of times when the two work hand in hand. Take building something, for example: you might want to make something but have no clue what to create. That’s where your imagination steps in, tossing out all sorts of creative ideas for what you could build. Once you settle on a concept, your knowledge takes over to work out the practical steps needed to make it real, pulling from everything you’ve learned about measurements, materials, and structure. That’s how the two work together perfectly.

It’s not all positive, though—both imagination and knowledge can lead to bad outcomes too. When you’re feeling down, your imagination might spiral into thinking you’ll never find anything to make you happy, dragging your mood down further. As a kid, letting your imagination run too far during games with friends could make the rules unfair, which might make you lose a friend. Then there’s the knowledge you gain in middle school, which can shape your test results for better or worse. If you get the highest score in class but brag about it to a friend who got one of the lowest, you might end up pushing that friend away.

Consider a 16-year-old boy looking for work. He might not be the most naturally clever student, but he has several failing grades because he never put in the effort to study. He could either land a decent job or end up unemployed, entirely depending on how much useful knowledge he’s picked up—and since he didn’t study, his options are slim. Other students with stronger knowledge and better grades will snap up the jobs he wanted. If this boy needed the job to cover the cost of food, he’d have to ask his friends to buy meals for him, since he has no income. Down the line, he might even end up homeless, because he has to pay back all the money he borrowed from friends just to get by.

Young children tend to have the most active imaginations, since they don’t have set expectations about how the world works. At night, a little kid might be convinced there are monsters hiding in their closet, and beg their parents to come check for themselves—only for the parents to reassure them there’s nothing there. Later that night, the child hears strange noises but can’t figure out where they’re coming from, so they scream for their parents again, still sure a monster is in the room. The parents insist again that there are no monsters. Eventually, the child works up the courage to leave the room, only to realize the noise wasn’t a monster at all—it was just their parents making sounds to scare them as a joke.

Moderntechnology lets people handle countless daily tasks without ever interacting with another person. We can borrow library books, buy groceries, and play video games without exchanging a single word with anyone. This sharp drop in face-to-face human contact caused by heavy tech use has harmed people’s lives deeply. The truth is, we rely on technology every single moment of every day—so much so that we would be lost without it.

Technology has hurt our lives in clear ways, starting with education. These days, teachers often share lessons through online slideshows, but this format does not show students how to actually complete their assignments. Without in-person teaching, there is no real bond between teachers and students. When I was growing up in my home country, we had almost no technology in schools. My teacher would write out assignments on the blackboard and walk us through each step. If anyone still did not understand, he would explain it again one-on-one. That is what school should focus on: building real connections between teachers and learners. I also remember hanging out with friends in the school cafeteria as a kid, where we would chat about our days. Now, thanks to smartphones, my friends just stare at their screens during lunch, and we barely speak to each other. This loss of human connection from reduced face-to-face interaction is a major problem.

Heavy tech use has even contributed to larger global issues, like wars between countries armed with nuclear weapons. On a personal level, many people no longer leave their homes at all. They stay inside watching movies, reading e-books, and playing video games, since technology gives them everything they need without stepping out. They stop caring about what happens in the outside world—some would not even notice if someone was dying right outside their front door, because technology has made them care less about others and made them weaker. We depend on technology far too much. When I was younger, if I wanted a book, I would walk to the local library to get it, instead of sitting lazily on my couch and ordering it online. Technology encourages laziness. I also remember going out to restaurants with friends to enjoy each other’s company and talk face-to-face. Nowadays, people just order takeout online, eat alone at home, and scroll through their phones instead of chatting with others. Real human connection is disappearing fast.

In the workplace, technology can be useful, but it also causes constant distractions. Humans are easily swayed—if a big game is on and their favorite team is playing, they will forget all about their work. They pull out their phones to watch the match, and often end up getting fired as a result. Then they have to hunt for a new job and figure out how to pay for food. We would not have this issue if technology did not exist. Tech is making more people lose their jobs than it helps, and sometimes it causes more harm than good.

Technology has also led to far more accidents than we saw in the past. Many drivers text while behind the wheel, which makes them miss turns or fail to see other cars, leading to serious crashes. One careless mistake can kill another person, and you will be held responsible for that death. Because of your actions, someone out there loses a husband, wife, or child in an instant.

To sum up, technology has a deeply negative effect on human life. It makes people less human, lazier, weaker, and even useless, and has erased almost all real human connection. We depend on technology so heavily that without it, we would be no better than cavemen—we rely on it for every single part of our daily lives.

A number of educational institutions now provide remote learning options, allowing pupils to join classes via the internet or video calls. However, I strongly believe that students will not gain much from this approach. Many learners struggle to stay focused when they are at home; they often do whatever they please instead of paying attention to the lesson. Without a teacher physically present to guide them, they simply won't absorb as much information.

Another issue is the lack of necessary attention. In a physical classroom, a teacher can see who is struggling, but online, students are often left to their own devices. On days when they feel unmotivated, they might ignore their assignments entirely or simply search for answers online without actually understanding the material. Since no one is watching, they might think this is acceptable, and surprisingly, many still manage to pass the course despite not mastering the subject.

Emotional well-being is another critical factor. Students often face personal challenges and need someone to talk to, whether it’s a teacher, a coach, or a counselor. If they are stuck at home, they may feel isolated and sad because there is no one available to listen. Furthermore, school counselors play a vital role in shaping a student's future. They guide young people toward the right career path and teach them about the professions they might want to pursue. Remote learners miss out on this valuable mentorship.

Remote education also makes it easier for students to cheat. Since there is no direct supervision, some might pay others to do their work or ask a sibling to complete their assignments. This means they aren't learning anything at all. Additionally, if a student is dealing with family problems, it can be difficult to concentrate on a screen. They might request extra help, but without a teacher physically beside them, that support is often unavailable, leading to failure on tests.

Social development is also at risk. Students who stayhome miss out on making friends and learning how to interact with others. This could cause trouble later in life when they enter the real world and need strong communication skills. Moreover, high school is about more than just books; it’s about experiences. For instance, a talented soccer player might miss the chance to play for their school team, potentially losing out on a scholarship that could have helped them become a professional athlete. Online classes take away these opportunities.

Video conferencing tools themselves are often insufficient. Sometimes the video doesn't explain a concept clearly, and students might feel too lazy to rewind and watch it again. In a traditional school setting, a teacher would immediately notice their confusion and offer assistance. Relying solely on digital communication hinders the learning process.

In conclusion, I do not believe students benefit from online classes. They learn less at home due to distractions and a lack of supervision. They need the personal attention of teachers and the emotional support of counselors. In my view, schools should not offer online or video conferencing options. Students will gain a better education and enjoy a richer high school experience if they attend school in person rather than staying behind a screen.

We tend to achieve far more when we focus on tackling the tasks and assignments given to us.

Whenever we put effort into finishing our given work, we almost always end up completing it successfully.

Consider employed people, for example: they put in hours day and night to finish the work, tasks, and assignments tied to their roles.

How do these workers manage to get so much done? Most map out clear, step-by-step plans before tackling any task or assignment. Skipping this planning stage makes it almost impossible to finish work on time. Take a person named Generic_Name, for example: he wants to finish a project, so he first outlines every step he needs to take and lists all the materials required. He follows this plan closely, gathers what he needs, and starts working through each step. By showing up and putting in work every day, he completes his project successfully.

We all have to put in consistent effort to finish any task or assignment we are given.

If you don’t plan ahead or keep working steadily, you will never finish what you start. That is why staying consistent is so important. Think of school students: they work hard to finish class assignments during school hours so they can have free time later, and they double-check their answers to earn good grades. These students are determined to complete all assigned classwork, so they don’t have to do extra homework at home instead of relaxing. Finishing work early is always better than putting it off until later. The same applies to jobs like car manufacturing: factory workers on assembly lines operate machines to attach parts to cars being built, so the finished vehicles can be shipped to dealerships. Almost every part of life depends on getting tasks done on time, to avoid bigger problems down the line. Whether you are a factory worker or a student, everyone has responsibilities to fulfill, which is exactly why we manage to get so much done overall.

Always finish what you start by taking action. There is a simple reason for this: when you complete current tasks and assignments, they won’t get in the way of the next thing you need to do. Clearing your to-do list is a great way to start fresh. Look at company CEOs, for example: they plan exactly what they want to achieve, then figure out the steps to make it happen. CEOs are skilled at getting work done efficiently because they run businesses, and they tell their employees what products (like food, drinks, or clothes) stores need to attract customers. Everyone needs to plan and work toward the goals they want to achieve, including long-term future plans. Putting real effort into your tasks and assignments is the only way to make progress. You have to be clear about what you want, then take consistent action to make it happen, so you can open up more opportunities for your future.

In conclusion, always put effort into the work, tasks, and assignments you are given. This will help you achieve your goals, both now and later in life.

We hear the word 'success' constantly in our daily lives, and nearly everyone has the goal of becoming successful at some point.

School is usually the first step a person takes toward success, and it is often described as the golden period of our lives. To make this time more enjoyable and comfortable for students, schools and teachers include activities like educational, engaging drama role plays, entertaining science experiments, and time for students to practice their favorite musical instruments.

Many of the talented actors, comedians, and actresses we see today were once students sitting in the same desks we use now. They worked hard, joined school role plays, and put in their best effort—and now we can see how far they have come. We can achieve similar success too, and one of the best ways to start is by taking part in school role plays to grow and improve now. On top of that, role plays are genuinely fun. They help us build confidence to speak in front of a crowd and present ourselves, as well as express our emotions. When we perform role plays, we bring joy to others, and nothing feels better than making someone happy.

Science and technology have advanced rapidly, with new experiments happening daily, and no one wants to stop this progress. That is why students need to learn how to conduct experiments. To make science more appealing, schools offer fun, safe experiments like creating rainbows in the air, mixing colors, or making a coin disappear. These boost students’ focus on science and are fun to do, as today’s students are the future of development.

Every student has hidden talents, whether in music, drawing, or sports. These will not stay hidden forever—they will eventually show. Music is the most popular talent among students, as it speaks directly to the heart and captures attention. There are many types of music, from happy to sad or angry, each making listeners feel those emotions. We hear music everywhere, from TV to school music classes. Listening to it lets us release emotions and clear our minds, which is enjoyable.

In the end, school is a place for learning. Anyone who wants to learn will enjoy their classes and gain new knowledge from each one. We should always enjoy our time at school while learning new things, because school is our main source of learning.

Most students look forward to summer vacation more than any other time of year. It’s a chance to relax with family and friends, try new activities, and take a break from school routines. Some teachers argue that the two-month break is too long, claiming students forget what they learned during the school year and struggle to catch up when fall classes start. But I completely disagree with this view.

For me, summer is the most meaningful part of the year because it’s the only time many of us get to really connect with the people who matter most. Most parents work 10 to 12 hours a day, Monday through Saturday, and sometimes even on Sundays. They hardly have any free time to spend with their kids during the school year, so summer vacation is the one chance we have to make up for that lost time. Every student deserves to have this opportunity to bond with their family.

I have so many happy memories of summer breaks spent with my family, and with God when we go on trips or attend church events. But the person I value most during this time is my mom. She’s always by my side, whether things are going well or I’m facing problems. She gives me daily advice on how to avoid mistakes she made when she was young, and her guidance helps me do better in school, at work, and at church. Summer is the time I get to spend the most hours with her, and she always encourages me to improve myself in every part of my life.

My mom is the most important person in my life. She’s always there to support me and help me grow into a kind, responsible person, both in my studies and in other areas. I also love spending time with God during summer, because I learn so many valuable lessons that help me navigate daily life. That’s one of the things I love most about the season.

Two months of summer break is the perfect length, especially after spending nine months in school. The school year can be really demanding, and sometimes you want to do fun things with loved ones but you’re too busy with classes and homework. Longer breaks give students the chance to actually enjoy time with the people who matter to them, instead of always stressing about schoolwork.

Teachers who say students forget everything over summer are wrong. All the information we learn about our schoolwork, projects, and homework is still stored in our brains. We don’t lose the basic, important facts – we just need a quick review when we get back to class.

I also don’t agree with the idea of switching to year-round school, where summer break is only 3 or 4 weeks long. That’s barely a month, and you can’t really enjoy yourself when you’re still thinking about school assignments. Summer is meant to be a time when you can relax with your parents, siblings, and extended family, especially since they usually have their own vacation time during these months too. Summer should be about making happy memories with the people you love, not worrying about classes.

Two months plus an extra two weeks of break is ideal, because it gives you time to clear your mind. You don’t have to think about homework or school projects for a while, which helps you feel refreshed. I learned this the hard way when I was living in Generic_City. Back then, all I could think about was my schoolwork: homework, group projects, presentations, and extracurricular programs. One day, my family invited me to go out with them, but I said no because I had too much work to finish. My uncle told me, “Generic_Name, it’s time to spend time with your family. You need to clear your mind of school stuff.” I refused again, saying I had to get my assignments done. So my whole family went out without me, and I stayed in my room working. Later, I sat there and realized I’d missed out on a wonderful time with my family just to finish school projects. I thought to myself: I should prioritize spending time with my family more, because they’re always there for me.

You never know when you might lose a loved one – your mom, dad, siblings, aunts, uncles, cousins, anyone. That’s why you should cherish every moment you have to spend with them. During the school year, make sure to finish all your work on time, so you don’t have to miss out on family time. Don’t treat your education as a burden. Instead, see it as a chance to grow. School is where you learn about people, animals, the solar system, water, and so many other important things that will help you in the future. You can even use what you learn to teach other people who need that knowledge.

There’s a time for everything: family, work, friends, school. It all depends on how you manage your schedule. That’s why I think we should stick to the rule: when it’s time for school, focus on school. When it’s time for family, focus on family. I’ve changed how I structure my life because of this. Now, I focus on my education from Monday to Friday. On Saturdays and Sundays, I spend time with God and my family. I make sure to give my full attention to whoever I’m with, and I’ve started spending way more quality time with my loved ones.

Summer vacation is especially important for students whose parents work long hours. During the school year, their parents might be out of the house for 8 or 10 hours a day, so they barely see each other. Summer is the only time they get to actually spend days together. You need to keep your life organized and make time for every important part of it. Education matters, but for me, family is even more important. One day, they won’t be here on Earth anymore, and you don’t want to regret not spending time with them.

Teachers also get to enjoy their summer break and spend time with their own families. When they come back to school in the fall, they just need to review old material with students – not everything is forgotten. The information is still in our brains, we just need a quick refresher.

Overall, two to three months of summer vacation is the perfect amount of time to enjoy with the people who mean the most to you. So make the most of it, and have a fun, memorable summer. To all the teachers reading this: don’t complain that summer is too long. For students, it’s a very short break. You enjoy your vacation too!

Many people are unfamiliar with how to play basketball, but I have a few tips that can help you improve your skills, set up games, or just enjoy the sport more.

First, consider the environment where you play. While some people prefer indoor courts, I recommend playing outside most often during the summer, since temperatures are more comfortable then than in other months. You should also avoid playing in extreme heat or cold, as these conditions make it hard to perform well. Strong winds are another issue to watch out for—high gusts will disrupt your gameplay, making it tough to control the ball or aim shots. The best seasons to play are spring and summer, when weather is mild. Finally, stick to daytime games: at night, visibility is poor, but during the day you can see the entire court and hoop clearly.

Having the right equipment is essential for basketball. First, you’ll need a proper basketball: make sure it’s fully inflated and has a firm, non-slip grip so you can handle it easily. The court itself needs to be large enough to fit standard gameplay, with a flat, even surface to stop the ball from rolling unevenly. You’ll also need a sturdy pole to hold the hoop, set at the proper height so the basket is reachable for shots. The hoop should be wide enough to fit the ball, with a net that’s not too long, so the ball drops through quickly after a made shot. Last, the court should have clear boundary lines: these help you line up your shots and know when the ball is out of bounds.

Basketball skills are key if you want to win games. Staying fit is especially important, as it boosts your stamina so you can keep playing hard for longer. Teamwork also makes a huge difference: even a simple pass to a teammate can turn a losing game into a win. If you want to get better at the sport, practice your shots regularly and work on creating open opportunities to score. Developing strategies with your teammates will help you outplay the opposing team, and planning ahead gives you backup options to avoid losing. At the end of the day, consistent practice is the only way to improve at any skill, basketball included.
