British Prime Minister Winston Churchill once said that true success means moving from one failure to the next without ever losing your passion. I think this is an incredibly valuable idea. Some people argue that if you keep failing over and over, it just proves you aren’t talented or smart enough to succeed. But I believe the opposite: as long as you hold onto your enthusiasm, you will eventually reach your goals.

The perfect example of this is Thomas Edison, who invented the first practical light bulb. He failed thousands of times during his experiments, but he never let those setbacks crush his excitement for the project. After countless failed attempts, he finally created a working light bulb that changed human life forever. This shows me that if you stay passionate about what you’re working on and keep putting in effort, you will eventually achieve the result you want, just like Edison did.

Another key reason I support this view is that you need to be brave enough to keep trying. When you go through failure after failure, the people around you—even your friends—might tell you to give up, insisting you’ll never succeed. They’re just offering their opinion, but that doesn’t mean you have to listen. If you stop just because others doubt you, you’ll lose the enthusiasm you had for something you truly cared about. Instead, trust in yourself, keep pushing forward, and never let go of that drive.

I also think enthusiasm isn’t something you can just summon out of nowhere. The only way to have it is to find something or someone that really captures your interest. For example, I can play video games for an entire day without getting bored, but sitting down to study for a whole day feels impossible. I strongly believe that achieving our dreams requires consistent effort, and we must stay clear on what we want out of life. It’s a fact that we get more done when we stay busy working toward our aims: keeping our minds focused on our goals or the person we want to become means we achieve far more than if we waste time on irrelevant activities.

Take school as a clear example. If we put in hard work and concentrate on our academic goals—like earning high grades and graduating—we set ourselves up to achieve great things later. Building a solid school record can lead to a fulfilling career where we earn enough to live comfortably, doing work we actually enjoy rather than settling for a boring, low-skill job.

Another case: once we settle on a specific goal, we should keep our minds fixed on it and put in the work to reach it, no matter how tough the process gets. Since this goal reflects what we truly want to be and what we enjoy, it will lead to a stable, happy future. A good job from reaching our goals means we won’t have to stress about money, so we can focus on enjoying life while still putting in daily effort toward our aims.

There’s another key reason to stay busy with activities we care about: it keeps us out of trouble that could block our progress. For instance, turning to drugs, alcohol, or other harmful habits ruins our lives, as these distractions pull us off our path and make us lose faith in ourselves. One single bad choice can wipe out all the hard work we’ve put in over years. That’s why we must stay focused on whether we really want to become a professional or build a meaningful future for ourselves.

On the other hand, some people argue that doing nothing has value too—that it’s okay to live life without working hard for our goals, and that everything that happens to us is just fate or destiny. I disagree with this completely. We have the power to decide who we want to become. That’s why God gave us free will: to choose what we want to fight for, and make decisions that help us achieve whatever we want in life.

In conclusion, I believe we can achieve amazing things if we work hard for our goals and keep our minds focused on productive, enjoyable activities—whether that’s school, our future career, or a job we love. Staying busy with useful tasks benefits our lives in countless ways. We also need to avoid distractions like drugs, alcohol, and other harmful habits. We should treat life as a precious gift from God, and be mindful of every decision we make. If we make a mistake, we can learn from it. It’s incredible how much we can achieve when we spend our time doing work we truly care about.

Reaching out to several people for help with a problem or question is far smarter than only consulting one person. When you gather responses from multiple sources, you’ll notice that while some replies overlap, many others offer unique perspectives you wouldn’t have heard otherwise.

Relying on a single person’s input is risky, as they might not have the right information or could even be mistaken. Instead, turn to people you trust: parents, aunts, uncles, close friends, anyone whose judgment you value. This way, you collect a range of opinions, which helps you make a more informed decision. Sticking to just one advisor has two major downsides: first, that person may simply not know the answer, and second, you’re limiting yourself to a single viewpoint, which isn’t the best way to solve a problem. You might also find that you don’t fully trust that one person’s suggestion, which makes it harder to act on their advice. Asking a group of people, though, greatly increases your chances of getting a clear, correct answer.

To sum up, seeking input from more than one person lets you gather diverse opinions, and it’s far more likely that someone in your circle will have the correct solution to your issue. Of course, some people avoid sharing their problems or questions with others. They might feel shy or nervous, or worry that the person they ask won’t understand what they’re trying to say. This can definitely happen: a friend of mine once had a tricky math problem, and when he asked his teacher, the teacher completely misunderstood what he was asking. The teacher tried to explain a different concept entirely, which wasn’t helpful at all. My friend then turned to the classmate sitting next to him, who immediately got what he meant, and helped him work through the exact question he had.

The word 'influence' covers a lot of ground. It can mean many different things, and there are countless ways to talk about it. Personally, I have a negative view of influence. Too often, it pushes people to make poor choices, pressuring them into actions they might not otherwise take. Take, for example, someone trying to get you to drink alcohol or use illegal drugs—that is a clear case of harmful influence. Or imagine a friend daring you to steal a bike, telling you it will be fun—that is another obvious example of bad influence. I also know people who copy the lifestyles of others even when those habits are unhealthy or unwise, which is another form of negative influence. Even small choices count: when someone pressures you to buy unhealthy items like McDonald’s meals, Red Bull, or potato chips, that is also a type of bad influence. To sum up, I believe influencing others is mostly harmful, as it often forces people to act against their better judgment and leads many young people down difficult paths. That said, influence is not always negative. It can also be a very positive force, helping people grow in their careers and personal lives.

This cross-age program offers a range of benefits for all participants: it supports students in picking up new knowledge, helps older students grow more responsible through teaching roles, gives younger students chances to meet new peers and practice communication, and trains older learners to plan lessons and stay organized. It also lets both age groups pick up new skills and explore different learning approaches.

The first major advantage of this program for younger and older students is that it gives younger participants access to new knowledge. I believe introducing new concepts to young learners early is valuable because it sets them up for success later in life. Through this program, younger students can discover interesting new topics and even start thinking about what career they might want to pursue in the future. When older students guide them through new material, younger learners can absorb that information and later share what they’ve learned with their peers. I think this setup works well because it lets young students apply what they’ve picked up to real-life situations later on—for example, math skills they learn now will help them handle taxes and bills as adults. This program truly supports young students in expanding their knowledge base.

Another key benefit is that teaching younger peers helps older students mature. I think this program is a great learning tool because it pushes older participants to focus on how to explain concepts clearly and choose appropriate material for their students. Since older students usually have more knowledge than the younger ones they work with, they have to figure out which topics their students struggle with, what content to cover, and the best way to present that information. This process makes older students more attentive to the needs of others, and taking on a teaching role helps them feel more responsible and grown-up. The program also encourages older learners to think more deeply: they have to come up with creative lesson ideas, consider how each activity will help their students, and ask themselves questions to refine their teaching approach.

The program also boosts communication skills for younger students, who get to interact with new people they might not have met otherwise. I think this is helpful because talking regularly with new mentors and peers reduces shyness over time, making it easier for young learners to speak to unfamiliar people. As they practice communicating with older students, younger participants gain confidence and stop feeling scared to talk to someone they don’t know. This increased comfort with new people also makes them more social overall, and helps them feel less nervous about public speaking tasks like presenting class projects or talking to a group.

A fourth benefit is that the program helps older students become more organized and prepared. To teach effectively, older participants have to identify which topics their younger students are struggling with, then plan lessons that address those gaps. They also have to schedule when and where they will hold their teaching sessions, which pushes them to manage their time and resources carefully. I think this program really helps older students build organizational skills because it requires them to structure their lessons step by step: they decide what material to cover first, how to present each part, and what activities will help their students learn best. Basically, they have to plan every detail of their teaching in a logical order.

The final reason I think this program is so valuable is that it lets both younger and older students support each other and improve their own learning skills. When participants work together, they can find easier, more effective ways to learn. Both age groups can share their preferred learning methods and trade ideas: younger students might pick up new study habits from older peers, while older students might learn simpler ways to understand complex topics from their younger students. This back-and-forth teaching helps everyone get better at areas they used to struggle with. The program also exposes all students to different learning techniques, like using flashcards, rereading material, or watching tutorial videos to solve math equations, so everyone can find the study method that works best for them. This helps all participants learn more quickly and easily, and lets them help others identify their own ideal learning styles.

Overall, this program helps both older and younger students strengthen their learning skills, and it is a great way to discover new, interesting knowledge that will benefit students long into the future.

Does the reduced face-to-face interaction caused by technology have a positive or negative impact on people’s lives?

Technology has a positive effect on people’s lives, including how they connect with others.

For one, digital tools make it simple to stay in touch with loved ones who live far away, like in other countries or states, even if you can’t visit them in person regularly. They also help people expand their social circles by meeting new friends online, and make it far easier to message nearby friends to plan outings.

Technology also plays a key role in the workplace. Businesses rely on it to store customer details, such as names and order history, and keep all important company documents organized. It also lets managers reach employees quickly, whether to share updates or let them know what tasks to complete the next day via email or phone calls.

Students benefit too. Many schools now let learners use laptops in class, which is much more convenient than lugging heavy physical books to school every day. A single laptop holds all the textbooks needed for every class. Students can also submit assignments and projects with just a click, so teachers receive their work instantly to grade. On top of that, teachers can use videos to explain difficult concepts more clearly to their classes.

Contrary to what some people claim, technology does not harm people’s lives. Its impact is overwhelmingly positive. Most of the people who argue otherwise are older adults who have not grown comfortable using digital tools in their daily routines.

To me, wisdom is best represented by my grandfather, who often shares stories of his early life in his home country. He grew up in deep poverty, sometimes struggling to find enough food to get through each day, and he always emphasizes how rare and valuable education was backthen. He also opens up about losing both his father and brother when he was between six and eight years old, as well as the immense challenges he faced when he first moved to the United States.

My grandfather was born into poverty, with one brother, a mother, and a father who worked in construction. His mother mostly handled household tasks: getting the children ready for school and preparing meals for the family. The nearest school was 3.4 miles from their home, so he had to walk there every day, but he never missed a day because he loved learning and found classes genuinely enjoyable. In his community, attending school was considered a huge privilege — most local children never got the chance to enroll at all, which made his education feel even more special.

My grandfather was only five years old when his father passed away. His dad had struggled with many personal issues and had gotten mixed up with gangs and dangerous people. He stayed hidden for a long time to avoid those who were looking for him, but one day, he went to work as usual and four men were waiting for him. He tried to run, but he was too slow — one of them shot him three times. He lay bleeding on the dirt ground, and he died before anyone could arrive to help him.

My grandfather’s brother later fell ill and stayed sick for two full months. He was a very smart man who had taught my grandpa how to read and write more fluently. My grandpa always said his brother was the reason he earned such high grades in school. When his brother got sick, my grandpa did everything he could to care for him and keep him alive, but medical care back then was very poor. This happened in 1976, outside the United States, and even if the right medicine had been available, it would have been far too expensive for the family to afford. All my grandpa and his mother could do was pray every night for his brother to get better, but he eventually passed away in his sleep. The family dug a grave for him, and everyone gathered to say prayers. His mother cried every day for a full month before finally coming to terms with his death.

As my grandfather grew older, he met my grandmother and they had two daughters and two sons together. He decided to take the test to move to the United States, which he said was very difficult. He had to study a notebook with 200 possible questions about US history and facts, then answer 50 random questions pulled from that material. After he passed the test, he packed his bags and said goodbye to his wife and four children. He wanted to settle in Virginia, and he made that happen, but life was hard at first because he only spoke a little English. He found a job at a restaurant, plus two other part-time roles, and as soon as he started earning money, he saved every extra cent to bring his family over. He said it took him about eight months to save enough for all of their travel costs. Once they joined him in the US, I was born shortly after. We have lived in Generic_City for as long as I can remember, and now my grandfather works at a local school. He is happy with how his life has turned out.

What happens if we choose not to take any action?

The founding father Thomas Jefferson once wrote, "Determine never to be idle... It is wonderful how much may be done if we are always doing something." Staying constantly busy makes it far easier to reach the dreams and goals we set for ourselves.

We get far moredone when we keep moving forward, for three key reasons: the people around us want us to succeed, taking risks and acting on our plans matters, and we need to stay true to who we are.

Some people argue that taking a break or doing nothing at all serves a purpose. They might say that God has a plan for our lives, so we don’t need to rush. Others claim that achieving big dreams takes patience, so there’s no need to act right away. A third group insists we should think carefully before making any move, so inactivity is smart.

There are several key reasons why staying active helps us achieve more.

1. The people around us offer support. Why? Our friends and family want us to do well. They hope we can build a good life, avoid struggling with poverty, and reach our full potential. They know what our dreams are because they care about us and understand who we are as people.

2. We must take risks and act. Why? When we work towards a goal, we learn more about our own strengths and limits. We prove to ourselves that we are capable of achieving what we set out to do. Every risk we take gives us experience, so next time we face a challenge, we know how to handle it and can do even better.

3. Stay true to who you are. Why? We all have dreams we hope to achieve one day. When you believe in your own ability, you can picture yourself reaching those goals. You know deep down that you are capable of making progress, especially when you have the encouragement of your family and your own inner drive. Reminding yourself "I can do this" helps, especially when you look back at all the things you have already achieved.

The more we believe in ourselves, the more we achieve. This is easier when we have people cheering us on, when we push ourselves to keep going even when risks feel scary, and when we stay focused on our dreams. If we never take action, we will never reach any of our goals or make our dreams come true.

I believe updating the cafeteria’s menu would be a positive step. At my school, the food is only decent occasionally, but most days it’s unappealing — often the same repetitive dishes served week after week. This is why so many students are unhappy with the current cafeteria offerings.

Lowering the prices on the menu is another smart change to make. Many students cannot afford to buy lunch right now, so some even skip meals entirely — even on days when the cafeteria serves better food. This is a big problem that needs fixing.

It would also be helpful to share the daily cafeteria menu with all students in advance. Everyone wants to know what’s being served each day before they head to the cafeteria.

I think the most important change is adjusting the length of our current one-hour lunch break. Most students want extra time to chat with friends, and some hope to head to classrooms after eating to discuss class material with teachers.

To sum up, all these changes would greatly improve the cafeteria experience for everyone. First, introducing a brand new menu is necessary because most students dislike the current food. At my school, meals are mostly unappealing because the staff refuse to switch up the offerings — all my friends complain about the food too, and they all say most people hate the current menu. Lowering prices is another key step, since the current menu is too expensive for many students. Cutting costs would let students with less money buy lunch regularly. We should also post the daily menu in advance: for example, putting a calendar on the cafeteria’s front door would let everyone see which days have better meals. Finally, adjusting the lunch break makes sense. My school gives us one hour for lunch, and after eating I can go anywhere, but I usually head to my classroom to do homework or chat with friends. These conversations often cover class topics, games, or plans with friends, and I learn a lot from them. Making all these changes to the cafeteria would benefit every student.

Modern technology has become a huge part of our daily lives, offering plenty of benefits but also some downsides. You can find tech tools in almost every space: our homes, workplaces, hospitals, schools, and even cars—it’s practically everywhere. While tech definitely simplifies so many parts of human life, it also has a habit of making people less active. Instead of heading outdoors to play soccer or other sports with friends, which would keep them healthier, many people choose to stay inside all day gaming or using apps.

I believe technology is overall a positive force in our lives today. It assists us with so many essential tasks, from saving lives to supporting education—you’d be hard pressed to find a place without some form of tech these days. We rely on it to live comfortably, and it even lets us help others more effectively. For instance, medical equipment in hospitals gives doctors the tools they need to save patients’ lives. At schools, computers let students complete assignments and learn more efficiently. Even in manual jobs like construction, specialized tools and machinery (which are all forms of technology) make physically demanding work far less difficult.

Another major benefit of technology is how it connects people. Whether you’re traveling or living in another country, you can stay in touch with loved ones 24 hours a day, 7 days a week through social media, messaging apps, or video calls. This makes it easy to maintain relationships even when you’re far apart. However, we still need to stay cautious, as some people use technology to carry out harmful activities.

To sum up, technology improves and even saves lives on a daily basis. We use it constantly in our everyday routines, and it is truly a valuable part of modern life. That said, we must use it responsibly, as overusing tech can lead to addiction. Just like with anything else, too much of a good thing can become harmful, so it’s important to find a healthy balance in how we use technology.

I agree with Ralph Waldo Emerson’s view on the value of individuality. When you stay true to yourself, some people will feel at ease around you, while others won’t. But nothing matters more than being your authentic self. You never know what you’re capable of achieving until you push past your own limits. The world will throw obstacles your way, trying to pressure you into making bad choices or pretending to be someone you’re not. But don’t let that break you—never give others the power to drag you down.

When people see the progress you make, they might start to resent you. But you don’t have to pay attention to their criticism, and you shouldn’t change your mind just because they’re talking behind your back. There will always be people who try to make decisions for you: for example, if you want to study a certain subject in university, but your parents or friends tell you to pick a major you have no interest in. If you’re an adult, you have the right to make your own choices. You should pursue what you enjoy, which is exactly why staying true to yourself matters, no matter what.

Take my own life for example. My father left when I was young, leaving my mom to raise me alone. She works very hard to give me the opportunities I have today, and seeing that sacrifice pushes me to stay true to myself every day. I work hard constantly, because her effort for me is amazing. Back in my home country, gangs often shoot people for no reason, and I grew up with my grandmother in a neighborhood full of gang members. But none of that changed me. I could have easily joined them, but I was raised with good values and education, so I never wasted my potential.

As the writer Ralph Waldo Emerson once said, “To be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment.”

Always stay true to yourself, no matter what. Life is hard, so you must work for what you want. Don’t listen to those who don’t want to see you happy. Trust in God and your own abilities. In conclusion, ignore anyone who opposes your decisions—they only want to hurt you.

Young people should decide on a career path before they start high school. When they have a clear goal in mind, they can figure out exactly how long they need to stay in high school and plan to graduate on time. Focusing on a specific career also helps them study more efficiently, so they can finish high school faster. On top of that, picking a career early lets students get ready for the field they want to enter while they are still in high school.

First, when students know which career they want, they can calculate exactly how many years they need to spend in high school to meet graduation requirements. This stops them from wasting time or staying in school longer than necessary. Many teens dislike going to school and want to finish as quickly as possible, often because they are eager to start working. Having a clear career plan helps them stay on track to graduate without delays.

Second, choosing a career early helps students focus better on their schoolwork. Instead of drifting through classes without a goal, they can direct their energy toward their future plans. High school gives young people a chance to explore career options early, so they can take classes that match the field they want to enter. If a student already knows their chosen career, they can study exactly what they need, which will make them much better prepared when they move on to college.

Third, having a set career path lets students use their high school years to get ready for their future studies or jobs. This pays off when they get to college, because they will not waste time stressing over what career to pick. They can avoid spending extra years in college or university, since they already made progress toward their goal while in high school. Some careers require years of skill-building, practice, and extra study, but starting that work in high school cuts down on the time they will need to spend on it later.

To sum up, students should be expected to pick a career by the time they enter high school. This lets them understand how long they need to stay in high school and plan to graduate on time. It also helps them focus on their studies so they can finish high school faster, and get prepared for the career they want to pursue. These are all key reasons why young people should commit to a career path at an early age.

I disagree with this idea, mainly because achieving success is hugely important, while experiencing failure is one of the worst things that can happen to a person. When people start to fail, they often lose all motivation to keep doing the activities they used to enjoy. If someone is stuck in a cycle of failure, they have very little ability to turn things around and boost their own success. By contrast, when successful people are at the peak of their careers, they have the freedom to do whatever they want. They can maintain their success, hold onto their position, and live in comfortable, favorable circumstances.

That said, being successful all the time can actually lead to failure in the end. If someone keeps doing the exact same tasks day after day, they will eventually grow tired and burnt out. This exhaustion is exactly how even thriving careers or stable jobs end up falling apart. People can avoid this outcome by addressing the issues that lead to failure early on. However, if they fail to spot the warning signs that they are starting to struggle, or if they stop paying attention to their work and stop caring about what they are doing, they will inevitably face decline.

On the other hand, people who face failure early in life often gain extra courage and push themselves to work much harder. This drive can help them become incredibly successful later on. After struggling with failure for a long period, many people manage to turn their lives around almost overnight. This is how many brilliant, talented people operate: after going through long stretches of failure, they work even harder, develop strong skills, and become highly competent in their chosen field, eventually achieving great success.

Summer should be a relaxed, ordinary time for students and all other people. It’s meant for enjoying quality time with family and friends, doing fun activities like shopping, swimming, or going on vacation. Summer doesn’t last forever, since winter will arrive soon, so it’s important to spend time with the people you care about. That said, some people can’t hang out with their loved ones because they have to work or handle other critical responsibilities.

Summer has some of the most pleasant weather of the year: it’s warm, not freezing cold, so you can head to the beach and have a great time. Many people count summer as one of the best times of year because there are so many water activities to try, plus options like camping and hiking. There are countless things to do during the summer months, like traveling to another state or having a sleepover at a friend’s house. Kids especially love summer because there’s no school, so they can stay home and play video games, or spend time with friends, family members, aunts, or uncles.

Summer is perfect for either staying indoors or heading out to have fun with friends. When the season starts, tree flowers bloom and eventually turn into fruit, while winter makes those flowers fall and temperatures drop drastically. Summer comes around every year, so we always have chances to bond with family and friends, or travel out of town to visit elderly parents. Even though summer is warm, it can also bring heavy rain sometimes, just like colder weather can.

Schools break for summer so students can have fun, and teachers get a well-deserved break too. Sometimes summer temperatures get extremely high, even passing 100 degrees Fahrenheit. Many people host pool parties during the season, and folks love summer because they have the freedom to do whatever they like, whether that’s fishing, camping, or diving. Summer can be a great or unpleasant experience, depending entirely on the choices you make.

Summer also brings local fairs with tons of games, which are fun to attend with friends or family. The warm weather is ideal for swimming with loved ones; public pools open for the season, and you can also swim in rivers or try other water activities. Many people use the summer to visit family, or travel to popular spots like California, Generic_City, and Florida. Summer is truly the best time of year because it returns every 12 months, giving everyone the chance to do exactly what they enjoy most.

I strongly believe that staying busy and active at all times helps us achieve far more in life. This is a view I fully support. When we keep ourselves occupied with meaningful tasks regularly, we naturally develop strong, positive routines. Consistent activity paves the way for real success, and you will never find traces of laziness along the path to achieving your goals.

Building these steady habits makes it far easier to tackle studying, learning new skills, or any other task we need to handle. We feel more confident and at ease when working, and others start to see us in a more positive light, treating us with greater respect. These useful routines also lay the groundwork for smooth, productive workflows.

Steady, active effort is what leads to genuine success. Think of a restaurant: it can only serve tasty, high-quality meals if the staff put in careful preparation work beforehand. The same applies to our own lives. No one becomes a skilled doctor, a talented architect, or excels in any other field without putting in focused, hard work over time. Staying busy and committed to our tasks is the ultimate key to unlocking success.

You will never spot signs of laziness on the road to achievement. If we slack off, stay inactive, or stop putting effort into learning and working, we will never see good results. Employers and colleagues alike avoid lazy people, since they contribute nothing and cannot deliver quality work. We should never feel too satisfied with what we have already achieved, as that overconfidence often leads straight to laziness. Instead, we need to keep working hard every single day, and dismiss the idea that doing nothing can ever help us reach our goals.

Hard work helps us build solid, productive routines, and those routines are what ultimately lead to success. We should never think we have done enough, or reached our limit. As Thomas Jefferson once wrote, “Determine never to be idle... It is wonderful how much may be done if we are always doing.”

Removing students’ favorite dishes from the school menu is a bad idea, especially the plan from the principal. If schools get rid of meals kids like, many might skip class entirely, since they won’t want to eat the bad lunch options. Offering more meal choices would make students like lunch more. This proposal from the principal is very poorly thought out.

Right now, some students already dislike the served food: it might be undercooked, or have cafeteria staff’s hair in it. All kitchen workers should wear hair nets whenever they cook, for both morning and afternoon meal prep. The same goes for bananas: throw out any that look bad, plus any food past its expiration date. Most students don’t care about nutrition rules—they only eat what tastes good. Schools shouldn’t remove chips or other snacks either, since most people like snacks more than full meals. The best choice is to keep the current menu as is, so everyone can enjoy the food they like.

I’d like to share my perspective on a well-known quote by author Ralph Waldo Emerson: staying true to who you are in a world that constantly pushes you to become someone else is the greatest accomplishment.

I completely agree with this idea. Trying to fit into a version of yourself that others expect is far harder when you have no one supporting you. Even if you put in your best effort, the journey feels like a really tough challenge. But if you have people around you who encourage you to stay authentic, the process becomes much smoother. That’s why I believe staying true to yourself when the world demands you change is one of life’s biggest achievements.

This makes sense to me, especially when you consider how hard it is to be your genuine self around people who spread negativity. Keeping your authenticity in the face of constant pressure to conform is truly a top accomplishment.

For instance, when you stick to being your authentic self and work toward your own goals, many people will dislike your confidence. They may try to tear you down or make you stumble. In a world that constantly tries to force you into a different mold, managing to stay true to who you are is always an amazing achievement.

It’s also wonderful if you’re in a space where people accept you exactly as you are, because being authentic lets you achieve anything you set your mind to. Even when the world pushes you to change, staying true to yourself is the best accomplishment of all. Life gets easier when you’re honest about who you are. We all have to make tough choices sometimes, and I believe being your genuine self will always lead you to make the right ones.

Is it better to be honest or to tell lies? We should always pick honesty. Think about the people you know best—the ones you assume would never trick you. If you lie to them, you will hurt them more than anyone else ever could. What’s more, if you are not truthful, people will never trust what you say.

These days, far too many people lie constantly and refuse to be truthful. If no one is honest, who can we possibly rely on? If you make a habit of lying, people will eventually cut you off, and no one will step in to help when you run into trouble. The truth is, lies always come to light eventually, so it is far better to be honest from the start. Lying to the people you care about most is especially disappointing, since they are the ones who support you through everything.

I believe that anyone who is not honest does not deserve to be trusted. Imagine trusting someone with a secret, asking them not to tell a soul, only for them to share it anyway. Would you ever trust that person again? I know I wouldn’t. If you want to earn people’s trust, you have to start over from nothing. Stop lying to the people you care about, and make a habit of telling the truth to everyone. Be kind, and avoid getting into unnecessary trouble. When people trust you, they will stand by you no matter what happens.

No one in the world enjoys being lied to. Most people value being able to trust others, so we should be honest all the time, not just when it feels convenient. Being truthful helps your parents trust you, which means they will not worry that you are doing or saying things you shouldn’t. Honesty also brings plenty of good things into your life: you can land great jobs, and handle all parts of your life responsibly.

If you are honest with everyone you meet, people will believe you every time you speak. They will trust every word you say. If you follow through on what you say you will do, or keep the promises you make, people will give you all the trust you need.

I know that being honest can sometimes hurt someone’s feelings. But instead of letting that get you down, turn that moment of weakness into a strength. You will feel better than you ever have before. Some people act mean when you tell the truth—just ignore them, stop talking to them, but give them another chance if they change their ways. Don’t listen to the things they say about you, since they are not even honest with themselves. In the end, the best choice is to be honest all the time.

The following text focuses on the idea that first impressions are not fixed, and can shift as time passes. It shares information with readers about the different reasons why these initial judgments change, and how such changes affect us. The piece uses real-life examples and supporting points to make the topic clearer, and stresses that impressions can alter at any moment, not just in the early stages of knowing someone or something.

A first impression forms the very first time you encounter a person, place, or object. It is the initial opinion your brain forms about that thing, but this early judgment often shifts as you get to know it better. When we first meet someone, our minds jump to a conclusion that might be accurate or completely wrong—we can only figure out which is true as time goes on.

These changes can work against us or in our favor. That means we might initially think something is great when it is actually flawed, or assume something is bad when it is actually good. A negative example would be buying a car that looks perfect on the outside, only to find out during a mechanical inspection that it has serious internal damage. A positive example is hearing a nasty rumor about a classmate or coworker, then meeting them yourself and realizing the gossip was completely untrue.

First impressions shift for all kinds of reasons tied to our own thoughts and feelings. Common causes include inaccurate initial judgments, letdowns, frustration, or even self-correction. All of these can shape how we view someone or something over time. For instance, when we are in a bad mood or feeling angry, even small things can seem irritating or unpleasant. Another example is when we correct our own earlier mistake—maybe we assumed a new cafe had bad coffee, but after trying it a few times, we realize our first opinion was wrong.

To sum up, first impressions matter a lot, but they are never set in stone as purely good or bad—our opinions almost always evolve. I believe it is better to wait a little before forming a strong positive or negative judgment about someone or something you do not know well yet. For this reason, I agree that first impressions can and do change as time passes.

Extending the school day is a terrible idea, and I’m strongly against it. Right now, students and teachers already have important tasks to handle after the final bell rings for both staff and students. Parents need to drive their kids to soccer practice or make it to doctor’s appointments, and these are the only free windows we have to get these essential errands done, from taking kids to sports practice to attending medical appointments. Some teachers live far away, like in Generic_City or other distant neighborhoods, and a longer school day would only make their already long commutes even worse. If we add more time to the schedule, parents will be stuck waiting to take their kids to football or soccer games, and students won’t get home until even later. Most of us already wake up at 7am and get home around 5 or 6pm, which is stressful enough—adding more school time would cut out all the hobbies and activities we usually do after class, like hanging out with friends or playing outside, leaving only time for homework. Before you know it, it’s 8pm and time to go to bed, with no chance to relax or prepare for the next day.

This plan is especially bad for students who commute from far away, often spending hours on buses or in cars just to get to class. I used to live in Generic_City, so I’ve experienced this firsthand, and even staying after school for a short time means I don’t get home until 7 or 8pm. Adding more school hours would make this way worse for kids in the same situation, and that’s only with the current schedule: they’d get home late, still have to finish all their homework, and that’s way too much to handle on a tight deadline. Longer days would also mess up schedules for both kids and their parents—maybe you can’t go to soccer or other extracurricular activities you’re signed up for, and their parents won't be able to attend their games or events either, just because school runs later. Classes are already 80 minutes long, which is tiring enough without adding extra time to sit in a classroom, and the current 80-minute classes already feel never-ending.

Even a small 30-minute extension would cause huge problems. Teachers might start assigning even more homework than we already get, which would eat into the only 3 hours of free time we have each day, which we currently barely have time to finish. For teachers who live far away, many of whom already leave home before the sun rises, leaving school at 6pm means hitting rush hour traffic, so they get home even later. Then they still have to grade papers after a full day of teaching, and wake up super early to get back to work the next day. Doing that same exhausting routine every day for years is way too hard—even as a student who doesn’t have a full-time job, I can see that would be awful, and I can’t even imagine how exhausting that would be.

If administrators really want to add 30 minutes to the school day for no real benefit, they should at least shift the start time to 8am instead. Waking up early and then leaving school even later doesn’t make any sense, especially since most students are already groggy and struggling to focus by the time the first bell rings. It would be way better to do the opposite: start later and end earlier. That would make everyone happier, no one would be in a bad mood, the whole day would feel more relaxed, and everyone’s energy levels would be higher.

Another issue is lunch times for 8th graders, who are already halfway through the school day by the time we eat. We already don’t get lunch until 1:40pm, which is way too late for growing teenagers, and adding 30 minutes would push that to 2:10pm. I already hate waiting that long to eat, and I don’t want to be starving through the afternoon. When you’re that hungry, you get “hangry” and can’t focus on your work—you just get frustrated and upset. It’s also unfair to bus drivers, many of whom rely on the bus to get to and from school, who would have to drop students off at 6pm. They need time for their own families too, instead of being stuck in traffic all day, not just driving back and forth picking up kids late.

Attending high schools that let students explore career paths early is a great option for learners like me. These programs give us plenty of time to figure out what we want to study after we finish high school. For example, I hope to become a pilot one day, so I could pick classes related to aviation and even learn the basics of flying planes.

The only downside is that not every school offers these perks. On top of that, many students can’t even get to these specialized schools easily. Not all of us can attend just any high school we want. If you have a car, you can drive yourself to and from campus, and getting a ride from someone else works sometimes too. But that’s not a reliable solution long-term—you’d constantly have to find people willing to drop you off in the morning and pick you up after class.

I also believe that deciding on a career path while we’re still young is a smart move, since it lets us graduate faster than we otherwise would.

Another big plus is that students at these schools get to learn a lot more than usual, and they can pick their college major well in advance. This opens up way more opportunities for them later on. Of course, many of these specialized high schools require applicants to have strong grades to get in, and you also need to keep your marks up to pass your classes there.

Put simply, if your grades aren’t up to standard, you won’t be able to enroll in these programs.

You need to be prepared at all times. If you manage that, you can get into the best universities and make your dreams come true.

My personal plan is to attend college and work in the computer field after I graduate. First, I need to finish high school at Generic_School. If you earn extra credits, you can finish high school early and head to college sooner.

It’s fine to get a part-time job after school to earn some money, but don’t take on too many hours. School should always come first, so remember to do all your homework and put effort into your schoolwork.

Many students can’t afford college, which is why they need to work after school. I know plenty of people who have enough money for college because they’re lucky enough to have parents who cover the costs. Higher education is very expensive, so a lot of people choose not to go to college at all. I feel bad for them, since I have the same problem—I don’t have the money to pay for school either. Some students also have to move out when they start college, which means they have to pay rent and other bills on top of tuition.

I think finishing high school in three years is a good option. You could work for a year after graduating, or delay college entirely if you’re not ready yet. Colleges don’t care how old you are when you apply—I’ve seen lots of older adults still attending classes there.

You can also take online classes during the summer or in the evenings to finish high school ahead of schedule. After your classes, you can work a few hours and then head home—this is a great way to get high school done faster. Just keep in mind that summer and evening classes cost money too, so you’ll need to work to cover those fees.

Whether you take three or four years to finish high school, you’ll still get your diploma in the end. Most importantly, you need to find a job you’re actually passionate about. Your future plan is your own choice, so pick the path that works best for you. Listening to helpful advice from others isn’t a bad idea, but if you don’t want to take it, that’s okay too—you should trust yourself.

I am writing to explain why I believe schools should ban student cell phones entirely. The biggest issue is that phones are a major distraction. Many students who bring them to class end up using them during lessons instead of focusing on the teacher. They often miss key explanations, so when the teacher asks them a question later, they cannot give an answer because they were not listening.

Another worrying problem is student safety. Some learners use their phones to message people they have never met in real life, sharing personal details or information about our school. They have no way of knowing who these strangers really are, and this puts them in danger, as the people they talk to could use the shared information to harm them.

Phones also cause unnecessary interruptions. If a student leaves their phone on during class, it might ring or ping with a new message while the teacher is speaking. This breaks the flow of the lesson, and the teacher has to stop teaching to ask the student to turn off the device or hand it over, which wastes time that should be spent learning.

Sincerely,
STUDENT_NAME

There are both upsides and downsides to working just four days a week, with ten-hour shifts each day. On the negative side, you might not earn enough to cover your monthly bills, afford a family vacation, or pay for other expenses. However, you get far more free time to spend with loved ones: you can relax, watch TV, or stay home with your wife and kids. This is valuable because many people rarely get to bond with family and friends during a standard work week. Overall, I think this is a strong proposal.

I also think this model would work well for schools, if they add two extra hours to each school day to fit the same weekly hours into four days. The benefits are clear: students get more time to study and finish all their assignments during the week, and then have three full days off to rest at home, do homework, or even pick up a part-time job and work those three days. All of these are clear advantages.

I believe this proposal has no real downsides, as it gives all students more opportunities at school and helps them become better learners.

To sum up, this plan offers a great chance to access better jobs and improve schools. That said, we should remember that every proposal has both benefits and drawbacks for different people.

Have you ever thought about trying skydiving? I’m convinced it’s an incredibly exciting activity, mostly because it lets you take in stunning views from way up high, and it’s also a great way to push past your fears. If you’re nervous about heights, you don’t have to go alone—you can jump with close friends or family members to make it feel less intimidating. Once you’re high up in the air, you’ll get a bird’s-eye view of the ground below: you can spot trees, grass, and all sorts of landscapes from far away. It feels just like flying, which is part of what makes it so fun. You might even see animals you’ve never encountered before, or spot weird, unexpected sights you’d never notice from the ground. Tiny houses, small animals like dogs or cats, and even people look like little dots from that height. There’s always something new to notice floating around in the air, too. Skydiving can also help you get over other fears related to heights. If you used to be too scared to ride a roller coaster, you’ll probably feel brave enough to try one after jumping out of a plane. The same goes for flying on regular airplanes: if you were once terrified of plane travel because of how high up they fly, you won’t feel that way anymore. After all, you’ve already jumped out of a plane at that exact same height! Once you’ve conquered your fear of heights, you might find yourself wanting to travel much more often. You can visit far-off places that are impossible to reach by car, like Bora Bora or other tropical destinations. Of course, skydiving isn’t just fun and games—it can be very risky, too. If you don’t know how to turn on the air bag that helps you float safely, you might crash when you land. Even if the air bag works, not knowing how to land properly could lead to injuries, or you might end up landing in the wrong spot entirely. If you don’t feel totally confident about safety, I’d recommend trying indoor skydiving first to get used to the feeling. At the end of the day, skydiving lets you spot weird, unique sights you’d never see otherwise, and it helps you face fears like flying on planes or riding roller coasters. I really think everyone should try skydiving at least once to take in all the incredible views. If you’re scared of high places—like tall mountains or tall buildings—this activity can definitely help you get over that. But if you’re worried you won’t know how to handle the air bag equipment, start with indoor skydiving first. If you decide to try outdoor skydiving, there will be an instructor attached to you the whole time: they’ll handle the air bag and the landing, so all you have to do is enjoy the flight. You don’t need to worry about a thing—just look around at the view and see if you can spot any interesting sights you’ve never seen before.

Another reason people ask more than one person for advice is that some of them have already gone through the situation you are facing. They know exactly what will happen, and what you might see or go through during the process, because they have been in your exact position before.

It lets you check that you understand what you are doing, and allows you to compare your own thoughts with others' opinions. You can see if other people agree with your plan, and you may find that you have a lot in common with these people when it comes to the situation at hand.

To sum up, the main reason people ask several people for their opinions is to hear different points of view and make sure they are on the right track with their choices. Many of the people you consult may have already gone through the exact situation you are currently dealing with.

Most people only seek advice when they feel unsure about which direction to take or which decision to make.

A bad decision can mess up someone’s life completely, especially when it hurts the people closest to them: a husband or wife, kids, or other family. For instance, if you end up in jail for a crime, you set a really bad example for young children. A lot of people who go to prison stay there for years and years. It’s awful for kids to not see their mom or dad for so long, and that kind of separation can make people feel really depressed.

On the other hand, making smart choices keeps you out of serious legal trouble, including federal charges. This sets a positive example for your children andgives them a better shot at a good future. Getting advice from the right person is a huge part of this. When you make good choices, your whole family benefits: your kids won’t have to visit you in prison, peering at you through a small glass window.

I’m speaking from my own experience here: I’ve been through all of this myself. Taking advice from the wrong person can hurt not just you, but your whole family. It’s the worst feeling to have your kids and spouse only able to see you through that tiny prison window. If you do get into minor legal trouble, like a parking ticket, a fine, or a misdemeanor, you can usually fix it easily. Don’t make choices that lead to bigger problems. Always do what you think is best for you and your family first, instead of worrying about what other people want.

Bad influences can also betray you: they might steal your things, take your money, stab you in the back, or turn on you when you need them most. My mom always tells me, “A friend is like a dollar in a pocket with a hole in it” — meaning people you trust can let you down easily. That’s why you should follow your own heart, not what other people tell you to do, because they can lead you straight into trouble.

Making the right choices opens up so many good opportunities. You can go to college, earn a degree in a subject you love, and land a well-paying job. With that, you can buy a nice home, a reliable car, and always have savings set aside for emergencies. You can even help your parents move into a good home, so you never have to put them in a nursing home. You’ll be able to buy your kids the things they want, whenever they need them, and you won’t have to struggle like so many people do just to put food on the table.

Have you ever had a teacher ask you to stay after class to finish your assignments? I strongly believe that after-school clubs are beneficial because they can help students succeed in their classes. These programs help learners finish their assignments more quickly, and they also make it easier for students to grasp difficult concepts. Many young people dislike doing homework at home, but if they can join fun activities after school, they’re often willing to complete their work first to participate.

For one thing, sitting alone to do homework can feel very boring for students. But when they combine schoolwork with engaging activities, they’re less likely to feel restless and more likely to focus on their tasks. When students are active and having fun, they tend to finish work faster and with less struggle. For example, if a student wants to join an after-school sports team, and is told they must complete their homework first to participate, a kid who loves that sport will definitely get their work done quickly. Nowadays, many students prefer doing academic work through interactive activities, like math games, card games, and other hands-on tasks. On top of that, teachers running these clubs can explain assignments more clearly to small groups, which helps students understand and remember the material better.

Another key point is that after-school clubs help students see how important their schoolwork is. When they take it seriously, they can improve their grades over time. Is finishing high school in three years better than the usual four? Many schools now offer early graduation programs, and I strongly support this option. Completing high school a year sooner gives students extra time to figure out their next steps, work to save for further education, and spend more time with family while planning ahead.

Many teens are unsure of their post-high school plans, which is another reason to support three-year graduation. They may not know which career to pursue, or whether to start working or keep studying. The extra year from graduating early gives them time to decide without rush. For example, a friend of mine finished high school last year with no idea what to study or what job to apply for. She stayed home for months unsure of her next move—something that would have been less stressful if that year was planned as part of a three-year program.

Many students who complete four years of high school take a gap year anyway to relax or figure things out, so why not build that into the high school timeline? Graduating in three years lets students use that year to work and save for college tuition. Others start entry-level work to get used to the professional world. Overall, finishing early is better, as it means students graduate younger, rather than being over 18 and feeling behind their peers.

Critics argue that three-year programs give students less time to learn, but this is not true. Students can prioritize core classes, or take evening courses and summer school to fit everything in. Many students who want to graduate early have specific goals they’re eager to reach, so they’re motivated to put in extra work. As online learning grows, it will also be easier for students to take any extra classes they need at their own pace.

In conclusion, graduating high school in three years is a smart choice. It lets students start college or enter the workforce a full year earlier, and gives them more time to research good colleges and prepare for the next stage. This also benefits parents, as their children can apply to their preferred colleges sooner, without wasting time after a traditional four-year program.

High school students should graduate in three years rather than following the traditional four-year schedule. To stick to this plan, learners will need to work harder, taking extra courses during summer vacation or in evening classes. This opens up two valuable options: starting a job a full year early, or enrolling in college ahead of schedule. Finishing high school sooner, joining the workforce earlier, and hitting personal milestones faster are all compelling reasons why a three-year high school track makes sense.

First, finishing high school ahead of schedule is a smart move for many students. For example, some sign up for summer classes or evening courses to earn credits faster. Others choose to skip optional elective classes, which also lets them complete all graduation requirements a year early. When students graduate sooner, they have more time to work toward their personal dreams.

Second, students gain an extra year to enter the workforce early. For example, many students work hard to save money for college expenses. When they enroll in college, they have to pay for the courses they take, so finishing high school early gives them a full year to work and set aside funds. With savings ready, they can focus on their studies without worrying about how to cover college costs.

Most importantly, finishing high school early gives students extra time to reach their goals ahead of schedule. For example, many students want to launch a strong career as soon as possible. When they achieve their early goals, they secure a good life for themselves down the line, with a stable job to support their needs. On top of that, students who hit their first targets early often get the chance to work toward even more ambitions. Reaching multiple goals helps them build an even better future.

Some people argue against three-year high school, saying students will miss out on elective courses. While this is sometimes true, skipping those optional classes lets students achieve their main dreams much sooner. What’s more, graduating early still gives learners the choice to join the workforce a year sooner or enroll in college early, and they can use that extra time to save up for their studies.

In conclusion, finishing high school in three years is a smart choice for many learners. It lets them complete their education early, join the workforce a year sooner, and reach their personal goals ahead of schedule. These are all strong reasons to support a three-year high school timeline instead of the traditional four-year track. Whether students take summer or evening classes to speed up their progress, work hard to save for college, or want to launch their career early, graduating in three years offers clear benefits.

Many teachers and other adults believe that some high school freshmen already have the ability and are expected to pick a future career path before they even start high school. They argue that only the students themselves can judge whether they are ready to take on this big responsibility. However, I strongly disagree with this view. I do not believe that young students are capable of handling the pressure of choosing a career so early, and I will explain my reasoning below.

First, we need to consider students who are already living independently. Many of these young people have part-time or even full-time jobs to cover their own expenses: rent, phone bills, groceries, and other daily costs. Balancing work and regular schoolwork is already a huge challenge for them, as they have to stay on top of homework while meeting their job duties. Adding the extra pressure of picking a long-term career path on top of this would be too much to handle.

Another key point is that many students lack the support they need to make such a big decision. Some cannot afford tutoring, extra classes, or materials required to explore career options. While a lucky few find mentors who want to help them figure out their path, most teachers and adults refuse to assist. These adults often assume that high schoolers are too immature to make career choices, so they do not even give students a chance to prove they are capable. They simply dismiss young people’s ideas without listening to their reasoning.

On top of this, many students are already struggling to keep up with their education. They put all their energy into passing classes and handling personal responsibilities, and some even drop out because the pressure is too high. Most, however, keep pushing forward even when they face family issues or home problems, trying their best to prepare for the future. Adding career decisions to their already heavy load would only make things harder.

It is also important to remember that many high school freshmen are still very young. They are just starting to understand how the adult world works, and how heavy adult responsibilities can be. If they are forced to pick a career right when they enter high school, they will have to take extra classes on top of their regular courses, which adds even more stress to their already busy schedules.

Most students entering high school are not even thinking about careers yet. They are focused on adjusting to new school responsibilities, or dealing with ones they already have. Many young teens make mistakes, like prioritizing their social life, how many friends they have, or how they look over their schoolwork. They need time to mature before they start focusing on academic goals, like getting good grades to make their family proud or working hard to reach their full potential.

Some people may argue that choosing a career early is easy for some students, while others disagree. However, I believe that pushing high schoolers to pick a specific career path is a bad idea. As I have explained, this process is difficult, stressful, and overwhelming for young people. They are simply too young to take on such a huge responsibility.

No matter what goal we set for ourselves, we can push through until we achieve it, even when we face challenges we have never encountered before. Nothing in life should hold us back from pursuing the future we want. If someone tells you that you will never reach your aims, do not let their negative opinions shake your confidence—you are capable of achieving anything if you stay true to yourself.

When many people work together on one specific task, the whole process definitely moves faster, letting us start other projects much sooner. This applies to large-scale work like building new cars or constructing homes—every team member has their own unique part to play. If someone has a goal they really want to achieve, they should dive in and keep going until they succeed, finally seeing their biggest dreams become reality.

A clear example of this is choosing a job you are passionate about, so you can be the best version of yourself, or even starting your own business to be your own boss. When you run your own company, no one tells you what to do, but you do have responsibilities: you need to keep track of your employees, pay those who work full days, and make sure everyone who shows up on time gets their wages. Of course, this applies to business owners. Most of us start out working for others—at retail stores, fast food joints, delivery services, or any other job you can think of. We all have to start somewhere: our first jobs help us save up to get our own place, pay our own bills, and buy the fun things we want with our own hard-earned cash.

Everyone starts out with small, simple steps, but when you want more out of life, you work to achieve your dreams and take on bigger, better projects. If there is something you have always wanted to do, give it a try first: see how it goes, and if it works out, keep moving forward until you reach that goal. Your own ideas can also make a real difference in the world, helping other people bring their own plans to life. Most people dream of owning a large, beautiful home with nice cars and a big backyard pool. When you do achieve your dreams and have plenty of money, it might be tempting to spend it all on parties and fun. But success is not just about spending cash on good times—it is also about doing the right thing and helping people who are struggling the most. Anyone can achieve whatever they want to be or become if they work hard for it. No one can stop you if you put your mind to your goal. You alone have the power to accomplish huge things in the future. The next step to your success is ahead, and the future is full of opportunities for new generations to achieve even bigger and better things.

Many people enjoy taking on new challenges, and learning a foreign language is a popular one. Around 67 languages are spoken across the globe, and 8.9% of the population speaks Vietnamese. It is ranked among the top 10 most difficult languages to master. I am lucky to speak Vietnamese fluently, which lets me do all sorts of useful things: I can translate between English and Vietnamese, teach my friends the language, and hold conversations with other Vietnamese speakers.

Since I speak both Vietnamese and English well, I can translate smoothly in either direction. This comes in handy on family trips abroad, especially for my mom. She does not speak or understand English at all, so I always act as her personal translator whenever we travel together.

My friends are really fond of Vietnamese, and they often ask me to teach them the language. Whenever I walk into class, some of them greet me with 'Xin Chao' – the Vietnamese word for hello. I am always happy to see how eager they are to learn. I once taught an American friend how to speak Vietnamese, and now he is so fluent that it sounds like his first language.

Being able to speak Vietnamese is also incredibly useful if you visit Vietnam or live in an area with a large Vietnamese community. Locals are always impressed when a foreigner can speak their language – they will definitely think you are really cool. I learned this firsthand during a family reunion trip to Vietnam. I got separated from my parents and started shouting in English that I was lost, but no one around me understood. Thankfully, I could switch to Vietnamese, ask where the nearest police station was, and find my way back to my family.

All in all, Vietnamese is a fantastic language to pick up if you want to push yourself out of your comfort zone. It will also be a huge help if you ever plan to travel to Vietnam in the future.

Every person is born with a unique mix of personality traits, which often makes it difficult to make sense of how others act around us. Many of us fall into the habit of assuming we are in charge of even the tiniest details of our lives, even though we do not fully control our own defining characteristics.

When a child is born, neither parent can predict what kind of adult their son or daughter will grow into. Broadly speaking, there are two kinds of people: those who put on a false front to act like someone they are not, and those who stay loyal to their true self. At some stage in life, many people start hanging around those who make poor choices and have bad judgment. By following these people, they gradually take on the same habits and attitudes over time.

We always have the choice to embrace who we really are, to value our inner self deeply, and to stop worrying about what other people think of us. The moment God chose to bring us into this world, he already knew exactly what our unique traits would be as we grew older. When we learn to love ourselves, we set an example that can encourage others to do the same in their own lives.

To sum up, we were not born to copy others or follow the crowd – we were born to be our own person and stand out. For every choice we make and every action we take, there will always be outcomes tied to those decisions.

A few years before my uncle qualified as a doctor, I watched him struggle with anxietyattacks brought on by the endless hours of studying he did in medical school. He eventually realized he needed to take part in other activities to distract himself a little, while also letting go of all that built-up stress. That experience made me realize that it is a fantastic idea for every student to take part in at least one extracurricular activity. They could play sports, join book clubs, or volunteer for community service, for example. If all students got involved in extra activities, their lives would be far more varied and fulfilling, with richer experiences and far less stress.

Getting active in sports is especially good for students’ physical health. Most students spend hours sitting at desks in school, then go home to sit on the couch for even more hours. The human body needs regular movement and exercise to stay healthy. Sports are a great way to make positive changes to your body — for teenagers, regular activity supports their metabolism, helping them grow taller and develop properly. Even just 20 minutes of exercise a day makes a real difference.

Book clubs are another fun, engaging option for students. Ever feel like your brain just needs a break? Books are the perfect solution — they can transport you to places all over the world, even imaginary settings, without you ever leaving your seat. You can discover new adventures, drama, romance, and experiences you have never had before, almost like stepping into a different world and taking a break from your daily routine. In a book club, you can talk to others about what you have read, and might even meet people who share exactly the same thoughts and opinions as you.

Volunteering for community service does not just benefit others — it helps you too. You might wonder how? Well, helping out in your local area teaches you the value of cooperation, and giving to others brings a sense of happiness and pride in how responsible you are becoming. On top of that, community service can earn students credits toward an advanced diploma, or even help them qualify for college scholarships. If you have never volunteered because you thought it would be boring, you should definitely give it a try as an extracurricular activity.

Every student should take part in at least one extracurricular activity after school, so their body and mind can get a productive, refreshing break. Any type of activity will help you relax when you need a pause from studying. Pick something you genuinely enjoy, and once the school day ends, throw yourself into that activity for as long as you can.
