People everywhere form quick first impressions of others, based on what someone says or does, and these initial judgments are very difficult to take back. A first impression shapes the thoughts, emotions, and opinions we form about a person right away. It’s easy to hurt someone’s feelings with a thoughtless comment, since we often don’t pause to choose the right words before speaking. By the time we realize we’ve caused harm and want to fix the issue, it’s often too late. First impressions are almost impossible to reverse, because they can wound others deeply and lead people to change how they act toward us.

First impressions can hurt others’ feelings deeply — I learned this firsthand with my sister just yesterday. My sister and I were discussing her wedding, which is set for next April, and we’re busy preparing for her big day. We need to pick out her dress and all the other items she’ll use for the event. She’s like a second mother to me, so I want to make sure she looks absolutely beautiful when she walks down the aisle. While we were scrolling through wedding dresses online together, she pointed out one she really liked. My immediate reaction was that it was ugly, and I blurted out that she’d look like a skeleton in it, since she’s thin. I didn’t mean to hurt her feelings at all — the dress really was not flattering, even if she liked it, and I just wanted her to have the prettiest dress possible for her wedding. I felt terrible afterward, because I hadn’t thought through my words before saying them. I apologized right away, but she was still a little upset with me for what I’d said. As the old saying goes, what you say is what you get back. For a while, my sister barely spoke to me, which made me really sad. I reached out to her again to say sorry properly, and she told me she knew I hadn’t meant it. We’re back to being close now, thankfully.

But another time, first impressions hurt me just as badly. My friend Generic_Name invited me to her birthday party, and one of her other friends told me in front of everyone that I looked ugly, and that I was an ugly, slow girl. Her harsh first impression of me really stung. Even though she took back her words later, it was too late — I left Generic_Name’s party early and went home, feeling miserable. The girl came to my house later to talk and apologize, and I told her she’d hurt my feelings but I was okay. I even gave her some advice about thinking before speaking, and then she left. That experience showed me again that first impressions are almost impossible to change, because they leave a mark on how the other person feels.

First impressions can also make people change how they act toward you, as I saw with my best friend. I once gave her my honest opinion about her boyfriend, telling her I didn’t think he really loved her because I’d seen him kissing another girl at school. She got angry and said I was crazy, just jealous because her boyfriend was the most handsome guy in the world. To be fair, he was good-looking, but he had a reputation for playing with girls' feelings. My best friend’s attitude toward me changed completely after that — she stopped wanting to hang out or even talk to me because of what I’d said. Later, I found out I’d made a huge mistake: the boy I saw kissing another girl wasn’t her boyfriend at all, but his twin brother. My snap first impression of him was totally wrong. I tried to apologize to my best friend, but she was still furious with me, and it was impossible to have a proper conversation. Now I only talk to her rarely, and even though I’ve changed my mind about her boyfriend, our friendship is never going to be the same. First impressions really do make people change how they treat you.

Some people might argue that first impressions can be fixed right away, since they’re no big deal, and that most people don’t even care about what others first think of them. But that’s not true at all. When someone gets a bad first impression of you, it hurts, and it can make them change how they act, even toward themselves. First impressions are almost impossible to reverse, no matter how big or small the issue is.

To sum up, first impressions are almost impossible to change, because the words we say in the moment can’t just be taken back. It’s hard to fix mistakes, especially when we say things we didn’t mean to say without thinking first. Apologizing after the fact is good, but sometimes it’s too late to undo the hurt caused. Some people are very sensitive and won’t forgive easily, and others might change how they act based on someone else’s opinion or feeling. In the end, first impressions are incredibly hard to reverse.

Success is the most important thing in the world. As former British Prime Minister Winston Churchill once said, "success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm." I completely agree with this view, because failure plays a critical role in helping people achieve success. Success means working hard to reach the personal goals you set, whether that is doing well in school or landing your dream job.

Graduating from school is a huge achievement, even though many students find it really hard to pass required exams or meet academic standards. They study for hours to pass their classes and earn their diploma. Take a student who moves to a new country and does not speak English, for example. They might fail core classes like English, history, and science at first, no matter how much effort they put in. But instead of giving up, they keep trying until they reach their goal. Even when a student fails a test, that setback shows them exactly what they need to fix for the next one. They can prepare more thoroughly and do better than they did last time.

A lot of people end up in jobs they enjoy, but not everyone gets their dream role right away. Some never give up, even when things get tough. Think of Remo D'Souza, now one of India’s best dance choreographers. When he first wanted to be a dancer, his father did not support his choice. He tried for a long time to convince his dad, but his father refused to listen. He eventually left home to follow his passion, even though he had nothing: no money, not even enough to pay for dance classes. But he still refused to quit. He started his own small dance workshop to earn money for his training, and now he is a huge success. The same is true for job interviews: some people get hired on their first try, but others have to apply again and again. They work on improving their skills each time, so they can finally land the job they want.

In conclusion, success is something everyone wants, but you will never achieve it if you are not willing to work hard. To become a successful person, you have to learn from your mistakes. Failure is truly the key to success: if you never fail, you can never improve for next time. Every person who is successful today has faced failures in their life too. To reach your goals, you have to use your failures as lessons to grow.

Thomas Jefferson once offered a memorable piece of wisdom: "Determine never to be idle . . . it is wonderful how much may be done if we are always doing." Reflecting on these words, I’ve realized that while a few small wins might come with no effort at all, the vast majority of meaningful achievements in life require consistent hard work. You need to put in real effort if you want to make real progress and reach big goals. I fully agree with Jefferson’s point about the value of staying active, because that is simply how life operates. You have to work for the things you want and need. Nothing in life is handed to you for free, and you will finish necessary tasks far faster by putting in steady effort and staying busy than you ever would by lounging around and doing nothing at all.

One key reason I stand by Jefferson’s words is that you have to earn everything you receive in life. You need to stay active and tackle tasks consistently to get things done. It is a powerful quote that many people overlook or never stop to consider. His message reinforces the idea that completing work requires both hard work and focus, and that tasks will never finish themselves if you sit back and wait.

Another important point is that no matter what path you choose, work is always a part of life. You should never take the things you have for granted, and you need to put in real effort instead of being lazy and leaving necessary tasks unfinished. This habit will benefit you in the long term, making daily life much smoother if you just handle what needs to be done. Jefferson’s quote is meant to inspire others to excel, pushing them to do everything possible to achieve their personal goals. It is a truly useful piece of advice that can support anyone who needs a little guidance.

A final reason I believe Jefferson’s quote is so valuable is that it reminds us life is not easy, and nothing comes for free. Every choice we make also carries consequences. It encourages people to appreciate what they have, since the quality of what you own reflects the amount of effort you put in, rather than just lying around doing nothing. This single quote packs a lot of meaningful ideas that can stick with people, and it has the power to motivate anyone who is feeling stuck or lacks drive.

To sum up, Thomas Jefferson’s quote can be a lifeline for people who need a boost of motivation. It shows them that it is incredible to see how much you can achieve just by consistently staying on top of your work. Finishing tasks also becomes far simpler when you stay active and avoid sitting still while doing absolutely nothing about your responsibilities. I support this quote because it helps people understand the way life works, and how they should live if they want to become both great and wise.

Is graduating from high school in just three years a smart choice? More and more students are finishing their secondary education ahead of the traditional four-year schedule. But do these students actually master the material they need to know? Many quickly forget what they learned in class, especially during summer break or after they stop attending school regularly. How much a student retains depends entirely on their individual learning style and memory. Some may find that extra time in high school helps them figure out their post-graduation goals, and taking elective courses can make them more creative and better prepared for future jobs.

Success with early graduation varies completely from student to student. Some have the capacity to absorb a lot of material without falling behind or losing focus, while others feel uninterested in certain classes, or get stuck in school programs that include subjects they don’t care about. But finishing early can be very helpful for students who want to enter the workforce right away, or start college sooner without high school obligations getting in the way. Other students prefer the standard four-year timeline, often because they want to earn an advanced diploma that opens up better opportunities later.

Spending more time in high school gives students space to work out what they want to do next. Students who rush to graduate often haven’t thought carefully about their future careers or goals, which can leave them struggling to find purpose after getting their diploma. For instance, a student might graduate early, only to spend weeks or months aimlessly unemployed because they have no clear direction. Anyone planning to finish high school early needs a concrete plan: maybe they need to earn money and will start working right away, or they want to pursue further education to gain more skills for their future. Generally, students who go straight to work after high school have clear goals, no matter how long their secondary education took. Those who choose to keep studying usually either aren’t ready to decide on a career yet, or are working toward a specific degree or certification.

Taking elective courses makes students more creative and better prepared for the workforce, as they learn new skills that help both in their future careers and daily lives. For example, an art class can boost creativity, while a music course might even help a student launch their own record label someday. Electives also offer far more opportunities than standard core-only programs, which many students find boring. Summer break is a great time to rest from schoolwork, but students who struggle to retain information during long breaks can also take online classes to keep their skills sharp.

To sum up, three-year high school graduation programs can be a great option for students who already have clear post-graduation plans, whether that means entering the workforce or continuing their studies. There’s nothing wrong with taking a little extra time to graduate, either — you never know what new things you might learn during those extra months, and you’ll have more time to think carefully about your future. For students who can retain information long-term, graduating in three years is perfectly fine. The most important thing for any student is to make a clear, detailed plan for life after high school, and be fully sure of what they want to achieve.

There are two common views on whether failure matters when working toward success. Some believe that failing is a key part of the journey, while others argue that failure has no role at all in reaching your goals.

Those who support the idea that failure helps point out that every time you fail, you learn how to pick yourself back up after a setback. To get things you’ve never had before, you have to try things you’ve never done, and that often leads to failure at first. Big failures tend to teach you bigger, more valuable lessons than small mistakes. Even if you fail once, you just have to keep trying again.

Everyone faces failures in daily life, but that does not mean you will never succeed. Life can be difficult to handle, but it is possible to get through tough times. Every failure gives you a chance to correct what went wrong. It’s normal for unhelpful, bad ideas to pop into your head when things go wrong, but you don’t have to focus on those – you should stay positive instead. When you fail, it’s easy to feel guilty, think you’re useless, or believe you can’t do the task at all. But there is something waiting for you if you keep going: that something is success.

Your own skills are valuable, and nothing can take that away from you. Many people worry too much about what others think of their achievements or the work they complete, but your work is your responsibility alone. You have to guide yourself toward success, and you are the one who will find the right path. There are plenty of ways to reach your goals, and you can get support from family, teachers, friends, and other people around you. At the same time, everyone is responsible for their own work and efforts.

I have a personal example of this from my biology class, where I had to pass the SOL exam. I took the test four times total, and only passed on my fourth attempt. It was very hard for me to get through the SOL, and I even grew to hate studying for it, but I never stopped trying to accomplish my goal. Everyone fails at some point in life, but that does not mean you have to lose your determination or avoid taking responsibility. You should make your ideas stronger, and work to turn the hopes you have for your life into reality. Sometimes, the best thing to do is calm down, take a deep breath, and focus fully on your work. When you fail a test, you learn exactly what material is covered, how to use different strategies to pass next time, how to keep trying, and what tools you can use during the exam, like a dictionary. This is exactly how failure plays a role in working toward success.

On the other hand, some people argue that failure has no place in the pursuit of success, because they feel like they fail every single time they try to reach a goal.

A young student grinned up at their older buddy and said, "Reading this book with you was so much fun!" Younger children, especially those in early grades, often look up to older students, seeing them as cool role models who make even simple tasks feel enjoyable. Many schools now run programs that pair younger and older pupils together, and these setups benefit both groups. Both kids pick up new, interesting knowledge, older students learn how to guide younger children, and all participants get a chance to share thoughts about school they might never feel comfortable saying in front of a teacher.

One clear way these programs help both younger and older students is through mutual learning. Both can pick up information they have never studied before, or focus on topics the younger student is curious about. Younger kids can teach their older partners new words or concepts they are currently learning, while older pupils can share the material they are covering in their own classes. This creates a low-pressure, informal arrangement where both sides gain something, with no grades or strict expectations to worry about.

Another key benefit is that these programs help older students prepare for future responsibilities, including part-time or full-time jobs. Many older pupils are close to entering the workforce, and working with younger kids teaches them how to manage, support, and communicate with children effectively. Younger buddies also share what learning methods work best for them, which helps older students adjust their approach. This builds a strong, lasting bond between the pair—years later, they might run into each other and still recognize the person who helped them when they were little.

A final way these programs support both groups is by giving students a safe space to share honest opinions. A lot of kids wonder why they’re assigned certain tasks, or whether the work even relates to their daily lives, but they’re often too shy to speak up in a full classroom. One-on-one with their buddy, though, they feel comfortable sharing exactly what they think about a topic or assignment. This helps both students practice explaining their ideas clearly, and makes them feel at ease opening up to others.

Overall, I believe these buddy programs boost students’ confidence in talking to others, and make learning feel fun rather than like a chore. I speak from experience: when I was in 6th grade, I joined a reading buddy program, and reading books with my younger partner was always the best part of my week. It made getting help with subjects I struggled with easy, and even helped me work through other small problems at school. The program encouraged me to learn more to share with my buddy, and I know it would help many other students too.

I believe art, music, and drama classes should be offered as electives, not mandatory requirements. Why force students to take these courses if they have no interest in them? Schools ought to let learners choose which classes they enroll in. When students get to pick their own electives, they enjoy school much more—we should look forward to our electives, not dread them.

Take a student forced to take art they hate: they will not put effort into assignments and likely fail the class. The same applies to drama: not everyone likes performing, so it should never be required. Not all students want to sing or play an instrument, so making music class mandatory is unfair.

While some students love these creative subjects, that is not true for everyone. That is why learners should have the freedom to choose their classes. If these subjects were electives, students would pick courses that interest them and actually try to complete work. More students would pass their classes as a result. For all these reasons, art, music, and drama should definitely be electives.

What does it really mean to succeed in life? I agree with Winston Churchill’s famous view that true success comes from facing failure after failure without ever losing your enthusiasm. Falling down, or experiencing setbacks, is an unavoidable part of life. It can feel incredibly hard to pick yourself back up when things go wrong, but if you stay strong and keep your passion alive, life becomes far less complicated. When you hit low points, it’s easy to get overwhelmed by negative experiences, and life often feels tougher than you expected. But enthusiasm opens up so many positive chances: it makes daily life smoother, helps you grow into a more patient person, cuts down on stress, and brings more happiness overall. Even if you fail, holding onto that drive means you’re still on track for future success. Every success you do achieve teaches you valuable lessons that point you toward new opportunities, letting you keep moving forward. Churchill’s statement is incredibly important, as it guides people toward a positive mindset that makes life easier for everyone.

Setbacks often come with a lot of negative baggage, and life is almost always harder than we first imagine. If you want better opportunities, you have to bring the energy to stay strong and never give up. Without enthusiasm, even the biggest dreams feel impossible to reach. Take someone who dreams of going to college, for example. If they fill their head with negative thoughts, skip studying, and feel too lazy to get a job to save for tuition, they’ll never make that dream a reality. Another common example: someone who wants to own a car, a house, get a dog, and travel the world. They might have a job, but if they’re lazy at work, they risk getting fired and won’t earn enough to afford all those goals. Negative thinking blocks you from getting the things you want for a brighter future, no matter how much you wish for them.

On the flip side, enthusiasm makes it easier to stay positive and focused on your goals. When you have that drive, you feel less stressed, have more energy, and can be patient even when things take time. Positive thinking powered by enthusiasm lets you tackle even supposedly hard tasks with ease. Consider a student who wants to pass their end-of-year SOL exams to graduate. If they stay enthusiastic, they’ll study regularly, pay attention in class, turn in homework on time, and stay organized. They can pass all their classes and exams without letting stress take over their mind. Or take a student who fails a math test: instead of giving up, they hold onto their enthusiasm and look for solutions. Teachers often offer extra help after school, or let students retake tests if they come back better prepared. Putting in that extra effort to learn the material makes passing the next time around much simpler.

Failing without losing your enthusiasm is the key to building a successful future. When you chase success with a positive mindset, you feel less stressed, learn important lessons from your mistakes, and spot better opportunities to keep moving forward. For instance, someone who doesn’t graduate because they failed one required class might feel defeated at first. But they have options: they can repeat the year, enroll in a program that helps students pass required exams, or look for extra resources to master the subject. Another example: a person gets fired from their favorite job after accidentally breaking a delicate plate. It’s normal to be upset, but they should start looking for other jobs right away. Since they already have relevant work experience, it won’t be hard to find a new employer. They just need to stay careful, keep a positive attitude, and bring their full energy to work—future employers will be impressed by how hard they work at a job they’re passionate about.

Of course, hitting low points in life does come with negative consequences. Letting negative thoughts take over will only lead you down a bad path, where you want to reach a goal but can’t make it happen. This becomes a huge problem if you’re trying to achieve something but act in ways that work against your own goals. But with enthusiasm, you can work hard and make even tough tasks feel manageable. Putting in effort while staying happy creates the kind of attitude that everyone admires. It’s hard to encourage people to stay positive in today’s world, since life is full of challenges, but there are always people who prove that you should never give up—you just have to keep moving forward. Failing without losing your enthusiasm is the only way to secure success in the future. This is a lesson everyone should take to heart, instead of making life harder for themselves. If you’re feeling negative, don’t get stuck overthinking, since that only adds stress and fuels more negative thoughts. Never give up, and always keep moving forward.

While it is true that many teenagers face frequent restrictions, those under 18 still have important responsibilities to both themselves and their families. These obligations center on three key needs: access to education, a stable home, and enough money to get by.

First, education is a core need for all teenagers, from elementary school all the way through high school. In just 5 to 10 years, today’s teens will grow up to support the national economy, contribute to their communities, and raise the next generation of citizens.

A safe, stable home is just as essential. Every teenager needs a place they can call their own, where they can relax and feel protected from the stress of the outside world. A good home is a space where someone is always waiting with a smile and a meal, even if they might scold you sometimes, because they care about your well-being and future.

Money is arguably the most important factor in a teenager’s life, and earning it usually means taking on a part-time job or working weekends. This is where the weekday curfew creates a major issue: teens aged 16 to 18 already have to use their limited free time after school to work. Most part-time shifts last around 6 hours. If a student works from 4 p.m. to 9 p.m., there is no conflict with the curfew. But if their shift falls between 5 p.m. and 10 p.m., they could be wrongly accused of breaking the law, even though they are just going to work. This is nothing more than unfair interference from the city government.

To sum up, today’s children will grow into tomorrow’s teenagers, and eventually become the adults of the next generation. A home is the best place for a teenager to feel comfortable, safe, and at peace. Money is the most important thing for a teenager both now and in the future, and they need enough free time to earn it.

My mom once gave me a piece of advice that stuck with me: she told me to stay positive in life, and good things would follow. After I started making a conscious effort to stay upbeat, my life really turned around. I landed the exact job I’d been hoping for, bought my first car, and my family and I even moved into a new home — everything just felt brighter overall.

From my own experience, I’d say everyone should try to stay positive, surround themselves with upbeat people, listen to feel-good music, and take part in activities that encourage a positive mindset. It’s also worth building a circle of friends who give off good energy and push you to grow, because sometimes the issue isn’t you at all. Instead, it’s the people around you who constantly say hurtful things or drag you down, leaving you in a bad mood day after day.

Switching up the music you listen to can also make a big difference. A lot of popular songs and artists nowadays focus on topics like drugs, violence, gang life, and other negative themes — none of which is helpful if you’re trying to stay positive.

Taking part in activities that boost a positive attitude helps too. Things like attending church, having movie nights with family, or going to motivational talks can lift your mood and help you forget about all the negative things happening in your life.

Staying positive has clear benefits: it makes you feel better and can lead to success in life. But it’s not a perfect solution for everything. Life can be unfair, and we have to face that reality. We can’t go through life pretending everything is great when the truth is the world is becoming more troubled every day.

Looking to the future, I hope the next generation will take up positive habits all around the world, helping everyone see life from a happier, more successful point of view.

I agree with Ralph Waldo Emerson’s famous idea that the greatest accomplishment a person can have is staying true to themselves when the world keeps trying to change who they are.

The phrase “never give up” captures our deep commitment to our goals, and gives us courage. Life is full of struggle, not comfort—everyone faces their own hardships. No one is as perfect as they seem. Success comes from overcoming struggle, not avoiding it. Successful people don’t achieve their goals overnight. They face many challenges, but never stop chasing their dreams. Years of persistence through hard times lead to success: they learn to handle difficulties, push through, and win, which is what makes them successful.

A soccer player, for instance, wants to score a goal to win. To do that, they must get past the opposing team first—only then can they succeed.

When you fail, people might call you a fool or a loser, saying your life is over and you should give up. It’s tempting to listen, but don’t. Failing once doesn’t mean you’ll never win. Don’t lose hope. You have hands, a brain, legs—use them. Keep working, and success will come. Then you can show everyone you did it.

For example, you might struggle with math but be great at social science. Show your talents! You don’t need to solve math equations to have value—you might excel at social science instead.

Time is more valuable than almost anything. Smart people use their time well. If you work hard but don’t succeed right away, don’t lose hope or blame yourself. Time brings more chances to try again—you just have to keep going. Laziness wastes time, and only leads to failure. Remember: time never comes back.

If you skip homework, you’ll fail the subject and waste time. But if you do it, even if it’s wrong, your teacher might let you fix your mistakes.

Inspiration helps you reach your goals. Learning how successful people achieved their dreams motivates you to do the same. It helps you figure out your future path, and plan your own life based on their examples.

The story of Robert Bruce and the spider shows this. Hiding in a cave, Bruce watched a spider fail seven times to climb a wall, then succeed on the eighth try. This inspired Bruce to keep fighting for his own goals.

Every good thing has an opposite: to know winning, you must know losing. Failure is normal—if you never fail, you never tried. It’s part of life, but don’t let it make you depressed. You can always start over. Before you quit, ask: should I try one more time? That one try could bring success.

Imagine digging for gold: you’re almost there, but give up. One more dig would have found the gold. Always think twice before quitting—one more try might be all you need.

Clear goals help you make good decisions. A person without goals will never succeed. Your choices shape your future. Make a daily routine and stick to it. Students may find this hard, but it’s possible. Focus on studies, finish homework before school, and consistent routine makes success easier.

Laziness is a weakness that stops success. Always work hard until you finish. Many people have dreams but won’t work for them—you can’t fulfill dreams without effort. Keep trying to reach your goals. We have time and life—try as hard as you can.

Some people will try to interfere with your dreams, bothering you and stopping your work. They are harmful to your progress. Ignore them, don’t engage, and they will eventually lose interest and leave you alone.

If someone bothers you every day, ignoring them will make them lose interest and leave you alone.

Success brings happiness and pride. When you prove the doubters wrong, they’ll feel ashamed of their wrong assumptions. Never be lazy. Work hard, keep trying, and make smart choices. In the end, you’ll have a happy ending, having erased all the wrong things people thought about you.

Children do not read books or have fun like in the past. Now everything had changed due to this issue.

While modern technology makes countless daily tasks easier—from attending remote classes to shopping online or staying in touch with others—I am convinced it has far more negative impacts on people’s lives. For one, heavy use of tech has sharply reduced face-to-face human interaction. It has also completely reshaped our daily routines: in the past, people would meet up at local parks just to chat, but now families rarely spend quality time together, students get distracted by phones during school hours, and children no longer read physical books or play outdoors as they used to. Nearly every part of daily life has shifted because of this trend.

One major downside is the harm it causes to brick-and-mortar stores. More and more people choose to buy clothes, school supplies, and other goods from online retailers like Amazon, which now generates far higher sales than any physical store chain worldwide. For instance, I recently learned about two local shops that are struggling because of this shift. One is about to shut down entirely, since most customers now prefer to shop from home instead of visiting in person. Both stores are holding massive clearance sales to sell off all remaining stock before closing for good. Foot traffic at physical stores has dropped so low that their sales can’t compete with online platforms, and many employees who work there will soon lose their jobs as a result.

Another clear negative impact is that once-popular public spaces like parks, lakes, and shopping malls now sit mostly empty. Instead of going out, most people choose to stay home playing video games or placing online orders.

Supporters of technology often argue it gives people better ways to express themselves, but there are plenty of offline options for this too: painting, drawing, playing sports, or even dancing. I take a dance class, and my instructor recently spoke about the problems tech causes. She pointed out that while we sometimes rely on our phones for everything, that shouldn’t be the case all the time. I agree with her completely. When I moved to the United States in 2016, I couldn’t speak or understand English at all, so I used Google Translate to communicate when I didn’t know difficult words—so tech has definitely helped me at times. But I’ve also seen many students scroll on their phones during lessons. When teachers ask them questions about the material, they can’t respond at all because they weren’t paying attention to the class.

On the other hand, many people argue that technology improves our lives in positive ways, such as making it easier to stay in touch with family and friends who live far away. But I think this comes at a cost: we now struggle to share our thoughts or ideas without reaching for a phone first, and it has even harmed parts of our culture. It also stunts children’s development, since most kids no longer want to go outside to play with friends. Instead, they stay home glued to laptops or phones. This generation rarely reads physical books or magazines anymore, all because of constant tech use. For example, my middle school cousin plays Fortnite every single day. He stays up late gaming, gets bad grades, and struggles to wake up on time for school. He never reads books, and he never goes outside to play either—he is always on his phone or gaming console. I truly believe life is too short to waste staring at a screen.

To sum up, technology will continue to erode our cultures further. People may soon stop going out entirely—whether to shop, to enjoy themselves, or to spend time with family. I am convinced tech has a deeply harmful effect on us, because it has already transformed who we are and the world we live in. Nearly every part of life is changing because of this trend, and tech limits our ability to come up with new ideas. It weakens our communication skills, reduces our knowledge and curiosity, and even makes us less happy.

For those who prioritize self-reliance, this trait means every person should trust their own gut feelings and personal ideas when making choices.

This makes perfect sense for everyone, since we all ought to shape our own life paths. We all face challenges constantly, and there are plenty of moments when we have to figure things out alone.

Whenever we get the chance to make a change, following our gut is key, and we have to own the responsibility of picking the best option. That’s exactly how we grow and learn on our own.

In daily life, people constantly hit roadblocks that cause stress. Maybe your car breaks down in heavy traffic, you fail a test you studied for weeks to pass, or your boss fires you unexpectedly.

But the good news is, we get to choose how to respond and even turn things around. You could ask someone for help, study harder or get tutoring for schoolwork, or start looking for other jobs that interest you more.

We all have countless options to choose from, and following our own instincts and ideas is the best way to improve our situations.

For me, I’ll be graduating high school soon, then joining the navy as an adult. I’ll be living my own life, handling everything independently.

My whole world will shift completely. My parents won’t be there to guide me on everyday common sense, my teachers won’t be around to share life lessons, and my friends won’t be on hand to help me out. Every choice will be mine and mine alone to make.

If I end up learning through tough mistakes, that’s just how it will be. Maybe my gut instinct will kick in and guide me through, you never can tell.

Being able to make your own judgments is one of the most vital life skills we all need to pick up. Everyone grows up eventually: you’ll have your own family and take on all sorts of responsibilities, and suddenly you’re the one making every decision, answerable not just for yourself but for your family too.

Your instincts will point you toward what your heart really wants. Sometimes they might lead you down the wrong path, but that’s okay, it’s all part of how we learn.

Success isn’t a straight, easy road. It’s full of adventures and setbacks along the way to the finish line. You’ll face way more failures than you can ever imagine before you hit your goal, and succeeding on your own terms means following your own instincts and ideas.

You might wonder if it’s better to ask experts or authority figures for advice on big life decisions. But here’s the thing: life is one big adventure, and you never know what’s coming next. No two people have the exact same life path, so while expert advice works for some, it won’t work for everyone. You might find a totally different solution that fits you better.

We can listen to what other people suggest, but remember: you’re the one making the final call, and you’re the one responsible for that decision, not anyone else’s advice or common opinions. It all comes down to you: follow your heart to set things right, or learn how to judge situations and pick the best path.

No one can change your life unless you let them, and no one can change your final decision unless you ignore your own instincts and heart. That’s exactly why we should make our own choices: not just to get things right, but to follow our hearts and figure out what really matters in life.

Schools now offer education to students who cannot physically attend classes. Many learners face significant barriers to getting to campus. For example, some live too far away and lack access to transportation, while others have special circumstances that make in-person attendance impossible. These days, manyschools provide the option to learn remotely from home.

To participate in remote learning, you need a computer or similar device that lets you communicate with school staff. Without these tools, you cannot join in. Internet access is essential for home learning, but not everyone can afford these resources, which leaves some students unable to take part.

Home learning has both advantages and drawbacks. On the plus side, remote students cover the same material as in-person learners, earn the same qualifications, and can apply to colleges and universities. However, a major downside is that they may struggle to adjust to a normal, healthy social life once they get to college.

One benefit of home learning is that you can finish your work at your own pace. You can spend as much time as you need on each task before moving on, but it is worth asking: what will you do once you complete your studies?

Students who learn from home often miss out on regular face-to-face conversations with peers. This is a serious issue that can harm their future lives. They may not know how to interact with others or navigate social situations, which can be very stressful. Many end up feeling isolated from their communities.

Home learning can let you skip the daily commute and avoid waking up early, but it is not the same as attending a regular school. In-person students can ask teachers questions the moment they have them, and they have access to many school resources that remote learners do not. If you study from home, you will have to look up answers and solve problems on your own.

We should not forget that students with special circumstances have access to dedicated school programs. Some schools can accommodate these students in person, while others offer home-based learning options. These programs are designed specifically for people who have been sick since birth or have had health issues their whole lives.

You cannot just choose to learn from home because you do not want to go to school. You need a valid reason to apply for remote learning. This is especially true for public schools, which require a formal letter and proof that you cannot attend in person. School staff will review your case before making a decision.

Remote learning is a resource available to many students today, but you should think carefully before choosing it. Avoid making choices that could harm your future, unless you have a genuine special case. There are plenty of support systems and solutions to help you succeed, no matter which learning path you take.

As you gain hands-on experience in that field, you’ll understand more about science and other topics naturally. The more you use your imagination to think through job-related experiences, the less you have to rely on memorizing existing knowledge to create something totally new, useful, and better than what’s already out there.

You can use it to decide what to create: a house, a long bridge, a watch, or even musical instruments like accordions, violins, guitars, and pianos. Imagination also helps you picture future careers, whether that’s teaching in a school, studying science, working as a doctor, building structures, managing a team, or training athletes for their next game. You’ll still use your brain and existing knowledge, but imagination is what drives you to put in the effort for any job.

You can invent, build, or study anything you want by using your imagination to explore the things you hope to do when you’re older. This combines with your existing knowledge and hard work to help you succeed in any role.

It’s clear that imagination is a more powerful tool than knowledge alone. When you use your imagination to plan, build, or invent things, you’ll pick up new information, gain support, and learn all the details you need to make your ideas happen.

Online schooling can be a great option, but it definitely isn’t right for every student. Some learners thrive when studying from home, but others struggle to keep up with the format. Online courses are far from simple, and not every student can successfully complete them, which is exactly why they aren’t a one-size-fits-all solution. Homeschooling is totally different from attending a traditional school: you don’t have to drag yourself out of bed at dawn, and you get to pick when you tackle your assignments.

While it’s nice to skip early mornings, the downside is that you have to dive straight into your work as soon as you start your day. This gets even tougher if you’re not getting the support you need, since you can’t just ask questions on the spot when you’re confused.

You also have to push yourself to do your absolute best, because if you fail an assignment, you can’t easily meet with your teacher to get extra help or make up the work the way you could in a regular classroom.

When you’re homeschooled, you miss out on all the non-academic experiences that make regular school memorable — not just classes, but things like fire drills, school dances, making friends, even the occasional fights between students. I know that when I’ve struggled in traditional school, I’ve thought about dropping out or switching to online classes, but homeschooling really isn’t a good fit for everyone. Probably at least 60% of homeschooled students either don’t complete their program or end up returning to regular schools.

Overall, traditional school is a better choice than homeschooling or online learning. You have a much higher chance of passing your classes when you work with peers, both getting help from others and offering your own support — after all, life works on a give-and-take basis. The most important thing is to try your hardest at whatever you do, never give up, and keep pushing forward. If you stay persistent, you’ll eventually reach your goals.

Dear Mr. Principal, today I want to discuss how many employers prioritize certain personal qualities in job candidates, even when those candidates have no prior experience in the role. I fully agree with this idea, because while someone might not know how to do a specific job right away, they can always pick up the necessary skills over time.

When someone first starts a new job, they often have no idea what to do at first. They need guidance from people who already know the ropes, like managers or senior staff. Even someone hired for a management position might have no prior experience in that exact role, but they can pick up what they need to know while working. For example, when I first moved to this country, I started working for my stepfather doing roofing work. I had no clue how to do the job at first, but I learned everything I needed to know over the months I worked with him. Last summer, I also worked as a cashier at a restaurant, and I struggled at first because I couldn’t tell the coins apart – the currency in my home country is very different. But the restaurant manager helped me get up to speed, and I put in a lot of effort to master the job, which helped me succeed.

Many people who already know the basics of a job still work hard because they want to keep learning more. Even those with experience can pick up new tips or methods from coworkers or managers. Here in the United States, a lot of people work hard not just to keep their jobs, but to support their families. They know that if they put in effort, their children can learn from their experience and grow into better people. Most parents want to set a good example for their kids, so children see that hard work is something to be proud of. Others work hard to reach their personal goals, or to build a better future for themselves and their loved ones.

That said, responsibility is another essential quality to keep in mind. Being responsible makes it much easier to get hired in the first place. If you show that you can be trusted to do your work, bosses will see that reliable staff help their company succeed. Many businesses grow and thrive because their employees are responsible and finish all the tasks their managers assign. When I lived in my home country, I saw many small stores fail not because their business idea was bad, but because the staff they hired were not responsible. Workers would show up late, or not complete their assigned duties at all, and the stores eventually had to close because they couldn’t make the improvements they wanted. Responsibility is a trait that will help you succeed in all areas of life. If you’re new to a job and you show up on time every day, your employer will see that you take your work seriously – and that is exactly the kind of responsible person most companies are looking for.

Another thing employers should keep in mind is that they need to hire people who are patient. In every workplace, there are managers, and those managers need to have the patience to train new hires who don’t know the job yet. For example, some managers are very impatient – they dislike helping new staff who lack experience, saying they don’t have time to train others. They might assume the new hire will never learn the job properly, or they have more important tasks to focus on than teaching someone new. But in most restaurants and retail stores, managers have a positive attitude and are always willing to help new team members.

To sum up, I believe a job candidate does not need to have prior experience in a role if they are responsible and genuinely interested in the work – they will pick up everything they need to know to succeed. It’s also important to remember that no one is born with work experience. We all have to learn from the challenges life throws at us, and we grow by learning from our mistakes.

A large number of students and teachers believe that online classes are bad for both students and their schools. Two key reasons drive this opinion: first, students often fail to take notes on the material teachers cover, and second, they are easily distracted during lectures. Since students are unlikely to record key information or stay focused on the teacher’s instructions, many argue that online learning offers no real benefits to those taking the classes.

One major issue is that students rarely take notes during online lessons. In a traditional classroom, teachers watch students work, so learners take notes to avoid trouble. But online, there is no supervisor, so students do not see the point of writing things down. Teachers on screen cannot tell if a student is jotting key points. Most learners won’t bother with notes, since they know the teacher cannot check. Taking notes helps information stick and makes topics easier to understand. Teachers cannot monitor this online, as they cannot see what students do off-screen. Many are not even paying attention to the lesson.

Distraction is another big problem, as students often fail to focus on online lectures. In a regular classroom, a student looking away from the teacher will miss important information. The same happens online: learners zone out and miss key details. This is serious, because distracted students might not know class updates, forget assigned tasks, or miss instructions for their work. Paying attention is key—no one wants to miss vital information. Students need to focus on the teacher to get details for assignments. When learners skip notes and stop paying attention, they miss key facts and may panic when solving homework problems, with no notes to check.

Overall, students gain nothing from online classes, since they neither take notes nor focus on the teacher’s lectures. They skip writing down useful information because no one is watching them while the teacher talks. This lack of focus means they miss valuable content, including instructions for assignments and how to complete tasks. The combination of no note-taking and constant distraction is exactly why online classes are not a good option. Teachers cannot track what students are doing during lessons, and many learners do not even care about the material being taught.

Requiring high schoolers to take summer classes so they can finish school a year early is not a smart plan. I hold this view because many learners may lack the required credits to graduate early, others have summer jobs that would clash with extra coursework, and plenty of students want to take a full year off before moving on to the next stage of their lives.

First off, pushing students to graduate in three years instead of four often creates credit problems. If a student wants to finish early but is short on required credits, they will have to pack extra classes into their schedule. This overload leads to unnecessary pressure and stress. A standard four-year high school timeline gives teens enough time to join clubs, play sports, and keep up with regular coursework without feeling buried. These extracurricular activities also make their college applications stand out. Trying to balance too many classes with sports or club commitments would leave most students feeling completely overwhelmed.

Another key issue is that many high school students take summer jobs. Most teens want spending money, and summer work is their main source of income. For a lot of learners, summer is the only time of year they don’t have to worry about schoolwork, so they can focus entirely on saving for a car, college tuition, or other big expenses. For many, summer work is not just a way to earn cash, but a hobby they enjoy. Adding summer classes to their schedule cuts into the time they can spend on this, as well as their ability to save for big goals.

Last but not least, not all students want to jump straight from high school to college. Some plan to take a full year off to work, figure out their future career path, or just rest after years of studying. This gap year lets them work full-time and save up for major expenses like a car, a house, or college tuition. True success takes time to build, so it’s better to move at a steady pace instead of rushing through school and burning out from stress and exhaustion.

To sum up, letting students take summer courses to graduate high school in three years is a poor idea. Many may struggle with credit shortages that force them to overload their schedules, others have summer jobs that conflict with extra classes and add stress, and plenty of students want a year-long break from school to work and save for their future needs.

Is our personality shaped by forces beyond our control, or do we pick our own character traits? British naturalist and politician John Lubbock once said, "Your character will be what you yourself choose to make it." I firmly agree with this view: every person has the independence and self-control to decide what kind of person they become. We get to pick the environments we spend time in, and we control how we respond to both good and bad situations. At the end of the day, each of us has the freedom to decide who we want to be.

No matter how difficult a challenge or how harsh a situation we face, we always retain full control over our own responses. Even when life feels unbearable, we can choose whether to meet it with tears or a smile, whether to adopt a negative mindset or a hopeful one.

I saw this truth play out in my own family, with my 78-year-old grandmother. She worked her whole life and was always incredibly self-reliant. She used to say, "If I don’t handle a job, no one else will do it to my standard." She was always energetic, never wasted time sitting idle, and kept a bright, positive attitude. Then one day, she suffered a severe stroke that left half her body paralyzed and took away her ability to speak. Her doctor told us she would need a wheelchair for the rest of her life. Watching such a lively, upbeat person confined to a chair was heartbreaking for our whole family, especially my mom. But even though my grandma understood exactly what had happened, her outlook never changed. She refused to let the stroke define her: she chose to stay positive, took charge of her recovery, and never gave up on herself. This experience taught me that even in the darkest of times, we have the power to decide what kind of person we will be.

We also have the freedom to shape the world around us. We can pick who we spend time with, where we live, and what kind of communities we join. Most people can recognize when they are surrounded by toxic individuals, or when a certain environment is pushing them to act in ways they don’t like. Even if our surroundings influence our daily habits, the final choice of how we let that environment affect us is ours alone. We can decide to turn a negative space into a positive one, or walk away from it entirely. At the end of the day, your character depends on your own choices, not the people or places around you. While the environment you live in can shape your daily habits and mood, you are the only one who decides who you want to be, how you let others affect you, and whether you stay positive or give in to negativity.

How we react to the people around us is one of the clearest signs of our character. Our responses can reveal our vulnerabilities, or show others whether we are calm and kind or short-tempered and harsh. Reactions make up a huge part of who we are, whether we feel in control of them or not. The way we respond to others is entirely our choice. Many people struggle to develop their own sense of self, especially when shifting moods make it hard to stay consistent. Some even try to copy the personalities of classmates they admire, but that is just borrowing someone else’s character instead of building your own. Last but not least, every single person has the freedom to choose what traits make up their personality.

In conclusion, every person is free to decide what their character will be. No matter how hard life gets, or how many people seem to be against you, you always have the option to either copy someone else’s personality or build one that is truly your own. But at the end of the day, whatever your character looks like, it is always the result of the choices you have made.

British naturalist and politician John Lubbock once stated, "Your character will be what you yourself choose to make it." This raises a key question: do we shape our own character traits, or are they formed by outside forces we cannot control? I believe we have control over our character, because we can actively choose traits like how quiet or outgoing we are, and even how we handle our ego. That is why I am convinced we choose our own character.

Take being quiet, for example. This trait is not strictly good or bad—it is fine to be reserved sometimes, but you cannot stay silent all the time, since you need to speak up occasionally to connect with others. It is all about finding a balance. I remember my 6th and 7th grade years in middle school: I was an extremely quiet kid with very few friends, never talking to anyone. I felt so lonely because of that. Then I made a choice to start talking to people more, and soon I had lots of friends. That is why I believe we can control our character traits, including how quiet we are.

Another clear example is being social. Being outgoing is a valuable trait, since talking to others helps you make friends, learn new things, and even discover more about the world. In 7th and 8th grade, I was very talkative—so much so that I worried I was annoying some people with how much I spoke. But through that experience, I learned how to approach and talk to different people properly. I also realized that people can change over time: some who seem nice at first become moody or mean, while others who start out unfriendly turn kind. Of course, some people never change at all, and that is just how the world works. All of this supports my view that we can control and choose our social character traits.

My next example is what I call "being over yourself"—that is, being confident or keeping your ego in check. This is a useful trait to have, but it can turn negative if you become too confident and come across as cocky. Many people dislike arrogant types, calling them "no fun" or "party poopers." I will admit that I was quite cocky and overconfident when playing sports, since I was very competitive as a kid. Sometimes I would scream and yell with excitement when I scored a point or won a game. Some people argue that our character traits are shaped by influences we cannot control, and I can see where they are coming from: when I screamed after scoring or winning, I did not feel like I was in control of that reaction at the time. I could have chosen to celebrate quietly, maybe raising my hands to the sky instead of shouting, but I did not make that choice. That moment actually proves my point: I had the option to act differently, so I did have control over that trait, even if I did not use it in the moment. This is why I believe we can choose traits related to "being over yourself."

To wrap up, when British naturalist and politician John Lubbock wrote, "Your character will be what you yourself choose to make it," he was likely considering two possibilities: either we choose our own character traits, or our character is formed by influences beyond our control. I believe he meant that we choose our traits—including being quiet, being social, and being over yourself. That is why I agree with his core message: we are the ones who shape our own character.

Suppose the school plans to extend the school day. I strongly disagree with adding more time, as longer hours would leave students feeling bored, overwhelmed, stressed, and irritated. Most kids have no desire for this change—they want to keep their regular, normal school day, just as it is now. They want to prove they can handle their current schoolwork without extra hours, and they believe in their own ability to succeed.

First, longer school days are incredibly boring for students. Kids look forward to their free time after class because they want to have fun and enjoy themselves, not sit in a classroom for extra hours. When schools start thinking about staying open longer, students begin to worry about all the fun activities they will miss out on. For example, my classmate Generic_Name always heads outside to play with friends immediately after the regular school day ends—longer hours would take that joyful time away from her.

Second, adding more school time causes intense stress. Students would feel panicked and anxious about the extra hours. This stress is harmful to both their minds and bodies—it can raise blood pressure, lead to heart problems, and in the worst cases, make kids feel so hopeless they consider hurting themselves. Of course, no one should ever act on those feelings, and students can take steps to protect their mental health instead. A clear example is when Generic_Name took a big test: she felt nervous, frustrated, lonely, and deeply upset from the pressure of schoolwork.

Third, longer days are deeply irritating for students. Kids will end up exhausted, lightheaded, and dizzy in class because their bodies simply do not have enough energy to handle extra hours of learning. For example, my best friend Generic_Name once studied for a big test for hours after school, and she ended up completely worn out by the end of it. I truly believe it is not right that so many students end up physically or mentally injured by school demands. Even if making changes to the school day is difficult, it is worth the effort. I want as many people as possible to be happy, not hurt or feeling down, and to feel positive about what is happening in their lives.

To sum up, I fully disagree with the school’s plan to add more time to the school day. It is a terrible idea that would leave students feeling irritated, bored, and stressed out. In my opinion, it is much better for kids if they do not have to worry about this extra burden. We can make small, steady improvements to the school day, step by step, and keep pushing forward until things get better for all students. We should not give up on making school a better place.

I also really think schools would be much better places if there were no bullies, and if the harsh, harmful teaching practices from the past were gone for good. Decades ago, many teachers hit children when they misbehaved, convinced that the kids deserved punishment. I know kids do not always get the right answer or act perfectly, but all teachers are different: some are kind, hardworking, and sweet, while others can be mean, inappropriate, or unkind. The teachers I have had from kindergarten all the way through eighth grade are nothing like those bad teachers of the past. They are nice, helpful, and caring, and they never hit us. Instead, they protect us and look out for our well-being. I want every other kid to have the exact same positive experience I have had with my teachers. My hope is that all children, and really everyone in the school community, can feel happy, safe, and protected at school.

There is a long-standing debate about whether having a positive mindset is the key to succeeding in life. While some argue that a cheerful outlook has nothing to do with achieving success, maintaining a positive attitude can improve a person’s life in countless ways. For one, optimistic people tend to make more friends, leave a lasting impression on others, and enjoy a happier day-to-day life.

When you approach life with a positive attitude, you become more willing to strike up conversations with others, and most people will respond warmly in return. This boosts your mood and makes you seem more approachable and friendly. Having a larger social circle also means you are far less likely to feel lonely. With more people in your life to spend time with, you stay busy enough that there is little room left for stress to creep in.

Many people believe that first impressions are the key to opening the door to love. Positive people naturally leave a strong, favorable impression on others, making them easy to remember. This also makes you feel more upbeat and friendly, whether you are at school, work, or anywhere else.

Research has shown that high levels of stress are harmful to human health. The best way to avoid excessive stress is to maintain a positive outlook, as this can shift many aspects of your daily life for the better. You might find yourself getting along better with neighbors, expanding your network of acquaintances, and having more trusted people to turn to when you need to talk. Overall, people who stay positive tend to lead both happier and healthier lives.

To sum up, a positive attitude is truly the key to success in life. When people stay positive, they are able to make more friends, leave a lasting impression on others, and live a life that is both happy and healthy.

Failure is something most of us fear and try to steer clear of in everyday life. While many go out of their way to avoid any scenario where they might mess up, far fewer people are willing to confront failure head-on. These individuals view setbacks as valuable learning opportunities, and often go on to achieve impressive things in their lives.

Fear shapes nearly every part of our lives. We worry about how we present ourselves, whether we’ve made the right choices, and if our actions will lead to good results. Most of the time, we fear failure because we can’t be sure things will work out, or we’re anxious about the fallout of our decisions. This mindset splits people into two groups with very different approaches: those who play it safe and avoid risks, and those who take bold chances. Both ways of living have their own benefits and drawbacks.

People who choose the safe route rely on years of accumulated knowledge to minimize their chances of failing. Calling them ‘shy’ isn’t always fair, unless they’re faced with something completely new and unfamiliar. They refuse to take risks that could lead to failure, which means they often avoid trying new things entirely, so they never actually fail. This could apply to anything: speaking up in class, joining a sports team, going to the gym, or even wearing a new outfit. The only thing standing between them and trying something new is fear. Since they never take the risk, they never find out what the outcome could be. If they do fail, they see it as a total loss. One upside to this mindset is that they really don’t lose much, but it also means they achieve far fewer successes. This doesn’t mean these people are constantly afraid, or that they never take risks at all. It’s just that they prefer to play it safe. The steps they do take to move forward are rarely scary, and often feel like no big deal. Most of these people have made mistakes in the past, and those experiences make them hesitant to try again: maybe they said something silly in class and everyone laughed, tried a sport and was terrible at it, or felt out of place at the gym because they weren’t as fit as the people around them.

On the flip side, people who seek out new experiences and learn from them are usually the ones who accomplish things that last a lifetime. A great example is former British Prime Minister Winston Churchill. His life proves just how important it is to keep trying. Becoming Prime Minister was never easy for him, as his biography shows he faced countless failures before finding success. People like Churchill see setbacks as life lessons. To them, failure is part of the process of perfecting ideas, making actions successful, picking the right path, or answering questions correctly. When a wrong move leads to a failure, they confront it head-on, and most importantly, they feel proud of what they’ve learned. They aren’t proud of failing, but of the growth and knowledge they’ve gained, which pushes them to avoid making the same mistakes again. They might slip up and repeat errors sometimes, but in the end, they come out on top. This is exactly where enthusiasm plays a key role.

Everyone works toward personal goals, and enthusiasm is what drives that effort. Winston Churchill led Britain to victory in World War II because his goal was to protect his people, humanity, and everything he had worked to build. Enthusiasm can take many forms: a sense of duty for a leader, joy for a musician, or the desire to bring happiness as a parent. How well you hold onto that enthusiasm depends entirely on you. The size of your goal doesn’t matter at all, whether it’s small, medium, or huge. What matters is the person pursuing it, not how big the goal is. For example, anyone could become president if they truly want to, but someone might not even manage to go to the gym a few times a week if they’re lazy and lack the willpower. This is closely tied to our life goals, whether they’re short-term or long-term. A failure can either crush your enthusiasm, or make it stronger than ever.

My own experience with martial arts is a good example of this. I taught myself to dual-wield nunchucks, and the learning process was really tough. I’m right-handed, so spinning the weapon with my left hand was painful at first. I hit my forearm hundreds of times, and my skin would be bright red after just an hour of practice. People often asked why I kept going instead of giving up. The only reason I didn’t quit was my enthusiasm for my goal: to master the nunchucks. After months of practice, I finally got the hang of it. I’m not a master yet, but at least I don’t hit myself anymore.

Of course, it’s important to note that some people face failure so extreme they can never try again. This includes situations where someone loses their life, which is a risk that’s too big to take. But it’s not just death that can stop us. Sometimes people end up unable to do things they once loved. On the other hand, there are also tragic situations where people come back stronger than before. I heard about a boy who loved riding his bike and doing tricks. He got into a car accident and lost his leg. He was in a wheelchair for months, until doctors offered to fit him with a prosthetic leg. He spent a long time in recovery, and as soon as he could move on his own, he wanted to get back to biking. For a long time, he couldn’t do anything on his bike. He felt angry and defeated, but he never gave up. After failing over and over, he finally got back on his bike. These days, he rides just as well as he did before the accident, all because he refused to quit. His story really inspires me.

I completely agree with Winston Churchill’s view. We need to fail to learn, and to truly appreciate what we achieve. We shouldn’t just practice until we get something right, but until we can’t get it wrong. We need clear goals to stay enthusiastic, and we should never let that drive fade. Instead, we should let every failure make our enthusiasm even stronger. We can either stay in our comfort zones and avoid failure at all costs, or we can face setbacks head-on and gain valuable experience.

Everyone has responsibilities to handle in life, and meeting those duties often comes with challenges we have to work through. Right now, our city council isdiscussing a new rule that would set a 10 p.m. weeknight curfew for teens, along with a midnight curfew for other nights. To the council members: I appreciate that you are trying to keep young people safe, but I do not agree with this proposed curfew, for a few key reasons. Many of us have after-school activities, part-time jobs, or even get caught in unexpected traffic that makes us run late. I get why you might think late-night driving is risky for teens. You’re probably worried that we’re too tired to focus properly on the road after a long day. But the truth is, teenagers can stay alert much later than most adults realize. We don’t stay up late just because we’re bored. We have real reasons: we work jobs, finish extracurriculars, and only go to sleep once we’re home from these obligations. We’re capable of managing our own schedules now. That said, I do agree that teenagers should not be driving on the roads past midnight. Late nights are when most drunk or impaired drivers are out on the streets. Depending on which part of the city you’re in, you might also hit wildlife like deer that are hard to see in the dark. There are plenty of hidden hazards at night: poor visibility makes it hard to spot obstacles, and there are sometimes people hanging around who might cause harm to young drivers. All drivers, even adults with years of experience, can get tired after long drives and risk getting into accidents at night. To wrap up, I understand why you want to keep teens off the roads at 10 p.m. on weekdays and past midnight entirely—late-night driving does come with real dangers. But I hope you also recognize that we aren’t out late for no reason. We’re doing important things like working or attending school activities, and we will be careful on the roads because we know the risks just as well as you do.

I strongly feel that the best way to build real-world experience, learn from past errors, and develop a strong work ethic is to stay consistently active and push yourself to achieve more. For me, staying busy and ticking off goals matters because it opens far more doors to long-term success.

Take my experience with soccer, my favorite sport, as a clear example. I made the school team initially, but I was one of the weakest players there—I struggled with basic skills and didn’t understand the game well. That changed when I started practicing every single day, both after classes and in my spare time. Regular training let me work through my weak points, fix the mistakes I kept making, and master the core rules and fundamentals of soccer.

Some people argue that doing nothing can actually help you reach your goals, but I disagree. You only gain meaningful life experience and grow from your errors when you’re actively working toward something and racking up achievements. My soccer practice paid off in more ways than one: along with fixing my weak spots, I picked up new tricks, learned how to pass the ball straight to teammates, and even trained to be a skilled goalkeeper who could catch tough shots. All of this gave me the confidence and experience I needed to keep pushing forward.

A perfect example of this came during one of our matches, where scouts were present to pick top players for the International Soccer Team. Their selections were based on how well players performed and whether they followed the game’s rules. Three days after the match, I got the news: I’d been nominated to join the international team, and I was even awarded the title of best player in that game. This opened up a huge, concrete opportunity for my future success in the sport.

To sum up, staying active and putting in hard work is the only way to gain valuable life experience, unlock more opportunities, and achieve your goals. Reaching any meaningful accomplishment is never easy—you will face countless challenges along the way, and learning to overcome those hurdles is exactly what accomplishment means. The path to achieving anything in life is full of obstacles, but if you keep going, work hard, and never give up, all that effort will eventually pay off with real, lasting success.

Many students find real value in taking classes from home, as they often have valid personal reasons for doing so, or face difficulties that make attending school in person hard. For instance, some learners dislike being part of a large school community, or feel overwhelmed by having too many people around them. If I had the chance to pick between remote learning and going to school in person, I would definitely choose to attend campus, since I want to meet more people and build new friendships.

Below are three key reasons why some students may prefer to take virtual classes from their own homes.

The first reason is that some students simply do not enjoy interacting with people outside their home. They may believe that most people are unkind, mean, or disrespectful toward others. In many cases, their parents also prefer remote learning, as they are scared of how their child will be treated by peers, or worry their child will be exposed to bad influences that push them toward making poor life choices. Other families choose home learning because their child has health issues, and they fear other students will laugh at them or make fun of their condition.

The second reason is that some students dislike the routine of a normal school day, and would much rather stay home to take their virtual classes. They often worry that other people will not like them, or spend time judging them for no reason. Sometimes, students avoid in-person school because they have health problems that make them feel self-conscious or embarrassed. Others may have gone through something bad while at school previously, which makes them not want to return.

Finally, if I had to pick between staying home and going to school, I would choose in-person classes every time. I would love to help other students understand why attending school on campus is so important, and give them advice that they do not need to feel embarrassed about their personal problems. I would tell them they just need to let those worries go, since many people who bully others do not even realize how much harm they are causing the person they pick on.

To sum up, students are completely free to choose remote learning from home if that works best for them. They will still get the same education as in-person students, and they have valid reasons for picking this option. That said, I would always remind people that they do not need to care about what others say about their choices.
