I think technology should not be permitted in a lot of everyday spaces. For one thing, it can cloud people’s thinking and leave many users hopelessly addicted. It also causes severe harm in multiple ways, from tearing families apart to enabling cruel online bullying.

First, homes are one place where technology often does more harm than good. Many families face constant conflict because children become obsessed with the latest devices. Overuse also takes a serious toll on users’ health: staring at a screen for hours on end does not damage your eyes right away, but it can lead to permanent vision loss over time. On top of that, heavy tech use can make people act irrationally, as if they have lost their grip on clear thinking.

Schools are another space where technology should be banned. It is far too easy for students to cheat using phones or tablets, and relying on tech for every task means they never learn basic skills like writing by hand. Tech also enables bullying: students can harass peers online or share inappropriate content like private photos. Worse still, devices distract learners from lessons, making it hard for them to focus in class.

Roads are yet another area where technology causes major problems. Reports show that phone use while driving is one of the top causes of traffic accidents. Tech also makes it easy for criminals to commit fraud: they can hack into people’s bank accounts to steal money, or access personal information to break into private accounts.

To sum up, more and more people are getting addicted to technology as new, faster devices hit the market. Overusing tech can ruin lives in countless ways, from permanent vision loss to splitting families apart. Many people lose their ability to think clearly because technology can be an incredibly harmful force in daily life.

Do you think that failing at something first is a good way to find success later in life? In this essay,I will explain why I believe failing at things is an essential part of life. When you mess up at least once, it helps you grow more confident, gets you ready to handle the real world, and teaches you that you have to work hard for the things you want.

My mom has always been my biggest supporter. She used to tell me, "I believe in you, so stay confident." When I was in first grade back in my home country of Honduras, one of my teachers warned my mom that I was struggling so much in math that I would definitely fail the grade. And I did. But my mom didn't blame my intelligence. She told me that failing didn't mean I wasn't smart—it just meant the work was too hard for me at the time, but she knew I could handle it. The next year, I had to repeat first grade. Everything was different that time around. My teacher actually pulled my mom aside to say she was shocked by how well I was doing, not just in math but in all my other classes too. I'm actually glad I failed first grade, because it taught me that one failure doesn't mean you have to quit. You have to push back and keep trying, just like I did.

Since then, I've always reminded myself to never give up on my dreams, no matter how hard things get. When I was little, I decided I wanted to be a lawyer when I grew up. One day in school, we had to stand up and share our future career plans. When I said I wanted to be a lawyer, a classmate laughed and told me I'd never be able to finish that degree. I told him he had no idea what I was capable of, no matter how many times I might fail along the way. I know I'm going to be a lawyer, because giving up on your dreams is what makes you a failure—and I am not a failure. I never let other people tell me I won't achieve my goals.

Failing once, or even multiple times, does not mean you will never succeed. In fact, it's the opposite. I'm 18 years old now, and I've failed plenty of times in my life so far. But I always keep one thing in mind: every time I fail, I learn a new lesson. I treat all those past failures as practice that helps me get ready for the real world and all the challenges it brings.

Some people might disagree with how I see failure, but they're the ones who are mistaken. No one is perfect. Every single person makes mistakes or fails at something at some point in their life.

If you want to be successful, you have to take things one step at a time. No matter how many times you fail, keep moving forward. You will achieve what you want, and you shouldn't let anyone else tell you what you can or can't do.

Becoming highly skilled in any field is an incredible achievement, as it means you have built up years of experience and know exactly how to handle your work. Like anything else, being a master of a craft comes with both benefits and drawbacks.

In my view, I disagree with Emerson’s perspective. Even if you are an expert in a specific field, you never stop developing. Every day, you gain new insights from your mistakes, learn lessons about life and how to live well, and pick up knowledge that applies to all parts of your life, not just your area of expertise.

However, there will always be people who challenge your views, since they have different mindsets or approach problems in completely different ways.

If you have a clear goal, you should never stop improving in that area, especially if it is something you truly want for your future and plan to pursue for the rest of your life. This is why it is so important to choose your path carefully: if you pick the wrong one, you may end up regretting it later. Regret is hard to undo, and it feels terrible to realize you have spent years working on something you never actually enjoyed.

Being an expert in a field brings many valuable perks, including:
You have full control over your work, so no one needs to tell you what to do.
You can complete tasks faster and with less effort than beginners.
You feel passionate and excited about the work you do, since you know you are good at it.
It is easier to access opportunities and resources that benefit you.
You can land high-paying, rewarding jobs in your field.
You may even be able to start your own business and work as your own boss.

There are also downsides to being a master, such as:
There are many other skilled experts working in the same field as you.
You have to compete with rivals who are also trying to succeed.
You face constant pressure to stay at the top of your game and be the best.
If you run a business, you have to fix any mistakes immediately, since errors can hurt your professional reputation and skills.

To sum up, I still disagree with Emerson. Even when you make mistakes, you can keep growing and reaching new goals. Personal and professional growth should never stop. You may stay in your current role or position, but there is always room to improve and become better every single day.

First, some companies have switched to a four-day work week with ten-hour days, mostly to cut energy use. Now, schools are considering slashing weekly class time to just two hours. This plan has three major flaws: it cuts instructional time, forces teachers to switch from salaried roles to hourly pay, and damages the economy.

I strongly disagree with cutting school hours to save energy. Students need eight hours of class daily. If weekly class time drops to two hours, teachers cannot cover all required material, severely disrupting students’ learning.

Another issue is how this affects teachers. Most earn a fixed salary, but under this plan, they would only be paid for two weekly class hours. Their paychecks would drop sharply, like other hourly workers. Many would need second jobs to make ends meet.

This shift also hurts the economy. When businesses cut hours to save energy, people take home less money. Workers have debts like credit card bills, health and car insurance to pay. With less income, households struggle to cover these costs, and food prices will rise significantly.

In conclusion, employers should not reduce working or school hours. While saving energy is good, this plan harms education, teachers’ finances, and the economy.

I strongly believe implementing a curfew for teenagers is a positive step, and there are plenty of reasons to support this policy. For one, most young people have school every single weekday, with the only exceptions being official holidays or days they are too sick to attend. If a curfew is put in place, fewer teens will be wandering the streets late at night, which is unnecessary in the first place—there is rarely a good reason for a student to be out past 10 p.m. on a school night. A 10 p.m. weeknight curfew makes sense: it gives teens enough time to socialize after school, while ensuring they get home before the riskiest hours. Staying out late often leads to trouble, and late-night streets are where most criminal activity happens. Fewer teens out after dark means lower chances of them becoming victims of violent crime, as attacks and robberies are far more common late at night. There is also a third key benefit: drug dealers are most active after dark, so if teens are required to be home early, they are far less likely to be exposed to illegal drugs or pressured into trying them.

The proposed curfew times are also very reasonable. For Monday through Friday, teens would need to be home by 10 p.m., and on weekends, the cutoff would be midnight. There is rarely a good reason to be out on the streets past those times. If someone is out later, they should have a very valid, extreme excuse for violating the rule. This policy would definitely keep young people out of far more trouble than they currently face. The allotted time is more than generous, not unfair at all. It does not disrupt anyone’s daily life: teens can still go out with friends, grab dinner, or attend events, just not stay out until the early hours of the morning. At first, I thought maybe the law should also apply to people over 18, since young adults often go to late-night parties. But on reflection, this law should only apply to people under 18. Adults over that age can make their own decisions about right and wrong, so it makes no sense to restrict them the same way.

This law is not meant to punish anyone, but to make the community safer by keeping teenagers out of harm’s way—a goal I fully support. That said, it is important to acknowledge that if a young person is already determined to misbehave, no new rule will magically change their behavior or keep them out of trouble if they do not want to follow rules. It is also worth noting the curfew does not stop teens from hanging out with friends: it just reduces the risks that come with being on the streets late at night. Every year, many innocent people are hurt or killed after being out after dark in areas where dangerous people are active. Teens have the entire afternoon after school to participate in sports, clubs, or other activities, so this rule does not take away their freedom to do what they enjoy. It is simply a way to protect them from avoidable danger. There may be valid reasons to be out past curfew, like attending a birthday party or family event, but there should still be clear limits on how late they can stay out. For people who break the rule, consequences should start with a warning, then get stricter with each repeat offense.

My position on this curfew law is that I understand why some people oppose it, even though teenagers generally know what they should and should not be doing. I have two different perspectives on this: reasons to be concerned, and reasons not to be. For one, many teens enjoy sleepovers—would these be allowed under the curfew? Do teens have to be in their own home, or can they stay at a friend’s house? These are valid questions. On the other hand, think about a teen who goes to a weekend party with a midnight curfew, loses track of time, and gets home at 1 a.m. They might be having fun with friends and simply forget the time, then get stopped by police after a neighbor calls to report suspicious activity. The police arrive, and now the teen has to face legal consequences for a simple mistake. Worse, this violation goes on their permanent record just because they stayed out a little too late. This would be incredibly frustrating: they get in trouble with their parents, and then face long-term consequences. Imagine a straight-A student with a high GPA who gets rejected from their dream college just because of one silly curfew violation years prior. That is a major downside, as colleges review all parts of an applicant’s history. Even a small mistake could ruin their chances, and they would carry that guilt for the rest of their life, knowing they missed out on their goal school because of one late night.

On another note, there is currently no general curfew for when teenagers must be home, but there are already strict rules for new drivers with learner’s permits: they are not allowed to drive late at night. This is already a big restriction, so you rarely see teen drivers out after dark, except right when school lets out. This proposed curfew has both pros and cons, but I believe the benefits far outweigh the drawbacks. Everything about the policy is reasonable and easy to understand. The only real downside I can think of is the risk of a violation going on a teen’s permanent record, which is a serious concern. But overall, there are far more positives to this law. It should be adopted across the entire United States, not just in one city or town. It will keep far more people safe. Of course, there will always be teens who try to break the rule as a joke, but this is not something to take lightly. All young people need to take the curfew seriously and follow the rules, as the goal is to protect them, not punish them.

In conclusion, a curfew would help prevent terrible crimes like child abduction and sexual assault, which are far harder to detect in the dark of night. Thieves often target young people walking alone after dark, sometimes abducting them to sell them or harm them. Putting this rule in place would greatly reduce how often these horrific incidents happen to anyone, but especially to young people. It will also keep teens out of all kinds of trouble by limiting their time on the streets during the most dangerous hours of the night, when they are most vulnerable to harm.

As a student, I find working in a group way better than handling assignments all by myself. There are a few clear reasons why I feel this way.

First, group work lets us complete assignments much more quickly. Second, each person takes on a different section of the task, so we split the work evenly. Third, if anyone gets stuck on their part, the rest of the group is there to help them figure it out.

Of course, group work has downsides too. For one, there are way more distractions when you’re working with other people. There’s also the issue of everyone wanting to add their own ideas to the project, which can lead to disagreements.

Now, let’s look at the benefits of working alone. The biggest plus is that you won’t face any distractions while you work. You also get to decide exactly how the assignment looks, since you’re the only one contributing ideas. Another advantage is that you can ask the teacher directly for instructions, so you’re more likely to complete the assignment exactly how they want it.

But working alone has its drawbacks too. For starters, it takes way longer to finish an assignment when you’re doing all the work yourself. You also have to handle every single part of the task alone, with no one to rely on but yourself.

No matter if you pick group work or solo work, you’ll run into pretty much the same struggles: you have to get a certain amount of work done, deal with conflicting ideas about how the assignment should look, and decide on the best way to approach it.

Even so, I still prefer group work. I know myself well enough to admit that I probably wouldn’t finish an entire assignment if I had to do it alone. When I work in a group, I only have to complete one small section, which feels manageable. Some people might say I’m just choosing group work to avoid doing as much work, and they’re right. But at least that way, the assignment actually gets done, instead of me leaving the whole thing unfinished.

To sum up, I’d always choose group work over working alone. After all, as the saying goes, "teamwork makes the dream work."

Does confidence come from accomplishing goals, or from getting praise from others? There’s a common debate about whether students need to already have self-confidence to learn effectively, or if self-esteem only develops after you reach a goal. While people have all kinds of opinions on this, I strongly believe you need to be full of self-confidence before you can achieve anything meaningful. I have three main reasons for this: first, you need self-esteem to work hard and keep learning new things regularly. Second, confidence and a positive attitude are essential to finish tasks successfully. Third, being confident means feeling certain about the actions you’re about to take.

Accomplishing big things feels great, but without confidence, how can you even trust your own ability to try? Let’s start with the need for self-esteem to work hard and keep learning. Take doctors, for example: they never stop studying, because new diseases pop up all the time, and new treatments are developed constantly. They can’t do their jobs if they don’t believe in their ability to keep learning. The same goes for learning a new language. Imagine someone who speaks Spanish fluently trying to learn English. It’s tough! Some words translate directly, but many don’t. One English word might have five different Spanish translations, and plenty of terms have no similar match at all. No one ever masters an entire language completely, not even native speakers. But if you stay confident, you’ll keep building your skills little by little, knowing you’ll never stop learning new words every day.

Next, you need confidence and positivity to actually get things done. Anger, for instance, makes it impossible to focus, and usually leads to messy, unproductive results. Think about when end-of-year exams and standardized SOL tests roll around, and you feel totally unprepared. The confidence you’ve built by showing up to school every day, even when you’re tired or having a bad day, is what helps you remember all the information you’ve learned. It gets you through those stressful “nightmare” test days. If you’ve put in the study time, you’ll feel ready to pass when the exam finally arrives.

Third, confidence is all about feeling sure of the steps you’re about to take. Consider job hunting: you never know exactly what a new workplace will be like, or how the hiring team will react to you. You have to trust in yourself, and let your confidence push past your fears. Fear stops you from trying at all. Since you can’t predict what will happen in that first interview, the people hiring you need to see that you’re capable of doing the job. If you seem unsure of yourself or lack confidence, they’re very unlikely to pick you for the role.

Of course, some people argue the opposite: that self-esteem only comes after you achieve something. They say when you reach a goal you’ve fought hard for, confidence follows as a natural result. For example, passing a big test isn’t easy. You have to combine all kinds of effort to get there. Adults often assume students only have to show up to school, but studying isn’t just about passing classes, it’s about retaining knowledge for the future. SOL tests are a perfect example: teachers spend eight months preparing us for tests that don’t take very long to complete, and that’s not even counting regular exams. When you pass, you feel huge satisfaction knowing it’s over, summer is here, and you don’t have to worry about school for a while after fighting for eight months. But if you fail the SOL twice, that can hurt your confidence for the next school year.

Another point they make is that after achieving something, people feel joyful that the hard work is over. If you stay up all night studying for your driving test and feel sure you’ll pass, that’s a great feeling. But if you fail, all that effort isn’t wasted, you just have to try again until you pass. If you do pass on the first try, you’ve achieved your goal, you’re happy it’s done, and you’re one step closer to owning a car and driving on your own. Your confidence shoots up, because if you could pass on the first try, you start to feel like you can tackle any scary challenge.

They also note that positive people are full of joy, confident in what they want, and willing to fight until they achieve it. There are all kinds of people in the world, positive and negative. Starting a new job is so frustrating at first, because you have no idea what you’re doing. Positive people always assume things will work out, and tell themselves they’ll eventually know the job like the back of their hand. Why? Because they have confidence that they can do anything if they work hard enough. No one is born knowing how to do things perfectly right away. Think about learning to walk: you fall over and over again until your knees are red, maybe even bleeding. But after all that effort, you realize you don’t need help anymore, you can walk on your own. Believing in yourself is exactly what confidence is. Even so, I still believe confidence has to come before achievement. Confidence is the courage you put in your heart to push past fear, and you need that courage before you can even try to reach a goal.

As I’ve said before, you can’t achieve anything without confidence. People need self-esteem to do well at work and keep learning new things. The confidence and positivity each person has makes it possible to finish tasks successfully, and confidence is a feeling of courage that chases fear away. My advice? Have confidence in yourself. Let that confidence cover your fears, and be sure of the choices you make. When you achieve a goal, the fear fades, but the confidence stays with you forever. I hope this essay was helpful to you. Thank you for reading!

Working on your own is more challenging than collaborating with a group, but it is far more effective for truly learning new material. Whether you work solo or with others, you will still complete tasks and pick up knowledge along the way. When I talk about learning, I mean actually discovering information—something that can happen in groups too, since every member brings their own unique ideas and facts about a topic. However, many people treat group work as an opportunity to copy answers just to finish tasks quickly. Copying others does not help you learn anything meaningful; it only gets the work done.

I prefer working alone because it supports my personal learning far better. Yes, I usually take longer to finish tasks this way, since I spend time carefully checking small details. Many people avoid independent work, but I choose it deliberately. One key reason I favor solo work is the sense of accomplishment I feel when I finish. If I complete a task entirely on my own, with no help except from the person who assigned the work, I know I have done a good job through my own effort.

Group work is not inherently bad—I just believe students and other learners should prioritize independent work to fully understand what they are doing, rather than just rushing to finish. It is possible to both learn and complete tasks at the same time. While some people do copy others’ work to get by, there are also groups where members all complete their own work and share useful insights with each other. Not everyone cheats, but a large number of students in particular use group work as a chance to copy others’ answers. Though working with a group is often easier than working alone, independent work offers far greater benefits for long-term learning.

People who are not used to independent work often find it difficult to adjust at first, since they are so accustomed to collaborating in groups. However, this challenge pushes them to seek out more details, facts, and clues relevant to their task on their own. If you do get stuck, you can absolutely ask a teacher or another person for help—there is no rule against seeking guidance when you need it. Working alone lets you focus far better on your tasks. In a group setting, you may get distracted by other people’s conversations, or find that hearing others share ideas pulls your attention away from developing your own thoughts.

Ideas shared by group members may also be incorrect, and if you use those wrong ideas in your work, you will end up with mistakes too. Too many people rely on others to provide answers, which is not a good habit. For some, communicating with a group is difficult, which makes independent work a better fit. When you work alone, you can approach tasks in whatever way works best for you. All of these points make it clear that working independently is better than collaborating in a group.

To be frank, telling the truth isn’t always difficult, nor is it always easy. When you’ve done something wrong, you’re bound to feel guilty, and carrying that secret around only adds extra stress. Admitting what happened lifts that weight off your shoulders, which is why being honest is always the better choice.

When you keep a secret, you’ll always feel like you’re hiding something, and you might even get too scared to speak up around the person you’ve lied to. That’s another reason why honesty is the way to go.

Take this common scenario: you accidentally break your mom’s favorite vase, but she hasn’t noticed yet. You might avoid talking to her entirely, torn between making up a lie or coming clean, and terrified that you’ll get punished if you tell the truth.

Honesty also helps build trust with your parents. For instance, if they leave you home alone to look after your younger siblings, being truthful about how you spent that time shows them you’re responsible. If you lie about it, they might assume you were lazy and didn’t actually care for your siblings while they were out buying groceries.

Lying repeatedly can damage your relationship with your parents over time. Remember, it’s important to be grateful for everything they give you and all the support they offer. If you have a friend who gets along really well with their parents, try to follow their example: make an effort to love and appreciate your own parents right now, while you still can.

Of course, no one is perfect. We all tell a lie or two now and then. But as soon as you realize you’ve been dishonest, say, “I’m sorry I wasn’t truthful earlier. Can you forgive me?” If you say this respectfully, with real love and sincerity, things will get better. The people you’ve hurt will feel loved and know how much they mean to you.

Switching school lunches to healthier options wouldn’t actually make much of a difference. Even now, the cafeteria still hasn’t made any real shift toward nutritious meals. Students have pushed for better lunch options for years, but nothing has changed so far. Even on days when the menu includes both healthy and less nutritious choices, students rarely pick the healthier option. For instance, when the cafeteria offers both pizza and rice with chicken, almost every student will choose the pizza.

To be fair, offering a fully healthy lunch menu would be a nice change. But we also have to think about students who struggle with eating habits — many skip meals entirely, sometimes going a full day without eating anything. If the school did decide to replace unhealthy options, they should get rid of pizza, hot dogs and chicken nuggets first. These could be swapped for dishes like rice and chicken, or pasta salad with tomatoes, onions and spinach. Vegan students should also get proper plant-based options, like veggie burgers or other vegetable-heavy meals. If the school is serious about updating the lunch menu, it should also stop wasting money on pointless upgrades, like replacing floor tiles. That money could go toward better food instead. Most people don’t even care that much about how bad the current lunches are — it’s not the end of the world. That’s why so many of us are smart enough to bring our own food from home, just like most other students do.

At the end of the day, changing the menu won’t fix much, because students still eat the school food anyway. Some complain that the meals taste terrible, but they still refuse to bring their own lunch — which makes no sense at all. To be honest, the lunches aren’t always bad; sometimes they’re pretty decent, even if they’re never amazing. There’s no point wasting time and money trying to change a system that should have been fixed years ago. Just pack your own meal from home, and you won’t have to stress about what’s on the cafeteria menu at all.

Taking classes from home is not a good option. I believe learning in a physical school setting is far better, based on my own experiences with remote learning. For one, you lose the immediate support of a teacher who is right there with you. Sure, there’s still an instructor for online courses, but they aren’t present in person to answer questions as they come up. You also can’t rely on classmates for help, since everyone is working alone in their own homes. When you’re in a physical classroom, if you don’t understand a concept, you can raise your hand right away, or ask a friend sitting next to you to explain it quickly. That kind of instant help just doesn’t exist with remote learning. Another issue is that students are much more likely to fall behind. Without a teacher watching over you, it’s easy to get distracted by the internet or other apps on your device. Instead of focusing on the work you’re supposed to be doing, you might end up scrolling through social media or watching videos, which means you don’t actually learn the material. I definitely don’t think students gain anything useful from taking classes at home for this reason.

In-person classes also make it easier to grasp complex topics. Teachers can give real-time examples, walk the class through problems step by step, and clear up confusion on the spot. With online courses, it’s way harder to understand the core point of a lesson, because you don’t have that live guidance. You’re forced to work completely on your own, with no classmates to bounce ideas off of. I had a really hard time with remote learning myself: I had to get through 3 to 5 lessons every day, take at least five quizzes daily, and write detailed notes for each session. I often had to read through lesson materials three times just to pick out the key points and understand what was being taught. Sure, you do learn to be more organized and self-reliant over time, but that benefit doesn’t make up for how much harder the learning process is. For that reason, I strongly recommend that students attend physical schools instead.

There’s also the problem of self-discipline. In a regular classroom, teachers enforce rules about using phones or laptops for non-school purposes during lessons. At home, there’s no one to stop you from checking your phone or browsing the web while you’re supposed to be working. Since you’re in your own space without a teacher present, it’s easy to feel like you can do whatever you want instead of focusing on your coursework. But if you’re not paying full attention to your classes, you won’t actually learn anything, which can lead to failing the course and having to retake it later. That’s a waste of time and effort that could be avoided by going to school in person.

I will admit that there are a few perks to remote learning that some students like. You can sleep in later, take your time eating breakfast, and don’t have to rush to catch the school bus or wake up super early. I’m someone who loves sleeping as much as possible, so I get why that’s appealing. But it’s still your responsibility to finish all your work and submit it before the deadline. If you don’t want to fail, you have to set aside enough time for schoolwork, not just for your own free time. School has to be a priority, not just something you fit in around your personal schedule.

In conclusion, I don’t think students benefit at all from taking classes at home. It takes a lot of self-discipline to remember to log in to classes, complete all assignments, and turn them in on time, with no teacher there to guide you in person. You have to handle all your work on your own, without any immediate help. For all these reasons, I believe remote learning is not a good choice for students.

It feels really great when you say ‘thank you’ or ‘please’ to someone, or offer a polite ‘you’re welcome’ in return. When you speak kindly to others and use good manners, you show you value their time and effort. Always make sure to show you’re grateful for anything someone does for you, whether they help you out with a task or even give you a small gift. Saying ‘thank you’ right away is the easiest way to do this. When you’re consistently kind and polite, people are far more likely to treat you the same way. Showing warmth and care to others not only makes them happy, but it can lift your own mood too. Be ready to lend a hand to anyone who needs it, too.

If you treat others with kindness and use good manners, they will almost always mirror that behavior back to you. That means if they say ‘thank you’ or ‘you’re welcome’ to you, it’s because you showed them that same politeness first. Good manners matter in every situation, big or small—you should say ‘yes sir’ or ‘thank you’ whenever it’s appropriate, but only if you genuinely want to receive that same respect in return. If you hope someone will thank you for a favor, you have to be the first to offer that politeness to them. At its core, being nice to others is the foundation of all positive interactions.

Try to stay upbeat and say positive things to people—this is also how you make new friends, since good manners make you approachable. Always say ‘thank you’ after someone helps you, or does something kind for you. Make sure you have something nice to say to them, because you never know if your small compliment or polite word made their whole day better. The rule is simple: be nice and use good manners, and you’ll get that same treatment back. We all want to be treated with kindness and respect, so we all have to put that energy out into the world first. Being a kind person says a lot about your character.

Maybe you’ve forgotten to say ‘thank you’ or ‘yes sir’ to someone before, and that’s okay—but making a habit of using good manners is always better, because people will be more likely to say ‘you’re welcome’ or ‘thank you’ to you. If you ever upset someone, apologize right away, be kind, and say something nice to them, and things will usually smooth over quickly. They’ll feel better around you too. It all comes down to manners: if you want someone to be nice to you, you have to be nice to them first. If you want someone to say ‘thank you for this’ or ‘you’re welcome for that’, you need to use good manners and say those phrases first. No one really likes spending time with someone who has no manners. If you want kindness from others, you have to either say something nice or help them out with what they need. If you want people to treat you with respect, say something sweet to them, and they’ll almost always do the same for you. For example, if you see someone drop their belongings on the floor, help them pick everything up. When they say ‘thank you’, just reply with ‘you’re welcome’.

Using good manners and being kind is always a good thing, because it shows the best parts of who you are. When you go out shopping and pay for your items, take a second to ask the person checking you out how their day is going. Make them feel seen and appreciated—if you want someone to treat you that way, you have to start by being nice and asking about their well-being first. It doesn’t matter if you don’t know them personally; if they’re a worker helping you, say ‘thank you’ and ask how their day has been so far. Just try to make them smile. Always say ‘thank you’ after you receive something, no matter how small—that shows a lot of respect to the other person. Even if you didn’t start the conversation, if someone tells you to have a good day, say ‘thank you, you too’—that lets them know you hope they have a nice day too, and it’s a really polite gesture. Never say anything mean or hurtful to someone, because they won’t want to be polite back to you if you do.

If you go out to eat at a restaurant, say ‘thank you’ to your server, and you can even leave them a tip to show extra kindness. If you notice a worker is having a bad day, you could even offer to share a meal with them, or buy them a small treat—anything nice counts, even just leaving a bigger tip than usual.

The bottom line is: always say something nice to people, because that’s the only way you’ll get that same kindness back. Good manners and kindness are so valuable if you want others to treat you well. Be happy when someone says something nice about you, and make sure to say something kind in return. The more you use good manners, the more often people will treat you with that same respect.

There is no doubt that keeping adolescents safe and out of harmful situations is a priority for families and communities alike. Implementing rules that require young people to stay off public streets after 10 pm can benefit them in four key areas: their school performance, social relationships, physical health, and financial situation.

The first major benefit of such curfews is improved academic outcomes. When teens are not permitted to wander outside late at night, they are far more likely to get sufficient rest. A well-rested student can pay full attention during lessons, rather than nodding off at their desk. What’s more, these rules keep young people at home for longer stretches of the evening, giving them extra time to complete assignments. Spending this time on schoolwork instead of loitering outdoors directly translates to stronger grades and better study habits. Over time, this consistent rest and focused study time helps teens build stronger learning skills that will serve them well beyond school.

A second compelling reason to adopt these curfews is better social integration. When teenagers are out on the streets in the middle of the night, many members of the public assume they are involved in risky or criminal behavior, such as gang activity. This leads others to avoid them or view them with suspicion, which makes it hard for teens to build positive social connections. By staying home at night, adolescents avoid this negative reputation. People are more willing to interact with them when they are not associated with late-night street activity, allowing teens to communicate more freely, make new friends, and develop healthier social skills without the barrier of others’ unfounded fears.

Medical safety is another key reason to support these regulations. Late-night street activity often carries a high risk of conflict: if a teenager is out past 10 pm, others may misinterpret their presence as proof they are up to no good, which can spark unnecessary fights. These fights can lead to injuries that require hospital treatment, which is easily avoidable if teens are home safe instead. Curfews remove teens from these high-risk environments, protecting them from physical harm and keeping them out of emergency rooms.

The final major benefit is economic growth for young people. For teens who still want to be out of the house during late hours, curfews can motivate them to find part-time work that operates at night, rather than spending time idly on the streets. Working a night shift lets them earn their own money, gain professional experience, and build savings for future needs or unexpected emergencies. This is far more productive than wasting late nights in public spaces, where they gain no financial or personal benefit. Even small amounts of saved income can give teens a sense of financial responsibility and security.

Overall, adopting late-night curfews for teenagers is a smart move for their safety and long-term success. These rules keep young people secure by keeping them off the streets after dark. They also support academic progress by giving teens more time to rest and complete schoolwork, social development by removing the negative reputation of late-night street presence, physical health by preventing fight-related injuries, and financial stability by motivating those who want to be out late to find paid work instead of loitering. All in all, these regulations help teens avoid trouble while building a stronger foundation for adulthood.

Former British Prime Minister Winston Churchill once noted that true success comes from moving through one failure after another without losing enthusiasm. Every time we mess up, we gain lessons that help us grow. We keep pushing forward until we reach the goals we’ve worked hard for. Failing is a key step toward success, and it matters for everyone—setbacks play a big role in daily life. Failing doesn’t mean the world is ending; we always get more chances to try again. Everyone has faced failure, and no one succeeds without stumbling first.

First, failing makes you feel crushed, like you’ll never get it right. But spotting the mistake that caused the setback lets you work harder until you pass. Last year, I failed my world history exam and was so upset I didn’t want to retake it. My teacher handed my test back so I could check my errors. I realized I hadn’t read the questions properly. After that, I always read every question carefully, and got the top grade in class. I learned not to guess, since that leads to failing, and to study the night before tests instead of cramming.

Second, you should put effort into studying all material, even if it feels hard. Just do your best. When I showed my mom my world history results, she said she knew I could pass if I tried. I was scared to retake the test, but she made me study daily. I also stayed after school for extra help. By trying my hardest to understand each question, I passed the final and the whole class. Paying attention in lessons helped too, letting me pass not just the final exam but the entire class. When I passed, I was over the moon—I’d aimed for at least an 89, and finally understood the material and stayed on top of all assignments.

Third, failing something on your first try isn’t bad—it just shows you need to keep working. One day I came home crying after failing the world history exam again. My mom told me failing doesn’t make me dumb, just that I need to fix my mistakes. She shared she failed classes as a kid too, but kept trying and now has a successful career. She said I should always do my best, even if results aren’t perfect, and she’d be proud of my hard work. When I studied hard, retook the test, and passed, I felt so proud. That’s when I knew failure leads to success.

However, some claim failure doesn’t play a big role in life, since there are other ways to succeed. They say you can achieve anything without failing, that you don’t need to work hard for your goals, and that you can accomplish everything just by doing it. But they’re wrong. Failure is the number one driver of success. It pushes you to try harder and learn from mistakes. Failing isn’t the end of the world. You keep trying until you reach the goals you’ve studied and worked hard for. Failure leads to success, and everyone needs to experience setbacks—they play a vital role in our daily lives.

Is it better to make all your own life choices, or should you always ask others for advice first? In my view, the best way to live is to follow your own path, but still lean on your parents for guidance—after all, they’ve already lived through the same stages of life you’re in now. Parents have been through life’s ups and downs, and their only wish is for us to do well; they never want anything bad for us. Take buying a car, for instance. You’d probably ask your parents for their opinion before making a purchase, since they’ve already gone through that process themselves.

But when it comes to figuring out what you want to do with your life, that’s entirely up to you. You decide if you want to be successful, if you want a big house, a reliable car, or a fulfilling job—no one else can make those choices for you. Everything I’ve learned so far tells me that nothing gets done on its own. If you want something, you have to get up and work for it yourself.

I really admire my older brother. When he moved out, he had a clear goal: to own his own car and apartment by the time he turned 21, all while studying part-time. I want to be just like him—hardworking, focused on his goals, and willing to do the work himself, even though he still listened to our parents’ advice. But that’s not the main point here. The key thing is that he left home with a plan, determination, and confidence in himself. He always says that making bold, risky decisions is a huge part of life.

No one can force you to take action except yourself—and the only person who can truly set you back is also you. Every choice you make will shape your own life. Once you’re out of high school, the real world is totally different. You’ll make both good and bad choices, and that’s completely normal. Mistakes are bound to happen, but they’re actually helpful: you learn from them, and grow as a person. I’ve come to see mistakes as a blessing, because even my parents have made plenty of their own. Some they regret deeply, but others turned out to be lucky breaks that taught them valuable lessons they still talk about today.

Having a role model or something that inspires you is really important, but you also have to trust your own instincts. You can always look to others for motivation, but the drive has to come from within. Maybe one day you’ll even be a role model for someone else, inspiring them to become the person they want to be. But success isn’t just handed to you. You have to work for it, and there will always be obstacles and challenges in your way. Collaborating with others is far more helpful because you can finish tasks much faster and more effectively. Plus, you get to talk with your peers about the work and receive useful feedback from them.

Working in a team also lets you discuss ideas with your classmates and get their input on your progress. Everyone can support each other and share feedback tailored to whatever task you’re working on.

Another huge plus of group work is that you get access to way more ideas than you’d come up with on your own. This is honestly the best part: everyone brings their own thoughts to the table, whether they’re similar or completely different. Groups can blend all these ideas together to create something amazing that no single person could have made alone.

Whether you’re working on a school group project or part of a top-level business team, it’s clear that collaborating with others is far more beneficial than working by yourself.

Have you ever found yourself with nothing to do, feeling restless and unmotivated? Thomas Jefferson once said, "Determine never to be idle... It is wonderful how much may be done if we are always doing." I completely agree with this sentiment. Whenever I have too much free time and do nothing, I start to feel down or even depressed, so I always try to avoid idleness at all costs.

There are plenty of ways to stay busy and keep boredom at bay. For example, last summer, my dad, who works as a carpenter, took me to his job site with him. But not everyone can do that, so here are three simple ideas to help you avoid sitting around doing nothing: hit the gym, go for regular walks, or find a part-time job.

First, consider going to the gym. You might hear this advice all the time, but it really works. Exercising regularly is great for both your physical and mental health. You’ll start to feel more confident in yourself, and you might even notice positive changes in how you look.

Next, try going for walks. This is something that helped me find calm and peace. I love strolling around, taking in the sights of the world around me and breathing in fresh air. You don’t have to do it alone, either—bring a friend or two, or take your dog along. It’s a simple way to appreciate the beautiful world God has given us.

The third and final suggestion is to get a job. Last summer, I worked with my dad on his carpentry jobs, and I earned quite a bit of money. I used it to buy nice clothes and shoes, and even got gifts for my family. But the job was about more than just cash. Working with my dad gave me a new perspective on life, encouraged me to change some of my habits, and showed me that the real world is not always easy. It’s also amazing to visit the building site now and see how much progress has been made since I last worked there—the finished structure now feels like a complex maze to me.

That’s why I believe being bored or idle is never a good thing. Just think of all the tasks you can complete and the experiences you can have if you stay busy. For that reason, I think Thomas Jefferson was completely right when he said, "It is wonderful how much may be done if we are always doing."

A common debate in education today is whether schools should manage students’ involvement in extracurricular activities and control how they spend their free time after classes. Some people argue that schools should take charge of these hours, adding more education-focused activities to help students expand their knowledge. However, I believe students should be the ones to decide how they use their after-school time. This is because many hold jobs to support their families, others need to care for younger siblings while parents are at work, and plenty have their own preferred hobbies, from sports to art to completing homework.

First, a significant number of students hold part-time jobs to support their families. Balancing work and school is already challenging: after a long day of classes followed by a shift, many are exhausted and just want to go home and rest. These students often struggle to find time to prepare for quizzes, study for exams, or complete homework assignments. While study halls might help them finish schoolwork, they simply do not have extra time to join school-run extracurricular activities. Many of these working students are also saving up for college tuition, which is a smart investment in their future. For this reason, they have to skip other activities they might enjoy, and schools should not force additional requirements on them.

Second, many students have to rush home after class to look after younger siblings while their parents are at work. Most families cannot afford to hire a babysitter, so this responsibility falls to the student. They might only be able to join a club or activity if a parent has a day off work. On top of their schoolwork, these students often have to cook meals, clean the house, do laundry, and care for their siblings. Juggling all these duties alongside school responsibilities is already difficult, so adding mandatory school activities would only make their schedules more overwhelming.

While some argue that sticking to tasks you have already perfected is the best way to reach your goals, others believe that taking on tougher challenges allows you to go even further than your initial aims.

Going beyond your goals pushes you further in life: it keeps work or hobbies engaging, and expands your education.

If you convince yourself you are not capable of handling a challenge, you are only holding yourself back by lacking self-confidence.

To reach your goals and find true happiness, self-belief has to come first.

Push yourself to take on more than you ever thought you could handle.

Success means moving forward, shaped by those around you, your environment, and your own effort.

Making progress is wonderful, as not everyone has the privileges to get ahead like you.

Take the example of a student who decided to push herself by enrolling in a chemistry course.

Never settle for less than what you are worth.

Making your work enjoyable is a great goal, but how do you actually make that happen?

Start by finding parts of your job that you genuinely like.

Framing work as a game helps: everyone likes games and challenges.

You can pick up new skills just by observing other people’s traits and habits.

There are plenty of ways to learn new things, no matter where you are.

Life is full of unexpected twists, and it will teach us both valuable lessons and hard truths as time goes on.

Always do your best, and learn from every experience.

This means you should push yourself to tackle new challenges and exceed your original goals.

Believe in your own abilities, and work to improve a little bit every single day.

Picking a career in early youth? In several cultures, young people are pressured to settle on a future profession by the time they enroll in high school. But the core question remains: is it wise for students to commit to a specific career path at such a tender age?

Committing to a career early can be a smart move for students who want to pursue lengthy, demanding qualifications. Take fields like medicine, law, teaching, or pediatrics: these require years of study and training. If learners start working toward these goals while they are still young, they will be well-prepared to build a bright future for their country.

Another upside is that starting a career path early leaves room for flexibility later on. For instance, if a young teacher decides they want to switch to a different field down the line, they still have plenty of time and energy to pursue that new goal, since they began their first career while still in their youth.

Of course, there are also downsides to picking a career so early. Some students may burn out from years of constant studying, or come to regret their choice years later when they realize the field does not actually interest them.

All in all, committing to a career at a young age is an excellent choice for most students. That is why we should do more to motivate and support them as they work toward their goals. It would also help greatly if teachers and career counselors stepped in to guide young people toward picking the right profession for their skills and interests.

Honestly, this feels pretty unsettling, but it is the reality we live in: most people just want to fit in and seem "normal" so they can get comfort and approval from others, even when theydo not actually need that validation. Another reason I reject Emerson’s stance is that my generation cares way more about technology than real face-to-face interaction. This makes it easy to understand why so few of us forge our own paths—we would much rather follow the crowd than pursue what we actually want. It blows my mind that we have to sit for mandatory exams just to prove how smart we are, when all you need to do is observe a student in a classroom to see their true abilities, no dumbed-down test required. But I am just a young student following the crowd to get my diploma. These days, a diploma barely gets you anywhere in life, but it looks good on a resume, so that is why I am taking this exact test: to follow the crowd of dead students just trying to graduate for a family that does not even care if I am dead or alive, as long as I have that diploma.

I believe seeking input from several people gives you better results when you need advice. I once came across a quote from basketball star LeBron James that said whenever you need guidance, you should always consult more than one person. His point was that one person might give you incorrect tips, while another could offer exactly the right suggestion. There’s no shame in reaching out to people you look up to, and gathering multiple perspectives usually makes it easier to find reliable, helpful advice.

Of course, not everyone feels comfortable talking to lots of people. If you’re someone who prefers keeping conversations private, or you just want a single opinion, make sure you choose someone you trust completely. I’d always pick a person who is known for making smart, thoughtful decisions, so they can help me avoid mistakes and pick the best option. No matter how many people you ask, it’s crucial to go to someone reliable. Bad advice can lead you to make poor choices, so always check that the person you’re asking has a track record of good judgment.

There are also times when asking just one person is the smarter choice. If you’re sharing very personal, private information, a single trusted person is more likely to keep it secret. Telling multiple people about sensitive details raises the risk that your info gets spread around, which could lead to bullying or make you lose faith in others entirely. For really important private matters, sticking to one confidant is often best. If you don’t feel like you can trust anyone in your life, you can always turn to a school counselor. She is required to keep your information confidential, and she will understand your situation better because she may have gone through something similar when she was young. That makes one trusted person a really helpful resource.

At the end of the day, asking for advice is always valuable, whether you get it from one person or ten. Both approaches can help you solve problems and make better decisions. The only rule is to avoid asking people who regularly make bad choices. If you go to someone with a history of poor judgment, they’ll probably tell you to do the same things they do, and you might end up following their bad example. Good advice has the power to change your life for the better, so always pick your advisors carefully.

Have you ever wondered how difficult it is to stay true to who you are when the world constantly pushes you to fit a different mold? Most of us spend our lives trying to copy those around us, rather than embracing our true selves and finding real happiness. This essay will explore how the world tries to reshape us bit by bit every day, how we give in to that pressure and change who we are, and how each passing year seems to make our generation worse off than the one before.

Every single day, the world looks for new ways to pressure us into changing. As people, we need to pause and reflect: what do we actually want for our future? Why would we want to be exactly like everyone else? Do we crave wealth and status in society? Do we have dreams we want to achieve? These are the questions we should be asking ourselves, not just following the crowd blindly. If we keep walking in the footsteps of everyone else, where will we end up? The truth is, real success only comes when you stay true to yourself—the world will never do that work for you.

We are constantly shaped by the world around us, from the activities we join to how we speak, dress, and even what we believe. If we don’t follow these unspoken rules, society labels us as uncool or out of touch. Take fashion as an example: if you don’t wear the latest trending clothes or shoes, people judge you as less stylish or fun. Maybe you can’t afford those items, don’t have time to shop for them, or simply don’t like the style—but to the world, that just means you don’t measure up. This is incredibly harmful, as many people get bullied for not fitting in, and some even fall into depression because they can’t keep up with these expectations. It’s heartbreaking to see how cruel the world can be when we don’t conform.

Sadly, our generation seems to get worse with every passing year, and a lot of that blame falls on the world’s negative influence. We are surrounded by harmful messages: new drugs that ruin lives, ongoing conflicts between countries, and popular musicians who only sing about substance abuse, violence, and sex. All of this sets a terrible example for young people. If we don’t start embracing who we really are and making better choices, we will only end up in a much darker place down the line.

Some people argue that the world is entirely to blame for all this bad influence, but that’s not entirely true. It’s not just the world pushing us—often, we choose to get involved in harmful things, then turn around and blame the world for our choices when we’re the ones who let it happen. There is still time to turn things around, though. I hope the world becomes a kinder, more welcoming place, and I really believe the next generation has the bravery to fix these problems and build a better society for everyone.

I fully agree that maintaining a positive attitude is one of the most important factors in achieving success in life. A positive mindset is essential in any workplace, and you’ll never meet someone with a sour attitude who’s fun to be around at a party, either. To be totally honest, keeping a cheerful outlook no matter where you are will make your life much easier. I don’t just value a good attitude because it helps me get ahead, though — it also lets me brighten someone’s day, chase away negative energy, and I’m really thankful that I’m naturally upbeat. Plus, staying positive at work can make the day fly by, so you can head home sooner to rest and do whatever you like. I work in a restaurant, and I’ve noticed that when I’m in a bad mood, every shift feels endless, but when I keep a smile on my face, the hours pass in a flash. First impressions matter a lot, too — if you come across as friendly and upbeat when you meet someone, it will benefit you for years to come. A good attitude can turn a terrible situation around in seconds, which is always a plus.

Beyond that, I think a good attitude at work can open up all kinds of long-term opportunities. You might meet your future partner, run into a famous person, or stumble across other amazing chances most people never even imagine. A lot of people don’t stop to think about how much a positive outlook can benefit them personally. It can take you to places others can’t even picture, helping you achieve success by landing a great job, earning promotions, climbing to the top of your field, and eventually making a lot of money. I know most people dream of being wealthy, and while some people naturally keep a good attitude in life, others don’t. Everyone has their own ideas and their own unique perspective on life and the people around them, but there are so many negative people out there. Many of them have had a really hard life, maybe growing up with very little money or feeling like they have nothing left to hope for, but that mindset is wrong. No matter what challenges you face, you have to keep your head up.

On top of that, I’ve mentioned before that small acts of kindness, like sharing a smile, can lift other people’s moods, make the world a nicer place for everyone, and help people appreciate what they have. Humans are social creatures — we don’t want to be alone, and we all want better lives for ourselves and everyone in our community. To be honest, everyone should try to build a more positive work environment by keeping a good attitude themselves. A cheerful outlook is extremely valuable in the workplace, and it benefits you in every other part of life too. People need to figure out what’s best for their own wellbeing and health, too. I know there are plenty of people out there with great attitudes, but sadly, there are still far too many who choose to be negative.

A creative mind is the source of truly great ideas. Summer projects would be far more engaging if students got to select them on their own. When learners pick a topic tied to a subject they care about, they feel more invested, are far more likely to complete the work, and actually enjoy the process too.

Right now, teachers often spend an entire summer break or even a full school year brainstorming topics for student summer assignments. But most of the time, learners put very little thought or effort into these assigned tasks. This wastes the teacher’s time and energy entirely. On the other hand, if students come up with their own project ideas and topics, they are far more motivated to actually finish the work.

When students get to choose their own projects, they pick topics they are genuinely curious about and want to learn more about. Curiosity drives people to dig deeper into a subject, stay engaged, and seek out more information on their own. Learners often come up with brilliant, unique ideas for their own projects, too. Picking a topic you’re passionate about pushes you to think in new ways and try things you never would have considered otherwise.

Summer projects can also help boost classroom grades. For instance, a student who struggles to keep up with the pace of regular lessons can use the summer assignment to work at their own speed. It also gives learners who do not do well in busy, crowded classrooms a chance to do independent study. Summer work gives students an opportunity to improve their marks. If they get to choose their own assignment, they can work at a pace that suits them, with no pressure from tight deadlines. They have the entire summer to complete the project, so if they fail to finish it, that is pure laziness, which will hurt their final grade.

The subject of the assignment plays a huge role in how students respond to it. If a learner is assigned work on a topic they have no interest in, they will likely procrastinate or not do it at all. They will have zero motivation to start the summer task. For example, I might have both a history and a science project to complete. Even if my science teacher assigns a research paper on how genes mutate, which sounds interesting enough, I would not do it, because science does not fascinate me the way history does.

Getting to pick your own project makes the work feel fun, so students actually look forward to doing it and stay engaged throughout. Students should be allowed to design their own summer projects. This cuts down on work for teachers, gives learners a chance to think outside the box, and lets them make their teachers proud by putting in real effort. It sets everyone up for a much better school year ahead.

Is a positive mindset something everyone needs to achieve success in life? In this essay, I’ll explore whether having an upbeat attitude really matters, and I firmly believe we should always keep a positive outlook. It helps us thrive at work, pushes people to give their best even when tasks feel impossible, strengthens our relationships, and boosts our self-confidence.

I experienced this firsthand when I worked at Mango Paradise. My boss was a constantly grumpy man who snapped at all the staff, but I refused to let his bad mood affect me—I always kept a bright smile, no matter how rudely he treated the team. One day, he was completely unlike his usual self: he was devastated, sad, and anxious because his wife had been hospitalized with a delicate case of cancer. I asked if we could chat, and I told him that no matter what happened, we were all there to support him however he needed. Tragically, his wife passed away soon after, but as I’d promised, our whole team stayed by his side. We kept a positive attitude, reassuring him that his wife was now at peace, free from suffering. He was so grateful for our support during that dark time that he offered us all pay raises. Some of us accepted, others didn’t, but he’d changed completely. To this day, many of us still work there, earning more than we did before that incident.

Everyone faces tough times that make them want to give up, but a positive person can help pull them back up. My family went through a financial crisis when my dad was laid off. We fell four months behind on rent, and almost lost the home we’d lived in for years. My dad was crushed—he’d been job hunting for three months with no luck, and we were terrified we’d lose our house. But my mom, like she always did, stepped in. She told him, “Don’t worry, sweetheart. We’ll get through this like we always do—I’m right here with you.” My dad’s whole mood shifted almost instantly. He smiled at her and said, “Thank you for always standing by me and believing in me.” He grabbed his car keys and headed out to apply for more jobs. Not long after, he landed a new role that paid even more than his old one, and our financial struggles disappeared.

Believing in yourself isn’t always easy—sometimes it feels impossible to see your own strengths, but a supportive person can help you realize how capable you are. When I was in 10th grade, my algebra teacher kept telling our class we needed to have more faith in ourselves. At first, most of us didn’t even try the assignments because we didn’t understand them, and we were so disappointed in ourselves that we gave up before starting. Nearly everyone in my class failed the first quarter, and we were convinced our grades would never get better. Then our teacher sat down with us individually, and talked to us until we started to believe we could tackle any challenge we set our minds to. Slowly, our attitudes shifted—not because we were forced to, but because we finally believed we could succeed. By the second quarter, our class was celebrating huge grade improvements: scores jumped from 50s to 90s. We started paying attention in class like we should have from the start, and we attempted every task even if we weren’t sure how to do it at first. To this day, I’m still grateful to that teacher. She pushed us to be our best, even when we made her frustrated by doubting ourselves. Every single one of us changed, and she became my favorite teacher, as well as a good friend to the whole class—she was always there to support and guide us. That experience proved to me just how powerful a positive attitude can be.

We should keep a positive attitude no matter what, even during the darkest times in our lives. Some people argue that you only need to be upbeat during big, happy events, but they’re completely wrong. A positive mindset is something we need every single day to succeed and find happiness. At home, grandparents, parents, and siblings should model this behavior for younger kids—when children see the adults around them staying positive, they’ll learn to be confident, capable people with their own upbeat outlooks.

Should schools let students take courses that will help them succeed later in life?

I strongly believe that students should enroll in classes that steer them toward clear career goals. Thinking about future jobs early on is smart, because it means you won’t end up stuck in a dull, low-wage role once you become an adult.

I’m currently in 11th grade, and I’ve already decided what I want to do when I grow up: I plan to join the U.S. Marine Corps as a soldier.

One course I’m taking right now that will help me reach this goal is JROTC. You might be wondering what JROTC is. It’s a class that covers the structure, values, and operations of the United States Armed Forces.

Another course I’m enrolled in that will support my future career is Econ and Finals. While Econ and Finals is a mandatory class I need to pass to graduate, I actually enjoy it because I know the skills I learn will be useful for my future job.

If we don’t start preparing for our future careers while we’re still in high school, we’ll graduate feeling lost, unsure of what to do, and probably end up struggling financially. Is it true that impressions are almost impossible to change? I completely disagree with this idea.

These days, many people make adjustments to their lives to work towards their future goals. However, quite a few individuals believe that making these changes is far too difficult, often citing personal obstacles or circumstances that hold them back. While everyone has their own unique aims, it is important to remember that nothing in the world is truly impossible when it comes to making changes. In fact, even small adjustments can open up a window full of new opportunities. Luckily, you do not need to go through extreme hardship to start making positive changes, which can lead to big opportunities down the line. In my view, choosing to start a new way of life to adjust and improve your goals can mark the beginning of fresh opportunities. This helps build your ability to chase the dreams you have in mind, set new targets for the future, and keep going until you reach success. Impressions are never impossible to change, as they can bring new opportunities throughout your life. These changes let you improve your goals and dreams for the future, and make plans to boost your ability to turn your ideas into reality.

New opportunities that arise later in life often come from specific changes, which can feel like opening a door to new job offers. These changes allow you to gain new knowledge, put it into practice, and get better at coming up with fresh ideas. This is incredibly helpful for advancing in society, no matter what job you take on, especially as technology progresses every single day. This means we have more chances than ever to learn new things and complete all kinds of projects that contribute to our communities.

Working to improve your goals and dreams for the future is the best way to adjust and refine the plans you have in mind to grow as a person. You get to discover new ideas, figure out how to bring them to life, and put your knowledge to use. Staying motivated to reach your goals is key, and it helps to dedicate time every day to fixing your mistakes and making adjustments based on what went wrong. Many people give up on their work after making errors, but the most important thing is to learn from those missteps and try to get better.

Making clear plans to boost your ability to achieve your ideas is simple: think carefully about what you want, and write down a list of things you hope to accomplish to expand your knowledge. You can learn new skills and create projects you have always wanted to pursue. Considering different ideas and plans that work best for your personal development in any field is a smart move. On top of that, turning your ideas into reality can improve your financial situation if you work hard at any job you take on. It also helps you grow in society and support your family better over time.

To sum up, making changes that help you create and carry out the plans you have in mind is always for the best. While making adjustments to your life can be really tough at times, everyone knows that it is the best way to improve your ability to develop all kinds of plans and ideas. These changes bring even better opportunities later in life, and you can achieve every single one of your goals if you start making changes to build a better life for yourself.

There is a lot of debate about whether people should push themselves to learn skills beyond what they already know how to do. If we only stick to what we have already mastered, we will never truly grow. Some people think that once they have earned a master’s degree or a key qualification, they can stop learning entirely, but this mindset misses the point. I fully agree with writer Ralph Emerson that we should keep challenging ourselves and picking up new knowledge until the very end. For instance, if you never step out of your comfort zone to try something unfamiliar, you will never develop as a person. Below are my reasons for supporting this view.

First, gaining more experience makes you a stronger candidate in life, not just in terms of money. Experience is a form of wealth that has nothing to do with financial profit. Take job applications as an example: if I only have a high school diploma because I decided that was all I needed, but another applicant has that same diploma plus a certification as a plumber, they will almost certainly get the job. That second applicant has more practical experience and more qualifications, because they took the time to prepare themselves better than I did. Sometimes, we need to be ambitious in a healthy, constructive way.

I side with Emerson because trying new ways of learning is the same as growing. The more you learn, the more mature you become: for example, you gain wisdom by learning from your own mistakes, which is far easier than it is for someone who only ever stuck to the simplest, most comfortable path. Far too many people quit the moment they face their first setback. Life is never easy, but we should not give up after the first, second, or even third try.

Another key reason to try things beyond what I already know is that I can achieve far more goals. In today’s society, a person’s worth is often tied to what they have accomplished: if you have more earned goals under your belt, you gain more privileges. For example, my current goal is to become a police officer, but once I reach that, I will not stop there. I plan to work toward a higher rank, which will help me grow economically, physically, and mentally. What’s more, as you work to master new goals, you are growing as a person at the exact same time.

To sum up, many people disagree with this approach because they prefer taking the easy route, but easy accomplishments have little real value. We will all face obstacles, and many people mistake these setbacks for the end of the road. As a result, they do not grow enough to realize that the more effort you put in, the more opportunities you will have to succeed. Still, I believe it is never too late to keep learning, because every bit of new knowledge adds to what you know, and every new thing you know helps you grow even more.
