School-offered online learning programs can lead to either positive or negative results, depending on how they’re run and who uses them. Individual schools handle these programs very differently: some do not offer remote classes at all, while others make them a core part of their curriculum. Public opinion on online learning is just as split. Some people argue it is a great option, but others believe it is a poor choice. There are clear perks to online classes: for one, you never have to wait for other students to finish tasks before moving on, and you can work entirely at your own pace. However, there are plenty of downsides too. Unstable or non-existent wifi can disrupt your work entirely. Many students find it hard to complete assignments when they are stuck at home alone, and without a classroom full of peers your own age, it is easy to fall behind on assigned work.

Students taking online classes often struggle to finish the work their teachers assign. Unlike in a physical classroom, you cannot raise your hand to ask a question the moment you get stuck. Instead, you have to solve problems on your own. Many educational websites do not provide the right support, and some even give incorrect information that can make you fail an entire assignment. Instructional videos can help, but there are often very few videos covering the exact topic you are stuck on. In a traditional classroom, a teacher can walk you through a problem step by step, which makes it much easier to understand. With online learning, teachers are rarely available to help exactly when you need them. Many students also run out of time to complete work, or simply put assignments off, telling themselves they will “do it later” and then never following through. This makes it very hard to turn work in by the deadline.

Surrounding yourself with peers your own age has real benefits. You can pick up good study habits from them, ask for help when you are confused, and work on assignments together. Online learning strips all of that away: it is just you, your computer, and your coursework. You might have friends, but they are unlikely to be taking the exact same classes, so you cannot study or work on projects with them. Remote learning also cuts down on opportunities to meet new people. You may have a job or other commitments, but the people you interact with there are often older, and you might not talk to many people at all during the day. A traditional classroom environment helps you learn more, because you are not alone: there are other students in the room with you, not just you sitting at home by yourself in front of a screen. Online classes mean you are never surrounded by people your own age.

Online classes sometimes assign a huge amount of work to be completed and submitted all in one day. This is especially challenging if you do not understand the material being taught. The only way to really learn is to do the work yourself and engage with the course content, not just search online for similar answers and copy them down. Many students get lazy with remote learning, putting assignments off until the very last minute. This laziness leads to poor grades, or even failing the class entirely and having to retake it. It is also very easy to get distracted by other things going on in your life when you are learning from home. If you do not stay on top of your work, you will make no progress and will almost certainly miss important due dates.

Schools typically offer students two options for attending class: remote online learning, or in-person classes in a physical school building. Online learning can be helpful for students who want to take more classes or have more free time in their schedules. However, some students take advantage of the program just to stay home and do nothing all day. Life can be unpredictable, and unexpected challenges make it even harder to keep up with online coursework when there is no teacher available to guide you through tough material. Ultimately, every student has to choose the learning format that works best for them. But online classes are often difficult to succeed in: you are not surrounded by peers your own age, and it is easy to fall behind on assignments. For many students, remote learning simply does not work out.

When it comes to deciding whether working alone or with a group is more rewarding, I firmly believe that collaborating with others brings far greater benefits. This is because group work combines diverse perspectives, fosters teamwork needed to succeed in competitive settings, and creates engaging experiences for audiences.

To start with, every individual in a group brings their own unique way of thinking and set of ideas. When these are shared and combined, the group can come up with creative, well-rounded solutions that no single person would have thought of alone. Even goals that seem nearly impossible to reach when working solo become attainable when the whole team brainstorms and works through challenges together.

Another key advantage is the teamwork required to win competitions. Everyone in the group takes on distinct roles and responsibilities. Some members may take leading performer roles on stage, while others support from behind the scenes. Groups often have to spend long hours rehearsing, which can mean less time with family, but this shared effort is what helps them reach their goals and achieve success.

Finally, keeping the audience entertained is a top priority for any group. Audiences come to events to have fun and enjoy the performance, so every group member works hard to deliver a show that captivates and delights them. Most groups have a clear leader who coordinates roles and timing, ensuring the performance runs smoothly and feels interactive for everyone watching.

All in all, amazing work is often produced when people collaborate as a team. Working together lets groups develop stronger ideas, create entertaining performances, and bring joy to their fans. When they succeed, their families, teachers, and supporters feel proud of their hard work. For me, there is no doubt that working in a group is far more enjoyable and rewarding than working alone.

I firmly believe Ralph Waldo Emerson was completely correct in his writing—an idea that rings true for most people. Think about it: you finish college, earn a degree, move back in with your parents even though you could easily get a job, save money, and buy your own place. But as long as you keep living under their roof, nothing really changes. No matter how old you get, your parents will always see you as the little kid they held when you were born, until you start building a life that’s fully your own, with your own responsibilities and achievements. That’s exactly what I think Emerson meant when he wrote those words.

To everyone else, you’re a fully grown adult once you have your life in order: your own car, your own home, a family you’d do anything to protect, just like your parents did for you. It’s the same cycle, just with you as the one telling the story now. Even when your kids grow up, you’ll never stop seeing them as your babies, no matter how old they get. I didn’t really understand this until I watched my older sister care for her daughter—that’s when I started viewing my own life from a new perspective. I might not be a full-grown adult yet by some standards, but I moved out of my family home when I was just 15. I thought keeping up with the expectations of the outside world would be impossible, but I’ve learned that true growth happens when you stop caring what others think and start following your own path. Family comes first, second, and third for me.

To me, the best way to grow up is to focus on being your true self first. You don’t even have to move out to do this—all it takes is shifting how you see the world around you. Growing up has nothing to do with how many candles are on your birthday cake. It’s all about your mindset: stop worrying about anyone else’s opinions, and only focus on the people who matter most: your family and your friends.

These are lessons I’ve learned from personal experience, having lived through this all at a very young age.

I strongly believe that schools should introduce after-school homework clubs. It is often difficult to make sense of homework assignments on your own, and many students are unsure exactly what is expected of them. Think about how many more learners would complete their work on time if these clubs were available.

Some people might argue that homework is not very important, but that is not true. Homework typically counts for 10% of a student’s final grade. While that might seem like a small amount, it can make a big difference to your overall result. It also helps you prepare for exams: finishing a single assignment can teach you the material needed to pass a test or quiz you would otherwise have failed.

Middle school students have a lot on their plates. We have to keep up with assignments for all seven of our classes, which is not easy. Most teachers assign at least one piece of homework per class, and some give two or three, adding to the already heavy workload.

These clubs let students ask questions about anything they do not understand. Teachers or club leaders can explain confusing lesson content, rather than just giving correct answers. This means students actually learn the material instead of guessing or copying work. Students who struggle to find time for homework at home would also benefit: staying after school for even one day a week could help them finish all assignments, and might even raise a grade from a B to an A.

This would help not just students, but the school as a whole. If more students complete homework, the school’s overall performance looks better. Teachers will also see that students are doing work themselves, rather than copying answers as some do now. Even students who can finish assignments but often forget to turn them in on time would find these clubs useful, as it removes that problem entirely.

In conclusion, after-school homework clubs would be a great addition to schools. Homework is a major challenge for many students, and most do not realize how much it impacts their grades. You might wonder why you failed a test or quiz, but often the answer is that you skipped homework covering that material. Teachers assign homework to help us improve in each subject, but it is easy to tell yourself it does not matter. The truth is, it does matter, and that will not change. If these clubs are set up, homework becomes one less thing to worry about. Students will understand their work better, feel less stressed about heavy workloads, and have free time after school, since assignments that used to take up most afternoons will already be finished.

Over half of all people now use their devices mostly for social media, rather than talking to others in person. Countless online sources report that people who spend long hours glued to screens are far more likely to struggle with depression. We should cut back on using tech just for entertainment. Doing so would improve our quality of life, and it would also save our eyesight, reducing the need for glasses. I have a close friend who needed glasses by the time he was just five years old, after spending hours sitting right in front of the TV screen.

To be fair, tech does have a few practical uses. It lets us send photos to loved ones who live far away, helps us finish homework, shows us the current time, and most importantly, allows us to call family and friends in other countries. But devices are also very expensive. In my opinion, though, tech doesn’t actually help us with anything that matters. Staring at screens for too long just rots your brain cells.

Tech can even make people less intelligent. If you waste time on your phone instead of studying for a quiz or test, you’ll end up with a terrible grade. That’s exactly why tech is bad for everyone. Using it too much literally eats away at your brain cells. I know a friend who cheated on a test using his phone—and the teacher didn’t even catch him, because he was sitting at his desk playing on his own phone. Even one of my favorite teachers gets distracted by his phone sometimes.

It’s not like most teachers act this way, but some do. Even in gym class, people sit scrolling on their phones instead of moving. I’m not like that—I play soccer, baseball, and sometimes basketball, with soccer as my main sport. This isn’t just a student issue—gym teachers do it too. Am I the only one who notices this? These problems happen every day, everywhere. Did you just find out?

Ralph Waldo Emerson’s famous words sum up a truth I strongly support: “To be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment.”

First, let’s clarify what “accomplishment” means here: it refers to successfully achieving the goals that matter to you, and living honestly is the only way to reach those true goals. When you stay true to who you are, you work towards aims that align with your own values, not ones pushed on you by others.

I once heard a story that proves this point perfectly. A large company was hiring a new director, a role that paid thousands of dollars a week. They wanted someone who was wealthy and well-known to fill the position. Two women applied: one was talented, had years of work experience, but was quite poor. The other was also qualified, but chose to live honestly. The poor woman decided to fake her background to get the job. She took out nearly $500,000 in bank loans to buy two houses and three brand-new cars, all to make people believe she was rich and famous. When she entered the competition, everyone assumed she was the perfect candidate, and she was certain she would win. The other woman, who did not pretend to be someone she wasn’t, was seen as less impressive at first.

After months of assessing both candidates, the time came to announce the winner. Both women sat waiting, their hearts racing. The poor woman was 100% sure she would get the role. But the judges’ spokesperson stood up and explained their decision: they had found evidence that one candidate had lied about her wealth and status, while the other had been completely honest. They chose the genuine woman for the director role. They pointed out that giving the job to the woman who faked her life would put the company at risk—she might steal money or lie to cover up mistakes, just as she had lied to get the job. The fake candidate’s loans and false lifestyle were exposed, and she ended up with nothing but debt and public shame. The honest woman, who stayed true to herself, got the job and achieved her dream.

To wrap up, I hope this convinces you, rather than confuses you: in a world that constantly pressures people to change who they are, staying true to your real self is the greatest accomplishment possible. If you try to fake your way through life, you will never achieve real success—you will only end up with public embarrassment if you are caught, just like the woman in the story.

For years, people have debated one key question: is it better to tackle tasks on your own, or collaborate with a group?

Most experts and everyday workers alike agree that group work tends to be far more rewarding.

A major reason supporting this view is that working with others exposes you to different perspectives, life experiences and problem-solving approaches. For instance, if you are organizing a large school event, or even just putting together a simple classroom presentation, there will always be moments when you hit a creative wall and have no ideas left. In a group, you can rely on your teammates to offer fresh solutions. Working alone, you might feel stuck with no way forward, like you are trapped on a road with no exit.

Group work also tends to be far more enjoyable. Even when you are facing tight deadlines or stressful challenges, working with others brings chances to laugh, relax and stay positive. You never have dull, uninteresting stretches when collaborating with a team. There is always something to chat about, and you will build shared memories that you will look back on and laugh about for years to come.

Another clear benefit is speed. When more people work on a task together, things get done much faster than if one person handles everything alone. This extra time also leaves room for creativity: you can refine small details, practice your skills, or even come up with entirely new ideas for the project.

Collaborating with others also shifts your mindset from focusing on just yourself to prioritizing the whole team. This is an incredibly useful skill for the professional world, where almost every job requires some level of teamwork. You learn to work with people who have all kinds of personalities and opinions, and these collaboration skills will stay with you long after the project ends.

When your team finally finishes all tasks, the sense of achievement is unmatched. Everyone feels proud of what they have accomplished together, and this shared success encourages everyone to keep pushing forward and never give up on future projects.

It is true that group work can seem tricky at first, especially if you are used to working alone. But the experience helps you grow as a person and build your character. You learn how to communicate clearly with others, and how to share your ideas in a way everyone understands. That is exactly why so many people agree that working in a team offers far more benefits than working solo.

Most other schools offer way more than three extracurricular choices, after all, rather than sticking to such a tiny selection. There are countless other activities the school could run: cooking classes, chess club, drama, science and math clubs, creative writing groups, and more. Sticking to only sports, yearbook, and student council over and over again is dull and repetitive, and ignores so many other valid interests students have.

It’s possible some students will be happy with the current plan, but plenty more will not. People have totally different personalities and hobbies, so what one student loves, another might hate. For instance, while some enjoy sports, others can’t stand them; the same goes for yearbook and student council. Personally, I really want art to be offered as an option.

There are several extracurriculars I’d jump at the chance to join: art, reading clubs, and drama. I’ve always loved drawing, and I’m a huge fan of Marvel comics—especially Dr. Strange, Spider-Man, the Guardians of the Galaxy, and Black Panther. Drama is another passion of mine, since I plan to work as an actor and director when I’m older. I’ve spoken to lots of other students, and this is a very common opinion among us: we don’t just want sports, yearbook, or student council. We have all kinds of other interests, just like I do.

If every student is forced to pick one of these three activities, the whole school will start to feel really boring. Of course, the final decision is up to the principal: if they want every student to take part in at least one of the three current options, there’s not much we can do about it. But that doesn’t mean we can’t disagree, or ask the principal to add more activities if none of the current three appeal to us.

Ifirmly agree that it is nearly impossible to change a first impression. This is because they are tied to a moment that only happens once: even if you have a similar experience later, it will never feel exactly the same as that initial encounter. The emotions you felt in that exact moment are fixed, and most of the time, you won’t even want to change them. After all, if you liked that first reaction, you might even hope to feel that same way again in the future.

A common example of this is seeing someone on the street wearing clothes that are totally different from what everyone else around you has on. They immediately grab everyone’s attention, since most people in that area have never seen someone dressed that way before, or it’s just not a common style locally. Some passersby will start gossiping and sharing their own opinions, while others will judge the person outright based on their outfit. But there are also people who are simply curious: they want to learn more about the person, their culture, or even spend time with them, try new activities together, or just have fun.

These kinds of first impressions happen all the time, because we are constantly surrounded by other people: our family, our friends, even total strangers we’ve never met before. That means we are always in situations where we will form these immediate reactions, no matter where we are or what we’re doing. It makes no difference where you are, because you will always encounter new things, and each of those will spark that same type of immediate feeling.

You’ll have these first impressions no matter who you’re with or where you go, even when you’re alone. You’ll probably end up talking about these moments with your friends later, using them as examples in your daily life, or getting new ideas from them. Sometimes first impressions can even help you improve yourself: you might notice something special about someone you met briefly, and decide to make positive changes to your own life based on that initial observation.

To conclude, first impressions are almost always impossible to change, because they are tied to a unique moment that you can’t recreate. You might shift how you think about that person or thing later, but if you encounter them again, it will never feel the same. You already know what to expect, so the initial spark is gone, and the experience might even feel pointless. First impressions also help you understand different people and the lives they lead, no matter their race or background. Everyone has something unique to offer, something we might even find useful in our own lives.

I strongly believe that distance learning can bring real advantages to learners all over the globe. Learners can sign up for courses run by schools anywhere in the world, no matter how remote their own home is. This is a huge help for young people who live too far from their nearest school to commute, or who have no access to reliable transport. Studying from the comfort of their own home also makes the learning experience far less stressful for many.

It is also a great option for students who want to access top-quality education from institutions abroad. They can take classes that are not available in their home country’s curriculum, all without leaving their house. For example, a teenager living in France could enroll in courses run by a school in the United States, gaining exposure to teaching methods and perspectives that differ from what they would learn locally. This is especially useful for young people living temporarily in a foreign country who plan to return to their home nation eventually, as they can keep up with their original school’s curriculum while abroad.

Distance learning also removes barriers for students who would otherwise struggle to access any education at all. I once saw a documentary about a young girl who had to hike for four hours through mountainous terrain just to reach her school each day. Many learners live in areas with extreme weather, or remote rural regions far from any urban center, where attending a physical school is simply impossible. This model also proved helpful in the United States recently, when schools in states with confirmed coronavirus cases closed, forcing students to switch to learning from home to avoid infection.

Traditional school environments can also be uncomfortable for some learners, leading them to lose motivation or fall behind in their work. Many feel unsafe or anxious around teachers and peers, but learning at home lets them study in a space where they feel secure, surrounded by family members they trust. Bullying and peer pressure are major issues in physical schools: some students are teased for their appearance or interests, while others are pushed to act in ways that do not reflect who they really are. I recall a viral video of a 7-year-old boy who told his mother he wanted to take a knife and end his own life. The reason? He was relentlessly bullied by classmates for being shorter than other kids, to the point where his parents had to pull him out of school, enroll him in homeschooling, and arrange therapy to help him recover and feel comfortable learning again.

Of course, learning from home is not for everyone. Some people argue that it harms students’ social skills, since they miss out on daily in-person interactions with peers and teachers. This can make it harder for them to communicate with others later in life, as they spend most of their time studying alone at home. A friend of mine who was homeschooled until high school is a good example: he speaks very little in class, has few close friends, and it takes a long time for new people to get to know him. Ultimately, taking classes from home only offers real benefits if you want to enroll in courses from a school in another region or country, cannot attend physical school due to your remote location or a very long daily commute, or feel uncomfortable and unsafe in traditional school settings. Last week, I had a math exam scheduled for first period. I’d studied hard for it—I’d even reviewed all the material twice the night before, so I knew the content well. But I overslept that morning and realized I was running late for school. I also missed my school bus, so I had to walk the entire way to campus. By the time I arrived, I was exhausted and stressed, which made it impossible to do my best on the test. If I’d been taking online classes, I could have taken the exam from home and avoided all that hassle.

This experience made me realize how much online classes could help students avoid unnecessary problems and save time. Some people argue that learning from home isn’t beneficial, since students might struggle to follow lectures or complete assignments without in-person support, leading to poor performance. But I believe online classes offer clear advantages: first, they let students keep up with schoolwork even when they can’t physically make it to campus, whether due to illness or being away from home. Second, they free up a lot of time for high schoolers to work extra hours, take additional courses, or pursue other hobbies.

Critics of online learning do have valid points. They note that some students find it hard to grasp lecture content or assignment instructions when classes are held remotely, which can hurt their grades. For instance, a student might get stuck on a group project or fail to understand a difficult topic covered in an online lecture, with no teacher right there to answer quick questions.

But these downsides don’t outweigh the benefits. For one, online classes let students attend school even when they can’t be on campus. If I come down with a cold, I don’t have to skip class entirely—I can log in from my bed and keep up with lessons. Even if I’m visiting relatives or staying at a friend’s house, I can still join my classes as long as I have an internet connection.

Another major plus is the time saved. Without having to commute to school, high school students can fit in more activities. If I didn’t have to travel to campus every day, I could adjust my schedule to work longer hours at my part-time job, saving more money for college. I could also finish my schoolwork faster and take extra courses that will help with my future career, or spend time on hobbies I enjoy.

To sum up, online classes are a big benefit for students. They let people keep up with schoolwork even when they’re sick or away from home, and they save huge amounts of time that can be used for part-time work, extra classes, or fun activities. Online learning doesn’t just cut down on wasted time—it also opens up chances to do more of what matters to us, making each day more flexible and enjoyable.

Is failure actually a good thing? In this essay, I will explore how failure and success relate to each other in daily life. When people fail, they often react in very different ways: some feel deeply upset, others manage to hold onto their motivation, and quite a few end up angry at themselves.

To begin with, many people feel miserable when they fail at a task, especially if they put in their absolute best effort to get everything right. They may have never even imagined that they would not succeed, so the disappointment hits hard. For some, this sadness is so intense that they end up crying after a failure.

Next, there are those who do not let their first failure crush their excitement for the task. They tend to have a very positive outlook, and tell themselves that they will do better the next time around. This means they hold onto their enthusiasm even right after facing a setback.

Finally, some people direct their anger at themselves after failing. They feel they did not perform well enough, and can get especially furious if the failure was caused by a tiny mistake. However, this reaction actually shows they are learning: the errors they make push them to understand what went wrong and improve.

There are many who argue that failure is harmful to achieving success. Yet people who keep their motivation alive through repeated failures often end up proving this idea wrong. Those who refuse to lose their enthusiasm keep trying until they find a way to avoid failing again. Every time they stumble, they pick up new lessons that help them get closer to their goals.

To sum up, there are plenty of people for whom failure is nothing but a bad idea.

Is it better for people to make their own decisions, or should they turn to others for guidance when choosing what to do?

We all make poor choices sometimes, not just at work but in our personal lives too, and it’s rarely just because we thought the option felt right in the moment. Every day, our emotions play a role in how we see the world, which shifts the way we form our opinions and make choices. Think about starting a new job or meeting someone new: even small details like these can change how we think, speak, and act, including how we decide what to do next. This is totally normal, and there’s nothing wrong with it.

The ability to make our own choices is one of the key things that makes us human. We have a deep need to share what we feel and want, and this drive has pushed us to achieve incredible things. Every invention, creation, or new skill we have today exists because people were free to share their ideas and make their own decisions about what to build, learn, or try.

At the same time, being independent means you don’t need someone to tell you what to do every moment of the day. But don’t get me wrong: I’m not saying people should be free to do whatever they want, no matter the impact. There are many situations where we need help, and our choices can’t always be made alone.

For example, you might need guidance in a courtroom, at your workplace, or when you are still a child in school. As you can see, there are specific places, scenarios, and life stages where you are not legally or practically able to make all decisions for yourself.

I firmly believe that most people are capable of making their own decisions. As long as we follow the rules and laws that govern our society, we can choose our own path in life and take full responsibility for the choices we make.

In fact, you have the freedom to make your own choices and own the consequences, even when you pick the wrong option. It’s not about never making mistakes; what matters is that you get the chance to try things out and figure out what you truly want. Making a bad call is okay sometimes, and getting it right is wonderful too. The most important thing is that you have the right to shape your own life, learn from your errors, and live freely.

Eighth graders in middle school are often introduced to a wide range of career options, which helps them start forming ideas about what path they might want to follow later in life. Young people should always have the final say in picking their future career, yet many are pushed into fields their parents prefer instead. This often happens because they feel they have no other option. These days, teenagers have the basic right to decide what they want to study and pursue as a career. High school helps students build all kinds of useful skills, not just academic knowledge, which benefits them long after they graduate. Why does this matter? Because having a diverse set of skills prepares teens for any job, or helps them handle unexpected problems that come up in the workplace or daily life. Encouraging kids to explore interests early on is a great approach, since it helps them keep learning and growing mentally every day. For instance, they might research their desired field on their own, or reach out to people already working in that career to ask about their experiences. By the time they finish middle and high school, students are prepared to start college, and they should be the ones deciding what path works best for them.

Sadly, many teens in parts of the world do not get the chance to attend school at all. Countries with limited resources, like Honduras, El Salvador, Guatemala, and Africa, have poor education systems. In these places, a lot of teenagers drop out to work instead of staying in school, since the education available is not high quality. This is why so many people migrate to the United States: they know the education there is key to building a better future. Most young migrants arrive with big dreams, even kids as young as 12. Their strong mindset and clear goals help them pick a solid career path once they’re in the US. From a young age, they understand they need to make their family proud, often aiming to be the most accomplished member of their family with a good career. On top of that, these countries’ populations are growing fast, making it harder to find work even if you have a good degree. In these societies, parents often stop their kids from going to school, telling them "education won’t lead to anything here." When parents throw away their children’s dreams like this, it can lead to bigger issues — including the high rates of terrorism seen in many of these countries today. All parents should let their teens go to school, explain why education is so valuable, and let them choose the career they want from a young age.

Thinking about the future early on makes a huge difference today. While many teens around the world ignore their long-term goals, skip school, or don’t care about getting a job or supporting their families, US teenagers have far more opportunities. They can access great education, find stable jobs, and build healthy, successful lives.

Teens with early career plans will have their lives set after high school. They will inspire others and land good, stable jobs.

Ultimately, students should have a clear idea of their career path by the time they start high school. This helps them learn more, prepare for college, and grow into people who inspire other teens to value education and plan their own successful careers.

Have you ever been pressured to pick a future career before you even start high school? I certainly have, and I strongly believe we, as young people, should take our time with this huge life choice instead of rushing into it too early. This decision depends entirely on who you are and when you’re ready—there’s no rule that says you have to commit to a career right away. In fact, choosing whether to pursue a career at all is totally up to each individual, since it’s not a mandatory requirement.

First, I completely disagree with the push to pick a career so early. Younger students are very easily swayed by what adults tell them to do, which often leads to them picking jobs they have no real interest in. Over time, this wastes their time, their money, and crushes their personal dreams. Young people need more inspiration when thinking about future careers—roles like doctors, architects, teachers, and other professions are much easier to commit to if you feel passionate about them. It also helps to have constant support from family members, like parents or other relatives. Sadly, many young people either ignore adult advice or lack family support entirely, which stops them from pursuing any career at all.

Second, we young adults need to learn way more about different types of work before making any choices. For example, we could watch informational videos or talk to people already working in various fields to understand what their daily tasks and responsibilities look like. It would also be helpful to hear two clear examples: one person who finished their studies, built a career, and now has stable income, and another who dropped out of school and now struggles to get by, maybe even asking for money on the street. Young people need to think seriously about their future, too—real work is hard, whether you’re stuck outside in extreme heat or freezing cold, and nothing about it is easy.

Everyone has their own vision for the future, whether that’s building a good life for a future family, a spouse, or children. High school is a great time to explore hobbies and interests that could turn into careers. If you love drawing, for instance, studying to become an architect makes perfect sense. People get inspired by all kinds of things—drawing buildings, natural landscapes, or anything else that sparks their creativity. I’ve seen amazing architecture in places like Dubai, and even if I don’t know all the details, the designs are beautiful, born entirely from someone’s imagination. Too many people don’t realize how important studying is for their whole life.

Many young people end up dropping out of high school to start working, because not everyone has the same opportunities. Some have to work to support their families because they don’t have other relatives to help them. I think we need more programs or school events to help people understand the value of studying. Education brings so many benefits, including the chance to learn practical skills and qualify for apprenticeships that lead to stable future jobs.

For many students who struggle with low grades or frequent tardiness caused by oversleeping or missed buses, online learning can be a far better option. Attending traditional in-person school also takes up a lot of time that students could spend on outside interests, like playing sports or just relaxing at home.

I believe online classes are better than in-person schooling for several key reasons. First, many students find they learn much better when they are in the comfort of their own homes, rather than in a busy school building. Another common issue is students oversleeping because they do not get enough rest, which makes them miss their bus and arrive late to school. Online classes typically start at a more reasonable hour, which makes it much easier for people who struggle to wake up early to log in on time. When students are not rushing or exhausted from oversleeping, they have more energy to focus on their work and get more done during lessons.

Getting sick is another big challenge for in-person students: they have to miss days of school, fall behind on assignments, and often feel stressed as their grades start to drop. With online learning, even if a student is ill, they can still join classes from home. They can also log in from a laptop while on family vacation, so they almost never have missing work. This is a huge advantage for keeping grades up.

However, some people argue that looking at a bright screen for long periods will strain your eyes. Others also say that cheating on tests and quizzes is easier in online classes than in person, because teachers do not know exactly what you are doing at home.

These are the main reasons why I think online classes are more beneficial than traditional in-person school.

Dear Manager,

I am writing to ask for permission to visit your company, as I want to find out if a career there would be a good fit for me. I’d love to see what kinds of tasks are available, and learn exactly how daily work is carried out on site.

I know your company is quite large, with enough staff to complete tasks much faster than smaller firms. Letting students visit would give us a chance to experience what it’s really like to work in a corporate setting, or even step into a manager’s role for a short time. We could learn about standard 7-hour work shifts, and get clear details on scheduled lunch breaks. You could also show us how the workplace is organized, and where all materials are stored so teams can access what they need quickly to finish products on time and get them ready for sale.

Many people are curious about how big companies operate, and I’ve heard night shifts can be especially tiring. I have a few questions about this: is there any limit to how large a company can grow, or how much space it can take up? What does it cost to build a new company from scratch? Do offices and facilities need to be renovated regularly, say every 5 or 6 years? Can companies be built in rural areas, or are they only located in cities? When do suppliers deliver the materials needed to make products for sale, since selling those products brings in revenue that can be reinvested to help the company grow? Also, what do all the raw materials cost to keep the company running smoothly, without overspending and risking bankruptcy?

Visiting a company is really helpful for anyone who thinks they might want to work in business later. Lots of us want to get a feel for what it’s like to be a regular employee or a manager, and understand how much time we’d need to commit to the role. I also have more questions: what happens if a company runs out of money or raw supplies? Do they have to sell the business? Do companies pay very high utility bills, especially for electricity? Can they get in legal trouble if the products they make are faulty? I’ve noticed that while all companies are sizable, some are far larger than others because they sell their goods faster, earn more revenue, and can afford better equipment to make products, as well as hire more staff. Every company produces its own goods, of course—they can’t steal supplies from other firms, or take credit for work done by managers at other companies.

Another thing I’m curious about: if one company steals an idea from another, do they get hit with huge fines, or even face jail time for intellectual property theft? Do companies have work available every single day? Do they operate on public holidays like Christmas or New Year’s Day? Do employees get paid vacation days? I assume all machines are turned off on holidays once all work is finished. If an employee gets sick, do they have to call their manager to report their absence, or just stay home and wait for the manager to reach out when they don’t show up? If someone gets sick during a shift, does a replacement worker come in to cover for them until they recover? My top talents and skills include drawing, painting, coloring, and writing—these are the creative activities I enjoy most. I use these abilities to make cartoons, create painted or drawn pictures, color illustrations, and write novels. Last year, I got really involved in art by joining every available art club and class. While I used to want to work as a professional cartoonist, this year my main goal is to focus on writing, though I’m still confident in my artistic abilities. I plan to take art classes again once I reach ninth grade next year. Whenever I’m bored at home or school with nothing else to do, I turn to these creative hobbies to pass the time.

When it comes to writing, my dream is to create novels and books that everyone can enjoy. I’ve been taking writing classes every summer lately to improve my skills. Last year, I started working as a cartoonist, writing articles and drawing cartoons for my school newspaper. At school, I joined the animation club, where I drew background scenes for cartoon projects—I really loved that work. Later, I also joined the yearbook club and wrote captions under photos to explain exactly what was happening in each image. Last year, I had FACS (Family and Consumer Science) for my third block class, and I used my art skills to decorate cakes, cupcakes, and even ice cream treats. All these experiences made me realize that art is a great fit for me.

Let me share more about my favorite skill: writing. The main reason I love it is that I get to write novels and full-length books. One of my favorite projects to work on is based on Transformers: Dark of the Moon—it’s my all-time favorite graphic novel, adapted from what is widely considered one of the most successful movies of all time. The story starts with the War of Cybertron, then covers the entire space race, and includes all the key events from the movie. But what I love most about writing is how it lets me play with words and express feelings. I also write poems often, which help me think about different emotions.

To break down exactly why I love writing so much, here are three key reasons: First, I find that good writing can really impress people. Second, written work can include both real facts and personal opinions. Third, writing isn’t just stories or articles—it can also take the form of poems.

Art, meanwhile, is everywhere around us. Writing also relies on a strong vocabulary, and it’s always important to check your spelling when you finish an article or essay. Written work often includes art elements too—for example, graphic novel creators draw speech bubbles for characters to show when they’re happy, sad, or feeling other emotions. These books use all kinds of languages to tell their stories, and bold text is used to highlight the most important points and their true meaning. This helps readers fully understand the message a book is trying to share.

In conclusion, I will keep reflecting on my talents and skills, and what they mean to me, for years to come. I still care deeply about these creative abilities, and I think they can be a favorite hobby for anyone. For example, I still love drawing and writing comics in my free time. That’s my final thought on the topic.

When it comes to making big life choices, there’s no single right approach. Some people prefer to decide things entirely on their own, while others turn to experts or authority figures for advice. Ultimately, the choice is up to each individual, but getting input from someone with specialized knowledge can be really useful when you’re brainstorming ideas.

Those who choose to handle major life decisions without outside help often have their plans fully mapped out already, which is a sign of being responsible. Making choices independently is always a positive thing, so there’s no need to ask others for guidance if you’ve already got everything sorted.

Many people pride themselves on being self-reliant, handling tasks like schoolwork, assignments, and jobs all by themselves. But even these individuals sometimes wonder if they should listen to experts’ advice. For my part, I would always seek input from professionals, since they have far more knowledge and have been through the same situations before. They understand exactly what the experience is like. Trying to do every single thing on your own can be incredibly tough and draining, and it’s easy to feel like quitting when you’re struggling alone.

To sum up, I believe everyone should gather ideas and seek help from experts and authority figures. As I’ve mentioned, these people have been through similar experiences and have much more practical knowledge. Their support can assist you with almost any challenge, and ultimately help you achieve success.

Should high school students be allowed to complete their studies in just three years, so they can start college sooner and enter the workforce earlier? Many students, parents, and even teachers support this idea of speeding up high school completion. I believe shortening high school to three years is a good idea. It lets students graduate from university earlier, land jobs faster, and become independent while they are still young, which ultimately improves their quality of life.

In this essay, I will explain why I support this change, drawing on examples from my home country of El Salvador. Some high schools there already use a three-year system. My older sister finished high school when she was 17 after just three years of study. She enrolled in university right away and will earn her nursing degree by age 21. Even so, I think switching all high schools to a three-year schedule would be even better. I am currently in a four-year high school program, and I will not graduate until I turn 19. I worry this will delay my university graduation, especially if I choose a career that requires eight years of study.

Recently, my school held a vote for students, parents, and teachers to share their views on moving to a three-year high school system. Seventy percent of voters said they supported the change. Many teachers argued that this would give more students a chance to graduate faster, especially those who struggle to pass classes or advance to the next grade each year. They are absolutely right. My brother failed ninth grade, so he has to repeat the year. Instead of finishing high school in four years, he will need five.

My mom also graduated from high school at 17, after just three years of study. She earned her medical degree by age 25 and immediately got a well-paying job at a local hospital. At the same time, she took night classes to become a heart specialist, and she earned that second degree by the time she was 30. Today, she holds two good jobs and has a very comfortable life. I am sure she was able to achieve all this because she finished high school so early.

Shortening high school to three years is clearly the better option for students. Some school districts oppose this change, but they are mistaken. Students who finish high school faster can secure good jobs sooner. I hope that in the near future, all high schools will switch to a three-year system instead of sticking to four years.

I’ve developed a range of talents and skills over time, but skateboarding stands out as my clear favorite. Skateboarding is far from easy to master. Picking up even a single trick can take hours, days, or even years of practice, which is exactly what makes it such a one-of-a-kind sport and skill.

I skate almost every day now, and it’s become my go-to way to shake off stress and forget about any problems I’m dealing with. That’s a huge part of why I love it so much. I ride my board to all sorts of places: the corner store, friends’ houses, and sometimes even to school. I’ve gotten my fair share of scrapes, bruises, and other minor injuries while skating, but I still adore the sport. It’s taught me so many valuable lessons: how to feel confident when trying new things, how to pick myself up right after a fall, and how to learn from my mistakes instead of getting discouraged.

To me, skateboarding is more than just a sport, a skill, or a casual hobby. It’s a way of life. Sure, it’s not the safest activity out there, but it’s still one of my favorite skills, and I don’t think I’ll ever get tired of it anytime soon.

I first got interested in skateboarding when I was nine years old. Most of my friends at the time skated, and I knew nothing about the sport back then. Watching them ride around was fascinating, since it seemed like such a unique activity. I’d watch them practice tricks and ride their boards all over the neighborhood, and their passion eventually pushed me to give it a try myself.

A few days later, I told my parents I wanted to pick up a new hobby: skateboarding. My mom said she’d think about it, worrying I might get hurt, but my dad was totally on board. He told me to just go for it, so that’s exactly what I did. The next day after school, I asked my mom if we could head to the closest skate shop, and she agreed.

When we walked into the shop, I was completely overwhelmed. I saw skate decks, wheels, and tons of other parts I’d never even heard of before. A staff member noticed me looking lost and came over to ask if I was looking for anything in particular. I explained that I was brand new to skating and had never even stood on a board before. He then walked me through all the basic parts: the deck (the board itself), grip tape, trucks, wheels, and hardware.

After that, I picked out all the parts I wanted for my very first skateboard. We paid for everything, and he started putting it together for me. By the time he finished, it was already getting dark out, so I couldn’t test it out that day, which was a huge bummer. The next day, I got home from school, tossed my backpack down, and headed straight outside to try my new skateboard. I only knew how to ride at the time, but I fell in love with skating right away.

Ever since that day, I’ve skated nearly every day. If I can’t make it out daily, I at least skate every other day.

The sound of giggling kids huddled around a console is a common one these days, but it’s not just children who love gaming—plenty of people in their 30s still spend hours playing too. It makes you wonder: are video games really that fun for people in their 30s?

To start with, why do children find gaming so thrilling? For many, it’s the rush of fast-paced action, the pretend danger, and the constant excitement that comes with every new level or match. Gaming can also act as a stress reliever for both kids and grown-ups. While some games can be annoying when you get stuck on a hard level, others are surprisingly calming—simple puzzle games like Tetris or cozy titles like Pokémon can soothe a busy mind.

Next, there are countless popular games out there that draw in players, from battle royales like Fortnite to competitive titles like League of Legends, and kid-friendly platforms like Roblox. Kids are drawn to these games purely because they’re entertaining, often playing in groups that act like a pack of wolves hunting for food, all focused on shared in-game goals. When playing, people use three key senses: hearing to pick up in-game sounds, touch to control the controller or keyboard, and sight to track what’s happening on screen. This works like a secret mental workout, even if players don’t realize it. Other senses, like smell and taste, are only used for daily activities like eating.

Of course, gaming isn’t without its downsides for both kids and adults. Staring at a screen for hours on end can damage your eyesight over time. It can also shorten your attention span, making it harder to focus on slower tasks. Too much gaming can also make people withdraw from the real world, feeling shy or uncomfortable around others. Even fun activities come with risks.

At the end of the day, kids love gaming so much they rarely think about the negative effects. Adults are more aware of the risks, and know they might face issues like poor eyesight or shorter attention spans later on, but they still choose to play anyway. Even with all the pros and cons, gaming is simply a fun pastime for people of all ages. Why do you think kids and adults play video games?

Former British Prime Minister Winston Churchill once said, “Success consists of going from failure to failure without losing enthusiasm.” I completely agree with this statement. Everyone faces setbacks at some point, but the key is to never give up. If you keep pushing forward, you will eventually reach the goals you have set for yourself. Even when you fail at the same task multiple times, don’t give up—work hard instead. One day, you will see that persisting pays off in ways you never expected.

To start with, some people believe that success means moving from one failure to the next without losing anything. These individuals feel secure when they don’t suffer any losses along the way. For example, imagine you dream of becoming prime minister one day, but those around you insist you will never achieve this goal. In this case, all you need to do is work hard and trust in your own abilities. If you put your mind to something, you can accomplish anything you want in life.

Secondly, other people argue that success comes from experiencing failure after failure, even when you do lose something in the process. They see value in this kind of repeated failure, because some people prefer to try the same task over and over again until they get it right. Even if they struggle to master a skill at first, they choose to keep trying the same thing again and again.

There are those who prefer the idea of succeeding through failure without any loss, as they dislike repeating the same task multiple times and feel safer this way. On the other hand, some people support the view that success involves failing repeatedly with losses, because they enjoy practicing the same thing until they improve.

In conclusion, there are times when it is helpful to follow Churchill’s advice: “Success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm” applies to everything you do. But there are also moments when it is okay for success to involve moving from failure to failure while losing enthusiasm along the way.

Does failing at something actually help you achieve success? As former UK Prime Minister Winston Churchill famously put it, true success meansmoving from one setback to the next while still staying eager and committed. Most people working toward personal goals or long-held dreams would nod in agreement with this idea.

When setbacks pop up on the path to achieving what you want, they can actually offer three key benefits: they boost your motivation, push you to figure out how to improve, and give you valuable real-world experience. Setbacks are not always negative, after all.

First, failing gives many people the extra push of motivation they need to keep going. Think about a student who stays up all night preparing for a big exam, hands it in feeling confident, only to find out they failed. They get a chance to retake the test, and choose to take it – because one bad result doesn’t mean they can’t meet their goal eventually. It just means they need to keep trying. When you set a really ambitious goal, you have to accept that setbacks will happen along the way. The moment you hit a failure, that’s when your motivation needs to kick in. If you give up the second things go wrong, you’ll never reach the success you’re aiming for. Would most people really quit forever just because they messed up once? Probably not.

A second key reason failure can lead to success is that it makes you think about how to get better. We all know the old saying that you learn from your mistakes, and it’s completely true. If you mess up because of a choice you made or a method you used, you’re not going to repeat that same error again. After a failure, you can look back at what went wrong, figure out where to fix things, and try a better approach next time. That process of improvement is exactly what pushes you toward success. Almost every person who has reached a big goal will tell you they wouldn’t be where they are today if they hadn’t failed at least once along the way.

Last but not least, failing gives you valuable experience you can use for future goals. If you never faced a setback, you’d have no practical experience to draw on when chasing your next aim. Once you finally reach your goal after pushing through failures, you’ll have an inspiring story to share. You can talk about the obstacles you faced, and how you kept going instead of giving up. Sharing these experiences can even encourage other people who have failed and are thinking of quitting – you can show them that one failure doesn’t mean they can’t still succeed.

To sum up, failure can be a huge step toward success if you handle it the right way. Don’t just sit and give up when things go wrong – failing actually brings you closer to your goal. Treat failure as a source of motivation, a chance to improve, and an opportunity to gain useful experience. When you look at it this way, failure is actually a very positive thing.

I completely agree with Ralph Waldo Emerson’s belief that a person can only grow if they attempt tasks that go beyond the skills they have already mastered. I think this is true because once you have already perfected a skill or achieved a goal, the only way to keep improving is to aim for harder targets. It is completely normal to fail when chasing these bigger goals, since no one is perfect. You should also try to master a variety of different skills, rather than sticking to just one thing you already know well.

The main reason I think you should raise your goals after mastering a task is that repeating the same thing over and over, even if you are great at it, stops you from growing. For example, imagine I play recreational soccer, where teams are formed by sign-up with no tryouts. If I score in almost every game and constantly perform better than my opponents, I will not get any better as a player. The games are too easy, with no real challenge, so I need to set a higher goal. In this case, that would mean moving up to a travel team, where the competition is tougher and I can actually see progress in my skills.

I know some people might disagree with Emerson’s idea, mostly because they are afraid to set harder goals after mastering something. They worry about failing, or looking foolish if they cannot do the new task perfectly right away. I have felt this way myself when working toward goals, like trying to score three goals in a single soccer game. I practice hard to hit this target, hoping to score three goals every match once I master it. Sometimes I fall short, and do not reach three goals at all. But I remind myself that this is okay—when you are working toward any goal, you will almost certainly fail at least once, probably more. That failure pushes me to work even harder. No one is perfect, and failing is actually helpful because it teaches you what mistakes you made, so you can fix them next time.

The final reason I support Emerson’s view is that you should try to master all kinds of different skills in life. If you only stick to the one thing you have already mastered, you will never develop talent in any other area. It is so valuable to have a range of skills, as this lets you do far more things. If you find you do not enjoy a goal you are chasing, or cannot seem to reach it, it helps to have other goals you are working on at the same time. Many people change their minds about what they want to do, and often want to pursue more than one goal at once.

To sum up, if you have already mastered a skill, you need to set harder goals to keep growing. When you aim higher, you will definitely fail at some point, but you should not let that worry you—failure helps you learn from your mistakes, so you do not repeat them. You should also try to master a variety of different skills, so you are good at many things, not just one. This is exactly why I agree with Emerson’s core message.

Summer is the hottest season of the year, and schools always schedule a full two-month break during this time. While some educators argue that this break is too long, and that schools should switch to a year-round schedule—with just one month of summer break plus a longer winter holiday—I strongly believe we should keep the traditional long summer break. My main reasons are that the extreme heat makes learning nearly impossible, and students need this time to travel with family and friends, or simply relax.

First, the summer heat is so intense that attending school becomes unbearable. On some days, temperatures climb to 96 degrees Celsius or even higher, which is far too hot for students to sit in classrooms. This extreme heat causes heavy sweating, frequent headaches, and rising stress levels during class, which often leads to poor grades or constant anger. Students trying to study or work in these hot conditions find even simple tasks much harder than those in milder, warm areas, as the heat makes it almost impossible to focus on schoolwork.

Beyond the weather, summer gives students a full two months to unwind and make plans with loved ones. Many families save up all year to take big vacations during this period, since the long break means no school days are missed. It is the ideal time to head to the beach, travel to other countries, or even pick up a part-time summer job. Without classes to worry about, students can focus fully on earning extra money, spending time with family, or doing activities they don’t have time for during the school year. Most students look forward to this break all year, as it is the only time they have enough free time for trips that take more than a few days.

To sum up, summer is far too hot to be spent in school, but it is the perfect season to travel, earn money, or rest. The government should not cut our summer break—this time is ours, our big break. It is a chance to relax for weeks without any worry about schoolwork, and it only comes once a year. Students work hard all school year, so we deserve this time to enjoy ourselves.

Many people, including educators and school staff, are asking whether switching to a year-round school schedule is really a good idea. I am fully in favor of this change. Right now, when the long summer break ends, most students return to class having forgotten nearly everything they learned the previous year. A year-round calendar would give us far more time to fully grasp new concepts and keep that information fresh in our minds.

Since we would remember past lessons better, teachers would not have to waste weeks reviewing old material at the start of each school year. That means we could jump straight into new topics for core subjects like math, history, and English much faster. The more time we spend in class, the deeper our understanding of the material becomes, and the longer that knowledge stays with us. When we practice concepts regularly in class and get extra help from teachers as needed, we feel far more prepared when it is time to take end-of-year tests or SOLs.

I have definitely experienced this myself: every time I return to school after summer, I struggle to recall what we covered the year before. I often forget how to solve basic math problems or remember key details from other classes. A year-round schedule might help fix this, since we would be learning continuously without a long gap to forget everything. I think the main reason students lose so much knowledge over summer is that we get out of the habit of focusing on schoolwork, or we did not pay close attention to begin with. With more school days spread throughout the year, teachers could experiment with different teaching styles to keep students more interested and focused on the lessons.

I really like the idea of year-round schooling overall. It creates more chances for students to learn, and the extra instructional days give us more time to stay focused on our work. The only clear downside is that summer break would be much shorter than we are used to. But we would get more frequent breaks throughout the rest of the year, which makes up for that lost summer time. Hopefully, this new schedule would make it much easier for all students to hold onto the information they learn in class.

I truly think a year-round school system could be very effective. It would help countless students hold onto what they learn, which would make their classes feel easier. They would remember what they studied the year before, so they would already know how to approach new problems or questions. This change would honestly help me a lot too: I would be able to complete more assignments confidently because I would actually know how to do the work. I believe this plan would work well and be very successful, so we should definitely give it a try to see the results!

Picture this: sprinting against the wind, the ball at your feet, weaving past opponents as you push yourself to the limit to help your team take the lead. That’s the feeling of doing something you’re truly passionate about—where every moment feels exciting, not like a chore. For me, the goal is clear: I want to keep getting better, build the right mindset, and eventually play professional soccer.

First, a huge part of my drive is the chance to improve. I plan to train every single day, and I’m not afraid to ask coaches or more skilled players for guidance when I need it. Whenever I make a mistake, I take it as a lesson to figure out what went wrong so I can do better next time. Joining a team would also help a lot—I could practice alongside players of all skill levels, compete in tournaments, and pick up new skills from the people I play with.

Next, having the right mindset is just as important. I need to focus on what it takes to play at a professional level: playing without fear, and treating the sport as a lifelong commitment. It’s all about believing I can reach that pro level. I know this mindset will help me handle all the challenges I’ll face as I work toward my goal, so staying positive and determined is key.

On top of that, playing professional soccer has been my dream for as long as I can remember. I’ve spent my whole life practicing for this exact goal, because it’s the thing I love most. Sure, the sport can be tough sometimes—there’s always a risk of injury—but it’s also an amazing way to meet new people and feel like you’re starting a whole new chapter of your life. Plus, the salary is a big draw for countless people who want to go pro, and that’s true for me too.

To wrap up, when you do something you’re truly passionate about, it never feels like a job. My three core reasons for chasing this goal are simple: I want to keep improving my skills, build the right professional mindset, and play pro soccer because it’s the thing I love most.

I firmly believe that having a positive attitude will always guide a person toward success. A positive outlook is the core foundation of achievement—even if you have lost absolutely everything, you should never give up hope. Pair that optimism with hard work, and you are bound to succeed sooner or later. When you face a difficult challenge with a positive mindset, the obstacle will feel far less daunting, and you will find it much easier to push through.

Optimism also supports good physical health, which in turn makes it easier to reach your goals. On the other hand, approaching situations with a negative attitude will only hold you back from achieving what you want in life.

A positive attitude does more than just transform your own life. It can also inspire people close to you to chase their goals, since your optimism will encourage them to work toward their own success.

We can look at famous successful people for clear examples. Steve Jobs, the co-founder of Apple, was forced to leave his own company early in his career, but he maintained a positive attitude through every setback. Three years later, he regained control of the company. He also suffered from a heart disease that doctors warned would be fatal, but his sheer willpower and optimistic mindset helped him survive. Another example is football legend Cristiano Ronaldo, who faced racial discrimination as a young player. He tackled every hardship with a smile, staying positive his entire life, and is now considered one of the greatest soccer players in history. By focusing only on positive thoughts, he overcame nearly all of the obstacles in his path.

Today, many people get discouraged too easily—if they lose a small game, they immediately give up on ever winning again. We need to change this mindset, because that is not how life works. Everyone faces hardships, no matter who they are, but greeting those struggles with a smile can make them feel far more manageable. Instead of losing hope, focus on how to solve the problem, and keep a positive attitude.

To sum up, every person faces difficulties, from one-year-old children to elderly people, but staying positive can completely turn a situation around because it gives you the strength to overcome anything. Always stay calm, take deep breaths, and hold onto a positive attitude rather than letting negativity take over.

I fully agree with Prime Minister Churchill’s observation that ‘success consists of failure, being successful’—a view that differs from what many people assume. Rather than being a straight, easy path, success is about tackling problems head-on to clear obstacles, which ultimately helps people grow and feel motivated.

Success is never just a far-off wish; it requires committing to small, consistent efforts every single day. It also pushes people to focus on what lies ahead, instead of falling back into outdated habits from the past.

Failing at something does not mean you have to abandon your dreams or ideas. Instead, it gives you the chance to push past your limits and work through any hurdles in your way. Setbacks can also bring back your hopes and make you better prepared for whatever challenges come next. It even teaches you how to lift up others, offering support and encouragement to help them meet their own needs.

Even when you face failure, it is never the end of the world. Instead, it acts as a test of your confidence and skills, helping you improve and even grow into a leader in your field or daily life. I remember taking a tough class test recently: I felt nervous at first, but I chose to stay confident that I would pass, rather than wasting energy worrying about failing. Many people chase success to find happiness, and as their skills grow, they prefer to get back on track without relying on others. It is vital for them to plan far ahead for their future, and they refuse to lose their enthusiasm. This is nothing like the person who loses a video game, gives up immediately, throws their console in the trash, and never plays again.

On the other hand, some people actively seek out challenges. These push them to think deeply, improve their abilities, and spot their own weaknesses as they move up each level. They refuse to be beaten, and instead aim to stay at the top of their game.

Once again, I stand by Prime Minister Churchill’s quote that ‘success consists of failure, being successful’—a perspective that goes against common assumptions. Success is about solving problems to clear every obstacle in your path, which helps you grow as a person and stay motivated. It is also never just an idle dream; it takes daily dedication to keep showing up. Success encourages people to look to the future, not focus on outdated habits from the past.

Imagination is a core human trait that serves a vital purpose. It acts as one of the most essential foundations of all knowledge, and it sparks every new concept or creation. Put simply, if humans lacked imagination, we would have no knowledge at all.

This skill plays a key role in every part of our daily routines, whether that’s work, family life, or school. Every time we carry out an activity, we use our imagination to map out the steps we need to take, and figure out which knowledge or skills will help us finish the task. Imagination is also the reason humans have been able to evolve over centuries: it lets us adapt to all kinds of changing daily circumstances.

Imagination always comes first, before any idea, task, or decision we make. It serves as the initial draft for every concept we come up with. For example, whenever someone designs an object to solve a specific problem, they first use their imagination to picture what people need, and how that object will meet those needs to help others. Every single idea starts with imagination, and we only draw on our existing skills and knowledge later to turn that idea into reality.

Without imagination, humans would have no knowledge to speak of. Imagination forms the basis of all knowledge: it is the ability to think up new possibilities, while knowledge is just the collection of ideas we use to carry out any activity we want. To give an example, it is pointless for someone to have strong math or science skills if they cannot apply those skills to come up with new ideas or complete tasks. At its core, imagination is the foundation of all creation.

In short, imagination is an essential skill for everyday life. Humans rely on it in every area of their lives, from work and school to family. It is the ability to think creatively and come up with new ideas.
