A truly successful professional is often someone who discovered their passion for a specific career early in life and dedicated years to studying that field. Young children absorb new information far faster than they do as they grow older. It is common for parents to ask their kids what they want to be when they grow up, suggesting options like doctors, teachers, dentists, police officers, or engineers. Schools often encourage this too: teachers frequently assign drawing activities where students illustrate their dream future job, and nearly every young child already has a clear idea of what they want to be later in life. For this reason, having students commit to a career path at a young age is a very positive step.

To achieve success in their chosen field, students need plenty of time to prepare properly.

For instance, every career requires years of study to master core subjects. Students may struggle to earn enough credits to pass required classes, forcing them to retake courses and delay their progress. This is especially true for careers like medicine: becoming a doctor takes many years of training and costs a large amount of money. Students pursuing this path often need to save up to cover tuition fees, though in some cases the government will fund their education if they meet certain academic requirements. Gaining the knowledge and skills needed to excel in any career takes significant time and effort.

Starting a career path early also gives students the chance to explore multiple fields before making a final decision. They can switch to a different career if they realize they prefer another option, and young people have countless opportunities to build a bright future for themselves. They can also weigh up which career paths offer the best job prospects and highest salaries. By beginning their studies at a young age, students have the flexibility to try out different fields and settle on the one that plays to their strengths.

Not everyone agrees with this approach, however. Some people argue that young students lack the life experience to make informed career choices. They claim kids need to be older to fully understand how to pick a suitable career and feel confident in their decision. Critics also point out that many children only want to follow in the footsteps of their parents, uncles, cousins, or other people they admire, without actually knowing what those jobs involve. They add that students often underestimate how challenging a career will be, and that young people are not yet responsible enough to make long-term decisions about their future. Many believe children are simply too young to commit to a career path so early.

In conclusion, while students ultimately have the final say in what career they pursue, starting to work towards that goal at a young age brings clear benefits. It gives them more time to pick up skills that will help them in their future job, and more time to correct any mistakes they make along the way. People who build a stable, well-paid career and a bright future are often those who started working towards their goals in childhood. High schools will encourage students to start focusing on career paths from an early age.

What are my future goals? I’ve thought about getting a place of my own, buying a car, or even starting a family someday. But if I’m being honest, my biggest dream is to become a billionaire. What about you—what do you hope to achieve, and what’s driving that goal?

There are plenty of reasons whyI want to reach billionaire status.

First off, if I ever become a billionaire, the first thing I’d do is get my own home. I can’t live with my mom forever, and I’m sure she’d be happy to have her space back too. I’d make sure it has a backyard pool—I’ve always wanted one so I can swim whenever I want without trekking to the water park, or just lounge in the water when I have free time. I’d also host parties for my friends there, so my mom wouldn’t have to keep telling us to lower our voices.

Next, I’d buy my mom a house, a new car, and plenty of nice clothes. She’s worked so hard for our family, and she deserves to be spoiled. I’d sell the house we’re living in now, and give her every cent from the sale. Her current car is pretty old and always has mechanical issues, so I’d take her to a dealership to pick out a model she loves. I’d also bring her to the mall to shop at all her favorite stores, so she can pick out any clothes she wants.

Another big goal is to buy a hospital. I’d make sure it doesn’t overcharge patients—every time I’ve gone to the hospital, the bills are way too high, and lots of people can’t afford that. I’d hire only the most skilled doctors and nurses, since some medical staff aren’t very good at their jobs. I’d also make sure the hospital accepts everyone, no matter where they’re from, what they look like, or their race. Too many hospitals judge people based on things like skin color or appearance, and I want to change that.

Last but not least, I’d use some of my money to help homeless people. Not all my wealth would be for my own wants—I’d set a big portion aside for those in need. I’d buy food and clothes for them, since some have decent clothing and others don’t, and many are just waiting for a meal. I’d also buy a whole city block to build apartments for homeless people. Whenever I’m in a car, I see so many homeless people sitting or sleeping on sidewalks, and they absolutely deserve a safe place to live.

Those are the main reasons why I want to achieve billionaire status.

You do not even need to be upbeat or cheerful all the time to make an impact. Take the movie *The Princess and the Frog* as an example. The main character, Tiana, dreams of opening her own restaurant because it was her father’s lifelong wish. She works tirelessly to save enough money to buy a building for the business. She faces setbacks early on, but by the end of the film, she achieves her goal. Her story proves that having a single clear aim, plus the motivation to keep working toward it, is enough to make progress and inspire others.

The first way to influence others is through consistent actions. Leading by example is often far more effective than just telling people what to do. For instance, if you start donating food to your local food bank regularly, your individual contribution might seem small at first. But if you keep doing it day after day, people will start to notice your habit of helping those in need. If your efforts get covered by local news, even more people might be encouraged to donate to support their community too.

A second key way to influence people is by setting clear goals. People who have specific aims tend to get more done than those who wander without a plan. Imagine you really want to buy a new video game that costs eighty dollars, but you have no savings left. You start doing chores around the house: cleaning your room, washing your parents’ car, mowing the lawn. Even after that, you still don’t have enough money. So you go door to door in your neighborhood, asking neighbors if they need small tasks done for a fee. Eventually, you earn exactly the amount you need to buy the game. This shows that when you set a goal and work steadily to reach it, you prove to others that they can do the same thing to get what they want.

The final way to influence others is through genuine motivation. You will not inspire anyone if you seem discouraged or unmotivated yourself. Instead, you need to come across as energetic and driven. When other people see how passionate you are about your goals, they are far more likely to adopt that same energy themselves. Motivation matters because it shows you have a clear purpose for finishing what you start, and it demonstrates how much effort you are willing to put in to achieve your aims.

Some might argue that a person’s general behavior is the best way to influence others, since it creates a positive mood that encourages people to feel motivated. However, behavior alone does not show people exactly how to take action toward a specific aim. That is why the most effective way to influence those around you is to demonstrate your actions, set clear goals, and stay motivated throughout the process.

Statistics show that 93% of people in the US reach out to more than one person when they need advice. I firmly believe that gathering multiple perspectives leads to smarter decisions than relying on a single person’s input.

Beyond just making better immediate choices, this habit also benefits you in countless situations later in life. That’s why it’s always better to consult several people instead of one: you gain access to diverse viewpoints, learn how others interpret your problem, and start to view challenges from angles you might never have considered on your own.

Every person you know processes information and problems differently. While two people might agree on a small part of your issue, they will almost always propose different solutions, because no two situations call for the exact same fix. Hearing these varied suggestions helps you weigh more options before deciding.

Another key point is that people interpret situations in their own way. Some of the people you ask may not fully grasp your circumstances, or see the problem the same way you do. If they don’t understand the full context, their advice could be unhelpful at best, or make your problem even worse at worst. That’s why it’s important to have a circle of trusted people you can turn to for guidance. Many of these trusted contacts will have gone through similar experiences themselves, so they’ll know exactly what to suggest.

Gathering multiple opinions also changes how you view problems yourself. Hearing different takes on your issue broadens your own perspective, making you more open-minded when facing future challenges. Over time, you’ll also get better at advising others when they come to you for help. Being a reliable source of guidance strengthens your relationships, as people learn they can trust you to listen and respond thoughtfully. That trust is invaluable: it means friends and family feel comfortable sharing anything with you, knowing you’ll handle their concerns with care.

To sum up, consulting more than one person for advice leads to better decisions in the moment, and supports you in many other areas of life long-term. This habit lets you collect diverse opinions, understand how others perceive your problems, and develop a more flexible way of looking at challenges. That’s why it’s always worth reaching out to several trusted people instead of relying on just one perspective.

Completing high school in three years to start college sooner is a smart option for many learners. While most follow the standard four-year timeline, a growing number choose to wrap up secondary education early. There are plenty of valid reasons to graduate ahead of schedule. For some, the goal is to enter the workforce sooner to save for college tuition, or free up time for family vacations. Older students, particularly those from Hispanic communities with work or family responsibilities, see early graduation as a path to securing a well-paying job that requires a high school diploma. High-achieving students who meet all graduation requirements can also opt to finish early. Ultimately, graduation timing depends on personal needs and goals.

Earning a diploma a full year ahead of schedule takes serious effort from students. Take a 16-year-old in 11th grade, for instance: if they have not yet earned enough credits or fulfilled all graduation requirements, they will not be able to finish high school early. On the other hand, pupils who have already ticked all the boxes for graduation can absolutely choose to wrap up their studies sooner. Very few high schoolers hold part-time jobs, have after-school caregiving duties, or participate in extensive extracurricular activities. Most schools also offer a wide range of after-school options, from clubs to academic support: students can stay late to retake failed quizzes or ask teachers for extra help with tough subjects.

Any student hoping to graduate early must work hard and meet all graduation requirements. This often means taking extra assignments. For example, if a learner struggles with a class, they need to stay after school for teacher help to pass and earn credits. A major downside is burnout: students with after-school jobs often feel exhausted juggling work and school, which can make it hard to keep up. They may fall behind on required work and risk not graduating. To succeed, they need consistent effort.

Many schools now run special programs designed to let students finish high school in three years. These options often include summer classes or evening courses, which make it simple to earn required credits in a much shorter timeframe. However, very few students end up enrolling in these accelerated programs. A common barrier is that many learners have part-time jobs during the summer, which conflicts with class schedules.

For students who cannot fit these in-person programs into their schedules, there is another option: they can take accredited courses online to earn the credits they need.

To sum up, letting students finish high school in three years to start college early is a positive idea, even though it comes with both benefits and downsides. On the plus side, schools often provide accelerated programs or online course options that make early graduation achievable. The main drawbacks are the heavy workload and risk of exhaustion, especially for students who work part-time after school to save money for college. At the end of the day, success depends entirely on the individual student. Those who put in the required work and effort will graduate on time, while those who do not will not meet their goal.

British naturalist and politician John Lubbock once said, "Your character will be what you yourself choose to make it." Many people agree with this view, and I am among them. I believe we each shape our own character traits, because even when others try to influence us, we are the ones who make our own choices. It is true that some people we meet in life may try to talk us into doing bad things, but it is up to us whether we keep those people in our lives or walk away.

To start with, your character is the core of what makes you who you are. It depends entirely on whether you choose to be a good person or a bad one, kind or unkind. The world is full of people with all sorts of different personalities, each shaped by their own choices.

Secondly, everyone is unique in how they act. Some choose to help others, give up their free time to support the elderly, or prioritize spending time with family and friends. Others might make harmful choices like stealing or other bad acts. But every single one of these actions comes down to your own decision, not anyone else’s – these choices make up the character traits that define you as a person.

Last of all, people with both good and bad character traits can change if they want to. No one else can make that choice for you – it is completely up to you. There are countless ways to adjust your behavior and grow as a person, but you have to be the one to decide that change is what you want.

In conclusion, John Lubbock, the British naturalist and politician, was right when he said, "Your character will be what you yourself choose to make it." I fully stand by this belief. It is also true that the people around us can influence how we act – such as the family we grow up with, the role models we look up to, or the people who motivate us throughout our lives. At the end of the day, though, we are the ones who decide who we want to be and how we behave. Those choices shape our character, and no one else can make them for us.

One of my strongest skills, which I’m always happy to talk about, is math—and I’d like to share how I built this ability over time. It didn’t happen overnight; I spent months studying and practicing until the concepts finally clicked. Putting in all that effort was completely worth it, and here are the key steps I followed.

First, I focused on actually grasping how math works. I always attended every math class and paid close attention while my teacher explained new topics. After each lesson, I went over my notes again and again until I fully understood the material, instead of just memorizing steps.

Next, I made sure to complete all my math homework, since that was the best way to work through problems and spot what I still didn’t get. If I got stuck, I’d ask a family member or my teacher for help. I also referred back to my class notes to find relevant information, or watched short tutorial videos online that broke down tricky problem types. This practice was essential to getting better at math.

The last, and maybe most important, habit I built was never giving up and trusting my own abilities. Whenever a problem felt too hard, I’d remind myself that I could figure it out. I also made a point of looking for different ways to solve a single question, so I didn’t get stuck if one method didn’t work. Over time, I learned to trust my answers when I knew I’d followed the right steps, which boosted my confidence even more.

To sum up how I developed my math skill: first, I learned the basics by attending classes and reviewing material until I understood it fully, so I could tackle any question. Next, I did all my homework to master problem-solving, using help from others, my notes, and online resources when needed. Finally, I never gave up, believed in my ability to solve hard problems, and learned to trust my own work. That is how I became skilled at math.

Building a strong, admirable personality requires us to constantly take on new challenges, since staying idle will never help us reach our goals. Many believe that hard work is the foundation of every achievement, and it is impossible to get anywhere meaningful without putting in effort. I firmly believe that people who avoid action have little chance of a bright future. That is why we should always push ourselves to try new things, work consistently, and grow—this is the only way to secure a successful life, earn respect in our community, and become the best version of ourselves.

Everyone dreams of a happy, fulfilling future, but the path to that life is shaped by how we handle difficult times. It is clear that we will never achieve anything if we refuse to put in the work. Accomplishments only come from consistent effort, not luck or chance. People who stay inactive rarely have promising futures ahead of them. When you have no plan for what comes next, life feels aimless—you lose hope and grow tired of your daily routine. That is why it is so important to start building our future today, instead of putting it off until later.

Success is something we all strive for, and everyone is looking for the secret to reaching it. But if you look at people who have actually succeeded, you will find they all made a habit of tackling new tasks and pushing their limits. To build a bright future, a stable career, and a good life, we need to work hard, focus on our core goals that support our career growth, and trust in our own abilities—these are all key parts of a happy life. Inactive people add little value to their communities, and staying idle means you will never reach your full potential in the years to come.

Most of us want to be seen as having a strong, positive personality in our communities, as this makes the people around us proud. To build that kind of reputation, we need to expand our knowledge, improve our way of thinking, and pursue education. Without a clear main goal in life, it is impossible to reach what we aim for. Education is the only path to success: when you have a good education and a solid career, you feel more connected to your community, and you earn the respect of those around you. Inactivity will never help us achieve more. I believe that staying idle serves no purpose—it only slows down our thinking, making it harder to reach any of our goals.

We should all try our best to build a life that feels easier and more secure, and that only happens through hard work. People who stay idle throughout their lives will only face regrets and struggles later on. Successful people always put in effort earlier in life, which is why they now have comfortable, stable futures. The root of all accomplishment is hard work, self-belief, and a clear focus on your goals—things that inactive people rarely value. For all these reasons, pushing ourselves to work hard and take action is the only way to achieve the things we want in life.

Dear diary, today in English class, my friends were arguing that first impressions are nearly impossible to change once they’re made. I talked to a few other people about this, and I still don’t agree with that idea. For one, someone might be going through a really tough time in their life and not acting like their usual self. Another point is that people don’t always treat everyone the same way. One classmate gave me a really good reason, too: sometimes people act out of character because of circumstances we don’t know about. I thanked him for sharing that thought.

The biggest reason I disagree is that people can be in a really rough patch of their lives, so their behavior doesn’t reflect who they really are. Maybe they just moved far away from their old home, leaving behind friends and family. Maybe someone in their family passed away, or they’re just feeling incredibly lonely. I’ve been in this situation so many times myself. My family moves a lot because of where my parents’ jobs take us, and at one point they told me we’d be moving every single year. That completely changed how I acted: I felt miserable, didn’t want to go to school at all, and only cared about having fun outside of classes. This year, we haven’t moved yet, but my parents are looking at a house an hour away from here, and we might move again in January. I’m already dreading that, because Generic_School feels like a second home to me. The teachers are so kind—they help you with anything you need, even problems that happen outside of school, and they always try their best to support you. I’ve also made so many close friends here, and I really don’t want to leave them. Everyone at this school is just great.

Another reason first impressions aren’t fixed is that people don’t always treat everyone the same way. I had a personal experience with this that I really didn’t enjoy. Once, I went to a party where I was supposed to meet up with a group of friends. When I got there, they all ignored me, and I had no idea why. A girl who saw me trying to talk to them pulled me aside and explained: they’d heard I did something awful, something I didn’t even know I was accused of. I went over to the group, explained that I hadn’t done anything wrong, and told them I have a twin sister I’d never mentioned before. She’s the complete opposite of me, so it must have been her they heard about. Once I cleared that up, everything was fine, and we all ended up hanging out and having fun for the rest of the night.

The classmate I mentioned earlier gave me another good point: some people act out of character because they’re dealing with things we can’t see. For example, some kids struggle to control their emotions at certain points in their lives, so they might be aggressive one day and kind the next. A lot of the time, this is tied to a medical condition. He told me about a kid he knew who would be super helpful and friendly most of the time, but would suddenly get really angry and say mean things to people he’d known for years. He couldn’t control his outbursts, but his teachers would explain his condition to the other students, so everyone understood and didn’t judge him unfairly.

Now that we’ve looked at all these examples, I’m certain I’m correct. People aren’t always perfect—everyone makes mistakes in life, or sometimes other people or situations cause them to act that way. Thank you for hearing me out today! Have a great day!

Dear Readers,

I’m truly grateful for this opportunity to share my personal opinions and experiences with you. While I might side with different views on various topics, I’ve always held that life is fleeting and unpredictable – we never know when it will come to an end. The same cannot be said for first impressions, though: unlike life, we can track exactly when and how they shift, because there is a massive difference between the two.

I strongly disagree with the claim that first impressions are almost impossible to change. I believe they can absolutely be altered, even if not instantly. Let me explain my reasoning based on what I’ve lived through.

First, many people argue that “first impressions are incredibly important.” I’m not entirely convinced this is always true, but it’s a common belief, so there may be some truth to it for certain people. For those who care deeply about what others think of them, first impressions matter a lot. But whether that initial impression sticks depends entirely on who the person is. If you meet someone you have a crush on, you’ll want to make a good first impression. But even then, as time passes, either you or they can shift that initial view, because you’ll get to know the real person behind the first meeting. Time is the key here: a first impression only lasts a split second, but it can change completely as you spend more time together.

Second, first impressions are often based on superficial things like your appearance or the expression on your face. This is another area where they can be easily changed. Take an experience I had about a year ago: I spoke to a girl who looked furious at first glance. She wasn’t actually angry at all – her face just had a naturally stern, serious look. As we spent more and more time together, my initial impression of her being mad faded entirely. Now, I think the exact opposite of that first assumption.

Time is one of the most powerful forces in our lives. We can’t stop it, but we can move past initial feelings. First impressions might linger in our minds at first, but they don’t have to stay there forever. Some fade away entirely, others get replaced as we learn more about a person. They aren’t fixed parts of our lives – we can adjust them, just like we move past other small, fleeting moments.

In conclusion, everything comes down to time. If you ask me whether first impressions can be changed, my answer is a definite yes. You’ll never fully forget the very first impression you got of someone, but your later experiences with them will shape your overall view far more. We’re always able to adjust how we see others, given enough time. Thank you for reading.

I believe I understand why Thomas Jefferson wrote this text for the people of his era. His goal was to check if they would take responsibility for their own work instead of wasting time on trivial matters, and he simply wanted his community to be able to chase their dreams. When he first shared this message, many people were afraid, as they or their ancestors had been enslaved not long before.

Later, Abraham Lincoln became president of the United States, and his rise to power highlights three key reasons why Jefferson wrote this work.

First, Jefferson dedicated time to observing the public because he wanted to see how well they would follow the advice in his writing. Too many people never stop to consider what they truly want to achieve in life. If we keep spending all our time socializing with others instead of working on our own goals, we will never reach our dreams. Some people feel shy or afraid to chase their ambitions because others might try to hold them back, whether out of jealousy of their potential success or because the dreamers themselves doubt their own abilities. Many people fail to achieve their goals because they assume the process will be too difficult, but the real issue is that they never even try. Anyone can reach their dreams if they make the effort.

Second, if we read Jefferson’s words closely and carefully, we can uncover deeper meaning. Most of us don’t reflect on our goals because we lack the commitment to improve our own lives. Many young people attend school only because their parents send them there, not because they see the many opportunities education offers for future success. By following the lessons in Jefferson’s writing, we can learn the value of hard work for building a better life. We just need to focus on our future, study harder to earn good grades, and work toward the dreams we have always wanted to achieve.

Third, today we have more free time than ever to pursue our interests, as we live in a free society. Yet most of us only want to hang out with friends and have fun, with few people prioritizing their long-term dreams. Instead of working toward our goals, we spend hours at parties or doing meaningless activities with peers. If we keep making the same choices, we will never improve our lives. We need to commit more fully to the future we actually want for ourselves.

In conclusion, young people like us have the chance to be more successful than previous generations, as we have more opportunities and energy to chase our goals. We can prove to others that we are capable of great things if we focus our thinking and concentrate fully on our work. No matter what obstacles we face, we can achieve our dreams because we are not alone: our families will always support us in whatever we choose to do with our future. Jefferson’s words give us the strength to keep pursuing our ambitions and never give up on the goals that matter to us.

If I had to tell my teacher whether I’d rather work in groups or by myself, I would definitely choose working alone. Working by yourself lets you come up with creative ideas that other people in a group might never think of. For instance, students who work independently often get higher grades in class than those who complete assignments in groups. Another issue with group work is that it’s easy to get sidetracked. You might end up chatting with teammates instead of focusing on the task you’re supposed to finish, which means you don’t complete the work you started. Many students prefer working alone because it’s easier to meet deadlines this way, so they don’t risk failing a class. Quiet, shy students also tend to work better alone. They don’t have to worry about falling behind because other group members are not pulling their weight.

When students work in groups, they often don’t get much useful help from their teammates. A common mistake is joining a group where only two people do all the work, while the other two contribute nothing. Some group members don’t do any schoolwork at all—they just sit around chatting with friends, scroll on their phones, or play games instead of focusing on the assignment. While some students love to slack off and chat, others take their work seriously. That’s why so many students end up preferring independent work to group projects. Parents also worry about this. They often think their child’s friends will lead them to fail a class, so they blame the friends rather than their own kid if grades drop. If a teacher calls home to say a student is failing because they’re not turning in work like they used to, parents usually assume their child is spending time with the wrong crowd, not that their kid is slacking off. Some parents even stop their kids from spending time with certain friends, worried that these peers will make their child fail a class. They’re quick to blame friends for poor grades instead of holding their own child accountable.

Overall, I strongly believe students are better off working alone than in groups. This also reflects a bigger life lesson: while we might want help to get what we want, we have to earn most things on our own, using our own skills and effort rather than relying on others.

Have you ever wished for extra time at school? I definitely want more hours in the classroom. It would let me learn new things, finish tasks, and relax without rushing. There are three key reasons why longer school days are a great idea.

First, it helps students get all work done during school hours. Longer days mean extra time to finish homework before heading home. That way, we won’t have unfinished tasks waiting for us after school, since we already completed everything in class. Getting work done early is a huge plus.

The second reason is more time with friends. School can get dull, but friends make it fun. You can team up with classmates to work on projects together, finishing tasks faster. Hanging out with friends during extra hours makes the day less boring and more enjoyable.

My third point is about improving grades. Struggling with low marks? Extra time lets you fix that. Completing more assignments and doing well on them raises your overall grade. You can also redo work you did poorly on earlier, so you don’t fall behind.

Those are my three reasons for wanting longer school days. I think they’re all solid, and I hope you agree. Even if you don’t, that’s totally fine. Just remember: school is a great place, so make the most of your time there!

I do not agree with the idea that first impressions are permanent, because anyone can fix a bad first impression if given enough time and a second chance, rather than being judged only for one mistake.

First of all, everyone deserves a second chance to fix a poor first impression. We all slip up sometimes—maybe you stammered through a business meeting, or acted awkward on a first date. You would not want others to only remember that bad moment. Instead, you would want them to give you another chance to show your true personality, once you have had time to settle in and do better.

Another common situation is a high-stakes business meeting. If you perform poorly or say something wrong the first time you meet potential partners or clients, they might think you are unprofessional. But if they give you a second chance, you can show up prepared and confident, changing their minds completely. Instead of remembering you as the person who messed up, they will be impressed by how much you have improved since the first meeting.

A third example is meeting a partner’s family for the first time. Imagine you are having dinner with your girlfriend and her parents, and you make a bad impression. Her dad might say you are not the right person for his daughter, just because of that one mistake, and end up disliking you. But if you visit again, you can show a better side of yourself, fixing that first bad impression so her dad no longer has a negative opinion of you.

In conclusion, we should always give people a second chance to improve their first impressions. This lets them show their true selves, rather than being stuck with a reputation based on one early mistake.

In the end, achieving your goals almost always requires failing more than once along the way.

Lots of schools team up with nearby businesses these days. These collaborations give learners a chance to try out different career paths. Young people need plenty of support to do well in life, and schools have a responsibility to give them the tools to succeed.

Schools should form these kinds of partnerships to support all learners in reaching their personal goals. These arrangements help students build practical skills and give them space to develop their critical thinking too. Working with partners makes things far simpler, since other people are there to step in when help is required.

Partnerships also spread out risk, which is a huge plus. If a business fails, everyone shares the loss instead of one person bearing the full burden. Shouldering all the risk alone is incredibly tough — it’s almost impossible, like trying to reach the sky. Taking on all that pressure by yourself is awful: for instance, you could end up homeless or lose every cent you’ve saved. I want to have a comfortable life when I’m older, so I definitely don’t want to take on all the risk myself. I’d hate to lose all my savings, so having a partner to lean on would make me feel much more secure. Besides, I’ve never liked working by myself. I’d much rather collaborate with others once I enter the workforce.

One of the best parts of partnerships is sharing. You don’t just split the risks — you also share the rewards. Partners swap ideas to boost profits, and pool money to expand the business. Sharing really is a key benefit of working with others. Partnerships aren’t lonely at all; they’re full of positive energy. Working solo is dull, but chatting with your partners makes the work fun. These interactions also help team members get to know each other better. At the end of the day, partnerships are built on trust and shared enjoyment.

Some people argue that partnerships are a bad idea. They claim that working with others offers no real benefits, but they’re mistaken — partnerships are very useful. Critics worry that team members might clash, leading the business to fall apart. Sure, getting along with colleagues takes effort, but choosing the right partners from the start is essential. While these critics have a point about potential conflicts, they’re still wrong overall. The biggest advantage of partnerships is getting to learn new things from the people you work with.

Many schools already team up with nearby companies, and this is a really positive move. These collaborations help learners build practical skills, and guide them toward reaching their goals and achieving success in adulthood. What’s more, partnering with others makes any venture easier, as no one has to shoulder all the risk alone. Schools should have the tools to help their students thrive in their future lives.

There is ongoing public debate about whether modern technology brings more benefits or harm to our daily lives. Some argue that digital tools let people finish tasks without interacting with others, while others claim tech is the main reason face-to-face human connection has declined. However, I firmly believe technology has overwhelmingly positive effects, as it offers countless advantages and makes a huge difference in how we live our lives.

These days, most people lead hectic lives full of work and other obligations. Teenagers especially have packed schedules: they have piles of homework, and many even work part-time jobs after school, leaving very little free time in the evenings. Thankfully, technology speeds up and simplifies so many daily tasks. For instance, if students had to complete all homework on paper without any digital tools, they would have to visit a library to buy supplies like printed pictures, colored pens, or reference materials for history assignments. That process would take far more time, and they might even need to wait for someone to give them a ride to get there. Without tech, we waste both time and money on basic tasks that now take minutes to finish.

Critics often point to negative effects of technology, arguing we should limit our use of it. They note that when families sit down to eat together, many people end up scrolling on their phones instead of talking, which hurts family relationships. While this is a valid concern, technology still offers far more help than harm. For one, it makes it easy to stay in touch with friends and family who live far away. It also helps when we travel to unfamiliar places and don’t know the address: tools like Google Maps let us find our way instantly. Almost anything you need to look up, you can find using technology.

I have seen firsthand how much technology improves daily life. I have relatives living in another country and friends spread across different states, and I often miss them. Thanks to tech, I can communicate with them easily: we can chat and even video call to see each other’s faces, which makes us all feel happy. Every year on my birthday, my family calls me first thing in the morning using FaceTime, and I do the same for my grandmother’s birthday to celebrate with her. Beyond personal connections, tech helps with practical tasks too. My mom picks my dad up from work every day, and we use Google Maps to track his location so she knows exactly when to leave, instead of waiting around unnecessarily. It is a huge help for our family.

It is clear that technology is a massive asset in life, as long as we use it wisely. Not everyone views it positively, but that is often a matter of personal perspective. In professional fields like science and medicine, tech is essential. Doctors use advanced machines to diagnose illnesses and save countless lives, and researchers rely on digital tools to find cures for diseases. Even our knowledge of history comes from technological advances: digital archives and online databases let us access information that would once have been impossible to find. Every benefit depends on how we choose to use the tools available to us.

In conclusion, technology has a net positive impact on people’s lives. It supports us in countless ways, from helping us feel closer to loved ones who live far away to assisting professionals in every field. The way we use tech is entirely up to us. Most people rely on it daily for good reason: it makes our lives easier, more connected, and more efficient. As long as we use it thoughtfully, technology will continue to be a force for good in our lives.

McDonald’s is one of the world’s most popular fast food chains, and the people who work there earn very low wages. If students visit a branch, they can see firsthand what happens to people who do not complete their education or slack off in school: they often end up in jobs like this. I would even choose a low-paying role at sucha place myself, just to show students the consequences of ignoring schoolwork or not paying attention in class.

Students might stop messing around in school after visiting this type of job. They will watch staff working incredibly hard, rushing to keep up with orders every day, only to take home very little pay. This would make most students not want to end up in a role like that later in life. It could encourage them to start putting more effort into their studies, stop slacking in class, and aim for a well-paying, successful career instead.

Some parents cannot afford to send their children to school, so those kids will have no choice but to take on tough, low-paying jobs when they grow up. But students who have the chance to get an education do not have to end up like that. They should seize this opportunity to build a successful career, rather than slacking off. On the other hand, teenagers who drop out of school or never finish their studies will likely end up working at places that pay very little.

If students do not take their education seriously, they waste the money their parents spent on their schooling. If they refuse to pay attention or put in effort, that money is thrown away, because they learn nothing while messing around. They will never be able to get a good, successful job. Visiting a low-paying job like this can change how students think about slacking off. When you take your education seriously, you can land a well-paying job and build a successful life. But doing nothing in school will get you nowhere.

I plan to write a letter to McDonald’s to make this happen. I want students to see what happens when they slack off in school, or when their parents cannot afford to pay for their education. The staff at McDonald’s work incredibly hard, but they earn very little. If students take their education seriously, they can get a successful job later in life. This experience might change their minds about whether to pay attention in class, and encourage them to seize their chance at education, so they never end up in a low-paying job like this.

While it is fine to prioritize your own needs occasionally, constantly putting yourself first, acting as if no one else matters, is not realistic. We must also consider the people around us: our parents, siblings, grandparents, friends, and even colleagues at times. After all, many of these people have supported us when we faced difficulties, so it is only right to care about their needs too.

Think about working in a team, for instance. When you are part of a group, other members will often ask for your input to solve problems, plan upcoming tasks, or manage projects. Teamwork requires putting the group’s needs first, not acting selfishly. If you ignore requests for help or refuse to contribute, your teammates will form a very poor impression of you. But if you step up to support the team, you can push yourself to do your best work and help everyone succeed.

This also applies to the workplace. Whether you work in a corporate office or another setting, employers pay close attention to how you interact with others. They consider whether you are worth hiring, how well you handle your responsibilities, and how you treat the people around you. The key is to avoid focusing only on your own wants and needs. Never forget about the people in your life who matter to you.

There is no doubt that completing high school in just three years is a fantastic chance for many learners. For one, it lets students get their high school requirements out of the way much sooner. Not everyone enjoys their high school years, so graduating early is a smart way to move faster toward getting accepted into their preferred college. The program lets students take extra classes over the summer to speed up their progress, which means they can leave high school earlier and have more time to figure out their next steps. They might use this extra time to plan their college major, or start working to help their parents cover essential costs like rent and utility bills.

Of course, this option is not right for everyone. Some students may find they do not have enough time to keep up with the extra work, which could hurt their sleep schedule or even lead to them not finishing school at all. Others argue that this faster pace means they miss out on a full learning experience: a normal school year lasts ten months, but students in this program spend their summers taking extra classes, which some say is like skipping an entire year of regular schooling. If I were to join this program, I would make the most of the summer classes and other extra courses to earn the credits I need for the colleges I plan to apply to. After graduating early, I would start working, apply for scholarships, and submit applications to the universities I want to attend.

To sum up, not every student will want to join this program, and that is okay—we all have different priorities and beliefs. But for many, this option is a great way to start thinking seriously about their future career or college major while still in high school. I would definitely suggest students consider taking this offer, to see how it might benefit them. I am confident that taking this path can help students achieve their long-term goals.

Distance learning offers numerous benefits to students across various aspects of their lives. Thanks to the internet, learners can attend classes remotely and communicate directly with their teachers without stepping foot in a school building. They gain the exact same academic knowledge as their peers in traditional classrooms, but through a far more convenient process. Bullying remains a widespread issue in many schools, yet offering remote learning options can eliminate this problem entirely. Peer pressure from other teenagers is another common challenge, with some teens pressuring classmates to drink alcohol, smoke, or even experiment with illegal drugs. A large number of students have after-school obligations to juggle: they might take extra online courses, care for younger siblings, or hold part-time jobs.

Even when teachers make efforts to curb bullying, it is extremely difficult to guarantee all students behave appropriately. Some ignore rules entirely, show no concern for others, or simply refuse to put in effort. Many students already face incredibly difficult personal circumstances: their parents may be uninvolved in their lives, they may feel overwhelmed by excessive schoolwork, or they may already be balancing a part-time job alongside their studies. Adding bullying to these existing stressors can have devastating consequences. In far too many cases, students take their own lives due to unbearable stress, or because they feel no one cares about their wellbeing or notices their struggles. There are even instances where teachers are aware of bullying incidents, but choose to ignore the fact that their school is no longer a safe environment. They avoid addressing the root of the problem, or contacting parents to take action, to avoid extra work. Most teenagers do not realize that their actions can lead to someone’s death, and that they could face years of jail time and ruin their own futures over small acts like making fun of a classmate or getting into a physical fight. Even seemingly minor incidents can have life-altering repercussions.

Other students act as negative influences on their peers, pressuring them into actions that can damage their lives permanently, leading to jail time, health issues, or entirely negative life changes. Nowadays, it is often seen as trendy or cool for students to drink, smoke, or use drugs, and they frequently pressure others to join in. Common tactics include threatening to end friendships, claiming a partner doesn’t truly love them if they refuse, or even blackmailing them by promising to share private secrets with others. These threats leave students terrified of losing friends or romantic partners, forcing them to make choices that offer no benefit to their lives. While high school teachers are often strict with students, many teenagers show no interest in their education at all. They attend school solely to socialize with friends or distract other learners, which harms the educational experience of their peers. Some students are always full of energy, get into trouble regularly, and disrupt classes, acting as negative role models. Rather than issuing disciplinary referrals or suspensions, it would be better to suggest these students switch to homeschooling to prevent any further issues.

Holding a part-time job is a great way for students to save money for college or their future, but balancing work and traditional school is extremely challenging. Students often feel stressed and frustrated when they have to attend full school days on top of job shifts, leaving little time for homework. Traditional schools also waste time on long lunch breaks or non-academic activities, whereas students doing remote learning can complete all their assigned work in a few hours at home, then focus on their other responsibilities. Learning from home allows students to work at their own pace, without rushing to finish assignments or tests, which reduces stress related to schoolwork. Waking up early for school is a struggle for most teenagers, and poor sleep quality negatively impacts their grades, ability to concentrate, and leads to falling asleep in class, missing lessons, constant fatigue, or skipping classes entirely, all of which can delay their graduation.

In conclusion, offering homeschooling or remote learning options can make a hugely positive difference for both schools and students’ educational outcomes. It provides a simple way to learn, allowing students to gain the same knowledge as their peers in traditional classrooms, but through a more convenient process. The internet offers access to countless educational apps that make learning engaging and fun, rather than sitting in a classroom for hours on end. Remote learning also lets students avoid peers who show no concern for their own lives or education, as these students are far less likely to care about the learning experiences of others. For many teenagers today, attending school in person no longer feels like a priority, and they can easily take any required class online instead.

The topic at hand focuses on people who struggle to make choices on their own, even when it comes to personal matters, and often rely on others to tell them what to do.

The core question asks whether individuals should make all their own choices, or turn to experts and authority figures for advice on major life decisions. Some people argue that letting someone else handle every decision is better, as it saves them from having to stress over any choices at all.

Others strongly disagree with this view, pointing out that it makes no sense for a stranger to make choices that shape your entire life. After all, how can someone who doesn’t know you well understand what you truly want or need?

This is a highly debated issue, with valid points on both sides, but I firmly believe people should make their own decisions. My life belongs to me, and I need to learn how to handle the challenges that come with it. Even if my circumstances are difficult, I will take responsibility for every choice I make. It is fine to ask for someone’s opinion now and then—especially from people older than me who have more life experience—but that is all it ever is: an opinion. I would never give anyone else the power to make my decisions or take charge of my life for me.

To sum up, it is always better to take charge of your own life, no matter how tough things get. You are the only person who fully understands your own experiences and what works best for you. For that reason, I stand by my view: everyone should make their own decisions.

What if our school decided to change its current lunch menu? Most students would probably be annoyed at first, since the existing options are full of the tasty, familiar dishes they already love. But just because these foods taste good does not mean they are good for us.

The United States is widely seen as the country where fast food is most distributed and consumed, and it also has very high rates of deaths caused by elevated cholesterol.

Nowadays, all the useful tech we have makes people exercise less and move around way less. For example, we drive to almost every place instead of walking, so we get far less physical activity. We don’t even need to walk over to talk to someone—we can just send them a text. We don’t have to stand up to check the weather outside, either; we can just look it up on our phones. We’ve gotten to a point where if we’re too lazy to go to the cinema, we can just stay home and watch movies or shows on Netflix, Hulu, Disney+, or other phone apps.

All these tech advances are great in many ways, but they’re also making people who are already inactive even lazier and more overweight. This is leading to more health issues, such as heart attacks and high cholesterol.

If we don’t make any changes now, this problem will only get worse in the years to come.

One way to help young people, including us students at this school, is to teach them that fast food isn’t the only option. There are lots of healthy foods that taste really good—some are even better than junk food. Examples include avocado, fresh fruit juice, Caesar salad, fish, and many others. These foods help balance what our bodies need to work well with what we crave to eat.

We can introduce this wider range of foods through our school lunch menu. The cafeteria could serve dishes that students have never tried before, which have far less fat than foods like pizza.

That way, when we grow up, we won’t only reach for burgers, Chinese takeout, or chicken wings. We’ll know there are other choices that are better for our bodies.

If we don’t build these healthy habits now, it will be much harder to get into them later in life.

As a member of this school community, I care about my own future and that of my classmates. That’s why I believe adding more healthy options to the school cafeteria menu is one of the best possible ideas for all of us. None of us wants to deal with health problems caused by the food we eat every day.

Thank you for your attention.

While most students look forward to summer vacation, some teachers argue that the long break makes students sluggish when they return in the fall, and that they struggle to remember what they learned during the school year.

Summer vacation is the only extended time off students get to handle tasks they can’t fit into the busy school year, plus it gives them a chance to rest properly. I disagree with those who want to shorten it, for three key reasons.

First, many students want to take on part-time jobs or pursue hobbies that take up a lot of time during the school year, but they can’t manage it. Between piles of homework and constant test preparation, they barely have time for anything outside of schoolwork. Summer’s three-month stretch gives them space to work, gain practical experience that will help them land better jobs in the future, and pick up new skills.

Next, students really need a break once the school year ends. Most feel overwhelmed by the assignments and exams teachers pile on, and their minds need time to switch off and recharge. It’s unhealthy to be in work mode nonstop, and kids get burnt out easily. Summer is the perfect chance to unwind and have fun: they can go to the beach, spend more time with family, hang out with friends, or even travel to new places. The warm weather only makes these activities more enjoyable.

Finally, during summer vacation, students don’t have to stress about assignments or exams they’ll have to turn in or take right after the break ends. Shorter breaks like fall, winter, or spring recess only last a week, and most teachers assign work or schedule tests for right after the break, so students spend that time studying or doing homework instead of resting. In other words, those shorter breaks don’t actually give students a chance to relax. Summer is different: there’s no looming schoolwork hanging over their heads, so they can fully enjoy their time off.

Some people might argue that more frequent shorter breaks throughout the school year would be better for students. But they fail to realize that those shorter breaks almost always come with assigned work or tests scheduled for right after, so students never actually get time to let their brains rest properly.

To sum up, summer vacation is the only extended break students get to rest and do all the activities they can’t fit in during the busy school year, when homework and test prep take up all their time. It’s important to keep summer break as long as it is now — it’s the best time of year for students to relax, have fun, and recharge before the next school year starts.

This proverb holds true because being honest is the core of telling the truth, and it also helps you form new, meaningful friendships in life.

I stand by the idea that honesty is the best policy, but misusing it can completely destroy the trust others have in you. Losing someone’s trust is incredibly hard to fix. I once saw a bad car accident where someone was badly injured, but the driver who caused the crash lied about what happened and won the court case because he wasn’t honest. My dad has always told me that honesty plays a huge role in people’s lives. He’s shared stories where his friends witnessed robberies, and their honest accounts helped police track down and convict the criminals. Even a tiny bit of truthfulness can make a big difference for anyone. That said, you should never use honesty as a way to hurt someone’s feelings. Once, when I was playing a sports game, the opposing team kept lying and cheating, which really upset the younger kids on my team. But people’s approach to honesty can change over time too. I had a friend who used to lie all the time, but as he got older, he started to see why being truthful matters so much. I’ve even made new friends just by being honest with people. Clearly, being truthful can bring real benefits.

When you’re always honest, people naturally respect you. I’ve had plenty of times where being truthful earned me respect from others. Showing that you’re willing to tell the truth creates a positive atmosphere around you, which helps you build strong, healthy relationships. On the flip side, when people aren’t honest with you, it feels like you’ve been hit by a train, or completely betrayed. I remember walking down my street once and seeing a lot of police cars outside a neighbor’s house. I later found out she’d been robbed months before, but a witness finally came forward and told the police exactly what they saw. Because that witness was honest, the police were able to catch the thief. It’s clear to me that honesty really is the best policy.

To sum up, no matter what situation you’re in, you should always choose to be honest. Even later on, your past honesty can justify the choices you made. Honesty is the best policy because it pushes you to do the right thing and builds a positive environment around you. Being truthful shows that you have strong self-esteem, which will benefit you a lot in the long run.

Everyone should take charge of their own choices, for three key reasons. First, relying on yourself is the only way to gain real life experience. Second, you can only grow by making your own decisions, rather than letting others choose for you. Third, making choices builds your resilience, so you know how to handle tough situations when they come up.

A single choice can alter the entire course of someone’s life.

First, depending on yourself to make choices is the best way to build up your own experience. Take students, for example: a learner will never get top marks if they don’t decide to focus in class and complete all their homework assignments. No one else can make that choice for them.

Second, you will never truly learn if you don’t make your own decisions. No one will be around to guide you through every difficult moment, after all. When facing a tough choice, you have to think it over carefully, consider the long-term effects, and weigh the possible consequences of each option before acting.

Third, a single decision can change the lives of everyone around you, which is another reason to trust your own judgment. No one will ever care more about your future than you do yourself. Look at most successful people: many started with nothing, but they made smart, deliberate choices that helped them build their success.

To sum up, everyone should take responsibility for their own choices. Relying on yourself builds valuable life experience, making your own decisions is the only way to learn and grow, and choosing for yourself makes you stronger and better prepared to handle whatever challenges come your way.

So, are you ready to start making your own choices from now on?

Many hardworking people put their full effort into hunting for new roles and building a stable future for themselves. Most of these job seekers are responsible and confident they can improve any workplace, even making it better than it was before. Yet they often struggle to land positions simply because they lack prior work experience, and many employers refuse to hire them for that exact reason.

While plenty of people argue that past work experience is a must for getting hired, that idea is far from true. Countless people have landed jobs and built successful careers without any prior background in their field. You just need to stay determined and never quit. Take my father, for example. He couldn’t find work at first: his mother was ill, he had me as a young son, and he had no experience in any industry. He desperately needed a job to cover rent and pay for my grandmother’s surgery. He applied over and over, never gave up, and now he is one of Morocco’s most well-known journalists. He had no prior experience in journalism, yet he performs better than many colleagues who have years of experience under their belts.

First and foremost, a job candidate does not need prior experience to succeed. What matters most is being loyal to the role, working hard, and acting with honesty. These qualities push a workplace to grow, and they also help build a culture of respect and kindness among all staff members.

Second, this is not limited to traditional office jobs. It applies to acting, sports, or any other career path you might want to pursue. You do not need experience to start, as boxing legend Muhammad Ali once said: 'Everyone start out as a beginner.' For standard jobs, you just need to show employers why you deserve the role and prove you are the best candidate for the position. That said, you do need to prepare properly. You don’t want to come across as someone who can’t handle the work or knows nothing about the role. My father told me that workers with no prior experience often work harder, bring fresh ideas that push the company forward, and have a positive attitude that makes bosses value them more than longer-tenured employees.

Third, I cannot understand why so many employers refuse to give inexperienced candidates a chance to prove what they can do. There are countless people who never even get the opportunity to show their skills, even though they might be the best fit for the role. I have a French friend who wanted to work as a teaching assistant for a French class in the United States. Every school turned her down because she did not have much teaching experience, which felt incredibly unfair. She is a native French speaker, from the very country where the language originated, so she could teach students far more effectively. That is exactly why I believe employers need to rethink their bias against inexperienced candidates.

Finally, lacking experience does not define your ability to get the job you want. If you believe in yourself, you can land any role you set your mind to, as long as you keep working hard. Employers who still insist experience is mandatory will regret their stance later when they see you climbing to the top of your field. To me, experience has nothing to do with job success. Everything depends on the work you will do, not the work you have done in the past. I am certain that people without prior experience will outperform those who have years of background, as long as they bring positive energy and determination. Just keep that in mind, and you will succeed, just like my father and my French friend did.

Most people are familiar with the concept of kindness, but have you ever stopped to think about what it really is, or why it leaves such a strong mark on the people around us?

To start with, what exactly counts as kindness? It refers to any act where we give something to others, whether that’s a grand gesture like donating money to a charity, or a tiny everyday action like holding a door open for a stranger. But why do we bother doing these things? We help others because we hope they will go on to help someone else in turn, creating a ripple effect that makes the whole world a little better. At its core, kindness is what lifts someone’s mood and inspires them to pay that same goodwill forward to others.

Next, why does kindness have such a massive effect on other people? Most of us care about giving back, even if some people might disagree. All of us want to live in a better world, not just for our own sake, but for the next generation too. We hope our kids grow up in a kind, welcoming society, because one day they will remember the small, thoughtful acts that made their day — maybe someone held a door for them when their hands were full, or gave them a genuine compliment out of the blue. That one small act can spark a rush of happiness inside them, proving that even the tiniest gesture can leave a huge impression.

To sum up, kindness has an enormous impact on everyone it touches. It means something different to each of us, but we can all agree that even the smallest act of goodwill can transform someone’s day — and that person might then go on to brighten someone else’s life because of your initial kindness.

I strongly believe that allowing school students to study from home is a poor choice. A large number of young people would only exploit this arrangement—most would much rather stay in their bedrooms than wake up early to get to school by 7 a.m. There are plenty of students who would skip in-person classes for no better reason than not wanting to get out of bed early, while others make the effort to show up to school every day. For this reason, I do not think remote learning is suitable for school-aged children.

Admittedly, there are a small number of students who struggle to learn effectively in a traditional school setting, but far more choose remote learning just for the sake of it. When I say students take advantage of the system, I mean many claim to be completing assignments from home, but actually end up napping and putting off their work until much later. Yes, school can be challenging, but that is exactly why we have teachers, school staff, and parents ready to support us. Even online classes offer support if students have questions, but some people are visual learners who need an instructor right in front of them to understand material properly. Since everyone learns differently—some prefer working alone, others thrive in group settings or with a partner—attending school in person is the better option.

This is not to say remote learning offers no benefits to the students who actually complete their work online. I simply argue that in-person schooling is more straightforward for most. Many students would not gain anything from studying at home—they would just sleep through class or mess around instead of focusing on their work. There are countless reasons why I oppose remote learning for school students: for one, you can never be sure who you are interacting with in online spaces. Additionally, not all young people have reliable internet access, so they would be unable to participate in remote classes at all. When you are at school, however, you have access to countless resources to support your learning.

My final view is that attending school in person is far better than studying from home. Students actually have a proper chance to complete their work when they are in a school environment, whereas at home many would just sleep and neglect their assignments entirely, simply because they are in a relaxed setting. In-person learning is much more helpful than online study, as there is always a teacher or staff member nearby to assist if needed. While there will always be a few students who succeed with remote learning, the majority work better when they have another person standing right in front of them to guide them.

First impressions are incredibly hard to shift, largely because when we meet someone new, the only information we have about them is their appearance. Since we lack deeper context, it’s tough to alter those initial judgments, and most people rarely revise their first impressions of others.

First, forming quick judgments is a natural human instinct every time we encounter a stranger. Take a student who meets a classmate with a slight, unathletic build: they might assume this boy can’t play any sports, even if they’re told he’s the team’s top player. Even after watching him perform incredibly well on the field, the student will struggle to let go of their first impression. The boy still doesn’t look like a typical athlete, and the student already has a fixed idea of his poor physical health, so the initial judgment sticks.

Second, first impressions are personal opinions, and people tend to hold onto their own views even when presented with new information. Consider a man who comes across as very shy, always avoiding conversation with others. Most people around him decide he prefers to be left alone, so they stop trying to talk to him. Later, he might open up to close friends and reveal he actually loves chatting with people. But because everyone’s first impression of him is that he’s quiet and unfriendly, they still can’t bring themselves to strike up a conversation with him, unable to shift their original judgment.

That said, there are rare cases where first impressions can shift, usually when someone builds a genuine relationship with the person in question. For instance, a man with a large frame and a permanently frowning face might intimidate everyone around him. But if a student plucks up the courage to start a conversation, they might discover he’s actually warm and easy to talk to. In these rare moments, people can adjust their initial judgment, which makes interactions much smoother for everyone involved.

Another way first impressions can change is if a person clearly demonstrates how different they are now compared to when they first met others. Imagine a student who used to be mean to their friends. After realizing their behavior was hurtful, they start acting kindly, helping others instead of teasing them. If they consistently show this new, nicer side, their friends might eventually let go of their original impression of them as a mean person. This shift can lead to happier relationships and stronger friendships for everyone.

Even with these few exceptions, first impressions remain almost impossible to change for most people. That’s why we should avoid putting too much weight on our initial judgments of others.

I fully agree with Winston Churchill’s belief that true success means moving from one failure to the next without ever losing your drive. While many people view failure as a setback that crushes confidence and makes you doubt your own abilities, I believe it plays a vital role in helping us grow. It pushes us to progress, opens up new paths to reach our goals, and makes us far stronger than we were before we stumbled.

Failure is an unavoidable part of life. Too often, we label it as something negative, but in reality, it is a core ingredient for success. It equips you to handle even tougher challenges down the line. How can you improve if you never stumble? Mistakes and failed attempts teach you valuable lessons, build your resilience, and remind you that worthwhile goals rarely come easy. You have to put in consistent effort to get what you want, and slip-ups are simply stepping stones to progress, not dead ends.

Failure also pushes us to find new approaches to problems. When you fail, you immediately rule out methods that don’t work, which opens up room to try new strategies. It also shows you exactly what you could have done differently to avoid the setback. When I first started playing soccer, I had no idea how to kick the ball properly, because I only knew one technique. I messed up countless times, but I refused to quit. Instead, I experimented with different ways to strike the ball: adjusting my foot placement to hit it with more power, or positioning my body differently for better accuracy. All those failed attempts taught me that there are countless ways to solve a problem, not just one rigid method.

Beyond that, failure makes you far more resilient. When you get knocked down by a failure, then pick yourself up and push through to reach your goal, you emerge as a completely different person. You become someone who won’t give up over a small mistake, someone who refuses to throw in the towel when things get tough. You return with greater confidence, determined not to repeat the same error again. That one setback ends up making you far stronger than you were before it happened.

Thomas Edison once faced a question about his many failed attempts to invent the light bulb. When asked how it felt to fail 100 times, he replied that he hadn’t failed at all. Instead, he explained that creating a working light bulb was simply a project that required 100 steps to complete.

In conclusion, mistakes and failures are valuable learning tools. They show us new paths to reach our goals, and make us far stronger than we were before we stumbled. I believe people should not fear failure, but instead be willing to take risks and accept that failing is part of the process. When you finally reach your goal after working through setbacks, the sense of accomplishment you feel will be far greater than if everything had gone smoothly from the start.

Many people claim that first impressions are nearly impossible to alter, but I strongly disagree with this idea. In my view, humans are constantly evolving, and a single initial meeting can never fully capture a person’s true character.

First, it is important to remember that people shift their behavior and personality over time, whether for the better or worse. Take a friend I met a while back: when I first encountered him, he seemed constantly angry, never smiled, and was extremely quiet and reserved. But as the days passed, he gradually opened up—he started smiling more, and that initial cold, irritable attitude faded completely. My view of him shifted entirely, proving that early impressions can be totally overturned. Another clear example is a teacher I had: during the first few weeks of class, he was kind, assigned almost no homework, and was patient with every student. But over time, his attitude changed drastically. Now he’s often short-tempered, piles on endless assignments, and even shouts at students in class. The initial positive impression we all had of him is long gone, replaced by a very different view of who he really is.

Beyond that, a first impression is never enough to define a person, just like a book’s cover tells you nothing about the story inside. I have friends who admit that when they first met me, they didn’t like me at all. They thought I was always angry, and that I only ever spoke to my close friends, never to strangers. They never imagined we would become friends, but as they got to know me better, they realized I was nothing like their initial assumption. Their view of my personality changed completely. This also applies to times when we’re having a bad day: if you meet someone when you’re stressed, upset, or dealing with personal problems, they might form a totally negative impression of you. But if they take the time to spend more time with you, they’ll see that your behavior that day was just a one-time thing, not your true self. As they get to know the real you, that first bad impression will fade away.

Clearly, first impressions are never permanent, because a single judgment can never define my personality or who I really am, and I can always change how others perceive me. You need more than two separate impressions to truly understand a person, since altering those early judgments is often quite challenging.
