Modern technology lets people handle a wide range of daily tasks without ever interacting with another human being. We can borrow library books, buy groceries, and even play video games without exchanging a single word with anyone else. Is this reduction in face-to-face interaction caused by technology ultimately good or bad for our lives? In my view, this growing lack of real human connection will eventually damage our society. This risk is even greater as smartphones become more advanced every year. If we do not change course, technology may even come to dominate human life entirely one day. I know a story that illustrates how screen interaction differs from real life. Two classmates who went to the same school only ever talked to each other through social media for months. When they finally decided to meet in person, they felt extremely awkward at first. But after that first meeting, they grew close quickly, becoming good friends. They started going to the movies together, browsing the mall, eating out at restaurants, and doing all sorts of other activities. Over time, their friendship turned into a romantic relationship, and they became boyfriend and girlfriend. This kind of relationship is really meaningful. When you care about someone deeply, it is not just about physical intimacy or following a set of rules. It is about showing up for that person, being there to support them whenever they need you. Finding that special person is a wonderful gift. So many people spend ages trying to work up the courage to talk to someone they like in real life. Sending a message through a screen feels much easier, but does that message ever carry the same sincerity? Telling someone "I love you" is a big deal, and hearing those words in person can make your heart feel warm. But when people only say these things through a screen, it feels less real. Ending a relationship over text is even worse—it shows you do not have the courage to tell the other person how you feel face to face. Anyone who only interacts with others through their phone should try real-life conversation at least once. You will quickly realize there is so much more to life than staring at a screen all day. Sooner or later, I believe people will get so fed up with technology that they will smash their own phones to stop a future where robots take over completely. If we work together as a community, we can push back against constant phone use and other electronic devices to break this unhealthy obsession for good. Opening up to another person feels like watching a flower bloom for the first time. Seeing someone you care about in person is one of life’s greatest joys. Overall, I believe technology’s reduction of human contact is a harmful force in our lives. I am confident that one day, we will come together as a species to solve this problem, just as we should.

A growing number of schools are exploring the option of offering remote learning, allowing students to join classes from theirhomes via online platforms or pre-recorded video lessons. While this setup may work well for certain learners, plenty of others are opposed to the idea. For my part, I do not support moving classes entirely to home settings.

First, studying from home comes with far more potential distractions. For example, snacks and meals are always within reach, and many students find it hard to focus on lessons when food is nearby. Television is another common distraction — if something interesting comes on, it is easy for a student to tune out of their class. The biggest distraction of all, though, is probably smartphones. When taking classes at home, there is no teacher or staff member present to remind students to put their phones away, so it is simple to get sidetracked by texts, social media, or games.

Second, students are less likely to take remote classes seriously. Being in their own homes makes them feel relaxed, even too relaxed — they might log in for some lessons but skip others entirely, since no one is checking whether they attend. Without the structure of classroom rules, they feel free to do whatever they want rather than focusing on their work. In a physical classroom, by contrast, students get far more support: teachers can give more detailed examples, answer questions right away, and pay closer attention to each learner’s needs. Every teacher sets clear classroom rules designed to help students succeed, and that structure is missing from home learning.

Third, students simply do not learn as much through remote classes. They cannot raise their hand to ask a question and get an immediate, clear answer from a teacher. They also receive far less individual attention than they would in a face-to-face classroom, which means gaps in their understanding are more likely to go unaddressed.

That said, many students are in favor of remote learning. They argue it saves a lot of time that would otherwise be spent traveling to and from school. Bad weather is another plus: schools often cancel in-person classes when it rains heavily or snows, but remote learning means lessons can go ahead no matter the weather. This setup also helps students who struggle with transportation. Some have to walk long distances or pay for buses to get to school, so being able to join classes online removes that barrier entirely.

To sum up, while remote learning via online tools or videos may be helpful for some, I believe it is not a good fit for most students. My view is that schools should keep in-person classes as the standard. Studying at home creates too many issues: family members or loud noises can break concentration, and students may get so tired of watching pre-recorded videos with no one to explain tricky concepts that they nod off. Without a teacher present to guide them and enforce expectations, students are less likely to take their work seriously, and they miss out on the full education, information, and individual attention they need. In-person classes with a teacher provide far more support, and that structure is key to helping students succeed in the long run.

Have you ever thought about taking classes from home instead of going to a traditional school? If not, you might be surprised to learn why more and more students are choosing remote learning, either through online courses or regular video conference sessions.

While some people argue that in-person schooling is better, homeschooling via remote tools is actually a far better option for many learners. It lets students focus more on their work, keeps them much safer, and helps them stay away from negative peer pressure.

The biggest advantage of remote learning is that it removes many common classroom distractions. In regular schools, it’s easy for students to lose focus because of disruptive classmates. Some kids are naturally very unruly, and even when teachers tell them to stop misbehaving, they refuse to listen. Sometimes these students even get angry and walk out of class mid-lesson, which disrupts everyone else’s learning too.

Safety is another major reason families choose homeschooling. Sadly, there are many risks in public spaces today, including schools. Tragic incidents like school shootings have killed far too many innocent students—for example, the deadly shooting at a Florida school that happened just a few months ago. When students learn from home, they are completely protected from these kinds of violent threats.

Remote learning also shields students from harmful peer influences. Many schools have very diverse student bodies, which means learners are exposed to all kinds of behaviors. Some peers might skip class to hang out at shopping malls, wander around aimlessly after school, bully classmates, get into physical fights, or even go to the homes of people they barely know instead of going back to their families. Avoiding these influences can help students make better long-term choices.

While traditional schools do offer some benefits, learning from home through online platforms or video calls provides far more advantages for most students. The top benefits include a safer environment to study, fewer distractions to help with focus, and protection from negative peer pressure.

Visionary figures throughout history have made groundbreaking discoveries that shaped the world we live in today—without their work, our society would be unrecognizable. There is a well-known saying that staying true to yourself, even when the world constantly pressures you to fit a certain mold, is the greatest accomplishment a person can achieve. I completely agree with this statement, and examples from successful people’s autobiographies and news articles prove it to be true.

One key reason why being authentic is far better than letting others control your path is to look at people who have already achieved remarkable things. Think of figures like Nikola Tesla, Martin Luther King Jr., Neil Armstrong, and Albert Einstein. Each of these individuals did work that transformed not just their own lives, but the lives of everyone on the planet. If they had followed government-mandated rules about going to school and sticking to pre-set expectations, they never would have reached their life goals. For a community to make real progress, its members need to pursue their own goals, not just do what authorities tell them to.

Beyond that, staying true to who you are boosts self-confidence, which in turn helps you reach major life milestones. Consider a hypothetical example: a man lands an opportunity to work with a much larger, more prestigious company than his current employer. He is invited to a business conference to present his ideas, but his self-confidence is so shaky—because he has not learned to embrace his authentic self—that he fumbles the presentation and ruins the opportunity. Every successful person shares one key trait: strong self-confidence. This quality helps you handle real-world challenges, and living as your genuine self every day is the best way to build it.

On the flip side, many communities struggle because they follow the government’s so-called “help” instead of forging their own paths. Only people with extreme self-discipline manage to succeed under these systems, which is why so many people keep following the rules set by authorities. Take public schools in Virginia, for example: almost all of them teach identical material and use the same standardized tests. The curriculum has barely changed in a decade, and many students have personal goals that are impossible to reach because of these school-imposed limits.

To sum up, when we look at the lives of people who have achieved great things for both themselves and society, the key to success is clear: communities need to change how they approach goal-setting, instead of relying only on schools that do not teach practical life skills for after graduation. Depending on the government is not a path to success. Self-confidence, paired with personal goals, is what creates truly successful people.

There’s one destination I’ve always dreamed of visiting: Puerto Rico. It seems like such a vibrant, lovely place to call home, and I’m eager to get a taste of what everyday life is like there, especially what going to school feels like for local kids. This trip could really shift my perspective—seeing how people live there might make me more appreciative of the things I have that they lack, and inspire me to lend a hand to others more often.

One big reason I want to travel to Puerto Rico is to notice all the little ways their daily life differs from mine. I’m curious about everything from the clothes they wear to the meals they eat, and even what they get up to on a normal day. It would be so fascinating to watch all these details unfold, and I’d love to sample local dishes, try on traditional clothing, and get a sense of what it’s like to be part of Puerto Rican culture.

Another thing drawing me to Puerto Rico is that I don’t always appreciate what I have here in the US. Visiting would let me compare my own lifestyle to theirs directly, which I think would make me far more grateful for my privileges. It would honestly break my heart to see them eating unhealthy meals, while I’m here tossing out perfectly good food just because I don’t feel like eating it.

My last main reason for wanting to visit is to learn about local approaches to discipline. I want to see how Puerto Rican parents respond when their kids misbehave, and how teachers handle students who get into trouble at school. I’m especially curious to compare this to El Salvador, where I know some teachers still hit students with rulers as punishment—something I think is completely unacceptable. So I want to see if schools in Puerto Rico use kinder, fairer methods instead.

To sum up, I’m excited to spot every difference between life in Puerto Rico and life in both the US and El Salvador. I can’t wait to taste all the local dishes, spend time with students there, and grow more grateful for all the resources I have that they might not. I also hope to share some of my own belongings with people who need them more. More than anything, I’m itching to visit Puerto Rico, try new experiences, and have an amazing adventure.

People often debate whether working in groups is better than handling tasks alone. Common questions come up: is group work more useful? Does it help you stay focused? Is it simple and enjoyable? Is it even easier than working by yourself? Everyone has their own answer to these, but I firmly believe that collaborating with others brings far more benefits than working solo. There are a few key reasons for this: you get to share ideas and brainstorm together, the work feels less stressful and more fun, you get the chance to team up with classmates you don’t usually interact with, and you’re far more likely to finish your work by the deadline.

First, group work makes it easier to come up with strong ideas. When you work alone, you only have your own perspective to rely on, but bringing multiple people together means you can pool everyone’s thoughts. You can talk through different opinions about the assignment, debate options, and make sure every group member fully understands the task before you start. This is valuable because it means everyone gets to contribute something unique, rather than one person shouldering all the thinking work.

Another major advantage is that group work helps you stay on schedule. Working by yourself can be really tough sometimes—it often takes much longer to finish a task, you might miss deadlines, and you could get stuck on a problem with no one to ask for help. That’s really frustrating. But when you work in a group of three or four people, everything moves faster. You can split up the work, giving each person a specific role or task that plays to their strengths, so the whole project gets done well before the due date.

Lastly, group work is often more enjoyable and less stressful than working alone. It also gives you the chance to collaborate with classmates you don’t usually speak to. A lot of people avoid talking to peers they don’t know, so they choose to work solo, which is fine. But I find that group work feels lighter and more relaxed. It’s definitely more fun—someone in the group might tell a joke or make a silly comment. Sure, that might cause a tiny distraction here and there, but it brings laughter and happiness to the whole team, which makes the work feel less like a chore.

To sum up, working in groups offers far more benefits than working alone. When you collaborate, you share ideas, get tasks done ahead of deadlines, and have more fun doing it. Groups let you talk through the task to make sure everyone is on the same page before you put in the hard work. Working together matters because it teaches us to support each other, stay determined, and value teamwork—all of which make any group project more successful in the end.

Nowadays, many people pressure others to conform to the latest trends, whether that’s copying a popular haircut, dyeing hair the same shade as everyone else, or striving for a body type that’s currently seen as ideal. Too many people are scared to show their true selves to the world, hiding who they really are to fit in. For all these reasons, I fully agree with Emerson’s famous statement: when you manage to stay true to who you are, you become one of a kind, you can chase your own dreams, and you build genuine confidence.

These days, everyone copies what others do, but think about how freeing it would be to be unique. You wouldn’t have to do the same activities as everyone else—you could play any sport you actually enjoy, or practice a hobby that speaks to you. You could develop your own personal style, even design your own clothes, and let your creativity run wild. You’d never have to worry about following every new fashion trend, because you’d have your own sunshine to follow.

We all have dreams, don’t we? Yours might be to become a doctor, while mine could be to be a singer—that’s the beauty of being different. But when you take the time to figure out who you really are and chase your own goals, you’ll be far happier than anyone trying to live someone else’s life. You’ll find joy in every single day, every little moment, no matter where you are. Even on your worst days, you’ll focus on the good things, because you’ll love both what you have and what you’re doing.

Confidence is something a lot of people struggle with these days, but if you stay true to yourself, you’ll stop caring what others say about you. Other people’s opinions won’t matter, because you’ll be too focused on your own goals. You’ll trust your own choices and believe in yourself, no matter what happens. You might even become a role model for people who haven’t found that same confidence yet, and inspire them to go after their own dreams.

To sum up, being yourself matters more than whatever other people expect of you or want for your life. You only get one life, so live it for yourself. Set your own goals, and don’t try to copy someone else’s style or path. If you pretend to be someone you’re not, you’ll never find true happiness, and you won’t achieve the things you really want for your future. Your own sunshine is already inside you, waiting to shine—all you have to do is be yourself. Love who you are, and stay true to that person.

When you meet someone for the first time, the way you present yourself creates a first impression—and I fully agree that these initial judgments are almost impossible to change. People form their earliest opinions of you during this first meeting, and those views tend to stick. This matters in daily life, whether you’re making new friends or applying for a job: a strong first impression can decide if you get hired. I learned this firsthand during an interview task in my English 10 class. When it was my turn, I greeted the interviewer with a firm handshake and a cheerful "good morning," then answered every question with courtesy. I later received a high grade for the assignment. This experience showed me how much first impressions matter in interviews. Employers often base hiring decisions on those early moments of professionalism. My English 10 interview went smoothly, and it taught me that if I ever apply for a real job, I need to put my best foot forward from the very first moment to have a good chance of being hired.

I fully agree with Ralph Waldo Emerson’s view on this, based on both my own observations and personal experience. If a person never takes action or tries new things, they will never reach their goals or pick up useful skills. That’s why it is so valuable to master practical abilities that serve you throughout life.

It is also important for everyone to develop skills in more than one area. Life can be very challenging, and if you limit yourself to only one set of abilities, navigating tough times becomes even more difficult. As Emerson famously said, "you will never grow" – this simple line means that success is impossible if you only ever stick to what you already know, without picking up new skills in different areas.

Think about someone who only knows how to do the work of their specific profession, and has no other practical skills for daily life. Would it be easy for them to get by? Of course not. Life throws all kinds of challenges at us, and to succeed, we need to try all sorts of new things, not just stick to the one area we have already mastered. For example, imagine an engineer who cannot find a job in their field. They decide to start their own small business, even though they have no background in running a company. At first, this will be very hard, since they know nothing about business operations. But if they keep trying, test out different strategies, and push through early setbacks, they will gradually pick up the skills they need to make the business work.

Having skills in more than one profession not only makes you more well-known and shows off your well-rounded personality, but also makes you a more responsible person overall. Mastering multiple different skill sets is a direct path to both fame and long-term success. Life never stays the same for long – it shifts and changes every single second. All people are different, and we all grow older every day. No one can predict what will happen next, except Allah.

We all need to take on different tasks and build new skills throughout our lives. Beyond that, the skills we learn are also vital for the next generation. Every person should work to gain useful abilities, because we have a responsibility to teach our children right from wrong, and show them how to handle life’s challenges. If you are a skilled, capable person, others will want to learn from you. People are drawn to those who have mastered useful abilities, and this can make you well-known. Fame often opens doors to success, but even without that, trying new things is the only way to reach your goals – without effort, success is nearly impossible.

Knowledge never runs out, much like the sea that never stops flowing. All human beings need to keep learning, and we have a duty to keep doing so. Real knowledge is not limited to textbooks or school lessons. You cannot pick up most practical skills just by reading books. You only become truly skilled when you go beyond textbook lessons and try something new. If you only ever learn from books, it will be far harder to gain all the skills you need. Reading alone is not enough: you must work hard, do your own research, and keep trying new things. Again and again, trial and error proves to be the best way to grow and succeed.

We all know knowledge is valuable, but it is useless without the skills to apply it. Without skills, you have no idea how to put what you know into practice. All skills come from trying new tasks – without stepping outside your comfort zone, success is impossible and your mind will never grow.

I stand by Emerson’s words, as his views are rooted in his own life experience. If we reflect on what he says, we can see the truth in his message. As I have noted, life is full of challenges, and we need a wide range of skills to move forward. Mastering more than one profession will make you both well-known and successful in the long run. Reaching that level of fame and success takes hard work, and requires you to try things you have never done before, not just stick to what you already know.

Work hard, stay active, and do not let fear hold you back. Time waits for no one, and both mental growth and true success come from pushing yourself to try difficult, unfamiliar things throughout your life.

Some people claim that a positive attitude is not the key to success in life, but I completely disagree. The world today is very different from how it used to be, and one major problem we face now is that people rush through everything: they want to finish work as quickly as possible, and get to where they are going without delay. This constant hurry often makes people treat others poorly, which has become a big issue in our society.

First, having a positive attitude can help you land your dream job. When you interact with others in an upbeat, friendly way, people are more likely to like you, remember you as a kind person, and even offer you life-changing opportunities. For example, a manager or colleague might be impressed by your positive energy, and later reach out with a job offer at a top company, or a role that aligns perfectly with your biggest passions.

Another important reason is that positivity lets you brighten someone else’s day. If someone is having a really bad day, taking a moment to talk to them with a cheerful attitude can turn their mood around completely. Even better, this happiness spreads: when you lift someone’s spirits, they are more likely to pass that positivity on to everyone they meet next.

One final reason is that a positive attitude improves communication. When you approach interactions with optimism, it is much easier to connect with others, build strong, healthy relationships, and even form close, lasting friendships.

For all these reasons, I am convinced that a positive attitude is truly the key to success.

Most employers look for candidates who are reliable, hardworking, and usually have prior experience in the field. I believe I deserve this role because I have the first two qualities, even if I haven’t worked in this exact type of job before. I’m fully qualified for this position despite my lack of direct experience.

First, I will put in maximum effort to succeed in this position and take the time to fully grasp all the tasks your team handles. It might take a little while to get up to speed, but the results will be worth the wait. I’m not a lazy employee—I pick up new skills quickly. I’ve held other types of jobs in the past and performed well in them, not because I was desperate for any work, but because I truly wanted to contribute to those teams. Putting in hard work is a life lesson that will pay off for both my future and this company. If I work harder, I can build a better life for myself, and I’ll be ready to handle any task this role throws at me.

A lot of people today take jobs just because they got accepted somewhere, not because they care about the work, only to earn enough to cover rent and basic bills. They don’t stop to think about how staying in low-paying, long-hour roles hurts their future. But I’m different: I’m applying for this role because I want to grow here, not just collect a paycheck.

Even though it may take me a little time to adjust to this role, switching between different types of work is always challenging. You can’t learn the ropes of a brand new job in a single day, but I’m willing to put in the effort to get comfortable here, and I’ll work tirelessly until I’m promoted to manager. A lot of people assume picking up a new job is easy, but that’s not true—especially when you’re moving from a completely different field. Some coworkers can be unkind, trying to make new hires quit, but I won’t stand for that. I plan to do my work without drama or interruptions.

It’s normal to want to move up the career ladder, even when you’re just starting out, and I’m no exception. If rude coworkers try to push me out, I’ll keep showing up and doing good work until they get tired of targeting me, and they’ll see how much I’ve improved and how far I’ve climbed. I’d love to watch the people who doubted me see my growth if I get this job. I won’t slack off—I’ll work hard to become a manager, and later, I’ll put in even more effort to open my own business someday. Almost everyone dreams of owning their own company, and I’m no different. That dream takes hard work to achieve, which is exactly what I’ll do in this role. Eventually, I’ll master all the tasks of this job and perform even better than my more experienced coworkers.

To wrap up, being hired for a role you have no experience in doesn’t mean you can’t succeed. If you’re a strong candidate, you have the potential to become a top employee, or even run your own business one day. You just have to work hard enough to reach your goals, whether that takes one year or three. You have to keep pushing until you get where you want to be. I’m willing to put in that time—whether it takes two or three years, I’ll do my absolute best. I’ll take the risk of starting fresh, and I’ll do the job better than anyone else, in this role or any other I take on. Learning new skills makes you more qualified for all kinds of work, and knowing how to handle different types of jobs makes you a stronger candidate for future roles, or even for running your own company. Work hard, and don’t be afraid to take a chance.

“Snore, snore” – that’s the sound of someone wasting time, and whenever I’m not doing anything, I feel completely lazy. I’m convinced we get far more done when we stay busy all the time. Keeping your mind active stops it from getting lazy, and you end up feeling productive too. For instance, going to school, holding down a job, and lending a hand to others all count as meaningful activity. If you stay busy day after day, you’ll eventually grow to crave doing things rather than sitting idle. I also realize you can be productive without taking on huge tasks – one simple way is just staying out of trouble. As Thomas Jefferson once wrote, “never be idle.” That means you shouldn’t become the kind of person who hates doing anything at all.

First, I’m sure going to school helps you achieve more, since it keeps your brain occupied. For me, sticking to a routine of waking up early, attending class every day, and finishing homework right after school makes me feel way more productive than if I just lazed around. When I get stuck on a topic, I ask my teacher for clarification, and if a classmate needs help, I do my best to explain what we’re learning. Keeping my mind busy feels good, especially since I get to chat and work with my peers along the way.

Second, having a job gives you useful experience that prepares you for the future. When I started my first job, I picked up all sorts of new skills, like using a computer. I never thought I’d figure it out, but I stuck with it, and now those skills help me with my schoolwork too. I’ve learned that getting things done takes genuine interest – if you can’t be bothered to try, or you’d rather do nothing at all, you’ll never achieve anything. The only real way to reach a goal is to take action. At my second job, I didn’t even know how to use a basic cellphone at first, but I put all my effort into learning, so I could help customers place their orders properly. Now, at my third job, I’ve mastered tasks like answering phones, taking orders, and most importantly, providing great customer service.

Third, I believe helping other people is a meaningful way to accomplish something valuable. When you assist people experiencing homelessness, for example, you get the chance to talk to them and learn why they lost their housing or don’t have family to lean on. A lot of people run away from home because they don’t like their parents’ rules, but that’s rarely the best choice – everyone needs some kind of support. For any goal, big or small, the best approach is to listen to and follow the advice of older people, who almost always know best thanks to their greater life experience. I speak from personal experience here: I was once homeless myself after my parents left me to care for my two younger brothers. We had no food, and every time my little brothers asked for something to eat, I’d tear up because they were too young to understand our situation. Now, whenever I see people asking for food on the street, I’m reminded of what I went through back then.

I picked this topic because I truly believe we get more done when we stay active instead of sitting idle. Going to school, working a job, and helping others are all ways to keep busy and achieve meaningful things. You can also reach goals by taking less traditional paths, but I’ve focused on improving my own life and supporting the people around me. I also know that even small, low-key actions count as productivity – like staying out of trouble, which is itself a form of being responsible rather than idle. All of these efforts make me feel like I’ve accomplished a lot already.

Is imagination more important than knowledge? I believe it is, mostly because imagination lets us dream up countless possibilities. It matters more than knowledge since it lets us picture what we want to do when we grow up, how we want to live our lives, or fun times with friends. We can come up with all these ideas just by thinking, or even acting on them when we choose.

I still remember when my mom asked what I wanted to be when I grew up. I told her I wanted to be a soccer player, and described imagining myself playing with some of the world’s best players. She said I’d need to practice very hard just to make a team, but I told her she’d see me on TV soon. Knowledge is not more important than imagination. You have to learn to build knowledge, to make sure you understand what you’re talking about. But imagination is picturing things in your life that you know will happen one day. That brings a joy as great as anything else in the world, and makes you happy throughout your life, even during difficult periods.

One time, I was playing soccer with my friends in the rain, and I imagined myself making the school team. I was very happy when I actually made the team later that season. The next day at school, they read out the names of everyone who’d made the team. When I heard my name, I was thrilled—all because I’d already pictured myself succeeding. Everything worked out perfectly after that. I became the best soccer player in middle school, and now I can’t wait to be famous, with everyone knowing my name.

In conclusion, imagination is more important than knowledge. It lets you picture what you’ll do long before it actually happens.

Modern tools let us handle plenty of daily tasks without ever interacting with another human being. We can borrow library books via self-service kiosks, order groceries online, and play video games without saying a single word to anyone. Yet technology brings both benefits and drawbacks to our lives. While some argue it is useful because anyone can turn to it in an emergency, many others worry it shifts how people behave, making them value online connections more than the friends and family right in front of them.

Supporters of technology often point to its lifesaving role in emergencies. Think of a family living in a remote area with no neighbors nearby who suddenly needs urgent help. In that scenario, a phone or internet connection is absolutely essential. Without it, even a minor issue could turn into a tragedy. I saw this firsthand when I lived in my home country: many households were settled far from urban centers, and some did not own any communication devices. These families often struggled terribly. If someone fell ill, there was no way to call for assistance, and in some tragic cases, people died simply because they lacked access to the technology that could have summoned help.

On the other hand, many criticize technology for damaging people’s attitudes and behavior. They argue that back in 1978, people were far more polite to one another, even if they had less formal education, and would go out of their way to be kind to strangers. While some blame media like movies, music, or cartoons for shifting social norms, it is clear that constant tech use takes a toll: regular users may develop mental health struggles, or strain their eyes from staring at screens for hours. I know one family with a 15-year-old daughter who watches countless TV shows. She acts much older than her peers, refuses to listen to her parents, and has very poor behavior overall. Her parents are largely to blame: they keep buying her new gadgets, but never check how she is using them. Letting children use technology from a young age is risky, as they often misuse it and pick up bad habits that become impossible for parents to correct as they grow up. Instead of handing kids devices, parents should spend quality time with them outdoors or doing other activities.

Another common complaint is that technology makes people prioritize online contacts over the real people in their lives. It is undeniable that most people spend almost all their time staring at a screen. Psychologist Generic_Name argues that in-person conversations are far better, as they allow people to communicate more clearly, and he is right: it is easy to lie when hiding behind a screen. Today, manufacturers keep releasing new devices with flashy features designed to keep users hooked for hours, deepening people’s obsession with technology even further. Surveys suggest around 90% of people pay more attention to their phones or laptops than to their family members or the people sitting right next to them. I read a book called *Behind the Wed* five months ago that illustrated this perfectly. The story followed a female teacher who chatted with a stranger online. The person she was messaging claimed to be a man, but was actually a girl pretending to be male. When the teacher asked for a video call, the stranger refused, as they were lying about their identity. This kind of deception happens to real people every day, far more often than we realize.

To sum up, technology is neither wholly good nor wholly bad. Its impact depends entirely on how each person chooses to use it. Tech advances are not slowing down anytime soon, so we all need to learn to use these tools at the right times, and in the right ways. When used properly, technology can transform lives for the better, opening up opportunities that were once out of reach.

Many people ask whether students gain any advantages from taking classes remotely from their homes.

I am fully convinced that learning from home offers no real benefits to students at all. I have three main reasons to support this view. First, students who take online classes often finish the semester having learned almost nothing. Second, it is far too easy for them to get distracted at home, so they never focus on the material they are supposed to study. Finally, face-to-face teaching in a physical classroom is much more effective.

To start with, we already know that students sometimes struggle to learn much even in a regular classroom—so it is hard to imagine them absorbing anything useful when sitting in front of a computer at home. When learning remotely, most students rush through assignments just to get them done quickly, so they can move on to other activities. They rarely put real effort into online lessons, and when it comes time to take a test or show what they know, they are completely unprepared. For instance, I personally find that staring at a computer screen when trying to learn new material makes it hard for me to focus, as if the screen light stops my brain from processing information.

Next, distractions are everywhere when students learn from home. They have easy access to phones, the same computer they use for class, televisions, and other devices that pull their attention away. On top of that, family members often interrupt them—for example, if a parent sees a student at home during school hours, they might ask them to watch younger siblings. This means the student has to supervise children instead of paying attention to the lesson. While friends can be distracting in a physical classroom, distractions at home are far worse: many young students have friends over to play video games while they are supposed to be in class.

Finally, learning in a physical classroom where you can see your teacher in person is far more effective. For example, I prefer to discuss lesson topics with both my teacher and classmates—this helps me understand the material better, and I often get new perspectives I would not have thought of on my own. Watching a teacher explain concepts face-to-face makes it much easier to absorb the information needed to pass classes. In contrast, students who learn from a computer screen usually forget what they studied almost immediately.

To sum up, the best way to learn is by attending physical classes and interacting with teachers and peers, as this ensures you get all the information needed to pass your courses. Taking classes from home almost always leads to failing the semester, since students cannot get the scores required to pass. Electronic distractions are far more accessible at home, and they grab students' attention very easily.

Many schools now offer distance learning as an alternative, letting students join lessons remotely via online tools or video calls. This setup is especially helpful for students who struggle with social interactions, finding it hard to connect with classmates or teachers in a traditional school setting. It also supports those who have had unpleasant experiences in school environments. Learners who study in a space where they feel comfortable are often more focused, with fewer distractions pulling their attention away.

Critics of remote learning argue that students should not take classes from home. They claim that home environments are full of distractions, making it hard for learners to complete their schoolwork. Others point out that some students struggle to learn independently without a teacher present, and that remote learning robs students of the chance to experience typical school life.

Every student grows up with different experiences, and some have had difficult childhoods that shape how they act in daily life. For these learners, being allowed to study in a place where they feel at ease gives them the opportunity to show what they are truly capable of. Traditional schools often force them to interact with others when they are not ready, which only serves as a distraction from their learning.

Remote learning also helps students who have had negative experiences at school. For example, those who have been bullied often lose the motivation to attend school or work toward success. Even today, bullying remains a major issue that holds many schools back from reaching high academic standards, as it has such a deep impact on students. For some, going to school feels like a nightmare, but online classes let them escape that environment and focus fully on their studies.

On top of this, studying in a familiar, comfortable environment helps students stay focused with fewer interruptions. Being in a space that suits their learning needs lets them reach their full potential. A proper learning environment makes a big difference for focused students, especially those who are determined to succeed and hold themselves to high standards. Family members can also provide support and motivation when students learn at home, encouraging them to keep going even when the work gets tough.

For all these reasons, I strongly believe schools should offer online classes or video conferencing as an option for students. Giving learners this choice will help many who struggle to socialize with peers or teachers, those who have had bad experiences at school, and students who focus better in their comfort zone. Providing this opportunity will ultimately help more students succeed.

I fully agree with Ralph Waldo Emerson’s view that while it is natural to feel content in your current situation, true growth only comes from pushing past what feels familiar. Staying in your comfort zone might feel safe, but without trying new things, you can never discover what you are truly capable of, nor will you develop as a person. There is nothing wrong with feeling satisfied with your life for a while, but when unexpected challenges arise, you need to step out and explore to uncover your real strengths. Emerson’s point also rings true in my own community: many people where I live are perfectly happy with where they are in life, even if it means missing out on new opportunities.

I have always believed that the more you explore, the more you grow. Take Bill Gates as an example: if he had been content with the skills he had already mastered and never looked for new opportunities, he would never have built Microsoft or become a billionaire. The same goes for Barack Obama: if he had been satisfied with the education and knowledge he already had, he would never have served as a senator, let alone become America’s first Black president, and he would never have had the chance to share his ideas with the country. The truth is, if you never push past what you already know, you will never understand your own potential. Stepping outside your existing expertise always brings surprises: you might discover a hidden talent, or find a new path for personal growth. You cannot uncover your true worth if you never even try. Some people hold the mindset that exploring new paths will only lead to failure, but that is not true. The more you push your boundaries, the further you will go in life. My mother always tells me to never settle for where I am: she says I should step out of my comfort zone and try new things, instead of staying at a level I have already mastered.

Exploring helps you figure out who you really are. Think about a situation where your boss quits and the company is looking for a replacement. Maybe you have the right knowledge and ideas for the role, but you stay in your current position because you are too scared to take a risk. You might even assume they will reject your application before you even try. This mindset stops many college graduates: some are happy with their master’s degrees and too afraid to pursue a doctorate, thinking a master’s is the final step in their learning, or worrying they are not smart enough for a higher degree. Sometimes the environment around you can make it easy to stay content with your current situation, rather than pushing for more.

Of course, there is nothing wrong with being happy where you are. But the more you explore, the more you will grow as a person. You should never settle for who you are right now: always fight for a better future and a better life. As Neil Armstrong once said, his moon landing was “a giant leap for mankind” — many of us need to take that same giant leap in our own lives. The more you explore, the more you learn about life and the possibilities it holds for you.

Many people claim that first impressions are nearly impossible to reverse. I strongly disagree with this idea, as I have often been told that I come across badly when people meet me for the first time. Strangers frequently say I look unfriendly or like I have a bad attitude, but that is not true at all. I only act cold if others are rude to me, but I am perfectly pleasant when people are friendly or start a conversation with me.

Recent studies point out that it is much simpler to lose a good reputation than to build one from scratch, which makes sense. But the truth is, you can never truly understand someone until you actually talk to them. It is unfair to form opinions about a person based on their appearance, the way they talk, or how they dress.

I saw this happen myself a few years ago, on my first day of middle school in the United States. Classmates judged me immediately because they assumed I was fluent in English. Whenever they tried to talk to me, I would just look down at my feet and stay silent. Months later, after I picked up English and learned how to hold proper conversations, one of those classmates came up to me and admitted, "I didn't realize you could speak English. I remember in 6th grade, you never said a word." Once I started talking to him regularly, he completely changed his opinion of me. This proves that first impressions can definitely be shifted.

It is obvious that first impressions are rarely the most accurate ones, but we all have the power to decide whether to adjust how others see us. I have been through plenty of first meetings where people misjudged me, but I always remind myself that my reputation is not defined by what other people think of me. Instead, it depends entirely on how I view myself. Each of us has the ability to change the first impression we make.

Have you ever wondered whether learning from home actually helps students succeed? Most students aim to get a good education and build a successful future, but plenty of obstacles make traditional public or private schools a poor fit for them. When they switch to online learning, many report huge improvements: before, they were failing classes or struggling to manage personal challenges while attending in-person school. Countless students who’ve made the switch have not only turned their academic performance around, but also found that remote learning works perfectly for whatever circumstances they’re dealing with right now.

Critics may disagree with this view, but I’ve seen proof of online school’s benefits firsthand through my own family, heard real stories on radio podcasts, and listened to celebrities share their own experiences.

Take my cousin, let’s call her Generic_Name, for example. She went through an incredibly tough time that made attending public school impossible. She struggled to keep her grades up and even get to school on time, all while battling an eating disorder — a condition that makes balancing school and personal health extremely hard. Her family decided to enroll her in online school, and it changed everything. She could complete assignments from home while eating regular meals and attending doctor’s appointments, and sometimes teachers even came to her house to work through homework with her, which helped her a ton. Over time, she overcame her struggle with her eating disorder and got more and more focused on her studies. It’s honestly amazing: despite all the challenges she faced, she ended up becoming a lawyer.

Some people argue that it’s unfair she reached that goal through online school, claiming remote learning can’t lead to success and only sets students up to fail. But that’s not true. When you hear so many personal stories from people who thrived with homeschooling, you have to acknowledge that what works for one person might not work for another — it’s not a one-size-fits-all solution.

I’ve also heard plenty of real-life stories about this on radio podcasts. One that stuck with me was from a mother talking about her son, Generic_Name, who had gotten very popular on social media. Throughout high school, he was bullied by peers and even older students, who would pick fights with him for no reason. His mom enrolled him in online school, where he attended video conferences with his teachers every other day. He found remote learning way easier: he could focus fully, with just him and his laptop, no distractions or classmates bothering him or trying to start fights. Since social media takes up a lot of his time, online school let him balance both his online presence and his education. Critics might say he should have toughened up and learned to deal with mean people, instead of hiding. That’s partly true — you can’t avoid conflict forever. But if he was at his breaking point, switching to online school was the best choice. No one can handle unlimited hate forever.

Celebrities have also opened up in interviews about choosing homeschooling over traditional school, and how much it helped them. There’s one young woman, Generic_Name, who said being a big social media figure is exhausting: you deal with constant hate, people digging up old content to cancel you for no reason, and your name being dragged into gossip nonstop. She was bullied repeatedly, and it got so bad she developed depression, making it almost impossible to keep attending public school. Her teachers suggested she try online learning, and she took their advice, doing homeschooling for the rest of high school and even through college. She says she feels more successful now than ever. Generic_Name added that switching to online school was the best decision she ever made, and while she plans to attend a traditional public college soon, she’ll keep up her social media work too. Some critics say they don’t see how this benefited her, since she already knew what she wanted to do with her life. But the change was huge: she’s no longer scared of what people say about her online. Sometimes, students just need a break from the pressure of public school, and they can always go back when they feel ready.

The key takeaway here is that students facing similar struggles should look at these past experiences to decide if online school is right for them. In the future, people can look back at stories like these to understand what students went through years ago, and compare it to the challenges kids face today. The clear solution for anyone who finds traditional school too hard, for any reason at all, is to try online learning. It’s also important to remember what’s been said over and over: for people with big social media followings, coping with constant hate is incredibly difficult. The best solution there is simple: stop spreading hate to others in the first place.

People these days seem more divided than ever, with endless conflicting advice on how to behave and what choices to make in life. It is true that human nature can be tricky, and no one ever promised that life would be smooth sailing all the time. I believe everyone should start taking charge of their own choices, as this helps them learn vital lessons about life, gain a clearer picture of how the world works, build self-worth, and grow into a capable, independent person.

Of course, plenty of people will try to tell you exactly how you should live your life. But you can only truly understand these things by going through them yourself. There will come days when you stumble, or face unexpected hardships that make you realize just how tough life can get. Making mistakes is also part of the process — no one is perfect, and life has a way of throwing surprises your way when you least expect them. You need to be prepared to face whatever comes, no matter how easy or difficult it might be. When you make your own choices, you are the one best placed to pick what works for you.

It is normal to find life confusing at times, but this is just a regular part of daily existence. Learning how life really operates can help you avoid stressing over small, unimportant issues. Life will throw challenges your way that only you, as the person responsible for your own path, have to deal with. The result you get will always depend on how you handle these situations. As we grow older, life can either make us tougher or more fragile — it all comes down to our choices. The best approach is to accept that anything can happen without warning, whether it is at a convenient time or the worst possible moment. Tough experiences that hurt you will ultimately make you stronger, and that is a clear sign that you are truly living.

Many people overlook this, but if you do not love yourself first, no one else will do it for you. You should never rely on others to make you happy — your happiness is your own responsibility. On top of that, no matter what you do, you can never please everyone, so you might as well focus on your own path. Learning to handle things on your own makes you more efficient, which in turn brings more good things your way. Be unapologetically yourself, and cherish everything around you. Just keep in mind that nothing comes easy, and life can still surprise you when you least expect it.

To sum up, everyone should start making their own decisions to gain a real understanding of what life is truly like. If you learn and grow through daily experiences, nothing that happens will catch you off guard. Loving yourself is also the first step to being able to love others well. I hope more people realize that life is about your own journey, not someone else’s. Every person has their own unique thoughts and way of looking at the world.

Character describes the way a person acts and behaves day to day. I firmly believe that we have full control over shaping our own character and picking which traits we want to show, and no one else can decide what our personality looks like. That said, some people argue that the people we spend time with—like our parents—shape our character, and that our personality is just a copy of those around us.

It is up to you to decide what kind of person you want to be, and no one else can make that choice for you—including your character. Choosing your own traits is incredibly important. If you don't take charge of this, you will likely feel unsure of yourself, and struggle to work out who you really are or what path you should take in life.

Developing your own distinct character is a huge achievement. Many people end up copying the personalities of their parents, or even famous people they admire, but having your own unique character means you stand out as one of a kind. A recent study from the University of Virginia found that people who deliberately choose how they act and behave, rather than imitating others, report higher levels of happiness than those who just copy other people’s personalities.

You belong to no one but yourself. From the moment you are born as a baby, you start building your own character and personality, and you have full say over what kind of person you want to become. Some people claim that parents are the ones who shape a child’s character and pick their personality traits, but this is not true. Your character is shaped by your own life experiences, as John Lubbock once wrote: "Your character will be what your self yoose to make it."

To sum up, you can grow into whoever you want to be. Your character is built by you, based on the experiences you go through in life, and no one else can decide what your personality will look like. People will always judge you, but you should always follow what your heart tells you. Be proud of your own personality and character, and never let anyone—even your parents—tell you how to act. Build your own character, and always choose to behave in a way that feels right to you.

The author argues that “to be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you someone else is the greatest accomplishment”—and this is undeniably difficult, given that our society prioritizes surface-level appearance over who a person truly is. Many people choose to pretend to be someone they are not, just to fit in. For instance, when others comment on someone’s looks or personality, it is common for them to feel discouraged. This makes staying true to yourself a major achievement, as people will criticize every small detail about you: how you walk, how you style your clothes, even how you go about daily tasks.

We live in a world where public opinion often holds more weight than our own self-perception. Constant judgment from others, who tend to care only about how things look on the surface, pushes people to conform. A key reason why staying authentic is such a meaningful achievement is that it requires showing the world exactly who you are, and pursuing your own interests, no matter what anyone else says.

I fully agree with the author’s point here. It really is an incredible achievement to resist the pressure to act how others want you to, just to keep them happy, or to fake a version of yourself that is not real. Valuing your own individuality and making choices for yourself is far better than letting negative comments or unfair opinions influence you—especially since many people who criticize others are often unhappy with their own personalities. That said, it is not easy to stay strong when society places so much value on outward appearance.

To sum up, staying true to yourself is never simple, especially when people refuse to let go of stereotypes about how others should act. Do not let other people make decisions for you, or let their negative thoughts influence your choices—people who try to drag you down in this way are not worth keeping in your life. While it takes effort to hold onto your true self, nothing is impossible. Believing in your own individuality and making the right choices will eventually silence the people who try to force you to change.

When teenagers are out on public streets after midnight, they are breaking a city law. I strongly agree that this kind of curfew is a positive step for communities.

First, it encourages young people to return home earlier. This means parents do not have to stay up late wondering where their children are, which reduces stress for families. It also helps teens avoid getting into trouble with both their parents and local authorities.

Most teenagers today love spending time with friends late at night, which is why many cities have introduced these curfews. While some might see the rule as restrictive, it actually keeps young people safer by getting them off the streets during late hours when risks are higher.

These laws also make entire neighborhoods safer. With fewer teens out late, there are fewer opportunities for crimes like robbery or violent disputes that often happen late at night. The curfew also cuts down on harmful habits among young people: fewer teens are out smoking, vaping, or drinking alcohol, all of which can cause serious long-term damage to their health and futures.

Another key benefit is that teens avoid serious legal trouble. If they are out past midnight, they might get arrested or even sent to jail. For immigrant teenagers, the consequences are even worse: they could be deported back to their home country. Any run-in with the law can also make it much harder for them to find jobs or build a stable life later on.

I disagree with the school board’s proposal to extend the school day by an hour and a half. This change would force students to take on more academic work, like math assignments and homework, and lead to more conflicts between students during the day. On top of that, many learners have other commitments outside of school, such as visiting family, that would clash with a longer schedule. Adding this extra time would hurt the school overall, as students would struggle to pay attention in class.

First, a longer school day would mean a heavier workload for students. They would have more in-class assignments, extra projects, and additional homework, all of which would make it harder to stay focused during lessons. Many would also find it difficult to finish studying or complete homework after the extended day. For example, most students already feel tired after regular classes; adding more time would leave them wanting to rest instead of tackling more school tasks, so they would quickly grow to dislike the extra time.

Second, the extra time would leadto more drama among students every day. With more hours spent in school, students would have more opportunities to start conflicts with each other, which would distract them from their lessons. Over time, this lack of focus would cause their grades to drop. Even though a longer school day comes with many other problems, students would likely face more drama than they ever have before.

Finally, many students would hate the longer schedule because it would clash with their existing plans. They might miss football or soccer games, family cookouts in the park, or visits with relatives. The extra time would also cut into hobbies they enjoy, like hanging out with friends or playing outside. This change would only bring more work, more drama, and more stress, and most students have other commitments outside of school they do not want to give up.

In conclusion, the school board’s plan to add an hour and a half to each school day would make students less eager to attend. The extra time would mean more classwork, more time spent studying for subjects, and more drama that distracts from learning. Students would also have to wake up each morning dreading the longer day ahead, and they would miss out on activities outside of school. Overall, this change would only cause more problems than it solves.

Have you ever wondered why some people rarely leave their homes to socialize with others? Since modern technology became widespread, daily life has become far simpler for millions of people. It has provided easy access to most of the everyday items and resources we need to live more comfortably and efficiently.

I strongly believe that technology has a largely positive impact on people’s lives, especially for young people. For example, school-aged teenagers now have far more chances to learn and pick up the skills they will need later in life. Most schools provide access to computers, letting students find extra information to support their classwork, and many even offer the option to take classes or sit exams entirely online, without needing to be physically present on campus.

Beyond education, technology also makes it possible to stay in touch with others without meeting in person. There is no need to be face-to-face to have a conversation or share updates. It also offers convenient solutions for busy people: you can order clothes, groceries, and other essentials online, skipping the trip to physical stores entirely. On top of that, tech gives us the tools to create inventions that would be impossible for humans to build on their own.

Of course, technology also has its downsides. Think about how children play today compared to before digital devices existed: it is now common to see 5 to 10-year-olds with their own smartphones or gaming consoles, and many are hooked on these devices. This addiction is not limited to kids, either—many young adults struggle with overuse too. Staring at screens for too long can damage eyesight, but this is not the fault of the technology itself. We are each responsible for managing our own usage to protect our health.

To sum up, while technology does cut down on in-person social interaction for many people, it also delivers a huge range of benefits for both our current generation and those to come.

Getting rid of students’ favorite lunches to replace them with only healthy food is a really bad idea. Students will hate the new options, end up hungry, and struggle to focus during class.

First off, many students will dislike the healthy foods they aren’t used to eating. Take Generic_Name as an example: he goes to the lunch hall and finds the only food available is a salad. He has never eaten salad before, and sees a pile of vegetables like lettuce, tomatoes, and onions on his tray. He is disgusted by the meal he is served, and would rather starve than take a single bite. What this means is that when schools serve vegetables students won’t eat, they just won’t touch their food at all. They’ll end up hungry, which is very bad for their bodies.

What’s more, students who skip lunch because they hate the healthy options will be in bad shape during lessons. They may feel hungry, sick, or even pass out. For example, Generic_Name gets back to class after lunch without eating a single bite, since he couldn’t stand the food served. While he tries to work on his assignments, he starts to feel unwell, and his stomach growls loudly because it’s empty. He loses all focus, starts begging for food, and can’t stop thinking about how hungry he is. This means hungry students will struggle to follow what their teachers are saying, because their stomachs distract them. The principal should keep the current lunch system instead of making these changes. That way, students’ bodies will stay in good condition, and they’ll have enough energy to get through the entire day.

Some people might disagree with my view that switching school lunches to only healthy food is a bad idea. They argue it’s actually a good move, because eating healthy meals will help students grow stronger, keep a balanced diet, and have more energy in their everyday lives.

While that might be true in theory, it’s not how things work in practice. Students are comfortable with the foods they already eat, and what suits them now will work for their future lifestyle too. With all this in mind, swapping students’ favorite lunch foods for only healthy options is a very bad idea.

Picture a world that’s dull, gray, and lifeless, filled with people struggling with depression. This bleak future could become reality if people keep believing that small, kind gestures make no difference to others.

Even tiny acts of kindness have the power to transform the entire world, starting with how people see you. You can build a positive personal reputation in many ways, but one of the simplest and most effective is being kind to those around you. This helps you form new relationships or keep existing ones strong. Another big benefit is that kindness is often reciprocated: when you treat others well, they’re likely to be nice to you in return, and this creates a positive ripple effect for everyone involved. I’ve seen this firsthand—sometimes I just give someone a quick, sincere compliment, and it brightens their whole day. Other times, when I’m feeling low and it shows, people go out of their way to be kind to me too. Being consistently kind also makes you stand out in any setting. People will start to recognize you as the nicest person in the room, so others will either seek you out for kind words or try to match your kindness themselves.

Beyond personal gains, small acts of kindness can also improve entire communities, or even the whole world. Our current world has many flaws, but we can start to fix them just by treating others with kindness. For example, if you’re nice to someone, they’ll feel happier, and that happiness will make them want to spread kindness to others too—it creates a never-ending loop. The more people who choose to be kind, the more people they’ll influence, and soon kindness becomes the norm. This also helps others build the reputation they want, like being more well-liked or noticeable. I saw this happen at my own school: when I made a conscious choice to be kind to everyone around me, I became more noticeable to my classmates. Soon, other students started acting nicer too, hoping to get the same positive attention I had. It was a win-win for everyone.

Most importantly, kind acts can make a huge difference to how people feel about themselves. As the ancient storyteller Aesop once said, "No act of kindness, no matter how small, is ever wasted." Even something as simple as a compliment can turn someone’s whole day around, and that positive energy spreads to everyone they interact with afterwards—it’s heartwarming to see. Kindness can even change someone’s life completely, as it did mine. When I was around 11, I was going through a tough time at both home and school. The people who are now my closest friends stepped in with small, kind gestures that turned my whole year around, and maybe even my whole life, because I knew they would stick by me no matter what. If you show kindness to someone who really needs support—like a person struggling with issues at home or school—you could help shift their life toward a much happier path.

All of these examples show that even the tiniest act of kindness has the power to completely change someone’s life for the better.

A growing number of schools now let students join their regular classes remotely, either through online platforms or live video calls. School administrators often argue that this setup is useful, especially for students who struggle to attend in person—whether they dislike going to school, or have medical conditions that make it impossible to be on campus. While remote learning and in-person classes share a few advantages, they are not equally beneficial overall.

In my view, remote learning has both pros and cons. It is definitely helpful for students with health issues, but it is not a good option for everyone—especially because students often do not learn as well at home as they do in a physical classroom.

First, remote learning can be a huge help for students facing specific challenges. For instance, young people with mobility issues or chronic illnesses, such as arthritis, may find it painful or impossible to travel to campus every day. For these students, joining classes via video call or online portal is far better: they can access all their lessons, work toward their diploma, and build a better future without struggling to get to school. This option also works for students whose parents do not allow them to attend in person, for whatever reason, or those who have experienced bullying or fights with classmates. These students can still get the support they need and learn their coursework from home, without the stress of being in a school environment that does not feel safe for them.

However, remote learning is not a good fit for students who simply do not want to attend school. Without a teacher present to guide them and keep them on task, these students are likely to get distracted and do whatever they please instead of focusing on their work. They also miss out on clear explanations of difficult topics, which makes it hard to learn properly. This is especially true for students who are still learning English. I am a non-native English speaker, not born in the US, and I know I would struggle to improve my language skills if I studied from home. At home, I would only hear English once a day at most, and progress would be very slow. In a school setting, though, I am surrounded by people speaking English all day: my teachers explain lessons clearly, and my friends help me practice. Even though learning a new language is hard, going to school has helped me improve my English faster than I ever could at home.

To sum up, remote learning is not a perfect solution for all students. It offers real advantages for a small group of learners, but many others find it difficult and do not learn as much as they would in a classroom. At the end of the day, whether you study at home or in school, you are still learning—this is not some extraordinary, unusual arrangement, but it only works if you are truly motivated to grow and build a successful future. For me, going to school has made a huge difference in my life. I learn something new every day, and my English is getting better all the time thanks to the teachers and classmates who support me. I feel more confident now, too: no one makes fun of me for being a language learner, because everyone around me wants to help me succeed.

Have you ever thought about how fulfilling it is to shape your life around the character traits you value most? Picking the personality that fits you best is a decision you’ll never look back on with regret.

Most people decide to define their own character because they know this choice will pay off in the long run. Making this decision can feel incredibly tough at first, since there’s no guarantee it will work out. But true, lasting success never comes easily — you have to stay true to the personality you’ve chosen for yourself.

When you pick a character that aligns with who you truly are, you gain the confidence to pursue your goals. That self-assurance makes it far simpler to handle whatever challenges life throws your way. You never choose a personality without first understanding yourself, which is exactly why tailoring your character to suit your own needs works so well. For example, life often brings hardships, but if you face them with the calm, steady character you’ve picked for yourself, it takes a lot of stress out of difficult situations and makes them much easier to navigate.

As long as you’re clear on what your character is, you’ll always make choices that fit your values and desires. Take marriage, for instance: you don’t just hope you’ll get along with a partner. Instead, you shape your character to complement theirs, because you know you can adjust your personality in ways that make your shared life happier. Even if you fall for someone whose character is stronger than yours, you can choose to adopt some of their positive traits — which is exactly why having the power to choose your own character matters so much.

Many people start figuring out their character when they begin school. They’re exposed to all kinds of personality types there, and start to recognize which traits feel natural to them. They also learn from their teachers, who almost always want to pass on good, positive behavior — which is why so many students settle on their chosen character during their school years.

Picking the character you want also helps you attract the right people into your life. You’ll feel far happier surrounded by others who share your personality, without having to pretend to be someone you’re not. Faking a character you didn’t choose is basically living a lie. Life feels simpler and more joyful when you stick to your own rules. No matter what happens, commit to being the person you’ve chosen to be!

I fully support Churchill’s view on the importance of failure, as it acts as a stepping stone toward success. There are several reasons I back this opinion. First, if we never experience failure, we will not truly appreciate success when we finally reach it. Failure also highlights exactly what went wrong in past attempts, guiding us on how to improve for future challenges. Beyond that, it reminds us of our original motivation for taking on a task in the first place.

Failure is far more common than many realize—most of us stumble constantly in daily life. There is no shame in these missteps, either: the more times we fail, the more we learn and grow. As my father always says, “No matter how many times you fail, it does not mean the world is ending.”

It is true that failure can make our lives feel difficult or unfulfilled at times. However, it also forces us to ask important questions: why are we working toward this goal? How badly do we want it? What level of effort will it take to finally succeed? People often say failure makes our brains grow, but that does not mean they get physically larger. Instead, it means we collect far more details and useful information each time we mess up.

For all these reasons, I stand by Churchill’s statement: failure plays a vital role in the journey toward success.
