I’d like to share why working in groups is so helpful. Personally, I think collaborating with classmates simplifies tasks and makes the process more enjoyable. Group work lets students swap ideas and pick up new knowledge from one another, plus it pushes us to consider perspectives we might not have thought of on our own.

First off, group work takes the pressure off individual students because tasks can be split up. For example, one person can handle research, another can draft the written content, and a third can find charts or extra materials needed for the assignment. It’s also more fun to work this way: you get to chat with peers, and even when someone makes a mistake, the group can laugh it off together instead of feeling stressed.

Beyond that, students don’t just learn the assignment topic when working in groups—they also learn from their peers. Collaborative work gives everyone a chance to share thoughts and hear different viewpoints. If one student is stuck on a question, chances are another group member knows the answer, so everyone gets the support they need.

What’s more, some students find group work far more comfortable than solo tasks. They can rely on each other for help and feel supported even when they hold different opinions or ideas. When the whole team works together, they tend to produce better results, and they gain more knowledge through discussions where everyone shares their unique perspectives.

To sum up, group work offers far more advantages than working alone. Students gain more knowledge, achieve better results, and learn to value and listen to opinions that differ from their own. They also pick up new skills from their peers and get to explore topics from multiple angles through open discussion.

This essay discusses a growing trend among some companies: adopting a four-day work week by adding two extra hours to each standard workday. I will share whether I think this model should be introduced at my high school, outline the key pros and cons of such a change, and suggest steps schools should take before rolling it out.

Picture getting a notice from your school saying they plan to switch to a four-day week, adding two hours to each remaining school day. I strongly disagree with this plan, as it would harm my high school rather than improve it. The first area to be hit would be after-school programs and activities. Adding two extra hours means each school day would stretch to ten hours total. Students would be far more exhausted by the time classes end, so far fewer would want to join after-school clubs or sports. Eventually, the school might have to scrap these programs entirely. This would affect high schoolers especially hard, since many juniors and seniors hold part-time jobs after class. With longer school days, most would have no choice but to quit their jobs.

Of course, this schedule change has both upsides and downsides. On the plus side, longer class periods would give students more time to work on assignments during school hours, cutting down on homework. It would also save the school money and resources: running buildings for four days instead of five uses less electricity, water, and heating. But the downsides are significant. As mentioned, after-school programs would likely close due to low participation. Another big issue is that students who work would struggle to adjust their job hours, which is rarely easy for part-time teen workers. Many would end up leaving their jobs altogether.

Schools should never roll out this change without taking key preparatory steps first. First, school staff should hold a meeting to discuss whether the four-day schedule is feasible. Next, they should host a separate meeting for parents, where administrators clearly explain every detail of the proposed plan. After that, the school should send a detailed letter home, requiring parents to sign and return it to indicate whether they support or oppose the change. Only after gathering all this feedback should the school make a final decision on whether to adopt the new schedule.

To sum up, I do not think my school should adopt the four-day week with longer days. It would cause far more harm than good. The downsides are numerous: after-school activities could be cancelled, many students would lose their part-time jobs, and everyone would get home more exhausted each day. Our current schedule works perfectly well. Right now, students can join sports teams, take part in after-school clubs, and hold part-time jobs without conflict. We are happy with how things are, and adding two extra hours to each day would only create problems, not benefits.

I see the logic behind the plan to extend the school day by an hour and a half, which is meant to give students more time for learning. But I side with the many students who think this change is a bad idea. After all, children already spend plenty of time in class, and adding even more hours is the last thing they want. Most students have commitments outside of class, whether that’s scheduled after-school programs, sports teams, volunteer work in the community, or even regular household chores. These activities matter a lot to them, even if they might seem unimportant to some. While school learning is valuable, cutting into the time students have for homework and test prep will only hurt their grades. Many already struggle to balance after-school commitments with schoolwork, and a longer day would leave even less time to review material or finish assignments. Poor grades can limit their future opportunities, and also cause stress for their families.

It would also wipe out time for families to spend together. Right now, many households use after-school hours to run errands, grab a meal at a restaurant, or take evening walks before bed. Adding 90 minutes to the school day would steal that time, leaving no space for relaxed family bonding. Some parents argue that if the school day must be longer, students should start at least 20 minutes later, so they get enough sleep to stay alert during class. But even that fix doesn’t solve the bigger problem of lost free time. On weekends, many families like to take trips further from home, but if students have piles of homework and projects to finish, those plans get ruined. That hurts both family relationships and student well-being.

Worse still, if students start performing badly because they have no time to study, families may pull their kids out of the school. They might transfer to schools with shorter days, or even switch to homeschooling. If enough students leave, the school district might cut programs, or even shut the school down entirely. That would leave teachers and other staff without jobs, making it hard for them to cover rent and bills. None of this benefits the community in the long run.

This essay explores the potential benefits and drawbacks of a four-day school week where each day runs for ten hours, a schedule some people believe could help cut down on energy use and school resources.

As a student, I can see why the three-day weekend sounds appealing at first glance, but I do not support extending the school day by two extra hours to make this schedule work. For many of us, eight hours in class is already plenty: sitting in a classroom for most of the day leaves people feeling drained.

You can already see students nodding off in almost every class, thanks to the heavy workload schools assign, part-time jobs many students hold after class, and after-school sports. We are already too tired to stay focused during regular lessons, so adding two more hours of class time just to get an extra day off at the end of the week is not worth it.

Many people claim this schedule saves energy, but that is not true. Adding two extra hours to each of the four school days adds up to eight total extra hours, which exactly matches the time we would normally spend in school on the fifth day we are cutting. We are still using the same amount of energy, just spreading it out differently, so no real savings are made.

Take my friend Generic_Name as an example: he is a big fan of the four-day week, since the extra day off gives him more time to finish homework and hang out with his girlfriend Generic_Name. For students like him, the new schedule works well and brings clear benefits.

On the other hand, my boyfriend Generic_Name enjoys studying but strongly opposes the schedule change. He has two hours of basketball team practice right after school, then works a four-hour shift to help his mom pay for his car insurance. If school runs two hours longer, he will get home even later, leaving him with barely any time to finish homework before bed. He already struggles to get enough sleep, and this change would make that worse. He is far from the only student in this position: many of us take on part-time jobs or caretaking responsibilities to help our families cover bills, and longer school days only add to that stress.

We also need to consider teachers’ views. They would have to talk for ten hours straight each day, and they are not robots programmed by the government to work without getting tired. Many teachers would likely oppose making the school day longer for both students and staff.

For all these reasons, my school should not adopt this model. Any schedule change needs to take into account the needs of students, teachers, main office staff, and all other school employees to make a fair decision for the whole community. There is no guarantee this system will work for our high school community, even if some businesses have seen success with similar schedules. High schools have very different daily activities and needs compared to offices, so a model that works for companies will not necessarily work for us.

When you work independently, your only focus is on yourself and getting the task done on time.

Of course, some people still insist that group work is the better option. But working with others often leads to lots of distractions. Studies have found that most people complain about group projects and would rather work on their own. Why would you want to team up with people when you can’t be sure they have the same skill level as you? When you’re in a group, you have to constantly check in with your teammates to see if they’ve finished their section. If someone is unreliable and doesn’t do their part, you end up picking up the slack to protect the whole group’s grade.

Dear Principal,

I am writing to share my thoughts on the proposed changes to the eligibility policy for sports and school activities. I believe adjusting the current rules to require a B average, rather than a stricter higher grade, is a smart move — but we should not lower the requirement further to a C.

Many students currently have C averages. If they participate in sports while holding a C, they often end up focusing more on games and practices than on schoolwork, which can pull their grades down even further, sometimes below a C entirely. We need to make sure students prioritize their classes first, because slipping into failing grades helps no one. If we keep the requirement at a B, students will be motivated to work harder to keep their grades up enough to keep playing the sports they love.

There are plenty of benefits to maintaining a B average rule. When students get their progress reports or report cards and see low grades, it is usually a sign they are spending too much time on extracurriculars instead of schoolwork. If we stick to the B requirement, students will push themselves to improve their marks. Over time, this would change how our school is viewed: right now, people might think of us as a school that lets C students join sports, but if most students raise their grades to Bs, we will be known for strong academic performance across the student body.

I know many students will complain about having to study more, but this rule is truly for their own good. Almost every student is capable of earning at least a B, even if they do not get straight As. We all have different strengths, but everyone has the intelligence to meet this standard. Students who struggle can go to tutoring, finish all their homework, and turn assignments in on time — if they put in real effort, they will reach a B. If a student truly does their best, attends extra help, and still falls just short, you could check with their teachers to see if an exception is fair. But students who slack off, sleep in class, or do not try at all do not deserve to participate. If they choose not to put in work, they only have themselves to blame for missing out.

Good grades are also essential for students to pass their grade at the end of the year. The B requirement will be challenging for some, but I am sure any student who cares about playing sports or joining clubs will step up to meet it. Those who want to succeed will keep trying until they hit the mark.

I strongly support keeping the eligibility policy at a B average. As I have said, every student is smart enough to pass their classes, even if they do not believe it yet. Trying your best in school is never a bad thing, even if the only reason you do it is to keep playing sports. If you used to be failing, meeting this requirement means you can say you are passing all your classes now. Do not worry about what others say — do it for your own future.

Across the United States, many teenagers are obsessed with their smartphones, texting or calling friends constantly—even during class or lunch when they should be focused on school. This habit has become a major issue in schools nationwide, with teachers often confiscating devices and sending them to the main office.

Principals across the country are now reviewing rules for phone use. Two options are on the table: the first would let students bring phones to campus and use them only during lunch or other non-class breaks. The second would ban all phones from school grounds entirely.

I believe the second policy is the better choice, and phones should be completely banned from schools. Some people argue that teenagers are mature enough to follow directions and won’t use their phones during lessons. But this is not true. While a small number of students might listen, many others will ignore the rules and text in class anyway.

Another problem is that phones cause constant distractions. Even if students promise to keep their devices on silent, it only takes one notification or ring to disrupt an entire class, bothering both teachers and other students.

Many people believe that hard work is the key to a good life. Some argue that being self-reliant—trusting only your own instincts and ideas—is the best way to live, while others prefer to follow their own plans without outside input. Both approaches are common, but I believe that when it comes to life’s most important decisions, people should seek advice from experts and trusted authorities. This guidance can make life much smoother, especially for those going through tough times. There are countless examples of how expert help improves lives, but I want to share two personal stories that show exactly how this works.

The first example is a true story from my own childhood. It was the summer of 2010, and I was attending a basketball camp in Generic_City for the first time. I was thrilled—my private school didn’t offer any sports programs, so summer camps were the only chance I got to do proper athletic training. On the very first day of practice, a teammate accidentally injured my ankle, and I had to be taken to the hospital. Lying there, I was convinced I’d never play sports again, and I felt completely devastated. Then my father came to visit me. He told me that life is full of both easy and hard moments, and it rarely goes exactly the way we plan. He said I needed to grow stronger to take charge of my own life, instead of just following the same path as everyone else. His words made me realize that life isn’t always simple, and I’d have to work harder than before to become a better version of myself. That advice stuck with me, and it’s shaped who I am today. This is one big reason why I believe outside guidance can make life far easier.

The second story was told to me by my mother when I was little. It takes place a long time ago, in the middle of winter. A young man lived in a rundown old house, and he wanted to make a hammer so he could build himself a new home. He traveled far and wide to find the perfect piece of iron for his hammer, passing over countless pieces that he thought weren’t good enough. One day, he came across an old man who was forging hammers. When he got closer, he realized the iron the old man was using was exactly the “perfect” iron he’d been searching for. He asked the old man how he’d found it, and the old man laughed. “Young man, nothing in this world is truly perfect,” he said. “If you want to make a hammer like mine, you have to treat every material with equal care. Things aren’t perfect on their own—you make them perfect by how you treat them.” The young man understood then that the iron he’d rejected earlier was actually good enough, if only he’d put in the effort to work with it properly. In the end, he made a sturdy hammer that served him well for years. My mother’s story taught me that advice from older, more experienced people can teach you lessons you’d never figure out on your own. That’s my second reason for believing expert guidance improves your life and helps you understand important life lessons better.

Some people prefer to make every decision on their own, without any outside input. Others choose to seek advice from experts and trusted authorities. I firmly believe that turning to experts for help is the better choice, especially when dealing with life’s major challenges. Their guidance can make day-to-day life easier, and it’s especially valuable for anyone going through a hard time. I’ve benefited so much from expert advice in my own life, and I’m sure it can help anyone who’s struggling with their own problems.

I fully agree with Winston Churchill’s view on the vital part failure plays in the journey toward success, as it is essential to hold onto hope for our goals and future even when things go wrong. Think about facing setback after setback, yet staying certain you will eventually reach your goals. What if you never let go of your passion and drive to keep chasing success, no matter how many times you stumble? This idea lines up perfectly with the famous words of former British Prime Minister Winston Churchill, who once noted that "Success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm." After all, how can you grow if you never face the risk of failing while working toward what you want?

First, it helps to clarify what success actually means: it is reaching goals you have worked hard to achieve. Nearly everyone has something they want to accomplish, whether big or small. Achieving these goals feels amazing, while failing at them is never pleasant. Still, making mistakes is unavoidable, and that is okay. Every error gives you a chance to learn, adjust your approach, and try again until you get it right. No one is perfect, so it is normal to slip up occasionally as long as you use those moments to grow.

This process is familiar to anyone who has applied for a job. You send in your application, wait to hear back about an interview, go through the interview, then wait days or even weeks to find out if you got the role. This is exactly how chasing success feels: you put in effort, wait for results, and have to hold onto faith that your hard work will pay off, rather than giving up when things take time.

You know you are truly working toward success when you keep making mistakes but refuse to stop trying until you reach your goal. No amount of errors should hold you back from what you are working toward. Even if you fail many times, you can still end up successful, because each failure teaches you valuable lessons that make you better prepared for future efforts.

Success is something some people reach and others do not, but we are all responsible for our own actions, mistakes, and even the words we say, as these can affect the people and world around us. As individuals, we have to stay driven to pursue our goals. If we give up on our dreams, someone else will step in and take the opportunities we left behind.

The principal’s rule that every student must join at least one extracurricular activity is completely reasonable, and I fully support it. These activities offer benefits that help students both right now and later in life.

I believe every student should take part in at least one, if not more, after-school activities. They boost your mental and emotional well-being, keep you healthy, and even help with college applications. Multiple studies back this up: for example, people who regularly play sports are far less likely to have heart attacks, breathing problems, or other serious health issues later in life.

One of the biggest perks is better physical health. Joining a sports team, whether that’s baseball, basketball, track, cheerleading, or any other option, pushes you to be more active and can even help you manage your weight. Research consistently shows that people who stay active through their school years see way more long-term health benefits than those who don’t.

These activities also help with emotional health. When you’re busy with something fun, you get a break from whatever stressors are weighing you down, so you stop constantly thinking about your worries. This doesn’t just apply to sports, either. Volunteering with the school counselor, helping put together the yearbook, or pitching in with other school tasks gets you out of your own head, instead of only focusing on your own problems. Right now, many students stay in their own bubbles, but if we group students into different extracurricular clubs or teams every day, they’d get to know new people and have fun socializing.

College admissions are another major benefit. Taking part in extracurriculars, whether that’s sports or volunteer work around school, makes your college application look far more impressive. Admissions officers look for more than just good grades: they want students who stand out from the crowd. They also want to see that you’re a kind, responsible person who can get tasks done on time, not just someone who gets good marks. A solid history of extracurricular involvement can even help you earn scholarships, since more colleges will take notice of you. They want to see that you can balance multiple responsibilities, work well with others, and handle tasks on your own. If you can’t take your high school classes and activities seriously, after all, how will you manage the harder workload of college? Admissions teams also check how independent you are and how well you get along with peers, both of which extracurriculars demonstrate.

Requiring all students to join at least one extracurricular activity comes with too many benefits to ignore, so I’d encourage everyone to give it a shot. There’s really no downside to trying something new. I fully agree with the principal’s decision here: sometimes, rules are put in place for your own good, even if they aren’t exactly what you wanted at first. Sometimes you just have to go along with it, and in this case, it will only help you.

Technology plays a huge role in modern daily life, and its influence will only grow stronger in the years to come. People have always looked for ways to improve their lives and simplify everyday tasks. While many praise tech for making life easier, others argue it brings serious downsides: we spend less time interacting in person in public spaces, many people refuse to leave places where tech is available, and some even act aggressively when others point out tech’s negative effects.

Decades ago, it was common for people to run into each other on the street and chat face-to-face. Back then, there were no smart devices that let you video call friends from a tiny screen with the tap of a finger. Today, this shift has harmed how our society connects. Many people no longer go out to meet friends or enjoy public spaces like city streets; instead, they stay home to talk to people they have never met in person. Some argue that chatting with strangers online is no different from talking to new people on the street, but online interactions carry unique risks. Many users create fake profiles to steal personal information or cause other harm. In the past, when you met a stranger in public, you could observe their behavior and actions to judge if they were trustworthy – that’s how people used to form real friendships. Now, the internet is the main way people meet new contacts, even though there’s no way to confirm if those online friends are who they claim to be.

For many adults today, childhood meant playing outside: running around neighborhood streets, visiting friends’ houses, or spending afternoons at the local park. But life has changed drastically since those days. Modern technology has brought video games, which are now the top pastime for children and teenagers. All it takes is plugging a device into a TV to start playing, but far too many young people spend entire days gaming instead of going outside to play sports or visit friends. At school, video games are the most common topic of conversation among students, which hurts their academic performance. Spending all free time gaming leaves no time to study for big tests or finish homework. When the first gaming consoles came out, they were seen as an exciting new invention, but many kids back then couldn’t afford them. Instead of saving up for a small console, they put money toward simple treats like ice cream or burgers, or saved for trips to amusement parks. Today, though, most kids and teens refuse to leave home where their tech devices are within reach.

The widespread use of technology has also led to a worrying new behavior: many people become aggressive when they are not allowed to use their devices. Families often argue when parents try to limit their children’s screen time, and this angry reaction is becoming common across the world. Doctors explain that this happens because heavy tech users live in an imaginary world where they have total control, and taking that away feels like a major loss. But with technology available in almost every public and private space, it is very hard to get kids to cut back on usage. Some teenagers even get so angry while gaming that they smash items within reach – including the very gaming consoles their parents spent money to buy for them.

To be fair, some people argue that technology is a force for good, since it creates tools that simplify daily tasks. But overall, technology harms our lives because it makes us act less like typical, socially connected people, as we prioritize convenience above all else. If we do not learn to control how much we use technology, it will shape our society in very negative ways for years to come.

Courses like music, drama, and visual art are typically offered as optional electives in most schools. Many argue they should stay that way, since these subjects rarely come up in everyday adult life, and they are not mandatory for earning a high school diploma. Students have wildly different career aspirations, so forcing everyone to take arts classes limits their ability to focus on subjects that align with their personal goals.

Think about the practical skills we actually use as adults: basic math for calculating taxes or splitting bills, for example. When was the last time someone needed to compose a song, perform a dramatic monologue, or paint a masterpiece to get through their day? These activities are fun hobbies, but they are not essential for building a stable, comfortable life. Most employers won’t care if you have acting experience or drawing skills listed on your resume unless you are applying for a niche role in the arts. Even for students who major in these fields, only the most naturally talented or highly trained individuals will build successful, sustainable careers. Electives serve a clear purpose: they give students a low-stakes way to explore what they might want to do later in life. If arts classes were mandatory for every student, we might see a second Renaissance sweep the globe, but that is a far-off cultural shift, not a reason to force uninterested students to sit through classes they do not need.

Arts classes are not a requirement for graduating high school, and colleges place far more weight on core subject grades and diploma prerequisites than they do on art or music experience. Admissions tests like the SAT do not assess skills like painting or pottery sculpting, so these subjects have no impact on whether a student gets into their preferred university. It is also very common for students’ goals to shift as they grow older and start college. For instance, a student who plans to become a doctor might decide halfway through their degree to switch to a career in scientific research instead. Since both fields fall under the broad science category, many of the classes they already took will still count toward their new major. Arts classes, by contrast, are highly specialized: they share almost no overlap with other subject areas, so they offer no value to students who change their career plans later.

To be fair, mastering music, theater, or visual art can lead to rewarding careers: writing hit songs for popular artists, starring in films, or selling prized artwork can bring both fame and high earnings. However, this level of success is only possible for a tiny fraction of people. Whether someone is born with natural talent or spends years obsessively honing their craft toward a single clear goal, very few will ever make a stable living from creative work. It is not a reliable career path, so it makes no sense to treat arts classes as a mandatory part of every student’s education.

Spending too much time on required arts classes would leave students with fewer options to explore other interests that might better match their future goals. These subjects are simply not as useful in day-to-day adult life as core academic classes. For these reasons, music, drama, and art should remain optional electives. Forcing every student to take them would strip away the freedom to choose classes that align with their own unique plans for the future.

I disagree with adding an extra hour and a half to the school day. First, we already spend 8 hours in school each day working on lessons and other tasks, which leaves both kids and adults feeling completely exhausted. Adding even more time would just be too much for us to handle.

Second, longer school days leave very little time for normal childhood activities. If the school day stretches to 9 hours and 35 minutes, there’s barely any free time left. For example, when you get home from school, you’re already tired and want to have some fun, but then you have homework that takes hours to finish. By the time you’re done, it’s too dark to go outside, and your parents won’t let you out anyway because of the long school hours. That’s my second reason.

Third, homework is another big issue. Almost every single day, we have extra work to do at home, which can take hours to complete. For instance, if school ends at 4:00 PM, you’re already worn out, but you still have to sit down and do homework. Finishing that often takes 2 or 3 more hours of work, so by the time you’re free, it’s too late to do fun things like hang out with friends. That’s the third point.

Fourth, appointments also become a problem. Many students currently get out of school at 2:45 PM, so if they have a doctor’s or other appointment at 3:00, they can make it. But with extra school hours, you’d miss the appointment, and leaving early just wastes valuable learning time for kids and adults. That’s the fourth reason.

I get that schools add extra time to help us get smarter, build good lives, and get good jobs. But kids and adults alike need time for ourselves too. Those are all my reasons and examples for why I’m against adding more time to the school day.

My answer is no: you can never fairly judge a person based only on your first impression of them. It is much better to take the time to get to know who they really are. Even if they act immature during that first meeting, that does not define their whole personality. You should ask them about their life and interests, instead of immediately deciding they are not good enough to spend time with. For example, if someone seems lazy because they are clearly tired, you cannot assume that is their true character. Basing your entire opinion of them on that one tired moment is completely unfair.

Is change impossible? Definitely not. Whether or not you change comes down to your mindset. In life, very few things are truly impossible if you put your mind to them. For example, someone who is usually unkind can choose to start treating everyone with kindness. People can grow and shift who they are over time. I know this from my own experience: I used to be extremely quiet. I was so shy that I never wanted to start conversations with new people. Now, though, I love talking to others. I introduce myself to everyone I meet, no matter who they are.

I fully agree with the idea that first impressions do not tell the whole story. When I first met some people, they thought I was unfriendly because I was tired at the end of a long day. I did not have the energy to chat, so I came across as lazy or rude. That is why I decided to shift my mindset. I did not want people to keep calling me lazy, which I found really frustrating. I turned my whole life around — I did not want to stay the same person forever. Making that change made me so much happier, all because I adopted a more open, energetic lifestyle.

When someone claims that change is impossible, they are wrong. Usually, they just do not believe in their own ability to grow. I never thought I would become such a different person, but I did. Now I really like who I am, and I smile all the time. In the past, I rarely smiled and was a pretty dull person. I will admit that I used to judge people quickly based on first impressions too. I would meet someone and think they were not cool at all, only to find out later that they were actually great. Judging people too fast is never a good idea. For that reason, I strongly agree: you can never fairly judge someone based only on a first meeting.

I firmly believe that art, drama, and music courses should be offered as electives rather than mandatory classes, as they have no place in core education. They provide no real benefit for students' futures, since the only skills that matter are those that help you secure a good job and pay for everyday necessities like electricity, food, fuel, and water bills. Since these subjects are irrelevant to students' long-term goals, they should be optional, so learners can choose to take them only if they are genuinely interested. The second key reason is that many students simply do not enjoy these classes: they find them boring, as creative work is not something they care about. Most students prefer activities like listening to music, partying, using social media, playing sports, gaming, chatting with friends, and keeping up with trends. They would much rather not be stuck in a class with a group of students who enjoy painting, working with clay, and drawing, which they dismiss as 'nerdy' activities. No student should be forced to take a course they dislike. These creative classes should be optional, just as band classes are in most schools. Mandatory enrollment could also lead to failing grades: students who hate the classes may skip sessions, while others may struggle because they lack talent in areas like clay sculpting or drawing. Drama classes should also be voluntary, as the work of rehearsing scenes and delivering speeches does not help students in their future careers or daily lives. Music courses may be the most appealing of the three subjects to students, but even they do not teach skills that will benefit them in adulthood. Ideally, creative classes should be something students pick because they find them easy, have a natural talent for them, or are genuinely interested in the material. For all these reasons, I believe art, drama, and music should all be elective courses, not mandatory requirements for graduation.

In my view, opting for online or at-home classes is a solid choice for many learners, since they can concentrate more effectively, stay fully engaged with their work, and avoid distractions from others. One downside of learning remotely, though, is that students are less likely to make new friends. Having classmates can be helpful, as friends can support you or keep you company, so there are clear benefits to attending in-person school instead of studying at home. On the other hand, students who learn online or at home tend to be better prepared for all kinds of situations, since they pay close attention to their lessons. That said, in-person classes are often more engaging, as you get to meet new people and avoid working alone. Both options have their advantages, so ultimately people can choose the learning style that fits their needs and goals.

Many people choose remote learning specifically because they can stay focused without interruptions. For instance, group work in a physical classroom often leads to chatting instead of studying, while working alone lets students complete tasks more efficiently. This is a big reason why more people are picking online classes: they get more done when no one else is around. Students who learn from home or online are often more intelligent and gain more knowledge, since they stay fully focused on their studies. In traditional schools, it’s common for students to lose focus by playing or talking with friends, which distracts not just themselves but others too. If you pitted a remote learner against a regular school student in a competition, the remote student would likely come out on top, as they are usually better prepared. Some regular school students only show up to hang out with friends, which is nice for socializing, but they often zone out or even nap while the teacher is explaining material. As a result, they fail quizzes and exams. In contrast, remote learners pay attention throughout lessons, so they pass assessments and show more responsibility for their own learning.

By the end of the school year, traditional students vary widely: some learn a lot, but others waste time playing, not paying attention, or sleeping in class. Remote learners, meanwhile, are well-prepared and have retained far more information, since they stayed focused and had no distractions. This comes down to personal motivation: some people want to learn and pass, others don’t, and everyone can make their own choice about how to study. I believe online learning is more effective and productive by the end of the year. At-home classes benefit students in countless ways, and they usually know more material when the school year wraps up. Regular school students take the SOL test at the end of the year, and many fail because they didn’t learn anything all year—they just sat in class doing nothing. Remote learners, however, are able to pass the SOL test, since they stayed interested in the material and avoided distractions throughout the entire year.

Is trying your hardest ever a bad thing? In my opinion, there’s nothing wrong with giving 100% effort to whatever you’re doing. You should always aim to do your best, no matter what task you’re working on. Unfortunately, a lot of people hate putting in effort—they quit so fast that they stop trying altogether. I try to give my all most of the time, but sometimes I slack off, and when I don’t put in full effort, I end up with disappointing results.

Take Paul George as an example. When the Clippers faced the Los Angeles Lakers, his shots just weren’t going in for most of the game, leaving him with a low score. But he didn’t give up—he kept pushing to grab rebounds and make steals to help his team win.

Another example is a student I’ll call Generic_Name. He took a test with several questions he couldn’t figure out. Even so, he worked through every problem, made educated guesses where he needed to, and gave it his full effort. He ended up with a 75—lower than his usual B or above. He’d forgotten the teacher had warned the class there would be some questions no one in the class would know, so he was caught off guard.

My final example is about my little sister, who plays basketball just like me. I go to ball handling training every Friday to sharpen my skills, and she decided to join me once. She’d never done this type of training before, and the class was advanced—it was easy for me since I’d been attending for years, but she really struggled. At one point, our trainer told her she was doing a drill wrong, so she dropped the ball and walked out of the gym. When we got home after training, I sat down with her and offered to help. She gave up the first time she struggled, but she was willing to try again—and the results turned out well because she put in the effort.

Picture this: you have an incredible skill that almost no one knows about. Plenty of people argue that you should never keep your talents a secret, but I’ve found that keeping mine private helps me concentrate better and improve faster. My talent is singing, and I’m passionate about it. I work on getting better through regular practice, and I put my skill to use by writing my own original songs.

I’m deeply committed to improving my singing through consistent practice. For starters, I spend a lot of time watching online vocal tutorials to pick up new techniques and warm up my voice, though I also set aside time to practice alone. The more I rehearse, the more confident I feel singing without any guidance. Developing this skill matters a huge amount to me, since becoming a singer is my biggest dream.

I also take formal singing lessons to sharpen my abilities. My teacher often gives me sheet music and exercises to work on at home, and sticking to these practice plans has made my voice sound clearer, more controlled, and more polished over time.

On top of that, I use my singing talent to write my own music. Putting my thoughts into lyrics has helped me build strong writing skills, and it often brings back forgotten memories of my past. I usually base my songs on old experiences, past emotions, or how I’m feeling right now. Writing regularly has taught me new songwriting methods, fresh ways to phrase lines, and creative lyric ideas.

To sum up, I use my talent to write original songs, which has boosted my writing abilities, and I develop my skills by watching online tutorials and attending singing lessons. Since singing is the dream I’m working toward, I always put my full effort into improving.

Have you ever been pressured by friends into doing something you knew was wrong? Most people have two kinds of friends in their lives: those who act responsibly, and those who make poor choices. Yet many teenagers today don’t pause to consider the long-term consequences when they copy bad behavior from others. I strongly believe that the most effective way to positively influence others is to model good behavior yourself. People naturally learn by watching what others do, not just what they say. If you spend time with someone who makes bad choices, you will almost certainly pick up some of their habits, whether you realize it or not. The people around us are always observing our actions, and they will judge us based on what we do.

My first reason for this is simple: good behavior is the strongest form of influence. If you are a kind, educated, and content person, others will look up to you and want to mirror your choices. Far too many young people have ruined their futures by following harmful influences. Some might argue that we are old enough to tell right from wrong, but we rarely stop to think about the long-term outcomes of our actions. The world has no shortage of unkind people, and many wonder why bad behavior is so common. The answer is straightforward: people learn bad habits by copying those around them. If we want to build a better world for future generations, we need to model good behavior for the children and teens who are watching us.

I have seen this play out in my own life, with friends and family members who ruined their lives by spending time with people who dragged them down. It is incredibly painful to watch someone end up in prison or even lose their life just because they copied the bad choices of their friends. People who model bad behavior never warn you about the consequences of their actions. Think about young children: when they are learning about the world, they copy exactly what their parents do, or what their parents teach them. Teenagers and adults are a little different—we don’t always do exactly what we are told—but we still end up picking up habits, good or bad, from the people we spend time with.

People are always quick to judge, so if you want to avoid harsh criticism, the best thing to do is be a positive example. When you are a good influence, people will trust you; when you act poorly, that trust disappears. Often, we only realize this when it is too late, and the people we care about start to distance themselves from us because they don’t want to be dragged down by our bad choices. My grandmother used to say, "You reap what you sow." That phrase has always stuck with me, because modeling good behavior is one of the surest paths to success in life. There are other ways to get ahead too, of course, but being a good person lays the foundation for all of them.

For all these reasons, I am convinced that leading by good example is the best way to influence the people around us. When others watch what you do, they will pick up the positive habits you model, and they will come to trust you. You will also feel a deep sense of pride knowing that you are helping others make good choices. If we all want to live in a better world, we need to start by being good examples for others, and stop wasting time on behaviors that drag people down.

Many schools now let students join classes from home using online tools or video conferencing, and I believe this is an excellent option for learners. It helps countless students who cannot stick to a regular in-person class schedule. Some lack the money, time, or face personal challenges that make attending school on campus impossible, and this remote option lets them complete their studies.

Online courses are a key choice for students who want to finish their education. They can join lessons from their own homes without commuting to campus, and fit studying around their existing schedule. Time is a major barrier for many who drop out: a lot of students leave school because they have to work after classes, leaving no time for homework or other school activities. They start falling behind in lessons, and eventually decide to quit school to focus on full-time work, often because they need to support their families. For some, family and finances are even bigger factors: they may have moved to a new area with no relatives nearby, so they have to balance studying and working to earn money to send back to their families.

Video conferencing is another valuable remote learning option. Like online courses, it lets students join from home, either at a time that works for them or following a schedule set by their teacher. Unlike pre-recorded online lessons, this format involves live, real-time classes where students and teachers interact via camera. This is especially helpful because students can ask questions immediately if they get confused, and get feedback just like they would in a regular school classroom.

One of the biggest advantages of remote learning is that students can keep working and handling their regular personal responsibilities while studying. Another plus is that these programs are not just for young people: adults can also join to finish their high school education. Many adults drop out earlier because they were over the age limit for regular high school, but remote learning has no such restrictions, so it welcomes learners of all ages.

These days, more and more teenagers are dropping out of school. Some have no other choice due to their circumstances, while others quit out of laziness. But with schools now offering remote learning, many former dropouts and other learners can benefit from this easy way to finish their studies and build a better future.

I believe that if more schools add distance learning as an option for students, even more people will be able to join these programs and gain better life opportunities. With schools now offering this flexibility, there are no longer any valid excuses for not finishing school.

Extending the school day even further is a terrible idea, and I definitely do not want to stay an extra hour—plus I doubt any other students would want to either. First, we already spend nearly the whole day in class: eight hours is plenty of time for lessons, and there is no chance I would agree to stay longer than that. Second, adding an extra hour to the school day would take away time we need to finish homework. Teachers already assign a huge amount of work, so if we lose an hour of our afternoon, we would probably be stuck doing assignments right up until bedtime. Third, longer school hours mean less time for homework and even less free time. We would have no time left to do things we actually enjoy, because the heavy homework load already takes up so much of our day, and the extra hour in school would just add to the time we have to spend on assignments, leaving almost no free time at all. That is why the school day should not be made longer by an extra hour: we already spend almost all day in school, it would cut into our homework time, and leave us with even less free time to ourselves.

While most students love summer vacation, some teachers argue that the long break makes it hard for kids to remember what they learned when they come back in autumn, and that summer is too lengthy. But these educators are ignoring how students feel about the issue. We should not switch to a year-round school calendar that would only give 3-4 weeks of summer break plus a single week off in spring and fall. Why? Because shorter breaks mean less time with family, and students already have plenty of other responsibilities to manage.

The first key reason is that longer breaks let students spend quality time with their families. During the school year, kids get home every day only to focus on homework, pack their bags for the next day, and work on projects. Some even have deadlines for big assignments that take up all their free time. When students are constantly stressed about schoolwork, they often stop talking to their parents about what’s happening in their lives. They might not mention problems they’re facing, or share small updates about their day. This can hurt their relationship with their families, since parents are left out of the loop. Many teachers already think current student breaks are too short, so making them even shorter with a year-round calendar would only make this problem worse.

The second point is that students have lives outside of school, too. They have responsibilities that they can only handle during longer breaks like summer, spring, and winter vacation. During these breaks, many students help their parents with chores, run errands, or use their free time however they like, without the stress of homework or projects hanging over their heads. On top of that, most students don’t think all the information they learn in class is actually useful — which is exactly why they forget so much of it when they come back to school anyway. So even if summer break were shorter, they’d still struggle to remember lessons, because they don’t see the value in what they’re learning. This is the second main reason to reject year-round schooling.

It’s true that some people argue summer break is too long, and that students lose learning retention when they return in the fall. But there are plenty of people who disagree with this view. The bottom line is that educators should not push for a year-round school schedule with only 3-4 weeks of summer break and short spring and fall pauses. This would take away time students need with their families, and ignore the other responsibilities kids have outside of class. That’s why we should keep the traditional summer, spring, and winter breaks, instead of switching to a year-round calendar.

Several schools across the United States now offer remote learning programs, letting students join classes from home through online tools or video conferencing. Many schools view this as a helpful choice for students, especially since bullying remains a common issue in middle and high schools. Students who face bullying often lose interest in attending in-person classes and ask to switch to home-based learning instead. However, while remote classes may seem convenient, they often lead to poor learning outcomes. Students frequently get distracted at home, struggle to adapt to the new learning environment, and even report feeling more stressed than they did in physical classrooms. On the other hand, some do find learning from home more relaxing.

Distractions are a major problem for students learning at home. Most have easy access to smartphones, which pull their attention away from lessons. Staying indoors for long periods also makes many students feel bored and unmotivated, so they end up doing very little schoolwork. Even students who used to doze off in in-person classes are more likely to nap during home lessons. On top of that, many students hold part-time jobs, which leaves them exhausted and uninterested in engaging with their studies.

Focus is another issue. Students who struggled to pay attention in physical classrooms often find it even harder to stay on task when learning from home. Many turn on music or play games during lessons instead of listening to their teachers.

The learning environment itself suffers when classes move online. Students usually grasp concepts better when a teacher explains them in person, but online lessons make this far more difficult. Even learners who already struggled to understand material in physical classrooms find it nearly impossible to keep up with home-based classes, leading to a drop in their overall academic progress.

Many schools continue to offer remote learning because they believe it benefits students. There are some clear perks: learners can feel more relaxed at home, have extra time to finish homework, and stay in a comfortable, safe space with their families. They also tend to get more sleep, which should leave them with more energy for online lessons. However, these advantages are often cancelled out by distractions from family members at home, which make students far less likely to pay attention to their teachers.

In conclusion, online learning from home is not a good option for most students. It is far too easy for them to get distracted, whether by phones, family, or boredom, so they rarely pay full attention to lessons. Most do not want to engage with online material, and their academic progress suffers as a result. Even students who felt frustrated and confused in in-person classes find online learning even harder to manage, leading to even less learning overall. The distractions and drop in academic performance make remote classes a poor choice for many learners.

Students who live far from school or have trouble keeping up with their lessons often struggle to pass their classes. Teachers are very worried about these students and have tried every possible way to help them, but when they show the principal the test scores, the results are still very low. The school staff knows they need to find a way to help these students succeed, so they hold a meeting and come up with a plan: students will do all their assignments at home, which they call the Homeschool program.

The homeschool program lets students complete all their homework, quizzes, assignments, and tests from their own houses. Many students say this setup helps them do better in their classes, since they find it much easier than going to a regular school building. One big benefit is that they can stay home all day: they can eat lunch whenever they want, watch TV during breaks, and still finish all their work by the deadline.

However, not all students like the idea of homeschool. Some say they get bored staying at home all day, and they miss out on making friends with their classmates. They also struggle because there is no teacher around to help them with tough assignments, so they often miss important information they need to learn. Many students end up in homeschool programs because there are no schools near where they live, but their parents want the best for them and will do anything to make sure they get a good education and succeed later in life.

If I had to give advice on this issue, I would tell students to choose regular school instead. You have a much higher chance of succeeding there than in a homeschool program. You will still have your friends around, and they can even help you with your schoolwork. You also have a better shot at getting into college, since teachers will guide you and make sure you learn all the information you need to be prepared for the future. Homeschool is still a good program that can help students do well in the short term, but it is not the best choice for long-term success. Anyone who wants the best possible chances in life should take regular school seriously.

Most cities enforce curfews, rules designed for residents to follow, though some people still break these regulations. A common debate asks whether these time limits keep teenagers out of trouble or unfairly interfere with young people’s daily lives. I believe curfews do keep teens safe from harm, as they teach young people to be mindful of time.

Curfews are public laws meant to support a stable, pleasant life for everyone. When residents follow these rules, communities can stay peaceful, and people do not have to fear for their safety.

These time limits apply to everyone, and sticking to them helps young people mature faster. As they learn to follow curfew rules, they develop the skills to take care of themselves independently.

Some argue that curfews unfairly restrict young people’s freedom, but I think they actually protect teens from trouble. Curfews leave teenagers plenty of time to finish schoolwork or chores in the morning and early evening. Most places set curfew for 10 p.m., and teens who follow this rule stay safe at night. This habit also helps them become more responsible as they grow older.

Overall, curfews are a helpful rule for teenagers. They keep young people out of risky situations, encourage faster maturity, and teach self-care skills. Parents no longer have to worry about their kids being out late at night, and teenagers have enough time to get ready for school or work the next day.

I’d pick basketball for my school sports team since it lets me compete against squads from other schools. On top of that, my friends can come cheer me on from the stands. Joining the school basketball team comes with plenty of perks. For one, the team gets sponsorship, and we get to do regular drills and face off against teams from schools across the county. Once you make the roster, you have to stay in top shape. High school basketball plays way differently than community leagues, so you’ll need to work out regularly to build stamina and strength. That way, you’ll have an edge when driving to the basket or sinking three-pointers against rival players.

One key thing to remember is that you have to listen to your coach and show good sportsmanship. When the whole team follows these rules, you’ll play better together and have a strong chance of winning the championship. College coaches often attend high school games to scout players who can handle the ball well and play solid defense to block opponents from scoring. If you excel at both of these skills, you’ll have a big advantage, and college coaches may choose you for their team.

My second favorite sport to pick would be football. In my personal opinion, it’s the best sport out there because you get to tackle opponents. If you try out for the school football team, you’ll have to attend training sessions run by both defensive and offensive coaches to help you earn a spot on the roster. These training sessions include deadlifts, hill sprints, drills, weightlifting, and scrimmage games. Coaches look for players who push themselves hard in training, because that shows they’re committed to putting in the work needed to make the team.

Finally, football is the best sport to choose overall. It’s an extremely aggressive sport, and it’s very tough to master—you need a lot of luck to make it to the NFL. This path is challenging for another reason too: you have to keep your grades up. If your marks slip, coaches might cut you from the team, since they expect players to have perfect academic records. If you make it to college and play well there, you could be lucky enough to get an invite to the NFL combine. But if football isn’t your thing, just go with basketball. At the end of the day, it doesn’t matter which school sport you choose to play.

A local city council is currently debating whether to introduce a curfew for teenagers, setting a 10 p.m. limit on weeknights and a midnight cutoff on weekends. While many adults support this policy, most young people strongly oppose it. However, I believe imposing these time limits on teens staying out late is a positive step. In my view, such a rule would help teenagers build healthier sleep routines, cut down on poor eating habits, and give them more opportunities to connect with their families.

First, requiring teens to be home by curfew times would directly improve their sleep schedules. When young people are forced to return home early, they are far more likely to go to bed at a reasonable hour instead of staying out until midnight. Teenagers need at least 7 to 8 hours of sleep every night to support their developing bodies and brains. Getting enough rest leaves young people feeling energetic and focused, while late nights disrupt sleep patterns, leaving teens sluggish, tired, and unengaged in daily activities. Sleep deprivation also creates serious safety risks, especially for teens who drive. Drowsy driving causes dizziness and slows reaction times, which can be deadly—many teenage car crash victims lose their lives because they were too tired to pay attention on the road, and late nights out also increase the chance of drunk driving incidents. To protect young people from preventable tragedies, curfews are necessary. I have personal experience with this: when I do not get enough sleep, I struggle to concentrate in my classes, which hurts my grades. I also find that staying up late leaves me disconnected from what is happening around me, since I am asleep or unfocused when the people around me are active and engaged.

Beyond sleep, curfews would also have a positive impact on teenagers’ eating habits. When teens spend late nights out with friends, they almost always end up eating greasy, processed junk food, which is terrible for their health. To stay energetic and active, young people need balanced, nutritious meals, not just adequate sleep. Eating well is especially important for teenagers, who have their whole lives ahead of them—poor diets at a young age can lead to serious health issues far earlier than necessary. Late nights out also often involve underage drinking, which is harmful to developing bodies. Unhealthy food weakens the immune system, raising the risk of early illness, and excess weight gain from junk food can hurt teens socially, mentally, and physically. When teens are home by curfew, they eat home-cooked meals prepared by their parents, which are usually far healthier and less oily than takeout or fast food. I have noticed that eating junk food makes me feel ill, and when I am unwell, people tend to keep their distance, which leaves me feeling isolated. I also have a relative who gained a lot of weight after years of eating mostly junk food—he now needs help standing up from a chair, gets teased constantly for his size, and gets winded after walking just a short distance. To avoid cruel comments and poor physical health, teens should stick to home-cooked, nutritious meals, which is easier to do when they are home by curfew.

Finally, curfews would encourage teenagers to spend more quality time with their families. Instead of going out with friends every night, teens would be home to interact with their parents and siblings, which helps close the generation gap that often forms when family members spend little time together. Simple activities like eating dinner as a family create space to talk about what is happening in everyone’s lives. For example, when my family gathers for meals, we talk about new experiences we have had—like when my sister and I made new friends after moving to this area earlier this year. We also discuss how to stay safe during local disease outbreaks, and share any problems we are facing. This lets us celebrate each other’s joys and support each other through struggles, strengthening our family bonds.

Overall, there are many reasons why introducing a teenage curfew would improve young people’s lives. With this policy in place, teens can get enough sleep, eat healthier meals, and build stronger relationships with their families. These changes are essential to raising a generation of healthy, focused young people who can contribute to the country’s growth and development. When teens are well-rested, they can work hard to achieve their goals. When they connect with their families, they become more empathetic, well-rounded members of society. Teenagers should view this curfew not as a limit on their freedom, but as a tool to help them live healthier, more active lives. It is not a restriction, but a way to prevent the early health issues and risks that come with poor lifestyle habits. By adjusting their routines now, teens can avoid the long-term harm of sleep deprivation, bad diets, and disconnected families, and instead build a strong foundation for their future.

Dear Principal, I believe students should be permitted to bring their cell phones to school throughout the regular school day. This is crucial because phones can be lifesavers in unexpected emergencies. If a student gets injured or finds themselves in trouble, they can quickly dial 911 or 311 to get immediate help. Phones also let students stay in touch with family during free periods, which is another key benefit.

Emergencies can strike at any time during school hours. A student who gets hurt on campus can use their phone to call for aid right away. If someone is being bullied by their peers, they can contact the school office immediately to report that they have been harmed by other students. If something bad happens to a student during the school day, their phone is always there as a backup resource.

Beyond major emergencies, plenty of smaller mishaps can also happen during the school day.

For example, lots of students have little accidents: maybe they spill milk on their shirt at lunch, or don’t make it to the restroom in time. In these cases, a quick call to mom or dad can get them a change of clothes without having to sit through class uncomfortable. Phones are useful for so much more than just sending texts.

We also can’t predict what might happen when we head home at the end of the day. There are plenty of potential dangers on the way home, and having a phone means we can call 911 immediately if we run into trouble. It would also be great to use phones during free classes, so we can use them at appropriate times during the day.

It’s common for people seeking guidance to reach out to several different people instead of just one. You might wonder why this habit is so widespread. For anyone who usually ignores input from others, learning to accept advice can be a game-changer. Listening to other people’s perspectives helps you make smarter decisions about your life, grasp complex situations more quickly and clearly, and pick up useful lessons along the way. This approach is especially critical for public leaders, like city mayors: they rely on feedback from local residents to identify and fix community issues. A city where leaders never listen to the people would quickly fall into disrepair, something no one wants. The core takeaway here is simple: being open to receiving advice matters.

Every day, we face all kinds of decisions, from tiny everyday choices to huge life-changing ones, and all of them shape our future and chances of success. Listening to others’ input makes you far wiser when you weigh your own options. Take Abraham Lincoln, for example: if he had never learned about the brutal treatment African Americans faced due to their skin color, he would never have signed the laws to abolish slavery. Without the advice and perspectives that opened his eyes to this injustice, he almost certainly would not have tackled the deep-rooted, toxic racism of his time. We have him to thank for ending that practice, and it all comes down to seeking out good information and guidance. Most of us have received advice from people we admire, too. Whatever wisdom they share adds to your own knowledge base. For instance, if a parent or guardian tells you to never give up when faced with tough, frustrating problems, you’ll carry that lesson with you for the rest of your life. Over time, this makes you more resilient when facing challenges, builds a strong work ethic, and helps you tell right from wrong thanks to guidance from role models like your parents. Seeking multiple opinions is a lot like sampling dishes from different chefs: if you only stick to what you know, you’ll never discover a new favorite. The same applies to advice: listening to different viewpoints opens up possibilities you might never have considered, helping you use your own judgment to make the best choice.

To sum up, advice exists to support you, and other people’s opinions are there to steer you toward smarter choices in life. Not every piece of input you get will be helpful or align with what you want, but it’s still worth listening to. Taking in different perspectives will make you wiser and more alert to all kinds of situations, helping you grow into the best version of yourself.

Dear Principal, I’ve done some research recently, and I really believe switching our school cafeteria’s menu to offer much healthier options is a great idea. I know this would be a big adjustment, but it would benefit every student here in so many ways. I have several key reasons why updating the menu is necessary, and how it would help all of us.

First, many parents currently stress about what their children are eating during the school day. Lots of families want their kids to follow a nutritious diet, but they can’t control what’s served in the cafeteria right now. If we switch to healthier meals, parents won’t have to spend all day worrying. They’ll know for sure their kids are getting good, balanced food every day instead of junk food.

My second point is that students’ health would improve a lot. We’d be stronger and more energetic, which means we’d be more active in class and ready to focus on learning. Right now, the junk food served in the cafeteria makes a lot of us feel sluggish and tired, so we end up dozing off or being too lazy to participate. Our brains can’t work properly when we’re fueled by greasy, sugary meals all day. That’s why you should seriously think about this change – it’s for the students who come here every day to grow healthy and pick up new knowledge.

Finally, eating better would mean students get sick far less often. We’d show up to school more consistently, instead of missing lots of class days due to preventable illnesses. This also helps our parents: when kids get sick, families often have to spend a lot of money on doctor visits and medicine. If the school serves healthy meals daily, we’ll stay well more often. On top of that, the school can use these meals to teach us why eating nutritious food matters, helping us build healthy habits that last.

These are all the reasons why I think the cafeteria menu needs to change. Please consider this proposal: we’d be so much healthier than we are now, and our brains would work better all day long. This would help us for the rest of our lives, since school is where we spend most of our time as kids – it’s basically our second home. Making this change would support our futures and make our school an even better place for everyone.

In my view, allowing students to use phones at school has both advantages and drawbacks, so there are valid reasons both for and against it. On the positive side, phones are far quicker and simpler to use than school computers, and since most young people use them constantly in daily life, they are already very familiar with how they work. However, the biggest downside is that phones are a major distraction during lessons. They stop students from focusing on their work and cause all sorts of other issues.

When students have phones in class, they often stop paying attention to the teacher and become reluctant to do schoolwork. After all, schools already provide computers and libraries for students to research topics for their classes. Phones just pull their focus away, making it hard for them to learn or complete assignments. These days, almost all teenagers rely on their phones for every little thing. For example, if a teacher lets students use their phones to look up information for a task, I am sure most would end up scrolling through social media or messaging friends instead. School is supposed to be a place for learning, where students focus on lessons and pay attention to their teachers.

It is also common for students to get angry when a teacher asks to take their phone, since they use them so often during lessons. Students actually learn more efficiently when they read materials, do their work, and think through problems on their own, without turning to their phones for every answer. One possible solution could be for teachers to collect all phones when students arrive at class, then return them once the lesson ends. Another serious issue is that students use phones to cheat on tests, looking up answers instead of trying to solve problems themselves.

On the other hand, there are clear benefits to using phones at school. They are easier to handle than desktop computers and load information much faster. If students are allowed to use them, they can look up details they don’t understand in class, find new learning resources, or explore different ways to grasp tricky topics. Many students are also faster at typing on their phones than on school computers, which could save time for some tasks.

Overall, I believe phones at school are both a help and a hindrance. They are definitely more convenient than computers, but the distraction they cause is a huge problem. Students end up focusing on their phones instead of the teacher, especially since they can access social media at any time. Phones also make cheating on tests far too easy. These days, young people need to cut down on how much they use their phones, since they are on them all day instead of focusing on their studies, which is exactly why many struggle to learn.

I fully agree with Emerson’s view on the value of individuality. If you want to stay true to yourself in a dull, repetitive world, you cannot stick to the same old routines. You need to adjust your lifestyle to match the life you actually want to lead, since every single person has their own unique thoughts and perspectives on how they want to live.

It’s often very difficult to reach this goal, though. Many people cannot pursue what they truly want, because chasing their dreams takes a lot of time, and failure is always a risk. So many of us fall into the trap of repeating the exact same tasks day after day. Take the common routine of waking up extremely early for work, working overtime until we are exhausted and bored—some people even start shifts as early as 3 or 4 a.m. They feel stuck, like they have no other options for their lives. But if people switch to a different path, they can grow into far better versions of themselves.

Even when people do change their routines, many are terrified of failing. That fear stops them from taking new steps or trying unfamiliar things. No matter what we do, we need to shift how we think about the world around us, so we can make choices based on what we actually like or dislike. Everyone has good options and sound decisions available to them, but the key is to clearly define the choices you make, and be more intentional about your decisions—that is how you improve. Look at all the famous people who have made huge differences in their own lives. Before they became well-known, they were just ordinary people like anyone else. They simply stayed true to who they were, planned their own unique path in life, and that made them different from others.

The world will never pick you—you have to be the one to choose your place in it.
