I’m convinced that each person shapes their own character through the choices they make, and those decisions have a huge impact on the person they grow into. Three key factors play into this: the friends you spend time with, the way you were raised and the home environment you grew up in, and your personal drive. Staying motivated, for instance, helps you develop strong, positive character traits that will benefit you for years to come.

The people you surround yourself with have a massive effect on your character, since you naturally pick up both good and bad habits from those around you. There’s a common saying that you become like the company you keep, and that holds true. If you spend time with people who only do good deeds, you’ll feel inspired to act the same way. On the other hand, if your friends are lazy, sit around the house all day and waste their time, you’re likely to fall into the same pattern and lose your drive to achieve anything.

Your childhood and the type of home you grew up in also shape your character significantly, because that’s the constant environment you’re exposed to every day. The vibe of your household is the energy you absorb all the time. For example, if your parents are constantly fighting and the home feels tense, you might start feeling depressed and down all the time. That low mood can make it hard to focus at school and hurt your academic performance. But if your home is warm, happy and full of positive energy, you’ll grow into a cheerful, optimistic person. That supportive environment will also help you do better in school, since you’re not weighed down by negative emotions.

In my view, motivation is the single most important part of building good character. Having a goal to work towards and staying driven is incredibly valuable. When you have that inner push, your past doesn’t define you, and you can become the best version of yourself possible. For instance, someone with strong motivation can achieve any goal they set their mind to. Even tough experiences, like watching your family struggle financially, can fuel your drive to work harder. As you push through those challenges, you’ll develop lasting positive character traits that stay with you for life.

To sum up, you are the one who builds your own character. You choose who to spend time with, you can take steps to improve your home life if it’s not working for you, and you decide what drives you to keep going. I don’t think anyone can be influenced beyond their control, because every action you take is a choice you make. If you don’t like the friends you have, you can find new ones. If your home life is toxic, you can arrange to stay with another family member or trusted adult. Everyone should remember that no one else has the right to control you: every choice you make, good or bad, is yours alone.

Is it a good idea to praise students’ work no matter how poor the quality is? On the surface, this might seem like a kind, supportive approach, but in actual educational settings, it is a very harmful practice. All people enjoy being recognized for their efforts. We only get better at something by practicing it repeatedly, and we tend to put even more effort in when we feel satisfied with what we are doing. That satisfaction often comes from receiving praise. But if students only ever receive praise, with no feedback on how to improve, there is little reason for them to keep learning. If every assignment gets an 'amazing job' comment or an automatic A+, they lose motivation to push themselves further. Even if they do make some progress, this approach causes major problems: it can make students completely unable to handle any criticism, and they may start demanding all the attention be focused on them at all times.

Artists provide a clear example of why this approach fails. Most artists are rarely fully happy with their own creations, even when they have made real progress. They might receive lots of praise from others, but that is not what pushes them to get better. Instead, it is their own dissatisfaction with their work that motivates them to improve. They learn to accept criticism calmly, without taking it personally, and use it to fix their work rather than getting upset. If we applied the 'praise no matter what' rule to students, we would be making a big mistake. The core purpose of being a student is to learn skills that you will use in the real world. In the workplace, people will criticize your work, and if you cannot handle that feedback, you are very likely to lose your job.

To be clear, I am not arguing that we should stop praising students altogether, or that we should make them dislike their work. Instead, I believe every bit of praise should be paired with gentle, constructive criticism. This balance helps students understand that for every positive, there is also room for improvement, and that the real world will not always be full of praise for their efforts.

I am convinced students achieve far better results when they stay busy with meaningful tasks, rather than sitting idle. Keeping active with purposeful work is far more valuable than doing nothing. When students engage in productive activities, they pick up new knowledge faster. Taking concrete action is the only way to make real progress. Students who stay active also advance further in life than peers who do little. On top of that, they grow more mature and gain a clear understanding of how the real world works. All these factors mean an active student will achieve far more over their lifetime than someone who never takes initiative.

The core reason I hold this view is simple: you can never reach a goal if you stay stuck doing nothing. First, we gain new knowledge every time we take action. I saw this firsthand in 4th grade, when I struggled with math. Instead of giving up, I practiced for 30 minutes every day after school for the rest of the year. After weeks of consistent study, my grades improved dramatically. I would never have made that progress if I had not chosen to act. Research also backs this up: students who stay busy with tasks after school achieve more than those who waste free time. They also get better at managing their schedules.

Students who achieve their goals also go much further in life than less active peers. My aunt, a doctor, is a perfect example. She dedicated herself fully to every task, from countless exams to long training shifts. She always balanced multiple responsibilities at once, and that hard work paid off. Another clear point is that people who push through challenges quickly learn success only comes to those who take action.

Another key benefit is that students who stay on top of work gain a better understanding of adulthood, and mature faster. Balancing school and a part-time job teaches young people to use time wisely. A student who works after class might have a heavy workload, but learns to use lunch breaks or free periods to get tasks done. Having positive role models also helps students grow more capable over time.

To sum up, the students who achieve the most are those who take action, rather than sitting idle. Active students pick up essential life skills, and go far further in life than peers who make no effort. They also grow into mature adults, because they choose to spend time on smart, productive choices.

I fully agree with Thomas Jefferson’s famous advice to never stay idle, and that constantly staying busy lets people achieve far more than they expect. The more effort you put into tasks each day, the more you will cross off your to-do list, which makes daily life far less stressful. There is no reason to put off a task you can finish today until tomorrow. After all, no one can spend their whole life doing nothing and still reach their goals. Success never comes to people who refuse to work hard. You have to push yourself to your full potential every day, but the rewards at the end will make all the effort feel worthwhile.

This idea has been a part of my life for as long as I can remember, because my mom used to repeat the same saying to me: “Never put off until tomorrow what you can do today.” That phrase has stuck with me permanently, and I use it to motivate myself whenever I’m working on school assignments or hitting the gym.It never fails to get me moving, and I plan to follow this rule for the rest of my life. In fact, my entire family lives by this same motto.

If more people adopted this mindset, the world would be a far better place. When individuals are determined to work hard for their own goals, far more people would be able to achieve success. We would see more people living comfortable, wealthy lives, and far fewer people struggling without a safe place to sleep. More people would also spend time creating new inventions to solve global problems, and no one would have to go without clean water or enough food.

Hard work also lets you make your family proud, and gives you the chance to give back to your community. You could even achieve things no human has ever done before, like traveling to every planet in our solar system to check if they could support human life. A world full of hardworking people would have lower crime rates and fewer lives lost to preventable issues, and there would be far more opportunities for everyone to reach their goals.

Thomas Jefferson did not share this quote by accident. He wanted to help people succeed in life, and he meant for readers to actually follow the advice instead of ignoring it. Jefferson hoped that people would go on to do incredible things, by staying active and productive instead of wasting time. If you stay determined and keep working, you will eventually reach your goals. Never give up.

A few years ago, a man accepted a dare to eat a ghost pepper, a chili so spicy it can cause severe health issues. Within hours, he was rushed to the emergency room, regret clear on his face. That’s a stark reminder of how bad decisions made without guidance can go wrong. I remember an incident from elementary school involving a friend we’ll call Generic_Name. Another kid walked by during lunch, knocked his tray off the table, and Generic_Name was ready to throw a punch. I stopped him and suggested he talk to a teacher instead of getting into a fight. Incidents like these show why turning to trusted authorities or loved ones for advice on big life choices is always a smart move. While some people might think handling everything alone is better, asking for professional guidance, talking to family and peers, and building self-confidence all prove that seeking help from experts and trusted figures for major life matters is a great idea.

The first key reason to seek support is the value of asking for expert help and guidance. A friend named Generic_Name was struggling to pick a college a while back. He had no idea which schools would fit his goals, so I urged him to meet with his school counselor. Following that advice, he got into Generic_school, a place that matched his needs perfectly. If he’d picked a college on a whim without checking if it was a good fit, he might have ended up at a school he hated, with no easy way to transfer. That’s why consulting experts who know the ins and outs of a topic is so valuable.

Another important aspect is talking to family, peers, and keeping communication open. I often ask my friends and family for advice on small and medium choices: which classes I’d enjoy, what sports I should try out, things like that. I think regular communication is great because it shapes how others see you, making you seem approachable. It also helps you build more friendships, since you can swap useful advice back and forth. People who avoid talking to others often struggle to connect, staying quiet and feeling lonely much of the time. This works because family and friends are always there to support you, no matter what.

Building self-confidence is the third major benefit of regular communication. When you talk to others more often, your confidence grows until you no longer get nervous speaking in front of a class. One of my close friends, also named Generic_Name, transferred to Generic_school a while back. He was extremely quiet at first, with a soft voice that was hard to hear. But after he started chatting with friends and family every day, he changed completely. Now he’s far more confident when speaking in public, almost like a different person. This shows how anyone can get over a fear of speaking by starting small: talk to family first, then friends, then people you don’t know as well.

At the end of the day, learning to talk to the people around you—family, friends, school staff—matters more than you might think. Some people have bad experiences with communication in the past, but the choice to improve is always theirs. No one likes feeling unable to speak up. I hope more people overcome their fear of communicating, because it’s a critical skill for the future. Most jobs require you to work well with others, and that starts with good communication. Even in fields like politics or media, people have to speak to millions of viewers on TV, which is impossible without strong speaking skills.

While plenty of students get distracted by their phones during lessons, others use these devices to their benefit. Even though many people argue that cell phones have no place in classrooms, I believe they should be permitted for research and project work during class. With a phone, we can learn about almost any topic instantly. For example, if a teacher is explaining a concept I don’t understand, I don’t have to interrupt the lesson to ask them for help. Instead, I can look up the topic online, find clear explanations and examples, and fill in the gaps in my knowledge on my own. I fully support the idea of letting students use cell phones in class.

People who want to ban phones in classrooms have their own reasons, of course. They often point out that phones are distracting, and that students lack the self-control to avoid checking them during lessons. They also worry that phones are addictive. But this isn’t always true. Most of us are capable of managing our own device use. If we use our phones responsibly, we won’t just learn more content—we’ll also build useful research skills that will help us become experts in whatever field we choose later on.

I have a personal experience that proves this point. A while back, I got sick during my English class and had to see a doctor, so I missed two days of school. When I returned, the teacher was going over instructions for our next assignment. I felt like I’d been away for weeks, not just two days. I told the teacher I’d missed a lot and asked what I needed to do, offering to complete all the work on my own. He explained that they’d covered new vocabulary, but he was in the middle of explaining another task, so I’d have to stay after school if I wanted help. I told him that wasn’t necessary—he could just give me the list of vocabulary words, and I’d look up their meanings online and write them down quietly so he could keep teaching. He agreed. If phones weren’t allowed in class, I wouldn’t have been able to finish that vocabulary work, and I wouldn’t have practiced finding reliable information online, which is a skill that’s not always easy to build. This is a clear example of why phones should be allowed in class: we can use them properly to support our grades.

Another example comes from my friend Generic_Name, who is 17 and has been my friend since middle school. We were both in a government class together last year, when the teacher assigned a group project: we had to invent a new country, giving it a name, choosing a location, and picking its rulers. At first, all students were given school computers to work on, but there weren’t enough to go around, and our group didn’t get one. We asked the teacher if we could use our phones for the project instead. She checked that there were no spare computers left, then agreed, as long as we only used them for the assignment. We immediately took out our phones and got to work, using them just like we would have used the school computers. We worked hard until the bell rang, and thanks to our phones, we used them for the entire project and submitted it on time with the rest of the class. This is more proof that phones are incredibly useful in class—they let us complete work even when school resources are limited.

To sum up, cell phones should be allowed in classrooms for research and project work. I know many people disagree with this stance, but phones offer real benefits to students. Technology is meant to make our lives easier, and we should take full advantage of it to support our learning. Phones can help all students understand class material better, no matter what school they attend. We should all think carefully about this issue, and decide for ourselves whether we believe phones belong in classrooms or not.

Success grows out of failure, as long as you never let your enthusiasm fade. Reaching your goals is rarely as straightforward as it sounds; it almost always requires long hours of hard work and plenty of missteps along the way.

Not everyone manages to achieve success, especially if they avoid failure or lack passion for their goals. Setbacks can knock you down, but it’s up to you whether you stay there or push yourself to work harder until you reach what you want.

Cristiano Ronaldo is widely regarded as one of the best soccer players in the world. When he first started his professional career, he was seen as just an average player, and he faced plenty of failures early on. There were matches where he didn’t score a single goal, or his team lost despite his best efforts. His strong enthusiasm pushed him to train harder and harder, and that dedication turned him into the player he is today. Many fans now call him the greatest soccer player in history, but his path to the top was far from easy. Each failure motivated him to work even harder to build a successful career, and even after 15 years in the sport, he still trains tirelessly to keep achieving in life.

Enthusiasm is what drives people to keep working toward success, even after repeated failures. It’s the feeling that pushes you to move forward no matter how many times you stumble. When you have that kind of inner motivation, failure becomes a small hurdle rather than a roadblock—most people with passion will keep trying until they finally reach their goals.

My mom is a perfect example of this. A few months ago, she was trying to get her driver’s permit, which required passing a test on all road rules. She failed the first time she took it, and felt really upset that she couldn’t get her permit right away. But she had a strong burst of motivation inside her that pushed her to study harder and retake the test. She actually failed the test five times in total, never gave up, and kept working to improve her knowledge until she finally passed and got her permit. A few months later, she earned her full driver’s license. She faced failure over and over, but never lost her drive. When you’re chasing success, it doesn’t matter how many times you fail—you just have to pick yourself up, work hard, and keep going until you win. As you can see, true success is all about moving from one failure to the next without ever losing your enthusiasm.

A topic that comes up often in current debates is whether schools should adopt the same schedule some businesses use to cut down on energy and resource use: a four-day week with ten-hour days, which would mean adding two extra hours to each school day.

Many people oppose this plan, arguing that making students, teachers and all school staff work longer hours each day would leave everyone exhausted far more quickly. They point out that four ten-hour days actually feel longer than a standard five-day week. There is also concern that schools might raise graduation requirements to make up for the lost day, which would mean students need even more time to finish their studies. Plenty of people also argue that schools could save energy without messing with the regular schedule at all – for instance, switching off lights when classrooms are empty, or opening windows to cool spaces instead of running air conditioning.

I believe adding two extra hours to the school day would be really hard for most of us. Nearly all students have after-school jobs, and some work full-time across more than four days a week. If school runs longer, we won’t be able to balance our work commitments. I also think that using energy properly in the first place would make a huge impact on conservation. On top of that, asking people outside the school community for their input could give us far better ideas for saving energy.

I also think that learning on a four-day schedule would be much tougher. Ten-hour school days would leave everyone feeling tired far more often, which makes it harder to take in new information. If we switch to this system, we’d have to wake up earlier and get home later than usual, but the amount of energy used would barely be different from a standard five-day week. There is almost no meaningful difference in total energy use between four and five school days. Tired students always struggle more to learn effectively.

To find the best solution, we need to share our opinions and talk through all the options. From my own experience, learning new material, units and information is already really challenging, and many students need more time to process things than others. Switching to a four-day week would make that even harder for countless students. As we have already seen, there are plenty of simple, easy-to-put-into-practice energy saving ideas – like the ones mentioned earlier – that cut energy use without removing any school days at all.

Isn’t technology amazing? Over the years, it has kept evolving, getting more advanced with every passing decade. But some people wonder: is all this progress cutting down on our face-to-face human interactions? I firmly believe technology has brought really positive changes to people’s everyday lives. Think about it: tech helps us build skyscrapers, design cars, and even fly airplanes. It’s also changed restaurants so much that you don’t have to tip staff anymore! Plus, stores use tech to make shopping way faster than it used to be.

Sure, it’s true that new technologies have replaced hundreds of traditional jobs. But even so, tech is one of the most valuable tools we have today. Take the Ford car company, for example. They use robotic systems to build their vehicles—these machines are so efficient they can finish a whole car in just ten minutes. That’s incredible! What’s more, Ford now sells trucks entirely online, no need to talk to a sales representative or deal with customer service at all. Ordering replacement car parts has also gotten way simpler: visit Ford’s official parts site, pick what you need, and get it delivered the very next day. Even the restaurant near my local Ford dealership runs entirely on technology, with no human staff handling orders.

Who would have thought that adding tech to restaurants would make everything run so much better? Ordering your favorite meal off a tablet is now easier than ever. Yes, this means fewer people are employed there, and you have less interaction with waiters or other staff. But there’s a big upside: you don’t have to worry about tipping, and there are no human errors in your order—you just tap exactly what you want right on the screen. While you enjoy your food, the few remaining staff can focus on other tasks unless a customer calls for them. Anyone who’s stood in a long Walmart checkout line knows how much tech has helped there too.

Have you ever watched a cashier take ages just to scan a package of chicken you’re trying to buy? I have, and it’s so frustrating to wait through that. Or had a cashier give you the wrong change? That happens all the time, and if you don’t check your receipt right away, you lose money for no reason. That’s exactly why self-checkout machines were invented—they make the whole shopping process way faster. Thanks to these machines, getting out of Walmart has never been quicker. You just scan your items and leave! It’s likely that soon every store in America will have these helpful machines. Sure, they glitch sometimes, but most of the time they work perfectly. It might feel odd at first not to see a person behind the checkout counter, but you’ll get used to it pretty quickly.

Having technology on our side has improved our lives and made day-to-day tasks feel less stressful. It’s brought so many good things into our world. Just imagine how hard it would be if Ford had to hire millions of workers to build cars, and only finished one every five hours? Or if you opened a restaurant and had to hire twenty workers who were rude or lazy with customers? And think about Walmart with hundreds of cashiers who take forever to scan and bag your groceries. All of that would be awful if we didn’t have the great technology we have access to today.

A growing number of companies now operate on a four-day workweek, whether to cut down on energy use or give their staff an extra day to rest. I strongly support the idea of switching schools to a four-day week too, with each school day running two hours longer than usual. One key reason I back this plan is that it would give students more time to finish homework, and also leave room for part-time jobs. On top of that, schools would slash their energy use by staying open one fewer day each week. School buildings burn through a huge amount of electricity, heating and water every day they are open, so cutting one day would make a big difference. Plenty of students have young children to look after once classes end, so a four-day week would be a huge help to them. They have to balance being both a parent and a student at the same time, which is incredibly tough. I feel really lucky to study at my current school, because they offer support to students who can’t find childcare for their kids while they’re in class.

From my own experience, this change would make a huge difference for me and many other students. We would have that extra day free to handle all sorts of tasks. For example, I work a job after school right now to cover my rent, groceries, clothing and other basic needs, and I also send money to help my mom. If I only had to go to school four days a week, I could work a full shift on the extra day off, earn more money and support my family even better.

I also agree with businesses that choose to close for one extra day each week to save on energy and costs. This hits close to home for me: when I lived in my home country, my family always tried to cut down on energy use because we couldn’t afford the utility bills. Sometimes I would forget to turn off the TV, and my mom would scold me, saying, "Turn that off, you’re not the one paying the electricity bill." I would get frustrated because I wanted to listen to music or watch my shows.

Many students have to juggle multiple roles at once: they are parents, students and workers, all at the same time. The week feels far too short to fit all of that in, so an extra day off would be a lifesaver. Balancing all those responsibilities is not easy for anyone. I admire my mom more than anyone — she had to act as both mother and father to me and my brothers. I used to wonder how she managed it all, until I realized she got up every single day because she wanted the best for us, no matter how exhausted she felt. We should never give up, because pushing through is what matters.

To sum up, I fully support moving schools to a four-day week with two extra hours added to each school day. Students often feel exhausted, and having an extra day to rest would help a lot, especially since many of us also work on weekends. Schools would benefit too, saving money on energy, food, water and other supplies. I hope the government will make this change happen, so my dream of a four-day school week can become a reality.

Is adding an art course to a student’s list of elective classes a smart choice? I firmly believe it is an excellent option for young learners. There are a few key reasons for this: many kids already have a passion for drawing, others get the chance to pick up new artistic skills, and these abilities can even come in handy in everyday life.

First, a lot of students who already love drawing will jump at the chance to take art as an elective. For instance, one of my close friends never had free time after school to work on her art projects. She spoke to her school counselor to request a spot in an art class, and once she was enrolled, she had dedicated time during the school day to focus on her creative work. Not only did she get to do something she was talented at, but she also earned a good grade for it.

Another benefit is that art classes give students who have never had the opportunity to learn drawing a chance to build that skill. Many young people want to create art but have not had access to proper instruction before. Beyond just teaching drawing techniques, art classes cover so much more—something many students do not realize at first. My own mother once signed up for an art class hoping to learn how to draw, but she ended up gaining knowledge about art history too, which she found fascinating.

Critics sometimes argue that art electives are a waste of time, since students will never use these skills once they finish school. I could not disagree more. Plenty of young people dream of becoming professional artists later in life, and I know many working artists who earn a comfortable living solely through their drawing work. Students who take art classes now could even grow up to become famous for their creative work one day.

To sum up, these are the main reasons art makes a great elective for students. Some love drawing already, others want to learn the skill, and many will use what they learn in real life later on. Art is such a rewarding activity—why not let students enjoy it during school?

There is a common belief that first impressions are impossible to change. I disagree with this idea, though, since you can never be sure what kind of day another person is having. When I first started my job, there was a male colleague who was rude to everyone around him. I later found out he was having an incredibly tough day when we first met. After a few days, his mood lifted, and he began acting kindly to all of us. That’s when I realized he was actually a really good person.

I had a similar experience when I transferred from Generic_School to Generic_School. At first, I thought the move would be awful—I had to start from scratch, meeting new teachers, making new friends, and learning how the new school worked. I was also really upset about leaving all the people I knew at my old Generic_School. But after just one week, the teachers and students I met turned out to be kind and friendly.

Of course, some people still think first impressions are permanent. For example, many companies look for confident, hardworking, and responsible candidates when hiring. If a job applicant comes across poorly in their interview, they are very unlikely to get the role.

That said, I believe people can shift how others see them over time. For instance, if someone performs badly in a job interview, giving them a second chance could completely change that initial negative impression. In the end, I am convinced that first impressions can absolutely be changed.

When I was a kid, my parents always encouraged me to take on new challenges in life. They told me to step outside my comfort zone and reach for goals even bigger than I’d ever imagined, since no one else would achieve them for me. Have you ever considered leaving your comfort zone to chase your biggest dreams? I fully agree with Emerson’s view on this, because pushing yourself helps you improve, lets you stand out from the crowd, and brings the incredible feeling of finally reaching a goal you’ve worked hard for. That’s exactly why I stand by what Emerson said.

The old saying ‘practice makes perfect’ is one you’ve probably heard a thousand times from family or friends, and that’s exactly the point Emerson is making. How can anyone get better at something if they never practice? Even more, how can a person grow if they don’t put in as much effort as they possibly can? Back when I was in middle school, I really wanted to join the basketball team, but I wasn’t very skilled at the sport. One of my close friends who was already on the team told me he’d teach me everything he knew, as long as I was willing to work hard and practice with him every single day. We stuck to that routine right up until tryouts. When the day finally came, I played really well and earned a spot on the team. I only got better because I worked hard and refused to give up on myself.

Another key part of Emerson’s message is doing things differently from everyone else. My dad always told me this whenever I brought up college plans. He wanted me to pursue something impressive, but more than that, he wanted me to choose a path that was unique, not the same thing everyone else was doing. During my final year of high school, I decided to sign up for an online course. I did this not just to earn a credit, but to see what taking an online class was really like. At first, it was really tough. I was way outside my comfort zone, imagining being at home or in a classroom with no teacher there to guide me through problems. But two weeks in, I started getting the hang of it. Two months after starting, I completed the class with a B+.

All the hard work and time you put in will pay off in the end. When I first started that online class, I was terrified, but now I feel confident I could take all my classes online if I wanted to. That’s because I’ve been through the experience myself. It all comes down to practicing, whether on your own or with someone else, plus pushing yourself out of your comfort zone. If you tell yourself you can achieve something beyond your current limits, you will.

Some people argue that you don’t need to try new, different things to grow as a person. They’re completely wrong, and here’s why: most people can’t adjust to new situations or skills without making an effort to try them first. What’s more, you don’t have to master a skill to grow from it. Even if you just try something, you’ll learn what works and what doesn’t.

In conclusion, if you work hard and push yourself to step out of your comfort zone to try new things in life, you will always grow and become a better version of yourself!

Can you really get to know someone from a single first impression? A lot of people think a person’s character is closely tied to how they present themselves, especially the clothes they wear. They assume that how someone looks tells you everything about their intelligence or personality. I disagree with this, though—I think first impressions are often misleading, and they can shift completely for a few key reasons. For one thing, what you wear or how you style yourself never fully reflects your true personality or who you really are as a person.

In my limited experience, building real connections with people takes time. A bad first impression can easily get in the way of forming meaningful friendships or romantic relationships at first, but that initial judgment rarely holds up once you get to know the person better. Over time, your original opinion of someone almost always changes as you learn more about them.

Most of the close, long-lasting friendships and relationships I’ve seen actually started out with people disliking each other, or at least having a very poor first impression of one another. As they spent more time together, though, they got the chance to see the other person’s true nature, and ended up finding they got along really well.

To sum up, first impressions are a useful way to introduce yourself to others, but they stop mattering once you really get to know someone. That’s why I’m certain that first impressions are never set in stone—they always change as you learn more about the person behind the initial appearance.

Every individual has their own unique ideas and viewpoints, so there is no reason to stay silent about what you think. I believe holding and sharing your own opinions is a great thing, as it lets you speak your mind without always needing to ask experts for advice. Tryingto voice your thoughts is always worthwhile, but if you let fear or panic stop you from doing so, you will never find real success in life. For me, it is far better for people to make their own choices rather than follow others blindly.

People who constantly seek guidance from experts rarely achieve real success in life. They end up spending money on professional advice instead of trusting themselves, but if they learn to share their own opinions, they will have far more chances of landing a good job.

Speaking up about your ideas now can lead to better job prospects in the future. If you have an opinion, it is always worth sharing it rather than keeping it to yourself.

Of course, not everyone will agree with your ideas, and that is okay. What matters most is that you make your own decisions, as this lets you express your thoughts freely and access more opportunities, like finding a well-paying job. Sometimes, your own ideas might even turn into a successful business. The key is to speak up without fear, keep trying, and work towards a bright future for both you and your family.

To sum up, people who share their own opinions have far more opportunities no matter where they go. Employers are always looking for staff who can make decisions independently, rather than waiting for instructions. Everyone should keep trying to voice their thoughts and never let fear hold them back.

It is widely accepted that a positive mindset is the foundation of achieving success. No matter what action you take, even tiny, everyday things like blinking, if you lack confidence in what you are doing, you are already setting yourself up to fail.

This does not mean failure is something negative, though. In fact, failure is a crucial part of reaching success. Not only do you learn from the mistakes that led you to fall short, but you also return with a clearer understanding of what you are up against. The next time you try, you will have a new perspective, a better plan, and even a shift in attitude—all because of that one thing everyone labels as "bad": failure.

Let’s be honest, though: why would anyone choose to fail when they have a chance to succeed? If you are not willing to do what it takes to get what you want, there is no point in trying at all—you might as well stay home, lie on the couch, and watch TV series. The world is full of truly hungry people out there, and giving just 75% of your full capacity will never be enough.

This is exactly where a positive attitude makes all the difference. If you recognize your own worth and are willing to give 100% of your effort, you have nothing to fear.

When you stay confident and positive, you will chase your goals no matter who stands in your way, no matter what others say about you, and even no matter what the cost may be. That is the true key to success.

I do not support the idea of students taking classes from home via video conferencing tools. The main reason I oppose this online learning setup is that many students will skip logging in, doze off during lessons, or fail to complete their work, which could lead to a lot of kids failing overall. I can speak to this from personal experience, since I am a student myself, and I want to explain my reasoning clearly.

The first issue is that many students will not log in to their online classes at all. They might tell themselves they will join the next session, putting it off again and again until they decide the classes are not worth their time. Instead of logging in, they might go outside to play with friends. Sometimes, even when their parents remind them repeatedly to join class, they ignore the instructions and instead spend time playing games on their PS4 or scrolling on their phones.

The second problem is that students often fall asleep during online lessons, and teachers have no way to stop this. If we were in a real, in-person classroom, a teacher could tell a sleepy student to wake up and make sure everyone is focused on the work they are supposed to be doing. Having students in a physical classroom makes the teacher’s job much easier, since they can monitor everyone directly.

The final, but very important, reason is that students often do not complete their own work. Even if they log in to class, there is no way to confirm that the student is the one actually doing assignments. They might ask a friend or even pay someone else to finish their work for them. Teenagers can be difficult, but they are also very smart when it comes to finding shortcuts. Some people argue that learning from home is the best option, since students do not have to deal with morning routines like getting dressed or commuting, they can just open their laptop and join the teacher via webcam to learn. However, not all students learn well this way, many need an instructor right next to them to explain things clearly and help them understand the material better. That is why I disagree with the idea of students attending school from home.

Life moves through clear, fixed stages: we are born, grow up, reach adulthood, grow old, and eventually reach the end of our lives. Listing these steps is easy, but living through all those years is a long journey—especially now that more people are living to be 100 years old.

I fully agree that being raw and direct is more effective. It lets you treat life like a game while still taking on responsibilities, and earn your own money instead of relying on handouts from your dad. When you work to build your own future, you gain a real understanding of how life works.

I can speak from my own experience here. Even when I was a little boy, I started learning how to handle daily life. By age 8, I was making my own breakfast, cleaning up, showering, and laying out my school uniform on my own. When I turned 15, I took on small part-time work, which let me pay for some of my own expenses. Now, I have a clear grasp of how life works, and what I need to do to reach my goals. I have a vision for my future, and dreams of building a great life not just for myself, but for the people who are close to me too.

If you cannot take care of yourself or handle responsibilities, your quality of life will be much shorter.

To wrap up, you need to truly understand life, figure out your own vision and dreams for both yourself and your family. Start making your own plans to achieve your goals, so you can be completely independent and free, relying on no one else at all.

I fully agree that change is possible, even though many people insist it’s out of reach. Most of the time, the only thing stopping us is the mindset we carry: a mental block that tells us we can’t make a difference. For me, changing the world starts with shifting how we view our surroundings.

We need to adjust our perspective to truly see the environmental crises unfolding around us. Even tiny adjustments add up to massive progress, no matter how small they seem at first. Take global warming: it’s a problem we created, and we have the power to fix it. The issue is that no one wants to be the first to act, but our current habits are doing us no favors. Change is already on the way.

Lots of people claim they can’t change their own behavior because it’s too difficult, or that no one will notice their efforts anyway. But we have to adjust how we act day to day. Sure, people get tired after long, hard days, but I refuse to give up. Just like a tree shifts its leaves to a new color each season, I can change the world, starting with myself. Working as a team makes the impact even bigger: we can bring in other countries, get more people on board. If I can improve myself, I can help others see the reality of the world we live in.

Personally, I want to become a better version of myself to support the people around me: I want to be courteous, kind, responsible, punctual, and always try my best in everything I do. Improving my own life and the lives of others is my top priority. Even though nothing in this world is perfect, we have to lift each other up when we can. We should take pride in the good choices we make, both now and in the future.

I’m passionate about technology and electricity, two fields I plan to study. With tech, I’d love to build a personal home robot: everyone wants one to help with daily chores, and it would let people rest more. I know there are risks, like a bad software update making the robot malfunction, but the benefits far outweigh the downsides. For electricity, I want to design the first smartphone that charges using sunlight, without needing huge amounts of energy to power up.

It’s never too late to start making changes. Making mistakes is actually a good thing, because that’s how we learn. If you never mess up, you’re missing out on the key to success: turning bad choices into good ones.

My mom always says that being passionate about life gives you the power to change the world—or at least the world inside your own head, where you can create all sorts of things to help others. Even if you can’t pull off a massive, global shift, a single small act carries more weight than a grand, empty gesture. Change is coming soon, but a lot of people refuse to believe that, or insist bad habits are fine. That’s really sad to see: they need to open their eyes to what’s really happening in their communities and the wider world.

People say first impressions are almost impossible to change, and that’s true in many cases. Some people will never shift their views, but others can. I write about what I’ve seen, heard, and experienced myself: my own capacity for change feels small sometimes, but dreams can come true—even if they don’t happen in the real world, they can still come alive in your head. I dream of changing the world for people who need a little help to reach their own goals. They’ll always thank you for transforming their lives, and then it’s their turn to pay it forward. I’m grateful for the help I’ve gotten, and now it’s my turn to do the same for others.

Change shows up in every part of life: how we act in school, at home, in our neighborhoods, our countries, and in every conversation we have. Turning something ugly into something beautiful starts at home, and teachers play a huge role in shaping us, helping us study better and build brighter futures. The most important step is simply getting started. If I don’t take the first right step, no one else will. My teacher always says that changing how systems are built gets you to the goal you want.

I love the way I think about change, but I know I need a little extra help sometimes. I’d love to make short videos or animations and post them on social media: that way, people all over the world can see them, and say “this is exactly what I’ve been looking for.” I’ve answered lots of prompts, but this one is the clearest: nothing is impossible if you don’t give up. The change you make will be something countless people are proud of.

Your perspective is valid, no matter what you believe. Just don’t quit, keep moving forward. If everyone does their part, change will happen faster. You might not see the results yet, but the process is already working. We all make mistakes, but if we fix them, we can turn the impossible into reality. Life moves way too fast, so we have to live each day like it’s our last, and never give up. I’ll do my best, because change is closer than you think.

Have you ever stopped to think about how many people are unhappy just because they are pretending to be someone they are not? Right now, millions of people around the world are not living life on their own terms. It can be really hard to stay true to yourself when society treats being different as a bad thing. But the truth is, the biggest achievement any person can have is embracing their uniqueness and showing their true self in every part of their life. Being yourself is the key to happiness, even though fighting against others’ unfair prejudice is never easy. Accepting yourself exactly as you are can feel like a battle when everyone around you is trying to force you to change.

Many people believe that having a successful, amazing life means having lots of money, holding an important position, or owning plenty of material goods. But none of these things actually matter when it comes to being your true self. A person might have all of these things, but they do not define who you are as a person, and they cannot bring you real happiness. One very important truth is that without happiness, you have nothing at all. Research shows that at least 60 percent of people are unhappy with their lives, but this can change if they choose to be honest with themselves and cut out the things they do not want from their lives. The first step to happiness is being yourself. You cannot go through life lying to who you really are, because that only leads to a miserable existence. You have to accept your own personality and interests, based on your own thoughts, not what others expect. A serious consequence of not being honest with yourself is mental health issues like depression. This is a very dangerous problem, and one of its most common causes is not being happy with the person you are or the way you are living. For all these reasons, being yourself is difficult, but it brings the biggest reward of all.

Throughout your life, you will have to make countless decisions, and it is crucial to always listen to your own inner voice. You should never let someone else make choices for you if those choices will affect who you truly are.

First, it is very important to know exactly what you want, because that is the same as being happy with yourself. Always put your own opinion first—that is the path to real happiness. It is far too easy to follow other people’s opinions shaped by their own lives, or to be influenced by a world that constantly tries to turn you into someone else, someone you are not. But at the end of the day, what you truly want is the real answer to being happy.

Every person in the world is trying to find the right path for their life, and being honest about your feelings and all the things mentioned above is the way to reach that goal and be happy with who you are.

It is a fact that the world right now is like a constant battle, because most people are fighting for their rights and trying to be honest with both themselves and the rest of the world. But this is never an easy task. The only person whose opinion you need to care about is your own—you do not have to worry about what other people think, only about what you think. Unfortunately, not everyone understands this. Sometimes, people just want the world to accept them for the simple fact that they are a person. It is very hard to be your true self when millions of people want to change your mind, and refuse to accept that everyone is different. There are things that do not need to be the same, and that is perfectly fine—diversity is part of what keeps the world balanced. Everyone, whether in their country or their local community, is here to learn about others and respect them, no matter their race, skin color, language, traditions, customs, or any other thing that defines a person. Nowadays, many people are working to make the world a better place where prejudice does not exist, and where every person can be who they want to be and have the rights they need and deserve. It is a difficult fight, but the result is the greatest accomplishment of all. Studies confirm that if you are happy with who you are, and accept your true self—including both your good qualities and your flaws—no one can bring you down. Once you reach that point, nothing can make you fall.

This is partly our own fault, because for too long people stayed silent when something was wrong. But it is never too late to change, and right now most people are trying to change the way society thinks about what is acceptable in the world. That is why accepting yourself exactly as you are can feel like a war when the whole world is trying to change you. We have to be strong and not let anyone question your decisions. Why is it worth cultivating a positive attitude? For starters, maintaining good manners and a pleasant outlook makes you far more likely to succeed in life. There are plenty of clear reasons why adopting this mindset helps, while having a negative, rude attitude will only hold you back. A bad attitude can make even simple tasks harder: you might struggle to land a job, miss out on good deals, or even end up with a harsher punishment if you act out in court, since judges are far less likely to be lenient toward someone who is rude or uncooperative.

First, people are naturally drawn to those with good attitudes. When you treat others with respect, they will usually respond by liking you and respecting you in return. This positive connection can boost your success in all areas of life. For example, if you go to a job interview with a rude, dismissive attitude, the hiring manager is almost certain not to pick you. On the other hand, if you are polite, friendly, and professional, your chances of getting the role jump significantly.

Second, having a good attitude helps you earn respect from those around you. When others respect you, they are far less likely to try to undermine your efforts or make you fail. If you act rude or hostile, though, people will often disrespect you in return, and may even go out of their way to block your progress. Earning this respect does take work, though: you have to start by treating others with kindness and respect yourself. You also need to be willing to help others when you can, since people are much more likely to support you if you have supported them first. Over time, this mutual respect will pave the way for greater success in your life.

Third, a good attitude makes it much easier to reach key milestones like landing a job or getting into a good college. If you have a rude, negative attitude, these goals will be far harder to achieve. For instance, if you are applying for your dream job or your top-choice college, having a pleasant, cooperative attitude will make the process far smoother. Employers and admissions officers notice how you treat others, and a positive attitude can set you apart from other candidates. In contrast, a bad attitude almost guarantees you will get rejected, or even kicked out if you already secured a spot and then start acting out.

To sum up, I believe that having a good attitude makes life significantly easier than dealing with the consequences of a bad one. A positive mindset will boost your success, help you win people over, earn you respect from others, and raise your chances of landing a great job or college spot. It is a simple change that can have a huge impact on your future.

Schools should not add two extra hours to the regular school day. Every student follows a fixed daily routine that includes part-time jobs, sports practice, or after-school club activities outside of class. Most students would much prefer a four-day school week over a longer daily schedule. If schools tried to adopt a four-day week but tacked on two extra hours each day, it would backfire: students would have almost no free time left, and might even have to start school earlier than usual. The biggest perk of a four-day week is a three-day weekend every single week of the school year. It also gives students more time to complete homework, finish missing assignments, and keep up with their grades in each class. There are also major downsides to extending the school day by two hours. Students would struggle to focus on lessons and assignments, and many would end up nodding off in class. If my own school ever added those extra two hours, I know I would stop paying attention to my teachers entirely. I would zone out or just nap until the final bell rang. Another advantage of a four-day week is that it could shorten the entire school year, allowing for longer winter holidays or spring break. These are just some of the pros and cons of switching to a four-day school week. Overall, I think it is a fairly good idea, as it gives students an extra day to rest and recharge. This is just my personal view on the idea of a four-day school week.

When I practice a task regularly, I find I can take on even more responsibilities. Many people believe that repeating an activity consistently helps us get better at it, since more practice builds our skills. Every time I do a task over and over, I perform better the next time I try it. For example, I have to read books to complete book projects for school. If I work on projects regularly, I earn higher grades and can even take on more projects. I also need to study for quizzes: if I prepare for them consistently, I get better results.

I often need to read all kinds of materials, including books, biographies, and more.

In my Generic_Name class, we have to read books to finish book projects. Reading regularly lets me complete more projects and earn extra points. For our ABC project, we need to read *The Lions* book: if I read it consistently, I can take on more related projects. In my History class, I have to read biographies, and the more I read, the better my grades are in that class. I truly believe that putting in more effort into a task lets me handle more work and earn higher grades.

Projects are a big part of my classes. In Generic_Name class, we always need to read books, since reading more lets us complete more book projects. Our ABC project is based on *The Lions*, and reading that book regularly means I can do more work for that project. In History, I read biographies to earn extra points: the more biographies I read, the more extra points I get. The more I study overall, the more extra credit I can earn.

I also have to study for quizzes all the time. In science class, I review my notes before quizzes, and the more I study, the better I do on the essay portions of the quizzes. I need to prepare consistently for my SOL exams too, since getting good grades on these standardized tests is very important. I take quizzes in History class regularly, and practicing for them always leads to good grades. It is much easier for me to study hard for quizzes than to end up with a bad grade.

Sometimes, doing the same task over and over again gets boring. But if I focus on what I am doing, I can achieve much better results. Whether I am reading a book, working on a project, or studying for a quiz, I need to concentrate. If I just go through the motions without paying attention, I will not get anything done. In my view, studying consistently while staying focused lets me do everything well and earn good grades. For all these reasons, I am sure that doing something regularly is always better than doing nothing at all.

The benefits of showing a positive attitude towards the people you meet are far-reaching. When you approach someone you’ve just been introduced to with kindness and openness, it often paves the way for meaningful connections, like strong friendships or even romantic relationships. People are far more likely to want to spend time with you if you leave them with a favorable first impression, as they’ll perceive you as someone pleasant to be around.

Take meeting a close friend’s parents for instance. If you want to make a good impression on them, you’ll need to stay pleasant and open to everything they say, rather than acting bored or uninterested. Workplace settings offer another clear example: maintaining a positive attitude at work cuts down on stress and makes the environment brighter for both you and your colleagues. When you avoid complaining about how tough your day is (remember, your coworkers are dealing with their own challenges too) and stop focusing on how unfair life feels, you create space for better connections. You might even start hanging out with coworkers outside of work, building new friendships and making people enjoy your company a little more. After all, the tough parts of life will stay the same whether you complain or not, so choosing positivity is the better option. Ultimately, showing a good attitude to the people in your life—whether they’re friends, family, or coworkers—almost always leads to better results.

Should students decide on a future career path at a young age? Many people argue this is a positive step, since schools give young people the chance to explore a wider range of subjects and skills. Others disagree, pointing out that many students already have heavy responsibilities outside of class: they may work part-time jobs, help with household chores, or take part in other activities common for people their age. Despite these concerns, I believe students should pick a career direction early, for several important reasons.

First, starting early means students will be fully prepared when they enter the workforce in their chosen field. If they pick a career they are passionate about, they will get far more practice and learn much more than peers who decide later. They can focus on their chosen path every day, and most importantly, they will have no trouble proving their skills and knowledge once they complete their studies.

Another benefit is that in many communities, high school students are already expected to identify a potential career. This system helps young people figure out their area of expertise, and lets them see how well they performed in that field during their school years—whether they excelled or struggled with the work.

It is also very valuable for young people to know what they want to do with their future. Many adults still have no idea what career they want, or what their long-term dreams are. But those who decide early can feel certain about their path and make the most of every opportunity that comes their way. We have to take advantage of the chances life gives us. For example, when I was a child, my dad always urged me to sign up for extra classes: English, basic computer skills, guitar lessons, dance, and more. I always said no, because I just wanted to play with my friends. Now, I understand how important it is to learn new things, gain skills, create work you are proud of, and show the world what you are capable of. There are no limits to what you can achieve if you put in the effort.

Students who commit to a career early will also have more chances to learn about their chosen field. Schools can offer summer internships or after-school work placements, which is a fantastic idea. I can see this benefit clearly when I compare it to my home country. There, schools do not offer any career-focused programs. Students are not prepared or skilled enough to work, because they get no practical practice and no elective courses related to different jobs. They only study academic subjects, so most do not work while in school—their parents are the ones who hold jobs instead.

To sum up, I believe all students should take career-focused courses while they are young, as this benefits both society and the students themselves. They will gain a wide range of knowledge and be ready to start work in the field they chose in high school, with no confusion or doubts about their ability to do the job well. They will end up with a profession they are truly skilled at. These courses are not just for showing off to others what you studied in high school—they are for your own future. Even if you go on to study further, these early classes give you a real advantage in life. You can gain real value from this opportunity if you take it.

Most people try their best to have a good day and bring joy to others too. For example, when I lived in Italy, there was an annual festival each year where everyone gathered in the town center to celebrate together. We’d chat, share food and drinks, and laugh for hours. You could have just as much fun without spending a cent, even if you had money to spare. This matters because happiness doesn’t come from your bank balance. It comes from surrounding yourself with people who lift you up and never make you feel small or upset.

In life, you should never follow the crowd blindly, and you can only truly rely on yourself. Do what you’re passionate about, and remember that you have just as much worth as anyone else. Some people in this world are jealous, and they might try to crush your dreams. If they say something mean or do something hurtful, you might lose confidence and stop chasing what you want. This is so important: never let someone else live your life for you, and don't let anyone control your choices or tell you what path to take.

Every day, I think about how much better the world would be if everyone made an effort to help those around them, especially younger people. Once, when I was in Italy, I went to the supermarket with my dad and a friend. We picked up all the groceries we needed, and when we got to the checkout, I noticed a guy trying to buy a sandwich. He told the cashier he only had 50 cents, but the sandwich cost $2. When he turned to put it back, I grabbed it and paid for it myself. He was so grateful and said, "My friend, you make my day better." I felt really happy that day too. This shows you don’t need to spend a lot of money to make someone else’s day brighter.

To sum up, I believe we achieve far more when we take time to help others. I want to tell everyone: live life on your own terms, and never give up on your goals. The moment you quit is the moment you stop believing in yourself, and that’s never a good place to be.

Being invited to teach elementary school students is one of the best things that can happen to you. You get to interact with all kinds of people: the students themselves, their parents, and even other family members who come to school events.

Leading lessons for young elementary students is a lot of fun. It also brings back clear memories of your own childhood days. You can choose any subject you like to teach, whether that’s math, English, science, or another topic the students are learning in class.

Teaching these young learners often brings back a flood of memories from your own time in elementary school. For example, if you are teaching a lesson on grammar and ask a student a simple question like "What is a noun?", and they give the correct answer, you might find yourself wishing you could go back to being an elementary student again. While teaching young kids can feel challenging at first, it gets much easier once you figure out how to connect with them. Trying out different lessons and activities also helps. Getting to know the students better and learning what they enjoy is really rewarding.

Spending time helping elementary students also gives you a better sense of what goes on in today’s elementary schools. You will get to meet many teachers, school principals, and guardians who come to pick up their kids. Sometimes, you might even run into a sibling or other family member at the school. Visiting elementary schools regularly can also improve your own learning skills and teaching techniques.

Being in an elementary school setting also reminds you of all the little things you used to do when you were a student there. You can even make friends with some of the older students, like 4th and 5th graders, who are often eager to chat with adult visitors.

Elementary students will sometimes challenge you with questions from other subjects, like math, science, English, and more. The games they play at recess or in class are also a lot of fun to watch or join in. When you teach them a new subject, it makes them more interested in learning every day. I relate strongly to this quote, as it highlights a common issue that affects countless families and communities worldwide. Too many people are pressured into pursuing careers or paths they have no real interest in, simply to meet the expectations of others. That is exactly why I disagree with Emerson’s statement. Everyone should have the freedom to pick a path they truly care about, rather than being steered toward a profession just because a parent or society claims “you’d make a great doctor or engineer.”

When you genuinely love what you study or the work you do, it brings a unique kind of joy. Every small breakthrough feels exciting, and you stay driven to keep improving until you reach your goals. Whether someone is passionate about learning a new language, writing, scientific discovery, healthcare, or helping others, they deserve encouragement to follow that interest. Being forced into a different path can take a real toll on both mental and physical health, which I’ve experienced firsthand.

For most of my life, I studied business in my home country because I dreamed of working in that field. When I moved to the United States last year, my parents and everyone around me insisted I become a nurse. I’ve never had any passion for nursing, but with no support for my business goals, I gave in and chose the nursing path. Now, I feel constantly anxious about the difficulty of the work, and I often doubt myself when I think about my studies. If I were pursuing something I loved, I wouldn’t mind the challenge at all. I’d focus on finding solutions, trust in my own ability to succeed, and stay fully committed to my goals. That is what it means to be truly motivated: having the support to chase what you love makes all the difference.

I know some people agree with Emerson’s view, believing that your surroundings and society shape who you become. But I think that’s only true if you let them. The people around you cannot force you to go against your own wishes unless you give them that power, as I did. If you stand firm, explain why you care about your chosen path, and show how achieving it would mean everything to you, you can stay true to what you want.

Some people argue that teachers and parents should praise students' work to boost their self-esteem, even when the work isn't the student's best effort. They say self-confidence is essential for learning. I agree with this view, because personal growth matters far more than staying stuck in the same place forever. If a student doesn't believe in their own abilities, they will struggle to finish tasks or reach their goals throughout their life. Also, this kind of positive feedback helps build a positive mindset that pushes students to keep going. All students need healthy self-esteem to lead successful lives.

When a student doubts their own capabilities, they often fail to complete important tasks later in life. Those who don't think they are capable of more will stay exactly where they are, unable to grow, and their self-esteem will only keep dropping. The truth is, there are no real limits to what a student can achieve if they trust in their own potential. If a learner knows they are capable of improving, they can grow easily by practicing more and holding onto that belief. Giving up on self-belief will hurt a student's future opportunities, so they should never stop trusting in what they can accomplish.

Creating a strong, positive mindset is key to helping students keep moving forward. To build healthy self-esteem, a student needs to set clear goals to prove to themselves that they can achieve more. After writing down these goals, they should decide which one to tackle first, based on their own priorities. Students also have many sources of support to choose from: personal goals, encouraging friends and family, or their own drive to succeed. Even if a student doesn't put in their full effort the first time, setbacks happen to everyone. This should never make them quit trying—instead, they should remember that a first attempt that isn't their best just means they can do better the next time. Students should always pursue the things they truly want. Building this kind of positive mindset is very important for developing strong self-esteem. The core reason we should praise students to boost their self-esteem is simple: no student should be discouraged, even if their first try at a task isn't perfect. Everyone deserves the chance to develop healthy self-esteem and keep growing throughout their life.

I strongly believe that collaborating with a group of people is far better than working alone. For one, time passes much more quickly when you are working alongside others, and you also get tasks finished far faster than when working solo, rather than slogging through work by yourself where the hours seem to drag on forever. You also feel more upbeat and motivated when you have teammates around, whereas solo work can turn boring in no time at all.

Group members can support each other whenever someone gets stuck on a task. If you do not understand a certain part of the work, your teammates can explain it to you, which also helps you learn how to handle similar tasks in the future. Another nice bonus is that group work lets you build new friendships with the people you collaborate with.

For example, imagine working on a project with four people. Presentations especially require thorough explanations and answers to many possible questions, which is much easier to manage as a team. That is why I am convinced that working with a group of people is the better option.

People hold all kinds of different opinions about community service, but I think making it a mandatory activity for students is a great idea. I also feel it would be fairer to listen to students more, as they currently don’t have enough opportunities to voice their opinions on this topic. Even so, my own view is that requiring students to take part in community service is a wonderful idea. I believe this kind of work is good for the local community, even though doing it can feel like a punishment. That is why I think offering it as an optional activity is a bad move. It should not be a choice for students. For instance, I once had to pick between two options: one was terrible, and the other was only slightly better. This experience taught me that having to make such choices is not a good thing. It also feels unfair to people who want to support their community, but don’t want to have to choose between helping out and enjoying their free time. Since having options is not ideal, I believe the best solution is to make community service mandatory for all students.

Studying remotely from home is not the best option overall. For one thing, learning in a physical classroom is very different from studying at home. When you attend school in person, you have far more learning opportunities. If you struggle to understand a topic, you can ask your teacher for help right away, and they can explain the material as many times as you need. That said, remote learning is unavoidable at times—for example, if you are sick or have another valid reason to stay home, online classes are necessary to keep learning. The most important thing is to stay motivated and work toward your goals.

Remote learning does have some benefits, though. It can make you feel more upbeat and focused, since you can take classes at whatever time works for you. You also get more chances to listen carefully duringonline lessons, and you can fit in other activities you enjoy alongside your studies.

Many schools now offer occasional home-based classes, which is a great idea. But in-person school is still really important: you can take more courses and graduate alongside your classmates. Video conferencing is somewhat similar to in-person learning because you see the teacher giving lessons, but the main difference is you cannot ask for help right away.

In conclusion, attending school in person is far more important and helpful than distance learning or video conferencing. In my view, in-person classes are necessary because they give you more opportunities to learn and keep making progress toward your goals.

It is common for some students to be expected to settle on a career path by the time they start high school. Figuring out a future job during high school can help students make more thoughtful choices and gives them extra time to decide, though they are not required to pick a career at this age.

First, selecting a career during high school allows students to build basic knowledge and hands-on experience related to their chosen field. Committing to a path at a younger age helps them develop a sense of responsibility for their future and gives them a clear goal to work toward. For example, a student who decides on a career early can take relevant classes, join related clubs, and gain experience that will make them better prepared when they apply to university.

Second, students who choose a career in high school have more time to research their options thoroughly. They can explore different aspects of the field they are interested in, and if they realize it is not the right fit, they still have time to switch to a different path without wasting time or money later. By the time they enroll in university, they will feel more confident about the subject they are studying, instead of risking spending tuition on a degree they do not actually want. For instance, if a high schooler picks a career path, then decides a few months later it is not for them, they can change course immediately, rather than wasting years and money on a university program they will end up dropping.

In conclusion, many students face the expectation to identify a career by the time they enter high school. Choosing a career during high school helps build experience and knowledge for their future field, and gives them more time to research options and switch paths if needed, avoiding wasted time and money on unwanted university studies. While this expectation exists, students do not have to settle on a career during high school.

I think a big reason many people struggle with these habits is that their parents did not guide them enough when they were young.

When I was a child, I lived with my grandmother, and she was a major positive influence on me. She told me that once I turned 13 or 14, I should never start smoking, because cigarettes would ruin my health and my life. She also warned me to stay away from beer. One piece of advice she gave me has stuck with me ever since: always keep working toward your goals, and never give up. I have never forgotten that lesson.

Another important influence in my life came when I moved to the United States. At first, I could not speak English at all, but now I am much more fluent. I got better by reading books whenever I stayed home or had free time. I also improved by asking my teachers for help whenever I did not understand a question or a lesson.
