People who prioritize self-reliance often define it as the need for each individual to follow their own instincts and ideas. Should they seek guidance from experts and authorities on life’s most important matters? Take a position on this issue, and support your response with reasons and specific examples.

People value all kinds of different things. For some, it’s material items like clothes, shoes, phones, and gadgets. For others, it’s their family, friends, home, or savings. Everyone has their own unique set of values, shaped partly by their background and upbringing. Everyone also has to make their own choices in life based on what matters most to them. For example, if a girl buys a $100 pair of shoes with her own money, she will care deeply about keeping them in good condition. Many girls would never spend that much on shoes, so she will get angry or upset if they get dirty, scuffed, or damaged in any way.

The same goes for guys who spend money on expensive sneakers from brands like Nike, Adidas, Jordan, or KD. If their shoes cost more than $300 and get ruined, they get extremely upset. They hate when other people mess with their shoes, avoid stepping in mud, and will never wear their pricey sneakers to do outdoor work or manual labor.

If someone knows they will be doing outdoor work, they should buy affordable, durable shoes instead of expensive designer pairs. Work-appropriate shoes only need to cost between $20 and $50, not hundreds of dollars. This way, they don’t have to stress about checking their shoes every minute to make sure they stay clean, or worry about ruining a costly pair that they worked hard to buy.

Many teenagers complain about having to get a job, but working is important, especially if they want expensive items. It’s common for teens to beg their parents for pricey sneakers or gadgets they can’t afford on their own. When teens work, they learn how much everyday items actually cost. If they just ask their parents for things without working, they will keep demanding more and more expensive items, which is not sustainable for most families.

Everyone should understand the value of money by working for the things they want, instead of asking others to buy them. When you pay for something with your own earnings, you learn to take good care of it, and you are less likely to waste money on overpriced items you don’t need. The more teenagers work instead of relying on their parents for handouts, the more responsible they will become.

I work part-time, and I like to save my earnings so I can buy the things I need. That said, I also deeply value gifts from other people, because I know they took time out of their day to pick out and buy something for me. Last Christmas, I bought a pair of AirPods for a close friend, as well as a pair for myself. When I gave them to him, I told him I hoped he would enjoy them. I am glad I was the one to give him that gift, instead of someone else. He was overjoyed with the gift. I was his first girlfriend, and when I told him I would be moving away soon, he got very sad. He told me that he values me a lot, because we are always there for each other, no matter what.

My core values are my sister and my friend RJ, who helped me find my current partner. My partner makes me happy every single day, and we get to do all kinds of fun activities together outside of school. He is the best person I know, and I love him with all my heart. No matter if I am sad, upset, or having a bad day, he always finds a way to cheer me up.

A number of schools now let students use mobile phones in class for learning activities. Supporters argue that phones are handy tools for quick research when students have questions. However, I believe mobile phones should be banned from classrooms entirely. My reasons are simple: most students spend all day glued to their screens instead of focusing on lessons, they often use phones for non-school activities, and these devices are a major source of distraction.

First, when students have access to phones all day, they rarely pay attention to what is being taught. The main reason young people attend school is to learn, not to scroll through their devices. While it is true that phones can help look up information quickly, this benefit is lost if students never actually listen to lessons. For example, a student might use their phone to check a fact during class, but if they spend the entire period messaging friends or watching clips, they will have no idea what to do when test or quiz time rolls around. They end up knowing nothing because they wasted class time on their phones instead of engaging with the material.

Another issue is that phones are rarely used for schoolwork when students have them in class. Instead, they text friends, play mobile games, watch videos, or listen to music rather than paying attention to the teacher. Many students also take photos or record videos to post on social media, or just to mess around. For instance, some learners take embarrassing pictures of classmates to share online, or even use them to bully others on social platforms. None of these activities have anything to do with learning, and they create a hostile environment for other students.

Some people claim that phones are useful for completing homework, working on projects, or clearing up confusion about a topic. While this is technically true, the distraction factor makes this benefit almost irrelevant. Students often get pulled into social media apps, text conversations, or video calls instead of doing the work they are supposed to finish. They might start looking up information for a project, then get distracted by a notification and forget all about their assignment. If this happens regularly, their grades will drop drastically—teachers may even give them a zero for unfinished work if they are too busy on their phones to complete tasks.

To sum up, even though some schools allow phones in classrooms for educational reasons, I believe this policy does more harm than good. Students will not absorb any useful information if they are focused on their devices for the entire class. We all know that most young people love spending time on their phones during the day, but these devices do not support academic progress. They will not help students master the material they need to learn to succeed in their education.

Thomas Jefferson once wrote, "Determine never to be idle. It is wonderful how much may be done if we are always doing." I completely agree with this view. Many people complain they never manage to complete tasks, but that is usually because they refuse to put in consistent effort. They prefer to lounge around doing nothing, which is exactly why they achieve so little. In contrast, if you stay busy and tackle tasks one by one, you will get far more done. For example, if you have a report to write, you work on it until finished, then move to the next task, and the next, building a long list of completed work. You do not just finish one project, then declare you are done forever and spend the rest of your life relaxing. All that consistent effort brings rewards. You are never working for no reason – every bit of hard work pays back. Jefferson’s words carry weight because he lived by this rule himself. He was constantly working on new projects, accomplished a huge amount in his lifetime, and never let himself sit idle. We should follow his example. I believe his core message is to encourage everyone to stay productive all the time, because when people take action, the whole world moves forward.

Some learners argue that an extended summer holiday is beneficial, as the long time off lets them hang out with friends. I, however, believe schools should operate year-round, with a 3–4 week summer break, a longer winter holiday, plus one week off in both spring and fall. This setup helps because studying the same material nonstop grows boring, and regular breaks give students more chances to rest.

Other supporters of the traditional long summer break point out that students always enjoy extended time off, and it lets them travel abroad if their parents are living in another country. For example, they can return to their home country to visit parents, friends and relatives during the months off.

My view is that the year-round schooling model with these shorter, regular breaks is far better. If students attend classes nonstop with no time off, they become much more stressed from repeating the same academic routine day after day. Also,

Also, regular short breaks throughout the year ease mental pressure, since students are not overwhelmed with work for months on end. What's more, many students feel reluctant to return to school after a very long holiday, so shorter, more frequent breaks are more effective than one extended summer off.

To sum up, I firmly believe the year-round school system with 3–4 summer weeks off, longer winter holidays, and spring and fall week-long breaks is the best approach. Studying the same subjects constantly can grow tedious, so regular rest periods are essential. Long holidays also make students lazier and less willing to return to classes, which is why shorter, spread-out breaks work better than one long summer break.

Have you set a big, ambitious goal for yourself?

Nearly everyone has goals they want to achieve, though some aim for big, challenging targets while others pick small, easy ones.

Big goals are often tough to accomplish, but you should never lower your target to an easier one just because it feels less stressful.

Even if you tick off a hundred small goals, that doesn’t equal the value of one ambitious target. A single big goal can lead to real success, while finishing a hundred tiny ones will almost never help you achieve anything truly meaningful.

Setting ambitious goals is key to becoming an outstanding person. When you push for big targets, you can excel at almost anything you try. By contrast, sticking to small goals will never let you achieve real success.

First, ambitious goals help you grow into a remarkable person. Take Keanu Reeves, the famous and successful actor, as an example. He is widely admired not just for his career, but for showing that money isn’t the most important thing in life. Sometimes, a big goal has nothing to do with wealth at all—it can be a personal target you set for your own growth.

Second, chasing a big goal lets you stand out in any field. Kobe Bryant, one of the greatest NBA players of all time, became the best in basketball because he was determined to reach the top of the sport. You are no different from him: if you work hard at something you truly love, you can become the best at that too.

Finally, settling for small goals will never make you successful. People who only aim for easy targets rarely learn from their mistakes, and they never grow as individuals. If you want to achieve something meaningful, you need to find a passion and chase after it with everything you have.

Big goals can feel impossible to reach, and they will definitely be challenging. But you should never give up. Telling yourself “I can do this” is the very first step on the path to success.

First impressions matter a great deal in our lives, and I fully agree they are almost impossible to change. For example, an unappealing dish will put you off eating it, no matter how tasty it is. A bad first impression of a person makes you avoid talking to them, and when shopping, we judge stores by their first appearance or reviews.

Take dining out: you wait 15 minutes for your meal, only for it to arrive looking so gross it makes you feel sick. Even if it tastes good, you won’t want to eat it. A nicely presented dish, though, will make you dig in without hesitation, regardless of how it actually tastes.

Another case: your parents introduce you to someone who never stops talking, rambling like a buzzing insect. If you hate constant chatter and prefer quiet, their behavior will immediately put you off. You’ll dislike them and stay away, and that negative first impression will keep you apart from them for good.

First impressions also guide shopping. If you and a friend visit a new area and search for stores on your phone, you might find one with pretty items. But if almost all reviews are bad, with only a few positive ones, you’ll pick a different shop, assuming the products are low quality.

Overall, first impressions are very hard to reverse. Once you form an initial opinion of someone or something, it stays in your head. No matter what new info comes later, that first impression always comes to mind first, because the impact of a first encounter is truly unforgettable.

I fully agree with the statement from the Association Church that defines success as pushing through one failure after another, never letting your excitement for your goal fade, until you finally achieve what you have been fighting for. That said, the era when this idea was first shared is very different from the world we live in today. Groups like the Company Association, churches, and governments no longer operate the way they used to. These days, if you are working toward a goal and happen to fail, people are quick to judge you as unfit to make your dreams come true, even though failure is actually a vital part of reaching success. I want to share a specific example that shows how failure can push you closer to your goals.

Take your first day at a new job as an example. Most people have been in this situation: you feel lost when your boss or supervisor gives you instructions, and you struggle to follow them correctly. Instead of stepping in to teach you, some coworkers laugh at your mistakes, and hardly anyone offers to help. They wait until you mess up, then act like they are assisting you after the fact. But as you probably already know, the world is not a kind, gentle place. It is harsh and unforgiving, and no matter how tough you think you are, life will knock you down and keep you there if you let it. No one—not you, not me, no one at all—gets hit as hard as life can hit you. But life does not care how badly it knocks you down. The only thing that matters is how much you can endure, how many setbacks you can take and still keep moving forward. If you know your own value, go out and claim what you deserve. You have to be able to withstand those blows, and never turn to blaming others, saying things like "I can’t become the person I want to be because of him, or her, or anyone else." That is how true winners are made.

To sum up, every failure plays a key role in helping you succeed in life. Sometimes, a setback is exactly the push you need to reach a higher level. On top of that, you have to be able to ignore the criticism of others. If you cannot do this, your enthusiasm will fade, and all your hard work will be for nothing.

I completely agree with this idea, because it’s true: if you never learn anything beyond what you already know, you’ll never find real success in life. I used to be guilty of this myself, and it’s upsetting to realize how much time I wasted doing nothing productive. This question made me think deeply—I’d never considered trying to do better than what I’d already achieved. Sometimes when I did try, I was terrified of failing or making mistakes. But I’ve learned that small changes add up, and knowing even a little more than you did before opens up more opportunities and helps you grow as a person.

Trying something totally new is scary for everyone, no matter how old you are or how brave you think you are. If you struggled with a task before, you’ll probably feel scared doing it again even if you already know how to do it. For example, I worked at a Japanese restaurant for a year and a half. It was my first job as a server, and I was terrified to start. I only took the job for the money, but I surprised myself by succeeding. My boss told me I was doing a great job, and I felt so proud—even though my English wasn’t perfect back then. Later, I had a lot of issues with him over pay, so I decided to look for a new job. A friend told me her boss was hiring servers, so I applied. But when I saw how big the new restaurant was, and how different it was from my old one, I panicked. Looking at the menu, I kept thinking, "You’re going to fail."

I felt awful that day. The whole process of adjusting was long and painful, full of mistakes I’d made along the way. But I pushed through and succeeded again. Now, looking back, I realize what I went through wasn’t actually that hard. I’m not an expert at serving yet, but I’m still learning every day.

A lot of people are content to stay exactly as they are and don’t want to learn anything new. Unfortunately, I used to be one of those people. I failed plenty of times because I thought I already knew everything—sometimes even more than the people around me. For example, one day I took a Spanish test. I’m a native Spanish speaker, so I felt totally confident. Most of my classmates were studying for the test, but I didn’t bother. I ended up failing, because there were questions I never even knew existed. That test was important for getting course credit, so I lost out on that. That day, I learned a key lesson: even if you know a lot about a topic, there’s always more to learn.

To sum up, you should try to get a little better every single day. Remember that there is always more to learn, even if you think you already know everything there is to know about a subject. Keep in mind that trying new things doesn’t have to be scary—every human has the ability to learn and achieve whatever they set their mind to. The only thing holding you back is the limits you set for yourself.

Some learners choose to take classes from home because they live too far from campus or have no way to get there, using recorded videos or online platforms to study. Even so, I believe attending school in person is far more helpful for learning. Teachers often assign plenty of homework to help their students pick up new material, but even students who live far from school still take buses, trains, or other transport options to get there, because they are focused on building a good future. Taking classes at home is not a bad idea, though, since everyone wants to achieve their long-term goals: whether you attend school in person or take online courses, education is key, even if not everyone has access to the same chances in life.

In my view, online classes are not as beneficial as in-person learning for most students. It is often hard to focus when studying at home, since there are many distractions that get in the way of understanding the lesson. Teachers may also struggle to deliver content effectively through a screen. At school, by contrast, students face fewer distractions and are more likely to pay attention when teachers lead lessons. Teachers can also push students to stay focused, since they want their classes to learn as much as possible.

That said, some people do not have the option to attend school in person. They pay for online courses because they work full-time jobs. For example, many Hispanic immigrants in this country work long hours to cover rent and other bills. Some want to learn English to qualify for better jobs, so they sign up for paid online classes to pick up the language or gain new skills. For these learners, online education is very beneficial, as not everyone has the same access to opportunities.

School plays a very important role in people’s lives, but not all students feel the same way about it: some enjoy going, while others dislike it. Students who want to build a good future need to have clear dreams, because people without goals rarely achieve anything meaningful. Parents often give their children access to educational opportunities, but many kids around the world still lack any chance to learn.

Overall, I think online classes are a good option for people who cannot get to a physical school. Even though remote learning is not the same as attending classes in person, anyone with big dreams can still succeed through online courses, because everyone has goals they want to reach.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once claimed that staying true to who you are, even when the world pushes you to change, is life’s greatest achievement. I disagree with this statement. In reality, most people fail to pursue their own goals, instead trying to become someone they are not, and rarely show their true selves to the world.

First, far too many people never reach goals that actually matter to them. When society, family, or peers pressure someone to take a certain path, they often stop chasing their own dreams entirely. People need to pick and work toward goals that feel right for their own lives, without outside voices dictating their choices. Too often, individuals adopt goals pushed on them by others, only to realize later they never wanted those things in the first place. Many people struggle to tell the difference between what they truly desire and what they want to avoid doing. Those who fail to set or reach their own goals usually end up trying to become a version of themselves that fits external expectations, rather than staying true to who they are.

Another key issue is that most people actively try to be someone they are not. Many have attempted to embrace their true identity but felt they could not figure out who that person really is. The vast majority of people choose to act like someone else rather than honoring the person they are inside. The world can feel like an overwhelming place, so many avoid sharing their true thoughts or personality publicly. Instead, they mold themselves to fit in with others, even if that means hiding their real self. Most people who take this path end up unhappy with their choice, since they are constantly suppressing who they really are.

On top of this, most people refuse to show their authentic selves to the world. Many are unhappy with who they are, so they avoid expressing their true personality in daily life. Instead, they keep their real identity hidden from others. It is common for people to dislike looking at their true selves, often because they have not yet taken the time to figure out who they really are. When given the choice, most people will prioritize becoming whatever society expects of them over chasing their own personal goals.

In conclusion, I do not believe being yourself is the greatest accomplishment, as Emerson claimed. Most people are not living as their true selves, instead hiding their identity to become what the world expects of them. This quote is inaccurate because so many people fail to reach their own goals, choose to imitate others rather than be themselves, and refuse to show their authentic personality to the world.

Thisguide for teenagers covers the topic of expectations. A key question many ask is: do students benefit from taking classes from home?

First, let’s discuss what students expect from their education. For many, learning from home is a valuable option. For instance, some teens have to work part-time to support their families, so home classes fit around these duties. Others face barriers to attending regular school, such as feeling they lack equal access to education, or believing they cannot succeed in a traditional classroom. I support programs where teachers or school staff visit students’ homes when needed, so learners never miss lessons even if they cannot get to campus.

Another important factor is personal responsibility. In the area where I grew up, students often have to walk very long distances to reach school. Sometimes teachers even travel to students’ homes to deliver lessons directly. Many families also cannot afford transport fares, or do not have access to reliable buses or cars to get kids to school. To finish school and gain more knowledge, you have to put in effort, but if you take responsibility for your studies, you can achieve a lot. Students who perform well in school often qualify for helpful scholarships that support both them and their families.

Many teens now take online classes. A lot of people choose this route, especially older students who already have jobs or other commitments. Some think a mix of in-person and online learning works best, which I agree with. It is also common for students to help each other navigate this path to graduation. Regular school attendance is often low because many students would rather go to work than sit in class, which is why so many switch to online learning. While some students do not care much about school at all, there are still plenty who take their education seriously.

Offering home-based classes at night is another useful option. Many people find this works better for their schedules, though not everyone has the chance to take home classes in the morning or late afternoon. A lot of students jump at the chance to finish high school online. They choose this path because they have other priorities, like full-time jobs, or because they would otherwise stay home without doing anything productive with their time.

To recap, home-based learning is a great option for many students. It works for those with family jobs, those in areas with long school commutes, and those who need flexible schedules. In my hometown, long walks to school and home visits from teachers are common, and students often support each other through their learning journeys. Night classes at home are also valuable for those who cannot attend regular sessions. I am currently finishing my high school diploma online, and I think it is wonderful to share this experience with others. Sometimes people doubt their ability to make good life choices, but having access to flexible education opens up so many opportunities for growth. Both in-person and home-based learning have their strengths, and combining them can work well for many teens.

I strongly prefer working in groups over completing tasks on my own, as I find collaborative work offers far more advantages. For one, team projects generate a much wider range of ideas than solo work ever could. When everyone works together, we collaborate closely on the task at hand, which helps us stay focused rather than getting distracted by outside things. Every group member contributes input on what the project needs, what topics to cover, what type of final product to create, and how to follow the specific instructions our teacher gave us.

Working together also gives the whole group a better shot at earning high grades. Even if some members don’t usually get top marks on their own, group work gives them a chance to improve their scores by contributing to a stronger final product. It also helps people who struggle to explain their thoughts when working alone: in a group, they can practice sharing ideas and collaborating with others, and get feedback on how to communicate more clearly for future team projects. If anyone needs help with a task or wants to improve how they express themselves in a group setting, their teammates can support them.

When we work in a group, we all bring different ideas to the table about what to tackle first, who should write the project title, or who has the best plan for presenting our work. We can discuss as a team to figure out the best approach for the task or project. By contrast, working alone makes it much harder to settle on a good idea, and I often end up disliking the work I produce when I have to do it by myself. I always feel I get more out of group work because when we make a key decision, everyone can weigh in—if someone likes an idea, they can say so, and we can adjust based on the whole team’s input.

Not every student enjoys working with others—some are quiet and hesitant to share their ideas, while others prefer to work entirely on their own. But even for these students, group work still offers clear benefits: it gives everyone a chance to share their thoughts and create better work than they could alone. When students work solo, many end up getting distracted by their phones or other things, and don’t pay close attention in class, which leads to either good or bad grades by chance. When we work in a group, though, teammates can remind each other of what the teacher explained in class, including what type of project or task we need to complete.

Overall, I believe all students gain more from group work when we complete tasks together to produce high-quality work. Of course, group work requires everyone to share their best ideas and support their teammates, and there is a risk that a member might not turn in their part of the work, which can hurt the whole group’s grade. But even with this potential issue, group work gives everyone a chance to improve their scores, learn more about the material our teacher covers in class, and make sure every member can pass the course.

All public and private schools should launch a new lunch menu, supported by a dedicated website where students can log in to fill out feedback forms, answer surveys, and note any food allergies. This system would help schools identify which dishes students actually enjoy, and keep track of allergy information to avoid any health issues during lunch. Right now, many students dislike the current school meals and choose to bring food from home instead, which is not ideal. The core issue is that every student needs to eat a proper meal to have enough energy to focus in class.

One practical step schools can take is to roll out new menu options every year, and let students vote on their preferences through the website. Once the results are in, the school can adjust the lunch menu accordingly. This would bring huge benefits for students: eating well-balanced, enjoyable meals helps the brain concentrate better on schoolwork and boosts energy levels. For example, offering fruit or coffee in the morning, followed by popular options like Popeyes, Chipotle, tacos, and other varied dishes at lunch would keep meals interesting. Students often get bored of eating the same food day after day, so introducing new options yearly keeps lunch appealing.

Schools should also establish clear routines to support better eating habits. For instance, students could do 10 minutes of light exercise first, then head to lunch around 10 a.m. to eat dishes like tacos, Popeyes, or Chipotle, paired with natural water infused with fresh fruit, before returning to regular classes. Offering diverse meal choices shows schools care about student wellbeing. Students will feel more focused, have more energy, and keep a positive attitude, since change can make a big difference to daily life and overall health.

When students eat meals they actually enjoy, they have more energy and a clearer mind when they get back to class, which is a major advantage. That is why it is so important for students to vote on different menu options, and for schools to update the lunch selection every year. Eating the same meals repeatedly makes students lose interest, so many end up skipping lunch entirely, going home early, or bringing food from home. Surveys show 50% of students do not like current school meals. Long, slow lunch lines also discourage students from eating, leading some to skip lunch or rely on home-packed food. Schools need to take these concerns seriously, as not eating properly during the day hurts students.

To wrap up, schools should create new surveys and feedback forms on the website every year, then compare responses over time to pick the best menu options for both students and teachers. Drinks should also include a variety of natural fruit-infused waters, since staying hydrated and eating well is essential for good health. Student athletes especially need proper, balanced nutrition to maintain full energy levels during training and games. Offering a wide range of meal choices that students and even teachers enjoy is a great way to support everyone on campus.

Good health should always be a top priority for schools. The key step is launching a website that students can visit each year before the school term starts to share their opinions, which will help update menus in both public and private schools. When new, varied menu options are available, more students will vote for their favorites and choose to eat school lunches instead of bringing food from home. Students and teachers will have better attitudes and feel happier overall when they get to eat meals they actually like. Schools should also add more lunch lines to reduce wait times, giving everyone enough time to eat properly. This will make students happier, and even long lunch lines will feel manageable when there is enough time to enjoy a good meal.

First, I think it is wise to listen to authority figures for life’s big matters. They have far more experience than someone making all choices alone, and we can learn valuable life lessons from them.

Second, even if some prefer making their own choices or sharing decisions with others, everyone should talk to trusted guides about their situation. This helps them gain experience and pick up useful new information.

In conclusion, we should learn more about making good decisions and seek out people with valuable life experience. This helps us make smarter choices as we go through life.

The local school board is considering extending the standard school day by an hour and a half. Is this a smart change to make? I strongly disagree with this plan, for three key reasons: it will cause excessive stress for students, disrupt after-school schedules and programs, and drive up already high electricity costs that could be better spent on school improvements.

First, adding 90 minutes to the school day will put a lot of pressure on students’ mental and physical health. Many teens already struggle to balance schoolwork with rest, and longer days will leave them exhausted from sitting in classrooms for even more hours. Overloading them with extra material to memorize can lead to anxiety or even depression, making them lose all motivation to study. They will have no energy left to complete homework after such a long day, and little to no free time at home to review what they learned. Before long, most students will stop caring about school entirely, and some may even start skipping classes regularly, which hurts their academic progress more than any extra class time could help.

Second, extending the school day will throw all after-school programs and activities off schedule. Most students will not want to stay on campus for clubs or sports if it means getting home even later than usual. Transportation is a major issue here: students who live in rural areas often have long commutes, sometimes up to an hour each way. These students already have to wake up as early as 5 a.m. to get to school on time. If the school day runs 90 minutes longer, they may not get home until after 7 p.m., which is too late for them to finish homework or get enough sleep. This makes after-school programs inaccessible for many, and disrupts the entire daily routine for rural families.

Finally, the financial cost of this change is too high to justify. The school board already spends over 6 million dollars every year just on electricity to keep the buildings running. Adding an extra hour and a half to each school day will increase that utility bill significantly. If so much money goes toward covering extra electricity costs, there will be almost nothing left in the budget to pay for other essential expenses, let alone much-needed updates to school facilities. This is a waste of funds that could be better used to support students directly.

To sum up, the school board should reject the plan to add 90 minutes to the school day. It will cause unnecessary stress for students, throw after-school schedules into disarray, and waste millions of dollars on extra electricity costs that could be used to improve the school instead. I firmly disagree with extending the school day, as the drawbacks far outweigh any potential benefits. Do you agree or disagree with the plan to extend the school day?

Have you ever thought about how much first impressions matter? I completely agree that it’s nearly impossible to shift someone’s initial opinion of you, since first encounters carry so much weight for all of us. Lots of people hide their true personality at first, trying to get everyone to like them, but eventually their real self comes out, and people end up pulling away. That first meeting says more about us than we might think. I’m convinced that if you’re open about who you really are from the start, people will accept you as you are, and they’ll trust you too.

We should always be honest with ourselves and with others. My personal rule is to stay true to who I am, never pretending to be someone I’m not, if I want people to be genuine with me in return.

I try to be warm, kind, funny and easy to get along with everyone I meet, and I’m always happy to help others using what I know and can do. A good example of this is my current job at a retail store. Every day, new staff members start working there, and I always take time to show them how to keep the store organized and run smoothly. I also smile at every customer I see, since that’s part of the first impression I want to give. It feels amazing when customers notice my smile, greet me with “Hi, how are you today? Great to see you, have a good day!” I’ve only been working there for a few months, but I already feel totally at ease with everyone. Even though regular customers don’t know me very well, they trust me enough to share little details about their lives. My coworkers and I get along really well too—we’re like a little family, and we always look out for each other.

School is a bit different for me, since I’m pretty shy there and only really talk to my closest friends. But I’m always open about how I feel, even around new people I meet at school. Unfortunately, sometimes people act nice when you first meet them, but their attitude changes completely over time. This happened to me a couple of years ago with two different people. The first was a girl I met in 9th grade, when we were both new to the school. We became inseparable, doing everything together. But as the years went by, she changed. One summer, a friend and her sister told me and my sister that this girl had been saying mean things about us behind our backs. I had always been honest and friendly with her, but she ended up acting nothing like the person I first met. Then there was another girl, who was a bit similar. She was jealous of my sister and me because we got good grades and were active in school activities, while she struggled with her classes. We tried to help her, but she never wanted to accept it. Eventually, my sister and I stopped hanging out with her, because even though she acted friendly to our faces, she was never a good friend to us.

I truly believe we should always be our true selves, no matter what other people think of us. It’s fine to make positive changes in your life, but you should never change your core personality. Something I always do is reflect on my own weaknesses, and figure out how to turn them into strengths.

To wrap up, I think being genuine sets you up for success in life. A good first impression can open so many doors. I’ve found that the best people are the ones who have a great attitude when you first meet them—you just get a feeling in your gut that they’re a good person. People will remember that they can trust you, and they’ll be happy to know someone like you. Of course, first impressions aren’t always fair. A lot of people don’t know me well, and they assume I’m stuck-up just based on how I look, without even taking the time to say hi or smile. In my opinion, everyone should try to be more empathetic, get to know more people, and make new friends—but always stay true to who they are while doing so.

When someone is determined, they usually have clear goals and dreams they are willing to work hard to reach. Even on days when they feel exhausted or start to doubt themselves, a little voice inside reminds them they can keep going. At those moments, they remember what they need for their own life and for their loved ones. Having a set direction in life makes the journey feel much less overwhelming than drifting without any purpose at all. I also think it’s really important for determined people to surround themselves with supportive family and friends who can encourage them when things get tough. My own daily routine is a perfect example of this. My main goal right now is to earn my high school diploma, but that takes a lot of hard work. I wake up at 6 a.m. every morning to make breakfast for my whole family, then gather everything I need for my full-time job. I work all day until 5 p.m., then head straight to night school, where I’ve been taking classes for a full year now. Sometimes I get so tired I want to give up, but then I think about my family, and especially the example I want to set for my daughter. The only way to reach my goals is to keep working hard, no matter how tired I feel.

Dear Principal, I am writing to express my full support for the school’s new cafeteria plans. Replacing current junk food options with healthier alternatives will do wonders for our health: it will help us avoid obesity, lower our risk of depression, and keep our bodies feeling energetic and active.

You might ask: does eating better really make our health stronger? Is obesity even a real issue for students our age?

The answer to both questions is a clear yes. Nutritious school lunches will boost our health significantly. Unlike junk food, which leaves our stomachs feeling weighed down and sluggish, healthy meals make it much easier to take part in sports and physical activities. Just look at professional athletes: they maintain their fitness and performance by sticking to balanced, healthy diets every day. Their example shows that healthy eating is key to staying fit and active, a lesson that applies to students just as much as elite sports players.

Eating well also protects our mental health. When we fill up on junk food with no nutritious options, we tend to gain weight quickly. Overeating these unhealthy foods can lead to obesity, and many students who struggle with obesity end up feeling depressed because they are unhappy with how their bodies look as the weight piles on.

Obesity is a serious threat to our health, not just for adults but for young people too. In severe cases, it can even make everyday tasks like walking difficult or impossible.

Beyond that, healthy food keeps students more active overall. When we eat nutritious meals, our bodies don’t feel weighed down, so we can move around faster and with more energy. Junk food, on the other hand, leaves our stomachs feeling heavy and makes us so tired after lunch that we don’t want to do anything at all. Healthy food even helps activate our brains, much like how physical exercise wakes up our bodies.

To sum up, I believe switching the school cafeteria menu to healthier options is an excellent decision. It will improve our physical health, protect us from depression, and keep us more active throughout the day. Providing nutritious food is the best thing the cafeteria can do for students: it helps us avoid obesity and takes proper care of our overall well-being.

People often claim that first impressions are almost impossible to change. I disagree — I think these initial views can definitely shift over time.

First, someone might come across as caring about no one and nothing at first. But once you get to know them, your whole perspective on who they are can change completely.

A personal experience backs this up. I once knew a woman I thought was the one — the person I’d spend my life with. My first impression was that she was a sweet, good person. But as I got to know her, I realized she was truly cruel, full of hate, and always looked for ways to blame me for things. She made up excuses to do whatever she wanted, and she had no clue that every one of these actions was making my love for her fade a little more each day.

In conclusion, this is why I believe first impressions are not impossible to change. People, including family and loved ones, grow and change, so the way we see them can shift too.

Is technology actually useful in our daily lives? I strongly believe it makes it possible for people to handle countless tasks with ease, and I view this as a clear benefit. For one, you no longer have to trek to the supermarket for groceries—online shopping lets you order everything you need from home. My sister often uses this option when she’s under the weather or too busy to visit a store, and her groceries are dropped right at her front door.

Another major advantage is that working from home is now an option for many. Even if your job is normally based in a physical office, you can use a laptop to complete all your work tasks without leaving the house.

It’s also a huge help if you don’t drive but need to get around. Ride-sharing apps let you book a car to take you anywhere you need to go in just a few taps. Clothes shopping is just as easy: if you don’t have time to browse in physical stores, you can look through options online and order exactly what you need. You don’t even need to visit a bookstore these days. You can read books on your devices, and even check out titles to read online without leaving home. Practically every chore can be done online, including paying bills and handling all sorts of errands. That’s a big part of why I think technology has improved people’s lives.

I have a personal example of this: my grandma lives in Generic_City, but thanks to video calling apps, we can chat with her face-to-face even though we’re in a different country.

Of course, there are some downsides. If people order everything online instead of going to stores in person, they get far less physical activity, which can lead to a more inactive lifestyle, or even laziness. Another issue is that many people barely interact in person anymore. They rely on texting or phone calls instead of talking face-to-face. For instance, whenever I visit my grandma’s house for holiday gatherings, my cousins spend the whole time on their phones instead of chatting with the rest of the family.

Even with these small drawbacks, I still think technology is mostly a force for good today. Take traveling, for example: whenever my family goes to Generic_City or any other destination, my older sister checks us in for our flights online. That means we don’t have to stand in long airport lines, and we already have our seats picked out before we arrive. As I mentioned earlier, my view is that technology has been helpful for everyone. You can handle almost any task with just your phone—forgetting your wallet at home is no longer a problem either, since you can use Apple Pay to make purchases anywhere that accepts it.

Some people argue that you can grow just by letting time pass, but that is not true. Ralph Waldo Emerson was right in his famous quote: people need to think beyond just their current beliefs. When you grow, you get closer to achieving your dreams, and reaching those goals pushes you to grow even more. The most important thing is to believe in who you are.

To grow, you have to aim to do things that earn respect, and always give your best effort. From my own experience as a student, I am constantly working to improve, and I try to encourage the people around me to do the same. We students all want a better world, and when we grow and reach our potential, it makes the people around us proud. If we refuse to keep an open mind, the opposite will happen: we will never grow, no matter what else is going on in our lives. We have to keep pushing ourselves to improve.

Over time, you will build the skills you need to support yourself, and better things will always come your way if you stay organized. The key is to stay true to yourself: never let other people control your choices, just be who you are. All final decisions about your life are yours to make.

Have you ever been in a situation where you have to choose between two paths? That is when you need to believe in yourself, and decide whether you want to grow or stay stuck where you are. If you choose to grow, more opportunities will open up for you, and not just for yourself—the people around you will benefit too.

Give your absolute best to reach your goals. For example, if you never try to grow, what kind of person will you turn into?

There are so many benefits to growing as a person. You become someone who can handle almost any task, and you will be more accepted and sociable. Emerson made a brilliant point with his statement, and we should value the wisdom he shared. In my opinion, he was completely right that trying things beyond your current abilities is the only way to grow. Just give it a try, and you can succeed.

There are plenty of ways to meet new people, both online and in person. You might cross paths with someone at a shop, library, or while doing outdoor activities, though some people are too shy to talk to strangers in these places. Everyone has their own approach to making friends: some chat to anyone they meet to build connections, while others are more reserved. No two people are the same, so everyone socializes differently. Avoiding strangers entirely is not a good idea. If you want to meet someone new, approach them, be friendly, and be yourself when you speak to them.

I love making friends whenever I can. Being kind to everyone is the key to building new friendships. There are many chances to meet people: group projects, class study groups, or even family connections, whether you have long talks or just say a quick hello.

Some people withdraw and stop talking to anyone, thinking it is pointless to speak to people they do not have to. I think it is better to take action. The benefit of being social is having lots of friends, while staying isolated might leave you only with a pet for company. That is why I always try to make new friends.

When I go out with my dog, sometimes I do not talk to anyone, but other times I run into a friend and we chat. When I go to a store, I talk to staff to find tools for my home. At school, I meet new people in my classes or around campus.

People can be kind or unkind. I dislike mean people who get angry quickly, but I love good people who are friendly to everyone.

It is absolutely true that a positive mindset is the key to success in life. Without it, you will never reach your goals, and others will not respect you. You need to show this positive attitude everywhere, not just when you are out in public. At home, school, the workplace, and every other place you go, you should treat the people around you with kindness. This means respecting your parents, siblings, and other family members, being friendly to your teachers, and getting along well with neighbors who live in your area. All of these people deserve your respect.

Having a positive attitude will help you grow into a better person overall. People will notice your cheerful, respectful nature, and they will be happy to recommend you to others when opportunities come up. On the other hand, people who lack a positive attitude are often seen as disrespectful, unmotivated, and full of themselves. Over time, others will start to dislike and avoid them. In contrast, everyone loves and gets along with people who stay positive.

I study at Generic School, where we learn about positive attitude every day. We also practice how to build good relationships with others who share this mindset—it is much easier to form strong, happy connections with people who are also positive.

A positive attitude turns you into a better person, and that helps you achieve your dreams. In a way, staying positive is like a superpower when it comes to reaching your goals. Positive people put in the effort to find the keys to success in their lives. They work hard to find the right path forward, use their brains to make good choices, and build a bright future for themselves.

We all know that positive attitude is the key to a successful life, and it is incredibly important. My advice to you is this: if you want to become a better, more successful, and braver person, treat others the way you want to be treated. If you hope that everyone will be kind to you, you need to be kind to them first. If you have a dream, don’t give up—keep taking the next step, even if progress is slow. It might just work out. Keeping our bodies active throughout the day is extremely important. People who move regularly are far less likely to fall ill, as constant activity boosts their energy levels.

We should aim to stay busy every day. Most people set daily goals, whether for work or other parts of their lives, and many enjoy working long hours just to keep their bodies moving. This is beneficial, as regular movement trains your muscles to handle physical tasks consistently. Once you finish your daily tasks, the only thing you’ll want to do is rest and unwind.

An active body is far healthier and less prone to illness. This is especially helpful, because if you’re someone who loves staying busy, getting sick can be really difficult – you’re so used to constant movement that being stuck in bed feels unbearable. Interestingly, people who stay active their whole lives are often the ones who live to be older.

Of course, staying active also requires proper nutrition. If you want to keep moving every day, you need to make sure you get enough vitamins and nutrients to fuel your body. A weak, undernourished body can’t handle constant activity, and pushing yourself too hard when you’re not properly fueled can be dangerous. The key is to take all activities with care – but there’s no doubt that daily movement is incredibly good for your body, which needs regular activity to stay healthy.

Most of us are naturally active, rarely staying in one spot for long. Even people who spend most of their time sitting should make sure to fit in some form of activity. Staying busy doesn’t just benefit your body – it also helps clear your mind, lifting your mood and making you feel better overall.

It’s wonderful to fill your days with whatever activities you enjoy, but it’s important to remember that everything has a limit. You should never push your body to do more than it’s capable of – overworking yourself will only lead to harm.

I believe that working as part of a team is far more advantageous than working alone, as it comes with numerous perks. For one, collaborating with others helps people come up with ideas more quickly and effectively. Team members can share knowledge, look up information in books or online together, and step in for one another if someone is absent, say, due to illness. While conflicts or disagreements sometimes pop up in group settings, experienced professionals can work through these issues to find solutions.

Another key benefit is better financial outcomes for both workers and the company. When a team performs well on a project, the business often rewards them with higher pay or extra work hours, since group work tends to be more efficient. Teams can also help the company attract more clients, including partnerships with other firms or even businesses in other countries, which is much easier to achieve when people support each other.

To sum up, I think group work is more beneficial for several reasons. It makes tackling difficult tasks easier, as team members can lean on each other for help. It is also more practical for boosting earnings for both the company and individual workers, and it opens up opportunities to work with external partners.

Why is conserving energy and resources in schools not a good idea?

Some people argue that reducing energy use at school is beneficial, as it lowers overall power consumption and preserves supplies. However, I disagree with this view. Many students do not have access to computers or reliable internet at home, so they depend on school facilities to complete their assignments. They often stay after class, use the library during free periods, or work in classrooms during break times. But what happens if the school cuts power to these devices?

Missing homework deadlines can lead to lower grades for that class. Think about how hard it would be if the school had no power for just two hours a day—now imagine that lasting four full school days. Students would struggle to finish assignments on time, which causes stress and even conflict with their parents, who may be upset about poor grades.

It is easy for students from wealthy families to support energy cuts, since their parents can afford home computers, high-speed internet, and other tech. However, many students are not so lucky. Their parents may not have the budget for these expenses, or they may live with a single mother who has multiple children to care for and must cover rent, car payments, and utility bills. There are countless reasons why a family might not be able to pay for home internet, and these students rely entirely on school resources.

While having access to school energy and tech is not a problem in itself—for many students, it is a reliable, free way to complete work without stress—cutting power for four full school days would create huge issues. There are hundreds of students in the school, and we cannot all use the same computers at once. We all have different assignments, and finding an available device takes time. Students with home internet would finish their work easily, but those without would fall behind, which is unfair. That is why I believe energy conservation at school is not a good solution for all students.

Some people argue against keeping school energy on because a few students waste their time on social media or online games, taking up devices that others could use. But this is not true for all students. Many rely on school internet to research for homework, read digital books, or complete other academic tasks. Punishing the whole student body for the bad behavior of a few is not fair.

Another key issue is climate control. If the school cuts power, air conditioning and heating systems will stop working. Extreme weather outside—like heavy snow or very hot days—will make classrooms uncomfortable for both students and teachers. Sitting in a freezing classroom during winter could make people sick, or cause joint pain for those with existing health issues. On top of that, no power means students cannot charge their phones. This cuts off communication with parents, and in an emergency, no one would be able to call an ambulance or get help quickly. Energy is essential for staying connected and handling urgent situations.

To be fair, there are some benefits to reducing energy use. Limiting power consumption lowers the school’s electricity bills, leaving more money for other important resources. Schools could also host more outdoor activities when indoor areas are not powered. However, these perks do not make up for the harm caused to students who rely on school tech.

In conclusion, going without power for four full school days would make every task much harder for students. While businesses can successfully cut energy use because their operations are very different from schools, schools need steady power to support student learning. Energy is a vital tool for accessing knowledge, and conservation measures that limit student access to tech do more harm than good.

I fully agree with Emerson’s claim that striving to create something new every single day is life’s greatest achievement.

To be your true self means you constantly crave new experiences, to test just how capable you really are. When you focus on your own growth, your days feel lighter and more fun. You are one of a kind—no one else in the world is exactly like you, and only you can make the best choices for your own life. This constant drive to grow into a better version of yourself is the most precious gift you will ever receive, and it deserves your full care and attention.

When you push yourself to grow every day, you pick up skills you never knew you had. You’ll surprise yourself by doing things you once thought impossible, and you’ll find that spontaneous new experiences are far more rewarding—they leave you feeling inspired and excited about what’s next. Trying new things also helps you improve bit by bit, which in turn lets you support others when they need it. Many people in the world struggle to believe in themselves, often because they’ve faced years of bullying and taken in cruel words that make them feel worthless. If you meet someone in this position, you should speak to them with love, respect, and kindness. Love is the most powerful tool we have to reach people who feel miserable, bitter, or resentful after being hurt by others. Far too many people suffer from depression, anxiety, and racism, and some even take their own lives because they can’t bear the weight of hateful words and unfair treatment. We don’t have to let things get that far. We can change the world by stopping bullying and racism, stepping up to support those who are struggling. This not only saves lives, but also makes us better people: it helps us see the world from new angles and find solutions to big problems. Nothing is impossible when you set out to be a kinder, better person.

It’s time to prioritize yourself. Listen to your heart and your own inner voice, and work to become a better version of you for your own sake, not to please anyone else. Stop doing things just to impress others or make them happy—pursue your own life, dreams, goals, and career path, because that is what will make you feel happy, confident, and fulfilled. You’ll enjoy your wins so much more when they’re yours. Hold onto kind words from people who truly matter, since they want the best for you. As for cruel, negative words? Throw them away immediately, so they can’t hurt you or hold you back. When you’re working toward a big goal, don’t broadcast it to everyone. Some people get jealous of others’ success, and their envy can turn into resentment or anger toward you. Instead, only share your plans with the people who are truly important to you—the ones who will support you and celebrate your victories with you when the time comes.

I’ve found that doing work on your own is far more effective. When you work individually, you get to use your own opinions, strategies, and solutions to solve problems, and the final result reflects your unique perspective. For me, group work often holds back creativity: I can’t share all my ideas, and we end up having to compromise on a single plan that might not even be the best one. That’s why I believe working alone lets you do your best work.

At its core, the drive to grow into a new, better version of yourself every day is the greatest accomplishment of all. It lets you learn and create things you never thought possible. We all want to change the world for the better, and that starts with being mindful of the words we say, so we never hurt others. Every person on earth should feel free to be different. Right now, too many kids just do whatever their parents tell them to, instead of following their own passions—that’s a mindset we need to shift.

Your sense of self is incredibly precious, and it needs to be protected. It defines who you are, what your values are, and it’s a delicate, important part of you. You should surround yourself with people who push you to grow, who bring positive influences into your life, and who stand by you through both good times and bad. The right people will want the best for you, and they’ll be genuinely happy when you succeed—and you should do the same for them. That’s why it’s so important to know exactly who your real friends are.

A true friend is someone who supports you and wants only good things for you; they care about you enough to encourage you to do what’s right and be your best self. Someone who doesn’t help you, or who doesn’t care about the things that matter to you, is not a real friend. Everyone needs to take a hard look at their relationships to figure out who their true friends really are.

Being yourself brings a kind of happiness you can share with your family, friends, and everyone important to you. When you’re comfortable in your own skin, you feel at peace—something many people struggle with, as they feel unhappy with their bodies and face a lot of pain because of it. When you’re confident in who you are and believe in yourself, you feel joyful and content. This is something we need to protect fiercely, so that negative people who disapprove of your choices can’t bring you down. When you believe in yourself, every second of every day feels brighter and happier.

Technology brings many positive changes to our daily lives. It helps us get prepared for our jobs by finishing work tasks more quickly, cuts down the time we spend on communication, and removes the stress of misplacing physical paperwork.

Using technology makes our work easier and faster. Sending emails lets us share key documents with coworkers or business partners without traveling to their offices or scheduling in-person meetings, which saves a lot of time. Emails also arrive reliably and on time, so we do not need to rely on printed paper as much. Cutting down on paper use benefits both the environment and our own convenience. Many people struggle with face-to-face communication, especially when they need to discuss work tasks or share important job-related information. They may feel nervous or uncomfortable speaking directly to colleagues or partners. Technology offers a simple solution here: sending an email to explain issues avoids the need for oral or in-person interaction, which puts these people at ease. Digital tools are also very useful for storing important materials like projects, documents, data, and presentations securely. Files saved on a computer or a flash drive stay safe, and students can use platforms like Office 365 to keep their assignments, presentations, and letters. This way, they do not have to worry about losing their work.

Some people claim that technology negatively impacts people’s lives, but this is untrue. It makes work far more efficient: we can build presentations in PowerPoint and access information from the internet quickly. We can also purchase anything we need online without visiting physical stores, start our own businesses, post job advertisements, and hire new employees.

Mobile phones have no place in schools, so students should never be permitted to bring them to campus. This rule exists because school is a space for learning, not for personal devices. If a student brings a phone anyway, they will face serious consequences. For example, staff might call their parents to inform them of the violation. Students who break this rule may also lose privileges, like eating lunch with their peers, or even face in-school suspension. Texting during class or while talking to teachers is especially prohibited. Anyone caught doing this will receive a detention slip, and continued misbehavior will lead to stricter disciplinary action. Ultimately, schools should ban student phones completely, with no exceptions.

Choosing to adopt a positive attitude can make everyday life far better. While some people go through life with a negative mindset, seeing every situation as bad and refusing to try new things for fear of making mistakes, those who stay optimistic view the world in a completely different light. For example, if someone delivers terrible news, a person with a positive outlook will stay calm and say everything will be fine, rather than falling apart. This same optimistic approach also helps in school settings.

When people keep this positive mindset in every part of their lives, they worry far less and feel much happier overall. Take school exams as an example: even if you have a huge, difficult test ahead and you’re sure you won’t pass, staying positive changes everything. A friend might encourage you, telling you that you will get through the exam. This works because when you truly believe you can succeed, you feel motivated, and even if the test is really tough, you never give up. Passing in the end feels incredibly rewarding.

Another clear example is when someone gets a medical diagnosis. If a doctor tells a patient they have an illness, a negative person might immediately think they will never be the same again, or even that they will die. But someone with a positive attitude will decide it is just a small sickness that will go away in a few days. They accept that their life might change a little, but trust that everything will turn out fine in the end.

Seeing life through a positive lens means believing that anything is possible. No matter how big a problem seems, you can choose to stay happy, and even the most frightening situations can be handled with hope instead of fear. There is no need to stress over every little thing that happens to you. Try to be as happy as you can, and train yourself to view even the biggest challenges as small, manageable issues.

Everyone makes mistakes at some point in their life. If you keep facing failure after failure without ever losing your enthusiasm, you will never actually learn from those errors. Sometimes, we need to feel upset about the wrong choices we have made, because if we never feel regret or sadness, we will just keep repeating the same mistakes and keep failing at the same tasks over and over.

Last year, my friend and I both took IB Math, which was really tough for both of us. One day, she pulled me aside and said, “Generic_Name, you’re not going to pass this class with your current grades. You should switch to an easier course, or you’ll have to retake it next year.”

I went home and felt anxious for an hour after hearing her words. Eventually, I had to admit she was completely right: I hadn’t prepared for the exam at all, and I didn’t even have the motivation to study.

On exam day, I wasn’t nervous at all – I felt totally fine. I asked my friend if she had studied, and she told me she hadn’t, saying she was just glad it was Friday. We both sat the test, and neither of us passed. But I felt terrible about my result. When I got home, my dad asked how I did, and I told him I’d failed because the class was too difficult for me.

He got really angry with me, and I stayed silent. He pointed out that not even trying to study was one of my worst mistakes, and that nothing is impossible if you put in your best effort. His words made me feel even more ashamed of my grade. I called my friend later, expecting her to be just as upset as I was, but she was completely cheerful – she didn’t care at all about failing.

That moment, I decided I wanted to be an A+ student in that class, and in all my courses. I resolved to chase success and push myself as hard as possible, no matter what. I spent the whole weekend studying for IB Math, putting in my absolute best effort.

On Monday, I asked my teacher if I could retake the exam. The retest was surprisingly easy because I had prepared so well. My friend didn’t follow my example, though – she got another poor grade. She kept failing repeatedly without ever losing her cheerful attitude, which is why she never changed her approach. She had to retake the class this year because she didn’t pass it the first time.

If she had felt even a little upset about failing, she would have done well in the class and other areas of her life. This shows that failure needs to feel negative – if it doesn’t, people will just brush off their mistakes and never improve.

When older students work alongside younger peers on shared tasks, they often form new friendships, and this setup also offers clear, practical benefits to learners of both age groups.

Friendships form naturally in these mixed-age groups because students have to communicate and cooperate to complete whatever task they are given. They spend time listening to each other’s ideas and sharing their own, which lets them learn about shared interests or differences in what they like and dislike. This back-and-forth exchange means both age groups pick up new perspectives from one another, and these friendly connections are especially valuable for younger children, who may feel more comfortable around peers closer to their own age than strict teachers.

Younger students gain a lot from working with older partners. They often understand class material better since they know there is someone patient to explain parts they find confusing—especially since their older partners have usually already completed the same lesson themselves, so they know exactly what parts are tricky. Sharing their own thoughts also feels less intimidating, because the age gap between them and their older partner is usually only 4 or 5 years—far smaller than the gap with a teacher. Unlike in regular classes where they might have to wait for a teacher to finish helping another student before asking a question, younger learners can turn to their older partner right away for answers. They don’t have to worry about raising their hand and waiting in a long line of students, because their partner is focused just on them. This one-on-one support makes it much easier for younger kids to speak up about what they don’t understand.

Older students benefit just as much from this arrangement. Working with younger children teaches them to stay patient and calm, rather than getting stressed when things do not go as planned. They have to speak slowly, avoid complex vocabulary, and explain ideas in simple terms, since younger kids may not know advanced words or long, difficult terms. Many older students have forgotten parts of lessons they learned years ago, so teaching the material to a younger peer helps them relearn those concepts quickly—since they already have a basic grasp of the content, it comes back to them faster than it would if they studied alone.

In short, when older and younger students work together, they build friendships and gain support that helps both groups. I strongly believe mixed-age collaboration is very valuable for all learners, since everyone involved walks away with clear advantages.

I strongly believe schools should ban students from bringing cell phones to campus. These devices are far too distracting, as students often text friends and boyfriends when teachers are not watching. When teachers ask them to answer a question, they usually admit they were not paying attention, or ask the teacher to repeat the lesson. Instead of concentrating on their schoolwork or future goals, they spend time messaging friends or boyfriends to talk about what they are doing. There is also a safety risk: when walking near the streets around school, many students text while crossing, not noticing oncoming cars, which can cause serious accidents. Some even skip class entirely because a friend texted them to stay away. They also use their phones to gossip about other people and spread rumors. For many of these students, school matters less to them than texting friends. This habit often leads to low grades, as they waste study time chatting with friends. All they seem to do is send text after text without stopping.

Do you agree or disagree with Emerson’s claim that people should base their choices and growth on their own personal experiences? I fully agree with this stance, and there are several clear reasons why.

First, the more real-world experience you gather, the more you progress in life, instead of slipping backwards. When you try new things and build up a record of past lessons, you open yourself up to far more opportunities and better positions. You never lose ground when you have a solid base of things you’ve already done and learned from. Experience also gives you the support and reasoning you need to finish tasks that would otherwise feel impossible to complete.

On the other hand, if you have no experience at all, you will never be ready to take on new tasks, let alone finish them. Without this background, you cannot grow or improve. Reading about a topic is never enough on its own—you cannot move forward just by studying. You have to practice the skill yourself first, to build that hands-on experience. Only then will you be prepared for whatever comes next. Many people struggle to move up in their careers or personal lives because they are not properly prepared for the challenges ahead. But for those who have built up experience over time, it becomes much easier to handle new obstacles.

Of course, gaining good experience is not always simple. It takes work to get to a point where you feel confident in your current position. Many people are not properly prepared for big opportunities, and the lack of experience holds them back. That is exactly why you need to get prepared early, by building up your experience bit by bit. Everyone has to start by being honest about where they are now: what skills you already have, what ideas you’ve picked up, and what you still need to work on.

If there is something you do not understand, do not be afraid to ask for help. Talk to your teacher, your boss, or a school principal—they can give you useful advice, answer your questions, and help you make sense of confusing parts of your work or life. Once you have completed a task or learned a new skill, everything becomes far easier to handle.

All in all, basing your choices and growth on your own experiences is the best way to move forward. So many people put off practicing or building experience, but those who do put in the work are the ones who succeed.

I agree with the statement that certain impressions cannot be changed. For one, some people have physical disabilities that are impossible to alter. Many others struggle with mental health issues that make them prone to anger. Someone with a mental health condition might get into fights, requiring a hospital visit for a medical check-up. While taking prescribed medication can sometimes improve their state, it does not erase the underlying issue.

People with physical challenges may shout in the street or run around, frightening passersby. Their families often have to keep them at home, but if their home environment is not safe, relatives may place them in a mental health institution. This is because they cannot stay home without wandering out and potentially harming others. Neighbors might call the police, who could arrest the individual, leading to legal trouble. Parents bear the responsibility of protecting their children from such disasters. If these individuals want to go outside, a parent must accompany them to keep everyone safe.

This situation causes great distress for parents, who must care for children with such severe conditions. They feel frustrated by the constant strain, as the condition is so hard to manage. These families cannot go out freely, spending most of their time at home. If a parent steps out even briefly, the child might wander outside and cause trouble in public. The individuals cannot walk alone, as they always need a parent by their side. Even when parents take their children to a park to play, there are many other kids there. If the child hurts another child, that would be a terrible situation. Mental health struggles like these are incredibly severe.
