I completely disagree with the idea that first impressions can never be changed. We form all kinds of first impressions about people, objects, and even animals every day. While some people stick to their initial judgments no matter what, usually because they are overconfident in their gut feelings, I believe it is always worth double-checking if those first thoughts are actually accurate.

I can back this up with my own experience. A while back, I was working out at home when I suddenly got a strong, nagging feeling that my girlfriend was cheating on me with my best friend. I was furious at first, since the idea seemed so far-fetched. It also made me realize how risky it is to act on negative first impressions without thinking: you never know how the other person will react.

I knew I needed to confirm if my suspicion was true before doing anything rash, so I called my girlfriend and we talked for a long time. I struggled to bring up my worry about her and my best friend at first, torn between wanting to clear my mind and fearing I’d ruin our relationship if I was wrong. In the end, talking to her helped me change my mind completely. I realized that not every strong first impression is correct: sometimes we get bad feelings because we’re uncertain about something, or we’ve misunderstood a person’s actions.

My main point is that first impressions are absolutely changeable. We all have both positive and negative initial judgments, but we don’t have to stick to them forever. Sometimes, the best approach is to keep your first thoughts private and let time reveal whether they were accurate. These days, I keep my initial impressions to myself when I’m not sure about them, and this habit has helped me adjust my first judgments more easily.

The popular saying goes, "Unless you try to do something beyond what you have already mastered, you will never grow." I strongly disagree with this idea. I believe that growth is always possible, even if you are not trying to learn something completely new. Growth does not only come from pushing past your current skills—it also comes from getting second chances to fix your mistakes, no matter what goes wrong.

First, I can explain this with a common school situation. When students work together on a group project, they often have very different ideas about how to approach the task. Usually, one person takes the lead of the team to keep everyone organized. Even when the work is nearly finished, it might still not be good enough to get a high grade. For example, the group might turn in their project to the leader, but the leader realizes it is incomplete, missing key points, or has very low quality writing. Instead of accepting it, the leader says the work is not good enough to submit. The team then talks more about the problem, listens to each other's ideas, and starts working on the project again. At first, the group members might argue about how to fix the work, but they always end up working together. No one in the group says they do not want to do the work, even if they are tired. Everyone wants to prove they can do a good job and contribute fairly. Even if the first version was bad, they do not give up. They take the second chance to redo the work, fix their mistakes, and make it better, which helps them grow. You should never feel like you cannot try again—growth is always possible when you get a second chance to fix your mistakes, no matter how bad the first attempt was.

Second, there are many times when you feel like the things you have done are wrong, but that is not the end. Everyone in the world gets second or even third chances to improve. Making a mistake the first time does not mean you have to repeat that mistake forever. You can always work to improve yourself, your community, your classes, and the people around you. For someone who tries to do good work every day, the idea of "not growing" does not even exist—you are always getting better, even in small ways. Another clear example is people who have committed crimes. Someone who is guilty of a crime and wants to get an education to grow as a person—just like any of us—should be given that chance. No matter what they did wrong, they deserve the same access to learning as everyone else, because all people have equal rights, no matter their past actions. Many people who are in prison take classes to earn degrees, which helps them find jobs when they get out. I know many people will disagree with me—they might think someone who committed a serious crime does not deserve a second chance, or any chance at all. But in my opinion, they do deserve that chance. They are already in jail paying for their crime, and most of them want to grow into better people once they are released. All people have second chances. If you do something you are not good at yet, or you make a mistake, you can always try again. You should never say "I can't do this" or "I don't have the ability to fix this"—that kind of thinking is wrong. Almost anything is possible in this world if you are willing to try again. I know some people will be annoyed by my opinion, but it is only what I believe. No one wants to be in jail and never learn anything that could help their future. People who get upset with my view should think: if you were in the same situation, locked away with no chance to learn, would you want a second chance? Thinking about both yourself and others, and giving people the chance to fix their mistakes, can make the world a little better for everyone.

In conclusion, all people always have second chances to grow. As human beings, we need to think about ourselves, but also about other people. For example, this essay is written to encourage a world where everyone gets a chance to live better. People in this country are very lucky to have so many opportunities to grow and prepare for the future. On the other hand, I come from a country that has very few opportunities, but my goal is to be a better person today, tomorrow, and in all my future days.

Most people are aware that technology can act as a companion for those who use it daily, such as staying in touch with relatives and friends who live far away. Beyond that, it serves as a useful tool for tasks like finding books or buying items you would normally pick up at a mall or your favorite local stores. In other words, technology has a real effect on society. For instance, job seekers can look for work without wandering the streets going door-to-door, and students can get college details without having to visit campuses in person. It also lets people buy what they need without making long trips to far-off shops. Technology also offers benefits when life gets tough. Many turn to video games to relax and take their minds off stress, and it can even help you find solutions for home repair or construction issues.

That said, technology often shows its best side to the public, but few people discuss its darker side, which can become a danger to you and those around you. For example, you might stumble on a website that looks completely safe and trustworthy, but you never know who built it or what their real goal is. In many cases, people use technology for harmful purposes. Terrorist groups, for instance, use online platforms to connect with teenagers and try to recruit them, a problem that often gets worse when parents do not pay attention to what their kids do online. Technology is also a tool that many people overuse, spending hours scrolling through Facebook or shopping online. Worse still, some bad actors use these platforms as weapons: they sell fake products and steal money from people they think are easy to trick.

We all know technology has both positive and negative sides, but what you experience depends entirely on how you choose to use it.

Do you think students would benefit from being able to attend classes from home?

I believe students should be allowed to take classes from home. This way, we don’t have to travel to school every day, which gives us more time to spend with our families. We also don’t need to wake up as early, and we can stay safe in our own homes.

Many students struggle with waking up early for in-person classes. Choosing online learning lets them skip the daily bus ride, and they don’t have to rush to arrive at school before the bell rings.

I think taking classes online is especially smart right now, since so many worrying things are happening around the world. The coronavirus pandemic is a perfect example – one of the biggest reasons I support home learning is that students can join classes remotely and stay safe and healthy at home.

Another major benefit of home classes is that parents always know exactly where their children are. A lot of students skip school without telling their families, who assume they’re sitting in class. When kids take lessons from home, parents can be sure their children are safe and accounted for.

Some students dislike using computers and prefer to go to school in person, while others don’t know how to use tech tools yet. Even so, letting students attend classes from home is still a great idea. It gives families more time together, removes the need to wake up early for the bus, and lets students do their work in a comfortable space with more chances to rest.

Many businesses now use a four-day work week, where employees work ten hours a day. Some suggest schools should try this model too, but after looking at the pros and cons, I am sure our school should not switch to a four-day week.

First, this change would cut into family time. Longer school days mean we stay on campus all day, with extra classes and lessons. By the time we get home, we are bored and exhausted from focusing on work all day. Instead of spending time with family, most students would go out with friends to play games or hang out. If adults try to stop them, students get upset—they already spent hours learning, so they want free time with friends. This leaves almost no time for family.

Second, students would get far more homework. To fit all material into fewer days, teachers add extra classes and subjects, which means more assignments. After a long day, students come home to piles of homework. Many skip meals or talking to family to finish work. Staying in one place for so long is tiring and difficult, and many lose enthusiasm for school. Some use phones to listen to music or watch movies during breaks, but this is not true for everyone. Long days also mean students get very hungry, as they have to wait hours for lunch.

Third, longer days cause problems for families of students under 18. Younger kids need parents to drop them at the bus and pick them up after school. Parents might work during the longer day, but have to leave early to meet kids at home. Principals sometimes call parents for emergencies, and parents worry kids are out late getting into trouble. Some students work part-time, which gives them money and experience, but those with extra cash might lose interest in school—they feel they don’t need to learn when they can buy what they want.

I do agree students can focus on learning for longer periods, but there are risks. Students have a lot on their minds, and while they pick up information quickly, learning too much at once is overwhelming. If schools only use English, students who want to learn other languages have no time. Long hours make many students bored and uncomfortable, even if some love learning. Today, schools use computers and phones a lot—they have maps, dictionaries, and calculators, which are useful. But many students don’t realize screens damage eyesight and mental health, a risk that grows with longer days.

Finally, school is not the only place that prepares us for a good life. Teachers give useful learning tips, but if we spend all our time at school, we miss out on real-world experiences. More free time lets us learn from family, friends, and everyday life, which gives knowledge we can’t get in class. Businesses may use four-day weeks, but this is different for students: workers already have job skills, but students have homework and classes. The model works for businesses, but not for our school.

Are there real benefits to working in a group? In my view, collaborating with others is much better than handling tasks on your own. For one, group efforts let you finish work far quicker than if you work solo. Beyond that, working with others helps you make new friends, and teaches you key teamwork skills. You have to be kind to your teammates, listen to everyone’s opinions, and learn to respect different perspectives—all valuable lessons you pick up when working in a group.

Group work offers far more advantages than working alone, especially for large projects. Suppose your teacher lets you team up with classmates for a big assignment, but you decide to work solo instead. You’ll likely struggle to finish on time, while groups that collaborate can complete the task early by helping each other out. This shared support is one of the biggest advantages of group work.

In group settings, every member takes on an equal share of the work, making it much easier to handle your specific part of a project. If you work alone, you don’t have anyone to turn to for advice or extra support, so you might not perform as well. For this reason, group work is always more beneficial.

Some people argue that group work should not be permitted, but I still think it is the best way to learn. It teaches you to treat others kindly and take responsibility for your tasks, since you have to complete the specific part your team assigns to you. Sharing ideas with teammates can also improve your final grade. All in all, group work always brings valuable benefits.

Taking summer classes to graduate high school in three years rather than four is a smart choice. When you finish early, you can leave school sooner to start working or pursue other goals. For example, you might land a well-paying job, earn your own money, or even help out your family at home. You could support your parents with household expenses, or save up to buy personal items like a car, new clothes, or other things you want. These are all great reasons to consider finishing early.

This option works especially well for students who are 17 or 18. They can graduate at a normal age, instead of staying in school until they are 22, which sometimes happens to Hispanic students. Many Hispanic students move to the US at 15 or 16, and are placed directly into 9th grade. For these students, graduating in three years means they finish at 18, not 22. They can enter the workforce right away, and still have time to improve their English skills. This situation is very different for American-born students, who do not start high school later than their peers.

Finishing high school a full year early is definitely challenging, but it offers real benefits for students aged 18, 19, or 20. They can complete all their required courses in less time, and move on to the next stage of their lives faster. This shorter timeline means they waste no time getting started on their careers or other plans.

That said, graduating early is not always the best choice for Hispanic students. They may not have enough time to fully master English, which can make finding work much harder later on. Many jobs require strong English skills, so rushing through high school could put them at a disadvantage. This is not a problem for American students, since English is their native language. If American students are the same age as their Hispanic classmates, they can easily get good jobs and graduate early without facing language barriers. Their fluency means they do not need extra time to practice the language while in school.

That is my opinion on finishing high school in three years instead of four. If my school offered me the chance to graduate early, I would absolutely take it. Finishing in three years works better for me, given my age and my future plans.

I believe taking elective courses is very beneficial for students. They help you stay on track to graduate, and if you want to finish your degree within four years, electives are even more useful, since they let you gain extra knowledge that is valuable for your personal and academic growth.

Once you decide to pursue your studies, you should commit fully, because the skills you gain will help you a lot in the future. Many people dislike studying, but I still think taking elective courses is the better choice, as they let you pick up extra information beyond your core classes.

Here are some examples to support my view:

1. In my home country, everyone speaks Spanish. When I visit El Salvador and can use two languages to communicate, I feel really proud of myself. My English is not very strong yet, but I practice every day, and I’ve learned that making progress little by little is what matters most.

2. If you skip elective courses, you will not learn anything new, which usually comes from being lazy. You need to push yourself to study instead. Completing electives will make your family proud, and it helps you earn a proper degree.

3. Having a good degree will help you land a stable, well-paying job in the future. Many people in our country are unemployed and struggle to make money because they did not go to school when they were children. We have a great opportunity to study now, and every student should work hard to build a bright future for themselves.

4. If others doubt your abilities, you should work hard to prove them wrong, always strive to exceed expectations, and make your mother proud of your achievements.

5. I do not think taking elective courses during the summer is a good idea. Summer break is only two or three months long, which is much shorter than the regular school year. You get far more information and learn better when you take electives during the full academic year, so summer electives are not worth it.

Winston Churchill, a well-known former British prime minister, once said that success in life or any other pursuit always comes with failure, and you should never lose your enthusiasm over small setbacks or a single failed attempt.

I fully agree with Churchill’s view here. True success is not just about reaching a final goal, but about improving your skills and getting better at what you do. When you fail, it does not mean you have failed forever—instead, it gives you a chance to learn. Every mistake teaches you how to solve problems more effectively, and shows you exactly how far you can push yourself by trying. The more you attempt something, even if you mess up at first, the more experience you gain. Eventually, you stop making the same errors because you have learned from past missteps.

I believe that working towards success helps you build up a lot of valuable life experience. If you give up after a failure and stop trying, you will never grow or discover your full potential. But when you push yourself to keep going, you realize just how much you can achieve when solving problems or fixing mistakes.

If you keep pushing yourself to try again and again, you will either solve the problem or at least figure out how close you are to a solution. Even when you are working on something totally unfamiliar, and you have no idea how to fix it at first, putting in consistent effort will usually lead you to an answer eventually.

Failing repeatedly does not mean you will never solve the issue. If you are doing your best but still coming up short, it just means there is a hidden problem you have not spotted yet. Failure is not a sign that your goal is impossible, only that you have not found the right solution yet.

To sum up, achieving success means working through countless problems and mistakes before you find the right answer. If you never push yourself to your full potential, you will never understand what is holding you back. But when you do explore what you are capable of, you can solve issues, learn valuable lessons, and gain experience. Putting in consistent hard work almost always leads to solutions for any challenge. This experience also lets you help others with their problems later—after all, as the saying goes, two heads are better than one.

Many high school students push themselves to be top of their class, and I think it’s a great idea to aim for good grades, no matter your age. The key is to focus on learning and building on what you already know. I really believe high school is full of valuable opportunities.

There’s a common debate about whether students should decide on a future career while they are still young. Some people argue that committing to a career path early has clear benefits, and I agree. When you choose a career direction in high school, you have time to learn more about that field, figure out if it’s truly the right fit for you, and even look into other options if you change your mind.

To start, plenty of students take regular classes and put in their best effort, which is completely fine. When you work hard and learn quickly, even at a young age, these habits will benefit you throughout your life.

Another important point is that students who earn strong grades in all their classes and pass every course successfully are in a great position to get into university. They’ve already covered the required material, so they’re ready for the next step.

Third, taking tough classes and working hard in high school means you already know the course material inside out, so you’re prepared for adult life. The effort you put in during high school pays off later.

To sum up, students who take challenging classes practice and learn every single day in high school. These are motivated students who want to prepare for their future. Being prepared puts you in a strong position: you’ll graduate from high school and university, and since you worked hard in high school and learned everything in your classes, you can find a great job. You might have a tough time in high school, but you’re building a happy future for yourself. Even students who take regular classes benefit, because they’re still learning and preparing during their high school years.

I also admire some societies that push all members to do their best for the community. It’s wonderful that in these places, every boy can go to high school, work hard, and have a positive experience. The classes offered in these high schools are chosen to guide students toward specific career paths. I believe in the value of every class I take, and I care about my grades. I also believe that opportunities are real, because smart boys are selected to excel in high school.

I can’t understand why so many people are foolish enough to pretend to be someone they’re not. To me, this behavior is completely ridiculous. For instance, I’ve noticed some Latinos copy the accents of other Latino groups just to seem cool, which makes no sense to me. To me, that shows they don’t take pride in their own home country and lack self-confidence. When they do this, they’re presenting a version of themselves that isn’t real. What’s even worse is when these same people act like they love their home country, as if their accent copying never happened. That’s just being two-faced, plain and simple. I really can’t stand people like that.

But this isn’t the only issue. Lots of people just follow whatever others say or do. Take hair, for example: if one person says they like short hair, others will cut their hair short too, just to get a bit of attention. What I’m trying to say is, there are plenty of people who feel unloved or ignored, so they copy their friends or other people just to get others to notice them.

For my part, I’m happy with the little I have, and I have no desire to be anyone other than myself. I’ve also started taking a more neutral approach to socializing. What does that mean? Well, if someone wants to be friends with me, that’s great. If they don’t want to get to know me, that’s totally fine too.

At the end of the day, I don’t pay much attention to other people. I only care about myself, my four close friends, and my family, and that’s all. I don’t feel any need to meet more people. I’m content with what I have, because the fewer people I get to know, the fewer people there are who can betray me.

For me, the absolute best choice is attending classes remotely from home through online learning.

My main reasoning is that this setup lets me handle other tasks during my free time, something that’s hard to do with in-person classes. Schools now offer great options for students taking classes, like after-school style sessions that you can join right from your house. Since I work, I often can’t spare a full hour to attend a class in person, so online learning works far better for my schedule. It’s more beneficial for me personally, though I know everyone has their own preferences.

For instance, if you don’t have a job, you’ll have plenty of time to keep up with all your online coursework. If you do work, taking online classes gives you more time to focus on both your job and your studies, so you can produce better work for both. This option is especially good for people who don’t have full-time availability, like those who work and can’t stay at school for the whole day.

When you turn 18, you usually have way more responsibilities, and juggling in-person classes on top of that is not easy at all. Teachers always say you need to take a certain class for a good reason, and you do have to complete it, but taking it online is a much better fit for most people. I actually think online home classes are even better than video conferencing sessions, for what it’s worth.

One big reason I pick this option is that my home is a relaxed space. I have access to food, it’s quiet with no distracting noises, and I can take as much time as I need to think things through. That’s really important for online work, which isn’t always easy, so having time to come up with good ideas and clear answers makes a huge difference. These days, students have way more options to handle any issues that come up with their studies. A lot of students are adults, or they don’t have enough time to commute to school because of work or other commitments. Another common reason to pick online classes is that you don’t have to travel, which helps if you don’t have a car or a ride to get to campus.

I really hope more students consider taking classes from home, because it’s the best option for almost any situation. If you want more free time, it’s way easier to fit in home-based online classes, and it gives you more flexibility with fewer hassles. The only small downside is that there’s no teacher there in person to explain any questions you have, so it can be a little tricky at first, but it’s definitely not impossible. Nothing in life is impossible, but most things take some sacrifice. You can still do great work and pass your classes without much trouble.

All in all, taking classes from home via online learning is the best choice, and it offers the most benefits for learning at home. It’s way easier to fit around your schedule or handle other problems, and I’m really looking forward to everything going smoothly for my own classes.

I completely agree with the speaker’s perspective. He makes a valid point that while everyone stumbles quickly at first, God’s help will guide us toward success.

This stance makes sense because when people stick to the right path and work together, no one gets left behind. British Prime Minister Winston Churchill had a brilliant insight here: success comes step by step, and we get even more help from God when we trust in both Him and our own abilities. Churchill’s famous words sum this up perfectly: “Success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm.”

I stand by this view. The speaker highlights how crucial failure is in the journey to achieving your goals. You have the strength to push through setbacks, and if you keep fighting, you will win success eventually and feel proud of yourself. His idea is valuable: setbacks happen everywhere, but the most important thing is to follow the proper guidelines. Success is built on failure, as long as you never let your passion fade. My thoughts are arranged logically here, and I back them up with Churchill’s quote about moving through failures without losing enthusiasm. At the core of this pursuit of success, I believe God’s help is key, but the speaker’s idea gives us all useful guidance too.

One day, you will reach your goals if you fight through every failure. Everyone who faces setbacks head-on ends up successful. Many people never achieve their dreams because they do not persevere, refuse to follow the right rules, and lack the positive mindset needed to move forward.

Winston Churchill’s words carry huge weight. They reflect good, practical thinking: anyone who follows the proper guidelines will climb to success. If you do not have the right mindset, you will never make progress toward your goals.

The core message here is simple: success and failure go hand in hand, and you have to battle through setbacks to reach your goals.

This is a brilliant idea that supports the path to success. We all know that without failure, there can be no success. You have to fall down first before you can rise up to achieve your dreams. If you do not fight against failure, you will never move up or reach success.

I agree with Winston Churchill entirely. Yes, success really is going from failure to failure without losing enthusiasm. His statement is spot on because every success story includes failure.

There is something really great about always staying busy. When we keep active and tackle tasks regularly, we end up gaining far more than we ever expected. Regular practice is essential for success, even when working on small tasks. It is especially important to practice the exact skills tied to the goals we care about most.

Does staying busy all the time help us achieve more? Definitely. First, identify exactly what you want, then push to go further than your original goal. For example, if I wanted to be a police officer, I’d study harder than required to surpass that basic role. If I wanted an iPhone 5, I’d work extra hours to buy an iPhone 8 instead. I might plan a trip to Generic_City with $600, but I’d save more to have $1000 to spend there. We must plan ahead and learn how to save money wisely.

Doing nothing gets you nowhere. Hard work is essential to get what you want. Take my Geometry SOL exam: if I want to pass it, I have to study, but if I skip studying, I will definitely fail. I want a good future, not a bad one from laziness, so I’ll study and work hard to build a better life. We need to think about our long-term goals before choosing to do nothing at all.

Never be idle. I have no desire to be lazy, because that would stop me from getting everything I want. I might start out hoping to buy a Toyota, but I will work hard to earn enough for a BMW instead. I need to pass all my classes to graduate, but I want a better diploma than the standard one, so I will finish all my homework to pass every class. Avoid idleness if you want to get what you hope for.

In conclusion, staying busy is wonderful. We achieve more when we keep active. Never be idle. To afford expensive things, avoid laziness to earn more money. To graduate and become a better person in the future, study harder than others. For all these reasons, we must stay active and reject idleness.

There are clear advantages for students who are able to join classes from their own homes. When learners take lessons online, they are encouraged to think more deeply about the material. They also have more flexibility with their schedules, since they can complete online coursework from home without commuting. Over time, this helps them become more organized and sharp. I personally prefer online learning because it feels far less stressful than attending in-person school. In a physical classroom, I often struggle to focus because so many students are shouting or making noise. For this reason, online classes work much better for me. They also help students build stronger study habits and pick up more information overall.

In-person school is not entirely a bad experience, but it is very easy to lose focus there. When students are in a physical classroom, they often start chatting with friends and stop paying attention to the lesson. By contrast, learning online from home is a great way to grow your knowledge. You become smarter, more capable, and more eager to learn new things. You also put more effort into your work, since you can focus solely on your online classes. There are no classmates yelling to distract you, so you can concentrate fully and think clearly. This also helps students build confidence in their own abilities. I am taking online classes this year, and I find myself pushing to achieve more than I ever did in in-person classes. That has really boosted my self-confidence, and I’ve learned that I can handle my work entirely on my own.

To start with, taking classes online from home saves students a lot of time. They can finish their work earlier, then move on to other tasks or hobbies. This also opens up more opportunities for them to qualify for better jobs in the future. Every student should have the option to take online classes, so they can complete their schoolwork and still have time to rest. All of this leads to happier, smarter learners.

For instance, many students pay for their online classes out of pocket, so they take the subject matter much more seriously. They also have more time set aside for studying. When you learn at home, the environment is quiet, which makes it much easier to focus. Over time, this turns you into a smarter, more critical thinker. Completing work independently also gives you a big confidence boost. You become more self-assured, a better thinker, and more willing to put in hard work. It also helps you build stronger study skills and gain more knowledge overall.

All in all, online learning helps you pick up more knowledge and practical skills. If students put a lot of effort into studying, they perform better in their courses. They start actively trying to understand the material, rather than just memorizing it. This focus leads to higher grades. Some people think online classes are boring, but that is only true if you do not engage with what you are learning. If you take an interest in the subject, you will actually enjoy the classes. This is a far better use of time than wasting hours on other activities, and students gain real benefits from it.

It is clear that taking classes from home saves a lot of time. Students know exactly what work they need to complete, so if they want to manage their schedule flexibly, online classes are one of the best options. Since I started taking online classes, I have saved time while also growing my knowledge base, and I have fixed poor study habits I had in the past. A lot of students dislike studying at home, and would rather play video games than open a textbook. But when they have structured online classes, they start studying regularly, which solves that problem. This is a great way to improve skills, and it encourages students to work and study harder. In the long run, this helps them qualify for good jobs.

This shows that online learning makes students more thoughtful, smart, and even talented. They work hard and learn to believe in themselves. As they achieve more, they feel proud of their progress, and they start pushing themselves to do even more. If you put a lot of effort into online classes, you will accomplish a lot, and that is a proven way to expand your knowledge. You will also feel prepared to take any test, with no fear of exams. Online classes change the way you study for the better, help you learn more, and give you valuable experience.

Obviously, online classes can solve a lot of problems for students. For example, if you are a senior who wants to graduate this year but is missing required credits, the best solution is to take the necessary online classes. This lets you finish all your requirements and graduate on time. Online learning saves time, helps you become more capable, and develops your skills. It turns you into a better thinker, and stops studying from feeling boring. It also helps you fix any academic gaps you have, and makes students more thoughtful overall.

In conclusion, students gain real benefits from being able to attend classes from home. It improves the way they study, and encourages them to spend time on online learning instead of playing games. Students become more thoughtful and work harder. Taking online classes from home is key to developing strong study skills. You save time, get smarter, and never have to deal with classmates distracting you. You will perform better than you did in in-person classes, and earn higher grades. If you study through online courses, you will improve in every way, and grow to believe in your own abilities.

I strongly believe that schools should not force students to take elective classes, as these courses hold little value for most learners and only end up wasting their time. Unlike core classes that are mandatory for graduation, electives are not required to earn a diploma. Because of this, many students do not put effort into these courses, often skipping assignments or even missing class entirely. This leads to poor grades, including failing marks, which drag down their overall GPA.

Instead of spending hours in electives, students could use that time to take more required credit courses that actually count toward their graduation. Some students want to finish all their mandatory classes early, and being forced to take electives only slows them down. For this reason, I think electives should be optional: schools should let students choose whether to take electives or focus entirely on the credit-bearing classes they need to graduate.

Since electives are not needed to graduate, most students do not take them seriously. They are far more focused on completing work for their core classes, which matter for their future plans. When they ignore elective work, they often end up with failing grades, which hurt their GPA. A low GPA can cause big problems later, especially if students want to apply to college after high school.

Many students skip elective classes altogether, because they know these courses do not affect whether they graduate. Some electives, like art, music, or drama, feel boring to students who prefer sports or just want to get all their required credits done quickly. When students skip these classes, they can get into serious trouble with their school. Worse, a pattern of skipping or failing electives can limit their future opportunities: it can hurt their college applications, and even make it harder to get certain jobs, like federal positions. Schools need to fix this issue by making electives fully optional for all students.

In conclusion, students should not be required to take elective classes. These courses are not important for graduation, so most students do not care about doing well in them. Schools should give students the choice to either take electives or focus on completing all their required credit classes instead. Since electives are not mandatory to graduate, students will not put in effort, and many will skip classes that do not match their interests—for instance, students who love sports may skip art or music electives, while those who enjoy drama may avoid sports classes. Skipping or failing these classes can lead to big problems that affect students’ futures. Schools have a responsibility to support their students, and making electives optional is the best way to do that.

Many people argue that a positive attitude is the most important factor for success in life. I fully agree with this idea, as I believe that staying upbeat and treating everyone with respect plays a huge role in both personal and professional achievements.

It is also clear that most people prefer spending time with those who have a cheerful outlook. I saw this firsthand when I lived in my home country, Generic_City. A woman named Generic_Name used to run a small restaurant there, located in a park right across from her home. I say "used to" because I am not sure if the business is still open today. Her menu included soups, chicken dishes, and pupusas, and at the time, she was looking for an extra pair of hands to help run the place.

One applicant was a woman also named Generic_Name. She was very intelligent and had plenty of prior experience working in restaurants, but she treated everyone around her very rudely. She applied for the open position at the restaurant, and her background showed she had solid experience in the food service industry. Another applicant was a different woman named Generic_Name. She was friendly, always willing to help people in the local community, and had a consistently positive way of interacting with others. Generic_Name, the restaurant owner, reached out to both women to schedule interviews, as she wanted to meet them in person, assess their personalities, and check their relevant work knowledge.

The first person to arrive at the owner’s house for an interview was the experienced Generic_Name. She didn’t even say good morning when she arrived—she just walked up to Generic_Name and stated she was interested in the job. The owner was taken aback, as the applicant hadn’t introduced herself at all, and simply told her that she had already found someone to fill the role. Generic_Name didn’t protest; she just said "ok, bye" and left.

An hour later, the other Generic_Name showed up. She greeted the owner with a warm "good morning," introduced herself properly, and confirmed she was at the right place to apply for the restaurant helper role. Generic_Name invited her in to talk, and while she realized this Generic_Name had very little previous restaurant experience, she noticed the applicant was quick-witted, and believed she would pick up the necessary skills quickly if given the chance. More importantly, Generic_Name’s friendly, positive attitude during the conversation made a great impression.

This experience proves my point: a positive attitude really can be the deciding factor in success. I also saw this recently with my own family. A few days ago, my father was extremely stressed because he had a large, important project to finish, and only two days left to complete it. He was planning to ask my brother if he could spare some time to help, and my brother immediately agreed. When he saw how anxious our father looked, he asked what was wrong. Dad explained the tight deadline for the project, but my brother, who always keeps an upbeat mindset, told him not to worry and assured him everything would work out. He promised to do his best to help, work as quickly as possible, and even said he would ask his friends to come pitch in to get the big project done on time.

Two days later, the team finished the entire project before the deadline. My father’s boss was thrilled with the high-quality work, and Dad was incredibly proud of my brother—not just for his help, but for his positive attitude and self-confidence that made the whole process run smoothly.

All of these experiences have convinced me that a positive attitude is truly the key to success. It helps you build better relationships with family, friends, and even strangers, and opens doors to opportunities you might otherwise miss.

There are two countries at the top of my travel wish list: Spain, and my home country of Honduras, which is located in Central America. I also have several other places I’d love to visit, including Generic_City, Generic_City, Japan, and the UK, mostly to experience their unique national traditions and landmarks. But Spain and Honduras are definitely my top two priorities.

You might be asking yourself why I’ve chosen these two places. Let’s start with Spain. I’ve heard so many great things about their national cuisine – people always say Spanish food is absolutely delicious, and you end up wanting to try more dishes every time you taste something new. There’s one place in Spain where the food is supposed to taste especially amazing: Generic_City. Generic_City is famous across Spain not just for its local dishes, but also for its football team, in case you’re not familiar with the sport.

FC Barcelona is one of the most well-known football teams in Spain and around the world – if you know any football fans, just ask them about Barca, and they’ll definitely have heard of it. Generic_City is home to this famous team, and it has an iconic stadium called Camp Nou. They’ve had some of the best players in history play there, including Lionel Messi, who I think is the greatest footballer of all time. I’d love nothing more than to watch a live match at Camp Nou, whether it’s a regular league game or the legendary El Clasico.

Of course, Barcelona’s biggest rival is Real Madrid, another top team based in Spain’s capital. When these two teams play each other, the match is called El Clasico – it’s a massive event for football fans, as it features two of the best teams in the world competing. I’m not a huge Real Madrid fan, but I still want to try Madrid’s local food to see what it tastes like, and I’d love to catch a game at their home stadium, the Santiago Bernabeu, which is just as famous as Camp Nou.

I also want to visit the stadium of Atlético Madrid, another top Spanish team. I think their home ground is called El Coliseo, though I’m not entirely sure of the name. There’s another Spanish city I’m eager to explore too: Generic_City. The reason I want to go there is to see the house of my favorite YouTuber. I’ve been following him on YouTube for four years now, and getting to see his home in person would be a total dream come true.

Another place I really want to visit is my birthplace, Honduras. Honduras is located in Central America, near Guatemala, Belize, and El Salvador. Did you know that Honduras shares land borders with several other countries? Most of my extended family still lives there, which is another big reason I want to go back. I’ve never actually been to a live football match in a Honduran stadium, even though I used to drive past the local stadium with my parents all the time. My dad, brother, and I would watch games on TV together, and I remember once when I was supposed to go to my first live match. But it started raining heavily, and my dad decided it would be too dangerous to go, so we stayed home. I was crushed – I think I even cried. That was about six years ago now, and I still really want to make it to a game there.

I have so many childhood memories in Honduras. I used to have a few pets there: first a dog, then a parrot, and later another dog named Ranger. Sadly, Ranger passed away after eating something he shouldn’t have, and we never figured out what it was.

This is the last place I want to visit: Generic_City. You’re probably wondering why I’d want to go there, so let me explain. Generic_City is home to the world’s tallest tower, and you see super fancy cars like Bugattis and Ferraris everywhere, driven by wealthy locals. Those are cars you almost never see anywhere else. I like this place because some people there keep lions or cheetahs as pets – it’s pretty crazy, if you ask me.

I almost forgot to mention another destination: Japan. I’ve always been drawn to adventurous, slightly spooky places, so I’d love to visit Japan’s famous haunted forest, and try all sorts of new local dishes and cultural sites. I’m a pretty adventurous person, and I like risky, exciting things – I’m not sure why, but that’s just who I am. I could even visit Australia, because I love all kinds of animals: snakes, lions, spiders, you name it. I grew up watching Steve Irwin’s wildlife shows – he died after a stingray accident, which was so sad. Watching his show made me go from being scared of bees, spiders, and frogs to absolutely loving all animals. I used to dream of having a job like his, working with wildlife every day. That’s all the places on my travel wish list for now – I hope you’ve gotten to know me a little better!

When older and younger students start spending time together, two very different outcomes are possible. They might become friends, sharing small details about their lives, or conflict could break out. For example, some older kids might pick on or tease younger ones, which would be a big issue. If that happens, younger students will likely fight back, turning the whole school into a war zone with older and younger kids clashing constantly.

No one really knows how the two groups will react at first. In the past, people had no way to predict how older and younger students would interact. I bet many hoped the two groups would get along well on the first day of school, and were curious to see their reactions.

Over time, though, things will settle down. Everyone will get used to the new setup, mind their own business, and treat younger students exactly the same as all other peers. Older students should also help younger ones—this work can count as service hours or earn them credit, and they should aim to do even more of these hours over time.

Some companies have started using a schedule where employees work 10 hours a day for four days a week. This setup works well for workers, since they can earn more money and still have an extra day off each week. But schools do not use this same model, and there is a clear reason why: if they did, students would stop coming to class every day.

Unlike workers, students cannot follow this 4-day schedule. They need to attend school every single day to learn. If schools adopted the business model, students would only show up for two days a week, because their jobs would take up all their time. That would mean they miss most of the schoolwork and lessons. More than that, going to school regularly helps young people grow into responsible, good adults, and they can always get jobs after they finish their studies.

Obviously, schools do not want students to attend class only two days a week. There are two big downsides to this. First, students would not get good grades. Second, if they skip most classes, they have no idea what material teachers have covered with the rest of the class. They would fail assignments, miss important lessons, and end up with very poor grades.

The main perk of the 4-day work schedule for adults is that they can earn more money. Working 10 hours a day for four days a week gives them plenty of time to earn a living, but students should not copy this. If they do, they will only focus on working and skip school entirely. A better option for students is to get part-time jobs after school hours. That way, they can still attend all their classes, keep up with schoolwork, and get good grades. They will also have time to pay attention in lessons, respect their teachers, and finish all their homework.

To sum up, schools and teachers want every student to graduate, grow into good people, and get stable, well-paying jobs later in life. They want to support all learners in building a bright future. The only way this works is if students come to school every day to learn. They can always take on part-time work after classes instead of following the adult work schedule.

While some people believe older students can support younger ones, others argue they cannot be of much help. However, I strongly believe older students play a key role in helping their younger peers: they offer useful advice, help them grasp school subjects more easily, and show them how to handle new tasks.

The first way older students help is by sharing advice. When older peers give tips to younger students, it helps them learn and grow. For example, when I was in fifth grade of elementary school, our principal asked my teacher to give ideas and information to third graders who were working on a class project. My teacher sent our whole 5th grade class to the third grade classroom, and my classmates and I helped the younger students with their work.

Another key reason is that older students help younger ones understand their school subjects better. They work to make younger peers more confident and knowledgeable in different topics. For instance, when I was in sixth grade, my best friend was a year ahead in seventh grade. Whenever I struggled with homework or assignments for other classes, she always stepped in to help. She supported me with homework, tests, and quizzes, which made me understand every subject much better. She also taught me how to work through and solve difficult problems.

Finally, older students can show younger peers exactly how to do new things, which is incredibly helpful when you need guidance. To illustrate this, when I first moved to America, I was in third grade and everything was unfamiliar. I did not know the school rules, I had no idea how the school worked, and I could not speak any English. Older students took the time to help me find my classroom when I got lost on campus. I even once walked into the boys' bathroom by mistake, and they quickly showed me where the girls' bathroom was. They also helped me practice speaking English, which made settling in much easier.

Overall, older students are always ready to assist younger peers in three important ways: they share helpful advice, help them understand school subjects more clearly, and show them how to handle new tasks. My own experiences prove just how valuable this support can be.

I support Thomas Jefferson’s core belief that no one should ever be idle, and everyone ought to stay busy with productive work. He thought people should ask for any extra time, tools, or materials needed to finish tasks properly. He wanted a society where all people worked, with no fighting, and no one stole money or possessions from others.

He stressed education’s value: people who finished school and found jobs earned more than those who dropped out, who got low-paying work.

In my view, Jefferson served the US in the military and as president from 1714 to 1769. He fought in the American Revolution, and his service helped many people improve their lives. He worked with Congress to make the US stronger, including expanding territory to compete with world powers. He hated idleness, always kept busy, and knew exactly what he wanted to achieve, using his strengths to reach goals.

His main aim was to help the US through speeches, making the country stronger by improving its people’s character. As president, he gave speeches telling people what was good for them, thanking good actors, and calling out bad behavior. Most admired him, stayed tolerant, and backed changes for the public good. Some disliked his actions and speeches, and even tried to kill him later. He did much work in Congress, focusing on key policies there.

Jefferson read widely when young, shaping his thinking. His speeches drew large crowds, and most people liked him. He never doubted his life’s purpose. Friends helped him plan war strategies, and he read letters from Washington, taking useful ideas from them.

Lessons for elementary school students should focus on the types of topics that each child is genuinely interested in. There are already plenty of subject options available, including science, English, math, history, and more.

The lesson I would most like to introduce to students is sign language. This would be a fresh addition to the curriculum, letting kids connect with others using only their hands. Very few people are familiar with sign language today. Teaching it to students is a great idea, because they may eventually meet someone who relies solely on sign language to communicate—this way, they will be able to talk to that person easily.

A number of schools already teach sign language to help students communicate in real-world settings. Sign language remains in use across the globe even today. But why was sign language created? It was designed for people who cannot hear or speak, so they can interact with others in their community.

While sign language is very different from speaking to communicate, the skills required are similar in some ways. When using spoken language, you memorize words to talk to others; with sign language, you memorize hand movements to convey your message. Ultimately, it is up to each person whether they want to pick up this new skill.

Sign language is not the only lesser-known communication method out there. People who cannot see often use Morse code, which works almost like reading, and is applied in real-world situations. Every letter and number has a specific code, just like in sign language. Though the two systems are very different, they are both unique ways to learn.

I disagree with this statement, as people are capable of acting in ways that are completely opposite to how they behaved earlier. It is also common for someone to come across as unfriendly when you first meet them, even if they have perfectly valid reasons for this. They might be shy, for instance, or they could have had negative past experiences with social groups. Think of a situation where someone spots a stranger in need of help, but does not offer assistance. Many people would assume this person is unhelpful, but that is not always true. They might simply be introverted, and worry that approaching a stranger to offer aid is not a good idea. There is also the case of someone greeting a person they are meeting for the first time with a cheerful "Hi", only to get a rude response. After this happens, the greeter might act less warmly toward other new people they meet, and hesitate before offering a friendly greeting again. But later, when the two meet once more, the person who was rude at first realizes that the greeter had been kind all along.

Yearbooks are a great tool to help people hold onto memories, and I’m a big fan of them, even though some people don’t like them. They stop you from forgetting important things, like homework assignments, what you need to do tomorrow, or plans for the whole next week. Now that we’re in 8th grade, we don’t get yearbooks anymore, which I really miss. I think they’re perfect for showing family all the school activities you took part in, proving you went to school, and even letting relatives see what your friends look like. Maybe one day, your family can even meet those friends in person. I fully agree that yearbooks are worth making for exactly these reasons: they let you share your school experiences and what your campus looks like, and help you hold onto memories. They’re also precious if friends move to a new place, because you can still remember them and how much you cared about them. All of this makes me really support keeping yearbooks around. I still love them, and I wish we could get them back, because they look so nice too. We only get one yearbook per year, and it takes forever to arrive once it’s ordered. You also have to pay for your own copy, but I don’t mind that at all—I especially love the photos inside.

Thomas Jefferson once wrote, “Determine never to be idle… it is wonderful how much may be done if we are always doing.” What Jefferson meant by this, I believe, is that we should make up our minds to never waste time being unproductive, and always stay busy with meaningful tasks. When we do this, we soon realize just how much we can accomplish. It’s also true that people generally fall into two groups when it comes to this idea.

Some fully agree with his words, while others disagree. Those who oppose the idea often argue that it’s not essential to work hard or stay busy all the time to get what we want. They claim we only need to put in effort when the timing feels right, or when a task is truly urgent, or when we have a strong personal desire for something.

I strongly agree that Jefferson’s statement is completely correct. To achieve great things in life, we need to keep working consistently, not stop and wait. As he noted, it is remarkable how much progress we can make when we are always taking steps toward our goals. His command to “resolve never to be idle” really resonates with me—I interpret it as a reminder to never let myself fall into laziness.

There are far too many negative people in the world who insist that we can never reach the goals we set for ourselves. This kind of pessimistic thinking is exactly why so many people give up on their dreams and become lazy. Everywhere you look, there are people searching for any excuse to sit back and do nothing.

To sum up, I fully stand by Jefferson’s words. If we keep working steadily toward our goals, we will eventually see the results of our hard work. All we need to do is keep taking action, so we can build a successful future and become the person we want to be.

Early planning for your future is a smart choice, as it helps you figure out exactly what you want to achieve. You can pick a career path that fits your life goals, and start preparing for university well in advance. By the time you become an adult, you will have already gained useful experience that makes it easier to find a job. Once you start earning your own money, you will be financially stable enough to support your family, and even help a partner if you have one. Think back to when you were younger: your parents were always there to guide you, telling you what steps to take in life. They set a good example for you, so you should listen to their advice instead of turning it down.

In many communities, students who start preparing for their future early are ready to handle big life changes, like starting a family, and can build a much better life for themselves. Studying hard opens up far more opportunities, and helps you grow into a capable, well-rounded person who is ready to take on work. No one will question your ability to do a job, because you will be fully prepared for the role, and might even work your way up to a management position. However, you need to stay focused on your studies, earn good grades, and work on skills like public speaking. All of this helps you land a good job that lets you support your friends and family.

Many people fail to reach their goals because they did not prepare early enough. They struggle to find good jobs because they did not make the most of opportunities when they had them, and by the time they realize this, it is too late to start over. That said, you can still build a happy life doing other work you enjoy, such as construction, truck driving, or working as a bank cashier—whatever role suits your interests.

For example, if you study hard now, you will be ready to handle all your adult responsibilities later. You might land an office job, or any other role that fits your personal goals. The key point is that early preparation leads to a better life where you can achieve everything you want. Your parents can support you through this: they will encourage you to work hard in school, because once you are prepared, you get to choose your own path in life. Never blame your parents for your future, saying they did not do enough to help you.

My recommendation is to prepare and study hard for your goals as early as possible. That is how you build a good life and get ready to chase your dreams. If you put in the effort, you will become the best version of yourself, and a great role model for your future children. They will be proud of you, and when they grow up, they will follow your example, working hard to build good lives for themselves because they saw your positive influence even before they were born. Remember, you have the potential to be amazing. Focus on what you want your life to look like, keep working hard, and never let anyone tell you that you cannot succeed.

Many people argue that working alone offers the greatest learning benefits for students. For instance, when students collaborate in groups, they usually split the workload between members. This means each person only handles a small section of the task, so they never get to engage with the full scope of the material. By contrast, a student working solo has to complete every part of the assignment themselves, which lets them grasp all the concepts involved.

Group work does have its own advantages, of course. It is often quicker and less stressful, since each member takes on a portion of the work. Another plus is that if a student struggles to understand a concept, their group mates can explain it to them, helping the whole team get up to speed. That said, a lot of students pick group work because it feels easier—and it is common for some members to avoid doing their fair share, leaving the rest of the group to pick up the slack.

Personally, I prefer working alone. I find that I learn and understand the material far better when I work solo. For example, when I handle an assignment by myself, I have to track down all the necessary information, create every example, and explain all the key points on my own. That said, both ways of working are valuable to practice, since in the future, we will likely have to work both independently and as part of a team at different times.

While both approaches have merits, I still believe working alone is the better choice overall, especially for students just starting out. Teachers tend to agree with this too: when students work solo, educators can get a clear sense of each person’s work process and way of thinking. They can accurately assess every student’s abilities, since not everyone performs the same way in group settings. This helps teachers understand each learner’s strengths and weaknesses far better.

No matter which method you use, the most important thing is to put in your best effort and complete every task to the best of your ability.

Thomas Jefferson once wrote the famous line "Determine never to be idle," which basically means we should avoid laziness and stay active. I agree with this quote because it is very possible to fill our time with useful tasks instead of doing nothing.

I believe we get more done when we stay busy with tasks, whether that means studying after class or heading to a job once school ends. Some students avoid schoolwork because they worry they are not smart enough, but I enjoy doing work every day – that is how I pick up new knowledge and skills. Getting a part-time job after school is also a great idea: you earn your own money, and you might even be able to help your parents pay bills.

To build a stable, responsible life, we have to work or study instead of wasting time. For instance, once you turn 18, you are responsible for yourself – your parents will not buy you everything you want anymore, so you need to find a job to pay for your own needs. This is a realistic goal that anyone can work toward.

Of course, not everyone believes that staying busy is the right choice. There are also people who claim that living an idle life is preferable. They say this because they never plan for the future, or they simply refuse to put in any effort – but this approach never pays off. Take me as an example: I have a long list of tasks to complete to graduate high school, including passing my ESOL classes and earning high grades. If I don't graduate, my only option will be low-paying manual labor. On the other hand, if I want real opportunities later in life, the best choice is to work hard in my studies and attend college, so I can get a well-paying job.

Many of us stay busy with different responsibilities, and this is entirely possible because we want to grow into responsible, capable adults. Keeping active and working toward our goals teaches us that it is not hard to stay productive – we just need to never give up.

Even though some people claim online classes are a good option, and they have valid points, I still think remote learning is better overall, even if it’s not perfect. For one, learning from home means you never have to step into a school building. You don’t have to drag yourself out of bed at dawn to get ready, and you can skip seeing classmates you’d rather avoid. You also get to pick your own meals instead of eating whatever the cafeteria serves, and you can eat whenever you’re hungry, not just during a set lunch break. You don’t have to follow strict school rules either—you can set your own schedule and routines. Taking tests is also simpler, since you can look up answers online to help you pass. In contrast, attending school in person comes with a lot of hassles. You have to wake up early, get dressed, and catch the bus to get there on time. You’re stuck sitting at a desk in a crowded classroom all day, following strict rules like arriving to class before the bell rings. If you’re even a few minutes late, you get sent to the tardy table. If you’re late more than three times, you end up in ISS—in-school suspension—where you sit in a silent room with no phone and aren’t allowed to talk to anyone. If you skip class entirely, staff will track you down and put you in isolation. They’ll call or email your parents to tell them you weren’t in school, even if you left home like you were supposed to go. For me, that would get my parents really angry, and I’m sure most other students would get in trouble too. If you talk back to a teacher, they’ll call security to come escort you out and scold you. Getting into a fight with another student leads to even bigger problems. Security will come to break it up, and if anyone gets hurt, they’ll call an ambulance. The principal, police, and both sets of parents will get involved, and the other student’s family might even press criminal charges. This leaves a mark on your permanent record, which colleges will see when you apply. They don’t want students with a history of bad behavior, so this can ruin your future chances of getting into a good school. Using, carrying, or selling drugs on school grounds gets you in huge trouble with both the school and the police, and your parents will be furious. If you’re over 18 and the offense is serious enough, you could end up in jail. You’ll probably get expelled, too, so you’ll have to transfer to a new school and lose all your current friends. That’s incredibly upsetting, and you’ll have to deal with jail time and all the other consequences on top of that. That’s why I think online classes are the better choice. It’s not just about getting to eat whatever I want—there’s so much drama and strict punishment in traditional schools that you have to put up with, and most of it is stuff you’d rather avoid. I think trying out remote learning is a great idea for any student.

It is often said that people can change the first impression others have of them. I completely agree with this idea, as initial judgments are rarely final and often shift as we get to know someone better.

For example, when I first met my girlfriend, I assumed she was a very cheerful person. However, as we spent more time together, I realized she struggled with sadness more often than I initially thought, and my first impression of her gradually shifted.

This also happens in professional settings. When applying for a job, many people put on a happy face and smile during interviews to make a good impression, even if they feel down inside. Over time, though, coworkers and employers will see their true mood, and that initial positive impression will change.

Most people behave differently when meeting someone new, especially if they want to be liked. You might act outgoing or relaxed during a first meeting, but as people get to know you, they will see your real personality, and their first impression will adjust accordingly.

Another clear example is starting at a new school. Many students act overly cool or say things they think their classmates will like just to fit in at first. But as weeks pass, people see who they really are, and that initial impression of them being effortlessly popular fades.

In my view, first impressions are never the full picture of who someone is. They only show a small, often fake, version of a person. Whether at work, school, or in relationships, people will eventually see your true self, and their initial judgment will change. That’s why it’s always better to be genuine from the start – that way, people’s impressions of you will be accurate from the beginning.

As young people grow older, they form views on the things that affect their lives. Many claim first impressions are nearly impossible to change, but this is wrong.

Everything about a person can shift over time, including how others see them at first. Sometimes, people come across as unfriendly or rude when they first meet someone, not because that is their true personality, but because they are having a bad day, feeling sad or angry, or dealing with personal problems that show on their face. In these cases, the first impression someone gets is wrong, and it can be fixed.

It feels good when others describe you as kind and respectful. You can work to be friendlier, and it is nice to know people have positive thoughts about you. Your personality is the first thing others notice when they meet you, so if you show your best self by doing good deeds and speaking kindly, you can make sure they see the real you. Even if you were upset when you first met someone, you can later show you are actually a happy, pleasant person.

Some say you only need to change a first impression if others think you are unfriendly, but this is especially important in the workplace. If you want a job that requires you to be friendly and smile, but you seemed grumpy during an interview, the employer might not hire you. You need to prove you have the friendly attitude the role needs, so people do not avoid working with you.

It is valuable to show others you are a nice person, so theyhave a good impression of you. When people see you as friendly and easygoing, interactions go more smoothly. A positive first impression is very important for any job, since treating people well is key in almost every role.

In conclusion, it is not impossible to change the first impression others have of you. You can always demonstrate that you are not the person they initially thought you were, by showing your true, kind personality over time.

I disagree with the idea that first impressions are easy to change. Many people argue that shifting how others see you initially is difficult and time-consuming. For instance, you have to fully grasp how the entire process works, but most people don’t understand it, so the whole thing often feels very confusing. I also think first impressions are frequently inaccurate because not everyone wants to stand out or be different from others.

Second, changing these initial perceptions is nearly impossible for most people, since they simply don’t have the time to focus on such things. Between work, dealing with bosses, handling household chores, and caring for their families, most people have too many responsibilities to put effort into shifting how others see them. On top of that, many argue that first impressions are often negative because it’s impossible to get them right the first time.

What’s more, many note that it takes a long time to adjust to trying to change an impression, as you need to be fully committed to making your goal a reality. This requires a huge amount of effort, and if you don’t have enough time to dedicate to it, you won’t succeed. For example, lots of people say first impressions are almost impossible to shift, even though we can’t always tell if the process should be easy or difficult.

To sum up, I disagree because managing how others perceive you is not simple. Trying to fix a bad first impression requires a lot of work in a short time, which can feel like it takes forever to get right. Many people say this process is extremely hard, and that is completely true — first impressions are very difficult to manage.

Here is my view on whether schools should switch to a four-day weekly schedule. Supporters of this change often point out that students and teachers would gain an extra day off each week. They say this free day could be used to catch up on sleep, study subjects not covered in class, spend time with family, work on personal growth, or pursue hobbies. But there is a major catch: the remaining four school days would each be two hours longer than usual.

We need to think carefully about this. Right now, school days are already seven hours long, which is tiring enough. Every morning, students wake up as early as 5:30 or 6:00 to get ready for school, then spend seven full hours there. Adding two more hours would only make things worse. If we switch to a four-day week with longer school days, we would lose time for important things. For example, I would not have time to sleep in, study topics I like, hang out with my family, work on personal projects, or do what I enjoy. This is because the school day would be stretched by two hours. More time in school means more class time, not less.

I do not want to give up the free time and happiness I get from the current five-day week. We need to really think about what will actually benefit students, not just sound good on paper.

I fully side with Ralph Waldo Emerson’s view that trying to take action stops people from growing, which makes it hard to connect with his ideas. At first, this idea might sound frightening to some, since it suggests putting in effort prevents growth. But when I agree with Emerson, it creates space for sharing different opinions, and we can work to understand each other better. Finding common ground with others is really important here. Emerson should not shut down agreement or push it away; when we do connect over shared views, we can achieve things together. We have a choice: we can keep pushing forward to grow, or stay stuck in place. We should aim to rise, not fall, because if we stay down, we will never grow. Growth requires us to keep moving, not stay still.

When we align with an opinion, we start to understand the original idea better. Not everyone agrees with Emerson, though — only some people do. Sharing opinions helps us make sense of new ideas, even if there are small, everyday uses of the word “agree” that mean something else. For example, spicy food might not agree with someone, meaning it upsets their stomach, just as some ideas don’t suit certain people. Someone might agree with a view without acting on it, but they still gain a better understanding of that idea. We should be open to agreement, because people who share common views grow together, drawing on their shared experiences.

Emerson should also be open to agreeing with others, so more people will come around to his views. If he does not, people will struggle to align with his ideas, which hurts everyone’s growth. Agreement is rooted in people’s opinions and shared experiences, so Emerson needs to build those experiences with others too. Emerson has his own views that he stands by, and he can act on his knowledge. But having ideas is not enough if you keep them to yourself. We should reach out to agree with others, and if we don’t understand something, we can ask people who do. This makes it easier to find common ground, and others will appreciate the chance to align over shared ideas.

If a practice benefits people, we should support it — it is good for everyone, whether individuals or groups. If someone refuses to agree with a view, others can still take action on what matters to them. If a person does nothing, they cannot expect others to align with them. For Emerson, if he takes action himself, he does not need people to agree with his ideas.
