I believe technology has brought mostly positive changes to people’s daily lives. It helps us solve all kinds of problems, whether small daily issues or bigger challenges, and also gives us easy ways to relax, like listening to music, watching films, or playing games.

People rely on technology for almost every part of modern life. We use it to search for jobs, run businesses, shop online, and even teach classes. Creatives like musicians and actors also depend on tech tools to produce their work, from recording songs to filming movies. Technology is now so common around the world that it is available to almost anyone who wants to use it. It also bridges language gaps: built-in translation tools let us convert words between dozens of different languages in just seconds.

We also use tech to stay in touch with friends, family, and parents no matter how far away they are. Some critics argue that too much technology makes people lazy, claiming we stop moving around or doing physical tasks. But that is not true. There are now fitness machines and sports tools powered by technology that help us stay active, and tech also lets us find information or even work full-time jobs from home without leaving their houses. It is also a huge help for students of all ages: it makes writing essays, taking quizzes, and preparing for exams much easier. Most schools now have tech tools and staff trained to use them, with plenty of related resources available on campus.

What if the school day was extended by two hours every day? This change should definitely not happen. Adding two extra hours to each school day would leave students with no free time once classes end. They would grow exhausted by the long hours and start to hate being in school, unable to maintain a normal daily life.

With those extra two hours, students would not be able to take part in any other activities. They would have no time to join sports teams or sign up for after-school clubs, and they could not practice the sports they are passionate about or do any other hobbies they enjoy outside of class.

Longer school days would leave students feeling drained, making them not want to go to school at all. Most students would dislike spending an extra two hours in the building, and some might even start skipping classes regularly. Those who do show up would be too tired and sleepy to focus during lessons.

Many students would lose the chance to live a normal, everyday life. Most would not get to spend quality time with their families, and they would have no time left for their own personal lives or the activities they love doing after school.

They would not be able to maintain a regular routine or take part in anysports or hobbies that interest them after school. Managing their time would become impossible, and they would feel stressed and too tired to do anything once the school day ends. For all these reasons, the school day should not be extended by two hours, so that students can keep living normal, balanced lives.

Thomas Jefferson’s famous quote talks about how people should never choose to be lazy, and how meaningful it is when a group of people comes together to achieve great things and fulfill their life’s purpose.

In my view, Jefferson was actually referring to the American colonies deciding whether to stay under harsh British rule or band together to fight for their freedom. We should remember that colonists shed blood and died fighting for Britain in the French and Indian War. But after we won, the king took control of all the new land we’d gained. We weren’t allowed to settle there—only the king’s noble friends and allies could move to those territories.

So why should we keep paying taxes to a king who doesn’t care at all about the people living in the colonies? He only wants more money and power for himself. If we don’t speak up, no one will stand up for us.

Jones Watches argues that if we don’t fight back, we’ll end up living like slaves. We won’t be able to speak out, and the British will take our homes, our food, and every penny we earn, leaving our wives and children with nothing. They might even kill us, since they’ll label all of us as traitors and claim it’s their duty to execute us for the king.

But think about the innocent women and children who will suffer and die if we refuse to fight for freedom and justice. If we die fighting for what’s right, we die with dignity, as free men—not as slaves.

Thomas Jefferson’s books and newspaper articles helped open Americans’ eyes to the truth: we don’t have to obey the king anymore. We are Americans, and we have a democracy where we get to vote for our own leaders.

Both Thomas Jefferson and Jones Watches are incredibly important figures. In the end, one man can never rule the entire world alone. When we come together as a group, there is nothing we can’t achieve.

I fully agree that we should always stay true to who we are, even when trying to move forward in life. We live in a society where people often pick apart others’ behavior while ignoring their own flaws. In this world, being yourself matters more than fitting someone else’s idea of who you should be. We have to hold onto our true selves, and always remember one key thing: we are the ones who can change the world, not the other way around.

Everyone faces challenges, but we have to learn from them and keep chasing our dreams. I plan to graduate this year, and there are days when I feel like I cannot keep going anymore. But I have a son who looks up to me, so I have to keep pushing. I want to build a better world for him, raise him to be a kind person who helps others, and make sure he feels free to follow his own dreams.

To change the world, we first need to shift how we think, and work to become better people. I want to help those in need—low-income families, and elderly people who often get overlooked. We need to improve our own character if we want a brighter future for our children, since they are the ones who will shape what comes next. They need to learn to be good, kind people, because they hold the future in their hands.

School taught me not to judge people based on their skin color, background, or nationality. None of that matters—all people are equal, no matter where they come from or what they look like.

I will not change my way of thinking, because staying true to yourself is what matters most. You do not have to give up your values or ideas just to seem successful in the eyes of others. In the end, do not waste energy worrying—life is too short to live for other people’s opinions. Follow your dreams instead.

I want to study at university, pass all my exams, and become someone my son can look up to. I want him to see that if you are willing to work hard and truly want something, you can achieve anything you set your mind to.

Together, we can turn this into a better world for everyone.

A number of schools now offer students the chance to learn from home as an alternative to in-person classes. There are many topics that are difficult to master at home on your own, but video lessons and online tools provided by schools make these subjects accessible to remote learners.

First, digital technology is now widespread across the globe, and it is accessible at almost any time. This means students can log on to their classes and attend them right on schedule, no matter where they are.

Third, students who are disciplined and committed to completing their coursework and homework from home will see real benefits. This setup makes it much simpler to work through all their learning materials at a pace that fits their schedule.

Certain school district programs allow students to finish high school in just three years. Many students choose this option because they feel they are too old to spend an extra year in school, or simply do not enjoy the high school environment and want to move on quickly. Families often push for this shorter timeline too. Many parents or guardians do not want their children to remain in high school for an extra year. Instead, they expect teens to start working to pay taxes or earn money for their own expenses. Since these families offer little support for students to complete a full four-year program, many teens opt to graduate early. On top of that, a lot of students want to finish high school in three years so they can start college sooner. Taking summer courses is a popular way for these students to earn the credits they need to meet graduation requirements ahead of schedule.

On the other hand, many other school district programs encourage students to stick to the traditional four-year high school timeline. This gives learners more freedom to pick the classes that interest them most. If a student struggles and fails a course, they have plenty of time to retake it without falling behind. There is far less pressure when students have four full years, as they can balance their studies with other activities. For example, they have time to pursue extra learning opportunities, relax by playing games, or set aside enough time to study for exams. Many students also prefer staying in high school for four years because they enjoy spending time with their friends, collaborating on group work with peers, and learning from teachers they admire. All of these reasons make the full four-year high school experience appealing to a lot of people.

Hi there! Today I’m going to talk about the differences between working alone and working with a group. First, let me ask you: do you prefer tackling tasks on your own, or teaming up with others? Personally, I much prefer working in a group, and I’ll explain why below.

Both solo work and group work come with their own upsides and downsides. I prefer group work because a team can offer fresh ideas and different approaches to finish a task, plus working together makes the process more enjoyable. Of course, groups have flaws too: there’s almost always one person who just goofs off, refusing to do any actual work and only wanting to have fun. On the other hand, working alone means you can complete tasks exactly how you want, without worrying about what others think. You’ll also get work done faster when you don’t have to coordinate with anyone. But the downsides are clear: it’s lonely, you have no one to share ideas with, and it’s much harder to come up with creative solutions on your own.

Overall, I think group work is far more beneficial. When you have a team behind you, there are more people to support you during presentations, which makes you feel way more confident about your work. Collaborating with others also improves your communication skills, boosts your self-esteem, and helps you become more social – you might even make new friends! By contrast, working alone often gets boring, and you might not even finish tasks because you have no one to talk through ideas with.

Spending all your time working alone can even harm your personality and how others see you. People might assume you dislike being around others, and that you’re only suited to working by yourself. This can create a lot of unnecessary conflict, and in the worst cases, someone might end up feeling isolated and falling into depression because no one accepts them. Sometimes, that negative outcome is pushed onto them by others, making them feel that way about themselves.

When you work in a group, you pick up important skills like respecting others, learning different methods for getting things done, and collaborating as a team. Take sports as an example: you can’t play most sports by yourself, since they require a team. How can you function well on a sports team if you never learn how to work in a group? If you want to succeed in your community and your future career, you need to master teamwork. Working with people you trust in a group setting also shows you that friendship is incredibly valuable. Having people you enjoy being around support you helps you grow in life, a feeling that’s hard to find anywhere else.

Friendship is a natural part of working in groups, and it’s one of the biggest keys to success. It benefits you in your daily life, your future education, and your later career.

Let’s look at a concrete example. Imagine you’re driving on the highway, minding your own business, when you realize you forgot to stop for gas and your car breaks down in the middle of the road. If you refuse to work with others, you’ll have to push the car alone. You might strain yourself and get sick, or even crash into another vehicle. But if you’ve learned how to work in groups, you’ll have four people helping you push the car, others stopping traffic to keep you safe, and someone calling the police to assist with the problem. This makes it clear why learning to work in groups matters so much. Beyond that, you’ll meet new people and make friends along the way. The core point here is that group work gives you crucial support when you’re facing tough tasks that are too hard to handle alone.

Of course, whether you prefer solo work depends a lot on your personality. If you really love working without anyone else around, that’s totally fine. But there will always come a time when you have to collaborate with a team or group, because some tasks are simply impossible to finish on your own.

When you work in a group, you earn respect and build strong friendships. If you pull your weight and help out with everything, people will enjoy working with you, and you’ll feel like you’re making a real difference and that you’re valued. That’s something that’s very hard to achieve when you work alone.

I hope you found this explanation helpful – I’ve done my best to lay out my thoughts clearly. I really believe we should all be more open to socializing with others and inviting them to join us, for the sake of building a better future. When we do this, everyone can make friends and never feel isolated. Let’s work together to make everyone happy, enjoy helping each other, and always treat one another with respect.

I believe offering classes through online platforms or video calls is a really useful approach for students. For one thing, many learners live too far away from their school to commute there regularly, so they have no other way to access education. For these students, online learning is often the only path to finishing their studies. These digital tools also make it easier for students to communicate with teachers and peers while they learn.

This option brings plenty of benefits. It is simple and quick to access, which saves time. It is also helpful during bad weather, like heavy snowstorms. When snow falls, schools often have to close because roads get icy and dangerous, making it almost impossible for students to travel to campus safely.

If I had the choice, I would definitely sign up for online or video chat classes myself. They feel much less stressful to manage, and I don’t think learning through these tools is any harder than in a regular classroom. Plus, I would have more free time to handle other tasks, including holding down a part-time job.

That said, this setup is not ideal for every student. Some don’t have access to a computer or reliable internet at home, which makes joining online classes impossible for them. While digital learning is a great choice for many, it only benefits those who have the right tools, leaving others at a disadvantage.

Online classes work especially well for long-distance learning, as they bridge communication gaps between people who are far apart. However, I think all online schools should be free for every student—no one should have to pay fees to access this type of education.

Another perk is that students who take online classes won’t fall behind. They can start lessons whenever it suits their schedule, so they never miss out on important material.

All in all, I think using online and video chat classes is a very positive step forward for education.

There are two common perspectives on how to handle big life choices. Some argue that every person should make their own decisions, while others believe it is wiser to follow the guidance of people with more expertise, hands-on experience, and time to weigh difficult options carefully.

I firmly believe that everyone should take charge of their own choices. After all, it is your life, and you are the one who understands what will serve your future best. That said, many people prefer to mirror the decisions of experts or more experienced individuals, assuming they will get the same positive results if they copy the choices these seasoned people make.

I faced a major, life-altering choice myself not long ago: I had to decide whether to stay in my home country or move to the United States to pursue better living standards and more career opportunities. At first, I was completely stuck. I had no idea which option was better, or what negative outcomes a wrong choice might bring. I even thought about asking people who had already made this move for their advice, to see what they thought was best for me. But in the end, I realized this was a decision only I could make. No one else could choose for me.

Of course, there are exceptions to this rule. Sometimes, the person who will be affected by a decision is not the one making it. For example, when you are a baby or still a minor, your parents are the ones who make choices on your behalf. They act based on what they believe is best for you, and while you might disagree with their choices at the time, these are the moments when more experienced, knowledgeable people are supposed to step in and make the right call.

Overall, I believe everyone should have the freedom to make their own decisions, whether they choose to do so alone or seek help from people with more time and experience. However, it is important to be fully aware of the choice you make. Every decision comes with consequences, and at the end of the day, you are the only one who can pick the option that is truly right for you.

Former British Prime Minister Winston Churchill once shared a famous idea about success. He believed that true success means facing one failure after another, but never choosing to give up. Many people agree with this view. Failing at something can feel like a huge loss, making you think all your plans were bad or that you did something wrong. If you want to succeed in life, you have to start by accepting that failure is part of the process.

I failed a class test once, then studied constantly and passed the retake. Students who fail a class are usually given a chance to retake it, which is a perfect example of how failure can lead to later success. Churchill spoke from experience, as he faced many setbacks throughout his own life.

This same rule applies to every goal we have, whether it is passing classes or achieving other life milestones. If you want to become the person you hope to be in the future, you need to build confidence in yourself and never stop trying, even when things go wrong. Every person in the world fails at something at some point, but every person also finds success in at least one area of their life.

Many people need support to pass their classes, build a happy life, and take care of their families, including helping their parents when they can. Failure is often described as being unable to do something you are supposed to do well, but with help and persistence, you can move past it.

In day-to-day life, many people allow their character to be shaped by the opinions of those around them. This is understandable, as most people care about what others think of them, and how they are judged. When it comes to close loved ones—friends, family, or romantic partners—this fear is even stronger. Many worry that if they act out of line, they might lose these important people, or cause them distress.

The writer John Lubbock once shared a powerful quote that captures a key truth: "Your character will be what you yourself choose to make of it." This single line completely shifted how I view the world. While many people disagree with Lubbock’s perspective, I fully stand by what he said. There is so much truth in his words: we should not fixate on others’ opinions, nor let painful experiences or past events dictate who we become. I firmly believe that our character is never out of our control. After all, we are the ones who decide how we think and how we respond to the things that happen to us. I have watched three of my closest friends ruin their lives after choosing to let negative events, past experiences, and other people’s opinions shape who they are.

The first, Generic_Name, let one painful childhood event define his entire personality, and it led to a tragic ending. As a young child, he was constantly hit by his parents. He grew up angry, and started using violence at school, getting in trouble constantly. His parents would punish him with more violence, claiming they were "teaching him a lesson." This cycle continued for years, even after he got married. Every time his wife made a mistake, he would hit her, still bitter about the abuse he suffered as a child. Eventually, he ended up killing his wife and taking his own life.

My second close friend, Generic_Name, also let bad experiences change his character for the worse. When he was younger, he often fell for attractive girls, only to have his feelings toyed with. None of these girls took him seriously. After years of this treatment, he grew tired of being hurt, and lost all his romantic feelings. He became exactly the kind of person he used to dislike: someone who plays with others’ emotions. He started playing with girls’ feelings, and ended up completely alone, never finding real love. Once, he actually met someone who truly cared for him, but his past bad experiences had made him unable to feel affection for any woman. He pushed away the one person who loved him.

The third, Generic_Name, let other people’s opinions control his life. He constantly tried to act like someone he was not, just to win the approval of the people he cared about. In the end, this only hurt him. He was never happy putting on an act, and was essentially lying to himself just to please others.

Do not let bad experiences, painful events, or other people’s opinions shape your character. You are the one in charge of who you become, or you might end up like my friends, who let others and past hardships decide their fate instead of taking charge themselves.

You can’t wipe away or change the impressions stored in your mind, no matter how hard you try. I still remember something my mother told me when I was a child: "You will have both good and bad impressions in life, but every single one teaches you something new." There are definitely some impressions I wish I could change. My memory isn’t very reliable overall, but I know altering past experiences is impossible. My earliest, most painful impression was when my parents almost got divorced. My whole life shifted because of that, and back then it felt crushing. Now that I’m older, I realize adults don’t always foresee the consequences of their actions.

A later, much happier impression was when my uncle asked if I wanted to move to the United States. I had always dreamed of leaving my home country to build a new life, so that moment filled me with joy. It’s a cherished memory, and it reminds me that even life’s struggles are necessary—they all teach us lessons we can use later. My most recent painful impression was losing my best friend back in my home country of Guatemala. He passed away from a rare, uncommon disease, and that grief changed my life forever. The pain still lingers, but I carry that memory with me.

My view on this topic is clear: we can never change past impressions, but we have full control over the ones we form in the future. Taking time to reflect on and understand what we’ve been through gives us a reason to keep moving forward.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once wrote that being yourself in a world that constantly tries to turn you into someone else is the greatest accomplishment. I do not agree with this statement about individuality.

First, no one can reach this greatest accomplishment alone. People need support from schools and teachers to gain the skills and knowledge required to succeed. You simply cannot become a high achiever without outside help.

To count as a great accomplishment, you need to study and work with groups, not just focus on your own efforts. Working alone makes it hard to understand new ideas or pursue your dreams effectively.

This is actually my most important reason for disagreeing with Emerson. Collaborating with others helps you understand how life works, which is key to becoming a great achiever. Interacting with different people teaches you lessons about the world you would never learn on your own.

Reaching a great accomplishment also means studying what you want to do and learning about the world around you. To be truly outstanding, you must master a wide range of knowledge, not just rely on your personal traits.

In conclusion, I disagree with Emerson’s view because being yourself alone in a world that pushes you to change is not the greatest accomplishment. True achievement comes from learning from others, studying, and working with groups, not just staying true to yourself in isolation.

Young people view the world through a completely different lens than older adults, who often lose that fresh, open-minded perspective over time. An older person might give up on a goal if they feel their natural talent or “gift” has faded, but young students keep pushing forward regardless—their natural curiosity and drive set them apart.

Of course, there are challenges to consider. Being young means you see endless possibilities, even things that older people might dismiss as impossible. You have access to opportunities that others might not notice, but the real world can be far tougher than your ideals. This is the main downside to committing to a career early: reality does not always match your expectations.

For example, imagine a 17-year-old in 10th grade whose mother is a single parent. The mother’s job does not pay enough to cover all their basic living costs, so the student has to take a job after school. Many people in this situation would drop their career plans entirely, convinced they have no choice but to focus on surviving. But a young person’s mindset is different. They might say, “I can help my mom with bills and still finish my studies to reach my career goals.” They believe that if they work hard enough, they can achieve whatever they want, no matter their current circumstances.

Young students have far more imagination than older people, and they truly believe that anything is possible. This mindset also opens up more opportunities for their future. As the saying goes, young people are the future of tomorrow—this is an undeniable truth.

Nothing can truly stop a young student from reaching their goals, except themselves. Your age does not matter as much as your determination. If you believe you can do something, you will find a way to make it happen. You can achieve anything, and the only person who can pause your career progress or abandon your goals is you—if you let that happen. Everything depends on the choices you make, both now and in the future. Young people are the leaders of tomorrow, and that is a fact I stand by.

Many older people doubt young students, claiming they are too young or not talented enough for certain careers. I once saw a video about young entrepreneurs who were told by older relatives that they were not “born” for their chosen fields, or that their dreams were stupid. Today, those same young people have built successful careers, with money and power, even though society tried to push them down. Why? Because they never gave up on the goals they set when they were young. They remembered exactly what they wanted for their futures, and ignored the people who told them they could not succeed.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once argued that the greatest achievement a person can have is staying true to their own identity, even when the world around them constantly pushes them to become someone different. I fully agree with this idea. In today’s world, being authentic and embracing your individuality is the healthiest, most natural way to live, and it helps you stand out from the crowd in a positive way.

We all strive to be one-of-a-kind people, whether we work as musicians, visual artists, teachers, or in other roles. Take teachers, for instance: if an educator tries a new method with their students that no one has used before, that makes them stand out. The results might be great or not so good, and people will definitely have opinions about it. But the world is always pushing us to change, to become someone we are not—which is exactly what Emerson meant when he talked about outside forces trying to turn us into “something else.”

There will always be people who try to pressure you to change, or judge you for who you are. I think even small acts of staying true to yourself can be really powerful. For example, people might criticize how you look or act, but if you stay strong and ignore that negativity, you win. No human being is perfect, after all. We can also draw inspiration from people who are no longer alive: a relative, a famous artist, or anyone who achieved something special. That can give us ideas for how to live our own lives. Think of the person who founded Facebook—he is unique because he built a platform that connects people all over the world, something that did not exist before. That is a positive shift in how our society works.

We all go through the same basic life cycle: we are born, we grow up, we might have children, and eventually we pass away. When we are in the growing-up phase, we are taught that we have to make choices about our future. Adults often ask kids, “What do you want to be when you grow up?” This is really about deciding how you will contribute to the world around you, to make it a better place. For example, a teenager picking a college major and a future career is making a choice to give something back to society. That choice should beentirely theirs, no matter what anyone else thinks. People might judge them or be unkind, but at the end of the day, those opinions do not matter. You only get one life to live, so how you spend it is up to you. The only thing to keep in mind is that you should make smart, thoughtful choices.

Schools should think about allowing students to use cell phones during class, since this gives us a useful chance to complete our work. We need to avoid wasting time on unrelated activities and stay focused on our assignments.

However, there is a common problem when teachers let us use phones to look up information or finish assignments. Instead of doing the work, many students start playing mobile games, checking social media like Facebook or Instagram, or doing other unrelated things. This makes them ignore the teacher’s instructions, waste class time, and hurts their own progress.

I saw this problem firsthand when I lived in my home country. During one class, our teacher told us to look up information about a historical figure online, or use our phones as calculators for math. Almost everyone followed the rules except for one girl, who spent the whole time scrolling Facebook and messaging friends who were sitting in the same classroom. Her constant notifications distracted the students she messaged, making it hard for them to focus. On the other hand, many students do follow the rules, and for them, phones are a huge help. For example, since I moved to this country recently, I sometimes struggle with unfamiliar English words or phrases when reading in class. I use my phone to look up their meanings quickly, so I can keep up with the lesson. I do the same in math class when I don’t recognize certain symbols – looking them up on my phone helps me understand the material better. When used this way, letting students use phones in class is a great idea. It helps us learn more, finish work in ways that suit our preferences, and even makes things easier for teachers too.

At the end of the day, whether phones help or hurt depends entirely on the student. They can be a distraction that pulls down your grades, or a useful tool that supports your learning. Schools give us this privilege, so we should be grateful for it. We need to use our phones only for class-related tasks, not for games or social media that could hurt our academic performance.

I believe the ideas Thomas Jefferson put forward are really sound. Of course, not everyone shares this view — some people agree with him, while others completely disagree. After all, people will always have their own opinions about the choices and actions of others.

There are several reasons why I stand by Jefferson’s ideas. For one, putting in consistent hard work every day and tackling tasks that need to be done is key. Plus, Jefferson’s writings are considered classics, and that timeless wisdom can inspire many people to keep pushing forward even when things get tough. Some people struggle to stay productive every single day, and while a few argue that doing nothing sometimes has its merits, most proactive people get their work done as quickly as possible. Inactivity never leads to any positive, exciting changes in life. To wrap up, I think we would all benefit from adopting Jefferson’s mindset to achieve success: stop complaining, and always take action instead of sitting idle.

In my science classroom last week, our teacher ran a demo where fire shifted from bright orange to vivid green, which is a classic example of a chemical change. That kind of hands-on experiment is exactly why science feels so engaging. Most science teachers genuinely love their work, and it shows—they get to explore how things on Earth function, even features that aren’t plants or obvious natural landmarks. But people don’t just wake up one day as a scientist. It takes years of school, college, and disciplined, methodical study to reach that point. For most, becoming a scientist was a lifelong dream they worked toward for years.

Scientists put in a huge amount of effort in their education. You can’t just decide to join the field overnight—it requires passing tough tests and sticking to structured, methodical learning. There are all kinds of branches of science, too. Take science fiction, for example: its stories are built around made-up scientific breakthroughs, massive environmental shifts, or space travel, but they’re often inspired by real discoveries and global exploration. Some science experiments are very specific, like testing a curved board sword with its edge on the convex side, or studying cows, which might need four or five scientists working together with special tools. Without science, we’d have no idea how the solar system or the sky works at all.

Then there’s scientific notation, which is a way to write numbers as a decimal between 1 and 10, multiplied by a power of 10. This system is super useful for doing math with very large or very small numbers.

We use scientific notation for math problems where 10 is raised to a power, for instance. My sister wants to be a nurse, and she had to go to college for four years, then nursing school for another four—that’s a type of science career too, even if it’s not lab work. I’m not totally sure how many years it takes to become every type of scientist, but it’s always a long process.

There’s also the term scintilla, which refers to someone with expert knowledge of one or more sciences—it can also describe throwing off sparks, or being really lively and brilliant. To reach that level, you have to study hard and gain lots of hands-on experience.

Then there’s phys, which describes a multistage nuclear reaction, like a self-sustaining chain where splitting one atom releases neutrons that split more atoms. It’s a series of reactions where one product becomes the reactant for the next, like a linked chain with teeth, or a portable saw. Scientists were the first people to learn that atoms can split into smaller parts.

Most scientists really love their jobs and get excited about running experiments. My own science teacher is so fun, and he always says if you want to be a teacher, you have to go to school and college first. My advice for anyone wanting to be a scientist is to follow basic rules: stay in school, work hard. My aunt (my mom’s sister) always tells us not to show off about things we do at home, which is good advice. Once, my sister asked me for help with her boyfriend, who wanted to be a scientist but wasn’t sure what to do. I told her to tell him to follow his heart. My sister wanted to be a nurse, but he was set on science. He ended up going to a tough college program, and they broke up because he was focused on his dream. I was happy for him, though—wouldn’t you be glad if your sister’s boyfriend followed his dream? Anyone who chases their passion deserves to be happy.

My advice to all scientists is to follow your dreams no matter what gets in the way. Chase them with your whole heart. We wouldn’t know anything about the solar system without science, so be grateful for what we have, and stay determined to reach your goals. My brother always says to be resilient, because no one can do your homework for you—you have to do it yourself. Going to school isn’t always easy, and the work that comes home can be overwhelming, but if you want to be a scientist, you have to work harder than you ever have before.

For a lot of people, science is in their blood—they live to work in the field. So if you want to be a scientist, don’t let anyone stop you. Even if your dream is to study cows, or walk dogs, or be a dancer, go for it.

There’s also chain change, which refers to a group of convicts chained together for outdoor labor, or smoking in close succession, or a chameleon, or cutting off a corner, or beveling, or carving a groove in a flute. When your teacher does a science demo, you just have to wait and watch. My advice is to be open to change—life has all kinds of different paths, and people have totally different ways of thinking. I love going to school: my English teacher is so nice and fun, my math teacher is great too, and my sister is really good at math. My art teacher is super kind, and I love drawing. My dream is to paint and be a nurse, which is a bit of a weird combination, but that’s okay.

Here’s an example that’s not about science: Generic_Name has a friend who fought with her best friend all the time. She asked her sister for advice, and her sister said she should just stop being friends with her. But then she asked her mom, who said if she wanted to stay friends, they needed to talk through their problems and find solutions. So they did, and worked things out. Scientists have problems with friends too, just like everyone else—that’s totally normal.

Another example: my sister had a boyfriend she thought was cheating on her, and she asked me for advice. She wanted to know if she had proof he was cheating. I told her I didn’t think she should accuse him without evidence, because it’s not right to make those claims. I advised her not to overthink things or be too nosy, but she said she could do whatever she wanted. I told her I didn’t care what she did, but scientists always say talking things out is key—if you don’t have someone to talk to, you’ll go crazy. So I told her we should sit down together and talk through the problem, like I’m doing now. I’m writing this essay to work through my own problems, and I’m learning that talking things out makes them feel smaller.

So scientists, come together and talk about your problems. Don’t act like other people who pretend they can handle everything alone. Talk to your friends, your wife (or future partner if you’re not married), your siblings, your family. Science is so important to the world, so don’t let other people tell you who to be or what to do. I hate when people try to do your work for you, or tell you what to study. I’m so glad we have science, and that we’re all part of this community. Let’s come together as one. To all scientists: please follow your dreams. Don’t let mean people bring you down. Many people wonder if first impressions can ever be reversed, but I firmly believe they are nearly impossible to alter. Take surprise gestures from loved ones as an example. When a friend or family member surprises me, my immediate reaction is to smile—I feel so overjoyed and thrilled in that moment that I stop paying attention to anything happening around me. I remember once a family member did something kind for me out of the blue, and my first thought was ‘oh my gosh, that’s amazing’—I’d never expected them to go out of their way like that.

That immediate feeling, the first words I blurt out, the obvious excitement everyone can see on my face—none of that can be changed later. It’s my personal experience, shaped by my own choices and feelings, so no one else can rewrite it. Even if new details come to light later, that initial rush of excitement never fades. Another reason first impressions stick is that a surprise from a family member, close friend, or partner can turn a terrible day completely around.

In those moments, I don’t think about any problems I’m facing or the stress I’m under. No one in the world could change how I feel when someone important to me is by my side—that special moment stays frozen in time. To sum up, if someone special surprises you when you’re having a rough day, that first impression will stay with you forever. First impressions never fade because they become part of your life story. They’re often positive reactions tied to pure happiness—even if you were having a bad day, that surprise turns the whole moment around, letting you forget about surrounding problems and stress. That’s why I’m certain first impressions can never be changed.

I believe introducing a teen curfew is a great idea. It keeps young people from dying in street incidents, stops them from being out alone in unsafe areas, and can even reduce feelings of loneliness for them. When teens stay off late-night streets, they’re far less likely to break laws, even if they weren’t looking for trouble. There will be fewer street fights, less crime, and no teens firing weapons. This policy offers temporary protection, though its impact can vary.

The government should also support homeless teens, many of whom dropped out of high school. Dropping out is a big issue: some students stop trying in class and refuse to work hard. Without education, these teens won’t succeed later. Employers won’t hire uneducated dropouts, so many end up homeless, fending for themselves on the streets.

Even if they only find low-paying jobs that cover basic needs, at least they’re doing something productive. Many make bad choices early: they’re lazy, skip school, get bad grades, have bad attitudes, show no respect, and waste time on phones. If they don’t change their ways, they’ll likely end up in trouble. Still, I hope all these teens can turn things around and succeed.

I agree that helping others is essential. While being honest and sincere is always important when telling the truth, it’s also good to stay mindful of your own background. We should always aim to be truthful, but we also need to remember that many people live with depression. For these individuals, simply talking to them and showing you care makes a huge difference – even telling them they are valued and kind can help a lot. But supporting someone with depression is not the same as talking to a person without mental health struggles, since they often feel sad all the time. I have a friend who lives with depression, and I’ve learned that I don’t need to say anything profound to help – instead, we go play soccer or hang out somewhere else, and I always try to encourage them whenever I can.

I believe making an effort to help others is always worthwhile, because we never truly know what someone else is going through – they might be dealing with mental pain or other hidden struggles. Whenever you have the chance to lend a hand, you should take it. For example, if you help a homeless person, you’ll walk away feeling a warm sense of satisfaction in your mind, knowing you made a positive difference. That feeling is really rewarding.

Sometimes people insist they don’t need assistance, but in reality, they need it more than ever. Everyone’s mental state is different, and when someone’s mental health takes a turn for the worse, it can be very hard to reach them. They might act out or seem unpredictable, but you should still show you support them – talk to them, do activities together, or just spend time with them. Psychologists have an especially difficult job: they speak to many people with all kinds of different problems, which is emotionally draining for them. It’s very hard for them to try to help every single person who comes to them.

Small acts of kindness can have a big effect on the people around us. When someone is not feeling their best, even a simple gesture like offering a smile or telling them "everything will be okay" can turn their day around. Positive words motivate people and make their day brighter, while negative comments only drag them down further. Everyone is born with a purpose, not just to exist without reason. But if we make someone feel like they don’t matter, they might start to wonder if their life has any value at all. In the worst cases, this could lead them to even take their own life, because they feel like no one cares about them.

There are really only two types of people in the world: those who are kind, and those who are cruel. No one can force us to be a certain way - we get to decide what kind of person we want to be. If kind people didn’t exist, the world would be full of nothing but hatred. When we say something mean to someone and hurt their feelings, we’re actually hurting ourselves too. Some people don’t even care about their own actions, only worrying about what others think of them, and end up making everyone around them feel terrible. If someone treats you poorly, you don’t have to pass that meanness on to others. You can choose to avoid people, or accept help if you need it. But no matter what, we should treat everyone with kindness, regardless of who they are. The golden rule applies here: treat others the way you want to be treated.

Kind people are still out there, so we should all make an effort to treat everyone with respect and kindness. That means being there for friends when they need us, not turning our backs on them - staying by their side through both good times and bad. Offering reassurance like "everything will be okay" and giving helpful, positive advice makes a huge difference. At the end of the day, being kind to one another is what really matters.

It’s common to hear about people being bullied, and I’ve never understood why this happens. Often, it’s over something as superficial as skin color, even though all humans are basically the same, with only our skin tones setting us apart. There are other possible triggers too—people who are bullied may end up taking their own lives because of the harassment, which is an incredibly tragic outcome.

Bullies often keep targeting others nonstop until a serious incident occurs, and I always wonder why they act this way. Maybe it’s because the people they pick on are different from them, or they feel a false sense of power over others. Sometimes, bullies come from wealthier backgrounds and think having more money makes them better than everyone else. But bullying is never acceptable—it doesn’t just hurt victims, it can also lead to terrible consequences for the people doing the bullying.

I know it’s incredibly difficult for anyone going through bullying. Dealing with constant harassment for no valid reason is exhausting and traumatizing for victims. There is never an excuse for bullying, and it’s absolutely heartbreaking to see vulnerable people targeted for no fault of their own. The people doing the bullying need to stop picking on those poor people who are already struggling.

What should we do about bullying? We need to collaborate to stop it entirely. Bullying can lead to terrible outcomes for the people doing the bullying, including jail time, especially if the victims they make fun of end up taking their own lives. That is a very real consequence bullies face if they refuse to stop their harmful behavior.

Everyone experiences failure at some point, but people react to it differently. Some lose all their motivation, while others keep pushing forward no matter what. I fully agree with the saying that success is all about moving from one failure to the next without ever losing your enthusiasm. This idea is really worth reflecting on, and I support it because every time I fail, I end up growing and getting closer to my goals.

I’ve found that every failure pushes me to get better. Last year, I started high school in New York – it was my very first year studying in the US. Since everything was totally new to me, I failed loads of tests, struggled to talk to classmates, and couldn’t make any friends at first. Every little task felt impossible, whether it was passing a class or even striking up a conversation with someone. So I kept working hard to improve my English skills. A full year has passed since then, and my English is way better than it was when I first arrived.

Facing setbacks has made me tougher and brought me real success. Last year, I ran into so many issues that I even considered moving back to Thailand. But every time I felt like giving up, I’d remind myself, “Hang in there, Generic_Name. You can give it another shot, you’re more than capable, and you’ll achieve what you want.” I held onto that belief, didn’t return to Thailand, and picked up so many new skills and experiences that made me a stronger person.

Failure plays a vital role in life. We only find success by learning from our mistakes, and we improve every time we stumble. If we give up and walk away from our failures, we’re nothing but losers.

I agree with the statement that Minister Winston, who holds far more power than most others, has a clear duty to support the people around him. He should offer practical help and talk to people about what they are capable of achieving. As a leader, he is responsible for encouraging those nearby, boosting their confidence in what they can do and how much they can accomplish.

To give a personal example, when my teacher in class asked us to collaborate with classmates, I knew I had to participate fully and show up ready to work. Working in groups means helping each other and sharing ideas we can add to our projects. The rule for our group work was simple: even if you struggle or fail at first, as long as you show up and put in effort, that is how you improve. Mistakes are no big deal—next time, you can do even better. I believe this is exactly the approach Minister Winston should take in his role.

Beyond that, Minister Winston should discuss plans with others to get their agreement. If some people do not agree with the statement at first, he needs to make sure they understand that the work being done is already leading to real, successful results.

Like many others, I moved to this country to find better opportunities that were not available in my home nation. We have to learn the local language, which is challenging, but we try our best to improve and show that we can build a better future here.

Many students here have difficult pasts, and some have not graduated because they have to pay rent and work long hours after school. Balancing work and study leaves very little time for sleep, but we still push ourselves to work hard. Many students prove what they are capable of and how much they can achieve. A lot of immigrants, including me, came here to find a safe place to live, since our home countries do not offer much security.

I work hard here every day. Sometimes, I help people who are confused about what to do, or who have gotten into trouble. I warn them to avoid bad choices, because getting in trouble can lead to big problems and leave a negative mark on their record. So far, I have done my best, even though it is sometimes hard to understand everything around me. When I get home each day, I practice English by reading books—this is a tip that can help anyone trying to learn the language. For example, reading for just 20 minutes a day helps you learn new words, pick up correct pronunciation, maintain your vocabulary, and read faster over time.

I am a student who enjoys helping others and sharing new ideas. I love talking with people about what we hope to achieve in the future. Before I finish, I want to say thank you to the program that supports us, and to all the teachers who teach us something new every single day.

I disagree with the proposed school policy that would ban students from joining sports teams or extracurricular activities unless they maintain at least a B average across all their classes. Earning a B in every single class is an unrealistic goal for many students, and most are deeply passionate about taking part in sports or other after-school activities.

A much fairer approach would be to only stop students from joining activities if their grades drop below a C. It is far simpler for most students to maintain a C average than a B, and many already have C grades in one or more classes while still passing their courses and putting in genuine effort. It would also be a hassle for teachers and students to check which specific classes have B grades to decide if someone can join activities. Students with A, B, or C grades should all be allowed to participate, while those with D or F grades should be barred. Failing students are at risk of repeating the year, and letting them take part in activities would only distract them further from their schoolwork, making it even harder for them to pass.

While the idea of linking activity participation to grades has some good points, it is deeply unfair to students who are working hard to earn Cs. These learners are doing everything they can to keep up with their coursework, and blocking them from activities they love just because they have not reached a B is punishing them for progress they have already made.

In short, I strongly oppose the proposed B average requirement. Students with Cs are passing their classes and deserve to take part in sports and other activities, while only those with failing grades should be excluded until they improve their academic performance.

High schoolers should not enroll in programs that let them graduate in three years instead of the standard four. Most students in these fast-track programs have to take extra classes after school or during summer breaks, and they are often barred from choosing elective courses. This leaves them with far less time to complete homework, hang out with family and friends, or relax during summer vacation. On top of that, they miss out on valuable elective classes, including foreign languages, nutrition, music, computer skills, and health and physical education.

Another downside is that these students sometimes have to take two levels of the same subject in a single year, such as English 9 and English 10. There are some potential benefits: students who plan to attend college can graduate earlier, and those who skip college can start working full-time sooner. But the rushed pace of these programs puts students at a much higher risk of failing or dropping out, a problem that students in traditional four-year programs do not face. In conclusion, this is why high school students should avoid early graduation programs.

The writer who came up with the quote "you will never grow" showed great insight into how people actually live. I fully agree with this idea: in today’s world, plenty of people are never happy with what they already have. Worse yet, some are greedy, act like they are superior to everyone else, and try to grab everything they want all at once.

First, greed is a huge issue. People who are greedy set a terrible example for others trying to progress at work, in school, or even within their own families. Take my brother, for instance: he quit school because he wanted quick cash, thinking that working more hours would solve all his problems. Now, he admits dropping out for money was a huge mistake.

Another problem is that these people believe they are better than everyone else. Their attitude makes society cold: they ignore others, reject people who don’t meet their standards, and even engage in bullying. I strongly disagree with this mindset. Just because one person achieves something amazing does not mean others cannot do the same—true greatness comes from staying humble, not looking down on others.

A third key reason is that some people want everything immediately. This is exactly why the author says "you will never grow"—personal growth has nothing to do with how many material possessions you collect. In the end, chasing material wealth is meaningless. If you want to grow, start by being content with what little you have. Education, for example, helps shape you into a principled, decent person, which matters far more than fancy items.

To wrap up, life offers countless opportunities, but it is up to you to choose which one to take. This is how you grow into a good, smart person—remember that vanity is a terrible guide for making choices.

I strongly believe that technology is a positive force in our lives. For one, it lets people handle everyday tasks without ever stepping outside: you can buy anything you need through online shopping, read full books on digital platforms, and even meet new people through online games, all while sitting in your living room.

Lots of people don’t have access to a car, or can’t drive to meet up with others in person. Instead, they stay home and use their phones to call loved ones who live on the other side of the world, chat with new friends they’ve met online, or play multiplayer games with people from all over.

Many people also turn to technology to pick up new skills, or scroll through social media platforms like Facebook and Snapchat to see what others are up to. It’s especially useful for students: kids can use tech for schoolwork, join online clubs, and schools can set up safe guidelines for its use, so teens learn how to use it properly.

Critics will argue that technology is harmful because it stops people from making in-person friends or going out to have fun. But supporters of tech have a valid point too: some people are much more comfortable staying home, or even working remotely, where they don’t have to interact with strangers face-to-face.

Older adults also get a lot out of technology. They can read digital books on any topic they’re interested in, from war history to car maintenance to sports, and learn how to use tech so they can video call family and friends whenever they want.

Another common use is ordering food online and having it dropped off at your door, which makes daily life way easier. People also use the internet to handle tricky tasks like taxes, either learning how to do them themselves or hiring someone online to file for them. For people who struggle with social anxiety and are scared to leave the house, technology is a lifeline: they can talk to others online and find people who share their hobbies, without the stress of in-person meetups.

When you order items online, they often arrive the very next day. This kind of convenience can improve anyone’s life, no matter their age or situation.

There are countless online games people love to play, or download to use offline. Some even make a living using technology, whether that’s through gaming or other online work. Teens especially enjoy spending hours playing games, and sometimes even win prizes or get paid for their skills. The point is, technology has so many uses: it can help you with work, make daily tasks simpler, and fit into almost every part of your life. Most people will end up relying on it to make their lives run more smoothly.

It’s also easy to meet new people and play games with them online, building friendships without leaving your house.

Using technology in our daily lives makes everyone’s life better. Older adults can stay connected and entertained, teens can finish homework way faster with online resources, and work tasks get done more quickly and with less effort. We should all make use of technology while it’s available, because almost everyone will find it helpful. As the years go on, tech will only get better and more useful, so it’s worth using now.

Here are my main reasons why students should not take their classes online from home.

My first point is that most students should not complete their schoolwork at home. Doing assignments at home can be very challenging, while working in a school building is much better because teachers are there to help. When you take classes online, you might not fully understand what your teacher expects for each task, and there is no one at home to guide you. I would much rather do my work at school, where teachers can assist me right away instead of struggling through online classwork alone.

My second point is that high-achieving students should be allowed to take online classes from home. Students who have passed their SOL exams and all their current classes, especially those with part-time jobs, should be allowed to leave school early. These students usually have high GPAs and need time to plan for college and their future careers, like starting their own business to earn money. Smart students who have already mastered all the material do not need to attend school in person.

My third point is that online classwork should only be offered to young children. Completing assignments at home is often easier for kids, and it also simplifies things for their teachers. While some parents prefer their children to attend school in person to complete their work, online classes for young kids can be more convenient for everyone. If schools offer online options for small children, both students and teachers will find their workload easier to manage.

My final point is that schools should offer online classes for students to take at home. I believe all high school students should be required to take classes online from home, since this makes things easier for both students and teachers. But there is a problem: students might copy answers from their friends, which is a major reason why online classes are not a good idea. Middle school students should also do their classwork online at home.

Colleges should definitely offer online classes. This makes it easier for students to complete their coursework from home, as they have more time to work and can often earn better grades. If students get A or B grades, they can finish their current classes faster and sign up for new ones sooner.

The main reason schools need this plan is to protect the earth. Our planet needs many more plants, and every school should have plenty of greenery, since it benefits both animals and humans. Another reason

I strongly believe that self-esteem is built through praise. In my view, getting positive feedback helps students develop confidence in their own abilities.

This is especially true when the praise comes from teachers. After all, everyone loves being told they’ve done well, right? I definitely don’t like it when my parents criticize me, and I’m sure most people care about what others say about them. Isn’t that true for everyone?

As a student myself, I know exactly how this feels. When I make a mistake, I usually realize it on my own already. If a teacher criticizes me harshly, it makes me really upset. No one is born with an unbreakable mindset—we’re all human, not perfect. So we shouldn’t put kids down when they run into trouble. Young people are fragile, and if you blame them too much, they’ll just push back against you more. Instead, we should encourage them: tell them they’re doing well. If a student has actually made a mistake, don’t just say ‘no’ or tell them they’re wrong. Say something like, ‘I think you can do even better next time.’

What matters most is that young people keep making progress as they grow. Good education isn’t built overnight—it’s nurtured step by step, starting from when they’re little. Think about the difference between telling a student ‘I know you can do this’ versus just blaming them for a mistake. Those two approaches couldn’t be more different.

Every person is one of a kind! I truly believe that’s a fact. I’ll accept that someone is right as long as they can show they understand a topic in their own way. Honestly, whether an answer is technically right or wrong isn’t the biggest deal. What’s really important is that students are willing to explore a problem and learn from it—we can’t put them down for that.

To sum up, even if I (or my friends) miss the ‘right answer’ sometimes, I’d rather people praise us and tell us we’re doing well, and that we can improve. I’m proud of myself too, and having self-confidence makes me strong enough to handle whatever anyone says about me. I can adjust my own mindset, and that’s more than good enough.

Every person’s life plays out like a short, unique story, shaped by the experiences they’ve lived through. The way someone thinks or acts always ties back to what they’ve already faced—some move from simple, easy challenges to far tougher ones, and everyone encounters all kinds of situations as they go through life. When people handle problems in their own way, it means someone who’s been through the exact same struggle can inspire them, or push them toward positive choices in their own life. After you’ve faced enough different situations yourself, it becomes even easier to draw inspiration from other people’s life stories.

There are endless different opinions and methods for influencing other people. Sometimes, things that happen in a person’s life might not lead them to seek inspiration from someone else’s actions or life story at all. That said, feeling inspired can give you a huge confidence boost when you’re stuck in a situation where you have no idea what to do next. Overall, the influence of other people is almost always a helpful thing.

It’s important to remember that setting an example is far from the only way to inspire others—there are countless other ways to motivate people. For instance, there are plenty of moments where you won’t need someone else to inspire you at all. Instead, you just need to think carefully about your own situation, because you’re the one who will work to improve it by making the decision you believe is right for you.

Another point to keep in mind is that we’re all human, and we’re bound to make mistakes—and it’s up to each person to learn from those errors. There are so many different approaches to trying to inspire someone, but there are also times when you won’t even think about looking to another person for motivation at all.

When people look for inspiration or motivation to do something, they don’t always realize they’ve probably been through similar situations before. But everyone is different: a solution that worked perfectly for someone else doesn’t automatically mean it will benefit you too. You should just treat their experience as a reference point, take the positive parts that apply to you, and adjust them to fit your own needs.

Sometimes it’s just a coincidence that another person has gone through the exact same situation as you, and you might relate to them without feeling specifically inspired. This can still be useful, though—it lets you see that people handle the same problems in totally different ways. You might ask yourself: why did that person handle this situation differently than I did? What could I do differently if the same thing happens to me again?

There are also times when you feel deeply moved because someone’s life or current situation is almost identical to your own. You might feel inspired by how they pushed through the same struggles, or relate to something that happened to a friend, family member, or even yourself. Sometimes, just knowing that someone else felt the exact same way you do in a tough situation, or made the same choices you did, can be incredibly influential—because it proves you aren’t the only person who’s ever gone through that.

That said, it can be incredibly helpful to have someone share their experience to inspire you. Sometimes people feel totally stuck, like they’re the only ones who’ve ever faced a certain struggle, and hearing from someone who’s been through the exact same thing can change that. If they made it through, you start to believe you can too. Sometimes it’s all in your head—you just need to look to someone else as an example to feel better about yourself, or to build up your confidence again.

Everyone goes through good and bad moments, and sometimes those experiences turn you into the kind of person who can inspire others—and I definitely think that can shape someone’s actions for the better. A person’s behavior can influence the people around them, but everyone thinks in their own way. Just because you see someone do something positive or negative doesn’t mean you’ll follow suit—it all comes down to how you want to act, the kind of person you are, and your own way of thinking. That said, it’s a wonderful thing to inspire other people by sharing what you’ve been through, and become a source of influence that others can relate to, or feel moved by, when they hear your story.

Thomas Jefferson argued that people should always push themselves to achieve more and take on new tasks. When schools offer more activities, students get curious about useful information they can share with peers and other schools, which helps spread better ideas. Without any activities at all, students often form negative, unfair views of their schools.

Adding fun new sports or creative activities that students actually enjoy helps them relax and shake off stress. While staying busy with meaningful tasks helps young people grow and develop skills, spending every waking moment chasing accomplishments means they miss out on the joy of being young—something that shouldn’t be sacrificed all the time.

Being totally inactive is just as problematic. People who do nothing at all pour all their time into unproductive habits, and sometimes end up drifting away from their families, missing out on precious shared moments with loved ones.

If you have big dreams you’re eager to turn into reality, you have the power to make that happen. When you spend time on things you genuinely enjoy, you’ll keep achieving more and more—the results are always worth it, since the more effort you put in, the more you get done. This also comes with real responsibilities. For instance, if you’re passionate about a sport, you have to train hard every single day to become a top player or take on big challenges. All it takes is staying focused, putting in the work, and waiting to see the results. Most importantly, find the goal that makes you truly happy.

Thomas Jefferson wrote all this to give people ideas for becoming more creative and enthusiastic about living life to the full, and to cherish the moments you have right now. You should always be ready to try new things, do your best, and never give up. No matter what problems come your way, stay strong and keep moving forward with your life. You might have bad days, but always keep your head up. Jefferson wanted to show just how wonderful it feels to work on your own projects and get results that bring you joy, and to see what you can achieve if you keep at it. Taking on responsibilities also helps you grow into a more reliable, mature person.

That’s my take on what Thomas Jefferson wrote: you have to try things out for yourself and explore all the choices you have, to become whoever you want to be or do whatever you want with your life. I especially love the phrase “never give up,” because Thomas Jefferson was a good person who always did his best, and he can be a great example for all of us.

Have you ever accidentally hurt someone’s feelings by telling the truth? Many people struggle with how honest to be with their close friends and family. While some value total openness with their loved ones, others hold back because they worry that the truth might cause pain, or even ruin their relationships for good.

I do not believe that we should be honest 100% of the time. You don’t need to share every single truth, even if it feels important, because it might hurt the other person. That said, there are moments when people deserve to know the truth. For the person who has to deliver that honesty, it’s never easy: you can never be fully sure if your words will wound the other person’s feelings, end your friendship, or mean they never forgive you.

There will be times when you have no choice but to tell a friend the truth, and other times when keeping a secret is better. But certain situations do require honesty: for example, if you need to share how you really feel about them, or if there’s something they do that bothers you. It’s better to be upfront about these things. If a friend can’t handle your honesty and decides to end the friendship, then that relationship probably wasn’t right for you anyway.

Not all friends react well to honesty, though. Some would rather avoid hard truths entirely, while others appreciate hearing the truth because it helps them grow as both a friend and a person. These are the friends you can truly trust, the ones who feel like the supportive, fun companions you’ve always wanted to have in your life.

If you feel like you can’t be honest with a friend about something, it’s better to stay quiet than to lie. But keep in mind that there will always be moments where honesty is unavoidable. You don’t have to tell the truth about every little thing, every single time. It’s always worth taking a moment to think before you speak. Remember that even well-intentioned honesty doesn’t always go the way you expect: it can blow up and cause major conflict, but it can also work out far better than you imagined.

Famous scientist Albert Einstein once claimed that "imagination is more important than knowledge," but I completely disagree with this statement.

I strongly believe that knowledge is far more valuable than imagination, not the other way around.

We need solid facts to think clearly about any situation, otherwise we cannot predict what will happen next. If you only rely on imagination, you will never gain proper, useful knowledge. For example, imagining new words without learning them first means you won't remember how to use them correctly. But if you learn the facts first, then use your imagination, you will be able to get things done much more easily.

Writing a story is a good example: you can't create a good one with just imagination. You need to understand the context, setting, and rules of your story's world first, or your ideas won't make sense. If you don't know basic details about your story's setting, you won't know where to put key plot points, and the final result will suffer.

I do not claim to know exactly what Einstein meant by his famous quote, since everyone has their own opinions on what works best for them. Different people value different things, and that is perfectly fine. For me, knowledge always comes first. When I write stories, I use research and facts to build a believable world, rather than just making things up as I go.

Knowledge acts as a solid foundation for everything we do. We need to seek out information to figure out our next steps, because relying only on imagination is almost never enough. For example, when you go to your job, you need to know exactly what tasks you have to complete that day, not just daydream about what you might do.

This is also true in school science classes. If you have to examine a plant for a project, you need to learn basic facts about that plant first, so you know where to start your analysis.

Many other real-life situations also require knowledge over imagination. For instance, if a person is killed, the police have to gather facts about the crime scene, identify suspects, and figure out exactly how the victim died. They cannot just imagine what happened; they need concrete evidence to solve the case.

Some people argue that imagination comes first and is more important, and I can see why they think that. Everyone views the world differently, and for some, creativity is the top priority. Imagination lets you form mental pictures of where you want to place ideas or objects, which is a useful skill.

But even if you have vivid mental images, you still need to learn the facts first. I think gaining knowledge is more essential, because once you know the basics, it becomes much easier to work with your ideas. When you have knowledge, the mental pictures you imagine become more detailed and specific, which makes them easier to use.

There are countless ways to look at the world, and what works for one person might not work for another. Some people see things very differently from others, and that is okay. Everyone has their own unique perspective, but for me, the most important thing is sticking to what makes sense for my own life and work.

First, I believe that facing failure while chasing success makes you a wrestler in life. The second reason is that failing while chasing success helps you become a better person. When you make a mistake, it teaches you what not to do next time, so you avoid repeating the same error. On top of that, failing pushes you to want to improve more every day, which helps you grow into a better version of yourself.

Third, I think that failing while working towards success makes you stronger in that pursuit. Every failure gives you new knowledge about life, which helps you make the right choices later on. It also teaches you how to pick yourself up and overcome obstacles, which makes you more resilient overall.

Overall, I stand by Winston Churchill’s words. Pursuing success will always involve failure, but you can get past every setback if you hold onto your enthusiasm. Everything becomes simpler when you stay passionate and keep moving forward in life, working steadily towards your goals.

I want to accomplish more whenever I have the motivation to take action, even though I sometimes wonder if being inactive has any purpose. My focus is on helping two groups of vulnerable children in Bangladesh: those who experience abuse, and kids with disabilities.

Many families refuse to accept them, believing they will never be able to contribute to the household. I see things differently: with proper guidance and support, these children can grow up to be valuable members of society.

To sum up, we should commit to never staying idle. It is amazing how much we can get done if we keep taking action regularly.
